rows.technique: engraved
rows.date_note: Working dates 'some time between 1875 and 1910' per Wilkinson (1999, p. 36) as cited by a dealer.
rows.what_it_tells: An English signature in cursive suggests an item made for exhibition; places the item in Thayetmyo, an up-country silver center that supplied the Delhi Exhibition of 1902-03.
rows.cautions: One dealer links a dancing-peacock base mark to Aung Myat; no source seen confirms that he used a peacock mark.

facts.text: Wilkinson (1999, p. 36) identifies Maung Aung Myat as a silversmith working in Thayetmyo some time between 1875 and 1910.
facts.quote: Wilkinson (1999, p. 36) identifies Maung Aung Myat as a silversmith who operated in Thayetmyo

facts.text: A gilt silver jug is engraved on the base in cursive 'made by Maung Aung Myat'.
facts.quote: 'made by Maung Aung Myat'

facts.text: Thayetmyo was one of the Burmese towns from which silver was procured for the Delhi Exhibition of 1902-03.
facts.quote: From RANGOON, MOULMEIN, TOUNGOO, PROME and THAYETMYO have been procured an extensive series of silver plate

facts.text: A dealer links a dancing-peacock (ka daung) base mark to a symbol engraved on Aung Myat's works.

rows.meaning: Retailer's engraved mark of Coombes Company Ltd, 12 Phayre Street, Rangoon, sellers of silver, curios, ivory and rubies
rows.punch_set: Engraved alone; no maker's mark recorded with it
rows.technique: engraved
rows.date_note: A marked bowl is dated c. 1890 by a dealer. An archive record (not read directly) gives the firm's activity as c. 1830s-1940s.
rows.what_it_tells: Names the Rangoon shop that sold the item, not the Burmese silversmith who made it.
rows.cautions: Despite the word 'Silversmiths', the firm was a retailer; its silver was most probably made by independent Burmese silversmiths. Burmese-made silver was also sold through Indian firms that struck their own marks: a Shan-made dish carries the marks and pseudo date marks of Hamilton & Co, Calcutta, so an Indian retailer's mark does not prove Indian manufacture.

facts.text: A bowl of c. 1890 is engraved on the underside 'Coombes Company Ltd / Silversmiths / Rangoon'; another item is reported engraved 'Coombe's Company Ltd. Silversmiths. Rangoon'.
facts.quote: 'Coombes Company Ltd / Silversmiths / Rangoon' (Backman)

facts.text: Coombes was at 12 Phayre Street (now Pansodan Street) and retailed upmarket silver, curios, carved ivory and rubies; its silver was most probably made by independent Burmese silversmiths.
An archive authority record describes the company as active roughly from the 1830s to the 1940s (seen only in a search summary).
A Shan-made dish has an inner tray added by Hamilton & Co of Calcutta, with that firm's marks and pseudo date marks.
facts.quote: The cover and base are the product of Shan silversmiths working in Burma.

rows.plain: Padeing Aung of Yawnghwe, Southern Shan States
rows.meaning: Maker's name label of Padeing Aung of Yawnghwe (Nyaung Shwe), Southern Shan States
rows.punch_set: Paper or applied label inside the box; no punched marks recorded
wares: silver betel sets inlaid with black composition (Shan niello-type work)
rows.technique: label
rows.date_note: The V&A example is dated 1923 and was shown at the British Empire Exhibition, Wembley, 1924.
rows.what_it_tells: Names a Shan silversmith working for the 1924 Wembley exhibition; 'S.S.S.' stands for Southern Shan States.
rows.cautions: Known from one museum record. Labels are easily lost or moved between items.

facts.text: A silver lime box inlaid with black composition, dated 1923, has inside a label with the maker's name 'Padeing Aung of Yawnshwe, S.S.S.'; it was exhibited at Wembley in 1924.
facts.quote: Inside is a label with the name of the maker "Padeing Aung of Yawnshwe, S.S.S."

rows.meaning: A dancing peacock engraved or punched on the base of Burmese silver, read by Wilkinson as the 'signature' of several different makers who used the royal emblem to claim past royal patronage
rows.device: Peacock with tail displayed (the dancing peacock, emblem of the Konbaung kings); several variant drawings
rows.punch_set: Usually alone on the base; may accompany an owner's inscription
rows.technique: engraved or punched
rows.date_note: Marked items are dated by dealers and auction houses to the later 19th century (c. 1880-1900). The peacock was the emblem of the Konbaung dynasty (1752-1885), so its use as a mark implies a claim to former royal patronage rather than a date.
rows.what_it_tells: Points to Burmese manufacture and, according to Wilkinson, to one of a small group of makers of good-quality work; it does not name the maker.
rows.cautions: The peacock is also one of the most common decorative motifs on Burmese silver (medallions, borders, panels), so a peacock on the base is not automatically a mark. One dealer argues that engraved base designs are decoration, not signatures. The claim that peacock use was restricted to royalty under Konbaung sumptuary law comes from a dealer, not a scholarly source seen here. No source seen ties any peacock variant to a named maker.

facts.text: Wilkinson (Indian Silver 1858-1947, 1999, p. 41) records several variations of the peacock 'signature', whose users were indirectly claiming past royal patronage.
facts.quote: there are number of different variations of the peacock signature, all of whom are are indirectly claiming past royal patronage by using this mark (see Wilkinson's page 41)

facts.text: Auction and dealer catalogues describe the peacock on the base as a maker's mark: 'the royal peacock maker's mark' (Bonhams 2003) and 'marked with the dancing peacock (KaDaung)' (ALJ).
facts.quote: inscribed on the base with the royal peacock maker's mark (Bonhams, 1 May 2003, lot 377)

facts.text: The peacock medallion was the emblem of the Konbaung dynasty, which reigned 1752-1885.
facts.quote: The majestic peacock medallion emblazoned into the salver's center was the emblem of the Konbaung dynasty (Bonhams 2022)

facts.text: A dealer disputes that designs engraved on the bases of Burmese bowls act as makers' signatures.
facts.quote: Some feel that such designs to the bases of Burmese bowls function as the maker's 'signature'. We do not concur, and feel that such design is simply that.

rows.meaning: An elephant engraved on the base of Rangoon silver, recorded by Wilkinson as a maker's mark
rows.punch_set: Alone on the base
rows.technique: engraved
rows.date_note: Marked bowls dated c. 1900 by a dealer.
rows.what_it_tells: Burmese (Rangoon) manufacture by one of the makers who used a pictorial mark.
rows.cautions: Known only from one dealer citing Wilkinson (1999, p. 41). Elephants are common Indian pseudo-hallmark devices too; an elephant punched among letters imitating English hallmarks points to India, not Burma.

facts.text: A Rangoon bowl of c. 1900 has its base engraved with the 'elephant' maker's mark recorded by Wilkinson (1999, p. 41).
facts.quote: Base engraved ith the 'elephant' makers mark, see (Wilkinson, Indian silver 1858-1947, 1999, p.41)

rows.meaning: A stylized tiger engraved on the base, described as the signature of a well-known 20th-century Burmese silversmith
rows.punch_set: Alone on the base
rows.technique: engraved
rows.date_note: Marked bowls dated c. 1900 by a dealer.
rows.what_it_tells: Burmese manufacture by a maker who signed with a pictorial mark.
rows.cautions: Known only from one dealer citing Wilkinson (p. 41); the maker is not named.

facts.text: A Rangoon thabeik bowl of c. 1900 has its base engraved with the stylized signature of a tiger, attributed (citing Wilkinson p. 41) to one of the best-known 20th-century Burmese silversmiths.
facts.quote: Base engraved with the stylized signature of a tiger

rows.meaning: Engraved motif in the center of the base of a Burmese bowl, sometimes read as a pictorial maker's mark
rows.device: Bird (hamsa), rosette, flower, sunburst or similar, often in a ring of petals
rows.punch_set: Often with an owner's inscription around it
rows.technique: engraved
rows.date_note: Found on bowls from the mid-19th century onward.
rows.what_it_tells: Typical of Burmese bowls; whether a given design is a maker's emblem is disputed.
rows.cautions: Disputed: one dealer says many silversmiths could not write and signed with a unique pictorial mark; another holds that base designs are simply decoration. Treat an engraved base design as a possible, not a proven, maker's mark.

facts.text: A dealer states that many Burmese silversmiths of the time were illiterate and signed with a unique pictorial mark rather than script.
facts.quote: many silversmiths were illiterate and signed their work with a unique pictorial mark rather than script

facts.text: Another dealer describes a flower or 'snow flake' motif on a base as possibly the silversmith's emblem.
The same dealer elsewhere rejects the view that such base designs are signatures.
facts.quote: We do not concur, and feel that such design is simply that.

rows.plain: Owner's inscription: '[name]'s silver bowl', often with a Burmese-era year
rows.meaning: Engraved Burmese inscription naming the owner (and sometimes the year) for whom the bowl was made
rows.punch_set: Engraved in Burmese script around or beside the base design
rows.technique: engraved
rows.date_note: Common on bowls made for Burmese clients, 19th to mid-20th century.
rows.what_it_tells: Names the owner, not the maker; when a year is included it dates the commission.
rows.cautions: Dealers sometimes read the owner's name as a maker's. Translations offered in sale listings are the sellers' own and should be checked. Honorifics such as Maung (Mg), U, Ma and Daw are part of the name, not a title of office.

facts.text: Silver for local Burmese clients was mostly unsigned; the owner's name was inscribed instead.
Recorded examples include '1908. Mr. Pa Thit's Silver Bowl' (Asian Civilisations Museum) and '1280 [1918 CE]. Mr Pho Saung's silver bowl' (dealer translation).
facts.quote: 1908. Mr. Pa Thit's Silver Bowl. (ACM 2014-00713, translation of the Burmese inscription)

facts.text: Other recorded translations (one dealer): 'This is Ma Pwa's bowl' and 'Daw A Kyi's cup [bowl]', where Daw is the Burmese prefix for 'Mrs'.

rows.plain: Year of the Burmese Era (Sakkaraj, 'ME' or 'BE' in English books)
variants: Burmese digits ၀ ၁ ၂ ၃ ၄ ၅ ၆ ၇ ၈ ၉
rows.meaning: A year in the current Burmese era, which began in AD 638; add 638 (639 for dates between January and the Burmese New Year in April) to get the Western year
rows.punch_set: Usually engraved with the owner's name; written in Burmese digits
rows.technique: engraved
rows.where_on_object: underside of the base, in the owner's inscription
rows.date_note: Burmese years 1162-1322 cover AD 1800-1960. Burmese New Year falls in April (month Tagu), so a Burmese year straddles two Western years.
rows.what_it_tells: Gives the year the bowl was commissioned or presented.
rows.cautions: Do not confuse with the Buddhist (Religious) Era, which in this period runs in the 2300s-2500s, or with the Thai Buddhist Era (Western year + 543) found on Thai silver. English-language books use 'B.E.' for the Burmese Era as well as for the Buddhist Era, so check the size of the number: a 1200s year is Burmese Era. Seller conversions are sometimes one year off because of the April new year. The name 'Kawza' is used differently in different books (Irwin 1901 gives it to an ancient era with epoch 9340 BC), so convert by the number, not by the era's name.

facts.text: The current Burmese era began in AD 638; Irwin equates B.E. 1263 with A.D. 1901-2.
facts.quote: 5. Yahan Poppasaw's Era, now current. Epoch, 638 A.D.

facts.text: The Burmese year begins with the solar new year in the month Tagu (April).
facts.quote: The Burmese Era commenced in A.D. 638 with the solar new year in Tagu

facts.text: Silver bowls carry inscribed years in this era, e.g. 1280 read as 1918 CE.
facts.quote: 1280 [1918 ce]. Mr pho saung's silver bowl (dealer translation)

facts.text: Irwin also lists the Religious (Buddhist) Era, epoch 543 B.C., among eras used in Burma.
facts.quote: 3. The Religious Era. Epoch, 543 B.C., the year in which Gautama Buddha is supposed to have departed this life.

facts.text: Burmese digits are encoded U+1040-U+1049 (၀-၉).

rows.meaning: Burmese unit of weight (the tical of English sources) used to record the weight of silver or bronze in inscriptions
rows.punch_set: Engraved with the owner's or maker's name
rows.technique: engraved
rows.date_note: Weight inscriptions in kyat are attested on Burmese bells from the 15th to 19th centuries; on silver bowls only one example was found.
rows.what_it_tells: Records the weight of metal, which can be compared with the item's present weight; it is not a statement of fineness.
rows.cautions: A number followed by kyat (tical) is a weight, not a silver standard. The ISO 15919-style transliteration 'kyap' reflects the spelling; the word is pronounced and usually written 'kyat'. The only silver-bowl example was seen through a search summary of a Smithsonian record and has not been confirmed.

facts.text: The word translated 'ticals' in Burmese inscriptions is kyat; a bell inscription of 1847 gives its weight in kyats.
facts.quote: No doubt, the word translated "ticals" in the inscriptions of 1454 and 1843 is kyat.

facts.text: A Smithsonian Burmese silver bowl is reported to carry a base inscription naming the maker and giving the weight of silver as 11 ticals (unverified).

rows.plain: Burmese grade names for silver: bo (baw), dain, ywetni
rows.meaning: Words used in pre-colonial and early colonial Burma for grades of silver bullion
rows.date_note: Bullion grades of the Konbaung period, recorded by Yule (1855) and later writers; coins (rupees) largely replaced bullion after 1852 in Lower Burma and 1885 in Upper Burma.
rows.fineness: Shan bo: purest recognized silver (reported to contain some gold); dain: about 89-93 per cent; ywetni: the standard current grade (figures vary by source).
rows.what_it_tells: Explains terms that may appear in old descriptions or dealer notes on Burmese silver ('baw silver').
rows.cautions: No source seen shows these words struck or engraved on silverware as a fineness mark; they describe bullion. Colonial-period Burmese silver was often made from melted coins of varying fineness and is usually unmarked for silver content.

facts.text: The purest Burmese silver, bo (baw), came from the Shan country (extracted from lead ore, per Temple; mined in the northern Shan states, per the ACM).
facts.quote: The purest recognised silver in Burma is called Shan bò, or pure silver (Indian Antiquary 1919)

facts.text: The second quality of silver, dain, ran about 89 to 93 per cent and was recognized by striations on its upper surface.
facts.quote: The second quality of silver is called dain running about 89 to 93 per cent.

facts.text: In the colonial period coins were more often melted down to make silver items.

rows.meaning: Statement of silver content (95 per cent) found on a Burmese repousse bowl
rows.punch_set: Not recorded
rows.technique: not recorded
rows.date_note: Undated in the catalogue.
rows.fineness: 95 per cent (950/1000) as claimed by the mark; not confirmed by assay
rows.what_it_tells: A maker's or seller's claim of fineness; such statements are rare on Burmese silver.
rows.cautions: Single example. Most Burmese silver carries no fineness mark at all; dealers rely on acid tests (often reported as '900+'). A later '875' or '925' may be an import or re-marking stamp, not Burmese.

facts.text: A Burmese bowl chased with mythological scenes, sold at Bonhams in 2021, was catalogued as marked '95% silver'.
facts.quote: A Burmese silver bowl marked '95% silver'

facts.text: A dealer notes that Burmese silver is usually unmarked for fineness and reports acid tests of '900+'; one of its bowls carries later Soviet import marks for the 875 standard (both listings from one dealer).

rows.plain: Colombo large assay mark: K and G either side of a mango tree with a dove
variants: mango tree with dove, K and G
rows.meaning: Large assay mark (grote keur) of the VOC assay master of Colombo, for silver of 11 penningen (about 917/1000) and above and gold of 20 carat and above
rows.device: Arms of Colombo: a mango tree without fruit with a dove perched on it; letter K at the left of the trunk and G at the right
rows.punch_set: Struck with the maker's mark; the assay master was not to test work that did not already bear its maker's mark

maker.name: Assay master (keurmeester) of Colombo, Dutch East India Company

rows.technique: struck with a punch
rows.date_note: The punches are described in the ordinance of 29 October 1760; an assay master is recorded at Colombo from 1666 but earlier punches are not described. Dutch rule in Colombo ended in 1796.
rows.fineness: Silver of 11 penningen (11/12, about 917/1000) and finer; gold of 20 carat and finer
rows.what_it_tells: Dutch-period (VOC) Colombo assay of high-standard silver, c. 1760-1796.
rows.cautions: Marked Ceylon silver of the VOC period is rare: decorated colonial silver was only exceptionally marked. The first assay placard (1666) applied only to Colombo and the adjoining coast (including Negombo and Kalutara), so Jaffna smiths were not obliged to submit work. Silver sold at auction also had to carry the assay master's mark (a rule extending this to silver held at home was dropped within six months), so a Colombo mark can occur without a maker's mark. The ordinance gives the letter positions 'on the punch or the mark'; as struck the order may read G-K rather than K-G. Batavia (Jakarta) silver uses the Batavia arms and term letters, not the Colombo tree. The reading of G and K as 'groote' and 'kleine' keur is an inference, not stated in the ordinance.

facts.text: The Colombo ordinance of 29 October 1760 required the assay master to stamp approved gold and silver with two punches, a large and a small mark, both bearing the arms of the city: a mango tree without fruit on which a dove sits; on the large mark a G stands at the right of the trunk and a K at the left.
facts.quote: beijde getekend met het wapen deser stad, 't welk bestaat in een mangus boom zonder vrugt waarop een duijf zit ... op de stempel of het merk van de groot keur aan de regter zij van de stam van de mangus boom een G: en aan de linker dito een K

facts.text: The large mark covered gold of 20 carat and above and silver of 11 penningen and above.
facts.quote: Onder de Grote Keur zal begrepen worden al het goud dat 20 Garaat en het Zilver dat 11 penningen en daar boven fijn is

facts.text: The mango tree with a dove is the device of Colombo; the same tree-and-dove device between letters was used as the assay master's mark on the edge of the 1787 Colombo silver rupee.
facts.quote: A mango tree with a dove (Columbus) on it between K-K (Lakdiva)

facts.text: Recorded Colombo assay masters: Manuel St. Pay (appointed 22 September 1666), Joost Hendrik Betger (died 1750), Johannes Jongbloet (from 29 September 1750), Johan Christiaan Pieters (from 6 April 1784).
Decorated VOC-period colonial silver is only exceptionally marked.

rows.plain: Colombo small assay mark: K and K either side of a mango tree with a dove
variants: mango tree with dove between K-K
edge mark on the 1787 Colombo rupee
rows.meaning: Small assay mark (kleine keur) of the VOC assay master of Colombo, for silver of 9 1/2 to 11 penningen (about 792-917/1000) and gold of 17 to 20 carat
rows.device: Mango tree with a dove perched on it, a letter K on each side of the trunk
rows.punch_set: Struck with the maker's mark

maker.name: Assay master (keurmeester) of Colombo, Dutch East India Company

rows.technique: struck with a punch
rows.where_on_object: not specified for wares; on the edge of the 1787 rupee
rows.date_note: Described in the ordinance of 29 October 1760; struck by assay master Christiaan Pieters on the edge of 20,000 silver rupees in 1787.
rows.fineness: Silver of 9 1/2 to 11 penningen (about 792-917/1000); gold of 17 to 20 carat
rows.what_it_tells: Dutch-period Colombo assay of lower-standard silver or gold, c. 1760-1796.
rows.cautions: See colombo-grote-keur. On the coin the mark was reduced in size and is hard to read.

facts.text: On the small mark a K stands on each side of the tree's trunk.
facts.quote: op die van de kleene keur aan weerskanten van gedle stam een K gesteld is

facts.text: The small mark covered gold of 17 to 20 carat and silver of 9 1/2 to 11 penningen.
facts.quote: onder de kleene keur, het goud van 17 tot 20 Garaat en het Zilver van gVi tot 11 penningen fijn

facts.text: In 1787 the Colombo silver rupees were assayed by the assay master for gold and silver work, Christiaan Pieters, and given the small mark on the edge: a mango tree with a dove between K-K.
facts.quote: they were tested by the sworn assayer and given a hall-mark (Kleine Keur) on the edge (Lakdiva)

rows.plain: Early Colombo mark: tree with a bird, with a further sign (cross over a trefoil, or key with arrow); maker's mark IB below H
variants: tree and dove with cross over trefoil
tree and bird with key crossed by an arrow
maker's mark: IB with H above
rows.meaning: Larger tree-and-bird mark without the K letters, attributed by Veenendaal to Colombo before the 1760 ordinance
rows.device: Tree (read as the Colombo mango tree) with a bird above, plus a cross over a trefoil, or a key crossed by an arrow
rows.punch_set: On a pair of spittoons: the tree mark, an assay scrape and a maker's mark of IB with H above; on a dish in the Wolvendaal Church, Colombo, a similar mark
rows.technique: struck with a punch
rows.date_note: The dish is engraved for a baptism of 17 June 1668; the spittoons are placed in the second quarter of the 18th century if the maker is Joost Hendrik Betger (died 1750), an unconfirmed attribution.
rows.what_it_tells: A possible pre-1760 Colombo assay mark; the attribution is a scholar's proposal.
rows.cautions: Attribution to Colombo and to Betger is a hypothesis by one author; the meaning of the extra sign is unknown (possibly a standard mark).

facts.text: Two spittoons in the C.N.O. collection carry an assay scrape and two previously unknown marks: a tree with a dove and a sign like a cross over a trefoil, and a maker's mark IB with an H above; Veenendaal attributes the first to Colombo and suggests the maker could be Joost Hendrik Betger.
facts.quote: Het andere merk, IB met een H erboven, is vermoedelijk het meesterteken van de zilversmid

facts.text: A similar mark, with a key crossed by an arrow, is on a large silver dish in the Wolvendaal Church, Colombo, engraved for the baptism on 17 June 1668 of Esther Ceylonia van Goens.

rows.meaning: Mark of the Kandyan Art Association, Kandy, founded 1882 to sell the work of Kandyan craftsmen
rows.device: Rectangle with KAA; struck with a separate mark showing an animal (described as a monkey)
rows.punch_set: KAA rectangle with a separate animal mark
rows.technique: struck with a punch
rows.date_note: Marked silver seen is dated c. 1920 by a dealer; the Association was founded in 1882 and still trades.
rows.what_it_tells: Item sold through the Kandyan Art Association, made by a Kandyan craftsman; not a fineness mark.
rows.cautions: The same KAA mark appears on brass and bronze, so it does not prove the item is silver. The animal mark's meaning (a maker's mark?) is not established.

facts.text: Kandyan moonstone platters are struck on the rim with a 'KAA' mark together with a separate mark showing an animal.
facts.quote: one contains an animal whereas the rectangular one bears the letters KAA (Antiques Atlas)

facts.text: On a silver dish of c. 1920 the animal is described as like a monkey, and 'KAA' is read as the Kandyan Arts Association.
facts.quote: a separate 'KAA' mark for the Kandyan Arts Association

facts.text: The same pair of marks occurs on a bronze platter.
The Kandyan Art Association was established in 1882 through the efforts of J. F. Dickson, Government Agent of the Central Province.

rows.meaning: Small stamp of unidentified meaning on Kandyan silver moonstone platters, c. 1920
rows.punch_set: Alone on the rim
rows.technique: stamped
rows.date_note: Platters dated c. 1920 by the cataloguers.
rows.what_it_tells: Associated with Kandy silver platters of c. 1920; whose mark it is has not been established.
rows.cautions: Meaning unknown. The two catalogue descriptions may be of the same platter.

facts.text: A Kandy silver platter of c. 1920 has a small stamp on the rim with the letters 'RPD'; a Bonhams moonstone platter of c. 1920 is described as stamped 'RPD' on the outer rim (seen only in a search summary).
facts.quote: The rim has a small stamp with the letters 'RPD.' (Backman)

rows.meaning: Device reported on Sri Lankan silver of the mid-20th century
rows.device: Stylized lion holding a sword (the Sinhala lion of the national flag)
rows.punch_set: Not recorded
rows.technique: struck
rows.date_note: Described as mid-20th century (after independence in 1948).
rows.what_it_tells: Suggests Sri Lankan manufacture around the mid-20th century; whose mark it is and what standard it guarantees are not established.
rows.cautions: Single collector-reference source; a collector discussion questions whether lion marks on Ceylon silver always hold a sword. Modern Sri Lankan hallmarks (assay office and standard marks, standards .999, .925, .800) are a different, later system.

facts.text: Silver made in Sri Lanka in the mid-20th century is marked with a stylized lion holding a sword; present-day silver carries the assay office and standard marks, with legal standards .999, .925 and .800.
facts.quote: Silver manufactured in the mid-20th century is marked with a stylized lion holding a sword

rows.plain: Chinese export pseudo-hallmarks: lion passant, crowned leopard's head, sovereign's head and maker's initials
variants: SS + pseudo lion and leopard's head
rows.meaning: Imitation English hallmarks struck by Canton (Guangzhou) export silversmiths, with a letter that is the maker's initial, not a date letter
rows.device: Lion passant, crowned leopard's head, sovereign's head, letter in a shield
rows.punch_set: Usually four or five punches in a row imitating a London set: maker's initials + lion + leopard's head + sovereign's head + letter

maker.name: Canton export silversmiths and retailers (Cutshing, Sunshing, Khecheong and others)

rows.technique: struck with punches
rows.date_note: Mostly 1785 to the 1840s; Khecheong items run to the 1870s.
rows.what_it_tells: A row of English-looking marks with crude animals and no consistent date-letter sequence on Asian-made silver points to Canton export silver of c. 1785-1870, not to India or Burma.
rows.cautions: Indian colonial makers in Calcutta, Madras and Bombay also struck pseudo-hallmarks (lion, elephant, crown, letter), so the punches alone do not settle China versus India: compare initials with Chinese and Indian maker lists. Burmese silver of the same period has no pseudo-hallmarks.

facts.text: Early Chinese export items, to about the 1840s, often carry imitation English hallmarks: a lion passant, a crowned leopard's head, a monarch's head and the maker's initials.
facts.quote: Early pieces, to about the 1840s, often carry imitation English hallmarks. (Mozeris)

facts.text: In these sets the date letter was replaced by a letter that may be the first Latin letter of the silversmith's name.
facts.quote: date letters were replaced by a letter that might have been the first Latin letter of the silversmith's name

facts.text: Makers using such marks include Cutshing (CS, early 19th century), Sunshing (SS) and Khecheong (KHC, 1830s-1870s), all of Canton.

variants: WH with a Chinese character mark
rows.meaning: Retailer's initials of Wang Hing & Co, Canton and Hong Kong, the most prolific Chinese export silver firm, late 19th to early 20th century
rows.punch_set: WH, often with '90' and a Chinese-character mark of the actual silversmith
wares: repousse export silver with dragons, bamboo, chrysanthemums
rows.technique: struck
rows.date_note: Late 19th to early 20th century.
rows.fineness: Usually with 90 (900/1000)
rows.what_it_tells: Chinese export silver from Hong Kong or Canton; the Chinese-character mark beside it names the workshop.
rows.cautions: Heavy repousse Chinese export silver (dragons, figures in landscapes) is sometimes sold as Burmese or Indian; a 'WH' with '90' and Chinese characters settles it as Chinese.

facts.text: Wang Hing's mark is 'WH', often with '90' and a character mark; it was the most prolific Chinese export firm.
facts.quote: WH, often with 90 and a character mark. (Mozeris)

facts.text: Wang Hing worked in Canton and Hong Kong from the late 19th to the early 20th century.

rows.meaning: Fineness number used on Chinese export silver: 90 per cent (900/1000)
rows.punch_set: With retailer's initials (WH, LH, HC, LW) and Chinese-character marks
rows.technique: struck
rows.date_note: Common on late 19th- and early 20th-century export silver from Hong Kong, Canton and Shanghai.
rows.what_it_tells: Points to Chinese (or Hong Kong / Shanghai) export silver, not to Burmese or Indian work, which rarely carries fineness numbers.
rows.cautions: Also used with retailers' initials that resemble English makers' marks. A lone '90' without Chinese characters is not by itself proof of China.

facts.text: Many Chinese export items are stamped 90 for 900 parts per thousand.
facts.quote: many pieces are stamped 90 for 900 parts per thousand (Mozeris)

rows.plain: Zu yin / zu wen ('full silver', fine silver)
rows.meaning: Chinese-character mark for high-grade (pure) silver, used on Chinese and Straits Chinese silver beside a shop mark
rows.punch_set: Shop mark in Chinese characters (e.g. 'Jin Ji', 'Li Chang', 'Jin Cheng') with the fine-silver mark

maker.name: Chinese silversmiths' shops in China and in the Straits Settlements (Singapore, Malacca, Penang)

rows.technique: struck
rows.date_note: Straits examples dated late 19th century.
rows.fineness: Claims high-grade (pure) silver; no number
rows.what_it_tells: Chinese or Straits Chinese work, not Burmese, Indian or Ceylonese.
rows.cautions: The sources give only the romanized readings; the characters shown in other_spellings are the usual forms and should be checked against the item. Straits Chinese silver with these marks is sometimes sold as 'Burmese' or 'Indian'.

facts.text: Chinese silver is most commonly marked 'Zu Wen' (high-grade silver) in Chinese characters.
facts.quote: Chinese silver is most commonly marked with 'Zu Wen' (high-grade silver) mark in Chinese characters.

facts.text: Late 19th-century Straits Chinese key hooks are stamped with local Chinese shop marks ('Jin Ji', 'Li Chang', 'Jin Cheng') and the pure-silver mark 'Zu Yin' (citing Ho Wing Meng 1984, p. 103).
facts.quote: 'Jin Ji' shop mark and mark for pure silver 'Zu Yin'.

rows.plain: Chinese chop marks on Thai (Siamese) silver
rows.meaning: Small Chinese-character workshop or retailer marks found on the minority of Thai silver that is marked at all, Bangkok c. 1850-1920
rows.punch_set: Usually a single chop on the underside
wares: Thai silver bowls, water pots, betel sets, nielloware
rows.technique: struck
rows.date_note: Firms appear to have operated in Bangkok between about 1850 and 1920.
rows.what_it_tells: Thai silver of the late Chakri reigns; the chop names a workshop or retailer, rarely an individual silversmith.
rows.cautions: Most Thai silver has no maker's or reign mark. Thai repousse bowls resemble Burmese ones; a Chinese chop does not rule out Thailand, and some Chinese export firms made Burmese-themed silver for the Thai market.

facts.text: The vast majority of Thai silverware has no reign mark or maker's mark; the marks that do appear are mostly Chinese chop marks on the underside, naming a workshop or retailer rather than a silversmith, of firms active mainly in Bangkok c. 1850-1920.
The 'Tan Yue He' mark is on items of outstanding quality, some made to palace order in the 1870s-1880s.

rows.meaning: Generic mark on Thai sterling silver, especially black-and-silver nielloware jewelry and small wares, mainly post-1945 to the 1970s
rows.punch_set: Usually alone; occasionally with a firm's name
rows.technique: stamped
rows.date_note: Most marked items date from after World War II to the 1970s. The country was renamed Thailand in 1939, briefly Siam again 1946-1949, but 'Siam' and 'Thailand' were used interchangeably on marks, so the word does not date an item.
rows.fineness: Claims sterling (925/1000)
rows.what_it_tells: Thai manufacture, generally mid-20th century; not Burmese or Indian.
rows.cautions: Dealers who date 'Siam' marks before 1939 or to 1939-1949 are using a rule of thumb that the sources do not support.

facts.text: Thai silver jewelry usually carries a variation of 'Siam Sterling' or 'Thailand Sterling', without individual makers' marks.
facts.quote: will usually have variations on the hallmark "Siam Sterling" or "Thailand Sterling" (Market Square Jewelers)

facts.text: Most vintage Thai niello jewelry on the market dates from after World War II to the 1970s; the country became Thailand in 1939, Siam again in 1946 and Thailand in 1949.
Collectors report that 'Siam' and 'Thailand' were used arbitrarily, sometimes both on the same item.

rows.meaning: Maker's mark read as Bao Xing (Bo Hing), a Chinese export firm whose items include Burmese-themed silver made for the Thai market
rows.punch_set: Not fully recorded
wares: silver boxes with Jataka and Burmese mythological scenes
rows.technique: struck
rows.date_note: Listed as 20th century; claimed Canton dates for the firm are unsupported.
rows.what_it_tells: A Chinese export maker; Burmese subject matter alone does not make an item Burmese.
rows.cautions: Single dealer source. Shows that Chinese export firms made silver with Burmese imagery for Southeast Asian buyers.

facts.text: A Chinese export silver box made for the Thai market, decorated with the Pandara Jataka and other Burmese mythological imagery, bears the maker's mark 'B.H' for Bo Hing (Bao Xing).
facts.quote: Hallmarked Chinese silver, Maker's mark B.H (B.H for Bo Hing, alternative of Bao Xing).

rows.meaning: The BIS logo (Bureau of Indian Standards Standard Mark) used as the first component of the Indian gold hallmark; certifies that a BIS-recognized assaying and hallmarking center tested the item.
rows.device: Triangle (chevron-like) with a dot at its center over two horizontal bars; printed blue with a red dot in the 2018 Gazette, struck monochrome on metal
rows.punch_set: 2000 to 31 Dec 2016 (gold): BIS logo + fineness number (e.g. 916) + assaying and hallmarking center's logo + year letter + jeweler's mark | 1 Jan 2017 to 30 June 2021 (gold): BIS logo + carat and fineness (e.g. 22K916) + AHC mark/number + jeweler's mark/number | From 1 July 2021 (gold): BIS logo + carat and fineness (e.g. 22K916) + six-character HUID
rows.technique: struck with punches or lasered (2000-2018); lasered on jewelry under the 2018 Regulations
rows.where_on_object: Small (0.5-1.5 mm high) and usually needs a 10x loupe; on every detachable part and on each item of a pair; on bangles and light items struck once only (IS 1417:1999). Trade guides say inside ring shanks and near chain clasps.
rows.date_note: Gold hallmarking began in 2000 (April 2000 per non-BIS sources); voluntary until mandatory in notified districts from 16/23 June 2021.
rows.what_it_tells: The item was tested by a BIS-recognized center and met the purity marked beside the logo; the marks next to it give the system (and so the period): bare fineness + year letter = 2000-2016, 22K916-style + center and jeweler marks = 2017-June 2021, 22K916 + six-character code = July 2021 onward.
rows.cautions: The logo alone does not date or proves genuine an item; read it with the other marks. A triangle-like logo without a purity mark, or a purity number without the logo, is not a BIS hallmark. Jewelers may add their own marks next to the hallmark (BIS FAQ). The logo is also used on bullion and coins (with fineness only) and on silver (with the word SILVER).

facts.text: BIS identified as the sole hallmarking agency in 2000 by the RBI Standing Committee on Gold and Precious Metals; the gold jewelry scheme was voluntary until 2021.
facts.quote: The Committee identified Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS) in the year 2000 as the sole agency to operate the Hallmarking Scheme in India

facts.text: Western and collector sources date the start of gold hallmarking to April 2000.
facts.quote: The hallmarking of gold jewellery in India has been applied on a voluntary basis since April 2000

facts.text: In 2004 BIS described the first component as the 'BIS Corporate logo'; later pages call it 'BIS Hallmark', 'BIS Mark', 'BIS Standard Mark' or 'BIS logo'.
facts.quote: BIS Corporate logo

facts.text: The Hallmarking Regulations 2018 (Schedule III) print the hallmark as the BIS logo followed by 'XX K XXX' for gold jewelry, 'XXX' for gold bullion and coins, and 'Silver XXX' for silver; the device is a triangle with a central dot over horizontal bars.
facts.quote: Monogram of the hallmark and proportionate content shall be marked in a linear design.

facts.text: Trade guides describe the logo as a small triangle.
facts.quote: a small triangular logo that represents certification by the Bureau of Indian Standards

facts.text: Jewelry hallmarks are laser-marked; bullion and coin hallmarks are punched or embossed (Regulations 2018). Before that BIS allowed either punches or laser.
facts.quote: Hallmark at Sl.No. 1 and 3 shall be marked by laser marking.

facts.text: Permitted hallmark heights: gold 1.5, 1.0, 0.75 or 0.5 mm; silver 4.0, 2.0, 1.5, 1.0 or 0.75 mm.
A hallmark is valid for the life of the item; jewelry with older hallmarks held by consumers stays valid after the HUID rule.
facts.quote: Hallmarked jewellery lying with consumers as per old schemes shall remain valid.

facts.text: On retesting a hallmarked item, IS 1417:2016 allows a negative tolerance of at most 2 parts per thousand; IS 1417:1999 allowed none.
Imported jewelry already hallmarked in the exporting country must be re-hallmarked in India before sale.
facts.quote: it is necessary to re-hallmark a hallmarked imported jewellery.

rows.meaning: BIS logo with the word 'SILVER' and a fineness number: the Indian silver hallmark.
rows.device: BIS logo (triangle with central dot over bars) followed by the word SILVER
rows.punch_set: 2005-2014: BIS logo + fineness + AHC logo + year letter + jeweler's mark; IS 2112:2014: BIS mark with SILVER + fineness + AHC mark + year letter + jeweler's mark; from 1 Sept 2025: BIS mark with SILVER + fineness + HUID
rows.technique: punched or lasered; lasered on jewelry under the 2018 Regulations
rows.where_on_object: On each detachable part; 0.75-4.0 mm high.
rows.date_note: Silver hallmarking from 2005 (month disputed); the word SILVER enters the standard in IS 2112:2014; HUID version from 1 Sept 2025.
rows.fineness: See the silver grade rows (800 to 999).
rows.what_it_tells: Indian silver tested by a BIS-recognized center; the presence of a six-character code dates the marking to Sept 2025 or later.
rows.cautions: Indian silver hallmarking has always been voluntary, so most Indian silver (including all colonial and earlier silver) carries no BIS mark. A '925' or 'SILVER' stamp without the BIS logo is a maker's claim only. Do not confuse with British, Burmese or Chinese export marks.

facts.text: BIS launched hallmarking of silver jewelry and artefacts (coins, utensils, idols) in 2005.
facts.quote: BIS launches Hallmarking of silver Jewellery/Artefacts like Coins, Utensils and Idols of God and Goddess

facts.text: The month is disputed: Wikipedia and the 925-1000 forum say December 2005; a BIS statement reported in 2025-2026 says October 2005.
facts.quote: Silver hallmarking has been voluntary since October 2005.

facts.text: IS 2112:2003 marking: BIS logo, purity grade, assay center's logo, year letter, jeweler's mark (Amendment 4, July 2008, changed 'BIS logo' to 'BIS mark').
IS 2112:2014 requires 'BIS Mark along with the word SILVER', purity grade, assay center's identification mark, year letter and jeweler's mark.
facts.quote: BIS Mark along with the word 'SILVER';

facts.text: Hallmarking Regulations 2018 print the silver design as BIS logo + 'Silver XXX'.
facts.quote: Silver XXX

facts.text: Under IS 2112:2025, from 1 Sept 2025, a hallmarked silver item carries the BIS Standard Mark with 'SILVER', the purity grade and a six-character HUID.
facts.quote: The revised silver hallmark consists of BIS Standard Mark with the word “SILVER”, Purity Grade and six-digit HUID.

facts.text: Silver hallmarking remains voluntary, but any silver item submitted for BIS hallmarking must carry the HUID hallmark.
Silver marking must be visible under a 10x magnifier (IS 2112:2003 and 2014).

rows.meaning: BIS hallmark on gold or silver bars and coins: BIS logo with a fineness number (999 or 995 for gold), plus the refiner's or mint's name or identification and a serial number.
rows.punch_set: BIS logo + fineness (999/995) + refiner or mint name/identification + serial number
rows.technique: punched or embossed (Regulations 2018)
rows.where_on_object: Face of the bar or coin; coin serial may be on the pack.
rows.date_note: Bullion and coin hallmarking by licensed refineries/mints from IS 1417:2016 (Nov 2016) and the 2018 Regulations; earlier coins could be hallmarked as artefacts.
rows.fineness: Gold: 999 (fine gold) or 995 (standard gold); silver 999 and above.
rows.what_it_tells: Bar or coin from a BIS-licensed Indian refinery or mint, of the stated fineness.
rows.cautions: No year letter or HUID on bullion/coins. Unhallmarked bars and coins are legal (exempt). A refiner's own '999.9' stamp without the BIS logo is not a hallmark.

facts.text: IS 1417:2016 brought bullion and coins into the standard; hallmarked gold bullion and coins carry the BIS Standard Mark, fineness, the manufacturer's name/identification and a serial number (for coins the serial may be on the packaging).
facts.quote: In case of coins, serial numbers may be marked on the packaging.

facts.text: Only BIS-licensed refineries and mints may hallmark 999/995 gold bullion and coins (46 licensed refineries operating on 31 July 2023).
facts.quote: Gold bullion/coins of 999/995 fineness are permitted to be hallmarked by BIS approved Refinery/Mints only

facts.text: The Regulations 2018 design for bullion and coins is the BIS logo + 'XXX' (gold) or 'Silver XXX' (silver), punched or embossed.
facts.quote: Hallmark at Sl.No.2 and 4 shall be marked by punching or embossing.

facts.text: The mandatory hallmarking order does not cover bullion or coins: gold bullion 'in any shape of bar, plate, sheet, foil, rod, wire, strip, tube or coin' is exempt.
facts.quote: gold bullion in any shape of bar, plate, sheet, foil, rod, wire, strip, tube or coin.

facts.text: Before 2016, coins could be hallmarked as 'artefacts' under IS 1417:1999 Amendment 2 (Dec 2007) and IS 2112 (silver), if of a listed grade.
facts.quote: Artefacts cover medallions, utensils and coins provided the purity of gold alloy for artefacts is as per 4.

facts.text: Silver bullion/coin licences cover finenesses such as 999, 999.5 and 999.9 under IS 2112:2025.

rows.meaning: Fine gold, 999 parts per thousand: a grade for bars and coins.
rows.punch_set: Struck after the BIS logo
rows.technique: struck or lasered by a BIS-recognized assaying and hallmarking center
rows.where_on_object: Small (0.5-1.5 mm high) and usually needs a 10x loupe; on every detachable part and on each item of a pair; on bangles and light items struck once only (IS 1417:1999). Trade guides say inside ring shanks and near chain clasps.
rows.date_note: Listed as 'fine gold' in IS 1417:1999 and IS 1417:2016; under IS 1417:2016 the fine and standard grades are for bullion and coins. (Standard dated Dec 1999; BIS hallmarking began in 2000.)
rows.fineness: minimum 999 parts per thousand gold
rows.what_it_tells: On a BIS-marked bar or coin: at least 99.9% gold from a licensed refinery or mint.
rows.cautions: On jewelry a bare '999' or '24K 999' is a trade claim, not a BIS jewelry grade.

facts.text: IS 1417:1999 and IS 1417:2016 list 'Fine gold' at minimum 999 ppt; the 2016 standard defines it as gold of 999 ppt and above.
facts.quote: Fine Gold — It is gold having fineness 999 parts per thousand (‰) and above.

facts.text: BIS's summary of IS 1417:2016 says the fine and standard grades are only for bullion and coins; jewelry grades are separate.
facts.quote: The grade of fine gold and standard gold is only for gold bullion and gold coins.

facts.text: A jeweler's blog calls '999' the 24-carat hallmark, but the BIS 24-carat jewelry grade is 995 (written 24KS995).

rows.meaning: Standard gold, 995 parts per thousand: bullion and coin grade; for jewelry written 24KS995 since 2021.
rows.punch_set: Struck after the BIS logo
rows.technique: struck or lasered by a BIS-recognized assaying and hallmarking center
rows.where_on_object: Small (0.5-1.5 mm high) and usually needs a 10x loupe; on every detachable part and on each item of a pair; on bangles and light items struck once only (IS 1417:1999). Trade guides say inside ring shanks and near chain clasps.
rows.date_note: 995 'standard gold' in IS 1417:1999 and 2016 (bullion/coins); added as a 24-carat jewelry grade by IS 1417:2016 Amendment 1 (7 July 2021) and brought under the mandatory order from 1 June 2022. (Standard dated Dec 1999; BIS hallmarking began in 2000.)
rows.fineness: 24 carat; minimum 995 parts per thousand gold (no negative tolerance at marking)
rows.what_it_tells: 24-carat jewelry hallmarked in or after mid-2021 (24KS995); or a standard-gold bar/coin (995).
rows.cautions: What the 'S' in 24KS stands for is not explained in the sources read. A 24-carat jewelry hallmark guarantees 995, not 999.

facts.text: IS 1417:1999 and IS 1417:2016 list 'Standard gold' at minimum 995 ppt.
facts.quote: Standard Gold — Gold having fineness 995 parts per thousand (‰) and above.

facts.text: BIS writes the 24-carat jewelry mark as '24KS995' (FAQ: '24KS(995)'); the BIS brief lists '24KS' with minimum 995.
20, 23 and 24 carat (995) were covered by mandatory hallmarking from the second phase (order of 4 April 2022, in force 1 June 2022).
facts.quote: three additional caratages of gold jewellery/artefacts viz. 20 carat (833 fineness), 23 (958 fineness) and 24 carats (995 fineness)

rows.meaning: 23-carat gold, 958 parts per thousand.
rows.punch_set: Struck after the BIS logo
rows.technique: struck or lasered by a BIS-recognized assaying and hallmarking center
rows.where_on_object: Small (0.5-1.5 mm high) and usually needs a 10x loupe; on every detachable part and on each item of a pair; on bangles and light items struck once only (IS 1417:1999). Trade guides say inside ring shanks and near chain clasps.
rows.date_note: Introduced in IS 1417:1999; deleted by IS 1417:2016 (Nov 2016, in force 1 Jan 2017); restored as 23K958 by Amendment 1 (7 July 2021), mandatory-order coverage from 1 June 2022. Not hallmarkable 1 Jan 2017 - July 2021. (Standard dated Dec 1999; BIS hallmarking began in 2000.)
rows.fineness: 23 carat; minimum 958 parts per thousand gold (no negative tolerance at marking)
rows.what_it_tells: A bare '958' beside the BIS logo with a year letter = hallmarked 2000-2016; '23K958' = mid-2021 or later.
rows.cautions: 958 is also the British Britannia silver standard; on silver it means something else (see silver-958).

facts.text: IS 1417:1999 introduced grade 958 (23 ct), deleting 500 and 970, because of its popularity in many parts of India.
facts.quote: a new grade of fineness 958 has been introduced on account of its popularity for manufacture of ornaments/artefacts in many parts of the country.

facts.text: 958 (23 carat) was among the six grades shown in BIS's hallmark design 2000-2016 and in the 2012 Government advertisement.
facts.quote: 958 Corresponding to 23 Carat

facts.text: IS 1417:2016 deleted 958 (23k) among other grades 'in consumer welfare'.
facts.quote: the grades of fineness 958(23k), 875(21k), 833 (20k), 791(19k), 708(17k), 666(16k) and 375(9k) have been deleted in consumer welfare

facts.text: 23K958 returned in 2021 and is in BIS's current list.
Before 2017 the purity mark was the fineness number alone (e.g. 916); IS 1417:1999 made showing the carat optional. From 1 Jan 2017 the mark is carat plus fineness (e.g. 22K916).
facts.quote: The purity mark along with purity/fineness grade (indicating caratage shall not be mandatory)

rows.meaning: 22-carat gold, 916 parts per thousand (grade 916.6): the commonest Indian jewelry standard.
rows.punch_set: Struck after the BIS logo
rows.technique: struck or lasered by a BIS-recognized assaying and hallmarking center
rows.where_on_object: Small (0.5-1.5 mm high) and usually needs a 10x loupe; on every detachable part and on each item of a pair; on bangles and light items struck once only (IS 1417:1999). Trade guides say inside ring shanks and near chain clasps.
rows.date_note: A BIS grade throughout: bare '916' 2000-2016; '22K916' from 1 Jan 2017; mandatory in notified districts from June 2021. (Standard dated Dec 1999; BIS hallmarking began in 2000.)
rows.fineness: 22 carat; minimum 916 parts per thousand gold (no negative tolerance at marking)
rows.what_it_tells: With the BIS logo: 22-carat gold tested by an assaying center; the written form ('916' vs '22K916') and companion marks date the marking.
rows.cautions: '916' without the BIS logo is a jeweler's own claim. Indian 22-carat jewelry has many solder joints; before hallmarking low-carat solder commonly brought items below the stated carat (BIS).

facts.text: IS 1417:1999 grade '916.6', minimum fineness 916, 22 carat; kept in IS 1417:2016.
BIS and the 2012 Government advertisement show '916' corresponding to 22 carat; the advertisement calls this 'a BIS 916 hallmark'.
facts.quote: Thus a BIS 916 hallmark would certify to a purity of 916 per 1000, that is 91.6%, translating to a 22 carat purity of gold.

facts.text: From 1 Jan 2017 the mark is written 22K916.
facts.quote: Purity in Carat and Fineness e.g 22K916

facts.text: 22, 18 and 14 carat were the three grades of the first mandatory phase (256 districts, June 2021).
facts.quote: 14, 18 and 22 caratages of gold jewellery and gold artefacts.

facts.text: Before 2017 the purity mark was the fineness number alone (e.g. 916); IS 1417:1999 made showing the carat optional. From 1 Jan 2017 the mark is carat plus fineness (e.g. 22K916).
facts.quote: The purity mark along with purity/fineness grade (indicating caratage shall not be mandatory)

rows.punch_set: Struck after the BIS logo
rows.technique: struck or lasered by a BIS-recognized assaying and hallmarking center
rows.where_on_object: Small (0.5-1.5 mm high) and usually needs a 10x loupe; on every detachable part and on each item of a pair; on bangles and light items struck once only (IS 1417:1999). Trade guides say inside ring shanks and near chain clasps.
rows.date_note: Grade in IS 1417:1999; deleted by IS 1417:2016 (in force 1 Jan 2017) and not restored. (Standard dated Dec 1999; BIS hallmarking began in 2000.)
rows.fineness: 21 carat; minimum 875 parts per thousand gold (no negative tolerance at marking)
rows.what_it_tells: A BIS-marked 875 dates the hallmarking to 2000-2016.
rows.cautions: A dealer reports Indian '22kt' items testing at 87-88% (about 21 ct); 875 itself was a legitimate grade.

facts.text: IS 1417:1999 lists grade 875 (21 ct).
facts.quote: 875 Corresponding to 21 Carat

facts.text: Deleted by IS 1417:2016.
facts.quote: Prior to that, hallmarking was done for more standards such as 23K, 21K, 17K, 9K.

rows.punch_set: Struck after the BIS logo
rows.technique: struck or lasered by a BIS-recognized assaying and hallmarking center
rows.where_on_object: Small (0.5-1.5 mm high) and usually needs a 10x loupe; on every detachable part and on each item of a pair; on bangles and light items struck once only (IS 1417:1999). Trade guides say inside ring shanks and near chain clasps.
rows.date_note: Listed among grades deleted by IS 1417:2016, so it was in IS 1417 before 2016 (amendment and date not found); restored as 20K833 in 2021; mandatory-order coverage from 1 June 2022.
rows.fineness: 20 carat; minimum 833 parts per thousand gold (no negative tolerance at marking)
rows.what_it_tells: '20K833' = hallmarked mid-2021 or later.
rows.cautions: When 833 first entered IS 1417 (after June 2010) is not established.

facts.text: IS 1417:2016 records 833 (20k) as deleted, so it existed in the standard before 2016.
20K833 is a current BIS grade, added in 2021 and covered by the second mandatory phase.
facts.quote: 20 carat (833 fineness)
