rows.meaning: Mark (logo, later logo or number) of the BIS-recognized Assaying and Hallmarking Center (AHC) that tested and marked the item.
rows.device: Each center's own logo (designs vary: initials, emblems); from 2017 a logo or number
rows.punch_set: 2000 to 31 Dec 2016 (gold): BIS logo + fineness number (e.g. 916) + assaying and hallmarking center's logo + year letter + jeweler's mark | 1 Jan 2017 to 30 June 2021 (gold): BIS logo + carat and fineness (e.g. 22K916) + AHC mark/number + jeweler's mark/number
rows.technique: struck or lasered
rows.where_on_object: Small (0.5-1.5 mm high) and usually needs a 10x loupe; on every detachable part and on each item of a pair; on bangles and light items struck once only (IS 1417:1999). Trade guides say inside ring shanks and near chain clasps.
rows.date_note: Gold: 2000 to 30 June 2021 (HUID from 1 July 2021; four-mark stock could be sold until 31 March 2023, declared stock to 30 June 2023). Silver: until the HUID system of 1 Sept 2025 (not confirmed when silver dropped it).
rows.what_it_tells: Which center (and so roughly which city) tested the item; its presence on gold means hallmarked before July 2021.
rows.cautions: Center logos are not a closed, published set (an archived BIS list of center logos exists at bis.org.in/cert/hallmarkass.htm); centers close and new ones open. Not a maker's mark.

facts.text: The AHC's mark was a hallmark component from 2000: 'the Logo of BIS recognized Assaying and Hallmarking Center where the jewelry has been assayed and hallmarked'.
facts.quote: The Logo of BIS recognized Assaying and Hallmarking Centre where the jewellery has been assayed and hallmarked

facts.text: From 1 Jan 2017 BIS calls it the 'Assaying and Hallmarking Center's Mark/number' (IS 1417:2016: 'Assay center's identification mark/number').
facts.quote: Assay centre’s identification mark/number;

facts.text: From 1 July 2021 the AHC mark and jeweler's mark were replaced by the HUID on gold; the center's details are now looked up from the HUID.
facts.quote: Under this 4-mark system, instead of the HUID, logo of the jeweller and logo of the Assaying and Hallmarking Centre was mentioned.

facts.text: Centres are private but BIS-recognized for three years at a time (IS 15820:2009 basis): 41 in 2006, 948 on 1 July 2021, 1,220 on 31 July 2022, 1,565 (gold 1,561; silver 327) on 15 Oct 2026.

Collector examples of AHC marks: Sree Vishnu Assayers (Hyderabad), MMTC Ltd (New Delhi), Cochin Assay Co. (Cochin), Gujarat Gold Center (Ahmedabad), Leo Analytics Lab (Mumbai), Jalan Hallmarking Center (New Delhi).

rows.meaning: The registered jeweler's or manufacturer's own identification mark (logo or code), part of the BIS hallmark set 2000 to June 2021.
rows.device: The jeweler's own logo, initials or code
rows.punch_set: 2000 to 31 Dec 2016 (gold): BIS logo + fineness number (e.g. 916) + assaying and hallmarking center's logo + year letter + jeweler's mark | 1 Jan 2017 to 30 June 2021 (gold): BIS logo + carat and fineness (e.g. 22K916) + AHC mark/number + jeweler's mark/number
rows.technique: struck by the jeweler (or lasered by the center)
rows.where_on_object: Small (0.5-1.5 mm high) and usually needs a 10x loupe; on every detachable part and on each item of a pair; on bangles and light items struck once only (IS 1417:1999). Trade guides say inside ring shanks and near chain clasps.
rows.date_note: As a required hallmark component: 2000 to 30 June 2021 for gold. Jewelers' own marks continue as optional marks.
rows.what_it_tells: Which BIS-registered firm took responsibility for the item's purity.
rows.cautions: After July 2021 a jeweler's logo beside a HUID hallmark is optional branding, not part of the hallmark. The BIS register identifies jewelers by registration number, not by logo.

facts.text: The jeweler's (sponsor's) logo had to be struck on each item before it was sent to the AHC.
facts.quote: Jeweller's/Sponsorer's logo on each article shall be marked beforc offering the lot to BIS recognized Assaying and Hallmarking Centre

facts.text: It is the fifth component (2000-2016) and fourth (2017-June 2021): 'Identification mark of BIS Certified Jeweller/Jewelry Manufacturer'.
facts.quote: Identification mark of BIS Certified Jeweller/Jewellery Manufacturer

facts.text: Replaced by the HUID from 1 July 2021; jewelers and manufacturers may still add their own marks beside the three mandatory marks, and a retailer may add its brand after hallmarking.
facts.quote: Beside these, the manufacturer or jeweller may put his/their mark on hallmarked Jewellery/artefacts.

rows.meaning: Hallmark Unique Identification: a six-character alphanumeric code, unique to each hallmarked gold item, laser-marked with the BIS logo and purity from 1 July 2021.
rows.punch_set: From 1 July 2021 (gold): BIS logo + carat and fineness (e.g. 22K916) + six-character HUID
rows.technique: lasered (system-generated code)
rows.where_on_object: Small (0.5-1.5 mm high) and usually needs a 10x loupe; on every detachable part and on each item of a pair; on bangles and light items struck once only (IS 1417:1999). Trade guides say inside ring shanks and near chain clasps.
rows.date_note: Introduced 1 July 2021; sole permitted form to be sold from 1 April 2023 (declared old stock to 30 June 2023).
rows.what_it_tells: Hallmarked on or after 1 July 2021. Entering the code in BIS CARE should return the matching article type and purity, the jeweler's registration number and the center.
rows.cautions: The code does not, on published information, encode a date or place; read nothing into its letters. A code that fails to verify, or verifies to a different article type or purity, is a warning sign. An item may carry both an old four- or five-mark hallmark and a later HUID hallmark (re-hallmarked stock). A HUID may still verify after the item was altered (up to 50% or 2 g) or even melted.

facts.text: HUID is a six-digit alphanumeric number, unique to each hallmarked item and traceable.
facts.quote: It is a six-digit alphanumeric number which is unique for each hallmarked item and is traceable.

facts.text: Introduced 1 July 2021 (HUID hallmarking portal launched that day); every article hallmarked after 1 July 2021 must carry it.
facts.quote: 6 digit HUID was introduced from 01 July 2021 and all articles hallmarked post 01 July 2021 have to be hallmarked with HUID only.

facts.text: The code is generated by the BIS server at the end of testing and laser-marked by the AHC with the BIS logo and purity; it replaced the AHC and jeweler marks because the old uniform hallmark 'was prone to be misused'.
facts.quote: This system was prone to be misused; hence, it was decided to automate the functioning of the AHCs

facts.text: No sale or display of gold jewelry/artefacts after 31 March 2023 unless hallmarked to IS 1417:2016 as amended 7 July 2021 (i.e. with HUID): Order S.O. 1047(E) dated 3 March 2023 (Gazette dated 6 March 2023); PIB release 4 March 2023.
facts.quote: No person shall, after 31st March, 2023, sell or display or offer to sell any Gold jewellery or Gold Artefacts unless it is hallmarked in accordance with the standards specified in IS 1417:2016

facts.text: Jewelers who had declared old stock with pre-1 July 2021 hallmarks could sell it until 30 June 2023 (S.O. 1555(E), 31 March 2023).
facts.quote: such person shall be permitted to sell or display or offer to sell such declared stock of old Gold jewellery or Gold artefacts upto the 30 th June 2023

facts.text: Old-hallmarked stock offered for resale by a jeweler must be re-hallmarked: the HUID may be added beside the existing marks, or the old marks erased at the AHC.
facts.quote: Jewellery may be re-hallmarked with HUID along with existing marks or the existing marks may be erased as desired by jeweller to AHC.

facts.text: Consumers check a HUID with 'Verify HUID' in the BIS CARE app (live 24 Dec 2021); it shows the jeweler's registration number, purity, article type and the hallmarking center.
facts.quote: It provides information of the jeweller who got the article hallmarked, their registration number, purity of the article, type of article as well as details of hallmarking centre

facts.text: From 8 June 2026 photographs and automatically captured weights of hallmarked gold articles are recorded and shown in BIS Care.
When HUID jewelry is melted, deactivating the old HUID was 'presently under development' (BIS FAQ).
facts.quote: the provision to deactivate/disable the old HUID is presently under development.

facts.text: Alterations up to 50% of the item's weight or 2 g (whichever is lower) are allowed without re-hallmarking (Regulations amendment of 27 Oct 2021); the online HUID record does not reflect alterations.
facts.quote: Alteration in the hallmarked jewellery upto fifty per cent. of the weight of jewellery or upto two grams, whichever is lower, shall be permitted

facts.text: Over 65 crore (650 million) gold articles were hallmarked with HUID between July 2021 and Oct 2026.

rows.meaning: Six-character HUID on BIS-hallmarked silver, with the BIS mark, the word SILVER and the purity, from 1 September 2025.
rows.punch_set: BIS logo + SILVER + purity (e.g. 925) + HUID
rows.technique: lasered
rows.date_note: From 1 Sept 2025.
rows.what_it_tells: Indian silver hallmarked on or after 1 Sept 2025; BIS Care also returns the hallmarking date for silver.
rows.cautions: Silver hallmarking is still voluntary; absence of a HUID says nothing against older or unhallmarked Indian silver.

facts.text: HUID-based silver hallmarking began 1 Sept 2025 under IS 2112:2025, on a voluntary basis; any silver submitted for BIS hallmarking must carry the HUID mark.
facts.quote: From 01 September 2025, HUID-based hallmarking for silver jewellery/artefacts was introduced on a voluntary basis

facts.text: Each HUID silver item bears the BIS Standard Mark, 'SILVER', the purity grade and a laser-marked six-digit HUID; consumers can check article type, purity, hallmarking date, center and jeweler number in BIS Care.
facts.quote: consumers can now verify the article type, purity grade, hallmarking date,

facts.text: Over 77 lakh (7.7 million) silver items had a HUID by Aug 2026; over 90 lakh by Oct 2026.

rows.meaning: Word struck on a non-gold part of a hallmarked gold item.
rows.technique: struck
rows.where_on_object: On the non-gold part (e.g. a base-metal pin or screw)
rows.date_note: In BIS's early AHC recognition criteria (page archived 2015); not found in IS 1417 or IS 15820, so its later use is unconfirmed.
rows.what_it_tells: That part is not gold and is excluded from the purity guarantee.
rows.cautions: Single source; not seen on an example.

facts.text: Early BIS AHC criteria: an article with a part made of another metal is additionally marked 'METAL' on that part.
facts.quote: will be additionally marked with the word 'METAL' on the metal part of the article/ ornament.

rows.meaning: Additional mark on hollow gold items filled with lac, cement or other filler: the word FILLED (early criteria) or the declared weight of gold (IS 15820, IS 1417).
rows.technique: struck or lasered
rows.date_note: 'FILLED' in the early criteria; declared-weight marking in IS 1417 Amendment 2 (Dec 2007), IS 15820:2009 and IS 1417:2016.
rows.what_it_tells: The item is lac- or cement-filled; its gold content is only the declared weight, not the gross weight.
rows.cautions: Lac-filled Indian bangles and pendants are common; most older ones carry no such mark.

facts.text: Early BIS AHC criteria: hollow items filled with cement, lac or other non-metallic substance are additionally marked 'FILLED'.
facts.quote: will be additionally marked with the word 'FILLED'.

facts.text: IS 15820:2009 instead requires such items to be marked with the gold or silver weight declared by the jeweler; IS 1417 (Amendment 2, 2007, and 2016) bars hallmarking of filled items unless the gold weight is declared and marked.
facts.quote: will be add itionally marked with the weight of gold or silver (as applicable) as declared by the licensee jeweller.

rows.meaning: Hallmarking of Gold Jewellery and Gold Artefacts Order, 2020 and its amendments: which districts and grades must be sold hallmarked, and when.
rows.technique: n/a (legal rule)
rows.date_note: Order of 15 Jan 2020; mandatory in notified districts from 16 June 2021 (Order) / 23 June 2021 (BIS); 392 districts after 3 Aug 2026.
rows.what_it_tells: Gold jewelry sold new in a notified Indian district since mid-2021 should be hallmarked; earlier and exempt items (Kundan, Polki, Jadau, under 2 g, small jewelers, non-notified districts) often are not.
rows.cautions: Absence of a hallmark on Indian gold is normal for older items and exempt categories and says nothing about purity either way.

facts.text: S.O. 205(E), 15 Jan 2020 (Gazette Extraordinary No. 195): gold jewelry and artefacts to be sold hallmarked to IS 1417:2016 by registered jewelers; to come into force 15 Jan 2021; bullion and coin, articles under 2 g, gold thread etc. exempt.
facts.quote: It shall come into force with effect from the 15th day of January, 2021.

facts.text: S.O. 3513(E), 9 Oct 2020: start moved to 1 June 2021.
facts.quote: the words and figure “1st day of June” shall be substituted.

facts.text: S.O. 2102(E), 1 June 2021: start moved to 16 June 2021.
facts.quote: the words and figure “16th day of June” shall be substituted.

facts.text: S.O. 2481(E), 23 June 2021 (Second Amendment Order 2021): order applies only to 256 listed districts and to 14, 18 and 22 carat; new exemptions include Kundan, Polki and Jadau jewelry, watches and fountain pens, and jewelers with turnover up to Rs 40 lakh.
facts.quote: special categories of jewellery, namely Kundan, Polki and Jadaau;

facts.text: BIS and PIB date the first phase from 23 June 2021, although the Order's commencement date is 16 June 2021.
facts.quote: implemented with effect from 23 June 2021

facts.text: S.O. 1594(E), 4 April 2022, in force 1 June 2022: grade limit removed (20, 23 and 24 carat covered) and 32 districts added (288).
facts.quote: It shall come into force with effect from the 1 st day of June, 2022.

facts.text: S.O. 1047(E), 3 March 2023 (Gazette 6 March): HUID-only sale after 31 March 2023. S.O. 1555(E), 31 March 2023: declared old stock to 30 June 2023.
S.O. 3967(E), 6 Sept 2023 (Third Amendment 2023): 55 districts added (343). Press reports date it 8 Sept 2023.
facts.quote: The total number of districts covered under mandatory hallmarking is 343.

facts.text: S.O. 4814(E), 5 Nov 2024: 18 districts added (361).
S.O. 3549(E), 31 July 2025: 12 districts added (373).
S.O. 1129(E), 2 March 2026: 7 added (380); S.O. 2117(E), 28 April 2026: 5 added (385); S.O. 4345(E), 3 Aug 2026 (Gazette 6 Aug): 7 added (392).
Earlier, BIS proposed mandatory hallmarking from 1 Jan 2008 in its 2006 draft regulations; this did not happen.
facts.quote: hallmarking of gold jewellery is proposed to be brought under mandatory certification w.e.f. 1 January 2008.

rows.meaning: '916' (or 'KDM 916') stamped by a jeweler without the BIS logo and other hallmark components: a seller's purity claim for 22 carat, not a hallmark.
rows.technique: struck or engraved by the jeweler
rows.where_on_object: Clasp, inside of ring or bangle
rows.date_note: Widely used before and alongside BIS hallmarking; dates not established.
rows.fineness: Claims 916/1000 (22 carat); not independently confirmed
rows.what_it_tells: The seller claimed 22-carat gold.
rows.cautions: Not a guarantee. A UK dealer reports Indian '22kt' items commonly testing at 87-88%. Test before relying on it. Compare with a genuine BIS hallmark (logo + 916 or 22K916 + center/jeweler marks or HUID).

facts.text: Only BIS-recognized centers may apply the hallmark, and only to jewelry they have assayed.
facts.quote: shall be hallmarked by BIS recognized assaying and hallmarking centres only.

facts.text: A 'BIS 916 hallmark' is the 916 together with the BIS logo; trade guides tell buyers to look for the logo followed by 916.
facts.quote: look for a hallmark stamp that includes the BIS logo followed by the number 916.

facts.text: '916 KDM' is a trade phrase for 22-carat gold made with cadmium solder.
facts.quote: cadmium soldering , for example 916 (22 carat ) KDM Gold

facts.text: Before hallmarking, BIS described buyers told their gold was 22 carat finding on resale it was 18 carat, and serious under-carating from low-carat solder in 22-carat items.
facts.quote: A buyer, for instance, will be told that he has bought gold of 22 carats. When he goes to sell or exchange it he discovers that the gold is actually only of 18 carats

rows.meaning: Jeweler's own carat stamp (22ct, 22K, 22KT, 18ct...) on Indian gold, used before and outside BIS hallmarking.
rows.technique: struck or engraved by the jeweler
rows.where_on_object: Clasp, inside of ring or bangle
rows.date_note: Long-standing trade practice; no dated series.
rows.fineness: Claimed carat only
rows.what_it_tells: The maker or seller's claimed carat.
rows.cautions: Not a hallmark; test it. Gulf, Singapore and other Asian jewelry uses the same stamps.

facts.text: India had a 1978 standard, IS 8844 'Guidelines for marking purity of gold on gold articles/ornaments', which was folded into IS 1417:1999 and withdrawn.
facts.quote: provisions of IS 8844 : 1978 'Guidelines for marking purity of gold on gold articles/ornaments' have been incorporated after suitable modifications.

facts.text: A UK dealer: Indian and Asian jewelry marked '22kt' often tests at 87-88% gold, about 21 carat, because of lower-carat solder or deliberate short-carating.
facts.quote: It is common to see Indian (and Asian) jewellery marked as '22kt', but when tested may only be between 87% to 88% pure

facts.text: BIS: the many soldered joints of traditional 22-carat items and low-carat solders caused serious under-carating; 24-carat plating over low-carat articles is also common.
facts.quote: In addition, 24 carat plating of articles of low caratage is also common.

rows.meaning: Trade term for gold jewelry made with cadmium-alloy solder (often '916 KDM'); not a hallmark or a purity grade.
rows.technique: struck or engraved by the jeweler
rows.date_note: Trade usage, dates not established.
rows.what_it_tells: The seller claimed cadmium-soldered (and implicitly full-carat) work.
rows.cautions: Says nothing verifiable about purity; cadmium solder is now restricted under BIS standards. Meaning rests on weak sources.

facts.text: KDM refers to cadmium soldering, as in '916 (22 carat) KDM Gold'.
facts.quote: cadmium soldering , for example 916 (22 carat ) KDM Gold

facts.text: A 2026 trade guide lists KDM among older gold terms superseded by hallmarking.
facts.quote: You may have heard terms like 916 gold , 750 gold , or even KDM gold

facts.text: BIS standards restrict cadmium: IS 1417:1999 required solders free from cadmium; IS 1417:2016 caps cadmium at 0.02% in jewelry alloys and solders.
facts.quote: The maximum permissible limits of Cadmium and each of Platinum group metals in gold alloys for manufacturing jewellery/artefacts and gold solders are 0.02 percent

rows.meaning: Tola (Hindi तोला, tolā): traditional South Asian unit of weight for gold and silver (180 grains, 11.66 g from 1833); a weight, not a purity mark.
rows.technique: struck on bars
rows.date_note: Standardised 1833; superseded by metric 1956 (Standards of Weights and Measures Act); bar use continues.
rows.what_it_tells: A bar or item marked in tolas states its weight (1 tola = 11.66 g).
rows.cautions: Not a fineness or a hallmark; a '10 TOLA' bar is not BIS-hallmarked unless it also bears the BIS logo and fineness.

facts.text: Regulation VII of 1833 fixed the tola at 180 troy grains (11.6638 g); it was the British Indian base unit and the standard measure for gold and silver bullion.
facts.quote: now standardised as 180 grains ( 11.6638038 grams ) or exactly 3 ⁄ 8 troy ounce

facts.text: Officially replaced by metric units from 1956 but still used for gold bars (ten-tola bars) in South Asia and the Gulf.

rows.meaning: Touch: the touchstone test of gold or silver purity by streak color, the traditional Indian bazaar method; a test, not a mark.
rows.technique: n/a
rows.date_note: Traditional; still used.
rows.what_it_tells: A 'touch' figure quoted on a bill or by a jeweler is a touchstone estimate, not an assay.
rows.cautions: Use of 'touch' or 'tunch' as a numeric purity term in the bazaar is not documented in the sources read.

facts.text: BIS's 1999-era control tables name touchstone or XRF as the non-destructive method for checking homogeneity, with fire assay (IS 1418) for the purity result.
facts.quote: By non-destructive method (touch stone or XRF)

facts.text: A 2026 trade guide still offers a touchstone test as a way to check purity without damage.
facts.quote: ask for a Touchstone test at a BIS-certified jeweller

rows.meaning: Fake, copied or misapplied BIS hallmarks and HUIDs: what BIS says about misuse and how to check.
rows.technique: any
rows.where_on_object: Where a genuine hallmark would be
rows.date_note: Throughout the scheme.
rows.what_it_tells: Warning signs: BIS logo without purity mark; purity number without logo; old-style four- or five-mark hallmark presented as new after 1 April 2023; a HUID that does not verify or verifies to a different article or purity.
rows.cautions: Specific BIS/PIB reports of seized fake hallmarks or forged HUIDs were not retrieved.

facts.text: BIS: the pre-2021 hallmark (logo, purity, center and jeweler marks identical on every item) was 'prone to be misused', which is why HUID was introduced.
facts.quote: This system was prone to be misused;

facts.text: Misuse of the Standard Mark including the Hallmark is punishable under section 29 of the BIS Act 2016: up to one year and a fine of at least Rs 1 lakh (s. 29(2)), or up to two years and at least Rs 2 lakh (s. 29(3)).
A buyer of hallmarked jewelry found below the marked purity is entitled to twice the value of the shortfall plus testing charges (Rule 49, BIS Rules 2018).
facts.quote: the buyer/customer shall be entitled for compensation which shall be two times the amount of difference

facts.text: Anyone can have hallmarked jewelry fire-assayed at a BIS-recognized center (Rs 200), and from 1 Jan 2022 can have unhallmarked jewelry tested there.

rows.meaning: Country-of-origin stamp: the item was made in India and marked for export.
rows.technique: struck with a punch or die-stamped on metal; stamped in ink, painted, or a printed paper or foil label on wood, papier-mâché and stone
rows.where_on_object: underside or base; on trays near the rim on the back; on boxes under the base or inside the lid
rows.date_note: Earliest likely use on goods for the US market is 1 March 1891 (US Tariff Act of 1890, sec. 6). Used throughout the 20th century and still used. Items made before August 1947 in what became Pakistan or Bangladesh were also marked INDIA.
rows.what_it_tells: The item was made for export, very probably after 1891 if it was meant for the US. On its own the word gives no latest date: INDIA was used before and after independence.
rows.cautions: Popular rule 'INDIA alone = before 1914 (or 1921); MADE IN INDIA = later' is not supported by the statute texts (see 'made-in-india'). Absence of a mark does not mean pre-1891: goods for Britain needed no mark. A stamp can be added later by an importer or dealer.

facts.text: From 1 March 1891 the US required foreign-made goods of a kind usually marked to show the country of origin in legible English words.
facts.quote: on and after the first day of March, eighteen hundred and ninety-one, all articles of foreign manufacture ... shall ... be plainly marked, stamped, branded, or labeled in legible English words, so as to indicate the country of their origin

facts.text: A bare country name met the rule; no US statute required the words 'Made in'.
Britain did not require a country-of-origin mark on imported goods unless they bore British-looking names or fell under a later Order in Council.
Collector guides for other countries' wares use the same rule of thumb: a plain country name (ENGLAND, CHINA) appears after 1891.
facts.quote: With very few exceptions 'ENGLAND' was not used until 1891.

rows.meaning: Country-of-origin stamp with the 'Made in' prefix.
rows.technique: struck, die-stamped, ink-stamped, painted, printed label, sewn fabric label on textiles
rows.where_on_object: underside or base; textile labels sewn at a corner or on the back
rows.date_note: No law fixes a start date for the 'Made in' wording. Collector books give 1914, 1915, 1919 or 1921 as the date it became 'required'; the statute texts checked (1890, 1913, 1930/1938) require only the country name in English.
rows.what_it_tells: Made for export. The wording suggests 20th-century use and is very common on mid- to late-20th-century export brass and handicrafts, but by itself it does not date an item more closely than 'after 1891'.
rows.cautions: Folklore vs primary rule: the 1914/1915/1919/1921 'Made in' dates are collectors' generalizations from European and East Asian ceramics, not a statute. The 1921 date belongs to the US customs decision that 'Nippon' was not acceptable for Japan, not to 'Made in'. 'Made in' is required today only when another place name appears on the item (19 CFR 134.46).

facts.text: The McKinley Act (1890) and the 1913 and current statutes require only the country of origin in English; none prescribes 'Made in'.
A collector reference states the 'Made in' prefix was never required by US import regulations or the McKinley Act.
facts.quote: the "Made in" prefix was never a requirement of US import regulations or the McKinley Tariff Act itself.

facts.text: Collector dating rules disagree: thepotteries.org says 'Made in England' was generally introduced in 1914 but not because the law specified the phrase; Gotheborg says 'Made in' was required from 1919; Kovels says it was usually used after 1915.
facts.quote: Not strictly in the sense that the law specified the exact phrase 'Made in ...'.

facts.text: The often-quoted 1921 date comes from the US decision that 'Nippon' had to become 'Japan'; it concerns the English name of the country, not the 'Made in' prefix.
facts.quote: In the year 1921 the USA however decided that Nippon had to be changed into the more commonly known term of Japan

facts.text: Under current US rules, 'Made in' or 'Product of' is required only where a US place or a foreign place other than the country of origin also appears.
The 'Made in [country]' wording has British roots: under the 1887 Merchandise Marks Act a place name alone did not comply and a statement such as 'manufactured in Germany' was advised.
facts.quote: a definite statement should be added

rows.meaning: Country-of-origin stamp or label that also claims the item was made by hand.
rows.technique: ink stamp, printed label or sticker, sewn label
rows.where_on_object: base or underside; label on the back of a rug or the corner of a textile
rows.date_note: No source dates this wording. It contains the country name, so it meets the US rule; 'hand made' is a trade claim, not a legal requirement.
rows.what_it_tells: Made in India for export; the 'hand made' claim is the seller's description and is not certified by any government mark found for the 1880s-1990s.
rows.cautions: Not a guarantee of handwork or of age; the same wording is used on current production. No primary source on when this wording came into use was found.

facts.text: Any wording that includes the English name of the country (here INDIA) meets the US marking rule; additional words are not regulated by it.
Under the 1889 Indian Merchandise Marks Act a 'trade description' covers statements about where goods were made; a false origin claim was an offence in British India.

rows.meaning: Origin stamp naming British India, the British-ruled provinces before independence.
rows.technique: ink stamp, struck mark or printed label
rows.date_note: British India ceased on 15 August 1947, when the Dominions of India and Pakistan were set up. The wording therefore points to a mark applied before that date.
rows.what_it_tells: If original to the item, a mark applied before 15 August 1947.
rows.cautions: No museum or primary record of this exact stamp on craft goods was found, so how common it was is unknown. Princely states (Kashmir, Jaipur, Mysore, Hyderabad and others) were not part of British India; their goods were usually just marked INDIA or with a place name. Do not confuse with stamps, coins or postal items marked 'BRITISH INDIA'.

facts.text: The Indian Independence Act 1947 set up two independent Dominions, India and Pakistan, from 15 August 1947.
facts.quote: As from the fifteenth day of August, nineteen hundred and forty-seven, two independent Dominions shall be set up in India

facts.text: The 1889 Merchandise Marks Act and the Sea Customs Act 1878 governed goods brought into 'British India'.

rows.meaning: Place stamp or label naming Benares (Varanasi), a center of engraved and enamelled brass and copper, silk and toys.
rows.technique: struck, ink-stamped or label
rows.where_on_object: base or underside; trays on the back
rows.date_note: The city's official name became Varanasi on 24 May 1956, but 'Benares/Banaras' stayed in everyday and trade use, so the spelling does not prove a pre-1956 date.
rows.what_it_tells: Names the city (or the 'Benares' style) and suggests the English-language export or tourist trade. Without INDIA beside it, the item may not have been marked for US entry.
rows.cautions: 'Benares brass' is used loosely for engraved Indian brass in general; items made at Moradabad and elsewhere were sold in Benares. A place name is not a country name for US customs, so 'BENARES' alone is not an origin mark in the legal sense.

facts.text: Kashi/Banaras was officially renamed Varanasi on 24 May 1956, as recorded in the 1965 Varanasi district gazetteer, p. 10.
facts.quote: The 'city of lights' which is known as Kashi or Banaras got renamed on 24 May, 1956 as Varanasi.

facts.text: A brass tray in the Horniman Museum carries a paper label naming its maker as Baldev Das, brass merchant, Benares, and showing it was exhibited in the North West Provinces and Oudh section of an exhibition.
A tray attributed to Moradabad (about 1880) in the Gardner Museum was probably bought at a hotel in Varanasi (Benares) on 5 March 1884: the place of sale is not the place of making.
US rules require the English name of the country; a city name alone does not meet it.

rows.meaning: Place name plus country: names the craft town and meets the country-of-origin rule.
rows.technique: struck, ink-stamped, painted or label
rows.date_note: No source dates any particular town stamp. The only date limits come from the country name (after 1891 for US export) and from place renamings (e.g. Benares to Varanasi 1956; Mysore State to Karnataka 1973 [not confirmed here]).
rows.what_it_tells: Where the seller said the item was made, plus export to a country requiring origin marks.
rows.cautions: A town name marks where the item was sold or finished as often as where it was made. No published catalogue of Moradabad, Jaipur or Agra export stamps was found.

facts.text: The country name INDIA in the mark meets the US rule; the additional town name is not required or regulated by it.
Place of purchase and place of making differ: a Moradabad tray of about 1880 was bought in Benares in 1884.

rows.meaning: Place mark or label naming Kashmir, usually painted or labelled on papier-mâché, carved walnut and textiles.
rows.technique: painted by hand, printed label, ink stamp
rows.where_on_object: base or underside, often painted in the ground color with the seller's name
rows.date_note: No source dates KASHMIR marks as a group. A museum example spelled 'Kashmere. India' on an old exhibition label was collected by F. J. Horniman in Calcutta; the record gives no year.
rows.what_it_tells: Names the region of making. 'Kashmere' and similar older spellings appear on 19th-century labels.
rows.cautions: Kashmir is not a country name, so for US entry the item would also need INDIA (or PAKISTAN after 1947). Kashmir was a princely state before 1947, outside British India. Painted 'KASHMIR' marks are easily added later and are still used today.

facts.text: A papier-mâché box in the Horniman Museum has an old exhibition label reading 'Papier mache on wood. Box. Kashmere. India', and was almost certainly collected by F. J. Horniman in Calcutta.
facts.quote: Papier mache on wood. Box. Kashmere. India

facts.text: US marking rules call for the English name of the country of origin; a region name alone does not meet it.

rows.meaning: Country-of-origin stamp for Pakistan.
rows.technique: struck, ink-stamped, label, sewn label
rows.date_note: Pakistan came into being in August 1947 (the Indian Independence Act sets 15 August). Until 1971 it included East Pakistan (now Bangladesh).
rows.what_it_tells: Made in Pakistan after August 1947. Workshops in Lahore, Peshawar, Multan, Sialkot or Karachi marked the same kinds of goods INDIA before partition.
rows.cautions: Between 1947 and 1971 'PAKISTAN' can also mean the eastern wing (Dhaka); see 'east-pakistan'.

facts.text: The Indian Independence Act 1947 set up the Dominions of India and Pakistan from 15 August 1947.
facts.quote: As from the fifteenth day of August, nineteen hundred and forty-seven, two independent Dominions shall be set up in India

rows.meaning: Origin stamp for the eastern wing of Pakistan, now Bangladesh.
rows.technique: ink stamp, label
rows.date_note: East Bengal was renamed East Pakistan under the One Unit reorganization; sources give 14 October 1955 or the 1956 constitution. The name ended with Bangladesh's independence in 1971 (declared 26 March, war ended 16 December).
rows.what_it_tells: A tight window: about 1955/56 to 1971.
rows.cautions: From 1947 to 1955/56 goods from the same region were marked PAKISTAN; after 1971 BANGLADESH. The exact renaming date is disputed between 1955 and 1956.

facts.text: East Bengal was renamed East Pakistan in the mid-1950s; a 1956 constitution followed.
facts.quote: Under Mirza, East Bengal was renamed East Pakistan

facts.text: Bangladesh declared independence on 26 March 1971; Pakistani forces surrendered in Dhaka on 16 December 1971.
facts.quote: The independence of Bangladesh was declared on 26 March 1971

rows.meaning: Country-of-origin stamp for Bangladesh.
rows.technique: ink stamp, label, sewn label
rows.where_on_object: base, label, or sewn textile label
rows.date_note: Independence declared 26 March 1971; victory 16 December 1971. In practice export marks from 1972 on.
rows.what_it_tells: Made in Bangladesh after 1971.
rows.cautions: Earlier goods from the same region read INDIA (before 1947), PAKISTAN (1947-1955/56) or EAST PAKISTAN (1955/56-1971).

facts.text: Bangladesh declared independence on 26 March 1971; Pakistani forces surrendered on 16 December 1971.
facts.quote: The independence of Bangladesh was declared on 26 March 1971

rows.meaning: Country-of-origin stamp for Ceylon (Sri Lanka before 1972).
rows.technique: struck, ink stamp, label
rows.date_note: Ceylon became the Republic of Sri Lanka on 22 May 1972. Country marks on US-bound goods date from 1891.
rows.what_it_tells: As a country-of-origin mark, made before about mid-1972.
rows.cautions: 'Ceylon' survives as a trade name (Ceylon tea, Ceylon sapphire, Ceylon cinnamon) after 1972, so on tea and gem packaging it does not date the item. Allow for old stock and molds used after 1972.

facts.text: Ceylon became a republic within the Commonwealth under the name Sri Lanka, with effect from 22 May 1972.
facts.quote: An Act to make provision in connection with Ceylon becoming a republic within the Commonwealth under the name of Sri Lanka.

rows.meaning: Country-of-origin stamp for Sri Lanka.
rows.technique: struck, ink stamp, label
rows.date_note: From 22 May 1972.
rows.what_it_tells: Made after May 1972.
rows.cautions: A Laksala or other label reading 'Ceylon' can still be found on stock sold after 1972; check both.

facts.text: Ceylon was renamed Sri Lanka on becoming a republic on 22 May 1972.

rows.meaning: Country-of-origin stamp for Burma.
rows.technique: struck, ink stamp, label
rows.date_note: The military government changed the English name to Myanmar on 18 June 1989. The US government still officially uses 'Burma', so the name alone is a weaker date limit than CEYLON.
rows.what_it_tells: Usually made before mid-1989.
rows.cautions: Because the US government continued to use 'Burma', the name may have stayed on some US-bound goods after 1989 (no customs ruling found; see gaps). Older Burmese goods may carry no country mark at all. Burmese export silver is often confused with Indian.

facts.text: In 1989, a year after crushing a pro-democracy uprising, the military changed the country's English name from Burma to Myanmar.
facts.quote: But in 1989, one year after the ruling junta brutally suppressed a pro-democracy uprising, military leaders suddenly changed its name to Myanmar

facts.text: The United Nations records 18 June 1989 as the date the Union of Burma notified its new name, Union of Myanmar.
Unlike most of the world, the US government still officially uses 'Burma'.
facts.quote: Unlike most of the world, the U.S. government still officially uses 'Burma.'

rows.meaning: Country-of-origin stamp for Myanmar.
rows.technique: struck, ink stamp, label
rows.date_note: From 18 June 1989.
rows.what_it_tells: Made after mid-1989.
rows.cautions: See 'burma': both names can appear on goods after 1989.

facts.text: The English name changed from Burma to Myanmar in June 1989.

rows.meaning: British origin indication allowed by the Merchandise Marks Act 1926 for goods made in the British Empire (which then included India, Burma and Ceylon), in place of the country name.
wares: goods of classes named in Orders in Council (from late 1927)
rows.technique: stamp, label or printed mark
rows.where_on_object: on the item or its packaging, as the Order specified
rows.date_note: Orders under s.2 of the 1926 Act began in late 1927-1928 and were kept for three years after the Trade Descriptions Act 1968 took effect. The 'Empire' option still existed in 1959.
rows.what_it_tells: Made for the British market, roughly 1927 to the early 1970s, somewhere in the Empire/Commonwealth; it does not say which country.
rows.cautions: No example of an Indian craft item marked 'EMPIRE' was found, so this row records a legal possibility, not an observed Indian stamp. 'Empire Made' was also used on British goods.

facts.text: The 1926 Act allowed the indication of origin to be the country of manufacture, or 'Empire' or 'Foreign'.
facts.quote: the present option of marking "Empire" or "Foreign"

facts.text: By 1929, six Orders in Council under the Act covered 36 classes of goods.

variants: Central Cottage Industries Emporium, Janpath, New Delhi
Central Cottage Industries Corporation of India Ltd
rows.meaning: Label of the Government of India's flagship handicrafts store in New Delhi (Janpath).

maker.name: Central Cottage Industries Emporium (government; managed by the Indian Cooperative Union from 1952; Central Cottage Industries Association from 1964; Central Cottage Industries Corporation of India Ltd from 1976)

wares: all-India handicrafts: brass, papier-mâché, carving, textiles, toys, jewelry
rows.technique: printed paper label, sticker, swing tag or price ticket (label wording not seen in sources; recorded here as the organization's name)
rows.date_note: Founding is disputed: 1948 (created by the Ministry of Commerce and Industry; Wikipedia, Maharam) vs 1952 (Ministry of Textiles: 'established in the year 1952 under the management of Indian Cooperative Union'). 1952 is the year the Indian Cooperative Union took over management and merged Refugee Handicrafts into it. Corporation incorporated 1976 (third-party registry source).
rows.what_it_tells: Bought from the government emporium in Delhi, so made in India after about 1948 and sold as a government-vetted handicraft. A label naming the 'Corporation' suggests 1976 or later.
rows.cautions: An emporium label shows where an item was sold, not who made it or exactly when. Labels can move between items.

facts.text: The Ministry of Textiles says the emporium was established in 1952 under the management of the Indian Cooperative Union and taken over by the Central Cottage Industries Association in 1964.
facts.quote: Central Cottage Industries Emporium was established in the year 1952 under the management of Indian Cooperative Union and was later on taken over by Central Cottage Industries Association in 1964

facts.text: Other accounts say the Government's Ministry of Commerce and Industry created the emporium in Delhi in 1948, and the Indian Cooperative Union took over its management in 1952.
The Central Cottage Industries Corporation of India Ltd was incorporated on 4 February 1976.

forms: Central Cottage Industries Emporium, Janpath, New Delhi
Central Cottage Industries Corporation of India Ltd
Central Cottage Industries Corporation of India

rows.meaning: Government of India board (1952) that promoted crafts, design centers and emporia. No label of its own on goods was found.

maker.name: All India Handicrafts Board (Ministry of Commerce and Industry; later Ministry of Textiles)

rows.technique: none recorded
rows.date_note: Set up by Government resolution dated 5 November 1952, replacing the All-India Cottage Industries Board (constituted January 1952). Abolished 2020 (Wikipedia; not confirmed).
rows.what_it_tells: Background only: a reference to the Board on a label or certificate would date it to 1952 or later.
rows.cautions: No goods label, stamp or certificate issued by the Board was found; do not assume one exists.

facts.text: The All India Handicrafts Board was set up by Government resolution in November 1952 (resolution of 5 November 1952), with Kamaladevi Chattopadhyay as chair.
facts.quote: set up by Government Resolution in November, 1952

rows.mark_text: Handicrafts and Handlooms Exports Corporation of India
rows.plain: Handicrafts and Handlooms Export Corporation of India
variants: The Handicrafts & Handlooms Exports Corporation of India Ltd
rows.meaning: Label of the government export corporation for handicrafts and handlooms (also ran retail shops).

maker.name: Handicrafts and Handlooms Exports Corporation of India Ltd

rows.technique: printed paper label, sticker, swing tag or price ticket (label wording not seen in sources; recorded here as the organization's name)
rows.date_note: Incorporated 1 June 1962 as a wholly owned subsidiary of the State Trading Corporation, merging STC's Handlooms Export Organisation (set up January 1959) and the Indian Handicrafts Development Corporation. Wikipedia's 1958 date is not supported by the audit text. Closure approved 17 March 2021 (Wikipedia; not confirmed).
rows.what_it_tells: An HHEC label points to export or sale through the corporation from 1962 on.
rows.cautions: 1958 is widely repeated online as HHEC's founding year; the CAG and Ministry of Textiles give 1962. Earlier labels may name the predecessor bodies.

facts.text: HHEC was incorporated on 1 June 1962 as a wholly owned subsidiary of the State Trading Corporation, after a November 1961 decision to merge STC's Handlooms Export Organisation with the Indian Handicrafts Development Corporation.
facts.quote: incorporated on 1st June, 1962 as a wholly-owned subsidiary of the State Trading Corporation of India

facts.text: The Handlooms Export Organisation was set up in January 1959 as a department of the State Trading Corporation.

forms: Handicrafts and Handlooms Exports Corporation of India
The Handicrafts & Handlooms Exports Corporation of India Ltd
The Handicrafts & Handlooms Exports Corporation of India

rows.meaning: Label of the Jammu and Kashmir state government's crafts emporium, Residency Road, Srinagar (with branches elsewhere).

maker.name: Kashmir Government Arts Emporium (Department of Handicrafts & Handloom, Government of Jammu & Kashmir)
maker.place: Residency Road, Srinagar (former British Residency); branches in Delhi and Bombay

rows.technique: printed paper label, sticker, swing tag or price ticket (label wording not seen in sources; recorded here as the organization's name)
rows.date_note: 1948: Sheikh Muhammad Abdullah's government turned the former Resident's house into the Government Arts Emporium. Both sources are secondary.
rows.what_it_tells: Sold through the J&K government emporium, so 1948 or later; a common label on Kashmir papier-mâché and walnut bought by visitors.
rows.cautions: Private shops also use 'Arts Emporium' in their names (for example 'Shah Kashmir Arts Emporium'); only 'Government' identifies the state store. The label dates the sale, not the making.

facts.text: In 1948 Sheikh Muhammad Abdullah's government converted the old British Resident's house in Srinagar into the Government Arts Emporium, and set up branches in Delhi and Bombay.
facts.quote: Established in 1948, the Kashmir Government Arts Emporium stands as one of the oldest and most prestigious platforms

rows.meaning: Label of the Rajasthan state government handicrafts emporium chain (Jaipur, Delhi and other cities).

maker.name: Rajasthan Small Industries Corporation Ltd (RAJSICO)
maker.place: Jaipur (M.I. Road); outlets in Delhi and other cities

rows.technique: printed paper label, sticker, swing tag or price ticket (label wording not seen in sources; recorded here as the organization's name)
rows.date_note: RAJSICO incorporated 3 June 1961. When the 'Rajasthali' name was first used was not found; one aggregator ties Rajasthali to a different body founded 1974 (unverified).
rows.what_it_tells: Sold through the Rajasthan government emporium, after 1961.
rows.cautions: The start year of the Rajasthali brand itself is not established; do not date a label to 1961 on that basis alone.

facts.text: The Rajasthan Small Industries Corporation was incorporated on 3 June 1961 as a Rajasthan state government company.
Rajasthali is RAJSICO's (the Rajasthan government's) handicrafts emporium brand.

other_spellings: Gujarat State Handloom and Handicrafts Development Corporation
rows.meaning: Label of the Gujarat state government emporium chain.

maker.name: Gujarat State Handloom and Handicrafts Development Corporation Ltd
maker.place: Ahmedabad / Gandhinagar; outlets in other cities

rows.technique: printed paper label, sticker, swing tag or price ticket (label wording not seen in sources; recorded here as the organization's name)
rows.date_note: Corporation incorporated 10 August 1973. Start year of the Gurjari / Garvi Gurjari name not found.
rows.what_it_tells: Sold through the Gujarat government emporium, after 1973.
rows.cautions: Label dates the sale, not the making; Kutch embroidery sold there may be older material.

facts.text: The Gujarat State Handloom and Handicrafts Development Corporation was incorporated on 10 August 1973 and sells through the Garvi-Gurjari emporia.

variants: Poompuhar, Tamil Nadu Handicrafts Development Corporation
rows.meaning: Label of the Tamil Nadu state government handicrafts showrooms.

maker.name: Tamil Nadu Handicrafts Development Corporation Ltd
maker.place: Chennai; showrooms in Bangalore, New Delhi, Kolkata and elsewhere

rows.technique: printed paper label, sticker, swing tag or price ticket (label wording not seen in sources; recorded here as the organization's name)
rows.where_on_object: base label, often on bronzes and wood
rows.date_note: Formed as a public limited company on 26 July 1973.
rows.what_it_tells: Sold through the Tamil Nadu government showrooms, after July 1973. Common on modern South Indian bronzes and brass lamps.
rows.cautions: A Poompuhar label on a bronze icon indicates modern (post-1973) retail sale, which is useful against claims of great age, but it does not date casting precisely.

facts.text: The Tamil Nadu Handicrafts Development Corporation (Poompuhar) was formed as a public limited company on 26 July 1973.
facts.quote: formed as a Public Limited Company on 26.07.1973

dates.title: Dates on Indian, Burmese and Ceylonese items: eras, digits, months and the Mughal rulers

eras.label: Vikram Samvat
eras.why_two: the Samvat year begins in March–April in the north and in October–November in Gujarat

as_written.note: abbreviation; also written before Śaka years in some places
Vikrama saṃvat; Ojha's own abbreviation throughout (e.g. वि. सं. १६१२)

as_written.script: Gujarati-language form in Devanagari or Gujarati letters (સંવત)
as_written.note: Gujarati script form સંવત follows the same spelling; no Gujarati-language source was read for it
Punjabi form; no source read (gap)

eras.where_used: Northern and western India (all of the north except Bengal), Gujarat and Kathiawar, Rajasthan (Rajputana), Jain and Hindu inscriptions and metal images; carried by Marwari and Gujarati migrants elsewhere.
eras.year_start: Luni-solar. Three new-year points are in use: Chaitra śukla 1 (March–April; north India), Kārttika śukla 1 (October–November; Gujarat), Āṣāḍha śukla 1 (June–July; parts of Kathiawar, Gujarat and Rajputana).

reckonings.name: Chaitrādi (northern)
reckonings.to_ce: CE = VS − 57 from Chaitra śukla 1 to 31 December; CE = VS − 56 from 1 January to the end of Phālguna.

reckonings.name: Kārttikādi (southern / Gujarati)
reckonings.year_start: Kārttika śukla 1, the day after Dīvālī (October–November)
reckonings.to_ce: CE = VS − 57 from Kārttika śukla 1 to 31 December; CE = VS − 56 from 1 January to the end of Āśvina (Dīvālī). A Kārttikādi year carries the same number as the Chaitrādi year from Kārttika to Phālguna, and one less from Chaitra to Āśvina.

reckonings.name: Āṣāḍhādi
reckonings.regions: parts of Kathiawar, Gujarat and Rajputana
reckonings.to_ce: CE = VS − 57 from Āṣāḍha śukla 1 to 31 December; CE = VS − 56 from 1 January to the end of Jyeṣṭha.

eras.used: c. A.D. 450 as 'Mālava' era; name 'Vikrama' from c. A.D. 840
eras.note: The usual era of north and west India except Bengal: Rajasthan, Gujarat and Kutch, and Hindu and Jain inscriptions and metal images. In the north its year begins in Chaitra (March–April), in Gujarat in Kārttika (October–November), so the month, where it is written, settles which Western year is meant.
eras.research_note: When only the year is legible, give both: CE (VS − 57) or (VS − 56). If a month is legible, apply the reckoning rows; for Gujarat assume Kārttikādi, for the north Chaitrādi. A further −1 is possible in the rare inscriptions that write the current (vartamāna) year.
eras.current_vs_expired: Normally expired (gata) years. Kielhorn found that out of 150 dated Vikrama inscriptions (A.D. 898–1877) only six had to be taken as current years; Ojha: inscriptions mostly write gata years, current years very rarely, and a current year is one higher. So a written VS year is almost always to be converted with −57/−56; allow −58/−57 only as an outside possibility.

facts.text: In the north the Vikrama year is Chaitrādi with pūrṇimānta months; in Gujarat it is Kārttikādi with amānta months; in some parts of Kathiawar and Gujarat it is Āṣāḍhādi.
facts.quote: In Northern India the year is Chaitradi, and its months purnimanta, but in Gujarat it is Karttikadi and its months are amanta.

facts.text: Subtract 57 or 56 from a Vikrama year to get the Christian year; subtract 135 to get the Śaka year.
facts.quote: इस संवत् में से ५७ या ५६ घटाने से ईसवी सन् और १३५ घटाने से शक संवत् आता है

facts.text: The northern (Chaitrādi) year begins seven months before the southern (Kārttikādi) year of the same number.
facts.quote: उत्तरी (चैत्रादि) विक्रम संवत् दक्षिणी (कार्तिकादि) विक्रम संवत् से ७ महीने पहिले प्रारंभ होता है

facts.text: Users of the Vikrama era normally quote expired years and only exceptionally the current year (Kielhorn, 150 dates, A.D. 898–1877).
facts.quote: It has been at all times the rule for those who use the Vikrama era to quote the expired years, and only exceptionally the current year.

facts.text: The word 'samvat' alone usually means a Vikrama year, but it has also been used for Śaka, Siṃha and Valabhī years.
facts.quote: the word "samvat" ... is used to denote the years of the Saka, Simha, or Valabhi eras indiscriminately.

facts.text: In some Madras/Mysore panchangs and Tamil solar panchangs the Vikrama year is shown as a solar Meṣādi year or as a current year.
facts.quote: there are extant solar panchangs of the Tamil country in which the year of the Vikrama era is represented as a solar Meshadi year.

eras.label: Śaka
eras.why_two: the Śaka year begins in March–April

as_written.note: locative 'in the Śaka [year]'; the usual Marathi form
e.g. शाके ११५७ quoted by Ojha from an inscription
name joined to the era from the 14th century
no Bengali source read; CLDR gives সাল for the Indian national calendar era

eras.where_used: All of India; almost exclusive in the Deccan and the south (except Tinnevelly and Malabar), Maharashtra (शके), Karnataka, Andhra; in the north alongside Vikrama in panchangs and horoscopes; the basis of the 1957 Indian national calendar.
eras.year_start: Chaitrādi (Chaitra śukla 1) for luni-solar reckoning; Meṣādi (sun entering Aries, about 13–14 April) for solar reckoning. Months pūrṇimānta in the north, amānta in the south.

reckonings.name: Luni-solar Chaitrādi
reckonings.regions: Maharashtra, Karnataka, Andhra; north India panchangs
reckonings.to_ce: CE = Śaka + 78 from Chaitra śukla 1 to 31 December; CE = Śaka + 79 from 1 January to the end of Phālguna.

reckonings.name: Solar Meṣādi
reckonings.to_ce: CE = Śaka + 78 from Meṣa saṅkrānti to 31 December; CE = Śaka + 79 from 1 January to Meṣa saṅkrānti.

reckonings.name: Indian national calendar (from 22 March 1957)
reckonings.year_start: 1 Chaitra = 22 March (21 March in Gregorian leap years)
reckonings.regions: Government of India gazettes, All India Radio, official calendars
reckonings.to_ce: CE = Śaka + 78 from 22 (21) March to 31 December; CE = Śaka + 79 from 1 January to 21 (20) March. Not a luni-solar date: month days are fixed to the Gregorian calendar.

eras.used: A.D. 78 epoch; widely used from early medieval inscriptions
eras.note: The era of the Deccan and the south and of Maharashtra (written शके), and of almanacs and horoscopes across India. Its year begins in March–April. Since 1957 India’s national calendar has counted its years the same way.
eras.research_note: When only the year is legible give both: Śaka + 78 or + 79. Ojha: add 78, but 79 in roughly the last three months of the Śaka year (January–March).
eras.current_vs_expired: Normally expired (gata) years. Some Tamil, Telugu and Kannada panchangs of the 1880s–90s print the current year (one higher), and Dikshit doubted the compilers knew the difference; an inscription is known where a current year was made 'doubly current'. So a written Śaka year is almost always + 78/79; allow + 77/78 as an outside possibility in South Indian printed almanacs.

facts.text: The Śaka era is used over the whole of India, exclusively in most of the south except Tinnevelly and part of Malabar; its years are Chaitrādi (luni-solar) and Meṣādi (solar), months pūrṇimānta in the north and amānta in the south; expired years are in use in most parts.
facts.quote: Its years are Chaitradi for luni-solar, and Meshadi for solar, reckoning. Its months are purnimanta in the North and amanta in Southern India.

facts.text: Adding 78 to an expired Śaka year (79 in roughly its last three months) gives the Christian year; adding 135 gives the expired Chaitrādi Vikrama year; adding 3179 gives the Kali year.
facts.quote: गत शक संवत् में ३१७९ जोड़ने से कलियुग संवत्, १३५ जोड़ने से गत चैत्रादि विक्रम संवत् और ७८ (अंत के करीब तीन महीनों में ७९) जोड़ने से ई. स. आता है

facts.text: The name of Śālivāhana is joined to the era in Sanskrit literature from about the 14th century; the earliest inscription with it is the Śaka 1276 grant of Bukka I of Vijayanagara.
Current (vartamāna) Śaka years are printed in some Tamil, Telugu and Kannada panchangs, but expired years are in general use.
facts.quote: Where the years are numbered, however, the expired year is in general use.

eras.label: Indian national calendar

as_written.note: CLDR era label for bn

eras.where_used: Government of India official use (Gazette of India, All India Radio, official calendars) alongside the Gregorian date, from 1957.
eras.year_start: 1 Chaitra = 22 March (21 March in a Gregorian leap year). Months: Chaitra 30 (31 in leap years), Vaiśākha–Bhādra 31 each, Āśvina–Phālguna 30 each.

reckonings.name: Fixed solar
reckonings.to_ce: CE = Śaka + 78 from 1 Chaitra to 31 December; + 79 from 1 January to the last day of Phālguna (20/21 March).

eras.note: India’s official calendar since 22 March 1957, used alongside the Western date; its years are Śaka years.
eras.research_note: Only from Śaka 1879 (A.D. 1957). A Śaka date on an item before 1957 is a traditional Śaka date (see shaka).
eras.current_vs_expired: Same numbering as the traditional expired Śaka year.

facts.text: A variant of the Śaka (Śālivāhana) calendar was standardized as the Indian national calendar in 1957; years are Śaka years; 1 Chaitra falls on 22 March, or 21 March in Gregorian leap years, when Chaitra has 31 days; Vaiśākha to Bhādra have 31 days, Āśvina to Phālguna 30.
facts.quote: In leap years, Chaitra has 31 days and starts on March 21 instead.

facts.text: Example: 9 June 2006 (Gregorian) = 19 Jyaiṣṭha 1928 Śaka.
facts.quote: 9th June 2006 by Gregorian Calendar, is same as 19th of Jyaistha in 1928 of Saka era.

facts.text: Month names of the national calendar in Indian scripts (Hindi चैत्र … फाल्गुन; Bengali চৈত্র … ফাল্গুন; etc.) are those of the traditional months.

eras.label: Hijri

as_written.note: written after a Hijri year, e.g. ۱۳۱۵ھ; contrasts with ء after a Christian year. Convention not found in a source read here (gap).
'year'; written before the year on coins and in inscriptions, also for regnal years (sanah … julūs)
modern Iranian abbreviation (CLDR fa); rare on Indian items
Ojha's abbreviation (e.g. हि. स. ९६३)

eras.where_used: Mughal and other Muslim courts of India, coins, Persian and Urdu inscriptions on metalwork, arms, jade, seals; Muslim religious and family items to the present.
eras.year_start: 1 Muḥarram; purely lunar year of 354 or 355 days; months begin with the first sighting of the crescent; the day begins at sunset.

reckonings.name: Tabular (arithmetical)
reckonings.regions: conversion tables (Wüstenfeld, Gumpach, Sewell & Dikshit Table XVI)
reckonings.to_ce: Epoch 1 Muḥarram AH 1 = Friday 16 July 622 (Julian). Leap years (355 days) are years 2, 5, 7, 10, 13, 16, 18, 21, 24, 26, 29 of each 30-year cycle (one school uses 8, 19, 27 in place of 7, 18, 26). Approximate start of AH year Y: CE ≈ 622.54 + 0.970224 × (Y − 1). An AH year almost always overlaps two CE years: give both. It falls entirely inside one CE year only when 1 Muḥarram falls within about the first 11 days of January (e.g. AH 1429 = 10 Jan – 28 Dec 2008, Gregorian).

reckonings.name: Observed (actual)
reckonings.to_ce: May differ from the tabular date by 1–2 days; month lengths vary with place.

eras.used: AH 1 = A.D. 622; first Indian examples on coins of Mahmud of Ghazni struck at Lahore, AH 418–419 (A.D. 1027–28)
eras.note: The Islamic lunar year, on Mughal and other Indian Muslim coins, Persian and Urdu inscriptions, arms, jade and seals. A Hijri year has 354 or 355 days, so it drifts through the Western year; the reader works it out by the calendar’s arithmetic, which can be a day or two from the dates kept by sighting the moon.
eras.research_note: No fixed difference: 33 Hijri years ≈ 32 Christian years. Use the tabular conversion and report the CE span of the AH year (e.g. AH 1315 = 2 June 1897 – 21 May 1898, so '1897 or 1898'). Before AH 1166 (1752) British tables give Julian (O.S.) dates; Sewell & Dikshit Table XVI is Old Style up to AH 1165.
eras.current_vs_expired: Current years (AH 1 began at the Hijra); no expired-year convention.

facts.text: The Hijra era dates from the flight of Muhammad: astronomically the evening of 15 July 622, in civil reckoning Friday 16 July 622.
facts.quote: according to the Hissabi or astronomical reckoning, on the evening of July 15th, A.D. 622. But in the Helali, or chronological reckoning, Friday, July 16th, is made the initial date.

facts.text: The year is purely lunar, 354 days, or 355 in the eleven leap years of each 30-year cycle; the leap-year lists differ between authorities (2,5,7,10,13,15/16,18,21,24,26,29 vs 2,5,8,10,13,16,19,21,24,27,29).
facts.quote: The years which have 355 days, instead of 354, are in some countries the 2nd, 5th, 7th, 10th, 13th, 15th, 18th, 21st, 24th, 26th and 29th.

facts.text: A Hijri year equals 0.970223 of a Gregorian year; 32 Gregorian years are about 33 Hijri years.
facts.quote: A year of the Hijra = 0.970223 of a Gregorian year ... Thus 32 Gregorian years are about equal to 33 years of the Hijra

facts.text: There is no fixed difference between the Hijri year and the Christian (or Vikrama) year; it must be computed.
facts.quote: ईसवी सन् (या विक्रम संवत्) और हिजरी सन् का कोई निश्चित अंतर नहीं रहता

facts.text: The Muslim day runs from sunset to sunset; Hindu almanacs enter the first day of a Muslim month against the following civil (sunrise) day; the start of a month can differ by a day between places.

Whitehead's accession dates for the Mughal emperors agree exactly (day and weekday) with the tabular calendar, Julian before 1752 and Gregorian after; Lane-Poole's table of Akbar's Ilāhī years differs from it by up to two days, as observed dates do.

eras.label: Mughal regnal year

as_written.note: 'accession, sitting (on the throne)'
'year … of the reign of tranquil prosperity'; the coin formula from Aurangzeb onward. Persian spelling given in its standard form; the sources read print it in Persian type that the OCR garbles.
'one': the first regnal year is usually written as this word, not a figure, on Mughal coins
Jahangir used 'Ilāhī' with the regnal year in the same way as julūs
Devanagari rendering seen in Hindi documents; no source read (gap)

eras.where_used: Mughal coins (from Jahangir onward, and Akbar's Ilāhī issues), farmans and seals, dated metalwork and arms of the imperial workshops; successor states and the East India Company kept Mughal regnal years on coins, often frozen.
eras.year_start: Year 1 begins at the emperor's accession (julūs). Akbar: solar Ilāhī years from Nauroz 1556 (see ilahi). Jahangir: solar years with Persian months, changing at Nauroz. Shah Jahan: solar (Ilāhī) on most coins from his 2nd year; see the ruler notes. From Aurangzeb: lunar Hijri years.

reckonings.name: Lunar julūs (Aurangzeb and later)
reckonings.year_start: anniversary of the accession in the Hijri calendar (Aurangzeb: 1 Ramazan from year 2)
reckonings.to_ce: RY n begins in AH (accession AH + n − 1) on the accession day/month; convert that Hijri date and the next to CE. Rough: CE ≈ accession CE + 0.97 × (n − 1).

reckonings.name: Solar regnal years (Jahangir; Shah Jahan's Ilāhī-type coins)
reckonings.to_ce: Jahangir: RY n (n ≥ 2) begins at Nauroz of CE 1605 + n; RY 1 runs from the accession (23 Oct 1605 O.S.) to the Nauroz at which RY 2 begins (see rulers).

eras.used: Jahangir (1605) on coins; Akbar's Ilāhī years from 1583/84 to 1858 (Bahadur Shah II); frozen regnal years continued on East India Company and state coins into the 19th century
eras.note: “San … julūs”: a year of the emperor’s reign, on Mughal coins from Jahangir on, and kept, often frozen, on the coins of successor states and the East India Company. It needs the emperor’s name, usually on the other face.
eras.research_note: Never convert a julūs year without knowing the ruler. With ruler known: compute from the ruler's accession (rulers table) and give the CE span of that regnal year, usually two CE years.
eras.current_vs_expired: Current: year 1 is the first year of the reign; the first year is often written as the word aḥad.

facts.text: The regnal year (jalus-san) follows the Hijri reckoning; the same tables convert it once the accession day of each sovereign is known; reigns are reckoned in lunar years.
facts.quote: The jalus-san (san-i jalus) necessarily follows the Hijra reckoning, and the same tables will answer for the solution of them when the accession day of each sovereign is known.

facts.text: Jahangir kept Akbar's solar reckoning and Persian months for the regnal year, using 'Ilāhī' like 'julūs'; Aurangzeb banished the solar years and Persian months, and thereafter the lunar reckoning was strictly used.
facts.quote: the solar years and Persian months were banished from the coinage and the exchequer by Aurangzib ... and thenceforward the lunar reckoning was strictly adhered to

facts.text: From Jahangir's reign the regnal year appears on coins; under Jahangir, Shah Jahan and Murad Bakhsh many coins carry the Ilāhī date and Persian month together with the Hijri year; from Aurangzeb the Hijri date is on the obverse and the regnal year on the reverse.
Discrepancies between the Hijri year and the regnal year on the same coin are not infrequent (old dies, careless mint-masters).
facts.quote: discrepancies between the Hijrah year and the regnal year are not infrequent.

facts.text: Hijri and regnal dates on Mughal coins are written in figures, except the first regnal year (usually the word aḥad) and the year 1000 (alf).
Aurangzeb's regnal years: year 1 from 1 Zu'l-qa'da 1068 (31 July 1658 N.S.); year 2 from 1 Ramazan 1069; every later year from 1 Ramazan.
facts.quote: the second and all succeeding years commenced on the first day of the month, in which the accession took place.

facts.text: Late Mughal regnal years were frozen on many East India Company and successor-state coins (e.g. Shah Alam II year 17, 26, 39, 46 or 49 kept unchanged while the Hijri year ran on), so a regnal year on such a coin does not date it.

eras.label: Ilāhī year
eras.why_two: the Ilāhī year begins at Nauroz in March
eras.where_used: Akbar's coins from about his 28th–30th regnal year, and coins and documents of Jahangir and (early) Shah Jahan, usually with a Persian month name; imperial documents and inscriptions.
eras.year_start: Solar year beginning at Nauroz (the sun's entry into Aries; Farwardīn 1), about 10–11 March Julian. Year 1 began 28 Rabīʿ II 963 = 11 March 1556 (O.S.), 25 days after Akbar's accession; the era was introduced later (A.H. 991–993 / A.D. 1583–85) and reckoned back to the accession year.

reckonings.name: Solar Ilāhī
reckonings.to_ce: CE = Ilāhī + 1555 from Nauroz (March) to 31 December; CE = Ilāhī + 1556 from 1 January to Nauroz. Example: Ilāhī 40 began 9 Rajab 1003 = March 1595 (Lane-Poole), so Ilāhī 40 = March 1595 – March 1596.

eras.used: introduced A.H. 991–993 (A.D. 1583–85), counted from 1556 to abandoned by Shah Jahan (on coins after his early years; Ojha: on his accession, 1628)
eras.note: Akbar’s solar “divine era”, counted from his accession in 1556 and written on his coins from about his thirtieth year, then on Jahangir’s and early Shah Jahan’s, usually with a Persian month. Its year begins at Nauroz in March.
eras.research_note: Give both when the month is not legible.
eras.current_vs_expired: Current (year 1 = the first year of Akbar's reign).

facts.text: The Tārīkh-i Ilāhī was established by Akbar and dates from his accession (Friday 2 Rabīʿ II 963 = 14 February 1556 O.S.); its days and months are natural solar, without intercalation, with ancient Persian month names; it fell into disuse early in Shah Jahan's reign.
facts.quote: It dates from his accession, which, according to the Tabakat-i-Akbari, was Friday the 2nd of Rabi-us-sani, A.H. 963, or 14th February, 1556 (O.S.)

facts.text: Its year 1 was taken to begin not on the accession day but 25 days later, on 28 Rabīʿ II 963 (11 March 1556), when the Iranian month Farwardīn began.
facts.quote: उससे २५ दिन पीछे तारीख २८ रबीउस्सानी हि. स. ९६३ (ई. स. १५५६ तारीख ११ मार्च …) से, जिस दिन कि ईरानियों के वर्ष का पहिला महीना फरवरदीन लगा, माना गया है

facts.text: Add 1555 or 1556 to an Ilāhī year to get the Christian year.
facts.quote: इलाही सन् + १५५५-५६ = ईसवी सन्

facts.text: Ilāhī months had 29 to 32 days; months with 32 days named the last two days rūz o shab ('day and night').

The year the era was introduced is reported differently: A.H. 992 / A.D. 1584 in Akbar's 29th year (Ojha) or 30th year (Prinsep, after Abu'l-Fazl); Lane-Poole infers from a rupee of Ilāhī year 28 that the change came at the end of the 28th solar year (A.H. 991, beginning 11 March 1583).

eras.label: Faslī (northern)
eras.why_two: the northern Faslī year begins in September–October

as_written.note: standard spelling; not seen in a source read here

eras.where_used: Revenue and land records, government documents, some dated items: northern Fasli in Bihar, Bengal, U.P. (N.W. Provinces) and the Punjab; Deccan Fasli in the Bombay Deccan and Maratha lands; Madras Fasli in the Madras Presidency (revenue year); the Nizam's Hyderabad also used a Fasli year (details not established here).
eras.year_start: Different in each region (see reckonings). All Fasli years share the number of the Hijri year at the time of their creation and have since been kept as solar or luni-solar years.

reckonings.name: Northern (Bengal, Bihar, U.P., Punjab)
reckonings.year_start: Āśvina kṛṣṇa 1 (pūrṇimānta), about September; luni-solar, days counted 1–30 through the month without fortnights
reckonings.to_ce: CE = Fasli + 592 from the Āśvina new year (Sept.–Oct.) to 31 December; CE = Fasli + 593 from 1 January to the next Āśvina.

reckonings.name: Deccan (Bombay, Maratha)
reckonings.year_start: sun's entry into the nakṣatra Mṛgaśiras, about 5–7 June
reckonings.to_ce: CE = Fasli + 590 from early June to 31 December; CE = Fasli + 591 from 1 January to early June.

reckonings.name: Madras
reckonings.year_start: originally solar Āḍi 1 (Karka saṅkrānti, mid-July); fixed at 13 July about 1800 (12 July in Prinsep); fixed at 1 July from 1855
reckonings.to_ce: CE = Fasli + 590 from 1 July (13 July before 1855) to 31 December; CE = Fasli + 591 from 1 January to 30 June (12 July).

eras.used: Akbar (north, from the A.H. 963/971 years); Shah Jahan (Deccan, from A.H. 1046 / A.D. 1636–38) to 20th-century revenue use (Madras Fasli still cited in Tamil Nadu revenue records)
eras.note: Akbar’s revenue year, in land and tax records and some dated items. The northern count (Bengal, Bihar, the United Provinces, the Punjab) begins in September–October; the Deccan and Madras counts run about two years behind it.
eras.research_note: Northern figures. For a Deccan or Madras Fasli date use + 590 / + 591. If the region is unknown, the candidates span + 590 to + 593: say so. The southern Fasli runs about two and a quarter years ahead of the northern.
eras.current_vs_expired: Current years.

facts.text: The Fasli year is the harvest year introduced (as some say) by Akbar, derived from the Hijri year and bearing its number, but beginning in July; it diverged by region.
facts.quote: This is the harvest year introduced, as some say, by Akbar, originally derived from the Muhammadan year, and bearing the same number, but beginning in July.

facts.text: Northern Fasli: add 592–593; southern (Deccan) Fasli: add 590–591.
facts.quote: उत्तरी फसली सन् + ५९२-९३ = ईसवी सन् … दक्षिणी फसली सन् + ५९०-९१ = ईसवी सन्

facts.text: Prinsep: add 592 to the northern Fasli and Vilāyatī years if less than four of their months have passed, 593 if more.
facts.quote: The number 592 must be added to convert the two first eras into Christian account, if less than four of their months have transpired, and 593 years, if more

facts.text: In Madras the Fasli year began on solar Āḍi 1; about 1800 the British fixed it at 13 July, and in 1855 at 1 July. In parts of Bombay it begins when the sun enters Mṛgaśiras (about 5–6 June). Fasli 1302 began 5 June 1892 in Bombay and 1 July 1892 in Madras.
Madras Fasli: current Fasli = A.D. year − 590; the revenue year 1 July 1910 – 30 June 1911 was Fasli 1320.
facts.quote: Its formula is "current Fasli=A.D. year minus 590".

facts.text: The Deccan Fasli originated under Shah Jahan after his Deccan settlement (1636), branching from the Hijri year later than the northern one.
The luni-solar northern Fasli runs its days 1 to 30 through the month from the full moon, without bright and dark fortnights.

eras.label: Faslī (Deccan and Madras)
eras.why_two: the Deccan and Madras Faslī year begins in June–July
