eras.label: Bengali San
eras.why_two: the Bengali year begins in mid-April

as_written.note: 'year', before the number (e.g. সন ১৩০৫)
'year', usually after the number

eras.where_used: Bengal (West Bengal, Bangladesh), Tripura, Assam (Barak valley); Bengali documents, horoscopes, shop and temple inscriptions, Bengali-made items.
eras.year_start: Solar; begins at Meṣa saṅkrānti, 1 Baiśākh (about 14–15 April); months take lunar names (Baiśākh first). Bangladesh (Bangla Academy reform 1966, adopted officially later) fixes 1 Baiśākh at 14 April.

reckonings.name: Solar Meṣādi
reckonings.to_ce: CE = San + 593 from 1 Baiśākh to 31 December; CE = San + 594 from 1 January to the end of Caitra.

eras.used: epoch A.D. 593–94 (Śaka 516 current); attributed to Akbar's reform, introduced 1584 and counted from 1556
eras.note: The Bengali year (Baṅgābda) of Bengal, Tripura and Assam, on Bengali documents, temple and shop inscriptions and Bengali-made items. It begins in mid-April.
eras.research_note: Give both when the month is not legible.
eras.current_vs_expired: Current years in common use (Pillai's tables print expired years: add 1 to them).

facts.text: The Bengali San is a solar year running with the solar Śaka year from the Meṣa saṅkrānti, with lunar month names, Vaiśākha first; Bengali San 1300 current = Śaka 1816 current = A.D. 1893–94.
facts.quote: It is a solar year and runs with the solar Saka year, beginning at the Mesha sankranti; but the months receive lunar month names

facts.text: Add 593 to the Bengali San for the first nine months, 594 for the rest.
facts.quote: also 593 for the first nine months of the Bengali san, and 594 for the rest.

facts.text: Ojha: the Bengali San (also called Baṅgābda) begins at the Meṣa saṅkrānti (solar Vaiśākha); adding 593–94 gives the Christian year and 650–51 the Vikrama year.
facts.quote: इस सन् में ५९३-९४ जोड़ने से ई. स. और ६५०-१ जोड़ने से वि. सं. बनता है

facts.text: Banglapedia: adding 593 to the Bangla year gives the Christian year; Akbar introduced the calendar in 1584, counted from 1556 (Hijri 963).
facts.quote: অর্থাৎ বাংলা সনের সঙ্গে ৫৯৩ যোগ করলে খ্রিস্টীয় সন পাওয়া যায়।

facts.text: A Bangla Academy committee under Muhammad Shahidullah (set up 17 February 1966) recommended fixed month lengths, with Caitra taking 31 days every fourth year.

eras.label: Kollam (Malayalam era)
eras.why_two: the Kollam year begins in August or September

as_written.note: spelling cross-checked on Malayalam Wikipedia only
common abbreviation; not confirmed in a source read here
cross-check only
Tamil name (Tinnevelly); S&D and Ojha give 'Kollam āṇḍu' in transliteration

eras.where_used: Kerala (Malabar, Cochin, Travancore) and Tinnevelly; Travancore and Cochin state documents, coins and dated items; Kerala almanacs to the present.
eras.year_start: Sidereal solar. South Malabar, Travancore, Cochin and Tinnevelly: 1 Chiṅṅam (Siṃha saṅkrānti, mid-August). North Malabar: 1 Kanni (Kanyā saṅkrānti, mid-September).

reckonings.name: Southern (Siṃhādi)
reckonings.to_ce: CE = Kollam + 824 from 1 Chiṅṅam to 31 December; CE = Kollam + 825 from 1 January to the end of Karkkaṭakam (mid-August).

reckonings.name: Northern (Kanyādi)
reckonings.to_ce: CE = Kollam + 824 from 1 Kanni to 31 December; CE = Kollam + 825 from 1 January to the end of Chiṅṅam.

eras.note: The Malayalam era of Kerala (Travancore, Cochin, Malabar), on state documents, coins and almanacs to the present. Its year begins in mid-August in most of Kerala.
eras.research_note: Give both when the month is not legible.
eras.current_vs_expired: Current years (the one Indian era Pillai treats as current).

facts.text: The Kollam year (Kollam āṇḍu, 'western year') is sidereal solar; it begins with Kanni in North Malabar and with Chiṅṅam in South Malabar and Tinnevelly; the first Kollam year began in A.D. 825–26; years are current; A.D. 1894–95 was Kollam 1070.
facts.quote: The year is sidereal solar. In North Malabar it begins with the solar month Kanni (Kanya), and in South Malabar and Tinnevelly with the month Chingam (Simha).

facts.text: Add 824–25 to a Kollam year to get the Christian year (Kielhorn's determination from inscriptions); its years are mostly written as current years.
facts.quote: कोल्लम् संवत् में ८२४-२५ मिलाने से ई. स. होना निश्चय किया … इस संवत् के वर्ष बहुधा वर्तमान ही लिखे जाते हैं

facts.text: Pillai: Kollam current year = A.D. year − 825 (A.D. 1900 = Kollam 1075, i.e. the year running in January–August 1900); Kollam 1086 Dhanus 20 = 3 January 1911.
The era runs in cycles of 1000 years in theory, but the number has been allowed to run past 1000 in modern use.
facts.quote: in actual modern use the number has been allowed to run on over the 1000, A.D. 1894—95 being called Kollam 1070.

eras.label: Vīra Nirvāṇa Samvat (Jain)
eras.why_two: the Jain year begins in October–November

as_written.note: common short form; not seen in a source read here
Gujarati form; no Gujarati source read

eras.where_used: Jain texts and colophons, Jain temple and image inscriptions (occasionally), Jain almanacs and printed books; usually alongside Vikrama Samvat.
eras.year_start: Kārttika śukla 1, the day after Dīpāvalī (Mahāvīra's nirvāṇa), in modern Jain almanacs (the era runs with the Kārttikādi Vikrama year + 470). Not confirmed for older inscriptions.

reckonings.name: Śvetāmbara standard
reckonings.to_ce: VNS = VS + 470 = Śaka + 605 = CE + 527. CE = VNS − 527 from the new year (Oct.–Nov.) to 31 December; CE = VNS − 526 from 1 January to Dīpāvalī.

eras.used: medieval Jain texts; rare in inscriptions
eras.note: The Jain era counted from Mahāvīra’s nirvāṇa, in Jain texts and almanacs and now and then on Jain images, usually beside a Vikram Samvat date. Its year begins in October–November.
eras.research_note: Give both when the month is not legible. Some Digambara writers used other intervals (see disputed).
eras.current_vs_expired: Not established in the sources read.

facts.text: Adding 470 to a Vikrama year, 605 to a Śaka year, or 527 to a Christian year gives the Vīra Nirvāṇa year (Śvetāmbara Merutuṅga, Vicāraśreṇi; Nemicandra's Mahāvīracariya); the year is mostly used in Jain books and sometimes in inscriptions.
facts.quote: विक्रम संवत् में ४७०, शक संवत् में ६०५ और ई. स. में ५२७ मिलाने से वीरनिर्वाण संवत् आता है

facts.text: Ojha's table: Vīra Nirvāṇa year − 527/526 = Christian year.
facts.quote: वीरनिर्वाण संवत् — ५२७-२६ = ईसवी सन्

facts.text: Prinsep put the first year of the Jain era of Mahāvīra in 529 B.C. and noted it as not in use.

eras.label: Burmese era
english: B.E. (Burmese Era, in older English usage)
Chulasakarat (Thai name of the same era)
words: ကောဇာသက္ကရာဇ်
eras.why_two: the Burmese year begins at Thingyan in mid-April

as_written.note: 'era'; spelling from general knowledge, no Burmese-language source read (gap)

as_written.native: ကောဇာသက္ကရာဇ်
as_written.note: modern name of the current era; no Burmese source read (gap). Irwin (1901) used 'Kawza Era' for a different, legendary era.
'year' after a year number; no source read (gap)

eras.where_used: Burma (Myanmar) and Arakan; Burmese silver, lacquer and inscriptions; the same era is the Magī San of Chittagong.
eras.year_start: Solar year from Thingyan (Burmese New Year, mid-April; in practice from Thingyan Tet, the end of the water festival); luni-solar months Tagu … Tabaung with an intercalary second Wazo (Burma) or second Tagu (Arakan).

reckonings.name: Thagayit (Burmese era)
reckonings.to_ce: CE = ME + 638 from Thingyan to 31 December; CE = ME + 639 from 1 January to Thingyan. Days at the very start of Tagu may be 'hnaung' (late) days of the previous year.

eras.note: The era of Burma and Arakan, on Burmese silver, lacquer, coins and inscriptions, in Burmese digits with သက္ကရာဇ် before the number or ခုနှစ် after it. Its year begins at Thingyan in mid-April. ခုနှစ် is also written after Western years: a number above about 1800 is a Western year.
eras.research_note: Give both when the month is not legible.
eras.current_vs_expired: Expired years: the era began with year 0 (Irwin). 1 January 1900 was 1261 Pyatho waxing 2.

facts.text: The era now in common use was started in A.D. 638–9, in Burma by King Poppasaw of Pagan and in Arakan by King Thareyarenu; the same era is current in Chittagong as the Magi San.
facts.quote: In A. D. 638-9 the era now in common use was started simultaneously, in Burma by King Poppasaw of Pagan and in Arakan by King Thareyarenu

facts.text: Core rule: Burmese era + 638 = Christian year from the new year (mid-April) to December, + 639 from January to the new year.
To reduce a Burmese vulgar-era year to the Christian year, add 638; the year begins with the new moon of the solar month Chaitra.
facts.quote: To reduce the Burmese vulgar year into the Christian, add 638.

facts.text: Thagayit counts expired years: 1 January 1900 was Burmese 1261 Pyatho waxing 2nd, so January–April dates take + 639.
facts.quote: The first of January 1900 was Burmese 1261 Pyatho waxing 2nd, which means the second day of the month of Pyatho after the completion of 1261 years

facts.text: Tagu is nominally the first month but the year number changes with the solar year, so up to 11 days at the start and end of a year share month and day names; the later ones are marked 'hnaung'. B.E. 1257 Tagu waning 10 was 18 April 1895; B.E. 1257 Hnaung Tagu waning 10 was 6 April 1896.
The solar year is taken to commence at Thingyan Tet (end of the Thingyan festival).
facts.quote: the actual practice for many years has been that it commences at Thingyan Tet.

facts.text: Ojha: Magī San (Chittagong) + 638–39 = Christian year.
facts.quote: इसमें ६३८-३९ जोड़ने से ई. स. … बनता है

eras.label: Buddhist era
eras.why_two: the Buddhist year changes in April–May in Ceylon and Burma

as_written.note: Sinhala; no Sinhala source read (gap)
Burmese; no Burmese source read (gap)

eras.where_used: Ceylon (Sri Lanka), Burma, Siam: monastic and religious documents, temple inscriptions, Buddhist presentation items.
eras.year_start: Traditionally from the Buddha's nirvāṇa reckoned in 544 B.C.; modern Sri Lankan and Burmese practice changes the BE year at Vesak / the full moon of Kason (April–May). New-year point not established from the sources read.

reckonings.name: Ceylon/Burma/Siam count
reckonings.to_ce: CE = BE − 543 or BE − 544 (give both unless the month is known; the split depends on whether the BE year changes in April–May or on 1 January).

eras.note: Counted from the Buddha’s death, in Ceylon, Burma and Siam, on temple inscriptions and presentation items.
eras.research_note: Give both.
eras.current_vs_expired: Irwin's Burmese thagayit counts expired years; for the religious era not established here.

facts.text: In Ceylon, Burma and Siam the Buddha's nirvāṇa is reckoned at 544 years before the Christian era.
facts.quote: सीलोन (सिंहलद्वीप, लंका), ब्रह्मा और स्याम में बुद्ध का निर्वाण ई. स. से ५४४ वर्ष पूर्व होना माना जाता है

facts.text: Prinsep: era of the Buddha's nirvāṇa, in India, Ceylon, Ava, Siam: first year = 543 B.C.; B − 543 = C.
facts.quote: Ditto, his nirvāna, in India, Ceylon, Ava, Siam, etc. 1st year = 543 B.C. ... B−543 = C

facts.text: The Burmese Religious Era dates from 543 B.C., the year in which Gautama is supposed to have attained nirvāṇa.

eras.label: Nepal Samvat
eras.why_two: the Nepal year begins in October–November, and sources differ by a year

as_written.note: abbreviation; not seen in a source read here

eras.where_used: Nepal (Kathmandu valley, Newar community): inscriptions, manuscripts, metal images; replaced by Śaka for official use after the Gorkha conquest (1768/69), still used by Newars.
eras.year_start: Kārttika śukla 1 (October–November); amānta months.

reckonings.name: Kārttikādi
reckonings.to_ce: Per Pillai (and modern Newar use, where N.S. 1146 began in October 2025): CE = N.S. + 879 from Kārttika śukla 1 to 31 December; CE = N.S. + 880 from 1 January to the end of Āśvina. Ojha's table gives + 878/879 instead (see disputed).

eras.note: The Newar era of the Kathmandu valley, on inscriptions, manuscripts and metal images. Sources differ by a year in converting it, so the reader gives both.
eras.research_note: One-year disagreement between sources (Ojha + 878/879). Give 878–880 as the range unless the month is legible and the item is modern.
eras.current_vs_expired: Mostly expired years (Kielhorn: only 2 of 25 dates current).

facts.text: The Newar era was in use in Nepal up to 1768, when the Śaka era was introduced; its years are Kārttikādi, months amānta, years generally expired.
facts.quote: Its years are Karttikadi, its months amanta

facts.text: Pillai: Nevar expired year = A.D. year − 879.
facts.quote: Formula " Nevar expired = A.D. year minus 879".

facts.text: Ojha's table: Nevār saṃvat + 878–79 = Christian year.

eras.label: the Western year

as_written.note: 'year' before a number; in Hindi usually means the Christian year (but san is also used for Hijri, Fasli, Bengali years: check context)

eras.where_used: Since British rule; on 19th–20th-century items, often with an Indian-era date beside it.
eras.year_start: 1 January (Julian in British territories until 2/14 September 1752, Gregorian after).

reckonings.name: Gregorian
reckonings.to_ce: identity

eras.note: The Western year itself, written the Indian way since British rule: सन् or ई. in Hindi, ઈ.સ. in Gujarati, খ্রিস্টাব্দ in Bengali, கி.பி. in Tamil, ء after the number in Urdu. Often there is an Indian-era date beside it.
eras.research_note: Beware: the bare word 'san' (सन्, سن, সন) also introduces Hijri, Fasli, Bengali and regnal years.
eras.current_vs_expired: Current.

facts.text: The Christian era has come into use in India only since English rule; its years are current years beginning 1 January.
facts.quote: This has come into use in India only since the establishment of the English rule.

facts.text: Modern abbreviations and names of the Christian era in Indian languages (ई., ईस्वी, ई. स., ઈ.સ., খ্রি., கி.பி., క్రీ.శ., ಕ್ರಿ.ಶ., عیسوی, ක්‍රි.ව., ခရစ်နှစ်).

as_written.note: no source read

eras.research_note: For expired years. Panchangs sometimes give current years (one higher).
eras.current_vs_expired: Panchangs give sometimes expired, sometimes current years, sometimes both (S&D).

facts.text: Its years are both Chaitrādi and Meṣādi; it is not often used in epigraphical records.

eras.label: Shuhur San

as_written.note: Ojha spells शाहूर सन्

eras.where_used: Maratha documents and accounts (17th–19th century); 'still occasionally met with' in 1911.
eras.year_start: Solar: the sun's entry into the nakṣatra Mṛgaśiras (about 5–8 June); months and days follow Hijri names.

reckonings.name: Solar
reckonings.to_ce: CE = Shuhur + 599 from early June to 31 December; CE = Shuhur + 600 from 1 January to early June.

eras.note: A Maratha era of documents and accounts, its years written in Arabic number words rather than digits. The reader does not read it.
eras.research_note: The year is normally written in Arabic number-words, not digits (see words).
eras.current_vs_expired: Current.

facts.text: The Shuhur (Sūr) San diverged from the Hijri year in A.D. 1344 (A.H. 745) and has since run as a solar year beginning when the sun enters Mṛgaśiras; add 599 (600 after its sixth month) for the Christian year.
facts.quote: It is nine years behind the Fasali of the Dakhan ... To convert it to an A.D. year, add 599.

facts.text: Its years are written with Arabic number-words (e.g. 1339 = तिस्सा अशर सलासे मया व अलफ), not with figures.
facts.quote: इस सन् के वर्ष अंकों में नहीं किंतु अंक सूचक अरबी शब्दों में ही लिखे जाते

eras.label: Vilāyatī or Amlī year

reckonings.name: Vilāyatī / Amlī
reckonings.to_ce: CE = year + 592 from the September new year to 31 December; CE = year + 593 from 1 January to the next new year.

eras.note: Years of Orissa and parts of Bengal, in business and court papers, numbered like the northern Faslī.
eras.research_note: Same number as the northern Fasli.
eras.current_vs_expired: Current.

facts.text: The Vilāyatī year (Orissa) begins with the solar month Kanyā; the Amlī year begins on lunar Bhādrapada śukla 12; both bear the same number; add 592–93.
facts.quote: विलायती सन् + ५९२-९३ = ईसवी सन्

eras.label: Magī San

eras.year_start: As the Bengali San (Meṣa saṅkrānti, mid-April).

reckonings.name: Solar
reckonings.to_ce: CE = Magi + 638 from mid-April to 31 December; + 639 from 1 January to mid-April.

eras.research_note: 45 years behind the Bengali San.
eras.current_vs_expired: As Bengali San.

facts.text: The Magi San of Chittagong is like the Bengali San in days and months but 45 years behind it (Magi 1200 = Bengali 1245); add 638–39 for the Christian year; Irwin identifies it with the Burmese era.
facts.quote: मगि सन् बहुधा बंगाली सन् के समान ही है. अंतर केवल इतना ही है कि इसका प्रारंभ बंगाली सन् से ४५ वर्ष पीछे माना जाता है

eras.label: Saptarṣi era
eras.where_used: Kashmir and neighbouring hill states (formerly Multan); Kashmiri manuscripts, Sharada inscriptions.
eras.year_start: Chaitrādi; months mostly pūrṇimānta.

reckonings.name: Century-less
reckonings.to_ce: Hundreds are omitted: written year y (1–100). CE = y + 24 or + 25 + a multiple of 100 that must be supplied from context (e.g. y 86 = A.D. 1910 per Pillai).

eras.note: The era of Kashmir, on Kashmiri manuscripts and Sharada inscriptions. Its years leave out the hundreds, so a year cannot be read without knowing the century; the reader does not read it.
eras.research_note: Plus an unknown number of centuries: never a single answer without context.
eras.current_vs_expired: Mostly current years (Kielhorn).

facts.text: In practice the hundreds of the Saptarṣi year are omitted, and the count restarts at 1 after 100; add 24–25 (and the century) for the Christian year.
facts.quote: But in practice the hundreds are omitted, and as soon as the reckoning reaches 100, a fresh hundred begins from 1.

eras.label: Mauludi era (Tipu Sultan)
eras.why_two: the Mauludi year does not begin on 1 January
eras.where_used: Mysore under Tipu Sultan (1782–1799): coins, arms and armor
eras.note: The era Tipu Sultan of Mysore introduced and wrote on his coins and arms, counted from the Prophet's birth. The Met catalogues Mauludi 1222 as 1793–94 and 1225 as 1796–97, which fits Western year = Mauludi + 571 or 572; the dating research did not find a second source for the rule.

rulers.name: Akbar
rulers.julus_rule: Akbar's coins are dated A.H. until about his 28th–30th year, then in Ilāhī solar years with Persian months. Ilāhī year n runs from Nauroz (about 10–11 March O.S.) of CE 1555 + n to the next Nauroz. Example: Ilāhī 40 began 9 Rajab 1003 = 10 March 1595 (Lane-Poole's table), so Ilāhī 40 = March 1595 – March 1596.
rulers.ilahi: Ilāhī era counted from 11 March 1556 (28 Rabīʿ II 963), 25 days after the accession; introduced A.H. 991–993 (see era 'ilahi').
rulers.note: Accession date confirmed by three sources (Whitehead; S&D citing the Ṭabaqāt-i Akbarī; Ojha).

facts.text: Accession 963-04-02 A.H. (1556-02-14 Julian (O.S.), Friday); dates computed by the tabular Hijri calendar agree with the source's A.D. date and weekday.

rulers.name: Jahangir
rulers.julus_rule: Solar regnal years with Persian months, the year changing at Nauroz (Lane-Poole). Coin evidence (regnal year 22 found with A.H. 1036 and 1037) places the start of regnal year 22 at Nauroz 1627, so regnal year n (n ≥ 2) begins at Nauroz (about 10–11 March O.S.) of CE 1605 + n, and regnal year 1 runs from the accession (23 October 1605 O.S.) to the Nauroz when regnal year 2 begins. Worked: regnal year 10 = Nauroz 1615 – Nauroz 1616. This anchoring is inferred from Lane-Poole's coin evidence (single source); Jahangir also wrote 'Ilāhī' with the regnal year.
rulers.ilahi: Jahangir abolished the Ilāhī era for the main date (reverting to A.H.) but kept solar regnal years and Persian months (Lane-Poole).
rulers.note: Death on 28 Ṣafar 1037 confirmed by Lane-Poole.

rulers.name: Dawar Bakhsh
rulers.note: Set up in Ṣafar 1037 (October–November 1627) after Jahangir's death; deposed 2 Jumādā I 1037 (30 December 1627 O.S.) (Whitehead).

rulers.name: Shah Jahan
rulers.julus_rule: Uncertain. First coins: Hijri and regnal years; from his 2nd year the regnal date is an Ilāhī (solar) year with a Persian month (Whitehead's 'Kalima-Ilāhī' type); Lane-Poole says regnal years were solar under Jahangir and Shah Jahan. Lunar reckoning from the accession is also plausible for documents. Rule: CE ≈ 1627 + regnal year (for the part after the anniversary) or 1628 + regnal year; give both. Over 30 years solar and lunar counts drift apart by about one year.
rulers.ilahi: Ilāhī months on coins; the Ilāhī era itself fell out of use early in his reign (S&D, Ojha).
rulers.note: Whitehead gives 18 Jumādā II 1037 (Thursday 14 February 1628 O.S.), which matches the tabular calendar; no second source for the day was read.

rulers.name: Aurangzeb ʿĀlamgīr I
rulers.julus_rule: Lunar. regnal year 1 from the first enthronement, 1 Ẕū al-Qaʿda 1068 (21 July 1658 O.S. = 31 July N.S.), to the end of Shaʿbān 1069; regnal year 2 from 1 Ramaẓān 1069 (13 May 1659 O.S. by the tabular calendar; the Indian Antiquary table gives 23 May 1659, i.e. N.S.); regnal year n (n ≥ 2) from 1 Ramaẓān of A.H. 1067 + n. Worked: regnal year 10 = 1 Ramaẓān 1077 = 15 February 1667 O.S. to 1 Ramaẓān 1078 = 4 February 1668 O.S. He died in regnal year 51.
rulers.note: Accession confirmed by Whitehead and the Indian Antiquary (1911); death 28 Ẕū al-Qaʿda 1118 (20 February 1707 O.S. = 3 March N.S.) confirmed by Lane-Poole and the Indian Antiquary.

numerals.used_for: Hindi, Marathi, Nepali, Sanskrit, Rajasthani; Jain and Hindu inscriptions in north and west India
numerals.older_forms: Not established from a paleography source in this pass. Bühler's plates follow the decimal figures only to the 11th–12th centuries, noting local differences in west, east and south from then on; Ojha's plates (lipipatra) of later numerals were not read. Practical note (no source): 18th–19th-century hands often write ५ and ८ in forms close to the Gujarati ૫ and ૮, and १ with a long tail.
numerals.confusable_with: १ (1) can look like Latin 9; ९ (9) and Gujarati ૯ are the same digit; ७ (7) and Gujarati ૭ are the same digit but Gurmukhi ੭ also differs only slightly; ५ (5) vs Marathi/Nepali variants (no source).
numerals.note: Digit identities from Unicode and CLDR (same organization, not independent); no paleographic second source for the modern shapes.

numerals.used_for: Gujarat and Kutch: silver, brass, Jain images, account books
numerals.confusable_with: Several shapes are close to Devanagari (૧/१, ૯/९, ૭/७) and read the same; Gujarati ૦ zero vs the letter-free circle used as a mark; ૮ (8) can look like Latin 6 rotated (no source).

numerals.older_forms: Not established (gap). Traditional Bengali currency fractions (৴ ৵ ৶ ৷ ৸ ৹, U+09F4–U+09F9) appear in accounts, not in dates.
numerals.confusable_with: ৪ (4) looks like Latin 8; ৭ (7) like Latin 9 or Devanagari ९; ৮ (8) like Latin 'b' (no source; standard reader warnings).
੧ (1) like Devanagari ९ (9): a dangerous confusion; ੭ vs Devanagari ७ (no source).

numerals.codepoints: U+0BE6–U+0BEF (zero U+0BE6 is a late addition); ௰ U+0BF0 = 10, ௱ U+0BF1 = 100, ௲ U+0BF2 = 1000; ௳ U+0BF3 day sign, ௴ U+0BF4 month sign, ௵ U+0BF5 year sign, ௺ U+0BFA number sign
numerals.used_for: Tamil Nadu, Tinnevelly, Ceylon Tamil; traditional documents, temple and silver inscriptions, marriage invitations
numerals.traditional_system: Non-positional, without zero: a digit written before ௰/௱/௲ multiplies it, a digit after adds. Example (composition rule from general knowledge, not from a source read): 1898 = ௲௮௱௯௰௮ (1000 + 8×100 + 9×10 + 8). The day, month and year signs ௳ ௴ ௵ follow the number they label.
numerals.older_forms: Bühler: the Tamil numerals 'greatly differ from the usual ones and preserve the old signs for 10, 100 and 1000'. Unicode: Tamil traditionally lacked a zero and adopted one from general Indian practice.
numerals.confusable_with: Unicode lists ௧ (1) ~ க ka, ௨ (2) ~ உ u, ௭ (7) ~ எ e, ௮ (8) ~ அ a: digits and letters can be identical in some fonts.

numerals.older_forms: Telugu base-4 fraction signs (U+0C78–U+0C7E) were used for measures and money, not dates (Unicode).

numerals.confusable_with: Close to Telugu digits; ೧ (1) like Telugu ౧ (same value).

numerals.codepoints: U+0D66–U+0D6F; archaic ൰ U+0D70 = 10, ൱ U+0D71 = 100, ൲ U+0D72 = 1000; fractions ൳ ൴ ൵ (¼ ½ ¾) and U+0D58–U+0D5E, U+0D76–U+0D78; date mark ൹ U+0D79
numerals.traditional_system: Archaic numbering with signs for 10, 100 and 1000 (Unicode); assumed to compose like Tamil (not confirmed in a source read). The date mark ൹ is written after the day of the month, like English 'th'.
numerals.older_forms: Unicode: the archaic system included numbers for 10, 100 and 1000 and fraction signs; the date mark is not much used today.
numerals.confusable_with: ൧ (1) resembles the letter ന (na) in some hands (no source).

numerals.used_for: Persian and Urdu inscriptions, Mughal coins, Hijri and julūs dates, Urdu documents in India and Pakistan
numerals.older_forms: Lane-Poole: Akbar's copper coins write the Hijri year in Persian number-words rather than figures.
numerals.confusable_with: Unicode: distinct glyphs for 4, 5, 6, 7 compared with Arabic-Indic (٠–٩, U+0660–U+0669), and 4, 6, 7 vary between Persian and Urdu. ۰ zero is a dot (do not read as a stray mark); ۵ five is a small circle or heart (do not read as zero); ۲ (2) and ۳ (3) differ only by one tooth; Urdu ۷ (7) and ۸ (8) are mirror shapes (V and inverted V).

chronograms.what: Persian abjad chronograms (tārīkh; māddah-yi tārīkh): a word, phrase or verse whose letters, valued by the abjad system, add up to the date of the event, normally a Hijri year.
chronograms.how: Add the abjad values of every written letter: ا 1, ب 2, ج 3, د 4, ه 5, و 6, ز 7, ح 8, ط 9, ی 10, ک 20, ل 30, م 40, ن 50, س 60, ع 70, ف 80, ص 90, ق 100, ر 200, ش 300, ت 400, ث 500, خ 600, ذ 700, ض 800, ظ 900, غ 1000. Persian and Urdu letters take the value of the nearest Arabic letter: پ = ب, چ = ج, ژ = ز, گ = ک; Urdu ٹ = ت, ڈ = د, ڑ = ر, ے = ی. In Urdu practice hamza counts as alif and a tashdīd (doubled letter) counts as an extra letter (Pritchett). The total is a Hijri year unless stated otherwise; convert it as a Hijri year.
chronograms.worked: Rekhta example: the phrase 'Dukhtar-e-Momin' gives 1340; the poem instructs that the value of 'Naal' (81) be subtracted (takhrīja), leaving A.H. 1259 = A.D. 1843–44.
chronograms.caution: The values of some letters are given here from general knowledge (Pritchett's page shows the full table only as an image; the text confirms alif 1, be 2, jim 3, dal 4, he 5, ze 7, ḥe 8, ye 10, lam 30, mim 40, nun 50, sin 60, re 200, te 400, khe 600, ghain 1000). Poets add (taʿmiya) or subtract (takhrīja) values by riddling instructions; spelling choices (hamza, long vowels, doubled letters) change the total; a chronogram can be composed after the event; and the stated event may not be the making of the item. Treat a chronogram reading as a claim to check, not as a date.

facts.text: A tārīkh is a word or verse made up of letters forming the date of an event 'in the Hijera style', the words also fitting the event.
facts.quote: a word or a verse is made up of letters forming the date thereof in the Hijera style.

facts.text: Dates in abjad chronograms are understood as Hijri dates.
facts.quote: Dates are always understood to be those of the hijrii dating system

facts.text: Chronogram devices: taʿmiya adds and takhrīja subtracts a stated value; in Urdu hamza is valued like alif.
facts.quote: Two such devices of prominence are Ta'amiya, that uses addition, and Takhrija, that uses subtraction.

facts.text: Persian/Urdu letters take the values of related Arabic letters (pe = be, che = jim, zhe = ze, gaf = kaf; Urdu retroflex letters = their dental counterparts; bari ye = ye).

decode_rules: A bare number is never read as a date. Read a date only when an era word (संवत्, सं., शके, सन्, سنه, جلوس, বঙ্গাব্দ, കൊല്ലവർഷം, ခုနှစ်, ء, ھ …), a month name, a fortnight word (sudi/vadi), a weekday, or a julūs formula is written with it. Purity marks (e.g. 916, 92.5), weights, inventory numbers and Mughal-style pseudo-dates on later items are not dates.

Identify the script of the numerals first (Devanagari, Gujarati, Bengali, Gurmukhi, Odia, Tamil, Telugu, Kannada, Malayalam, Persian/Urdu, Burmese, Sinhala, Western). Watch confusable shapes: Bengali ৪ (4) looks like 8; Gurmukhi ੧ (1) like Devanagari ९ (9); Persian ۰ (0) is a dot and ۵ (5) a circle; Tamil ௧ ௨ ௭ ௮ look like the letters க உ எ அ; Burmese ၀ (0) like the letter ဝ.

Tamil (and old Malayalam/Sinhala) numbers may be non-positional: digits before ௰ (10) ௱ (100) ௲ (1000) multiply, digits after add. Saptarṣi (Kashmir) years omit the hundreds. Shuhur San years are written in Arabic number-words. Sanskrit verse dates may use word-numerals read right to left (Bühler).

Which era from the number alone: you cannot tell eras apart by the number alone in general; the era word or the place must decide. As a guide for 1700–1950 items: 1750–2010 is typical of Vikrama; 1620–1880 of Śaka; 1100–1370 of Hijri (Hijri 1300 = 1882–83); 1150–1360 of Bengali San (also Fasli 1150–1360, Vilāyatī/Amlī); 870–1130 of Kollam; 1060–1310 of the Burmese era and Magī San; 2240–2500 of the Buddhist era (and also of Vīra Nirvāṇa: VNS 2400 = 1873–74 vs BE 2400 = 1856–57 — they overlap); 4800–5050 of Kali. Overlaps: Hijri and Bengali/Fasli ranges overlap entirely (e.g. 1300 could be Hijri 1882–83, Bengali 1893–94, northern Fasli 1892–93, Deccan Fasli 1890–91); Vikrama and Buddhist/Jain ranges do not overlap Śaka but VS 1900–2010 overlaps Gregorian numbers (a Western date 1950 vs VS 1950 = 1893–94).

'Samvat' (संवत्/सं.) alone: read as Vikrama in north and west India and Gujarat; it has also been used for Śaka and other eras. 'Shake/Śake' = Śaka. 'San' (सन्, سن, সন): Christian, Hijri, Fasli, Bengali or regnal; decide from script, region and the size of the number.

When to give two candidate Western years: always, unless the month (and for Kārttikādi/Āṣāḍhādi years the fortnight) is legible. Year-only conversions: Vikrama −57/−56; Śaka +78/+79; Bengali +593/+594; northern Fasli and Vilāyatī/Amlī +592/+593; Deccan and Madras Fasli +590/+591; Kollam +824/+825; Vīra Nirvāṇa −527/−526; Burmese era and Magī +638/+639; Buddhist era −543/−544; Ilāhī +1555/+1556; Kali −3101/−3100; Shuhur +599/+600; Nepal Samvat +879/+880 (Ojha +878/+879); Hijri: the CE span of the AH year (usually two CE years, rarely one).

With a month: use the reckoning's new-year point. The first figure applies from the era's new year to 31 December, the second from 1 January to the end of the era year. New-year points: Chaitrādi VS/Śaka and Kali at Chaitra śukla 1 / Meṣa (March–April); Kārttikādi VS and Vīra Nirvāṇa at Kārttika śukla 1 (October–November); Āṣāḍhādi VS at Āṣāḍha śukla 1 (June–July); Bengali, Magī, Burmese, Tamil solar at mid-April; Kollam at Chiṅṅam (mid-August) or Kanni (mid-September); northern Fasli and Vilāyatī in September; Deccan Fasli and Shuhur in early June; Madras Fasli 1 July; Ilāhī at Nauroz (about 10–11 March O.S.).

Vikrama in Gujarat (and among Gujarati makers elsewhere) is Kārttikādi: a Gujarati date in Kārtak–Āso before January takes −57, after January −56. In Kathiawar and parts of Rajputana an Āṣāḍhādi year is possible, sometimes stated by the word आषाढादि. Do not assume the north-Indian Chaitrādi year for a Gujarati item.

Expired vs current: Vikrama, Śaka, Kali, Nepal and the Burmese era are normally written as expired years; Kollam, Bengali (in common use), Fasli and the Christian era as current. A rare 'current' Vikrama or Śaka year makes the true year one earlier; mention this only as a remote possibility.

Hijri: convert with the tabular algorithm and give the CE span. Observed month starts can differ by 1–2 days; British-period tables give Julian dates before 1752. Never subtract a fixed number from a Hijri year.

Julūs (regnal) years: compute from the named ruler's accession (rulers table). Aurangzeb and later: lunar years. Jahangir: solar years from Nauroz. Akbar: Ilāhī solar years from 1556. Shah Jahan: uncertain; give the range. On East India Company and successor-state coins the regnal year is often frozen and does not date the coin; prefer the Hijri year if both are present, and note any disagreement.
Abjad chronograms give Hijri years; report them as a claimed date with the computation shown, and flag that riddling additions/subtractions may apply.

If an Indian-era date and a Christian date are both written, check them against each other; if they disagree by one year, the Indian year may be current rather than expired or the month may straddle the new year.

A written date dates the inscription, which may be later than the item (re-dedications, presentation inscriptions, owner's marks) or copied from an older item; on reproductions dates are often copied. A date is evidence, not proof.

examples.material: gum tempera and ink on palm leaf (manuscript colophon folio)
examples.written_date: Samvat 1336, the fifth day of the bright half of Jyestha (museum's partly translated transcription: 'Sri Anahillapure Maharajadhiraja Sri Sarangadevasya Vijayarajye Likhitam on the fifth day of the bright half of Jyestha, Samvat 1336')
examples.method: Jyeṣṭha falls in May–June. Chaitrādi year: VS 1336 − 57 = 1279. Kārttikādi year (usual in Gujarat): Jyeṣṭha comes after 1 January, so VS 1336 − 56 = 1280.
examples.where_on_object: colophon text on the palm-leaf folio
examples.notes: Manuscript colophon, kept because it shows the full era + month + fortnight + day pattern and a regnal phrase (in the victorious reign of Sāraṅgadeva, r. 1275–97), which brackets the year. The museum's 1279 assumes the Chaitrādi year; the Kārttikādi reading gives 1280. A collector is unlikely to hold such a folio.

examples.date_as_catalogued: after 1782 (event dated 1782 AD in the museum's translation)
examples.where_on_object: inscriptions on the cloth (Takri and Persian)
examples.notes: A VS date written inside a Persian-language inscription: the era word is Samvat even in Persian. The museum dates the painting 'after 1782' because the inscription dates the event shown, not the painting.

examples.material: gum tempera and gold on cotton cloth
examples.written_date: saṃvata 1938 poṣa kṛṣnā [pakṣe] 1 gadādhara prasāda (museum transliteration)
examples.method: VS 1938 − 57 = 1881. Pauṣa kṛṣṇa 1 read pūrṇimānta (usual in Rajasthan) is the day after the Mārgaśīrṣa full moon, about 6 December 1881 (meeus_check); read amānta it would be early January 1882 (VS − 56).
examples.notes: Shows the spelling saṃvata, the month poṣa (Pauṣa) and kṛṣṇā [pakṣe] for the dark fortnight. The museum's gloss 'December–January' covers both month systems.

examples.material: gum tempera and gold on paper
examples.written_date: … samat 1806 rā āsoj bīd 10 rī vaire dīn / nijar huvo cītāro jugarno jīvā ro (museum transliteration of the reverse; museum translation: 'In Samvat 1806, on Friday, the tenth day of the dark half of Asoj … artist Jugarsi, son of Jiva, presented [the painting] as nazar')
examples.method: Āśvina (Asoj) falls in September–October. Chaitrādi: VS 1806 − 57 = 1749. Kārttikādi: Asoj comes after 1 January of that year, so VS 1806 − 56 = 1750.
examples.notes: The museum's 1747 does not follow from 'samat 1806' by either reckoning (1749 or 1750). Weekday test (meeus_check): Asoj badi 10 read pūrṇimānta fell on a Friday on 29 September 1747 (which would be VS 1804) and on 25 September 1750 (VS 1806 in the Kārttikādi reckoning); in 1749 it fell on Sunday 5 October. So either the year is 1804 misread as 1806 (Devanagari ४ 4 and ६ 6), or the year is Kārttikādi and the date is 25 September 1750. The weekday word in the transliteration ('vaire dīn') is unclear; the museum translates it as Friday. Needs the inscription photo. Note also that the date records when the artist presented the painting, not necessarily when it was painted.

examples.object: Maharao Guman Singh Riding an Elephant in Procession
examples.material: opaque watercolor, black ink and gold on tan paper
examples.written_date: samvat 1827 (as cataloged: 'dated 1770 (samvat 1827)'; the inscription text is not given in the API)
examples.method: VS 1827 − 57 = 1770 (or − 56 = 1771 if the day fell between 1 January and the next new year).
examples.where_on_object: not stated in the API record
examples.notes: Only the year is cataloged, so both candidate years stand; the museum gives the first.

examples.object: Krishna playing with the gopis, folio from a Rasikpriya (artist Ruknuddin)
examples.holder: National Museum of Asian Art, Smithsonian Institution
examples.material: opaque watercolor and gold on paper
examples.written_date: Verso, in nagari script: 'rukdin ro sam. 1743 pota raskapriya am.52' (museum transliteration)
examples.method: 'sam.' = saṃvat. VS 1743 − 57 = 1686 (− 56 = 1687 for January to the next new year).
examples.notes: The abbreviation 'sam.' with no month: a year-only date, so two candidate years. Also carries the painter's name (Ruknuddin) and folio number (am. = aṅka, number 52).

examples.object: A nobleman (portrait inscribed Abul Hasan, ruler of Bhaganagar; by the son of Ruknuddin)
examples.holder: National Museum of Asian Art, Smithsonian Institution
examples.material: opaque watercolor and gold on paper
examples.written_date: Verso, in nagari script: 'Pata Saha bhaga nagar ro kam rukdi re bete ro sam. 1744 jeth Abul Hasan' (museum transliteration)
examples.method: Jyeṣṭha (jeth) falls in May–June. Chaitrādi: VS 1744 − 57 = 1687. Kārttikādi: − 56 = 1688.
examples.notes: Month name in its spoken Rajasthani form 'jeth' (Jyeṣṭha). Bikaner used the Chaitrādi year, which gives the museum's 1687.

examples.object: Thakur Ajit Singh worships the Goddess
examples.holder: National Museum of Asian Art, Smithsonian Institution
examples.material: opaque watercolor and gold on paper
examples.written_date: Verso, in devanagari: 'Ghera Khulayo 1864 Bhadrapad Sud 14 Jada Sare' (museum translation: 'This was opened in V.S 1864 Bhadrapad (August-Sept) in the crescent lunar phase (Shukla Paksha) 14')
examples.method: Bhādrapada falls in August–September. Chaitrādi: VS 1864 − 57 = 1807 (Bhādrapada śukla 14 = about 15 September 1807 by meeus_check). Kārttikādi: − 56 = 1808.
examples.notes: The museum's own translation reads V.S. 1864, which converts to 1807 (or 1808), not 1817. Either the catalog year is a slip for 1807 or the museum dates the painting from other evidence; the inscription itself records an opening ('ghera khulayo'), so it may date an event rather than the painting. Note the year is written with no era word at all.

examples.object: Maharao Umed Singh hunting tigers (Hans Raj Joshi)
examples.holder: National Museum of Asian Art, Smithsonian Institution
examples.material: opaque watercolor and gold on paper
examples.written_date: Verso, in devanagari: 'samvat 1844 vasakih sudi 14, hitvarah din …' (museum translation: 'Samvat 1844 (1787 CE), fourteenth day of Caisakh, Sunday…')
examples.method: Vaiśākha falls in April–May. Chaitrādi: VS 1844 − 57 = 1787. Kārttikādi: − 56 = 1788.
examples.notes: Weekday test (meeus_check): Vaiśākha śukla 14 fell on Tuesday 1 May 1787 but on Sunday 18 May 1788. The written 'Sunday' (hitvār = ādityavāra) therefore fits the Kārttikādi year (1788), not the museum's 1787; the Chaitra śukla 14 of 1787 (1 April) was also a Sunday, if 'vasakih' is misread. Confirm with Pillai's tables. Same pattern as the Mewar example: weekdays on Rajasthani inscriptions can decide the reckoning.

examples.object: Altarpiece or shrine (Jain, image of Suvidhinatha)
examples.licence: not open (V&A images non-commercial; text cited only)
examples.material: copper alloy, silver; cast and inlaid
examples.written_date: 'Vikrama Samvat 1520 Chaitra-badi 8' (museum translation of a Sanskrit inscription in Devanagari)
examples.method: Chaitra badi falls in March–April and comes after 1 January, so VS 1520 − 56 = 1464 under either reading: pūrṇimānta Chaitrādi (Chaitra badi closes the year 1520) or amānta Kārttikādi as used in Gujarat (Chaitra of the year that began in Kārttika 1463).
examples.where_on_object: inscription on the altarpiece (position not stated in the text read)
examples.notes: The usual dated item in Western collections: a Jain brass or copper-alloy shrine with a donor's inscription on the back. The year agrees. The day does not: by meeus_check 23 March 1464 (Julian) was a full moon; amānta Chaitra kṛṣṇa 8 fell on Friday 30 March 1464 and pūrṇimānta Chaitra badi 8 on Thursday 1 March 1464. Image not open; date fact cited from the published text only.

examples.material: bronze
examples.region: Northern India, Uttar Pradesh (as cataloged); donor from a village in Nepal
examples.written_date: '… saṃvat / 500 10 3 // …' (museum transliteration; numerals written as separate signs for 500, 10 and 3)
examples.method: Read as the Śaka era: 513 + 78 = 591 (or + 79 = 592 for January to the next new year).
examples.where_on_object: front and right side of the separately cast pedestal
examples.notes: The inscription says only 'saṃvat'; the era is the museum's identification (asianart.com: 'Śaka Samvat 513, 591 CE'). Read as Vikram Samvat the same number would give 456, and as the Gupta era about 832, so 'saṃvat' alone never fixes the era. The numerals are the older non-place-value kind: one sign each for 500, 10 and 3.

examples.object: Jain Altarpiece with the Jina Parshvanatha flanked by the Jinas Mahavira and Neminatha (?)
examples.holder: Los Angeles County Museum of Art
examples.licence: public domain (LACMA page data publicDomain: 1; download offered)
examples.material: brass inlaid with copper and silver
examples.written_date: Devanagari dedicatory inscription; museum: '… in 988 CE (Shaka era 910)'
examples.method: Śaka 910 + 78 = 988 (+ 79 = 989 for January to the next new year).
examples.notes: A western-Indian Jain bronze dated in the Śaka era, not Vikram Samvat: the era must be read from the inscription, not assumed from the region.

examples.written_date: 1675 (cataloged as 'alternate calendar date: 1675')

examples.notes: Ahom coins are dated in the Śaka era. The record gives the number only, not the script; collectors meet these as octagonal gold and silver coins.

examples.object: Vessel in the Form of a Skull Cup
examples.material: copper alloy
examples.written_date: 'samvat 524' (cataloged); 'A Nepalese inscription around the body of the cup records its consecration in the year Samvat 524 (1404 C.E.)'
examples.method: Nepal Samvat + 879/880: the year began in the autumn (Kārttika), so NS 524 ran from about October 1403 to October 1404.
examples.where_on_object: around the body of the cup
examples.notes: Brief-coverage era (Nepal Samvat). Item made for tantric ritual; the date fixes the consecration.

examples.object: Colophon, folio 188 (recto), from a Manuscript of the Perfection of Wisdom in Eight Thousand Lines
examples.material: gum tempera and ink on palm leaf
examples.written_date: '… [siddham] samvat* ā la ña aśvaniśuklāṣṭamyāṃ | śrīvikramaśīlamahāvihāre …' (museum transliteration; translated 'In the year 239 [Newar Era], on the 8th [tithi] in the bright fortnight of Āśvina')
examples.method: NS 239 + 880 = 1119 for Āśvina (September–October), before the Kārttika new year.
examples.date_as_catalogued: Sunday, September 14, 1119 (year 239 of the Newar Samvat in the month of Ashvina)
examples.notes: The year 239 is written in letter-numerals (akṣara-saṅkhyā: 'ā la ña'), not digits. A date reader must recognize syllables used as numbers on Nepalese and eastern Indian manuscripts. Manuscript colophon; unlikely to be in private hands.

examples.material: steel, gold, textile
examples.written_date: A.H. 1126 (as cataloged: 'hilt, dated A.H. 1126 /1714–15 CE'; inscription tagged Arabic)
examples.method: Tabular Hijri: AH 1126 = 17 January 1714 to 6 January 1715.
examples.notes: Date applies to the hilt only; the blade is European and earlier. A dated part does not date the whole weapon.

examples.material: steel, gold, ivory, wood, enamel, velvet, silver, textile
examples.written_date: A.H. 1162 (as cataloged: 'blade, A.H. 1162/1748–49 CE')
examples.method: Tabular Hijri: AH 1162 = 22 December 1748 to 10 December 1749.
examples.date_as_catalogued: hilt, scabbard, and belt, early 19th century; blade, A.H. 1162/1748–49 CE
examples.notes: AH 1162 began only nine days before the end of 1748, so almost all of it is 1749; '1748–49' is correct but a reader should not take 1748 as likely. The fittings are later than the dated blade.

examples.material: steel, silver, diamonds, enamel, leather
examples.written_date: A.H. 835 (as cataloged: 'blade, dated A.H. 835/1673 CE'; inscriptions tagged Arabic and Persian)
examples.method: Tabular Hijri: AH 835 = 9 September 1431 to 27 August 1432. 1673 CE would be AH 1083–1084.
examples.notes: The catalog's two numbers contradict each other: AH 835 is 1431–32, not 1673. Either the AH figure or the CE figure is wrong (a misread digit, or a date in another era). The inscription text on the web page was not reachable (HTTP 429), so the written form could not be checked.

examples.material: gold coin
examples.region: Agra (Mughal, reign of Jahangir by date)
examples.written_date: 1028 AH (as cataloged: 'dated 1028 AH/1619 CE')
examples.method: Tabular Hijri: AH 1028 = 9 December 1618 to 28 November 1619.
examples.notes: The catalog gives only 1619; the AH year also covers the last three weeks of 1618. The same museum writes the neighboring year two ways: coin 99.35.6553 'dated 1027 AH/1617–18 CE' and coin 99.35.2385 'dated 1027 AH/1618 CE' (AH 1027 = 29 December 1617 to 18 December 1618).

examples.written_date: 0972 (cataloged as 'alternate calendar date')
examples.method: Tabular Hijri: AH 972 = 9 August 1564 to 28 July 1565.
examples.notes: Early Akbar coin dated by the Hijri year alone (before his Ilāhī era).

examples.holder: National Museum of American History, Smithsonian Institution (National Numismatic Collection)

examples.material: gold coin
examples.written_date: 1220 AH (cataloged)
examples.method: Tabular Hijri: AH 1220 = 1 April 1805 to 20 March 1806.
examples.notes: The catalog gives the first CE year only; the AH year runs into March 1806. Company-period coins in the Mughal style may carry frozen (fixed) dates; this record does not say whether 1220 is frozen.

examples.holder: National Museum of American History, Smithsonian Institution (National Numismatic Collection)
examples.licence: CC0 (metadata_usage access as stated); no image online
examples.material: gold coin
examples.written_date: 1109(41) (cataloged: Hijri year with regnal year 41 in parentheses)
examples.method: Tabular Hijri: AH 1109 = 20 July 1697 to 9 July 1698. Regnal year (san julūs) 41 of Aurangzeb, counted in lunar years from his accession in Ramaḍān 1068, ran from about Ramaḍān 1108 to Shaʿbān 1109, so the coin was struck in the first eight months of AH 1109: about July 1697 to March 1698.
examples.where_on_object: coin faces (Hijri year on one side, regnal year on the other, as usual)
examples.notes: Two dates on one coin narrow each other: the regnal year limits the Hijri year to its overlap. The regnal-year rule should be recomputed from the dating tables' Aurangzeb accession date.

examples.holder: National Museum of American History, Smithsonian Institution (National Numismatic Collection)
examples.licence: CC0 (metadata_usage access as stated); no image online
examples.material: gold coin
examples.written_date: 1170(40) (cataloged)
examples.method: Tabular Hijri: AH 1170 = 26 September 1756 to 14 September 1757. But regnal year 40 with a CE date of 1696–97 fits Aurangzeb (AH 1107–1108), not AH 1170.
examples.notes: Catalog error, probably a transposed '1107' typed as '1170'. No ruler reigned 40 years by AH 1170 (Alamgir II acceded in 1167). A reader should check the Hijri year against the regnal year: they must overlap.

examples.holder: National Museum of American History, Smithsonian Institution (National Numismatic Collection)
examples.licence: CC0 (metadata_usage access as stated); no image online
examples.material: silver coin
examples.written_date: 0038 (cataloged as 'alternate calendar date'; an Ilāhī year, the era of Akbar's later coins)
examples.method: Ilāhī year 1 began at Nauroz (the March equinox) 1556, so year N begins in March of 1555 + N: Ilāhī 38 = March 1593 to March 1594.
examples.where_on_object: coin face (Ilāhī year with a Persian solar month name, usually)
examples.notes: The catalog is one year early, as if it counted Ilāhī year 1 from 1555. The same collection's half rupee NU.69.192.20 ('0047') is cataloged 1600–1601, though Ilāhī 47 = 1602–03. The epoch must be confirmed by the dating tables before publication.

examples.material: steel, wood, gold, silver
examples.written_date: Mauludi era 1222 (as cataloged: 'dated Mauludi era 1222/1793–94 CE')
examples.method: Tipu Sultan's Mauludi era (used 1784–99), counted from the Prophet's birth, which Tipu reckoned as 572 CE: the year begins in CE = Mauludi + 571 and ends in Mauludi + 572. 1222 + 571 = 1793; + 572 = 1794.
examples.where_on_object: not stated in the API record (usually the barrel or lock)
examples.notes: Era not here's list but common on Tipu Sultan's arms and coins (1784–99). A Mauludi year read as Hijri would be about 1807, after Tipu's death in 1799: a clear sign the era is Mauludi. The conversion needs to be added to the dating tables.

examples.material: steel, wood, silver, gold, copper alloy
examples.written_date: Mauludi-era 1225 (as cataloged: 'dated Mauludi-era 1225/1796–97 CE')
examples.method: CE = Mauludi + 571 at the start of the year, + 572 at its end: 1225 + 571 = 1796; + 572 = 1797.
examples.where_on_object: not stated in the API record
examples.notes: Second Mauludi example from the same museum, consistent offset (+571/572).

examples.written_date: 1214 (cataloged as 'alternate calendar date: 1214')
examples.method: Burmese era (Sakkaraj) + 638 = 1852 (+ 639 = 1853 after 1 January, before the April new year).

Shaw (1977) gives 1214 BE '= 1852 AD' in his text and 1853 AD in his catalog, and records the Mandalay mint as formally opened in November 1865; the peacock series is therefore dated 1214 (the year of Mindon's accession) but struck from 1865. 'BE' in numismatic books means Burmese Era, not Buddhist Era.

examples.written_date: A.H. 1042 (as cataloged: 'dated A.H. 1042/1632–33 CE')

examples.written_date: A.H. 1026 (as cataloged: 'dated A.H. 1026/1617–18 CE')
examples.method: Tabular Hijri: AH 1026 = 9 January 1617 to 28 December 1617 (an AH year can fall wholly inside one CE year).

examples.material: black stone
examples.region: India (western India by the donor's Prāgvāṭa lineage)
examples.written_date: Carved inscription, museum translation: 'This image was caused to be made in samvat 1165 in the dark half of the month Jyestha, 5th day, a Wednesday, by Jaluka, son of Avasara ?, in the poravata lineage …' (translation by Phyllis Granoff)
examples.method: Jyeṣṭha falls in May–June (pūrṇimānta Jyeṣṭha badi falls in April–May). Chaitrādi: VS 1165 − 57 = 1108. Kārttikādi: − 56 = 1109.
examples.where_on_object: on the cushion (base) of the image
examples.notes: Weekday test (meeus_check): Jyeṣṭha badi 5 read pūrṇimānta fell on Saturday 2 May 1108 but on Wednesday 21 April 1109; read amānta it fell on Sunday 31 May 1108. The written Wednesday fits a Kārttikādi year with pūrṇimānta months, giving 21 April 1109. Stone, not bronze, but the same donor-inscription formula as Jain metal images.

examples.object: Maharaja Shri Anand Singh-ji and His Consort
examples.material: gum tempera, silver and gold on paper
examples.written_date: '… ustai murāda nijara kīvī dīvālī rī saṃ[vata] 1786 mītī kāti suda 1 …' (museum transliteration)
examples.method: Kārttika śukla 1 falls in October–November, before 1 January: VS 1786 − 57 = 1729 under both Chaitrādi and Kārttikādi years (it is the Kārttikādi new-year day). meeus_check: 23 October 1729, the day after the Diwali new moon.

examples.object: Maharao Ram Singh II of Kota (r. 1828–66) Hunting Buffalo
examples.material: gum tempera, gold and silver on paper
examples.written_date: '… darabāra kotā ko samata 1889' and '… chabī darabāra sarī rāma sīga jī rī cha samata 1889 posa badi 5' (museum transliteration)

examples.object: Muktâvalî nâṭikâ (Bengali play by Saurîndramohana Ṭhâkura [Sourindro Mohun Tagore], 1840–1914), printed book
examples.licence: CC0 (metadata_usage access as stated); no image online
examples.material: printed book (paper), 3 p. l., 61 p., 18 cm
examples.written_date: 1283 (cataloged imprint date: '1283 [san, i.e. 1875]'; note: 'Date in the Bengali San era.')
examples.method: Bengali San + 593 from the mid-April new year (Baiśākh 1) to 31 December, + 594 from 1 January to mid-April: San 1283 = April 1876 to April 1877.

gaps: Paleographic second source for 18th–19th-century digit shapes in each script (older forms of 1, 5, 8, 9): Bühler's plates stop in the 12th century and Ojha's numeral plates were not read; all modern-digit entries are single-sourced (Unicode/CLDR).
Burmese-language and Sinhala-language sources: none read (web search budget exhausted). Burmese and Sinhala script spellings of era words and Burmese months are from general knowledge and flagged.
Urdu convention of writing ء after a Christian year and ھ after a Hijri year: not found in a source read.

Malayalam-language source for Kollam spellings (ml.wikipedia used only as a cross-check; the Kerala government encyclopedia site was unreachable); traditional abbreviations കൊ.വ. and ക്രി.വ. unconfirmed.
Gujarati-language source for Kārttikādi practice and Gujarati spellings (સંવત, સુદ, વદ); Kutch-specific new-year practice (Āṣāḍhī bīj) not confirmed from any source read.
Indian national calendar: Government of India pages could not be reached; adoption date 22 March 1957 not confirmed from an official text.
Vīra Nirvāṇa Saṃvat rests on Ojha alone among sources read (+527); modern new-year day (after Dīpāvalī) not confirmed.
Buddhist era: the point in the year at which Ceylon and Burma change the BE number (Vesak/Kason vs 1 January vs Thingyan) not established.
Nepal Samvat: one-year disagreement (Ojha +878/879 vs Pillai and modern usage +879/880) unresolved from sources read.

Mughal rulers: day-level accession dates rest on Whitehead (Brown 1920 copies him); a second independent source (Persian chronicles, Hodivala) was not read. Shah Alam II's accession day not established. Jahangir's RY 1 boundary and Shah Jahan's regnal-year reckoning (solar vs lunar) not settled.
Hyderabad (Nizam's) Fasli calendar with Persian month names not researched.
The 60-year (Bṛhaspati) cycle year names used in Tamil and Telugu dates are not tabulated here.
Kaṭapayādi letter-numerals (Kerala) are noted by Bühler but not tabulated.
dates.rulers_note: Dates follow Whitehead (1914), who gives the Hijri day:month:year with weekday; his A.D. dates are Julian (O.S.) to 1752 and Gregorian (N.S.) after, and every pair was recomputed here with the tabular Hijri calendar (civil epoch 16 July 622 O.S.). accession_ce is in the calendar Whitehead used; accession_ce_gregorian is always given. Day-level dates rest on Whitehead alone unless another source is listed; reign years (A.H./A.D.) are confirmed by Lane-Poole (1892). Claimants and interim rulers (Dawar Bakhsh, Aʿẓam Shah, Shah Jahan III, Nīkū-siyar, Ibrāhīm, Bīdār Bakht) struck few or no coins; their regnal years are 1 (rarely 2).

sources.name: Weekday and tithi check computed for this file: lunar and solar longitudes after J. Meeus, Astronomical Algorithms (2nd ed., 1998), ch. 25 and 47 (main periodic terms), Lahiri ayanamsa approximated, tithi read at local sunrise
sources.notes: Approximate (error well under an hour of tithi time except near boundaries). Used only to test which reckoning a stated weekday fits. Every such result should be confirmed against Sewell and Dikshit, The Indian Calendar (1896) or Swamikannu Pillai, Indian Ephemeris before publication. figures.title: Figures in Indian, Burmese and Himalayan art, by what they hold and ride

rows.name: Shiva
rows.features_other: Tiger or leopard skin worn as a garment; a man's earring in the right ear and a woman's in the left; a blue scar on the throat (Nilakantha). In Pahari paintings his skin is usually white or ash-grey (token wanted: white or ash-smeared skin), with three horizontal ash lines on the brow.
rows.identify_by: Matted hair piled up with a crescent moon (often with a small river-goddess face), a third eye, and in four-armed images the back hands holding an axe and a deer (or a drum and trident). In paintings: an ascetic with white, ash-smeared skin, tiger skin, snake at the neck and a trident.

look_alikes.name: vishnu
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Four-armed standing Vishnu holds the discus and conch in his back hands and wears a tall cylindrical crown; Shiva's back hands hold axe and deer (or drum and trident) and his hair is a pile of matted locks with a crescent.

look_alikes.name: chandrashekhara
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Chandrashekhara is the standard four-armed standing Shiva of South Indian bronzes; use that row for a lone standing bronze.

look_alikes.name: adhikaranandi
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Adhikaranandi looks like Chandrashekhara but his front hands are joined in salutation.

rows.regions_styles: All of India and Nepal. Bronzes: Chola and later Tamil Nadu (with Kerala and Karnataka variants), Kashmir, Himachal; stone: everywhere; paintings: Pahari (Chamba, Kangra, Mandi), Rajasthan, Kalighat (Kolkata), Mithila.
rows.dating_clues: Style places an image in a region and broad period (Chola, Pala, Kashmir); it cannot by itself show that a given piece is old.
rows.cautions: An identification names the figure; it says nothing about age, or whether the item is old or a recent casting. Traditional forms are still made: Gangoly (1915) records hereditary bronze-casters at Swamimalai near Kumbakonam and illustrates a Nataraja cast by a Swamimalai sculptor in 1909; the Met holds a Gangadhara bronze dated 1945 (Chennai). Items over 100 years old count as antiquities under India's Antiquities and Art Treasures Act 1972, which bars their export except by the Government; stolen South Indian temple bronzes have been returned to India (the National Gallery of Australia's Chola Nataraja, bought in 2008, went back in 2014). Facts only, not legal advice.

facts.text: Sastri's general (Rudra) form of Shiva: matted locks in a crown with the crescent on the left and the face of Ganga over the hair, three eyes, a tiger skin, a woman's earring in the left ear and a man's in the right, and a blue scar on the neck.
facts.quote: The left ear of the god wears a woman's ornament called lamba-patra, while the right wears a man's ornament called makara-kundala.

facts.text: Coomaraswamy lists features that belong to Shiva generally, not to one form: braided yogi's locks, the skull of Brahma, Ganga in the hair, cobras, the two different earrings, four arms.
facts.quote: Such are the braided locks, as of a yogi : the Cassia garland: the skull of Brahma : the figure of Ganga ... : the cobras: the different earrings, betokening the dual nature of Mahadev

facts.text: Standing four-armed images: the front hands show protection (fear-not) and boon-giving and the back hands hold the axe (tanka) and antelope.
facts.quote: The fore-arms exhibit the protecting and the boon-giving postures ; while the hind arms hold the tanka and the antelope.

facts.text: In Pahari paintings Shiva is usually painted white, with a snake round his neck, a third eye, a trident, an animal-skin garment and the crescent at his brow; Chamba paintings keep a white, three-quarter-view Shiva for over a century.
facts.quote: he seems alluringly approachable despite his white body, the snake around his neck, his third eye, trident weapon, animal-skin garment, and the crescent moon at his brow.

facts.text: Cleveland describes a Pahari Shiva as ash-smeared with triple-line sectarian marks, a garland of severed heads and a leopard-skin loincloth (Shiva and Devi on Gajasura's hide, 1952.587).
facts.quote: white skin smeared with ash from funeral pyres, the third eye of true knowledge, triple-line sectarian marks, a garland of severed heads, and the leopard-skin loincloth.

rows.name: Shiva Chandrashekhara (standing Shiva)
rows.features_other: Stands straight with level feet (samapada) on a lotus base; the crescent sits on one side of the matted-hair crown (jatamakuta). With Uma at his side he may embrace her with the lower left arm.
rows.identify_by: The plain four-armed standing Shiva of South Indian bronzes: back hands holding axe and deer (sometimes drum or trident), front hands in fear-not and boon-giving, feet level, no animal and no dance.

look_alikes.name: vishnu
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Vishnu's back hands hold discus and conch and he wears a tall crown (kirita); Chandrashekhara holds axe and deer and wears piled matted hair with a crescent.

look_alikes.name: adhikaranandi
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Same axe and deer in the back hands, but Adhikaranandi's front hands are joined at the chest in salutation.

look_alikes.name: vrishabhantika
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Vrishabhantika stands with legs crossed or one leg bent and rests a bent arm high, on the bull (often lost); Chandrashekhara stands straight with both front hands in gestures.

look_alikes.name: lingodbhava
look_alikes.how_to_tell: The same figure emerging from a linga, feet hidden, with a swan and a boar at the sides, is Lingodbhava.

rows.regions_styles: South Indian bronzes and temple stone, Chola (c. 900–1300) and later; modern castings from Tamil Nadu workshops.
rows.dating_clues: The form has been made continuously from Chola times to now; form alone dates nothing.
rows.cautions: An identification names the figure; it says nothing about age, or whether the item is old or a recent casting. Traditional forms are still made: Gangoly (1915) records hereditary bronze-casters at Swamimalai near Kumbakonam and illustrates a Nataraja cast by a Swamimalai sculptor in 1909; the Met holds a Gangadhara bronze dated 1945 (Chennai). Items over 100 years old count as antiquities under India's Antiquities and Art Treasures Act 1972, which bars their export except by the Government; stolen South Indian temple bronzes have been returned to India (the National Gallery of Australia's Chola Nataraja, bought in 2008, went back in 2014). Facts only, not legal advice.

facts.text: Chandrashekhara alone stands with level feet, holding the antelope and the drum (or axe) in his back arms and showing fear-not and boon-giving with the front arms.
facts.quote: When alone, he stands on the pedestal with level feet (samapada), holding the antelope and the kettle-drum (or, axe) in his back arms and presenting the abhaya and the varada postures in the fore-arms.

facts.text: Rao describes Adhikaranandi as made exactly like Chandrashekharamurti with axe and deer in the back hands, except that the front hands are in salutation; this confirms the axe and deer as Chandrashekhara's back-hand attributes.
facts.quote: sculptured precisely like Siva in the aspect of Chandrasekharamurti, carrying the parasu and the mriga in the back right and left hands respectively

facts.text: With the goddess (Alingana form) the lower left arm passes round the goddess; some Agamas allow it only to reach her arm. A Bagali example holds trident and drum instead of axe and deer.
facts.quote: The right lower hand shows the abhaya posture and the left lower passes round the back of the yielding goddess

rows.name: Shiva Nataraja (Lord of Dance)
rows.features_other: Locks fanned out on both sides of the head (or tied into a crown); a scarf flying; the dwarf (Apasmara or Muyalaka) lies on a double lotus base, often holding a snake; one earring male, one female; peacock-feather or Cassia crest. Rarer Tamil forms have eight arms (Kalika-tandava) or a leg raised to the head (Urdhva-tandava).
rows.identify_by: A four-armed Shiva dancing on one leg on a prostrate dwarf inside a ring of flames: upper hands hold drum and fire, the lower right shows fear-not and the lower left points across to the raised left foot.

look_alikes.name: natesha
look_alikes.how_to_tell: North and Central Indian dancing Shivas (Natesha) usually have eight or more arms, no flame ring and no dwarf under the foot.

look_alikes.name: ganesha_dancing
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Same pose, elephant head and pot belly: dancing Ganesha.

look_alikes.name: gajasamhara
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Eight arms stretching an elephant hide behind him, foot on the elephant's head: Gajasamhara, not Nataraja.

look_alikes.name: sambandar
look_alikes.how_to_tell: A small dancing child with one leg raised is the saint Sambandar, two-armed and without drum or fire.

look_alikes.name: sandhya_tandava
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Sastri's evening dance (Sandhya-tandava) has no dwarf under the foot.

rows.regions_styles: Tamil Nadu bronzes, Chola (c. 900–1300), then Vijayanagara and Nayaka; still cast at Swamimalai. Gangoly notes the eight-armed Nataraja is rare in the Tamil country.
rows.dating_clues: Many sizes; Coomaraswamy says rarely over four feet. Style (fanned locks vs tied crown, ring with or without flame tongues) varies by period and workshop, but form cannot date a piece.
rows.cautions: An identification names the figure; it says nothing about age, or whether the item is old or a recent casting. Traditional forms are still made: Gangoly (1915) records hereditary bronze-casters at Swamimalai near Kumbakonam and illustrates a Nataraja cast by a Swamimalai sculptor in 1909; the Met holds a Gangadhara bronze dated 1945 (Chennai). Items over 100 years old count as antiquities under India's Antiquities and Art Treasures Act 1972, which bars their export except by the Government; stolen South Indian temple bronzes have been returned to India (the National Gallery of Australia's Chola Nataraja, bought in 2008, went back in 2014). Facts only, not legal advice. Natarajas are the most reproduced Indian bronze type; tourist castings are sold as old.

facts.text: The upper right hand holds the drum, the lower right is raised in fear-not, one left hand holds fire and the other points down toward the dwarf; the left foot is raised.
facts.quote: One right hand holds a drum, the other is uplifted in the sign of do not fear: one left hand holds fire, the other points down upon the demon Muyalaka

facts.text: The lower left hand thrown across the body and pointing down is called gaja-hasta, the elephant-trunk hand.
facts.quote: The position of this hand is known as gaja-hasta, "the elephant-trunk."

facts.text: He dances on the back of the dwarf demon Apasmara (Musalagan, Muyalaka); Cleveland calls the dwarf a figure personifying ignorance.
facts.quote: With every step in his dance, he lands on a dwarfish figure personifying ignorance.

facts.text: The aureola is ringed with flames like the fire held in the left hand; the pedestal is a double lotus.
facts.quote: being surmounted all round with flames of fire similar to the one which is held in the pot or cup in one of the two left arms of the image.

facts.text: In the hair are a cobra, a skull, the mermaid-like figure of Ganga and the crescent moon.
facts.quote: In His hair may be seen a wreathing cobra, a skull, and the mermaid figure of Ganga ; upon it rests the crescent moon

facts.text: The Agamas speak of seven dances; in the evening dance (Sandhya-tandava) the dwarf is absent, and in the Kalika-tandava Shiva has eight arms.
facts.quote: The Agamas speak of seven dancing postures of Siva.

facts.text: Gangoly found the hereditary image-makers of Swamimalai, three miles west of Kumbakonam, still at work in 1915, and compares a Nataraja cast at the Victoria Technical Institute by a Swamimalai sculptor in 1909.
facts.quote: which was executed at the Victoria Technical Institute by a sculptor from Swamimalai in 1909.

facts.text: India's Antiquities and Art Treasures Act 1972 bars anyone but the Central Government (or its authorised agency) from exporting any antiquity or art treasure; the Act's definitions use a 100-year threshold.
facts.quote: it shall not be lawful for any person, other than the Central Government or any authority or agency authorised by the Central Government in this behalf, to export any antiquity or art treasure.

facts.text: The National Gallery of Australia bought a Chola bronze Nataraja (c. 1100) from the New York dealer Subhash Kapoor in 2008 for AUD 5.6 million; it had been stolen in January 2006 from a temple at Sripuranthan, Ariyalur district, Tamil Nadu. The Gallery removed it from display in March 2014 and the Australian Prime Minister returned it to India in September 2014.
facts.quote: In 2014, the Gallery relinquished the work, and the Australian Prime Minister returned it to India.

rows.name: Dancing Shiva of North and Central India (Natesha)
rows.features_other: Usually a stone relief or temple niche figure, the bull Nandi and musicians often at his feet; no ring of fire and no dwarf underfoot in most examples. Attributes vary from piece to piece.
rows.identify_by: A many-armed dancing Shiva in stone, often with Nandi and drummers at his feet, without the Tamil flame ring and dwarf.

look_alikes.name: nataraja
look_alikes.how_to_tell: The Tamil Nataraja has four arms, a ring of flames and a dwarf underfoot.

look_alikes.name: ganesha_dancing
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Elephant head.

look_alikes.name: gajasamhara
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Holds an elephant hide stretched behind him.

rows.regions_styles: Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh (Pratihara, Chandela), Odisha, Bengal (Pala), Nepal.
rows.dating_clues: Regional temple styles; dating needs a specialist.
rows.cautions: An identification names the figure; it says nothing about age, or whether the item is old or a recent casting. Stone temple sculpture of this kind is a common target of theft; Items over 100 years old count as antiquities under India's Antiquities and Art Treasures Act 1972, which bars their export except by the Government; stolen South Indian temple bronzes have been returned to India (the National Gallery of Australia's Chola Nataraja, bought in 2008, went back in 2014). Facts only, not legal advice.

facts.text: Museum examples of the type: an eight-armed dancing Shiva between two pillars (Cleveland 1958.288, Chandela, 10th–11th century) and a dancing Shiva (Natesha) from Rajasthan (AIC 1986.1288, 10th/11th century).
Sastri contrasts the Tamil Ananda-tandava with other Agamic dances, e.g. the eight-armed Kalika-tandava, showing that dancing Shiva is not always four-armed.
facts.quote: In the fifth form, called Kalika-tandava, the god has only two eyes, but eight arms.

rows.name: Somaskanda (Shiva, Uma and the child Skanda)
rows.features_other: Group on one pedestal: four-armed Shiva seated at ease (right leg pendant), two-armed Uma on his left (left leg pendant), and between them the small child Skanda, standing, seated, on Uma's lap or dancing. Skanda was often cast separately and is often missing.
rows.identify_by: Shiva and Uma seated side by side on one base with a small child between them.

look_alikes.name: umasahita
look_alikes.how_to_tell: The same pair without the child is Umasahita; a Somaskanda that has lost its separately cast Skanda looks the same.

look_alikes.name: uma_maheshvara
look_alikes.how_to_tell: In Uma-Maheshvara Uma sits on Shiva's lap and he embraces her; in Somaskanda they sit apart.

look_alikes.name: vrisharudha
look_alikes.how_to_tell: A group with the bull is Vrisharudha or Vrishabhantika.

rows.regions_styles: Tamil Nadu: Pallava stone panels behind the linga (Mahabalipuram, Kanchi) and Chola bronzes; one of the commonest processional bronze groups.
rows.dating_clues: Sastri notes the panel behind the linga is Pallava and is not found in later Chola temples; bronzes continue to today.
rows.cautions: An identification names the figure; it says nothing about age, or whether the item is old or a recent casting. Traditional forms are still made: Gangoly (1915) records hereditary bronze-casters at Swamimalai near Kumbakonam and illustrates a Nataraja cast by a Swamimalai sculptor in 1909; the Met holds a Gangadhara bronze dated 1945 (Chennai). Items over 100 years old count as antiquities under India's Antiquities and Art Treasures Act 1972, which bars their export except by the Government; stolen South Indian temple bronzes have been returned to India (the National Gallery of Australia's Chola Nataraja, bought in 2008, went back in 2014). Facts only, not legal advice. Groups are often split up: a lone seated Shiva, a lone seated or standing Uma, or a small dancing child may each come from a Somaskanda.

facts.text: On one pedestal Shiva and Uma are seated with the child Skanda standing or seated between them; Sastri calls it the commonest of Shiva's sportive forms.
facts.quote: On one and the same pedestal are seen Siva and Uma with the child Skanda standing (or seated) between them.

facts.text: Rao: the pair alone is Umasahita; with the child added between them it is Somaskanda, and the child may stand, sit on the seat or on Uma's lap, or dance.
facts.quote: between these, there is the additional figure of the child Skanda. The figure of Skanda may be standing, sitting on the seat or on the lap of Umadevi, or dancing

facts.text: Both sit at ease with one leg hanging down, the right in the case of Shiva and the left in the case of Parvati.
facts.quote: Both the god and the goddess are seated comfortably (sukhasana), with one leg (right in the case of Siva and left in the case of Parvati) hanging down

facts.text: Open-license museum groups exist: Met 1982.220.10 (Tamil Nadu, early 11th century) and AIC 1966.334 (Vijayanagara, about 1400).

rows.name: Umasahita (Shiva seated beside Uma)
rows.features_other: Four-armed Shiva and two-armed Uma seated side by side on one seat or pedestal, not touching.
rows.identify_by: Shiva and Uma seated side by side, apart, with no child between them.

look_alikes.name: somaskanda
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Somaskanda has the child Skanda between them (often lost).

look_alikes.name: uma_maheshvara
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Uma-Maheshvara: Uma on Shiva's knee, in his embrace.

rows.regions_styles: South India, bronze and stone; Mahabalipuram panels.
rows.dating_clues: As Somaskanda.
rows.cautions: An identification names the figure; it says nothing about age, or whether the item is old or a recent casting. Traditional forms are still made: Gangoly (1915) records hereditary bronze-casters at Swamimalai near Kumbakonam and illustrates a Nataraja cast by a Swamimalai sculptor in 1909; the Met holds a Gangadhara bronze dated 1945 (Chennai). Facts only, not legal advice. A shared base with an empty place between the two figures may once have held a Skanda; it cannot be proven from the base alone.

facts.text: Rao: Shiva and Uma in these relative positions, with prabhamandala, are the Uma-sahitamurti; adding the child makes it Somaskanda.
facts.quote: is known as the Uma-sahitamurti. In the case of the Somaskandamurti, the same relative positions are maintained by the figures of Siva and Uma

facts.text: Sastri describes Sukhasana or Umasahita panels at Mahabalipuram with Shiva seated on a lion-pillared pedestal with the bull between.
facts.quote: Sukhasana or Umasahita

rows.name: Uma-Maheshvara (Shiva embracing Parvati)
rows.features_other: Uma sits on Shiva's left knee; his left arm goes round her shoulder and her right arm round him; Nandi (bull) and Uma's lion often lie under the seat, with small Ganesha and Skanda at the ends of the base.
rows.identify_by: Shiva seated with Parvati on his left knee in a mutual embrace, usually with the bull (and often a lion) below.

look_alikes.name: umasahita
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Umasahita sits apart from Uma.

look_alikes.name: lakshmi_narayana
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Vishnu with Lakshmi on his knee (Lakshmi-Narayana) has Garuda below and holds discus and conch; Uma-Maheshvara has the bull and Shiva's trident.

look_alikes.name: ardhanarishvara
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Ardhanarishvara is one body, half male and half female, not two figures.

rows.regions_styles: Mostly North and East India and Nepal: Pala stone (Bihar, Bengal), Uttarakhand, Kashmir, Nepalese bronze; Karnataka (Haveri) and Trivandrum ivory per Rao.
rows.dating_clues: Pala-style black stone steles and Nepalese bronzes are repeatedly copied; style needs a specialist.
rows.cautions: An identification names the figure; it says nothing about age, or whether the item is old or a recent casting. Stone temple sculpture of this kind is a common target of theft; Items over 100 years old count as antiquities under India's Antiquities and Art Treasures Act 1972, which bars their export except by the Government; stolen South Indian temple bronzes have been returned to India (the National Gallery of Australia's Chola Nataraja, bought in 2008, went back in 2014). Facts only, not legal advice. Rao (1916) illustrates an Umamaheshvara newly carved in ivory at the Trivandrum School of Arts: traditional forms were being made fresh, in ivory too, a century ago. Ivory raises its own legal limits.

facts.text: At Haveri Uma sits on Shiva's left lap and embraces him; Shiva holds trident, drum and rosary in three hands and throws the fourth round Uma's shoulder.
facts.quote: Uma is seated on the left lap of Siva and embraces him with her right hand ... the remaining hand is thrown in embrace over the left shoulder of Uma.

facts.text: The Art Institute of Chicago's Madhya Pradesh relief shows Shiva seated in embrace with Uma on the bull Nandi.
facts.quote: Here, he is seated on his bull Nandi, with Uma resting on Shiva

facts.text: Open examples catalogued as Uma-Maheshvara: Cleveland 2011.208 (Almora, 10th century), Cleveland 1964.50 (Pala, 9th century), Met 1978.253 (Bihar, 10th century).
Rao illustrates an ivory Umamaheshvaramurti made at the Trivandrum School of Arts.
facts.quote: Umamahesvaramurti ; Ivory: Trivandram School of Arts.

rows.name: Ardhanarishvara (Shiva half woman)
other_names: the Lord who is half woman
rows.features_other: Right half male (matted locks, flat chest, tiger skin to the knee, male earring); left half female (crown or hair-knot, one full breast, wide hip, long skirt, woman's earring, often only one left arm holding a flower or mirror). Often leans on the bull with the right elbow.
rows.identify_by: One figure split down the middle: male right side, female left side with a single breast and a long skirt.

look_alikes.name: harihara
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Harihara is half Shiva, half Vishnu: both halves male, the left half with Vishnu's tall crown and discus or conch.

look_alikes.name: uma_maheshvara
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Two separate figures embracing.

look_alikes.name: vrishabhantika
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Leans on the bull like Vrishabhantika but has the female left half.

rows.regions_styles: All India and Nepal; Chola bronzes and stone (Tamil Nadu), Nepal, Pahari and Bengal paintings (Kalighat Ardhanarishvara).
rows.dating_clues: Form persists to the present.
rows.cautions: An identification names the figure; it says nothing about age, or whether the item is old or a recent casting.
