Facts only, not legal advice.

facts.text: The left half is the woman (Parvati) and the right half the man (Shiva), with jewelry and dress distinguished side by side.
facts.quote: an image of which the left half represents the woman (Parvati) and the right half, the male (Siva).

facts.text: The image may have two, three or four arms; one right arm may rest bent on the bull's head.
facts.quote: The image of Arddhanarisvara may have two, three or four arms.

facts.text: On Cleveland's Chola trident finial the female side has crown, earring, full breast, broad hips, long skirt and only one arm; the male side holds an axe and leans on the bull.
facts.quote: The female side has a jeweled crown, earring, full breast, broad hips, long skirt, and only one arm.

facts.text: Sastri: tiger skin to the knee on the right side; fine muslin to the ankle on the left; right hands hold a hatchet and show protection, the upper left holds a flower.
facts.quote: The drapery on the right side is the tiger's skin of Siva reaching only to the knee, while on the left side it is the finely embroidered muslin

rows.name: Bhikshatana (Shiva the naked beggar)
rows.features_other: Naked but for snakes round the waist; wears sandals; a bell tied at the ankle; the lower right hand reaches down to a leaping antelope; a trident decked with peacock feathers over the left shoulder; a pot-bellied dwarf carries his begging bowl on his head.
rows.identify_by: A naked, walking four-armed Shiva in sandals, his lower right hand offering grass to a leaping deer, a skull bowl in a left hand and a small dwarf with a bowl on his head beside him.

look_alikes.name: kankala
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Kankala is the same walking beggar but clothed, carrying a staff with a skeleton.

look_alikes.name: vinadhara
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Vinadhara Dakshinamurti stands still with hands posed for a vina and is clothed.

look_alikes.name: annapurna
look_alikes.how_to_tell: In Bengal paintings Shiva begs from Annapurna, who ladles food into his bowl.

rows.regions_styles: Tamil Nadu bronzes and temple niches (Tanjore big temple south wall); Karnataka; Chola onward.
rows.dating_clues: Form persists; the figure's nudity makes it a popular modern casting subject.
rows.cautions: An identification names the figure; it says nothing about age, or whether the item is old or a recent casting. Traditional forms are still made: Gangoly (1915) records hereditary bronze-casters at Swamimalai near Kumbakonam and illustrates a Nataraja cast by a Swamimalai sculptor in 1909; the Met holds a Gangadhara bronze dated 1945 (Chennai). Items over 100 years old count as antiquities under India's Antiquities and Art Treasures Act 1972, which bars their export except by the Government; stolen South Indian temple bronzes have been returned to India (the National Gallery of Australia's Chola Nataraja, bought in 2008, went back in 2014). Facts only, not legal advice.

facts.text: Having cut off a head of Brahma, Shiva had to wander as a naked beggar until the skull fell from his hand.
facts.quote: Siva had to wander about as a naked beggar (bhikshatana)

facts.text: Rao: no clothing at all, not even a waist band; a snake is tied round the waist; front left hand carries the skull (kapala), back right the drum.
facts.quote: But there should be no kind of clothing on the person of Siva, not even the waist zone. Instead of this latter there should be a snake tied round the waist

facts.text: Sastri: the lower right hand touches an antelope's mouth, the upper right holds the drum; he stands on sandals, a bell at the ankle; the dwarf Kundodara carries a begging bowl on his head.
facts.quote: A demon called Kundodara, with protruding teeth, stands on the left side of the god, carrying on his head a begging bowl.

facts.text: Rao and Sastri agree that Bhikshatana and Kankala share the same walking posture.
facts.quote: the general posture of Siva is the same as in the Kankalamurti aspect

rows.name: Kankalamurti (Shiva with the skeleton staff)
rows.features_other: Clothed (unlike Bhikshatana); carries the skeleton (kankala) on a staff, peacock feathers; a knife at the waist; followed by women, demons, birds and beasts.
rows.identify_by: A walking, clothed four-armed Shiva with a staff carrying a skeleton, surrounded by admiring women and animals.

look_alikes.name: bhikshatana
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Bhikshatana is naked and holds a skull bowl; Kankala is draped and carries the skeleton staff.

rows.regions_styles: Tamil Nadu bronzes (Tenkasi) and stone (Dharasuram).
rows.dating_clues: As Bhikshatana.
rows.cautions: An identification names the figure; it says nothing about age, or whether the item is old or a recent casting. Traditional forms are still made: Gangoly (1915) records hereditary bronze-casters at Swamimalai near Kumbakonam and illustrates a Nataraja cast by a Swamimalai sculptor in 1909; the Met holds a Gangadhara bronze dated 1945 (Chennai). Facts only, not legal advice.

facts.text: Kankalamurti is closely allied to Bhikshatana and almost the same in appearance; per the Mayamata he is draped in fine cloth and holds peacock feathers and the skeleton.
facts.quote: Kankalamurti is a form closely allied to Bhikshatana and almost similar in appearance.

rows.name: Dakshinamurti (Shiva the teacher)
rows.features_other: Seated under a banyan tree, right foot on the dwarf Apasmara, left leg folded across; sages seated at his feet; sometimes the bull and forest animals. Attributes vary: rosary, water pot, book, antelope; Agamic texts also give fire and snake.
rows.identify_by: A youthful four-armed Shiva seated under a banyan tree, one foot on a dwarf, a hand in the teaching gesture, with sages at his feet.

look_alikes.name: vinadhara
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Vinadhara is a Dakshinamurti whose front hands play a vina (usually lost), often standing.

look_alikes.name: nataraja
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Both have a dwarf underfoot, but Nataraja dances on one leg.

look_alikes.name: buddha
look_alikes.how_to_tell: A seated teacher under a tree with a teaching gesture but no third eye, crescent, deer or dwarf, and with a cranial bump, is a Buddha.

rows.regions_styles: Tamil Nadu: Chola temple niche on the south wall of the central shrine; stone and bronze.
rows.dating_clues: Placement on the south wall is a temple convention, not a date.
rows.cautions: An identification names the figure; it says nothing about age, or whether the item is old or a recent casting. Stone temple sculpture of this kind is a common target of theft; Items over 100 years old count as antiquities under India's Antiquities and Art Treasures Act 1972, which bars their export except by the Government; stolen South Indian temple bronzes have been returned to India (the National Gallery of Australia's Chola Nataraja, bought in 2008, went back in 2014). Facts only, not legal advice.

facts.text: He is a youthful teacher seated beneath a banyan tree, teaching aged pupils by his silence.
facts.quote: He is always conceived to be a youthful teacher, seated beneath a banyan tree, teaching aged pupils and removing their doubts by his very silence.

facts.text: The right leg is bent and placed on the dark dwarf Apasmara, the left folded across the right thigh.
facts.quote: his right leg bent vertically at the knee and placed on the body of the dark demon Apasmara and the left leg bent across so as to rest upon the right thigh.

facts.text: In Chola temples the image usually occupies a niche on the south wall of the central shrine.
facts.quote: In Chola temples this image generally occupies a niche in the south wall of the central shrine.

facts.text: Rao (from the Agamas): seated under a banyan, on the right side of its trunk, on a seat covered with tiger skin, surrounded by rishis.
facts.quote: under a banyan tree, on the right side of its trunk, on a jewelled pitha covered with a tiger's skin and he should present a benign look

facts.text: Attributes vary between images: rosary and water pot in the back hands, or water pot and antelope above with rosary (in jnana-mudra) and book below.
facts.quote: the upper hands hold the water-pot and the antelope and the lower hands the rosary (with jnana-mudra) and the book

rows.name: Vinadhara Dakshinamurti (Shiva as Lord of Music)
rows.features_other: Front hands held as if playing a vina (stick zither) across the body; the vina was cast separately and is usually missing. Token wanted: vina (stringed instrument).
rows.identify_by: A standing four-armed Shiva with axe and antelope above and both lower hands posed, empty, as if plucking an instrument held across the body.

look_alikes.name: tripurantaka
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Tripurantaka's empty hands are posed for a bow (left raised) and an arrow (right low), not for an instrument held across the chest.

look_alikes.name: vrishabhantika
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Vrishabhantika rests a bent arm high on a (lost) bull.

look_alikes.name: saptamatrikas
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Shiva playing a vina also leads panels of the Seven Mothers (AIC 2021.206).

rows.regions_styles: Chola bronzes, Tamil Nadu (Vadaranyam, Madras Museum examples in Rao).
rows.dating_clues: As other Chola forms.

Facts only, not legal advice.

facts.text: Cleveland's Chola 'Shiva as Lord of Music' (1971.117): the vina is missing but the lowered hands are in the position of playing it; the other attributes are the axe and rearing antelope.
facts.quote: He holds a stringed instrument called the vina, which is missing in this example, but the fingers of his lowered hands are in the position of playing it.

facts.text: Rao and Sastri list Vinadhara as a form of Dakshinamurti and illustrate bronze and stone examples.
facts.quote: Vinadhara-Dakshinamurti

rows.name: Lingodbhava (Shiva appearing in the pillar of fire)
rows.features_other: Shiva in Chandrashekhara form framed in an opening of a tall linga, legs below the knees or ankles hidden; a swan (Brahma) flies up at one top corner and a boar (Vishnu) digs down at the foot; Brahma and Vishnu may also stand at the sides with hands joined.
rows.identify_by: Shiva's upper body seen inside a tall linga, with a swan above and a boar below.

look_alikes.name: mukhalinga
look_alikes.how_to_tell: A mukhalinga shows only a face or faces on the linga shaft, not a four-armed figure.

look_alikes.name: chandrashekhara
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Same figure, but free-standing with feet visible.

rows.regions_styles: Tamil Nadu: Chola temple niche on the west wall of the central shrine; stone, rarely bronze.
rows.dating_clues: Stone niche figure; Met 62.81 is catalogued late 12th–13th century.
rows.cautions: An identification names the figure; it says nothing about age, or whether the item is old or a recent casting. Stone temple sculpture of this kind is a common target of theft; Items over 100 years old count as antiquities under India's Antiquities and Art Treasures Act 1972, which bars their export except by the Government; stolen South Indian temple bronzes have been returned to India (the National Gallery of Australia's Chola Nataraja, bought in 2008, went back in 2014). Facts only, not legal advice.

facts.text: Shiva is shown within a huge linga with the feet below the ankles hidden; Brahma as a swan soars up and Vishnu as a boar delves down.
facts.quote: he is represented within a huge linga, the portion of the feet below the ankles being hidden in the linga.

facts.text: Placed on the west wall of the central shrine in Chola temples; named Lingapuranadeva in the Tanjore inscriptions.
facts.quote: In the Tanjore inscriptions, Lingodbhava is mentioned by the name Lingapuranadeva

facts.text: Sides differ between sources: Sastri puts the swan on Shiva's left and the boar on the right; Rao's Agama text puts the swan on the right of the linga near the top and the boar on the left at the foot.
facts.quote: On the right of the linga and near its top Brahma should be represented in the shape of a swan (hamsa) while Vishnu should be carved in the form of a boar on the left at the foot

rows.name: Gangadhara (Shiva receiving the Ganges)
rows.features_other: One right arm raised holding out a single lock of hair on which the small Ganga sits with hands joined; the other arm round a sad-faced Parvati; the sage Bhagiratha may pray nearby. In Pahari paintings the river streams from Shiva's topknot.
rows.identify_by: Shiva lifting one long lock of his hair on which a tiny goddess (Ganga) sits, often with Parvati at his side.

look_alikes.name: nataraja
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Ganga also appears small in Nataraja's fanned locks, but he dances.

look_alikes.name: uma_maheshvara
look_alikes.how_to_tell: An embracing pair without the raised lock and tiny goddess.

rows.regions_styles: Tamil Nadu bronzes and stone (Trichinopoly rock-cut panel), Ellora; Pahari paintings of the Descent of the Ganges.
rows.dating_clues: The Met holds a Gangadhara bronze dated 1945 from Chennai: the form was being cast in the 20th century.
rows.cautions: An identification names the figure; it says nothing about age, or whether the item is old or a recent casting. Traditional forms are still made: Gangoly (1915) records hereditary bronze-casters at Swamimalai near Kumbakonam and illustrates a Nataraja cast by a Swamimalai sculptor in 1909; the Met holds a Gangadhara bronze dated 1945 (Chennai). Facts only, not legal advice.

facts.text: One right arm holds up a lock of his hair on which the goddess Ganga is seen; he embraces and consoles Gauri.
facts.quote: One right arm holds up a lock of his hair, on which is seen the goddess Ganga.

facts.text: Rao (Trichinopoly panel): the back right arm is lifted to hold one lock; at its end Ganga sits with hands joined in salutation; a front hand holds a snake and a back hand an antelope.
facts.quote: at the end of this jata is the river goddess Ganges seated with hands folded on her chest in the anjali pose.

facts.text: In Pahari paintings the Ganges flows from Shiva's topknot while Bhagiratha stands on one leg in penance.
facts.quote: the gift of the Ganges River, which flows from Shiva's topknot of hair.

facts.text: The Met's 'Shiva Gangadhara, Bearer of the Ganga' (2009.101) is catalogued as dated 1945, India (Chennai).

rows.name: Vrishabhantika (Shiva leaning on the bull)
rows.features_other: Stands with one leg bent or crossed, the right elbow raised and resting on the head of the bull standing behind him. The bull was often a separate casting; without it the raised, bent arm rests on nothing. Usually with Parvati as a separate figure.
rows.identify_by: A standing Shiva with his right arm bent at elbow height as if leaning on something (the bull), legs relaxed or crossed.

look_alikes.name: ardhanarishvara
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Also leans on the bull, but is half female.

look_alikes.name: vinadhara
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Hands posed for an instrument across the body, not an arm propped up.

look_alikes.name: vrisharudha
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Vrisharudha sits on the bull.

rows.regions_styles: Chola bronzes (Vedaranyam, Tiruvenkadu), Tamil Nadu stone.
rows.dating_clues: As other Chola forms.
rows.cautions: An identification names the figure; it says nothing about age, or whether the item is old or a recent casting. Traditional forms are still made: Gangoly (1915) records hereditary bronze-casters at Swamimalai near Kumbakonam and illustrates a Nataraja cast by a Swamimalai sculptor in 1909; the Met holds a Gangadhara bronze dated 1945 (Chennai). Items over 100 years old count as antiquities under India's Antiquities and Art Treasures Act 1972, which bars their export except by the Government; stolen South Indian temple bronzes have been returned to India (the National Gallery of Australia's Chola Nataraja, bought in 2008, went back in 2014). Facts only, not legal advice. A lone figure with the bent arm is often sold as 'Shiva'; the missing bull is a sign of a separated group.

facts.text: When Shiva stands leaning against the bull and is not mounted on it, the Kasyapa-Silpa calls him Vrishavahana; the right elbow rests on the bull's head.
facts.quote: In this case the elbow (kurpara) of the right hand of Siva rests on the head of the bull

facts.text: Rao on the Vedaranyam bronze: it is the right arm, not the left as the text requires, that rests on the bull's head; this example has only two arms.
facts.quote: it is not the left arm that is resting on the head of the bull but the right.

rows.name: Vrisharudha and Shiva on Nandi (Shiva riding the bull)
rows.features_other: Shiva seated on the bull, right leg hanging, often with Parvati behind or beside him; in Pahari and Kalighat paintings the couple ride a white bull. Ganesha and Skanda may walk alongside in family scenes.
rows.identify_by: Shiva (often with Parvati) seated on a bull.

look_alikes.name: maheshvari
look_alikes.how_to_tell: A goddess alone on a bull, with Shiva's emblems, is Maheshvari, one of the Seven Mothers.

look_alikes.name: uma_maheshvara
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Uma-Maheshvara sits on a throne with the bull lying below, not on its back.

look_alikes.name: nandi
look_alikes.how_to_tell: A bull alone is Nandi.

rows.regions_styles: South Indian stone and bronze; North Indian stone; Pahari, Rajasthani, Kalighat and Mithila paintings.
rows.dating_clues: Painting style, not subject, dates the work.
rows.cautions: An identification names the figure; it says nothing about age, or whether the item is old or a recent casting. Popular prints and 20th-century copies repeat these forms; the painting style, not the figure, is the dating evidence (see the paintings guide).

facts.text: Vrisharudha is Shiva seated on the bull with the right leg hanging and the left resting on the bull; he holds axe and antelope in the upper hands.
facts.quote: Vrisharudha is a figure of Siva seated on the bull with the right leg hanging down and the left bent so as to rest on the bull.

facts.text: AIC's Madhya Pradesh relief (1961.775) shows Shiva seated in embrace with Uma on the bull; Met 1989.362 (Kashmir) shows Shiva and Parvati with Karttikeya, Ganesha and the bull; Cleveland 2005.87 is a 20th-century Mithila 'Shiva and Nandi'.

rows.name: Tripurantaka (Shiva, destroyer of the three cities)
rows.features_other: Stands with one leg bent; the front left hand raised as if gripping a bow and the front right lowered as if holding an arrow; bow and arrow were separate and are usually lost. Some forms put a foot on the dwarf. His consort (Tripurasundari) stands as a separate figure.
rows.identify_by: A standing Shiva whose empty front hands are posed for a bow (left, raised) and an arrow (right), with axe and deer in the back hands.

look_alikes.name: rama
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Rama also poses with bow and arrow but has two arms, a tall crown and no axe or deer.

look_alikes.name: vinadhara
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Hands posed for a vina held across the body.

look_alikes.name: vrishabhantika
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Right arm bent high, resting on the bull.

rows.regions_styles: Chola bronzes (Tamil Nadu, Thanjavur district) and stone; Madurai.
rows.dating_clues: Met 2018.757 (Shiva Tripuravijaya) is catalogued ca. 1000–1020.
rows.cautions: An identification names the figure; it says nothing about age, or whether the item is old or a recent casting. facts.text: Images of Tripurantaka have the right leg on the pedestal and the left bent; the front right hand holds the arrow and the left the bow; the others hold axe and deer.
facts.quote: The right fore-hand in the simha-karna posture holds the arrow and the left fore-arm, the bow. The other hands hold the tanka (or the axe) and the deer respectively.

facts.text: Rao gives several Agamic variants, one with the left foot on the Apasmara dwarf, another with the front hands grasping the point and tail of the arrow.
facts.quote: In the second form of Tripurantakamurti the left foot of Siva must be kept upon Apasmara-purusha

rows.name: Kalyanasundara (wedding of Shiva and Parvati)
rows.features_other: Shiva takes Parvati's right hand in his right (panigrahana); Parvati, two-armed and shy, stands on his right in the South Indian texts; Brahma officiates at a fire, Vishnu may give away the bride; in North Indian reliefs Parvati may hold a mirror. Bengali paintings show Parvati garlanding Shiva.
rows.identify_by: Shiva holding Parvati's right hand in his right hand, she standing on his right, with Brahma tending a fire.

look_alikes.name: umasahita
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Ordinary pairs put Parvati on Shiva's left and do not join hands.

look_alikes.name: sita_rama_wedding
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Rama's wedding: Rama holds a bow and has no axe, deer or matted locks.

rows.regions_styles: Tamil Nadu bronzes (Madurai temple cult) and stone; Ellora and Elephanta panels; Madhya Pradesh; Kalighat paintings.
rows.dating_clues: AIC 1969.673 is a Madurai bronze catalogued c. 1600.
rows.cautions: An identification names the figure; it says nothing about age, or whether the item is old or a recent casting. facts.text: Parvati, the bride, stands on Shiva's right; he holds her right hand in his own.
facts.quote: On his right side stands Parvati, his bride, whose right hand he holds with his own.

facts.text: AIC's Madhya Pradesh relief: Shiva takes the bride's right hand (panigrahana) while she looks into a mirror; Brahma officiates.
facts.quote: Shiva formally accepts the bride by taking her right hand in his (panigrahana). He gazes upon Parvati while she looks into a handheld mirror.

facts.text: Shiva holds an axe (or tanka) and black buck in the back hands; the lower left shows boon-giving.
facts.quote: In his back hands are seen the symbols, tanka (or sometimes the axe) and the black buck.

rows.name: Virabhadra (Shiva's wrathful champion)
rows.features_other: Fierce face with tusks; flaming hair or a crown with a small linga in it; sandals and hero's anklet; the small goat- or sheep-headed Daksha stands at his right with hands joined; Bhadrakali may stand by him.
rows.identify_by: A fierce, tusked warrior form holding sword and shield or bow and arrow, with a tiny ram-headed man (Daksha) praying at his side.

look_alikes.name: bhairava
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Bhairava is naked, pot-bellied and has a dog; Virabhadra is armed and clothed, with Daksha.

look_alikes.name: skanda
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Skanda holds a spear and has a peacock.

rows.regions_styles: Karnataka and Andhra (Lepakshi, Vijayanagara), Tamil Nadu; brass folk images in Karnataka and Maharashtra.
rows.dating_clues: Popular in later South Indian and Deccan art.
rows.cautions: An identification names the figure; it says nothing about age, or whether the item is old or a recent casting. Traditional forms are still made: Gangoly (1915) records hereditary bronze-casters at Swamimalai near Kumbakonam and illustrates a Nataraja cast by a Swamimalai sculptor in 1909; the Met holds a Gangadhara bronze dated 1945 (Chennai). Facts only, not legal advice.

facts.text: Shiva created Virabhadra from a lock of his hair to destroy Daksha's sacrifice; Daksha was revived with a sheep's (Rao: goat's) head.
facts.quote: he created out of a lock of his hair the terrible Virabhadra

facts.text: Rao (Sritatvanidhi): four arms, three eyes, fierce tusks; bow and mace in the left hands, sword and arrow in the right; garland of skulls; sandals; Daksha with a goat's head and hands in salutation on his right; Bhadrakali beside him.
facts.quote: On the right side of Virabhadra there should be the figures of Daksha with a goat's head, two eyes and two horns, and with hands held in the anjali pose.

facts.text: Sastri: seated forms are Yoga-Vira, standing Bhoga-Vira, walking Vira-Vira; the head has a crown with a linga in the middle; a skull garland.
facts.quote: Seated figures of Virabhadra are called Yoga-Vira, his standing figures, Bhoga-Vira and those in a walking posture, Vira-Vira.

rows.name: Bhairava (Shiva the terrible)
rows.features_other: Bulging round eyes, fangs, hair standing on end or a crown of skulls; may carry the severed head of Brahma on a staff; a dog stands behind or beside him. Nepalese Bhairava masks and heads (often gilt copper or wood) are common in the trade.
rows.identify_by: A naked, fanged, pot-bellied Shiva with skull ornaments, trident and drum, and a dog at his side.

look_alikes.name: virabhadra
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Virabhadra is armed, clothed and has Daksha with a ram's head, not a dog.

look_alikes.name: mahakala
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Buddhist Mahakala (Tibet, Nepal) is dark, squat, holds a chopper and skull cup and stands on a figure; Bhairava's sign is the dog.

look_alikes.name: bhikshatana
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Bhikshatana is naked too but serene, with a deer and a bowl-carrying dwarf.

rows.regions_styles: All India; Odisha and Karnataka stone; Nepal (masks, heads, gilt copper); Tamil Nadu bronzes of Bhairava with dog.
rows.dating_clues: Nepalese masks are still made for festivals.
rows.cautions: An identification names the figure; it says nothing about age, or whether the item is old or a recent casting. Stone temple sculpture of this kind is a common target of theft; Items over 100 years old count as antiquities under India's Antiquities and Art Treasures Act 1972, which bars their export except by the Government; stolen South Indian temple bronzes have been returned to India (the National Gallery of Australia's Chola Nataraja, bought in 2008, went back in 2014). Facts only, not legal advice. Nepal and Tibet items are often sold as Indian.

facts.text: Bhairava's symbols are trident, sword, noose and drum; he is naked, followed by spirits, and rides a dog.
facts.quote: His symbols are the trident, sword, noose and the kettle-drum. He is naked and is represented as being followed by all kinds of demons and spirits and riding on a dog

facts.text: Hemadri, quoted by Sastri: pot-bellied, round red eyes, protruding teeth, garland of skulls, snake ornaments.
facts.quote: Hemadri describes Bhairava as a pot-bellied god with round red eyes, terrible face, protruding teeth and wide nostrils.

facts.text: Cleveland's Odisha Trikala Bhairava: crown of skulls and cobras, bulging eyes, fangs, hair on end; three heads for past, present and future.
facts.quote: His ferocity and fearsome attributes include the crown of skulls and cobras, bulging eyes, fangs, and hair that stands on end.

facts.text: A Hoysala guardian at Cleveland holds a drum and a staff topped with Brahma's decomposing head.
facts.quote: he holds a staff surmounted by a decomposing head of the god of creation, Brahma.

rows.name: Gajasamhara (Shiva flaying the elephant demon)
rows.features_other: The two uppermost hands stretch the elephant's flayed hide behind him like an arch, its legs and tail showing at the edges; one foot on the elephant's head; Parvati may look on holding the child Skanda. Token wanted: elephant hide held behind.
rows.identify_by: A many-armed dancing Shiva holding an elephant's skin spread out behind him like a halo, an elephant's head under his foot.

look_alikes.name: nataraja
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Nataraja's halo is a ring of flame, not an elephant hide.

look_alikes.name: natesha
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Northern dancing Shivas lack the hide.

rows.regions_styles: Tamil Nadu (Perur, Valuvur, Darasuram), Karnataka (Hoysala); Pahari paintings of Shiva and Devi on Gajasura's hide.
rows.dating_clues: Chola stone panels; Cleveland 1962.164 is catalogued 11th century.
rows.cautions: An identification names the figure; it says nothing about age, or whether the item is old or a recent casting. Stone temple sculpture of this kind is a common target of theft; Items over 100 years old count as antiquities under India's Antiquities and Art Treasures Act 1972, which bars their export except by the Government; stolen South Indian temple bronzes have been returned to India (the National Gallery of Australia's Chola Nataraja, bought in 2008, went back in 2014). Facts only, not legal advice.

facts.text: Usually eight hands, sometimes four; the two uppermost stretch out the elephant hide like an aureola with the legs hanging at the sides; the left leg is on the elephant head.
facts.quote: The two uppermost hands are stretched out and hold the hide of the elephant with its tail bent upwards in the form of an aureola

facts.text: Cleveland's Chola panel: eight arms, wrathful face; the flayed hide stretched behind with the hind feet sticking up; Parvati looks on.
facts.quote: He has just successfully flayed the skin of an elephant demon and triumphantly stretches it out behind him

rows.name: Linga (Shiva's emblem)
rows.features_other: An upright rounded pillar, usually set in a spouted base (pitha or yoni) that drains offerings; may be stone, metal, crystal or a natural river pebble; sometimes a snake hood rises over it; small portable lingas are carried in silver boxes. Token wanted: linga (aniconic pillar).
rows.identify_by: A smooth upright pillar with a rounded top, often in a ring-shaped base with a spout.

look_alikes.name: mukhalinga
look_alikes.how_to_tell: A face or faces carved on the shaft.

look_alikes.name: lingodbhava
look_alikes.how_to_tell: A figure of Shiva shown inside the linga.

rows.regions_styles: Everywhere Shiva is worshipped; sizes from pocket to temple.
rows.dating_clues: Plain lingas are almost impossible to date by form.
rows.cautions: An identification names the figure; it says nothing about age, or whether the item is old or a recent casting. Lingas from temple sanctums, and their bases, are protected antiquities in India when over 100 years old.

facts.text: Worship in the central shrine of a Shiva temple is offered only to the stone linga; metal figures are used for processions.
facts.quote: while worship is offered in the central shrine of a Siva temple only to the formless stone linga, for processional purposes images made of metal are used

facts.text: Museums describe the linga as a stylized phallus installed in the sanctum, symbolizing Shiva's creative power.
facts.quote: Taking the form of the phallus, it symbolizes Shiva's yogic control of the cosmic creative force.

rows.name: Mukhalinga (linga with a face of Shiva)
rows.features_other: One to five faces carved on the shaft, the fifth on top. Separate metal covers or masks (kosha) with Shiva's face were made to fit over a linga in Himachal and Nepal and are often sold as 'heads of Shiva'. Token wanted: face on a linga.
rows.identify_by: A linga shaft with one face (or four facing the directions) of Shiva carved on it: third eye, matted hair, crescent.

look_alikes.name: linga
look_alikes.how_to_tell: No face.

look_alikes.name: sadashiva
look_alikes.how_to_tell: A full multi-headed figure with arms, not a linga.

look_alikes.name: head_of_shiva
look_alikes.how_to_tell: A detached metal face with a hollow back may be a linga cover (kosha) rather than a broken statue.

rows.regions_styles: Early North Indian (Gupta Madhya Pradesh, Mathura), Kashmir, Himachal (brass covers), Bihar (Pala), Nepal (four-faced lingas).
rows.dating_clues: Gupta and Kashmir examples are early; style needs a specialist.
rows.cautions: An identification names the figure; it says nothing about age, or whether the item is old or a recent casting. Stone temple sculpture of this kind is a common target of theft; Items over 100 years old count as antiquities under India's Antiquities and Art Treasures Act 1972, which bars their export except by the Government; stolen South Indian temple bronzes have been returned to India (the National Gallery of Australia's Chola Nataraja, bought in 2008, went back in 2014). Facts only, not legal advice.

facts.text: The mukhalinga is distinguished from other lingas by one or more human faces; it may have one to five faces for the aspects Vamadeva, Tatpurusha, Aghora, Sadyojata and Isana.
facts.quote: it might have one, two, three, four or five faces corresponding to the five aspects, Vamadeva, Tatpurusha, Aghora, Sadyojata and Isana, of Siva.

facts.text: The face shows Shiva's third eye, matted ascetic hair and crescent moon.
facts.quote: the prominent vertical third eye, the matted hair indicative of his ascetic practice, and the crescent moon affixed above his left forehead.

facts.text: Metal linga covers exist: AIC 2021.231 'Linga Cover with Head of God Shiva' (brass, Himachal, 8th/9th century); Met 'Head of Shiva (lingakosha)'.

rows.name: Sadashiva and Mahesha (many-headed Shiva)
rows.features_other: Five faces (four round, one on top, often only three visible in relief) and ten arms, or three faces in Kashmir images: a gentle front face, a female face (Uma) on one side and a fierce face (Bhairava) on the other.
rows.identify_by: Shiva with three or five heads; in Kashmir, a calm central face flanked by a woman's face and a fanged face.

look_alikes.name: brahma
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Brahma has four bearded heads, a water pot and book, and a swan; no third eye or crescent.

look_alikes.name: vaikuntha
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Kashmiri Vaikuntha Vishnu's side heads are a boar and a lion.

look_alikes.name: heramba
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Five elephant heads.

rows.regions_styles: Kashmir (three-faced), Bengal/Bangladesh (Pala Sadashiva), Maharashtra bronzes, Nepal.
rows.dating_clues: Regional; specialist needed.

facts.text: Hemadri, quoted by Sastri, gives Rudra five faces, ten arms and skull garlands, riding the bull; Sastri lists Sadasiva among the Agamic forms.
facts.quote: Hemadri describes Rudra as riding on a bull and having five faces all of which are mild-looking, except the one on the right side of the central face. He has ten arms

facts.text: Cleveland's 8th-century Kashmir 'Standing Shiva Mahadeva': front face sovereign, left face Parvati, right face Bhairava; fear-not hand; citrus fruit; Ganesha, Skanda and Nandi at his feet.
facts.quote: She emanates as his wife Parvati, here seen as his left face. His right head is Bhairava, whose fearsome face embodies Shiva's powers of destruction.

facts.text: AIC catalogues two 'Cosmic Form of Shiva (Sadashiva)' images: a Pala schist from Bangladesh (c. 11th century) and a Maharashtra bronze (c. 18th century).

rows.name: Ravananugraha (Ravana shaking Mount Kailasa)
rows.features_other: Shiva and Parvati seated on Mount Kailasa with attendants; below, the ten-headed, many-armed Ravana strains to lift the mountain; Parvati clings to Shiva in fear while Shiva presses down with his toe.
rows.identify_by: A scene with Shiva and Parvati above and a many-headed, many-armed demon below heaving at the rock.

look_alikes.name: uma_maheshvara
look_alikes.how_to_tell: No Ravana below.

look_alikes.name: krishna_govardhana
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Krishna lifts a mountain overhead with one hand; Ravana shakes it from beneath.

rows.regions_styles: Ellora, Elephanta, Central Indian temple reliefs; Hoysala; Madurai paintings.
rows.dating_clues: Mostly temple relief fragments.
rows.cautions: An identification names the figure; it says nothing about age, or whether the item is old or a recent casting. Facts only, not legal advice.

facts.text: Shiva presses down his toe to quell the ten-armed Ravana, who tried to carry off Kailasa; Parvati clings to Shiva in fear.
facts.quote: he presses down his big toe to quell the ten-armed demon Ravana, who tried to steal Mount Kailasa and take it away to his island.

facts.text: Rao on the Ellora panel: Ravana tries to uproot Kailasa; Parvati in fear embraces Shiva, who is calm and reassures her.
facts.quote: Parvati, in great fear, embraces the well-proportioned and well-built body of Siva, who is calm and unperturbed

rows.name: Parvati (Uma, Shiva's consort)
rows.features_other: As Shiva's companion: two arms, the right hand bent as if holding a flower (blue lily, often missing), the left hanging loose; standing with a hip-shot bend on a lotus base, tall conical crown (karandamakuta) or hair-knot. Alone: four arms with lotuses (or noose and goad) above and fear-not, boon-giving below. In Bengal paintings she often holds the infant Ganesha.
rows.identify_by: A slender two-armed goddess standing with a sway of the hips, right hand raised holding (or once holding) a flower, left arm hanging; she stands on Shiva's left when paired.

look_alikes.name: lakshmi
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Sridevi (Lakshmi) beside Vishnu looks almost the same in South Indian bronzes; without the partner or an inscription the two often cannot be told apart. A breast-band is a sign of Lakshmi or Durga in Sastri's reading, not of Parvati.

look_alikes.name: shivakami
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Shivakami is Parvati as Nataraja's consort; a loose standing Parvati can only be called Shivakami if its history ties it to a Nataraja.

look_alikes.name: durga_standing
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Durga holds discus and conch in her upper hands and may stand on a buffalo head.

look_alikes.name: tripurasundari
look_alikes.how_to_tell: The consort of Tripurantaka stands in the same way; only the group tells.

rows.regions_styles: Chola and later Tamil Nadu bronzes; Kerala; Nepal (Uma turning toward a lost Shiva); North Indian stone; Pahari and Kalighat paintings.
rows.dating_clues: The type has been cast without a break from Chola times; form cannot date a piece.
rows.cautions: An identification names the figure; it says nothing about age, or whether the item is old or a recent casting. Traditional forms are still made: Gangoly (1915) records hereditary bronze-casters at Swamimalai near Kumbakonam and illustrates a Nataraja cast by a Swamimalai sculptor in 1909; the Met holds a Gangadhara bronze dated 1945 (Chennai). Items over 100 years old count as antiquities under India's Antiquities and Art Treasures Act 1972, which bars their export except by the Government; stolen South Indian temple bronzes have been returned to India (the National Gallery of Australia's Chola Nataraja, bought in 2008, went back in 2014). Facts only, not legal advice. Lone goddess bronzes are often given the name the seller prefers; Cleveland catalogues one Chola goddess simply as 'Goddess Holding a Lotus'.

facts.text: With Shiva she has two hands, holds a blue lily in the right and lets the left hang 'like the tail of a cow'; alone she has four hands, with lotuses above and varada and abhaya below.
facts.quote: In the former case she is fully decorated, is standing or seated on a lotus pedestal, holds a blue lily in the right hand, while her left hangs down loose "like the tail of a cow."

facts.text: She stands to the left of Shiva or of the linga and wears a tall crown (karandamakuta, kiritamakuta) or hair-knot.
facts.quote: she stands to the left of the image of Siva or the Siva-linga and wears the head-dress karandamakuta, kiritamakuta or kesabandha

facts.text: Cleveland catalogues a Chola goddess only as 'Goddess Holding a Lotus' (1984.2): museums too leave such figures unnamed when the partner is lost.
A Nepalese Uma at Cleveland turns toward a lost companion figure of Shiva.
facts.quote: she is depicted here as turning toward her consort, the Hindu god Shiva, a companion sculpture from which this image of Uma has been separated.

facts.text: Bengal (Kalighat) paintings show Parvati with the infant Ganesha in her arms.
facts.quote: The goddess Parvati is portrayed here with the infant Ganesh in her arms.

rows.name: Shivakami (Parvati as Nataraja's consort)
rows.features_other: Same standing type as Parvati: right hand raised as if holding a flower, left arm hanging, hips swayed; made to stand on Nataraja's left.
rows.identify_by: Only her setting makes her Shivakami: a standing Parvati made as the companion of a Nataraja (the goddess of Chidambaram).

look_alikes.name: parvati
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Iconographically the same; the name depends on the lost partner.

look_alikes.name: lakshmi
look_alikes.how_to_tell: See Parvati.

rows.regions_styles: Tamil Nadu bronzes, Chola onward; Chidambaram.
rows.dating_clues: As Parvati.
rows.cautions: An identification names the figure; it says nothing about age, or whether the item is old or a recent casting. facts.text: Gangoly publishes a Chola goddess bronze as 'Siva-kama-Sundari' alongside other Gouri (Parvati) figures.
facts.quote: Gouri (Plate XXXIV) and Siva-kama-Sundari (Plate XXXIII)

facts.text: Sastri: Shiva dances in the presence of Parvati, and at Chidambaram the dance group has Parvati standing on the left.
facts.quote: Siva is said to dance in the evening in the presence of the goddess Parvati

rows.name: Ganesha
rows.features_other: Right tusk broken; the trunk usually turns to his left, rarely to his right (Valamburi); a snake as belt or sacred thread; the trunk often reaches into a bowl of sweets; the rat sits beside or below the seat rather than being ridden.
rows.identify_by: Elephant head on a pot-bellied human body, one tusk broken, holding goad and noose with a sweet or the broken tusk, a rat nearby.

look_alikes.name: heramba
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Five elephant heads, on a lion (mostly Nepal).

look_alikes.name: vinayaki
look_alikes.how_to_tell: An elephant-headed goddess (Vinayaki/Ganeshani) has breasts; see other_hindu.

look_alikes.name: buddhist_ganapati
look_alikes.how_to_tell: In Tibetan and Nepalese Buddhist art Ganesha may be trampled by a Buddhist protector; then the main figure is the protector.

rows.regions_styles: All India, Nepal, Southeast Asia; bronze, brass, stone, wood, ivory, papier-mache, paintings and prints.
rows.dating_clues: One of the most reproduced figures in modern brass and resin; form gives no age.
rows.cautions: An identification names the figure; it says nothing about age, or whether the item is old or a recent casting. Traditional forms are still made: Gangoly (1915) records hereditary bronze-casters at Swamimalai near Kumbakonam and illustrates a Nataraja cast by a Swamimalai sculptor in 1909; the Met holds a Gangadhara bronze dated 1945 (Chennai). Items over 100 years old count as antiquities under India's Antiquities and Art Treasures Act 1972, which bars their export except by the Government; stolen South Indian temple bronzes have been returned to India (the National Gallery of Australia's Chola Nataraja, bought in 2008, went back in 2014). Facts only, not legal advice. Rao (1914) illustrates an ivory Ganapati newly carved at the Trivandrum School of Arts, so ivory Ganeshas need not be old.

facts.text: Ganapati is the eldest son of Shiva and Parvati, with elephant head and ears and four arms; the back hands hold goad and noose, the front an elephant's tusk and a wood-apple (or boon-giving and a water pot).
facts.quote: In the two back hands he holds the hook and the noose and in the front arms an elephant's tusk and the wood-apple.

facts.text: The right tusk is broken and must never be shown whole; he rides a rat or bandicoot; a snake girds the belly and forms the sacred thread.
facts.quote: The right tusk of the god is broken and must in no case be shown complete.

facts.text: The trunk generally turns to the god's left; images with the trunk turned to the right are rare (Tamil Valamburi Vinayaka).
facts.quote: Generally however, it is turned towards the left; only in rare cases do we meet with figures with the proboscis turned to the right.

facts.text: The seat may be a lotus, a mouse, or rarely a lion; Getty notes he was seldom shown actually seated on the rat.
facts.quote: The seat may be a padmasana or a mouse or in rare instances, a lion.

facts.text: His fondness for sweets is shown by his pudginess and the modaka he carries.
facts.quote: his weakness for sweets, as indicated by his pudginess and the sweet modaka he carries.

facts.text: Rao illustrates an ivory Kevala-Ganapati carved at the School of Arts, Trivandrum, influenced by Western art.
facts.quote: a very pretty ivory image of Kevala-Ganapati carved in the School of Arts at Trivandram.

rows.identify_by: Ganesha on his feet rather than seated.

facts.text: Sastri illustrates standing Ganapatis in stone (Lepakshi) and metal (Pattisvaram).
facts.quote: Ganapati standing (metal) ; Pattisvaram

rows.name: Dancing Ganesha (Nritta Ganapati)
rows.features_other: One leg bent on the lotus, the other lifted; one hand often swings free for the dance; musicians or the rat at his feet.
rows.identify_by: Ganesha with one leg lifted in dance, often many-armed.

look_alikes.name: nataraja
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Human head; drum and fire.

look_alikes.name: ganesha_standing
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Both feet down.

facts.quote: This is a representation of Ganesa as dancing. This image should have eight hands

facts.text: Cleveland's Central Indian example has six arms and holds a bowl of sweet cakes and a radish, mimicking Shiva's dance; AIC's has twenty arms with the rat at his feet.
facts.quote: Ganesha has six arms instead of four, and he holds a bowl of sweet cakes and a radish instead of a tongue of flame.

rows.name: Ganesha with consort(s) (Shakti Ganapati, Lakshmi Ganapati)
rows.features_other: A goddess sits on his lap holding a lotus, or two consorts stand at his sides (in Rajasthani and Pahari paintings Riddhi and Siddhi, or Siddhi and Buddhi).
rows.identify_by: Ganesha with a goddess on his knee or two women beside him.

look_alikes.name: uma_maheshvara
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Human-headed Shiva with Uma.

look_alikes.name: lakshmi_ganesha_pair
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Lakshmi and Ganesha as two separate seated figures (a common Diwali pair) is not a Shakti Ganapati.

rows.regions_styles: Tamil Nadu (Madura, Tenkasi), Bundelkhand and Bhumara stone; Rajasthani and Pahari paintings.
rows.dating_clues: As Ganesha.
rows.cautions: An identification names the figure; it says nothing about age, or whether the item is old or a recent casting. Traditional forms are still made: Gangoly (1915) records hereditary bronze-casters at Swamimalai near Kumbakonam and illustrates a Nataraja cast by a Swamimalai sculptor in 1909; the Met holds a Gangadhara bronze dated 1945 (Chennai). Items over 100 years old count as antiquities under India's Antiquities and Art Treasures Act 1972, which bars their export except by the Government; stolen South Indian temple bronzes have been returned to India (the National Gallery of Australia's Chola Nataraja, bought in 2008, went back in 2014). Facts only, not legal advice.

facts.text: Rao: Shakti-Ganesha is a class including Lakshmi-, Uchchhishta-, Maha-, Urdhva- and Pingala-Ganapati; Lakshmi-Ganapati holds a parrot, pomegranate, lotus and other items.
facts.quote: Sakti-Ganesa represents a class of images consisting of Lakshmi-Ganapati, Uchchhishta-Ganapati, Maha-Ganapati, Urddhva-Ganapati, and Pingala-Ganapati.

facts.text: Sastri: Maha-Ganapati is embraced by his wife seated on his lap holding a lotus; ten hands with sugarcane bow, discus, conch, noose, lotus, paddy ear and tusk.
facts.quote: He is lovingly embraced by his wife who, seated on his lap, holds a lotus in her hand.

facts.text: AIC's early 19th-century painting shows Ganesha enthroned with goad, modaka, rosary and tusk, with female attendants presumed to be his consorts Riddhi, Siddhi and Buddhi.
facts.quote: Ganesha is accompanied by his mouse vahana (vehicle) and female attendants, presumably his consorts Riddhi, Siddhi, and Buddhi

rows.name: Heramba Ganapati (five-headed Ganesha on a lion)
rows.features_other: Four elephant heads facing the directions and a fifth on top (often only three to five visible); rides a lion. Most examples collectors meet are Nepalese.
rows.identify_by: An elephant-headed god with several heads riding a lion.

look_alikes.name: ganesha
look_alikes.how_to_tell: One head, rat.

look_alikes.name: durga_lion
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Goddess on lion.

look_alikes.name: sadashiva
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Human heads.

rows.regions_styles: Nepal (bronze, painting), Bengal; rarer in South India.
rows.dating_clues: Nepalese castings continue today.
rows.cautions: An identification names the figure; it says nothing about age, or whether the item is old or a recent casting. Traditional forms are still made: Gangoly (1915) records hereditary bronze-casters at Swamimalai near Kumbakonam and illustrates a Nataraja cast by a Swamimalai sculptor in 1909; the Met holds a Gangadhara bronze dated 1945 (Chennai). Items over 100 years old count as antiquities under India's Antiquities and Art Treasures Act 1972, which bars their export except by the Government; stolen South Indian temple bronzes have been returned to India (the National Gallery of Australia's Chola Nataraja, bought in 2008, went back in 2014). Facts only, not legal advice. Nepalese figures are often sold as Indian.

facts.text: Heramba has five elephant heads, four facing the cardinal points and the fifth on top, and is seated on a powerful lion.
facts.quote: It has five elephant heads, four facing the four cardinal points and the fifth placed above these so as to be looking upwards. It should be seated upon a powerful lion.

facts.text: Getty illustrates Nepalese bronzes of Ganapati-Heramba, one ten-armed with his shakti, standing on a lion and a rat.
facts.quote: Ten-armed Ganapati-Heramba and sakti standing with one foot on a lion and the other on a rat. Nepalese bronze.

rows.name: Skanda / Karttikeya (god of war)
rows.features_other: A youthful god with a spear (shakti, vel) and often a cock (rooster) held or on a banner (token wanted: cock); rides or stands by a peacock. In Kalighat paintings a dandy on a peacock.
rows.identify_by: A youthful god with a spear and a peacock (and often a cock).

look_alikes.name: kaumari
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Kaumari is the goddess with Skanda's peacock and spear.

look_alikes.name: subrahmanya
look_alikes.how_to_tell: South Indian Subrahmanya usually has four arms with vajra and spear, and consorts.

look_alikes.name: shanmukha
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Six heads.

rows.regions_styles: Early North India (Mathura, Gandhara, Kashmir) and Bengal; Kalighat paintings.
rows.dating_clues: Mathura and Gandhara images are ancient; specialist needed.
rows.cautions: An identification names the figure; it says nothing about age, or whether the item is old or a recent casting. Stone temple sculpture of this kind is a common target of theft; Items over 100 years old count as antiquities under India's Antiquities and Art Treasures Act 1972, which bars their export except by the Government; stolen South Indian temple bronzes have been returned to India (the National Gallery of Australia's Chola Nataraja, bought in 2008, went back in 2014). Facts only, not legal advice.

facts.text: Skanda or Kumara is a son of Shiva, born of Shiva's fiery energy, commander of the gods' army, rides a peacock and is known as Karttikeya, raised by the six Krittikas.
facts.quote: He is represented with six faces (Shadanana) and as riding on a peacock.

facts.text: Rao links the cock (kukkuta) and peacock with Subrahmanya; the Saktidhara form holds the shakti (spear) in the right hand and the vajra in the left.
facts.quote: The left hand should bear a vajra and the right one the sakti

facts.text: Early museum examples: AIC 'Karttikeya, God of War, Holding a Spear' (Mathura, 2nd century); Met Karttikeya from Gandhara (6th–7th century) and Kashmir (8th century); Cleveland Kashmir Karttikeya (5th century).
A Kalighat painting shows Kartikeya astride his peacock as a dandy in European shoes.
facts.quote: Sitting astride his vehicle, the peacock, Kartikeya has a Prince Albert hairstyle and buckled European shoes.

rows.name: Shanmukha (six-headed Skanda)
rows.features_other: Six heads (in relief only three may be visible) and up to twelve arms, mostly holding weapons; on a peacock.
rows.identify_by: A god with several heads and many weapon-bearing arms riding a peacock.

look_alikes.name: kaumari
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Female, among the Seven Mothers (Sastri gives her six faces and twelve arms too).

look_alikes.name: brahma
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Four bearded heads and a swan.

rows.regions_styles: South India (Andhra, Tamil Nadu temples), Chidambaram.
rows.dating_clues: AIC 1962.203 is a 12th-century Andhra basalt.
rows.cautions: An identification names the figure; it says nothing about age, or whether the item is old or a recent casting. Stone temple sculpture of this kind is a common target of theft; Items over 100 years old count as antiquities under India's Antiquities and Art Treasures Act 1972, which bars their export except by the Government; stolen South Indian temple bronzes have been returned to India (the National Gallery of Australia's Chola Nataraja, bought in 2008, went back in 2014). Facts only, not legal advice.

facts.text: AIC's Andhra basalt shows Karttikeya on a peacock with six heads (shanmukha) and twelve arms, ten holding weapons.
facts.quote: the commander of the gods is shown with six heads (shanmukha) and twelve arms, ten of which hold weapons aloft.

facts.text: Sastri: images may have two, four, six or twelve hands; a Chidambaram sketch shows three visible faces and ten arms on the peacock.
facts.quote: Skanda with three visible faces, ten arms and the peacock vehicle

rows.name: Subrahmanya / Murugan with Valli and Devasena
rows.features_other: Four-armed youthful god (back hands vajra and spear, front fear-not and boon-giving), peacock behind; Valli stands on one side and Devasena on the other, each two-armed, one hand holding a lotus and the other hanging.
rows.identify_by: A four-armed young god with spear and vajra, a peacock behind, flanked by two small goddesses.

look_alikes.name: vishnu_with_consorts
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Vishnu with Sridevi and Bhudevi holds discus and conch and has Garuda, not a peacock.

look_alikes.name: skanda
look_alikes.how_to_tell: North Indian Karttikeya is usually alone with spear and cock.

rows.regions_styles: Tamil Nadu (Kumbakonam, Tiruvorriyur, Samayapuram), Kerala, Karnataka, Sri Lanka; bronze and stone; modern brass.
rows.dating_clues: As other South Indian bronzes.
rows.cautions: An identification names the figure; it says nothing about age, or whether the item is old or a recent casting. Traditional forms are still made: Gangoly (1915) records hereditary bronze-casters at Swamimalai near Kumbakonam and illustrates a Nataraja cast by a Swamimalai sculptor in 1909; the Met holds a Gangadhara bronze dated 1945 (Chennai). Items over 100 years old count as antiquities under India's Antiquities and Art Treasures Act 1972, which bars their export except by the Government; stolen South Indian temple bronzes have been returned to India (the National Gallery of Australia's Chola Nataraja, bought in 2008, went back in 2014). Facts only, not legal advice. The consorts were often separate castings; lone small goddesses from such groups are easily mistaken for Parvati or Lakshmi.

facts.text: Rao illustrates Subrahmanya with his consorts Devasena and Valli in stone (Kumbakonam) and bronze (Tiruvorriyur), with his peacock behind.
facts.quote: Subrahmanya with his two consorts Devasena and Valli

facts.text: Sastri: Kumara on the peacock, single face and four arms, attended by Valli and Devayana (Devasena); his marriage with the forest maid Valliyamman.
facts.quote: Kumara on the peacock vehicle, with a single face and four arms and attended by the goddesses Valli and Devayana

facts.text: Kumara-tantra (quoted by Rao): Valli is dark, holds a lotus in her left hand, right hanging; Devasena is red and stands the opposite way.
facts.quote: Mahavalli should be of black complexion and should have a smiling face. ... She should be holding in her left hand a padma (lotus) and her right hand should be hanging by her side.

rows.name: Nandi (Shiva's bull)
rows.features_other: A humped zebu bull lying down with legs folded, head up, wearing bells, garlands and a saddle-cloth; faces the shrine. Token wanted: bull (as the figure itself).
rows.identify_by: A recumbent humped bull, ornamented with bells and garlands.

look_alikes.name: adhikaranandi
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Nandi in human form with axe and deer and hands joined.

look_alikes.name: maheshvari
look_alikes.how_to_tell: A goddess riding the bull.

look_alikes.name: vrishabhantika
look_alikes.how_to_tell: A standing bull with Shiva's arm on it belongs to a Vrishabhantika group.

rows.regions_styles: Every Shiva temple; stone, bronze, brass, enamel (Jaipur).
rows.dating_clues: Form gives no date.
rows.cautions: An identification names the figure; it says nothing about age, or whether the item is old or a recent casting. Temple Nandis over 100 years old are protected antiquities in India.

facts.text: Nandi (Nandisha, Nandikeshvara) is now represented by the recumbent bull placed in front of the chief shrine in a Shiva temple.
facts.quote: now represented by the recumbent bull placed in front of the chief shrine in a Siva temple

facts.text: Rao: Nandikeshvara is more often a bull than a bull-faced human or a double of Shiva; the bull lies before the central shrine of all Shiva temples.
facts.quote: Nandikesvara is more often represented as a bull than as a bull-faced human being or as a duplicate of Siva.

facts.text: Cleveland holds a Jaipur enamel plate with Nandi as Shiva's white bull in the center (c. 1800).

rows.name: Adhikaranandi (Nandi in human form)
rows.features_other: Made like Chandrashekhara (axe and deer in back hands) but the front hands joined at the chest; may have a bull's face (token wanted: bull head). Processional versions ride a bull-headed vahana.
rows.identify_by: A Shiva-like four-armed figure whose front hands are joined in salutation.

look_alikes.name: chandrashekhara
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Chandrashekhara's front hands show fear-not and boon-giving.

look_alikes.name: saint
look_alikes.how_to_tell: A saint with hands joined has two arms and no axe or deer.

rows.regions_styles: Tamil Nadu (Valuvur) bronze and stone.
rows.dating_clues: As other South Indian bronzes.
rows.cautions: An identification names the figure; it says nothing about age, or whether the item is old or a recent casting. Traditional forms are still made: Gangoly (1915) records hereditary bronze-casters at Swamimalai near Kumbakonam and illustrates a Nataraja cast by a Swamimalai sculptor in 1909; the Met holds a Gangadhara bronze dated 1945 (Chennai). Items over 100 years old count as antiquities under India's Antiquities and Art Treasures Act 1972, which bars their export except by the Government; stolen South Indian temple bronzes have been returned to India (the National Gallery of Australia's Chola Nataraja, bought in 2008, went back in 2014). Facts only, not legal advice.

facts.text: Rao's Adhikara-Nandin at Valuvur is sculptured exactly like Chandrashekhara with axe and deer, but with the front hands folded on the chest in anjali.
facts.quote: Nandikesvara has them folded on the chest in the anjali pose.

facts.text: Hemadri (via Sastri): three eyes and four arms, a tiger skin, trident and short javelin, one hand raised over the head, one with a pointing finger.
facts.quote: He is stated to have three eyes and four arms and to wear a tiger's skin.

rows.name: Durga Mahishasuramardini (slaying the buffalo demon)
rows.features_other: She spears or beheads a buffalo; from its cut neck the demon emerges in human form, often bound by her noose; her lion attacks him. Early (Kushan, Gupta) images show her pressing the buffalo's back with no lion. Bengal clay and Kalighat images: ten arms.
rows.identify_by: A many-armed goddess killing a buffalo, the demon coming out of its neck, her lion biting it.

look_alikes.name: durga_lion
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Durga on her lion with no buffalo.

look_alikes.name: durga_standing
look_alikes.how_to_tell: A calm Durga standing on a buffalo head.

look_alikes.name: chamunda
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Sastri warns that Chamunda, Durga, Mahishasuramardini and Maha-Lakshmi killing the buffalo are often hard to tell apart; Chamunda is skeletal.

rows.regions_styles: All India and Nepal; Gupta and medieval stone, Kashmir and Himachal bronzes, Bengal (Pala; Kalighat; clay festival images), Odisha, Tamil Nadu (Mahabalipuram relief).
rows.dating_clues: Many 20th-century bronzes (AIC holds a 20th-century Odisha one) follow old forms.
rows.cautions: An identification names the figure; it says nothing about age, or whether the item is old or a recent casting. Traditional forms are still made: Gangoly (1915) records hereditary bronze-casters at Swamimalai near Kumbakonam and illustrates a Nataraja cast by a Swamimalai sculptor in 1909; the Met holds a Gangadhara bronze dated 1945 (Chennai). Items over 100 years old count as antiquities under India's Antiquities and Art Treasures Act 1972, which bars their export except by the Government; stolen South Indian temple bronzes have been returned to India (the National Gallery of Australia's Chola Nataraja, bought in 2008, went back in 2014). Facts only, not legal advice.

facts.text: Silparatna (via Rao): ten hands; at her feet a buffalo with its head cut off, blood gushing, from whose neck the real asura half emerges, bound by the snake noose.
facts.quote: At her feet should lie a buffalo with its head cut off and with blood gushing from its neck. From within this neck should be visible the half emerged real asura bound down by the naga-pasa

facts.text: Sastri: a man emerging from the buffalo's neck holds a weapon; the lion she rides attacks the giant; her right leg on the lion, the other on the demon.
facts.quote: The lion too on which Chandika is riding attacks the giant with its mouth while the noose held by the goddess is tightly fastened round his neck.

facts.text: Cleveland: his more vulnerable demonic form emerges from the neck and she slays him with her sword.
facts.quote: His more vulnerable demonic form emerges from the neck, and she, calm but powerful, slays him with her sword.

facts.text: Sastri: it is not always easy to say whether a buffalo-slaying goddess is Chamunda, Durga, Mahishasuramardini or Maha-Lakshmi.
facts.quote: It is not always easy to distinguish the images which are thus engaged in the act of killing the buffalo-demon

facts.text: The AIC holds a 20th-century Odisha bronze of Durga, Slayer of the Buffalo Titan (1995.460), beside an 11th–12th-century Chamba one (1995.458).

rows.name: Durga standing on the buffalo head (Tamil Durga)
rows.features_other: Stands calm and upright on a lotus or on the severed head of a buffalo; wears a breast-band (often of snakes); upper hands hold discus and conch like Vishnu; lower right fear-not, lower left on the hip; sometimes a parrot.
rows.identify_by: A calm standing goddess holding discus and conch above, one hand on her hip, a breast-band across her chest, often on a buffalo head.

look_alikes.name: vishnu
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Vishnu also holds discus and conch but is male (no breasts, no breast-band) and wears a tall crown with a dhoti.

look_alikes.name: lakshmi
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Lakshmi holds lotuses, not discus and conch.

look_alikes.name: vaishnavi
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Vaishnavi (Seven Mothers) also carries Vishnu's emblems but rides Garuda and appears in the Mothers' row.

rows.regions_styles: Tamil Nadu (Pallava Mahabalipuram, Chola temple niche on the north wall), Kerala.
rows.dating_clues: Specialist needed.
rows.cautions: An identification names the figure; it says nothing about age, or whether the item is old or a recent casting. Stone temple sculpture of this kind is a common target of theft; Items over 100 years old count as antiquities under India's Antiquities and Art Treasures Act 1972, which bars their export except by the Government; stolen South Indian temple bronzes have been returned to India (the National Gallery of Australia's Chola Nataraja, bought in 2008, went back in 2014). Facts only, not legal advice.

facts.text: Rao: Durga's back hands carry discus (right) and conch (left), front right fear-not, front left on the hip; she stands on a lotus or on a buffalo's head, or sits on a lion; her breasts are bound with a snake.
facts.quote: The image of Durga should be made to stand erect upon a padmasana, (See PI. C.), or on the head of a buffalo, or be seated on the back of a lion. Her breasts should be bound with a snake

facts.text: Sastri: Durga holds conch and discus above, abhaya and hand on waist below, with a breast-band of serpents; a Mahabalipuram Durga stands on the buffalo's head with discus and conch uppermost and a parrot on one hand.
facts.quote: She holds the conch and the discus in her upper hands, while her right lower hand presents the abhaya posture and the left lower rests on the waist.

facts.text: Sastri suggests figures with a breast-band standing upright on the severed buffalo head are generally Durga-Lakshmi.
facts.quote: figures with a breast-band standing upright on the severed head of the buffalo are generally those of Durga-Lakshmi

rows.name: Durga on her lion (Simhavahini)
rows.features_other: Seated on or riding a lion; in later North Indian paintings and prints the animal may be drawn as a tiger; a peaceful form (Kshemankari) sits above two lions back to back.
rows.identify_by: A many-armed goddess seated on or riding a lion, with weapons, and no buffalo.

look_alikes.name: ambika
look_alikes.how_to_tell: The Jain goddess Ambika also has a lion but holds a child or mango branch and sits under a mango tree; see the Jain topic.

look_alikes.name: heramba
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Elephant heads.

look_alikes.name: bhadrakali
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Sastri's Bhadrakali also rides a lion but has fangs, a long tongue and a skull garland.

look_alikes.name: parvati
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Parvati may have a lion beneath her seat (in Uma-Maheshvara), but is two-armed and beside Shiva.

rows.regions_styles: North and Central Indian stone; Nepal; Pahari and Rajasthani paintings; Kalighat; modern prints and brass.
rows.dating_clues: Painting style dates paintings.
rows.cautions: An identification names the figure; it says nothing about age, or whether the item is old or a recent casting. Popular prints and 20th-century copies repeat these forms; the painting style, not the figure, is the dating evidence (see the paintings guide).

facts.text: Rao allows Durga to be seated on the back of a lion; Sastri's Mahishasuramardini and Bhadrakali ride a lion.
facts.quote: or be seated on the back of a lion.

facts.text: AIC's ten-armed Madhya Pradesh Durga (11th century) is the pacific Kshemankari, seated over addorsed lions.
facts.quote: This sculpture presents the supreme goddess Durga in her pacific form as Kshemankari, wherein addorsed lions are positioned beneath her seat.

facts.text: In a Pahari painting (c. 1830) Durga rides a chariot drawn by two tiger-like lions.
facts.quote: The goddess in her warrior aspect in which she is named Durga rides a chariot pulled by two leonine tigers

facts.text: The Met holds a 9th-century 'Four-Armed Durga Seated on Her Lion Vehicle' (1990.15, probably Uttar Pradesh).

rows.name: Kali (standing on Shiva)
rows.features_other: Black or blue skin, tongue out, blood at the mouth; holds a sword and a severed head (token wanted: severed head); skirt of cut arms; stands or dances on the supine white body of Shiva (token wanted: Shiva or corpse underfoot); cremation ground with jackals.
rows.identify_by: A dark, four-armed goddess with tongue out, sword and severed head, standing on a white male figure lying on his back.

look_alikes.name: chamunda
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Chamunda is skeletal and sits on a corpse; Kali is full-bodied and stands on Shiva.

look_alikes.name: tara_mahavidya
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Other Mahavidya goddesses on Shiva (Tara, Chhinnamasta) differ in attributes; see gaps.

look_alikes.name: bhadrakali
look_alikes.how_to_tell: South Indian Kali is seated or standing alone, usually without Shiva underfoot.

rows.regions_styles: Bengal (Kalighat paintings, clay festival images, brass), Pahari Tantric Devi series (Mandi, Kangra), modern prints.
rows.dating_clues: Kalighat paintings were made for pilgrims and tourists from the 19th century; the subject continues in 20th-century prints.
rows.cautions: An identification names the figure; it says nothing about age, or whether the item is old or a recent casting. Popular prints and 20th-century copies repeat these forms; the painting style, not the figure, is the dating evidence (see the paintings guide).

facts.text: Kali on Shiva: the goddess is active and her consort Shiva lies like a corpse (shava); the scene is a cremation ground.
facts.quote: Kali appears active, while the male principle, personified as her consort Shiva, is like a corpse (shava).

facts.text: A Bengali hymn to Kali, quoted by Coomaraswamy, puts Mahakala (Shiva) beneath her dancing feet in the burning-ground.
facts.quote: With death-conquering Mahakala neath Thy feet Do Thou enter in, dancing Thy rhythmic dance

facts.text: The Kalighat Kali is black, four-armed, tongue out, with sword and severed head in two hands and the other two in protection and blessing; Cleveland calls it a pilgrim souvenir replicating the temple image.
facts.quote: she holds a sword and a demon's severed head in two hands while the other two hands are in gestures of protection and blessing.

facts.text: Sastri: Chamunda is called Kali when she has four arms.
facts.quote: Chamunda is known by the name Karali or Bhadrakali when she has eight arms, Kalabhadra when she has six arms, and Kali, when she has four.

rows.name: Kali of South India (Bhadrakali)
rows.features_other: Fierce face, fangs, often flame-like hair spread in a halo (token wanted: flaming hair); fat breasts; may stamp on the buffalo-demon's head; in Chola bronzes usually seated with one leg pendant. The sources read give no fixed set of hand attributes for the bronze type.
rows.identify_by: A fierce, fanged goddess, often with flaming hair and a skull garland, seated at ease or standing alone.

look_alikes.name: kali
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Bengali Kali stands on Shiva.

look_alikes.name: chamunda
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Chamunda is skeletal.

look_alikes.name: durga_lion
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Durga is calm and not fanged.

rows.regions_styles: Tamil Nadu and Kerala bronzes and stone, Chola and later.
rows.dating_clues: Cleveland 1956.7 is catalogued Chola, 900s–1000s.
rows.cautions: An identification names the figure; it says nothing about age, or whether the item is old or a recent casting. Traditional forms are still made: Gangoly (1915) records hereditary bronze-casters at Swamimalai near Kumbakonam and illustrates a Nataraja cast by a Swamimalai sculptor in 1909; the Met holds a Gangadhara bronze dated 1945 (Chennai). Items over 100 years old count as antiquities under India's Antiquities and Art Treasures Act 1972, which bars their export except by the Government; stolen South Indian temple bronzes have been returned to India (the National Gallery of Australia's Chola Nataraja, bought in 2008, went back in 2014). Facts only, not legal advice.

facts.text: Sastri: Bhadrakali has a terrible face, fat breasts, protruding teeth and long tongue, a skull garland, rides a lion and stamps the buffalo-demon's head.
facts.quote: Bhadrakali has a terrible face, fat breasts, protruding teeth and a long tongue and wears a garland of skulls. She rides on a lion and stamps under her foot the head of the buffalo-demon.

facts.text: Cleveland catalogues a Chola bronze as Kali, the wrathful form of the goddess born in battle to drink the demon's blood.
facts.quote: Kali is the wrathful form of the goddess generated in the midst of a battle with a demon that the gods failed to conquer.

facts.text: Rao: Parvati created Bhadrakali and sent her with Virabhadra against Daksha's sacrifice.
facts.quote: Parvati, in her turn, created Bhadrakali and sent her also with Virabhadra

rows.name: Chamunda (the skeletal goddess)
rows.features_other: Skeletal body with visible ribs, sunken belly and sagging breasts, sunken eyes, hair standing up; seated on a corpse (token wanted: corpse seat); tiger skin; may sit under a fig tree; the seventh of the Seven Mothers.
rows.identify_by: An emaciated, skeletal goddess with a skull garland, often seated on a corpse.

look_alikes.name: karaikkal_ammaiyar
look_alikes.how_to_tell: The saint Karaikkal Ammaiyar is also emaciated but is two-armed, human and without weapons.

look_alikes.name: kali
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Kali is full-bodied and stands on Shiva.

facts.text: Per the Mayamata, Chandesha has the axe (parasu) behind his folded arms; at Chidambaram he holds it between his folded arms.
facts.quote: According to the Mayamata Chandesa has behind his folded arms the weapon parasu (axe).

facts.text: In Chandeshanugraha Shiva, seated with Parvati, ties a flower garland round the head of the devotee Chandesha, who sits or stands below with hands joined (Gangaikondacholapuram, Chola, early 11th century).
facts.quote: the right front hand holds the end of a flower garland and the left front one is tying it round the head of Chandesa.

facts.text: Rao: Chandesvara's image is essential in a Shiva temple, in the north-east corner of the central shrine; the Agamas give two- and four-armed, seated or standing forms.
facts.quote: The image of Chandesvara is essential in a Siva temple and should be set up in the north-east corner

rows.name: Vishnu (standing)
rows.features_other: Tall cylindrical crown (kirita-makuta); long garland (vanamala) to the knees; discus and conch in the two back hands (the South Indian discus often shown edge-on); often flanked by Shridevi (his right) and Bhudevi (his left).
rows.identify_by: A crowned four-armed standing god with the discus in one back hand and the conch in the other; the front hands give fear-not or boon, or one rests on the hip or holds a mace.

look_alikes.name: Shiva four-armed (shiva_devi topic)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Shiva's back hands hold an axe and a deer and he wears matted hair with a crescent moon; Vishnu holds discus and conch and wears a tall crown.

look_alikes.name: vishnu_24_forms
look_alikes.how_to_tell: The 24 named forms are all this same standing figure; only the order of discus, conch, mace and lotus in the four hands changes, so a plain standing Vishnu may carry any of the 24 names.

look_alikes.name: venkateshvara
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Venkateshvara is a standing four-armed Vishnu too; in pictures he is shown as the Tirupati image, heavily garlanded, with the large white forehead mark.

look_alikes.name: Harihara (shiva_devi topic)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Harihara is split down the middle: one half with matted hair and Shiva's emblems, the other with crown, discus or conch.

rows.regions_styles: All of India and beyond: Gupta and later stone from North and Central India; Pala stone and bronze of Bengal; Chola and later bronzes of Tamil Nadu; Kashmir; Nepal and Southeast Asia (Cleveland and AIC hold Cambodian, Nepalese and Balinese examples).
rows.dating_clues: Style, not the attributes, carries date: e.g. Gupta-period heads have a squarish crown with a lion-head medallion (Cleveland 1942.498, 1969.57). Attributes do not date an item.
rows.cautions: An identification names the figure only; it says nothing about age, origin or whether the item is old or genuine. Traditional forms are still made: Rao (1914) already notes small Krishna figures sold in bazaars as toys and new ivory figures carved at the Trivandrum School of Arts. Nepalese, Cambodian and Balinese Vishnu figures follow the same scheme; the region must be read from style, not from what the hands hold.

facts.text: Vishnu is shown standing, seated or reclining; the three attitudes are named sthanaka, asana and sayana.
facts.quote: The principal image in a Vishnu temple is generally represented in one of three attitudes, that is, standing, sitting or reclining.

facts.text: Discus and conch are the constant signs of Vishnu, with the garland and the Shrivatsa mark.
facts.quote: the Vaishnava symbols, viz., the discus and conch, the garland vanamala and the auspicious mark Srivatsa always remain the distinguishing features of Vishnu.

facts.text: Standing Vishnu (yoga type): four arms, discus in back right hand, front right in fear-not or boon, front left on the hip, conch in back left.
facts.quote: The back right hand has to carry the chakra, while the front one is to be in the abhaya or varada pose. The front left arm should rest upon the hip

facts.text: The discus is normally in the right hand and the conch in the left, but the order can be reversed.
facts.quote: The discus is generally held in the right hand and the conch in the left; but this arrangement is reversed in the case of an image found in the Bellary district

facts.text: Cleveland identifies a Chola bronze Vishnu by crown, four arms, discus seen from the side (upper right) and conch (upper left).
facts.quote: His upper right hand holds a discus, seen from the side. In his upper left hand he holds the conch shell.

rows.name: Vishnu seated (Yogasana / Bhogasana)
rows.features_other: Yoga type: legs crossed, front hands in the lap in meditation, eyes half closed. Bhoga type: on a lion throne with Lakshmi and Bhudevi seated either side, one leg pendant.
rows.identify_by: A seated four-armed Vishnu: discus and conch in the raised back hands, with the front hands either in the lap (meditating) or giving fear-not/boon.

look_alikes.name: vishvaksena
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Vishvaksena also sits with one leg down holding conch, discus and club, but his fourth hand makes the threatening raised forefinger (tarjani).

look_alikes.name: yoga_narasimha
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Yoga-Narasimha sits with knees up held by a band and has a lion's face.

look_alikes.name: buddha_avatar
look_alikes.how_to_tell: A seated Buddha has no discus or conch and wears the monk's robe; in Hindu sets he sits in meditation among the avatars.

rows.regions_styles: Stone at Badami, Aihole, Ellora (Rao's plates); South Indian bronzes; ivory at Trivandrum.
rows.dating_clues: Not datable from iconography.
rows.cautions: An identification names the figure only; it says nothing about age, origin or whether the item is old or genuine. Traditional forms are still made: Rao (1914) already notes small Krishna figures sold in bazaars as toys and new ivory figures carved at the Trivandrum School of Arts.

facts.text: In the Yogesvara form Vishnu sits cross-legged with eyes nearly closed, front hands in the lap, discus and conch in the raised hands.
facts.quote: The two front hands should be kept on the crossed legs in the yogamudra pose.

facts.text: In the Bhogasana form Lakshmi and Bhumidevi sit on either side of Vishnu on the throne.
facts.quote: In this aspect Vishnu is seated on a simhasana, with his consorts Lakshmi and Bhumidevi on the right and left sides respectively.

rows.name: Vishnu reclining on the serpent (Anantashayana)
other_names: Vishnu sleeping on the cosmic ocean
rows.features_other: Lies on the coils of the serpent Ananta/Adishesha, whose five or seven hoods arch over his head; a lotus stalk rises from his navel bearing four-faced Brahma; Lakshmi (often at his feet) and Bhudevi attend; the demons Madhu and Kaitabha may appear at his feet.
rows.identify_by: A crowned figure lying on a coiled many-headed serpent, with a lotus and small Brahma rising from his navel.

look_alikes.name: ranganatha
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Ranganatha is the named Srirangam form of the same reclining Vishnu; the name depends on the temple, not on a different pose.

look_alikes.name: vatapatrashayi
look_alikes.how_to_tell: The baby Krishna lies on a banyan leaf, not on a serpent, and usually sucks his toe.

look_alikes.name: Reclining Buddha (buddhist topic)
