look_alikes.how_to_tell: The dying Buddha lies on his side in monk's robes with no serpent couch, no crown and no navel lotus.

rows.regions_styles: Mahabalipuram (Pallava), Deogarh (Gupta), Rajasthan; temple forms at Srirangam (Ranganatha) and Trivandrum (Padmanabha); Nepalese Budhanilkantha type (water-reclining).
rows.dating_clues: Not datable from iconography.
rows.cautions: An identification names the figure only; it says nothing about age, origin or whether the item is old or genuine. Traditional forms are still made: Rao (1914) already notes small Krishna figures sold in bazaars as toys and new ivory figures carved at the Trivandrum School of Arts.

facts.text: The reclining Vishnu lies on the serpent; a lotus from his navel carries Brahma.
facts.quote: on the lotus issuing from the navel there should be Brahma.

facts.text: The serpent couch may have five or seven hoods.
facts.quote: the serpent, the couch of Anantasayana, may be of five or seven hoods

facts.text: In the bhoga type Lakshmi sits at the head-side and Bhudevi at the feet; Madhu and Kaitabha are shown near the feet.
facts.quote: On the head-side of this recumbent figure of Vishnu there should be the figure of Lakshmi seated

facts.text: Srirangam and Trivandrum are the chief temples of the reclining form; Tamil name Palligondan.
facts.quote: The temples at Srirangam and Trivandrum may be specially mentioned as the places where this form of Vishnu is worshipped. In Tamil he is known as Palligondan.

rows.name: Ranganatha (Srirangam)
rows.features_other: The temple name at Srirangam for the reclining Vishnu on the serpent; Rao classes the image as the yoga-reclining type (two arms, one hand near the head).
rows.identify_by: A reclining Vishnu on the serpent called by the Srirangam temple's name; the form itself is the Anantashayana.

look_alikes.name: vishnu_reclining
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Same iconography; 'Ranganatha' is a temple-specific name, so a label saying Ranganatha needs a Srirangam connection (or a painting caption) to be meaningful.

look_alikes.name: Padmanabha (Trivandrum)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Also reclining; Padmanabha is the Trivandrum temple name. Only captions or provenance separate them.

rows.regions_styles: Srirangam, Tamil Nadu; paintings and prints of the shrine; Rao calls Srirangam 'the temple' of the Srivaishnavas.
rows.dating_clues: Not datable from iconography.
rows.cautions: An identification names the figure only; it says nothing about age, origin or whether the item is old or genuine. Traditional forms are still made: Rao (1914) already notes small Krishna figures sold in bazaars as toys and new ivory figures carved at the Trivandrum School of Arts. Do not upgrade a generic reclining Vishnu to 'Ranganatha' without a caption or provenance.

facts.text: Ranganatha of Srirangam is of the yoga-reclining type.
facts.quote: The god Ranganatha is of the type of the Yogasayanamurti already described.

facts.text: Sastri gives Ranganatha as one of the names of the reclining form and explains it as 'lord of the assembly hall'.
facts.quote: Ranganatha is "the lord of the ranga, the assembly-hall."

rows.name: Vishnu riding Garuda (Garuda-Narayana)
rows.features_other: Vishnu sits or stands on the shoulders of the man-bird Garuda, whose hands support his feet; with an elephant and crocodile below it is the rescue of Gajendra (Gajendramoksha), the form worshipped as Varadaraja.
rows.identify_by: Vishnu (discus and conch) carried on the shoulders of a winged, beaked man.

look_alikes.name: Lakshmi-Narayana on Garuda
look_alikes.how_to_tell: If a goddess sits with him on Garuda, read the pair (Cleveland 1959.256: Vishnu and Shri on Garuda).

look_alikes.name: Vishnu on Garuda from Nepal or Bali
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Same subject; region shows only in style (AIC holds Nepalese 17th-18th c. and Balinese 19th c. examples).

look_alikes.name: vaikuntha_chaturmurti
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Vaikuntha also rides Garuda but has four faces (human, lion, boar, demon).

rows.regions_styles: From the Gupta period (Cleveland 1961.46, Bihar, 300s CE) to Nepalese, Cambodian and Balinese examples; South Indian temple pillars (Kumbakonam).
rows.dating_clues: Not datable from iconography.
rows.cautions: An identification names the figure only; it says nothing about age, origin or whether the item is old or genuine. Traditional forms are still made: Rao (1914) already notes small Krishna figures sold in bazaars as toys and new ivory figures carved at the Trivandrum School of Arts.

facts.text: Garuda-Narayana: Vishnu riding Garuda, holding bow and arrow, conch and discus.
facts.quote: Vishnu is seen riding on Garuda, holding a bow and arrow, conch and discus.

facts.text: Garuda's hands support Vishnu's feet when he carries him.
facts.quote: the two hands, carrying respectively the pot of ambrosia and the umbrella, should both be engaged in supporting the feet of Vishnu, riding astride on the shoulders of Garuda.

facts.text: Cleveland's Gupta-period example: Vishnu straddles Garuda, who has a human head and a serpent tied round his neck.
facts.quote: Vishnu straddles his vehicle, the man-eagle called Garuda, here shown with a human head, wings outstretched

rows.name: Lakshmi-Narayana
rows.features_other: Lakshmi sits on Vishnu's left thigh or beside him, her right arm round his neck, a lotus in her left hand; his left arm round her waist; Garuda small at the base.
rows.identify_by: Seated four-armed Vishnu with a goddess on his left knee, the two embracing.

look_alikes.name: lakshmi_narasimha
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Same embrace but the god has a lion's face.

look_alikes.name: Uma-Maheshvara (shiva_devi topic)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Shiva with Parvati on his knee: matted hair, trident, and usually the bull below, not Garuda.

rows.regions_styles: Hoysala stone (Belur), Namakkal; North Indian and Nepalese bronzes (AIC 1995.463, Himachal Pradesh, 'Narayana and Lakshmi').
rows.dating_clues: Not datable from iconography.
rows.cautions: An identification names the figure only; it says nothing about age, origin or whether the item is old or genuine. Traditional forms are still made: Rao (1914) already notes small Krishna figures sold in bazaars as toys and new ivory figures carved at the Trivandrum School of Arts.

facts.text: Lakshmi sits on Vishnu's left, her right hand round his neck and a lotus in her left; his left arm round her waist.
facts.quote: The right hand of the goddess should be thrown round the neck of Narayana, whose left hand in turn should be made to embrace the goddess round her waist.

rows.name: Vaikuntha Chaturmurti (four-faced Vishnu)
rows.features_other: A human face in front, a lion face to one side, a boar face to the other and a fierce demon (Kapila) face at the back (often hidden); in Kashmir the back hands may rest on the heads of the personified discus and mace; an earth goddess may emerge between the feet.
rows.identify_by: Vishnu with a lion head and a boar head growing from either side of his human face.

look_alikes.name: Brahma (other_hindu topic)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Brahma's faces are all bearded human faces; Vaikuntha's side faces are lion and boar.

look_alikes.name: narasimha_ugra
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Narasimha has a single lion head; Vaikuntha has the lion head beside a human face.

look_alikes.name: varaha
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Varaha has a single boar head on a man's body.

rows.regions_styles: Kashmir above all (c. 8th-10th c.); also Chamba, Mathura, Khajuraho (Lakshmana temple image).
rows.dating_clues: The type is chiefly early medieval Kashmir in Banerjea's account; later copies exist. Style, not form, dates.
rows.cautions: An identification names the figure only; it says nothing about age, origin or whether the item is old or genuine. Traditional forms are still made: Rao (1914) already notes small Krishna figures sold in bazaars as toys and new ivory figures carved at the Trivandrum School of Arts.

facts.text: Vaikuntha has four faces; Rao (after the texts) gives eight hands and Garuda as the mount.
facts.quote: Vaikuntha or Vaikunthanatha should have four faces and eight hands, and be seated upon the mythical kite Garuda.

facts.text: In Kashmir images the front face is human, the side faces lion and boar, and a demonic face is at the back.
facts.quote: the central face is human, the side faces on the right and left are stylised ones of a lion and a boar.

facts.text: Banerjea ties the faces to the four Pancharatra emanations (Vasudeva, Samkarshana, Pradyumna, Aniruddha) rather than to the avatars.
facts.quote: The lion- and the boar-faces are thus primarily associated with the Pancaratra Vyuhas and not with the Nrsimha and Varaha incarnations

rows.name: The twenty-four forms of Vishnu (Keshava, Narayana, Madhava ...)
rows.features_other: Each of the 24 names is a plain standing four-armed Vishnu; the name is fixed by the order in which conch, discus, mace and lotus are held in the four hands.
rows.identify_by: A standing four-armed Vishnu holding all four emblems; which of the 24 names applies depends on the order of the emblems, read hand by hand.

look_alikes.name: vishnu
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Same figure; a museum label such as 'Vishnu as Shridhara' (Cleveland 1932.116) reflects this order-of-emblems rule.

rows.regions_styles: Medieval temple walls in North and South India; Bengal and Odisha steles often carry such names.
rows.dating_clues: Not datable from iconography.
rows.cautions: An identification names the figure only; it says nothing about age, origin or whether the item is old or genuine. Traditional forms are still made: Rao (1914) already notes small Krishna figures sold in bazaars as toys and new ivory figures carved at the Trivandrum School of Arts. Texts disagree on the order of emblems for some names, so a specific name is a reading that should cite the text followed.

facts.text: The 24 forms are standing four-armed figures holding conch, discus, mace and lotus in different combinations.
facts.quote: are represented each by a standing figure of the god with four hands holding the four symbols sankha (conch), chakra (discus), gada (club) and padma (lotus), in different combinations.

facts.text: Hence temple images named Trivikrama, Vamana, Narasimha or Krishna may be plain standing Vishnus, without the story.
facts.quote: we may often find in Vishnu temples images named Trivikrama, Vamana, Padmanabha, Narasimha or Krishna represented as plain standing figures of Vishnu

rows.name: Shridevi (Sri Devi), Vishnu's consort at his right
rows.features_other: In South Indian bronze sets she stands at Vishnu's right, one hand raised in the holding (kataka) gesture for a lotus (often lost), the other hanging; she usually wears a breast band (kuchabandha), which Bhudevi lacks; golden-yellow in painted images.
rows.identify_by: A two-armed goddess on Vishnu's right with one hand raised to hold a lotus; in bronzes the breast band is the usual sign that she is Shridevi rather than Bhudevi.

look_alikes.name: bhudevi
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Bhudevi stands on Vishnu's left, mirrors Shridevi's pose, holds a blue water lily, and in bronzes usually has no breast band.

look_alikes.name: Parvati/Uma (shiva_devi topic)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: A lone consort bronze may be Uma; without the pair or a Vaishnava context the identification stays open.

look_alikes.name: sita
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Sita belongs to a Rama group and stands near Rama and Lakshmana, who hold bows.

rows.regions_styles: Chola and later bronzes of Tamil Nadu (Cleveland 1963.104.1; AIC 2006.181 'Goddess Shridevi, Consort of Vishnu', Madurai c. 1100).
rows.dating_clues: Not datable from iconography.
rows.cautions: An identification names the figure only; it says nothing about age, origin or whether the item is old or genuine. Traditional forms are still made: Rao (1914) already notes small Krishna figures sold in bazaars as toys and new ivory figures carved at the Trivandrum School of Arts. Separated consort bronzes are often sold singly; side and hand position depend on which side of Vishnu she originally stood.

facts.text: Shridevi stands on Vishnu's right with a lotus in her right hand, the left hanging; golden-yellow.
facts.quote: In the right hand of this goddess there should be a lotus flower, and the left hand should be allowed to hang freely by her side.

facts.text: The breast band (kuchabandha) distinguishes Shridevi from Bhudevi in South Indian bronzes.
facts.quote: distinguished from Bhu Devi by the breast band (kuchabandha)

facts.text: Cleveland describes its Chola Shri holding the lotus in her left hand, so hand side varies between sets.
facts.quote: One of Vishnu's two wives, Shri, the goddess of abundance and good fortune, holds the lotus flower in her left hand.

rows.name: Bhudevi (Earth goddess), Vishnu's consort at his left
rows.features_other: Stands at Vishnu's left holding a blue water lily (nilotpala), mirroring Shridevi; dark or light green in painted images. Alone she may have four arms with vessels of gems, grain and herbs, seated on four elephants; Sastri's Prithvi holds a pomegranate and steps on a treasure pot.
rows.identify_by: A two-armed goddess on Vishnu's left holding a water lily; as Varaha's rescued Earth she sits on the boar-god's arm or thigh.

look_alikes.name: sridevi
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Shridevi stands at the right and usually wears a breast band; Bhudevi at the left, usually without one.

look_alikes.name: andal
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Andal, the woman saint held to be Bhudevi, carries a parrot and has her hair in a side knot.

rows.regions_styles: As for Shridevi; Cleveland 1963.104.3 (Chola, 10th c.).
rows.dating_clues: Not datable from iconography.
rows.cautions: An identification names the figure only; it says nothing about age, origin or whether the item is old or genuine. Traditional forms are still made: Rao (1914) already notes small Krishna figures sold in bazaars as toys and new ivory figures carved at the Trivandrum School of Arts.

facts.text: Bhudevi stands at Vishnu's left holding a blue water lily in her left hand, the right hanging; dark in color.
facts.quote: In her left hand she should be made to hold the blue water-lily, and her right hand should be made to hang freely by her side.

facts.text: Sastri's Prithvi: two hands, right in fear-not, left holding a pomegranate, left foot on a treasure pot.
facts.quote: has only two hands of which the right is raised in the abhaya posture and the left holds the fruit of the pomegranate.

facts.text: Standing alone she may have four arms with vessels of gems, grain and herbs, seated on four elephants.
facts.quote: She should be seated upon the back of four diggajas or elephants of the quarters.

rows.name: Lakshmi (Shri)
rows.features_other: Sits or stands on a lotus, lotuses in the upper (or both) hands; a bilva fruit and a pot of nectar are the other usual objects; two-armed when beside Vishnu, four-armed in her own shrine. Kolhapur Mahalakshmi carries a small linga on her head.
rows.identify_by: A goddess seated or standing on a lotus and holding lotuses, without Vishnu's discus and conch as her main emblems.

look_alikes.name: gajalakshmi
look_alikes.how_to_tell: With two elephants pouring water over her she is Gajalakshmi.

look_alikes.name: Sarasvati (other_hindu topic)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Sarasvati holds a vina, book and rosary and has the swan; Lakshmi holds lotuses.

look_alikes.name: Durga (shiva_devi topic)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Durga carries weapons (trident, sword, discus) and rides the lion.

rows.regions_styles: All India; brass and bronze household images; Bengal (Lokkhi) clay and paintings; Kalighat pictures.
rows.dating_clues: Not datable from iconography.
rows.cautions: An identification names the figure only; it says nothing about age, origin or whether the item is old or genuine. Traditional forms are still made: Rao (1914) already notes small Krishna figures sold in bazaars as toys and new ivory figures carved at the Trivandrum School of Arts.

facts.text: Lakshmi is seated on a lotus holding a lotus in each of her two hands.
facts.quote: She is seated upon a padma and holds in each of her two hands a lotus.

facts.text: Two-armed beside Vishnu, four-armed in her own temple (lotus, bilva fruit, pot of nectar, conch).
facts.quote: The figure of Lakshmi should have only two hands when she is by the side of Vishnu. But when she is worshipped in a separate temple she should have four hands

facts.text: Kolhapur Mahalakshmi carries a linga on her head.
facts.quote: On her head is a Linga

rows.name: Gajalakshmi (Lakshmi bathed by elephants)
rows.features_other: Two elephants, one each side, pour water over her head from pots held in their trunks; a common emblem on door lintels.
rows.identify_by: A goddess on a lotus with an elephant on each side tipping a water pot over her head.

look_alikes.name: lakshmi
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Without the elephants she is simply Lakshmi.

look_alikes.name: Indra on Airavata
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Indra rides a single elephant; Gajalakshmi is flanked by two that bathe her.

look_alikes.name: Buddhist and Jain Shri/Lakshmi
look_alikes.how_to_tell: The same bathing scene appears on early Buddhist and Jain monuments; context, not the motif, gives the religion.

rows.regions_styles: Door lintels of temples across India (Sastri); Mahabalipuram relief; brass lamps and plaques.
rows.dating_clues: Not datable from iconography.
rows.cautions: An identification names the figure only; it says nothing about age, origin or whether the item is old or genuine. Traditional forms are still made: Rao (1914) already notes small Krishna figures sold in bazaars as toys and new ivory figures carved at the Trivandrum School of Arts.

facts.text: Two elephants pour water over Lakshmi's head from pots.
facts.quote: Behind her are represented two elephants pouring water from two pots held by their trunks over the head of the goddess.

facts.text: Gajalakshmi is the most popular of the eight Lakshmis and is usually on door lintels.
facts.quote: Of these, Gaja-Lakshmi is the most popular. She is generally found figured on the lintels of door-frames

rows.name: Venkateshvara (Balaji of Tirupati)
rows.features_other: Standing four-armed Vishnu of the Tirupati hill; in pictures and souvenir images a very large white U-shaped sectarian mark (namam) covers much of the forehead and eyes, with heavy garlands; Rao notes a snake bangle on the right forearm of the temple image.
rows.identify_by: A standing four-armed Vishnu shown as the Tirupati image, with conch and discus in the back hands, one front hand on the hip, and (in pictures) the broad white namam over the eyes.

look_alikes.name: vishnu
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Without the Tirupati setting, garlands or forehead mark, he is just a standing Vishnu; Sastri says his form is that of one of the 24 forms.

look_alikes.name: vithoba
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Vithoba has only two arms, both on the hips.

look_alikes.name: Harihara (shiva_devi topic)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Rao and Sastri report a view that the Tirupati image is partly Shaiva; a true Harihara shows the split body.

rows.regions_styles: Tirupati (Andhra Pradesh); very common in Thanjavur and Mysore gilt-and-gesso paintings, brass and silver plaques, and modern prints.
rows.dating_clues: Not datable from iconography.
rows.cautions: An identification names the figure only; it says nothing about age, origin or whether the item is old or genuine. Traditional forms are still made: Rao (1914) already notes small Krishna figures sold in bazaars as toys and new ivory figures carved at the Trivandrum School of Arts.

facts.text: Venkatesa (Srinivasa, Balaji) is the god of the Tirupati hill, a standing four-armed form.
facts.quote: Venkatesa is a standing image with four hands, the back two of which carry the sankha (?) and the chakra; the other right hand is held in the abhaya pose

facts.text: Both authors report the view that the Tirupati image combines Vishnu and Shiva.
facts.quote: the image on the Tirupati Hill is a combined form of Vishnu and Siva.

facts.text: The white namam is applied over the eyes of the temple image, leaving a narrow slit.
facts.quote: a portion of white Namam is applied partially over the eyes of the idol

rows.name: Garuda (Vishnu's man-bird mount)
rows.features_other: Human body with a beak-like nose or bird's head, round eyes and wings; hands joined in salutation facing the shrine, or carrying Vishnu; kneeling on the left knee in metal processional images; snakes worn as ornaments or held. Token wanted: wings / beak.
rows.identify_by: A winged figure with a beaked nose, usually kneeling or standing with joined hands, often with snakes as ornaments.

look_alikes.name: Hamsa/Brahma's swan
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Brahma's mount is a goose, not a man-bird.

look_alikes.name: Kinnara and other bird-men
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Garuda faces Vishnu or carries him, with snakes; decorative kinnaras play music.

look_alikes.name: Nepalese and Southeast Asian Garuda
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Same subject: AIC holds Nepalese kneeling Garudas with joined hands; Cleveland Khmer Garudas with serpents. Style shows the region.

rows.regions_styles: Opposite the shrine in every South Indian Vishnu temple (Sastri); Nepalese pillar Garudas; Kerala wood (Rao: Palur, carried an elephant and a tortoise).
rows.dating_clues: Not datable from iconography.
rows.cautions: An identification names the figure only; it says nothing about age, origin or whether the item is old or genuine. Traditional forms are still made: Rao (1914) already notes small Krishna figures sold in bazaars as toys and new ivory figures carved at the Trivandrum School of Arts.

facts.text: Garuda has a kite-like beak and legs, round eyes, wings, and hands joined in salutation.
facts.quote: the beak and the legs should be made to resemble those of a kite. The eyes should be roundish

facts.text: As a metal processional image Garuda kneels on the left knee with a serpent on his head.
facts.quote: Garuda is represented as kneeling on the left knee, the right foot being firmly placed on the ground and a serpent decorating his head.

facts.text: Garuda may carry the pot of nectar (amrita), recalling the story of his theft of it.
facts.quote: Occasionally, Garuda may be made to carry in his right hand a pot of nectar.

rows.name: Sudarshana Chakra (Chakrattalvar), the personified discus
other_names: Sudarshana with Narasimha on the back
rows.features_other: A fierce many-armed figure standing inside a flaming wheel (often on a six-pointed star); on the back of the plaque a seated Yoga-Narasimha inside a triangle. Personified weapon (ayudhapurusha).
rows.identify_by: A many-armed fierce figure framed by a wheel of flames, with Narasimha seated on the reverse.

look_alikes.name: Durga or other many-armed goddesses (shiva_devi topic)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Sudarshana is male, fanged, inside a wheel, with Narasimha on the back.

look_alikes.name: ayudhapurusha
look_alikes.how_to_tell: A small personified discus standing beside Vishnu (with the wheel behind his head) is the Chakrapurusha attendant, not the temple Sudarshana.

rows.regions_styles: South Indian Srivaishnava temples (Tirupati, Kumbakonam Chakrapani temple, Dadikkombu bronze in Rao).
rows.dating_clues: Not datable from iconography.
rows.cautions: An identification names the figure only; it says nothing about age, origin or whether the item is old or genuine. Traditional forms are still made: Rao (1914) already notes small Krishna figures sold in bazaars as toys and new ivory figures carved at the Trivandrum School of Arts.

facts.text: Sudarshana is a fierce many-armed figure within the discus; Narasimha sits on the reverse.
facts.quote: On the reverse there should be the figure of Nrisimha in the yoga attitude

facts.text: Sixteen arms with weapons (conch, discus, bow, axe, sword, arrow, trident, noose, goad, lotus, thunderbolt, shield, plough, pestle, club, spear); sometimes eight or four arms.
facts.quote: sixteen arms holding the weapons conch, discus, bow, axe, sword, arrow, trident, noose, goad, lotus, thunderbolt, shield, plough, pestle, club and spear.

facts.text: In Tamil the Sudarshana is called Chakrattalvar.
facts.quote: In Tamil it is known as Chakrattalvar.

rows.name: Personified weapons of Vishnu (Chakrapurusha, Gadadevi, Shankhapurusha)
rows.features_other: Small figures standing beside Vishnu, often with the weapon on or behind the head (a wheel behind the Chakrapurusha's head); the mace is personified as a woman (Gadadevi). Vishnu may rest his hands on their heads.
rows.identify_by: Two small attendants at Vishnu's feet, one with a wheel behind his head, one a woman for the mace, on whose heads Vishnu's lower hands rest.

look_alikes.name: sridevi
look_alikes.how_to_tell: The consorts are as tall as Vishnu's shoulder and hold lotuses; the weapon figures are dwarfish with the weapon as a headdress.

look_alikes.name: Jaya and Vijaya (door guardians)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Door guardians stand at shrine doors holding clubs, away from the image.

rows.regions_styles: Gupta and post-Gupta North India, Kashmir (AIC 2021.232), Pala Bengal (Cleveland 1945.367, 1964.453).
rows.dating_clues: Common in early (Gupta to early medieval) North Indian Vishnu images; that is a tendency, not a date.
rows.cautions: An identification names the figure only; it says nothing about age, origin or whether the item is old or genuine. Traditional forms are still made: Rao (1914) already notes small Krishna figures sold in bazaars as toys and new ivory figures carved at the Trivandrum School of Arts.

facts.text: The weapons are personified; the mace (and the spear) as women.
facts.quote: the Sakti and the Gada are worked out as females

facts.text: Hemadri's Vasudeva places his lower palms on two dwarf figures, male and female, who are the personified discus and mace.
facts.quote: These dwarf figures are stated to be the personified weapons chakra and gada

facts.text: Cleveland: a personified discus with the wheel behind his head, broken from a Vishnu image.
facts.quote: This personification, with the chakra behind his head, has broken away from the main image of Vishnu.

rows.name: Hayagriva (horse-headed Vishnu)
rows.features_other: Horse's head on a four- or eight-armed Vishnu body; god of learning; may have the four Vedas personified at his hands, or rosary and book with the teaching gesture.
rows.identify_by: A Vishnu figure with the head of a horse holding Vishnu's emblems or a book and rosary.

look_alikes.name: kalki
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Kalki is usually a rider on a horse with a sword; when Kalki is horse-headed he carries sword and shield, not the book.

look_alikes.name: Hayagriva (Buddhist, buddhist topic)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: The Buddhist Hayagriva is a wrathful red deity with a small horse head in his hair, flames and a staff.

look_alikes.name: Ashvins
look_alikes.how_to_tell: The twin horse-faced physicians come as a pair.

rows.regions_styles: Hoysala stone (Nuggehalli, inscribed); South Indian bronzes and Mysore/Thanjavur paintings; Cambodian Vajimukha (AIC 2016.427).
rows.dating_clues: Not datable from iconography.
rows.cautions: An identification names the figure only; it says nothing about age, origin or whether the item is old or genuine. Traditional forms are still made: Rao (1914) already notes small Krishna figures sold in bazaars as toys and new ivory figures carved at the Trivandrum School of Arts.

facts.text: Hayagriva has a horse's face and eight arms, four with Vishnu's emblems and four on the personified Vedas.
facts.quote: Hayagriva should have the face of a horse and possess eight arms

facts.text: The Pancharatragama gives him four hands with conch, rosary, book and the teaching gesture.
facts.quote: The Pancharatragama mentions only four hands in which are seen the conch, rosary, book and the jnana-mudra.

rows.name: Vishvaksena (Vaishnava chamberlain and remover of obstacles)
rows.features_other: Looks like a seated four-armed Vishnu, but the fourth hand makes the threatening raised forefinger (tarjani). Token wanted: threatening finger (tarjani).
rows.identify_by: A seated Vishnu-like figure with conch, discus and club whose fourth hand raises the forefinger in warning.

look_alikes.name: vishnu_seated
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Vishnu's free hands give fear-not or boon or rest in the lap; Vishvaksena's raised forefinger is the sign.

rows.regions_styles: South Indian Srivaishnava temple bronzes (Sastri fig. 160 c).
rows.dating_clues: Not datable from iconography.
rows.cautions: An identification names the figure only; it says nothing about age, origin or whether the item is old or genuine. Traditional forms are still made: Rao (1914) already notes small Krishna figures sold in bazaars as toys and new ivory figures carved at the Trivandrum School of Arts.

facts.text: Vishvaksena holds conch, discus and club and shows the threatening finger; seated with the right leg hanging.
facts.quote: In three of his hands he holds the usual Vaishnavite symbols, viz., the conch, discus and the club and in the fourth exhibits the threatening finger-pose called tarjani.

facts.text: Rao lists Vishvaksena among the attendant figures of the reclining Vishnu group.
facts.quote: the images of the ayudhapurushas, of Garuda, of Vishvaksena

rows.name: Dattatreya
rows.features_other: Sage-god uniting Brahma, Vishnu and Shiva: either three gods side by side, a seated yogi Vishnu with the swan, Garuda and bull carved on the pedestal, or (as Hari-Hara-Pitamaha) many faces and six arms holding the emblems of all three; often followed by four dogs (the Vedas). The three-headed six-armed form with cow and dogs common in modern Maharashtra prints is not described in the sources read (gap).
rows.identify_by: A figure combining the emblems of Brahma (water pot, rosary), Vishnu (discus, mace) and Shiva (trident), or a mendicant followed by four dogs.

look_alikes.name: Trimurti (other_hindu topic)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: A three-headed bust from Elephanta type is Shiva Maheshamurti; Dattatreya has the mixed emblems and dogs.

look_alikes.name: Bhairava with dog (shiva_devi topic)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Bhairava is naked, fierce, with skull cup and one dog; Dattatreya is a serene sage, often with four dogs.

rows.regions_styles: Maharashtra and Karnataka especially; Rajputana stone (Rao's Ajmer example).
rows.dating_clues: Not datable from iconography.
rows.cautions: An identification names the figure only; it says nothing about age, origin or whether the item is old or genuine. Traditional forms are still made: Rao (1914) already notes small Krishna figures sold in bazaars as toys and new ivory figures carved at the Trivandrum School of Arts. Also recorded by the other_hindu topic; keep one row in the final table.

facts.text: Dattatreya is a form of Vishnu associated with all three gods.
facts.quote: Dattatreya is an incarnation of all the three deities of the Hindu trinity, although in a special sense he is an incarnation of Vishnu in particular.

facts.text: He may be a seated yogi Vishnu with the swan, Garuda and bull on the pedestal.
facts.quote: his triple nature is indicated by the lanchhanas, the characteristic emblems, the swan, the Garuda and the bull, of the three gods Brahma, Vishnu and Siva, being carved on the pedestal

facts.text: He is followed by the four Vedas in the form of four dogs.
facts.quote: He is represented as a wandering mendicant with ashes rubbed over his body and followed by the four Vedas in the form of four dogs.

rows.name: Salagrama stone
rows.features_other: A smooth, rounded black (or colored) river pebble, a fossil ammonite from the Gandaki river, with a hole showing spiral grooves read as Vishnu's discus. Not a figure. Token wanted: aniconic stone.
rows.identify_by: A dark, heavy, rounded pebble with a hole or split showing spiral (ammonite) markings, kept in a household shrine or box.

look_alikes.name: Bana-linga (shiva_devi topic)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Shiva's bana-linga is an egg-shaped river stone (Narmada) without the spiral fossil markings.

look_alikes.name: Ordinary ammonite fossils
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Worship use is shown by context (box, shrine, sandal paste); the stone itself is a natural fossil.

rows.regions_styles: Gandaki river (Nepal and north Bihar); used across India in household worship.
rows.dating_clues: A natural stone: no dating from form.
rows.cautions: Natural fossils; value and identity depend on religious use, not age. Sastri notes devout owners do not buy or sell them, only give and receive them.

facts.text: The salagrama is a river-worn fossil ammonite from the Gandaki, whose spirals are read as Vishnu's discus.
facts.quote: fossilified ammonite shell, which is river worn and thus rounded and beautifully polished.

facts.text: Devout owners only give or receive salagramas, never buy or sell them.
facts.quote: Strictly religious people never sell or purchase Saligramas but only acquire them by gift or by transfer.

rows.name: The ten avatars as a set (Dashavatara)
rows.features_other: Ten small figures in a row, a grid of panels (Kalighat, Rajasthan and Odisha paintings, ganjifa cards) or round the arch (prabhavali) of a Vishnu image, starting from the fish. Usual order: Matsya, Kurma, Varaha, Narasimha, Vamana, Parashurama, Rama, Balarama or Krishna, Buddha (or Jagannath, or Krishna), Kalki.
rows.identify_by: A fish, a tortoise, a boar-headed and a lion-headed figure among ten small figures is the ten-avatar set; the ninth place tells the local tradition.

look_alikes.name: Navagraha (nine planets, other_hindu topic)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: The planets are nine figures (Surya, Chandra ... Rahu, Ketu); avatars are ten and include the fish and tortoise.

look_alikes.name: Jain tirthankara rows (jain topic)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: 24 near-identical meditating figures; avatars are all different.

rows.regions_styles: All India; on Chalukya and Hoysala Vishnu images the set fills the arch around the god; Bengal Kalighat sets put Jagannath ninth; Odisha patachitra sets likewise vary.
rows.dating_clues: The choice for the ninth avatar reflects region and sect, not date.
rows.cautions: An identification names the figure only; it says nothing about age, origin or whether the item is old or genuine. Traditional forms are still made: Rao (1914) already notes small Krishna figures sold in bazaars as toys and new ivory figures carved at the Trivandrum School of Arts.

facts.text: The ten avatars are Matsya, Kurma, Varaha, Narasimha, Vamana (Trivikrama), Parashurama, Rama, Krishna, Buddha and Kalki; some put Balarama in place of Buddha.
facts.quote: Some Hindu authorities do not consider Buddha to be an avatara of Vishnu, and substitute in his place Balarama, the elder brother of Krishna, as an avatara.

facts.text: In South Indian reliefs Buddha may be left out and replaced by Krishna.
facts.quote: Buddha is sometimes, though rarely, omitted in south Indian Dasavatara reliefs, his place being occupied by Krsna.

facts.text: In some modern sets Jagannath takes the ninth (Buddha) place.
facts.quote: In some modern representations of the ten incarnations of Vishnu the place of the ninth or Buddha incarnation (avatara) is occasionally occupied by the figure of Jagannath.

facts.text: On Chalukya and Hoysala images the avatars run round the arch (prabhavali) from the fish at Vishnu's right over the top to his left.
facts.quote: The most favourite position for the sculptor to introduce these avataras seems to have been in the prabhavali round the figure of Vishnu.

facts.text: Only five avatars are commonly worshipped in South Indian temples (Varaha, Narasimha, Vamana-Trivikrama, Rama, Krishna).
facts.quote: There are ten such avatars recognized as of primary importance; but of these only five are commonly represented for worship.

rows.name: Matsya (fish avatar)
rows.features_other: Either a plain fish, or a crowned four-armed man above a fish tail; in paintings he may fight the demon (Hayagriva or Shankhasura) who stole the Vedas.
rows.identify_by: A crowned man with a fish's lower body, or a fish in a row of avatars.

look_alikes.name: Makara or naga figures
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Nagas have snake tails and hoods; the makara is a crocodile-like beast; Matsya has a fish tail and Vishnu's discus and conch.

look_alikes.name: kurma
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Kurma's lower body is a tortoise shell.

rows.regions_styles: In avatar sets everywhere; rarely a main image (Sastri). Rajasthan enamel jewelry (Cleveland 1916.119, Pratapgarh).
rows.dating_clues: Not datable from iconography.
rows.cautions: An identification names the figure only; it says nothing about age, origin or whether the item is old or genuine. Traditional forms are still made: Rao (1914) already notes small Krishna figures sold in bazaars as toys and new ivory figures carved at the Trivandrum School of Arts.

facts.text: Matsya is shown as a fish or as half man, half fish, with four hands holding conch and discus and giving boon and fear-not.
facts.quote: The image of Matsya may be made either like an ordinary fish, or in a form which is half fish and half man, the upper portion being that of man and the lower that of the fish.

facts.text: Cleveland's Pratapgarh pendant shows Matsya defeating a demon emerging from a shell.
facts.quote: Matsya appears in the middle, defeating the demon Hayagriva, who emerges from a shell, grasping him by the hair.

facts.text: Fish and tortoise avatars appear on temple walls and ceilings but are not usually the main image.
facts.quote: the Fish, the Tortoise, Parasurama, Buddha and Kalki though represented largely on walls, pillars and ceilings of temples ... are not generally worshipped as the chief deity

rows.name: Kurma (tortoise avatar)
rows.features_other: A tortoise, or a four-armed crowned man above a tortoise shell; in churning-of-the-ocean scenes the tortoise supports Mount Mandara.
rows.identify_by: A crowned man with a tortoise's lower body, or the tortoise under the churning mountain.

look_alikes.name: matsya
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Matsya has a fish tail.

look_alikes.name: Yamuna on her tortoise (other_hindu topic)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: The river goddess Yamuna stands on a tortoise holding a water pot; she is a woman, not Vishnu.

rows.regions_styles: In avatar sets everywhere; Sastri notes a stone at Kanchipuram of the tortoise worshipping Shiva.
rows.dating_clues: Not datable from iconography.
rows.cautions: An identification names the figure only; it says nothing about age, origin or whether the item is old or genuine. Traditional forms are still made: Rao (1914) already notes small Krishna figures sold in bazaars as toys and new ivory figures carved at the Trivandrum School of Arts.

facts.text: Kurma is half man and half tortoise (lower part tortoise), with conch and discus, or simply a tortoise.
facts.quote: The image of this avatara is generally worked out in a form which is half man and half tortoise, the lower part being that of the tortoise.

facts.text: The tortoise supported the churning mountain at the churning of the ocean.
facts.quote: Vishnu assumed the form of the tortoise for supporting on its back the mountain employed in the churning of the ocean

rows.name: Varaha (boar avatar) lifting the Earth
rows.features_other: Man's body with a boar's head; the rescued Earth goddess (Bhudevi) sits on his bent arm, elbow, thigh or tusk; one foot on the serpent king (Adishesha) and his queen; or a whole boar covered with small figures.
rows.identify_by: A boar-headed god with a small goddess perched on his arm or tusk, his foot on a serpent.

look_alikes.name: vaikuntha_chaturmurti
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Vaikuntha has a boar face only at the side of a human face.

look_alikes.name: Varahi (shiva_devi topic, Matrikas)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Varahi is a boar-faced goddess, female, often with a fish or skull cup and a buffalo mount.

rows.regions_styles: Gupta Udayagiri, Eran (whole boar); Chalukya Badami; Pallava Mahabalipuram; Central India (Cleveland 2011.148); Rajasthan and Himachal (AIC 1997.707, 2012.686); royal crest of the Chalukyas and Vijayanagara.
rows.dating_clues: Not datable from iconography.
rows.cautions: An identification names the figure only; it says nothing about age, origin or whether the item is old or genuine. Traditional forms are still made: Rao (1914) already notes small Krishna figures sold in bazaars as toys and new ivory figures carved at the Trivandrum School of Arts.

facts.text: Varaha has a boar's face on a man's body, four arms with conch and discus, one foot on the serpent Adishesha, and Bhudevi seated on his bent leg.
facts.quote: the left hand should be shown as supporting the legs of Bhumidevi, seated on the god's bent right leg

facts.text: Some texts have him carry the Earth on his tusk or elbow, or make him wholly a boar.
facts.quote: it may be worked out wholly as a boar with a thick snout, broad shoulder-blades, long tusks

facts.text: Cleveland: the earth goddess sits on one of Varaha's elbows.
facts.quote: Varaha holds out one of his four elbows as a seat for the earth goddess who he has rescued.

rows.name: Narasimha tearing open Hiranyakashipu (Ugra-Narasimha)
rows.features_other: Lion head with thick mane on a man's body; the demon king Hiranyakashipu laid across his thigh, belly torn open by the god's claws, the entrails held up like a garland; may burst from a pillar; Prahlada with joined hands nearby.
rows.identify_by: A lion-headed god disembowelling a man laid across his lap.

look_alikes.name: yoga_narasimha
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Calm, seated with knees up in a band, no demon.

look_alikes.name: Durga on the lion / Simhavahini
look_alikes.how_to_tell: There the lion is an animal mount under a goddess; Narasimha has the lion's head on a human body.

look_alikes.name: Narasimhi (Matrika)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: A lion-faced goddess (female) among the Mother goddesses.

look_alikes.name: Sharabha (shiva_devi topic)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Shaiva images show the bird-beast Sharabha overpowering Narasimha.

rows.regions_styles: Ellora, Ahobilam, Hampi (monolith of 1528); Central India (AIC 1987.361.3); Pala Bengal (AIC 2020.550); Odisha (AIC 1996.88); South Indian bronzes.
rows.dating_clues: Not datable from iconography.
rows.cautions: An identification names the figure only; it says nothing about age, origin or whether the item is old or genuine. Traditional forms are still made: Rao (1914) already notes small Krishna figures sold in bazaars as toys and new ivory figures carved at the Trivandrum School of Arts.

facts.text: Narasimha has a lion's face and mane on a man's body and splits the demon's breast with his nails.
facts.quote: splits the breast of the giant, thrown flat upon his thigh, with the sharp nails of both his hands.

facts.text: Two hands hold up the drawn-out entrails like a garland.
facts.quote: holding the drawn out entrails of Hiranyakasipu in the form of a garland.

facts.text: Conch and discus are in his upper hands in all his forms.
facts.quote: The usual Vaishnava symbols, sankha (conch) and chakra (discus), are seen in the two upper hands of the image of Narasimha in all his forms.

rows.name: Yoga-Narasimha (seated in meditation)
rows.features_other: Sits with both knees raised, held by a meditation band (yogapatta) round knees and back; front arms stretched forward resting on the knees; discus and conch in the back hands. Token wanted: yoga band (yogapatta) / knees-up seat (utkutika).
rows.identify_by: A lion-headed god sitting with knees up bound by a band, hands resting on his knees.

look_alikes.name: narasimha_ugra
look_alikes.how_to_tell: No demon, calm pose.

look_alikes.name: Yoga-Dakshinamurti or yogi figures (shiva_devi topic)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: They have human faces; Yoga-Narasimha has the lion head.

look_alikes.name: sudarshana
look_alikes.how_to_tell: The same seated Narasimha appears on the back of Sudarshana plaques, inside a triangle.

rows.regions_styles: Hoysala Halebid; Tirupati hill; Chola bronze (Cleveland 1973.187, c. 1250); Ahobilam, Sholinghur.
rows.dating_clues: Not datable from iconography.
rows.cautions: An identification names the figure only; it says nothing about age, origin or whether the item is old or genuine. Traditional forms are still made: Rao (1914) already notes small Krishna figures sold in bazaars as toys and new ivory figures carved at the Trivandrum School of Arts.

facts.text: Yoga-Narasimha sits with the legs held up by the yoga band; four arms, discus and conch in the upper hands, the others stretched forward on the knees.
facts.quote: the forelegs being maintained in the required position by the yoga-patta belt going round them and the back of the body.

rows.name: Lakshmi-Narasimha
rows.features_other: Calm lion-headed Vishnu seated with one leg down and Lakshmi on his bent knee, embracing; Garuda may be shown below.
rows.identify_by: A lion-headed god with a goddess on his lap.

look_alikes.name: lakshmi_narayana
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Same embrace, human face.

rows.regions_styles: South Indian bronzes (Madras Museum pair in Rao); Thanjavur paintings (AIC 1939.339 'Narasimha and Consort', c. 1910, not open).
rows.dating_clues: Not datable from iconography.
rows.cautions: An identification names the figure only; it says nothing about age, origin or whether the item is old or genuine. Traditional forms are still made: Rao (1914) already notes small Krishna figures sold in bazaars as toys and new ivory figures carved at the Trivandrum School of Arts.

facts.text: Lakshmi sits on the knee of the seated Narasimha; his upper hands hold discus and conch, lower right fear-not, lower left embraces her.
facts.quote: On the lap so formed by the bent leg Lakshmi is seated with both her legs hanging down

facts.text: Lakshmi-Narasimha is the god after his anger subsided at Prahlada's prayers.
facts.quote: When, however, his anger subsided at the earnest prayers of Prahlada he became serene and in this form he is known as Lakshmi-Narasimha.

rows.name: Vamana (dwarf avatar)
rows.features_other: A small boy-student (brahmachari): tuft or knot of hair, sacred thread, deerskin, umbrella in one hand and water pot in the other; sometimes a stunted, pot-bellied dwarf. Token wanted: umbrella.
rows.identify_by: A small two-armed boy-priest holding a parasol and a water pot.

look_alikes.name: trivikrama
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Trivikrama is the same story at the next moment: a giant with one leg raised; the dwarf may stand beside him.

look_alikes.name: Dwarf attendants (ganas)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Ganas are pot-bellied but carry no umbrella and water pot.

look_alikes.name: Kubera (other_hindu topic)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Kubera is pot-bellied with a money bag or mongoose.

rows.regions_styles: Temple walls; boundary stones of land grants in the south (Sastri); Rajasthan and Pahari paintings of the Bali story (Cleveland 2018.142).
rows.dating_clues: Not datable from iconography.
rows.cautions: An identification names the figure only; it says nothing about age, origin or whether the item is old or genuine. Traditional forms are still made: Rao (1914) already notes small Krishna figures sold in bazaars as toys and new ivory figures carved at the Trivandrum School of Arts.

facts.text: Vamana has two arms, holding a water pot and an umbrella, with a tuft of hair, sacred thread and deerskin, as a boy-student.
facts.quote: It should have two arms, one of which should carry a kamandalu and the other an umbrella.

facts.text: Some texts make him a misshapen, pot-bellied dwarf.
facts.quote: the image should be worked in the form of an ill-shaped man with hunch back, protruding joints of bones and a big belly.

facts.text: Vamana figures appear on boundary stones of land granted in charity in the south.
facts.quote: on demarcation stones of fields granted in charity, were quite common even down to the end of the nineteenth century.

rows.name: Trivikrama (Vishnu taking the three strides)
rows.features_other: A giant Vishnu standing on one leg, the other raised to knee, navel or forehead height (or straight up); Brahma may wash the raised foot; King Bali and the dwarf Vamana at the base; Rahu's face may appear in the sky.
rows.identify_by: A many-armed crowned Vishnu with one leg kicked high, small figures of Bali and the dwarf at his feet.

look_alikes.name: Shiva Urdhva-tandava (shiva_devi topic)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Shiva's leg-raised dance has matted hair, drum and fire; Trivikrama has crown, discus and conch, often a sword and shield.

look_alikes.name: vamana
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Vamana is the small boy with umbrella before the giant form.

rows.regions_styles: Mahabalipuram, Badami, Ellora; Odisha (AIC 2001.428); Pala Bengal (AIC 2019.724); Mewar painting (Cleveland 2018.142).
rows.dating_clues: Not datable from iconography.
rows.cautions: An identification names the figure only; it says nothing about age, origin or whether the item is old or genuine. Traditional forms are still made: Rao (1914) already notes small Krishna figures sold in bazaars as toys and new ivory figures carved at the Trivandrum School of Arts.

facts.text: Trivikrama is the giant form of Vamana: Vishnu standing on one leg with the other raised across the sky, Bali and the dwarf at his feet.
facts.quote: Trivikrama as striding over the earth, the mid-world and the heaven-world respectively

facts.text: The raised foot may reach the knee, the navel or the forehead, for the three worlds.
facts.quote: with the left foot raised up to the level of (1) the right knee, or (2) to the navel, or (3) the forehead.

facts.text: Mahabalipuram's Trivikrama has eight hands with discus, club, sword, bow, shield and conch, Brahma touching the raised toe.
facts.quote: Here the god has eight hands.

facts.text: Tamil name Ulagalanda-Perumal, 'the lord who measured the universe'.
facts.quote: the Tamil Ulagalanda-Perumal ... "the lord who measured the universe (with three strides)."

facts.text: Cleveland's Mewar painting shows Vishnu with one foot on the ground and the other in heaven where Brahma washes it.
facts.quote: Vishnu stands monumentally with his one foot on the ground and the other foot reaching to heaven where Brahma washes Vishnu's foot

rows.name: Parashurama (Rama with the axe)
rows.features_other: A Brahmin warrior with matted hair (jata-makuta) and sacred thread, carrying a battle axe; may wear a deerskin.
rows.identify_by: A two-armed Brahmin with piled matted hair holding a battle axe.

look_alikes.name: Shiva with axe (shiva_devi topic)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Shiva's axe comes with the deer, trident, third eye and crescent moon; Parashurama is two-armed and human.

look_alikes.name: rama
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Raghava Rama carries bow and arrow and wears a royal crown.

look_alikes.name: balarama
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Balarama carries a plough and pestle.

rows.regions_styles: In avatar sets; own shrines in Kerala and the west coast (Sastri).
rows.dating_clues: Not datable from iconography.
rows.cautions: An identification names the figure only; it says nothing about age, origin or whether the item is old or genuine. Traditional forms are still made: Rao (1914) already notes small Krishna figures sold in bazaars as toys and new ivory figures carved at the Trivandrum School of Arts.

facts.text: Parashurama holds the axe in his right hand and wears the jata-makuta and sacred thread; four-armed versions carry axe, sword, arrow and bow.
facts.quote: in the right hand the parasu should be held

facts.text: He is worshipped in special shrines in Malabar as the founder of the west coast.
facts.quote: He is, therefore, often worshipped in Malabar in special shrines dedicated to him.

rows.name: Rama with the bow (Kodandarama)
rows.features_other: Human, two-armed prince in a tall crown, standing in a triple bend: in South Indian bronzes the left hand is raised as if gripping the top of a bow and the right lowered as if holding an arrow; bow and arrow were separate and are often lost; a quiver may show behind the shoulder. Blue or green skin in paintings (green in Kalighat pictures).
rows.identify_by: A crowned two-armed prince whose raised left hand grips (or once gripped) a tall bow and whose lowered right holds an arrow, usually with Sita and Lakshmana.

look_alikes.name: lakshmana
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Lakshmana holds the bow the same way; by text he lacks the royal crown (hair knot instead) and stands to the side and is smaller.

look_alikes.name: venugopala
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Venugopala raises both hands to one side at mouth level (flute) and crosses one leg over the other; Rama's hands are at different heights and his legs are not crossed.

look_alikes.name: krishna
look_alikes.how_to_tell: In paintings Krishna rarely carries a bow; he wears a peacock feather and is with cows, gopis or Radha. A bow-carrying blue prince with a quiver, crown, Sita or a monkey is Rama.

look_alikes.name: madanagopala
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Madanagopala's bow is of sugarcane and he also plays the flute, with eight or more arms.

rows.regions_styles: Chola and later bronze sets (Rao's Shermadevi group, 12th-13th c.); Rameshvaram; Pahari and Rajput Ramayana paintings; Kalighat; Mysore and Thanjavur paintings of the coronation.
rows.dating_clues: Rao dated the Shermadevi bronzes by workmanship and a later Rameshvaram set to the 16th-17th c.; dating from style needs a specialist.
rows.cautions: An identification names the figure only; it says nothing about age, origin or whether the item is old or genuine. Traditional forms are still made: Rao (1914) already notes small Krishna figures sold in bazaars as toys and new ivory figures carved at the Trivandrum School of Arts. A lone bronze with empty raised hands may be Rama, Lakshmana or a Krishna; read it with its group when possible.

facts.text: Rama has only two arms, with arrow in the right hand and bow in the left, a crown, and the triple-bend stance.
facts.quote: It should never have more than two arms; in the right hand the bana or arrow should be held, and in the left hand the dhanus or the bow.

facts.text: In bronzes the left arm is raised to grip the top of the bow; bows, arrows and quivers are often missing.
facts.quote: the left arm is lifted up and bent so as to hold the top of the bow

facts.text: Rama with the bow is called Kodandarama; Sastri notes a four-armed independent Rama with bow, arrow, conch and discus.
facts.quote: The bow is called kodanda and so Rama with the bow is sometimes known as Kodanda-Rama.

facts.text: Cleveland's Kalighat pictures paint Rama green and still with bow and arrow when enthroned.
facts.quote: King Rama still holds his signature emblems of bow and arrow.

rows.name: Rama with Sita, Lakshmana and Hanuman (Rama parivara)
rows.features_other: A set of three or four bronzes, or a painted court: crowned Rama with bow, Sita with a lily, Lakshmana with bow (or holding a parasol or fly whisk in paintings), and a smaller Hanuman with joined hands or hand to mouth; Bharata and Shatrughna may be added.
rows.identify_by: A crowned bowman with a lady and a second bowman, and a kneeling or bowing monkey.

look_alikes.name: rajagopala
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Krishna with Rukmini and Satyabhama: two ladies, no monkey, Krishna holds a stick, not a bow.

look_alikes.name: radha_krishna
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Krishna's group has cows, gopis, a flute and a peacock feather; Rama's has bows and Hanuman.

rows.regions_styles: South Indian temple processional sets (Cleveland 1980.26 Hanuman 'would have been paraded with a group'); Mysore and Thanjavur coronation paintings; Kalighat (Cleveland 2003.152, 2003.134.a).
rows.dating_clues: Not datable from iconography.
rows.cautions: An identification names the figure only; it says nothing about age, origin or whether the item is old or genuine. Traditional forms are still made: Rao (1914) already notes small Krishna figures sold in bazaars as toys and new ivory figures carved at the Trivandrum School of Arts. Sets are often split and remade; a matching patina and base do not by themselves show the items were made together.

facts.text: Sita, Lakshmana and Hanuman accompany Rama; Hanuman stands smaller, humble, hand at the mouth or hands joined.
facts.quote: Hanuman, the faithful monkey-messenger, should be shown as standing a little in front and also to the right of Rama

facts.text: Sita's side differs: the Vaikhanasagama puts her on Rama's right, but temple groups usually have her on his left.
facts.quote: Rama is generally seen to be a standing figure with his queen Sita on the left and his faithful brother Lakshmana on the right.

facts.text: Cleveland's Kalighat court: Rama and Sita under a parasol held by Lakshmana, Hanuman kneeling.
facts.quote: Rama and Sita sit enthroned under a royal parasol held by Rama's brother Lakshmana. A diminutive Hanuman kneels before them in adoration.

rows.name: Sita
rows.features_other: Two-armed lady with a blue water lily (or lotus) in one hand, the other hanging; in South Indian bronze sets she stands in a bend opposite to Rama's.
rows.identify_by: A two-armed lady standing with Rama and Lakshmana or Hanuman; alone she cannot be told from other consort figures.

look_alikes.name: sridevi
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Shridevi belongs with a four-armed Vishnu; Sita with a two-armed bowman.

look_alikes.name: bhudevi
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Same pose and lily; only the group tells.

look_alikes.name: radha
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Radha accompanies the flute-player Krishna.

rows.regions_styles: As for rama_group.
rows.dating_clues: Not datable from iconography.
rows.cautions: An identification names the figure only; it says nothing about age, origin or whether the item is old or genuine. Traditional forms are still made: Rao (1914) already notes small Krishna figures sold in bazaars as toys and new ivory figures carved at the Trivandrum School of Arts. A single goddess bronze sold as 'Sita' is a reading unless it comes with its group.

facts.text: Sita holds a blue water lily in the left hand, the right hanging; reaches Rama's shoulder.
facts.quote: In the left hand there should be a nilotpala flower and the right hand should be hanging down freely.

facts.text: Rao (vol. 1 pt. 2) lists Sita, Rukmini, Satyabhama and Radha as the consorts of the human avatars.
facts.quote: Sita was worshipped as the consort of Rama, and Rukmini, Satyabhama and Radha as the consorts of Krishna.

rows.name: Lakshmana
rows.features_other: Like Rama in pose (bow grip) but smaller and, by the Vishnudharmottara, without the royal crown: hair tied in a knot on the crown of the head. In paintings he may hold the royal parasol or fly whisk over Rama.
rows.identify_by: A second, slightly smaller bowman beside Rama, hair tied in a knot rather than a tall crown.

look_alikes.name: rama
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Rama wears the tall crown and is the larger central figure.

look_alikes.name: Bharata and Shatrughna
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Further brothers in full sets; by text Bharata may carry sword and shield.

rows.regions_styles: As for rama_group.
rows.dating_clues: Not datable from iconography.
rows.cautions: An identification names the figure only; it says nothing about age, origin or whether the item is old or genuine. Traditional forms are still made: Rao (1914) already notes small Krishna figures sold in bazaars as toys and new ivory figures carved at the Trivandrum School of Arts.

facts.text: Lakshmana stands beside Rama, like him in all respects; by the Vishnudharmottara without the crown.
facts.quote: the figure of Lakshmana should not have the kirita-makuta on the head.

facts.text: In the Shermadevi bronzes Lakshmana's hair is tied in a knot on the crown.
facts.quote: of Lakshmana has the hair shown as tied up in a knot on the crown of the head

rows.name: Balarama (Krishna's elder brother; avatar in some lists)
rows.features_other: Pale or white-skinned in paintings (Krishna is dark); plough share and pestle (or club); a canopy of serpent hoods behind the head (he is held to embody the serpent Shesha); palm-tree banner (taladhvaja); one earring only.
rows.identify_by: A white-skinned or snake-hooded figure holding a plough, often beside the dark Krishna.

look_alikes.name: krishna
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Krishna is dark or blue with a flute or herding stick; Balarama is white with a plough.

look_alikes.name: Nagaraja / naga figures
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Naga kings have hoods but no plough or pestle; many have serpent tails.

look_alikes.name: balabhadra
look_alikes.how_to_tell: At Puri the white Balabhadra is a wooden figure with large eyes and stump arms.

look_alikes.name: Parshvanatha (jain topic)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: The Jain Parshvanatha under a snake hood is a nude meditating or standing-stiff figure without plough or pestle.

rows.regions_styles: Early Mathura and Gwalior stone (snake canopy); Pahari and Rajput paintings (white Balarama, blue Krishna); Puri as Balabhadra; Kalighat.
rows.dating_clues: Not datable from iconography.
rows.cautions: An identification names the figure only; it says nothing about age, origin or whether the item is old or genuine. Traditional forms are still made: Rao (1914) already notes small Krishna figures sold in bazaars as toys and new ivory figures carved at the Trivandrum School of Arts.

facts.text: Balarama carries the pestle (musala) and the plough (hala); his color is white.
facts.quote: The figure of Balarama should carry the musala in the right hand and the hala in the left. The complexion of Balarama should be white

facts.text: He stands under a canopy of snake hoods in many images.
facts.quote: the canopy of snakehoods and the ploughshare in one of the hands are almost invariably mentioned.

facts.text: Some lists put Balarama in Buddha's place among the ten avatars.
facts.quote: substitute in his place Balarama, the elder brother of Krishna, as an avatara.

rows.name: Buddha as the ninth avatar of Vishnu
rows.features_other: In Hindu avatar sets the Buddha sits in meditation in a monk's robe with short curls and a hair knot; only his place in the set makes him an avatar.
rows.identify_by: A meditating robed figure in the ninth place of a Hindu ten-avatar set.

look_alikes.name: Buddha (buddhist topic)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Identical type; a lone Buddha figure is a Buddhist image unless it belongs to a Vaishnava set.

look_alikes.name: Jain tirthankara (jain topic)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Digambara tirthankaras are naked; Rao notes the Buddha wears the robe and has the hair knot.

look_alikes.name: jagannath
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Bengal and Odisha sets may put Jagannath in this place.

rows.regions_styles: Chalukya and Hoysala Vishnu images (in the arch); Rajput and Pahari avatar paintings.
rows.dating_clues: Not datable from iconography.
rows.cautions: An identification names the figure only; it says nothing about age, origin or whether the item is old or genuine. Traditional forms are still made: Rao (1914) already notes small Krishna figures sold in bazaars as toys and new ivory figures carved at the Trivandrum School of Arts. Rao warns that even educated people confuse Buddha and Jain images.

facts.text: In Hindu avatar sets the Buddha sits in meditation with legs crossed and hands in the lap.
facts.quote: In all these instances Buddha is represented in the Dhyana attitude, with his legs crossed and his hands placed upon the lap in the yogamudra pose.

facts.text: Buddha and Jain images are easily confused; the robe and hair knot mark the Buddha.
facts.quote: even highly educated people are not able to distinguish the one class of images from the other.

facts.text: The Buddha avatar is counted but rarely worshipped in Hindu temples.
facts.quote: The Buddha incarnation of Vishnu is, no doubt, counted among the ten avatars but is rarely found worshipped in Hindu temples.

rows.name: Kalki (the avatar to come)
rows.features_other: Usually a warrior on horseback with a raised sword; some texts give him a horse's face on a man's body instead.
rows.identify_by: The last figure of an avatar set: a sword-swinging rider on a horse, or a horse-faced warrior with sword and shield.

look_alikes.name: hayagriva
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Horse-headed Hayagriva holds Vishnu's emblems or a book, not sword and shield.

look_alikes.name: Revanta or horsemen hero stones
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Revanta, Surya's son, rides with hunting dogs; hero stones show a fallen warrior; Kalki comes last in an avatar set.

rows.regions_styles: In avatar sets; Rajput and Pahari paintings; Kalighat.
rows.dating_clues: Not datable from iconography.
rows.cautions: An identification names the figure only; it says nothing about age, origin or whether the item is old or genuine. Traditional forms are still made: Rao (1914) already notes small Krishna figures sold in bazaars as toys and new ivory figures carved at the Trivandrum School of Arts.

facts.text: Kalki is expected to appear riding a horse, sword in hand.
facts.quote: expected to appear as a powerful hero riding on horse-back, sword in hand

facts.text: The Vaikhanasagama gives Kalki a horse's face on a man's body with four hands (conch, discus, sword, shield).
facts.quote: have the face of a horse and the body of a man with four hands

rows.name: Krishna (general; how to know him in paintings)
rows.features_other: Dark (blue in paintings) skin; peacock feather(s) in the crown or hair knot; flute; cows, cowherds and gopis around him; Radha as companion. Token wanted: peacock-feather crown.
rows.identify_by: In paintings: the blue- or dark-skinned youth with a peacock feather in his crown, among cows or milkmaids, often with a flute. In sculpture: the specific forms below.

look_alikes.name: rama
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Rama also has blue/dark skin in paintings, but carries a bow and quiver and appears with Sita, Lakshmana or monkeys; Krishna has the peacock feather, flute and cows.

look_alikes.name: vishnu
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Vishnu is four-armed with discus and conch and no peacock feather; four-armed Krishna temple images exist, so the flute or story scene is the sign.

look_alikes.name: Shiva in paintings (shiva_devi topic)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Shiva is pale or ash-gray (sometimes blue-throated) with matted hair, crescent moon and snakes.

look_alikes.name: balarama
look_alikes.how_to_tell: The white-skinned brother with the plough.

rows.regions_styles: Everywhere: Rajput (Mewar, Bundi, Kota, Kishangarh), Pahari (Basohli, Guler, Kangra), Malwa, Deccan, Bengal and Odisha paintings; South Indian bronzes and Thanjavur paintings; Nathdwara pichhwais.
rows.dating_clues: Iconography does not date; painting school and materials do (see paintings guide).
rows.cautions: An identification names the figure only; it says nothing about age, origin or whether the item is old or genuine. Traditional forms are still made: Rao (1914) already notes small Krishna figures sold in bazaars as toys and new ivory figures carved at the Trivandrum School of Arts.

facts.text: Krishna's complexion is dark (black or rain-cloud colored; blue in paintings).
facts.quote: The complexion of the image of Krishna should be black

facts.text: A peacock feather in the hair is a mark of Krishna, especially as cowherd and child.
facts.quote: A peacock's feather stuck into the tuft of hair knotted overhead is, along with the other golden jewellery peculiar to children, a special feature of Krishna as a boy.

facts.text: Krishna is worshipped as baby, boy and youth, unlike any other avatar.
facts.quote: Krishna alone, among the avataras of Vishnu, is worshipped as a child, a youth etc.

rows.name: Venugopala (Krishna playing the flute)
rows.features_other: Stands on one leg with the other crossed in front or behind, resting on the toes; both hands raised to one side holding the flute at the lips (in bronzes the flute is often lost, leaving the hands curled at mouth height); peacock feathers; in paintings often leaning on a cow; temple images may have four arms with discus and conch and consorts beside.
rows.identify_by: A standing youth with legs crossed at the ankle and both hands lifted to one side of the mouth as if playing a transverse flute.

look_alikes.name: rama
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Rama's hands are at different heights (bow above, arrow below) and his legs are not crossed.

look_alikes.name: madanagopala
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Same flute pose but with eight or ten arms holding Kama's sugarcane bow and other emblems.

look_alikes.name: Shiva Vinadhara (shiva_devi topic)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Shiva holding a vina stands with matted hair, crescent and four arms with axe and deer; the hands hold a stringed instrument, not at the mouth.

look_alikes.name: radha_krishna
look_alikes.how_to_tell: With a lady beside him it is a Radha-Krishna pair (or Krishna with consorts in the south).

rows.regions_styles: Hoysala stone (Halebid); Chola and Vijayanagara bronzes; Bengal and Odisha brass; Rajput and Pahari paintings; Nathdwara.
rows.dating_clues: Not datable from iconography.
rows.cautions: An identification names the figure only; it says nothing about age, origin or whether the item is old or genuine. Traditional forms are still made: Rao (1914) already notes small Krishna figures sold in bazaars as toys and new ivory figures carved at the Trivandrum School of Arts.

facts.text: Venugopala stands on one leg, the other crossed and resting on the toes, holding the flute in both hands to the mouth.
facts.quote: the right leg is thrown across behind or in front of the left leg so as to touch the ground with the toes. The flute is held in both the hands

facts.text: Temple images may be four-armed with conch and discus and consorts on either side.
facts.quote: When the figure is intended for worship in temples the two upper hands will hold the conch and the discus

facts.text: In paintings he often leans against a cow with cowherds round him.
facts.quote: In paintings Venu-Gopala is often represented as leaning against a cow

rows.name: Madanagopala (many-armed flute-playing Krishna)
rows.features_other: Venugopala's pose with extra arms carrying Kamadeva's sugarcane bow and flower arrow alongside Vishnu's emblems.
rows.identify_by: A many-armed Krishna playing the flute with two hands while others hold a sugarcane bow.

look_alikes.name: Kamadeva (other_hindu topic)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Kama holds the sugarcane bow and flower arrows but does not play the flute and rides a parrot.

look_alikes.name: Lalita / Tripurasundari (shiva_devi topic)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: The goddess also holds a sugarcane bow, noose and goad; she is female and has no flute.

rows.regions_styles: Pandya pillar at Tenkasi (1447); Kanchipuram Varadaraja mandapa (ten arms).
rows.dating_clues: Not datable from iconography.
rows.cautions: An identification names the figure only; it says nothing about age, origin or whether the item is old or genuine. Traditional forms are still made: Rao (1914) already notes small Krishna figures sold in bazaars as toys and new ivory figures carved at the Trivandrum School of Arts.

facts.text: An eight-armed flute-playing Krishna holds lotus, axe, discus, sugarcane bow, noose and conch; the Sritattvanidhi calls it Madanagopala.
facts.quote: Here Krishna is represented with eight arms; in three of the right hands he holds a padma, a parasu, and the chakra, and in three corresponding left hands he carries a bow made of sugar-cane, a pasa and the sankha.

rows.name: Krishna dancing on the serpent Kaliya (Kaliya-mardana)
rows.features_other: A boy standing on one foot on the hoods of a many-headed cobra (whose upper body may be human, with joined hands), the other leg lifted to stamp; one hand grips the serpent's tail stretched out like a streamer, the other gives fear-not.
rows.identify_by: A dancing boy on top of a many-hooded serpent, holding its tail up in one hand.

look_alikes.name: navanita_nritta
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Same dancing pose; the butter-dance Krishna holds a butter ball and has no serpent underfoot.

look_alikes.name: Nataraja (shiva_devi topic)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Nataraja dances on a dwarf inside a ring of fire with drum and fire; Kaliya-Krishna dances on a serpent holding its tail.

look_alikes.name: vishnu_reclining
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Vishnu lies on a serpent; Krishna stands on one.

rows.regions_styles: Chola, Vijayanagara and Nayaka bronzes (AIC 1995.62, 14th c.); Ellora; Rajput paintings (Cleveland 2018.141, Mewar).
rows.dating_clues: Not datable from iconography.
rows.cautions: An identification names the figure only; it says nothing about age, origin or whether the item is old or genuine. Traditional forms are still made: Rao (1914) already notes small Krishna figures sold in bazaars as toys and new ivory figures carved at the Trivandrum School of Arts. Sastri notes small Kaliya-Krishna figures among household shrine images, so many are domestic, not temple, items.

facts.text: Krishna's left foot is on the serpent's hood, the right raised; one hand holds the serpent's tail, the other shows fear-not.
facts.quote: In the hand stretched out and held in the flag-pose the tail of the serpent Kaliya is caught.

facts.text: Kaliya-Krishna is a decorative or household image, not a main temple image.
facts.quote: Kaliya-Krishna is found only as a decorative figure in temples but not as the object of worship in the central shrine.

rows.name: Navanita Krishna (crawling baby Krishna with butter)
rows.features_other: Plump naked baby on hands and knees (one hand raised holding a ball of butter), child's jewelry, a tiger-claw pendant may hang at the neck; in South Indian paintings he may have a butter pot under his arm.
rows.identify_by: A crawling baby with a ball of butter in his raised hand.

look_alikes.name: Bala-Ganesha / child Ganesha (other_hindu topic)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Ganesha has an elephant head; his round object is a sweet (modaka); the crawling human baby is Krishna.

look_alikes.name: Child Skanda / Bala Subrahmanya (other_hindu topic)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Skanda as a child is usually with Shiva and Parvati (Somaskanda) or with a spear and peacock.

look_alikes.name: vatapatrashayi
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Lies on a leaf sucking his toe.

look_alikes.name: Jain child or donor figures
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Look for the butter ball and Vaishnava context.

rows.regions_styles: South Indian bronzes (AIC 1949.599 'Krishna the Butter Thief', 15th c.; AIC 1949.600 'Infant Krishna'); household brass child-Krishna figures (called Laddu Gopal in the north); Thanjavur paintings.
rows.dating_clues: Not datable from iconography.
rows.cautions: An identification names the figure only; it says nothing about age, origin or whether the item is old or genuine. Traditional forms are still made: Rao (1914) already notes small Krishna figures sold in bazaars as toys and new ivory figures carved at the Trivandrum School of Arts. Small Bala Krishna figures were and are made in large numbers for household worship and as toys (Rao, Sastri).

facts.text: As a baby Krishna is shown crawling on all fours, sometimes with a ball of butter in his hand.
facts.quote: As a baby Krishna is represented as crawling on all fours, sometimes with a ball of butter in his hand

facts.text: Miniature gold and silver child Krishnas are part of the daily household shrine.
facts.quote: Gold and silver images of this form of Krishna in miniature are among the set of idols worshipped daily in an orthodox Brahmana's house.

facts.text: A necklace with tiger's claws is part of the child's jewelry in the Silparatna's description.
facts.quote: He wears also a necklace with a pair of tiger's claws decorating it.

rows.name: Dancing child Krishna with butter (Navanita-nritta)
other_names: Krishna dancing with a butter ball
rows.features_other: A child standing on one slightly bent leg, the other lifted and bent inward (often propped on a small lotus for stability), one hand holding a butter ball or in fear-not, the other flung out; nude or in short drawers.
rows.identify_by: A child dancing on one leg with a ball of butter in one hand and the other arm thrown out.

look_alikes.name: kaliya_mardana
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Kaliya-Krishna dances on a serpent and holds its tail.

look_alikes.name: Dancing Ganesha (other_hindu topic)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Elephant head, pot belly, four or more arms.

look_alikes.name: Dancing Sambandar (shiva_devi topic)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: The Shaiva child-saint Sambandar also dances with one finger raised pointing up to Shiva and no butter ball (AIC 1949.602).

rows.regions_styles: Chola and later South Indian bronzes (Madras Museum examples in Rao and Sastri).
rows.dating_clues: Not datable from iconography.
rows.cautions: An identification names the figure only; it says nothing about age, origin or whether the item is old or genuine. Traditional forms are still made: Rao (1914) already notes small Krishna figures sold in bazaars as toys and new ivory figures carved at the Trivandrum School of Arts. Rao (1914): such figures 'may very often be even purchased in bazaars as a toy for children to play with'.

facts.text: The Navanita-nritta Krishna dances on the left leg, right leg lifted, holding a butter ball or showing fear-not, the left arm thrown out.
facts.quote: In the hand the ball of butter is invariably shown. This is a common piece of sculpture in South India, and may very often be even purchased in bazaars as a toy for children to play with.

rows.name: Baby Krishna on the banyan leaf (Vatapatrashayi)
other_names: Baby on a leaf sucking his toe
rows.features_other: A baby lying on a banyan (fig) leaf floating on the cosmic waters, holding his foot and sucking his big toe. Token wanted: leaf as couch.
rows.identify_by: A baby on a large leaf with his toe in his mouth.

look_alikes.name: vishnu_reclining
look_alikes.how_to_tell: The adult Vishnu reclines on the serpent; the baby lies on a leaf.

look_alikes.name: navanita_krishna
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Crawls with a butter ball.

rows.regions_styles: South Indian ivory and bronze (Rao's Trivandrum ivory); Thanjavur and Mysore paintings; Kerala.
rows.dating_clues: Not datable from iconography.
rows.cautions: An identification names the figure only; it says nothing about age, origin or whether the item is old or genuine. Traditional forms are still made: Rao (1914) already notes small Krishna figures sold in bazaars as toys and new ivory figures carved at the Trivandrum School of Arts. Rao's example is a modern ivory from the Trivandrum School of Arts; ivory carries legal restrictions.

facts.text: The child Krishna lies on a leaf of the banyan (Indian fig), symbolizing God over the waters after the dissolution of the world.
facts.quote: lying upon a leaf of the [vata] tree (Indian fig) and is hence known as the Vata-patra-sayi.

rows.name: Yashoda nursing the baby Krishna (Santana-Gopala)
rows.features_other: A seated woman with a baby on her lap at the breast, the baby looking up at her, one hand on her breast; worshipped by those wanting children.
rows.identify_by: A mother suckling a baby who looks up into her face, in a Vaishnava context.

look_alikes.name: Parvati with Skanda or Ganesha (shiva_devi topic)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: An elephant-headed baby is Ganesha; Parvati's group usually includes Shiva or the bull.

look_alikes.name: Hariti / Jain mother goddesses (buddhist, jain topics)
