look_alikes.how_to_tell: Hariti carries several children and a pomegranate; Jain Ambika sits under a mango tree with a child and a lion.

look_alikes.name: Maya and the infant Mahavira or other nativity scenes
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Context and attendants decide.

rows.regions_styles: South Indian bronzes and Thanjavur paintings (AIC 2018.592, 20th c., not open).
rows.dating_clues: Not datable from iconography.
rows.cautions: An identification names the figure only; it says nothing about age, origin or whether the item is old or genuine. Traditional forms are still made: Rao (1914) already notes small Krishna figures sold in bazaars as toys and new ivory figures carved at the Trivandrum School of Arts.

facts.text: Santana-Gopala: the infant Krishna on Yashoda's lap, sucking at her breast and looking up at her.
facts.quote: the infant Krishna should be portrayed as lying on the lap of Yasoda and sucking milk from her breast

rows.name: Krishna lifting Mount Govardhana (Govardhanadhari)
rows.features_other: One arm raised straight up holding a hill (on one finger in North Indian paintings) as an umbrella over cows and herders sheltering from Indra's storm; the other hand gives a boon, rests on the hip or holds the flute.
rows.identify_by: Krishna standing with one arm raised overhead supporting a hill, cows and cowherds beneath.

look_alikes.name: hanuman_mountain
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Hanuman carries his mountain flying or striding and has a monkey face; Krishna stands still with cowherds sheltering below.

look_alikes.name: shrinathji
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Shrinathji is the Nathdwara image of this same act: raised left arm, but the hill itself is not shown, and the figure is a flat black relief.

rows.regions_styles: Pallava Mahabalipuram; Hoysala (Nuggehalli, signed); Kangra paintings (Cleveland 2001.45); Phnom Da, Cambodia (Cleveland 1973.106).
rows.dating_clues: Not datable from iconography.
rows.cautions: An identification names the figure only; it says nothing about age, origin or whether the item is old or genuine. Traditional forms are still made: Rao (1914) already notes small Krishna figures sold in bazaars as toys and new ivory figures carved at the Trivandrum School of Arts.

facts.text: Krishna holds the hill aloft with one raised hand, cows and cowherds sheltering below.
facts.quote: Krishna stands in the centre with his left hand raised straight up to support the hill, while his right hand is held in the posture of offering boons

facts.text: The Silpasara has one hand with the flute at the waist and the other supporting the hill.
facts.quote: the god is described as having one hand with flute resting on his waist and the other supporting the hill.

rows.name: Radha and Krishna (the pair)
rows.features_other: A pair: Krishna (often playing the flute) with Radha beside him; in paintings in groves, pavilions or on terraces; in North and East Indian brass and marble shrine pairs the two stand side by side.
rows.identify_by: Krishna with one beloved woman as an equal pair, in a Braj, Bengal or Rajput setting.

look_alikes.name: rajagopala
look_alikes.how_to_tell: South Indian Krishna with two wives (Rukmini and Satyabhama) is a different group.

look_alikes.name: Rama and Sita
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Rama carries a bow; Krishna the flute.

look_alikes.name: Shiva and Parvati (shiva_devi topic)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Shiva has matted hair, trident, bull; Krishna the flute and peacock feather.

rows.regions_styles: Bengal and Odisha (Gaudiya and other Vaishnava traditions), Braj, Rajasthan (Kishangarh, Mewar), Pahari kingdoms; AIC and Cleveland hold many paintings.
rows.dating_clues: Not datable from iconography.
rows.cautions: An identification names the figure only; it says nothing about age, origin or whether the item is old or genuine. Traditional forms are still made: Rao (1914) already notes small Krishna figures sold in bazaars as toys and new ivory figures carved at the Trivandrum School of Arts. Courtly paintings of a lover pair are not always Radha and Krishna; the blue skin and peacock feather decide.

facts.text: Radha was the most beloved of the gopis, and Radha-Krishna is a name by which Krishna is addressed.
facts.quote: the most beloved was Radha, so much so that Radha-Krishna is the name by which he is addressed

facts.text: Cleveland labels many Pahari and Rajput paintings of the pair; Radha is 'the blue god Krishna's beloved'.
facts.quote: Radha, the blue god Krishna's beloved, raises one hand, reddened with henna

rows.name: Radha
rows.features_other: Fair-skinned young woman in the dress of the painting's region; she has no fixed emblem and is known by her companion, Krishna, or by a caption.
rows.identify_by: The woman with Krishna in a pair or love scene; alone she is identifiable only by caption or series context.

look_alikes.name: sita
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Sita is with the bowman Rama.

look_alikes.name: Gopis and heroines (nayikas)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: In Rasikapriya and Gita Govinda series many heroines appear; inscriptions or the series decide.

rows.regions_styles: Paintings above all; Bengal and Braj shrine pairs in brass or marble.
rows.dating_clues: Not datable from iconography.
rows.cautions: An identification names the figure only; it says nothing about age, origin or whether the item is old or genuine. Traditional forms are still made: Rao (1914) already notes small Krishna figures sold in bazaars as toys and new ivory figures carved at the Trivandrum School of Arts.

facts.text: Radha is counted among Krishna's consorts in Vaishnava worship.
facts.quote: Rukmini, Satyabhama and Radha as the consorts of Krishna.

rows.name: Krishna with Rukmini and Satyabhama (Rajagopala, Mannar)
rows.features_other: Two-armed Krishna in the triple bend, right hand holding a curved cowherd's stick (often a separate, lost stick passed through the curled fingers), left arm raised or resting on a consort's shoulder; Rukmini at his right, Satyabhama at his left; Garuda may stand by.
rows.identify_by: A two-armed Krishna holding a short curved stick, between two consorts.

look_alikes.name: vishnu
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Vishnu with Shridevi and Bhudevi is four-armed with discus and conch; Rajagopala is two-armed with a stick.

look_alikes.name: rama_group
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Rama holds a bow; his group has one woman and a monkey.

look_alikes.name: venugopala
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Venugopala's hands are raised together to the flute.

rows.regions_styles: Tamil Nadu (Mannargudi; Rao's Shermadevi bronze, 11th-12th c. by style); Nathdwara-tradition Dvarakanathji at Kankroli is a different, four-armed image (Cleveland 2001.161).
rows.dating_clues: Rao dated his examples by style; iconography itself does not date.
rows.cautions: An identification names the figure only; it says nothing about age, origin or whether the item is old or genuine. Traditional forms are still made: Rao (1914) already notes small Krishna figures sold in bazaars as toys and new ivory figures carved at the Trivandrum School of Arts.

facts.text: Krishna holds a curved stick in the right hand; Rukmini stands at his right, Satyabhama at his left; this form is enshrined as Mannar.
facts.quote: In the right hand a peculiarly curved stick should be carried

facts.text: The right hand of the metal image is curled to receive a separate stick.
facts.quote: is obviously intended to receive a separate metallic stick, which might be passed through the ring formed of the forefinger and the thumb

facts.text: South Indian temple Krishnas stand between the two consorts Rukmini and Satyabhama.
facts.quote: there will usually also be the images of his two consorts Rukmini and Satya on either side

rows.name: Krishna as Arjuna's charioteer (Parthasarathi)
other_names: Krishna and Arjuna on the chariot
rows.features_other: Krishna on (or mounting) a chariot drawn by horses, reins in one hand and a whip in the other, teaching the kneeling or seated Arjuna who holds a bow; the Triplicane temple image is a two-armed standing Krishna with conch. Token wanted: chariot; reins/whip.
rows.identify_by: Krishna on a horse-drawn chariot holding reins or a whip, with an archer (Arjuna) before him.

look_alikes.name: Surya (other_hindu topic)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Surya's chariot has seven horses and he holds two lotuses; Krishna's chariot carries Arjuna.

look_alikes.name: rama
look_alikes.how_to_tell: The bow belongs to Arjuna, not to Krishna.

rows.regions_styles: Triplicane (Chennai) temple; Pushpagiri relief; 19th-20th c. prints and calendar art.
rows.dating_clues: Not datable from iconography.
rows.cautions: An identification names the figure only; it says nothing about age, origin or whether the item is old or genuine. Traditional forms are still made: Rao (1914) already notes small Krishna figures sold in bazaars as toys and new ivory figures carved at the Trivandrum School of Arts.

facts.text: The Vaikhanasagama describes Krishna holding the reins and a cane, mounting a chariot, with Arjuna standing with joined hands.
facts.quote: Krishna is represented as holding the reins in one hand and a cane in the other, and as in the act of mounting a chariot

facts.text: Parthasarathi is the god of the Triplicane temple; the scene is the teaching of the Bhagavad Gita.
facts.quote: Hence Krishna is also known by the name of Parthasarathi, the name of the god in the famous temple at Triplicane.

rows.name: Shrinathji of Nathdwara
rows.features_other: A flat black stone relief image of the child Krishna lifting Govardhana: left arm raised high above the head (the hill itself not shown), right hand closed at the waist; large eyes; in paintings dressed and jeweled for the day's festival, with a pichhwai cloth behind and priests offering lamps. Sources differ on the right hand (Cleveland's pendant label reads a herdsman's staff). Token wanted: one arm raised overhead.
rows.identify_by: A dark, frontal, stiff figure with the left arm raised straight up and the right hand at the waist, set against a painted cloth with cows and gopis.

look_alikes.name: govardhanadhari
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Govardhanadhari shows the hill and the sheltering herd; Shrinathji is the Nathdwara icon with the hill implied.

look_alikes.name: rajagopala
look_alikes.how_to_tell: The Kankroli Dvarakanathji of the same sect is four-armed (Cleveland 2001.161).

look_alikes.name: jagannath
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Jagannath is a dark wooden figure with huge round eyes and stump arms, with white and yellow siblings.

rows.regions_styles: Nathdwara, Rajasthan: pichhwai temple cloths, souvenir paintings, prints, jewelry pendants (Cleveland 1946.257, 1937.454; AIC 2013.80). Pushtimarg sect.
rows.dating_clues: Nathdwara painting continued into the 20th c.; souvenir paintings (AIC 2018.581-582, 20th c.) and prints are common. The icon type does not date an item.
rows.cautions: An identification names the figure only; it says nothing about age, origin or whether the item is old or genuine. Traditional forms are still made: Rao (1914) already notes small Krishna figures sold in bazaars as toys and new ivory figures carved at the Trivandrum School of Arts. Old pichhwais are usually worn and faded from use (Cleveland); new ones are made in large numbers in Nathdwara.

facts.text: Shrinathji's raised left hand refers to the lifting of Mount Govardhan.
facts.quote: Even in the tiny composition, Krishna's raised left hand can be seen clearly, referencing his miraculous lifting of Mount Govardhan.

facts.text: The Shrinathji image was first on Govardhan hill (temple of 1520 by Vallabhacharya) and was moved to Nathdwara in Udaipur territory under threat of Aurangzeb's raids.
facts.quote: In anticipation of one of Aurangzeb's raids, the image of the god was removed to Nathdwara in Udaypur territory, and has remained there ever since.

facts.text: The icon is a dark stone relief on a rectangular slab carved with rocks and animals.
facts.quote: the dark stone sculpture of Shri Nathji with its monolithic rectangular slab depicting stylized rocks and wild inhabitants in low relief.

facts.text: Pichhwais are painted cloth hangings behind the image; long use leaves them faded and worn.
facts.quote: As a result of long-term exposure, these textiles are usually faded and worn.

rows.name: Jagannath of Puri
rows.features_other: Black-faced wooden figure with a large round head, enormous round eyes, no neck, stump arms projecting forward at head height, no legs; with the white Balabhadra (larger) and yellow Subhadra (smaller, armless) between them; a Sudarshana image beside them. Token wanted: stump arms; huge round eyes.
rows.identify_by: A black, roughly cylindrical figure with huge round eyes and stump arms, usually with a white and a yellow companion.

look_alikes.name: balabhadra
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Same shape, white face, usually the tallest of the three.

look_alikes.name: subhadra
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Yellow, smaller, without arms, in the middle.

look_alikes.name: Folk and tribal wooden figures
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Many folk images are block-like; the black-white-yellow triad, round eyes and Puri context (temple, chariots, patachitra) decide.

look_alikes.name: buddha_avatar
look_alikes.how_to_tell: In some Bengal and Odisha avatar sets Jagannath occupies Buddha's ninth place.

rows.regions_styles: Puri (Odisha): wooden temple images, Odia patachitra paintings, souvenir figures; Bengal Kalighat pictures (Cleveland 2003.114.b; AIC 1917.425, Calcutta c. 1875).
rows.dating_clues: Souvenir figures and pictures have been made for pilgrims for centuries; style and materials, not the form, date them.
rows.cautions: An identification names the figure only; it says nothing about age, origin or whether the item is old or genuine. Traditional forms are still made: Rao (1914) already notes small Krishna figures sold in bazaars as toys and new ivory figures carved at the Trivandrum School of Arts. Nineteenth-century writers' theory that the triad began as a Buddhist symbol (reported by Rao and the Puri Gazetteer) is a period opinion, not an identification aid.

facts.text: The three Puri images are wooden, with round shapeless heads and stump arms; Balabhadra, Jagannath and Subhadra are painted white, black and yellow.
facts.quote: They are painted white, black, and yellow respectively

facts.text: The brothers have arms projecting forward; the sister has none.
facts.quote: The two brothers have arms projecting horizontally forward from the ears. The sister is entirely devoid of even that approximation to the human form.

facts.text: Krishna is worshipped at Puri as Jagannath with his sister Subhadra and brother Balarama.
facts.quote: The famous temple at Puri-Jagannath contains figures of Balarama and Krishna with their sister Subhadra standing between them.

facts.text: The wooden bodies are periodically renewed (Navakalevara).
facts.quote: Its celebration is said to depend on certain astronomical conditions, viz., the occurrence of two months of Ashadha in the same year

rows.name: Balabhadra of Puri
rows.features_other: The white-faced member of the Puri triad, same block form as Jagannath (stump arms, round eyes), the tallest of the three (six feet against Jagannath's five in the Gazetteer). Token wanted: white face (Puri).
rows.identify_by: The white figure of the Puri triad.

look_alikes.name: jagannath
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Jagannath's face is black.

look_alikes.name: balarama
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Elsewhere Balarama is a full human figure with plough and snake hood.

rows.regions_styles: As for jagannath.
rows.dating_clues: As for jagannath.
rows.cautions: An identification names the figure only; it says nothing about age, origin or whether the item is old or genuine. Traditional forms are still made: Rao (1914) already notes small Krishna figures sold in bazaars as toys and new ivory figures carved at the Trivandrum School of Arts.

facts.text: Balabhadra (Bara Thakur) is the elder brother, six feet high, painted white.
facts.quote: The elder brother Balabhadra is six feet in height, the younger Jagannath five feet, and their sister Subhadra four feet.

rows.name: Subhadra of Puri
rows.features_other: The yellow, smallest, armless figure standing between Jagannath and Balabhadra. Token wanted: yellow face; armless.
rows.identify_by: The small yellow figure in the middle of the Puri triad.

look_alikes.name: jagannath
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Black, with stump arms.

look_alikes.name: balabhadra
look_alikes.how_to_tell: White, with stump arms.

rows.regions_styles: As for jagannath.
rows.dating_clues: As for jagannath.
rows.cautions: An identification names the figure only; it says nothing about age, origin or whether the item is old or genuine. Traditional forms are still made: Rao (1914) already notes small Krishna figures sold in bazaars as toys and new ivory figures carved at the Trivandrum School of Arts.

facts.text: Subhadra is Krishna's sister, painted yellow, four feet high, without arms, standing between her brothers.
facts.quote: Even Subhadra, the sister of Krishna, is associated with Vishnu worship at Jagannath.

rows.name: Vithoba (Vitthala) of Pandharpur
rows.features_other: Two-armed, standing straight (no bends), both hands on the hips, feet together on a brick; tall round-topped cap with a linga mark (Rao); long earrings to the shoulders; often paired with his consort Rakhumai (Rukmini). Token wanted: brick pedestal; tall cylindrical cap.
rows.identify_by: A straight-standing two-armed figure with both hands on the hips, standing on a brick, in a tall cap.

look_alikes.name: venkateshvara
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Venkateshvara has four arms with discus and conch.

look_alikes.name: Jain tirthankara standing stiff (jain topic)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: A kayotsarga Jina stands straight with arms hanging down, not on the hips, and is nude or plainly robed.

look_alikes.name: Khandoba (other_hindu topic)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Khandoba of Jejuri rides a horse and carries sword and trident.

rows.regions_styles: Pandharpur (Maharashtra) and Karnataka; brass household images; Maharashtrian prints; Sastri illustrates examples at Tirupati and Ahobilam.
rows.dating_clues: Not datable from iconography (the Gazetteer's stylistic dating of the temple image is a period opinion).
rows.cautions: An identification names the figure only; it says nothing about age, origin or whether the item is old or genuine. Traditional forms are still made: Rao (1914) already notes small Krishna figures sold in bazaars as toys and new ivory figures carved at the Trivandrum School of Arts.

facts.text: Vithoba stands straight with two arms, both hands resting on the hips.
facts.quote: The characteristic feature of the image is that it has two arms which, being bent at the elbow, are placed on its hips.

facts.text: He stands on a brick, after the legend of Pundalik.
facts.quote: believed to be a brick to suit the Pundlik story of Vithoba waiting on a brick.

facts.text: The Pandharpur image's hands hold a conch (left) and a discus (right) and the head has a long round-topped cap.
facts.quote: the left hand holding a conch and the right hand a chakra or discus.

facts.text: Rao records the Pundalika legend and the consort Rukmabai (Rakhumai).
facts.quote: The name of his goddess is Rukmabayi.

rows.name: Hanuman as Rama's humble devotee
rows.features_other: Monkey face and tail on a man's body; stands bowed a little, smaller than Rama, either with hands joined, or with the right hand held before the mouth (a servant's posture of respect) and the left hanging to the knee; tail hanging to the feet. At Rameshvaram he may carry two lingas. Token wanted: hand before the mouth.
rows.identify_by: A monkey-faced figure standing respectfully, hands joined or one hand at the mouth, usually part of a Rama group.

look_alikes.name: Sugriva, Vali, Angada and other monkey heroes
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Other monkeys appear in Ramayana scenes (Cleveland 1973.103); the one serving Rama with joined hands, or carrying the mountain, is Hanuman. Captions may hesitate (Cleveland 2003.120).

look_alikes.name: Jambavan (bear king)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: A bear face, not a monkey's.

look_alikes.name: Nandi in human form / ganas
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Shaiva attendants with joined hands have bull or human faces.

rows.regions_styles: Chola bronze sets (Cleveland 1980.26, c. 1000); Rameshvaram; Central Indian stone (AIC 1997.720); Pahari and Kalighat paintings; Khmer images (Cleveland 1991.169) are not Indian.
rows.dating_clues: Not datable from iconography.
rows.cautions: An identification names the figure only; it says nothing about age, origin or whether the item is old or genuine. Traditional forms are still made: Rao (1914) already notes small Krishna figures sold in bazaars as toys and new ivory figures carved at the Trivandrum School of Arts.

facts.text: In the Rama group Hanuman stands smaller, humble, the right hand at the mouth and the left reaching the knee.
facts.quote: the right of which is placed upon the mouth in token of loyalty and the left is made to hang down so as to reach the knees

facts.text: He is shown humble and devoted, hands folded, tail hanging to the feet, when with Rama, Lakshmana and Sita.
facts.quote: in a humble and devotional attitude, with the two hands folded together, the tail hanging down close to his feet.

rows.name: Hanuman flying with the mountain of herbs (Sanjivani)
other_names: Hanuman with the medicinal herb mountain
rows.features_other: Heroic Hanuman in his own shrines: flying or striding, a hill of healing herbs held up on one hand, a mace or club in the other, tail often raised.
rows.identify_by: A monkey-faced hero in mid-flight or stride, holding a small mountain aloft.

look_alikes.name: govardhanadhari
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Krishna (human face) holds a hill as an umbrella over cows.

look_alikes.name: hanuman_devotee
look_alikes.how_to_tell: The devotee stands with joined hands; the hero flies with the mountain.

rows.regions_styles: Own shrines across India (Sastri: 'even insignificant villages'); Thanjavur paintings (AIC 1939.348, c. 1910); Bengal paintings (AIC 2018.605); Khmer flying Hanuman (Cleveland 1987.43) is Cambodian.
rows.dating_clues: Not datable from iconography.
rows.cautions: An identification names the figure only; it says nothing about age, origin or whether the item is old or genuine. Traditional forms are still made: Rao (1914) already notes small Krishna figures sold in bazaars as toys and new ivory figures carved at the Trivandrum School of Arts.

facts.text: In his own shrines Hanuman is the hero who flew to the Himalaya and brought back a hill of healing herbs.
facts.quote: In shrines exclusively dedicated to him he is always the heroic Hanuman

facts.text: Hanuman may show the fear-not and boon gestures.
facts.quote: Sometimes Hanuman may also be represented with hands showing the abhaya and the varada postures.

rows.name: Hanuman carrying Rama and Lakshmana on his shoulders
other_names: Hanuman with Rama and Lakshmana on his shoulders
rows.features_other: A giant Hanuman with the small brothers Rama and Lakshmana (bows in hand) seated on his shoulders. Popular in Bengal (Kalighat) and Mithila painting.
rows.identify_by: A big monkey figure with two small bowmen riding on his shoulders.

look_alikes.name: Garuda carrying Krishna and Balarama
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Cleveland 2003.134.b shows Garuda (man-bird) carrying the two brothers Balarama and Krishna; a beak and wings mean Garuda.

rows.regions_styles: Kalighat (Cleveland 2003.120, c. 1890); Bihar Mithila (AIC 2018.565, late 20th c.).
rows.dating_clues: Not datable from iconography.
rows.cautions: An identification names the figure only; it says nothing about age, origin or whether the item is old or genuine. Traditional forms are still made: Rao (1914) already notes small Krishna figures sold in bazaars as toys and new ivory figures carved at the Trivandrum School of Arts.

facts.text: Kalighat and Mithila painters show Hanuman carrying Rama and Lakshmana on his shoulders.
facts.quote: Riding on Hanuman's shoulders, the hero Rama—painted green—and his brother Lakshmana search for Rama's abducted wife Sita.

rows.name: Five-faced Hanuman (Panchamukha)
rows.features_other: Five faces: Hanuman (front), Narasimha, Garuda, Varaha and Hayagriva; eight or ten arms with weapons. The arrangement of faces varies between images.
rows.identify_by: A monkey face in the middle with lion, eagle, boar and horse faces beside and above it.

look_alikes.name: vaikuntha_chaturmurti
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Vaikuntha's main face is human; Panchamukha's main face is a monkey's and it includes horse and eagle faces.

look_alikes.name: Panchamukha Shiva / Sadashiva (shiva_devi topic)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Shiva's five faces are all human.

rows.regions_styles: South India (Tamil Nadu, Karnataka) and Maharashtra; Thanjavur and Mysore paintings; modern brass.
rows.dating_clues: Not datable from iconography. Wikipedia reports the form is late (associated with Tantric worship); no scholarly source checked.
rows.cautions: An identification names the figure only; it says nothing about age, origin or whether the item is old or genuine. Traditional forms are still made: Rao (1914) already notes small Krishna figures sold in bazaars as toys and new ivory figures carved at the Trivandrum School of Arts. Weakly sourced here; verify with a museum or scholarly text before publishing.

facts.text: Panchamukha Hanuman has five faces: Hanuman, Narasimha, Garuda, Varaha and Hayagriva.
facts.quote: Hanuman facing east, Narasimha south, Varaha north, Garuda west, and Hayagriva toward the sky

rows.name: Alvar saint (Vaishnava poet-saint), general
rows.features_other: Human saint (not a god): usually standing with hands joined in salutation, or seated with a teaching gesture; Vaishnava forehead mark (urdhvapundra) and sometimes small conch and discus on the shoulders; installed in Vishnu temples in bronze or stone. Token wanted: kind 'saint'; Vaishnava forehead mark.
rows.identify_by: A two-armed human figure with hands joined, wearing simple ornaments and a Vaishnava mark, from a South Indian Vishnu temple.

look_alikes.name: Nayanar (Shaiva saint, shiva_devi topic)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Shaiva saints (Appar, Sambandar, Sundarar) wear rudraksha beads and Shaiva marks; Sambandar dances pointing upward (AIC 1949.602). Conch-and-discus marks on the shoulders mean Vaishnava.

look_alikes.name: hanuman_devotee
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Also joins his hands, but has a monkey face.

look_alikes.name: garuda
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Garuda joins his hands but has wings and a beak.

look_alikes.name: Donor or royal portrait figures
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Royal and donor portrait figures also join their hands; crowns, dress and inscriptions identify them.

rows.regions_styles: Tamil Nadu temple bronzes and stone (Chola to Nayaka and later).
rows.dating_clues: Not datable from iconography.
rows.cautions: An identification names the figure only; it says nothing about age, origin or whether the item is old or genuine. Traditional forms are still made: Rao (1914) already notes small Krishna figures sold in bazaars as toys and new ivory figures carved at the Trivandrum School of Arts. Saint bronzes are temple processional images; several have been traced as stolen and returned (see tirumangai_alvar).

facts.text: The Vaishnava saints, the Alvars, are twelve in number and are installed in temples in metal or stone.
facts.quote: Saiva and Vaishnava saints (called Nayanars and Alvars), the former of whom are sixty-three in number and the latter twelve are also occasionally installed in temples, their images being made either of metal or of stone.

facts.text: Their hymns form the Nalayira Prabandham.
facts.quote: the hymns of the Vaishnava saints (Alvars) ... are also collected under the name Naldyiraprabandham

rows.name: Nammalvar (Sathakopa)
rows.features_other: Chief of the Alvars; the hagiography places him as a child under a tamarind tree at Tirukkurugur, where he sat in silent meditation. Iconography beyond the general Alvar type was not found in the sources read (gap).
rows.identify_by: A seated or standing Alvar named by inscription or temple context; no unique emblem found in the sources read.

look_alikes.name: ramanuja
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Ramanuja is shown as a monk with the triple staff.

look_alikes.name: alvar
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Without a label, an Alvar bronze cannot be assigned to Nammalvar on these sources.

rows.regions_styles: Tamil Nadu temples (Alvar Tirunagari).
rows.dating_clues: Not datable from iconography.
rows.cautions: An identification names the figure only; it says nothing about age, origin or whether the item is old or genuine. Traditional forms are still made: Rao (1914) already notes small Krishna figures sold in bazaars as toys and new ivory figures carved at the Trivandrum School of Arts.

facts.text: As a baby Nammalvar (named Maran) was laid in a cradle under the holy tamarind tree.
facts.quote: disposed it in a gold gem-made cradle under the Holy Tamarind Tree

rows.name: Andal (Goda), the woman Alvar
rows.features_other: A young woman saint standing in a slight bend, one hand raised; a parrot perched on her forearm or hand; hair wound into a large bun or knot (dhammilla), often to one side. Token wanted: side hair knot.
rows.identify_by: A slender standing woman with a parrot on her raised forearm and her hair in a large knot.

look_alikes.name: bhudevi
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Bhudevi stands beside Vishnu with a water lily and crown; Andal (held to be Bhudevi's incarnation) has the parrot and the hair knot.

look_alikes.name: Minakshi (shiva_devi topic)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Minakshi of Madurai also holds a parrot; she is a crowned goddess, often with Shiva-Sundareshvara.

look_alikes.name: Kamadeva / Rati with parrot (other_hindu topic)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Kama rides a parrot; Rati accompanies Kama.

rows.regions_styles: Tamil Nadu (Srivilliputtur); bronzes (LACMA M.86.94.2, Madurai District, 14th c.).
rows.dating_clues: Not datable from iconography.
rows.cautions: An identification names the figure only; it says nothing about age, origin or whether the item is old or genuine. Traditional forms are still made: Rao (1914) already notes small Krishna figures sold in bazaars as toys and new ivory figures carved at the Trivandrum School of Arts.

facts.text: Andal is the only woman among the twelve Alvars and is held to descend from Shri and Bhu.
facts.quote: Only one of them is a woman-Saint, the blest Andal (saviour) or Goda-Devi.

facts.text: She carries a parrot on her forearm and wears her hair in a bun (dhammilla).
facts.quote: She carries a parrot on her right forearm.

rows.name: Tirumangai Alvar (Parakala)
rows.features_other: A former chieftain shown as a warrior saint with sword and shield; small conch and discus on the shoulders mark him as Vaishnava.
rows.identify_by: A standing human saint holding a sword and a shield, with small conch and discus marks on the shoulders.

look_alikes.name: Bhairava or Virabhadra (shiva_devi topic)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Shaiva fierce gods with sword and shield have fangs, many arms, skulls; Tirumangai is a two-armed calm human with Vaishnava marks.

look_alikes.name: Hero stones and warrior portraits
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Shoulder conch and discus marks and temple context.

rows.regions_styles: Tamil Nadu temple bronzes (Ashmolean EA1967.42, 15th c.; a 16th-c. bronze from Thadikombu returned by the Ashmolean in 2026).
rows.dating_clues: Ashmolean dates by style (15th and 16th c. bronzes); iconography does not date.
rows.cautions: An identification names the figure only; it says nothing about age, origin or whether the item is old or genuine. Traditional forms are still made: Rao (1914) already notes small Krishna figures sold in bazaars as toys and new ivory figures carved at the Trivandrum School of Arts. Repatriation case: the Ashmolean returned a Tirumangai Alvar bronze bought at auction in 1967 after a researcher matched it to a 1957 photograph of the image in the Soundararaja Perumal temple, Thadikombu (French Institute of Pondicherry archive); handover at the Indian High Commission, London, March 2026.

facts.text: Tirumangai Alvar is always shown with sword and shield; conch and discus on his shoulders mark him as Vaishnava.
facts.quote: he is always depicted holding a sword and a shield.

facts.text: The Ashmolean returned a 16th-century Tirumangai Alvar bronze to India in March 2026; it had been photographed in the Thadikombu temple in 1957 and bought at auction in 1967.
facts.quote: A 1957 photograph in that archive shows the same idol at the temple.

rows.name: Ramanuja (Ramanujacharya)
rows.features_other: A Vaishnava monk: hands joined in salutation (or the teaching gesture), the triple staff (tridanda) beside him, a head-dress or shaven head, the Vaishnava forehead mark (urdhvapundra, white clay and red).
rows.identify_by: A seated monk with joined hands, a tall triple staff and the Vaishnava U-shaped forehead mark.

look_alikes.name: Shankaracharya
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Shankara is a bald monk with book, single staff, water pot and the teaching gesture, rudraksha beads, ash marks, often on a tiger skin, with four pupils.

look_alikes.name: Madhvacharya
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Madhva is bald with the teaching gesture, book, staff and water pot, and conch-discus marks painted on the body.

look_alikes.name: Vedanta Desika
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Another Srivaishnava teacher shown similarly (Sastri fig. 160 b); identification needs a label.

look_alikes.name: alvar
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Alvars are not monks and carry no triple staff.

rows.regions_styles: Tamil Nadu and Karnataka Srivaishnava temples (Srirangam, Sriperumbudur, Melkote); bronze and stone.
rows.dating_clues: Not datable from iconography.
rows.cautions: An identification names the figure only; it says nothing about age, origin or whether the item is old or genuine. Traditional forms are still made: Rao (1914) already notes small Krishna figures sold in bazaars as toys and new ivory figures carved at the Trivandrum School of Arts.

facts.text: Ramanuja has hands joined in worship, the triple staff (tridanda), a head-dress and the Vaishnava urdhvapundra marks.
facts.quote: Ramanujacharya has the sanjali-mudra, i.e., hands folded together over the breast in a worshipping posture, the triple staff (tridanda) and a head-dress. He wears the Vaishnava caste marks urdhvapundra

facts.text: Rao credits Ramanuja with spreading the Pancharatra agama in South India and with keeping Tirupati for the Vaishnavas.
facts.quote: which was propagated in S. India by the great Vaishnava reformer Ramanujacharya

rows.name: Brahma
rows.features_other: Four heads (in a relief usually three show); sacrificial ladles (sruk and sruva), a ghee pot and a bundle of kusha grass are prescribed and have no token; deer skin worn over the left shoulder; a beard on one or all faces in many images; consorts Sarasvati and Savitri.
rows.identify_by: Four heads and four arms with an ascetic's rosary and water pot, often a ladle or book, and the goose (hamsa) at his feet. The many heads are the decisive sign: no other common Hindu figure with these attributes has four faces.

look_alikes.name: agni
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Agni is also bearded and may hold a ladle, rosary and water pot, but has one head (or two), flames behind him and a ram or goat.

look_alikes.name: navagraha
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Brihaspati among the planets carries a rosary and water pot and is bearded, but has one head and stands in a row of planets.

look_alikes.name: varuna
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Varuna may also ride a goose, but has one head and holds a noose.

look_alikes.name: jain yaksha Brahma (see jain topic)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: The four-faced Jain yaksha named Brahma sits beside a Jina (tirthankara); the main figure of the piece is the Jina, not Brahma.

look_alikes.name: sarasvati
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Sarasvati shares the book and rosary but is a goddess with one head, often with a vina.

rows.regions_styles: Mostly a subsidiary deity: in South India set in the north-wall niche of Shiva and Vishnu temples; Chalukya-Hoysala standing images; rare South Indian bronzes; Kalighat paintings of c. 1890 in Bengal.
rows.dating_clues: Rao reports bronze images of Brahma, especially processional (utsava) ones, as very rare. Style of crown and face places a piece by region and school; it cannot date a single casting.
rows.cautions: An identification says who the figure is, not how old it is or whether it is genuine; the same forms are still made today. Bearded and beardless Brahmas both occur, so a beard is not a test.

facts.text: Brahma is shown with four heads facing the four quarters and four arms; he may stand, or sit on a lotus seat or on a goose.
facts.quote: The four heads should be respectively facing the four quarters. Brahma should have four arms ; he may be standing, seated on either a padmasana or a hamsa (swan).

facts.text: Items in his hands vary by text: rosary, kusha grass, ladles (sruk, sruva), ghee pot, water pot, book; Cleveland's Kalighat painting shows a manuscript, lotus, rosary and water pot.
facts.quote: He would typically hold a rosary and water pot in his left hands

facts.text: No sect is devoted to Brahma alone, but an image of him belongs in the north niche of the central shrine of Vishnu and Shiva temples.
facts.quote: The niche on the northern wall of the central shrine of the Vishnu's or Siva's temple should contain an image of Brahma and must receive daily puja.

facts.text: Disputed: Rao says the Rupamandana prescribes a beard; Banerjea notes that the elaborate texts do not explicitly call his faces bearded (only his attendant sages). Images exist both ways.
facts.quote: in none of these elaborate accounts there is an explicit reference to his face or faces being bearded

facts.text: Bronze processional images of Brahma are very rare.
facts.quote: Bronze images of Brahma are very rare and especially the one like the Madras Museum image, which is an utsava-vigraha, is met with very rarely, if at all.

rows.name: Sarasvati
rows.features_other: The vina (stringed instrument, often held across the body) is her commonest sign in later images but has no token; dressed in white in paintings; in Pala triads she stands at Vishnu's left with a vina.
rows.identify_by: A goddess with book and rosary, very often playing a vina, seated on a white lotus. (Her goose or peacock mount, common in later pictures, was not confirmed in a read source.) The vina together with the book is what separates her from Lakshmi.

look_alikes.name: lakshmi (see vishnu_krishna topic)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Lakshmi holds lotuses and is often bathed by elephants; she does not carry the book or the vina.

look_alikes.name: nagini
look_alikes.how_to_tell: A Nagini playing a vina (Khiching) has a snake hood behind her head.

look_alikes.name: brahma
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Brahma shares book and rosary but has four heads and a goose.

look_alikes.name: jain shrutadevi or Sarasvati (see jain topic)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: In Jain art Sarasvati presides over the sixteen Vidyadevis; context (a Jina nearby, Jain inscription) decides.

rows.regions_styles: Hoysala sculptures; Pala Bengal and Bihar triads with Vishnu and Lakshmi; Kalighat and chromolithograph pictures of the 1880s-1900s.
rows.dating_clues: Not datable from attributes; style only.
rows.cautions: An identification says who the figure is, not how old it is or whether it is genuine; the same forms are still made today.

facts.text: Sarasvati sits on a white lotus, has four hands with rosary, teaching gesture, book and white lotus; another text has her standing and holding a vina.
facts.quote: She is seated upon a white lotus, is of white complexion, and is draped in white clothes. She has four hands

facts.text: The Devimahatmya gives her a goad, vina, rosary and book, the form followed in Hoysala sculpture.
facts.quote: describes her as holding in her hands an ankusa, a vina, an akshamala, and a pustaka. It is in this fashion that the Devi is represented in the Hoysala sculptures

facts.text: In Bengal and Bihar she often appears as one of Vishnu's two consorts, with Lakshmi.
facts.quote: Vishnu Accompanied by Lakshmi and Sarasvati

rows.name: Surya
rows.features_other: Holds a lotus in each hand, raised to the shoulders; northern images wear a long coat and high boots (udichyavesha) and a waist-girdle (avyanga); the legless charioteer Aruna drives the one-wheeled chariot; attendants Danda and Pingala (pen and inkpot), archer goddesses Usha and Pratyusha; a halo behind the head.
rows.identify_by: A standing god holding two lotuses at shoulder height, with seven horses on the pedestal. In North and East India the boots and coat clinch it.

look_alikes.name: revanta
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Revanta, Surya's son, also wears boots but rides a single horse, often hunting with a whip and attendants.

look_alikes.name: navagraha
look_alikes.how_to_tell: In a planet row Surya is the first figure; Chandra beside him holds water-lilies and is not on a seven-horse chariot.

look_alikes.name: vishnu (see vishnu_krishna topic)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: The crowns of Vishnu and Surya differ little; Vishnu holds conch and discus, Surya two lotuses.

rows.regions_styles: Kashmir brass of the 600s-700s; Pala Bengal and Bihar black stone and bronze; Chalukya and Hoysala Karnataka with two goddesses; Tamil images bare-legged, often without attendants.
rows.dating_clues: North vs South: southern Surya raises half-open lotuses to the shoulders, wears an udara-bandha (belly band) and has bare legs; northern Surya holds full-blown lotuses and wears boots. This places region, not date.
rows.cautions: An identification says who the figure is, not how old it is or whether it is genuine; the same forms are still made today.

facts.text: Texts give Surya two hands each holding a lotus (southern texts: raised to the shoulders), a crown and halo, and a one-wheeled chariot of seven horses driven by the lame Aruna; the Brihatsamhita has him hold two lotuses by their stalks.
facts.quote: the figure of the sun-god should be sculptured with two hands, each holding a lotus

facts.text: North Indian Suryas wear a close coat and boots (udicyavesha) and the avyanga girdle; these are absent in South Indian images.
facts.quote: The most important characteristics of a north Indian Surya are its udicyavesa (consisting of the close covering of the body and top-boots of the legs

facts.text: Cleveland explains the boots and tunic as Central Asian riding dress; Bhattasali gives the Puranic reason, that the sun god's feet must not be shown. Two explanations of one feature.
facts.quote: Surya wears a long tunic and boots suitable for riding horses across the grassland steppes of Central Asia.

facts.text: Attendants: Pingala with ink-bottle and pen on his right, Danda with a staff on his left.
facts.quote: on the right of Surya there might be Pingala with an ink-bottle and a pen and on the left Dandi with a danda in his hand.

rows.name: Navagraha (the Nine Planets)
rows.features_other: A group of nine: Surya (Sun), Chandra or Soma (Moon), Mangala or Bhauma (Mars), Budha (Mercury), Brihaspati or Guru (Jupiter), Shukra (Venus), Shani (Saturn), Rahu (a bust with no body) and Ketu (serpent-tailed). Carved in a row on door lintels; in Tamil temples set as nine separate images in a shrine.
rows.identify_by: A row of eight or nine small male figures, one only a head and shoulders (Rahu) and one with a snake's tail (Ketu). Rahu's bodiless head identifies the set.

look_alikes.name: saptamatrika (see shiva_devi topic)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: The Seven Mothers are female and usually flanked by Ganesha and Virabhadra; the planets are male and include the bust-only Rahu.

look_alikes.name: dikpala_set
look_alikes.how_to_tell: The eight Guardians of the Directions each ride a different animal (elephant, ram, buffalo...); the planets mostly stand without mounts.

rows.regions_styles: Lintels over temple doors in Orissa, Central India and Bengal (700s onward); Bengal slabs led by Ganesha; Tamil Navagraha shrines (Suryanarkoyil bronzes).
rows.dating_clues: Banerjea: early lintels show only eight planets; Ketu appears in Orissa from the Ganga period on; early Orissan Brihaspati and Shukra are beardless, later ones bearded; some later Bengal slabs begin with Ganesha. These are tendencies by region, not dates for a piece.
rows.cautions: An identification says who the figure is, not how old it is or whether it is genuine; the same forms are still made today. Saturn is identified by his lameness or one-leg stance only where carved clearly.

facts.text: The nine are the sun, the moon, Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn and the two lunar nodes Rahu and Ketu.
facts.quote: the sun, the moon, the five planets—Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter and Saturn, and also the ascending and the descending nodes of the moon, called Rahu and Ketu

facts.text: Near temple entrances the nine were shown in an orderly row; Cleveland's 700s lintel shows the Sun first, a bodiless Rahu and a serpent-tailed figure.
facts.quote: Near temple entrances, the nine celestial bodies were depicted in an orderly row, often in figural form.

facts.text: Earlier lintels carried eight planets; Ketu was added later (Orissa: from the Ganga period).
facts.quote: the slab seems to have contained the figures of eight 'grahas' only ... and this seems to have been the earlier convention in architectural use of these 'planets', Ketu being a later addition.

facts.text: In some later Bengal slabs the row begins with Ganesha (Kankandighi relief).
facts.quote: In some of the later such slabs (specially hailing from Bengal), the group representation begins with the figure of Ganapati

facts.text: Chandra holds a white water-lily in each of two hands; Brihaspati and Shukra hold water pot, rosary and staff; Shani is black, small and lame; per the Rupamandana table Mangala rides a goat and Brihaspati a hamsa.
facts.quote: He should have two hands, each of which should hold a white water-lily (kumuda).

rows.name: Rahu
rows.features_other: Shown only as a head and upper chest with no lower body; grinning face, round bulging eyes, hair rising in spiral coils; hands, when shown, in tarpana (offering) gesture. Token wanted: 'head or bust only'.
rows.identify_by: The bodiless head in a row of planets.

look_alikes.name: kirtimukha
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Kirtimukha is a lion-like horned mask spewing foliage over doors and niches and stands alone; Rahu has a human face, often hands, and sits in the planet row.

look_alikes.name: ketu
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Ketu has a body ending in a snake's tail.

rows.regions_styles: Navagraha lintels of North, Central and East India; Tamil Navagraha shrines show him full-bodied.
rows.cautions: In separate South Indian Navagraha images Rahu may be given a whole body (texts give him four arms with sword, shield and trident), so the bust form is a northern-lintel sign.

facts.text: Rahu is shown only to the breast, with a grinning face, round protruding eyes and hair in rising spiral coils.
facts.quote: the fierce-looking Rahu is shown only up to the breast with a grinning face, round protruding eyes, hair tied up in a bunch of spiral coils rising upwards

facts.text: Cleveland: the bodiless head is the eclipse, who swallows the moon until it falls out of his neck.
facts.quote: The bodiless head is Rahu, the eclipse, who swallows the moon until it falls out his neck.

facts.text: Texts differ: one gives Rahu four arms with sword, shield and trident; another two hands with a book and blanket.
facts.quote: Rahu should possess four arms, one of his hands should be in the varada pose and the remaining three should carry the khadga, khetaka and sula.

rows.name: Ketu
rows.features_other: Lower body a serpent's tail (token wanted: 'snake lower body'); hands joined in salutation in some texts; dark in color.
rows.identify_by: The last figure of a planet row, with a snake's tail in place of legs.

look_alikes.name: naga
look_alikes.how_to_tell: A naga has a hood of cobra heads behind the head; Ketu has the snake tail but stands in a planet row, usually without a hood.

look_alikes.name: rahu
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Rahu is a head or bust without any lower body.

rows.regions_styles: Navagraha lintels; Tamil Navagraha shrines.
rows.dating_clues: Absent from the earliest lintels (eight planets only); added later.
rows.cautions: Disputed reading: Cleveland calls the serpent-tailed figure a comet, Rao an ascending/descending lunar node; both refer to Ketu. In Rao's printed Rupamandana table the snake-tail remark appears against the name Rahu, which looks like a misprint or misreading of the scan.

facts.text: The serpent-tailed figure at the end of a planet row is Ketu.
facts.quote: The serpent-tailed figure is a comet.

facts.text: Ketu is dark, two-armed, one hand in fear-not and the other holding a mace (Amsumadbhedagama); Rupamandana: arms folded in salutation.
facts.quote: Ketu is to be of dark colour and should have two arms, one of his hands is to be in the abhaya pose and the other should carry a gada.

rows.name: Shani (Saturn)
rows.features_other: Black or very dark; small in stature; lame in one leg. In Tamil practice his mount is a crow (no token; not confirmed from a read source here).
rows.identify_by: In a planet row, the figure standing on one leg or visibly lame; in paintings very dark.

look_alikes.name: yama
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Yama also holds a staff and is dark but rides a buffalo and holds a noose.

rows.regions_styles: Planet lintels; separate Shani shrines and images are common in modern worship.
rows.cautions: An identification says who the figure is, not how old it is or whether it is genuine; the same forms are still made today.

facts.text: Shani is black, small, lame in one leg; right hand holds a staff, left in boon-giving.
facts.quote: He should be small in stature and somewhat lame in one leg.

facts.text: Cleveland: Saturn stands on one leg because a goddess wounded him to stop him moving swiftly.
facts.quote: Saturn was wounded by a goddess to prevent him from moving swiftly, so he stands on one leg.

rows.name: Ganga (river goddess)
rows.features_other: Stands on a makara (crocodile-like creature, often with a foliate tail), under a tree, with small attendants, one sometimes holding an umbrella; placed on the proper right jamb of a temple door, opposite Yamuna; also shown as a small figure in Shiva's hair (see shiva_devi).
rows.identify_by: A graceful woman with a water pot standing on a makara, usually on a door jamb.

look_alikes.name: yamuna
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Yamuna stands on a tortoise; Ganga on a makara.

look_alikes.name: yakshi
look_alikes.how_to_tell: A yakshi or tree goddess holds a branch but stands on no makara.

look_alikes.name: varuna
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Varuna also rides a makara but is male and holds a noose.

rows.regions_styles: Gupta and early medieval door jambs (Besnagar, Kharod, Tigowa); Mathura region c. 700; Bengal steles (Rajshahi); Kalighat paintings of c. 1890 show Ganga on a fish-like makara.
rows.dating_clues: Banerjea: the river goddesses on temple doors are typical of the Gupta and early medieval periods. A detached door-jamb figure is an architectural fragment.
rows.cautions: An identification says who the figure is, not how old it is or whether it is genuine; the same forms are still made today. A door-jamb fragment comes from a temple; such items raise the export and provenance questions in the general cautions.

facts.text: Ganga stands on a makara, holding a fly whisk and lotus (Vishnudharmottara); at Kharod she stands on the proper right jamb with a full water pot.
facts.quote: Ganga of moon-like white colour and possessing a pretty face should be standing on a matsya or makara, with a chamara in one hand and a padma in the other

facts.text: Sculptures of Ganga were placed at temple doorways; her purifying waters cleanse those who enter.
facts.quote: Sculptures of Ganga were placed at the doorway of temples, for the image of the purifying waters symbolically cleanses those who enter the sacred space.

facts.text: The river goddesses of temple doors grow out of earlier female figure types: Coomaraswamy derives them from the yakshi tree-spirits, Banerjea from the early apsaras-type figures. Both agree they are older types re-used.
facts.quote: From these types of Yaksi dryads are evidently derived three types ... the Buddha Nativity, the asoka-tree dohada motif in classical literature, and the so-called river-goddesses of medieval shrines.

rows.name: Yamuna (river goddess)
rows.features_other: Stands on a tortoise; holds a blue water-lily (nilotpala) and fly whisk; on the proper left door jamb; dark like the blue lotus in painted images.
rows.identify_by: A woman on a door jamb standing on a tortoise.

look_alikes.name: ganga
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Ganga stands on a makara, Yamuna on a tortoise.

look_alikes.name: kurma avatar (see vishnu_krishna topic)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Vishnu's tortoise incarnation is the tortoise itself or half-man half-tortoise, not a woman standing on one.

rows.regions_styles: Same door-jamb tradition as Ganga (Tigowa, Kharod).
rows.dating_clues: As for Ganga.
rows.cautions: An identification says who the figure is, not how old it is or whether it is genuine; the same forms are still made today.

facts.text: Yamuna's seat or mount is the tortoise.
facts.quote: cf. the river goddess Yamuna who is kurmasana

facts.text: She holds a fly whisk and a blue water-lily (Vishnudharmottara); at Tigowa she stands under a tree on a tortoise.
facts.quote: should be standing on a tortoise with a chamara in one hand and a nilotpala in the other.

rows.name: Kubera
rows.features_other: Money purse or a mongoose that spits jewels (token wanted: 'money bag / mongoose'); pots of treasure under his feet; the two treasures Shankhanidhi and Padmanidhi as dwarfish figures; a man as his vehicle (naravahana, token wanted); crown set slanting to the left; moustache.
rows.identify_by: A pot-bellied, richly jewelled seated god with a purse or mongoose and pots of treasure. The mongoose or purse is the sign.

look_alikes.name: jambhala (see buddhist topic)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Jambhala is Kubera's Buddhist form; a citron in the right hand and Buddhist setting (Buddhas in the halo, Nepalese or Tibetan style) tell them apart.

look_alikes.name: yaksha
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Generic yakshas are also pot-bellied; without purse, mongoose or treasure pots the figure is better called a yaksha.

look_alikes.name: ganesha (see shiva_devi topic)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Ganesha has an elephant head.

rows.regions_styles: Kushan Mathura red sandstone (moustached); Gupta; medieval guardian of the north on temple walls; Nepalese and Tibetan Jambhala bronzes.
rows.dating_clues: Cleveland: Kushan-period Kubera heads are usually moustached.
rows.cautions: An identification says who the figure is, not how old it is or whether it is genuine; the same forms are still made today.

facts.text: All authorities give Kubera a big, slightly pendant belly; he may sit on a lotus seat or on a man's shoulders; the Amsumadbhedagama gives him a ram.
facts.quote: All the authorities are uniform in asserting that Kubera should have a rather big and slightly pendant belly.

facts.text: In Buddhist representation Kubera is recognized by a mongoose on his left lap or side.
facts.quote: he is immediately recognised as Kubera by a mongoose which is generally also shown either as sitting upon his left lap or placed on his left side.

facts.text: Kubera is lord of the yakshas and guardian of the north; the corpulent body is that of a yaksha.
facts.quote: the corpulent body in any case is that of a Yaksa

facts.text: Kubera wears the crown slanting on the left side (vama-kiriti).
facts.quote: Kubera should be vama-kiriti, i.e., the kirita should be placed slantingly on the left side of his head.

rows.name: Indra
rows.features_other: Third eye set horizontally on the forehead; the elephant Airavata (white, four tusks in texts); eyes all over the body in some accounts; consort Indrani on his lap.
rows.identify_by: A crowned god with a thunderbolt (vajra) riding an elephant; a horizontal third eye if present.

look_alikes.name: shiva (see shiva_devi topic)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Shiva's third eye is usually vertical and he rides a bull; Indra's is horizontal and he rides an elephant.

look_alikes.name: sasta_ayyappa
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Sasta/Aiyanar may also ride a white elephant but holds a crooked stick, not a vajra.

look_alikes.name: shakra in Jain painting (see jain topic)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: In Jain Kalpasutra pages Indra (Shakra) venerates the embryo of Mahavira; the setting tells.

rows.regions_styles: Kushan Mathura; East on Ashtadikpala ceilings and wall corners; Jain manuscript paintings of Gujarat.
rows.cautions: An identification says who the figure is, not how old it is or whether it is genuine; the same forms are still made today.

facts.text: Indra's mount is the white four-tusked elephant; he holds the thunderbolt; his cognizance is a third eye placed horizontally.
facts.quote: The elephant (mount) of Mahendra (Indra) is white and has four tusks ; (the god) has a thunderbolt in his hand, and has as his cognisance the third eye placed horizontally on his forehead

facts.text: Agama texts give him two arms with spear (sakti) and goad, or vajra and goad; seated on a lion throne or on Airavata.
facts.quote: Indra should carry in his right hand the sakti and in the left the ankusa.

rows.name: Agni
rows.features_other: Flames rising behind him or his hair standing up like a halo of fire; sacrificial ladle (sruk) in hand (no token); beard and moustache; two heads, seven arms and three legs in the Vedic description; mount a ram or goat; consort Svaha.
rows.identify_by: A bearded god with flames rising behind him and a ram or goat below.

look_alikes.name: brahma
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Brahma has four heads and a goose; Agni one or two heads, flames and a ram.

look_alikes.name: navagraha
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Mangala (Mars) in a planet row may ride a goat but has no flames.

rows.regions_styles: Medieval North India (Uttar Pradesh steles c. 1000); South-east corner of Ashtadikpala sets; Kerala and Tamil temple reliefs (Kandiyur two goat heads).
rows.cautions: An identification says who the figure is, not how old it is or whether it is genuine; the same forms are still made today. The Met's 3rd-century Kaushambi bronze is titled with three alternative readings (ascetic, deified king, Agni): early figures are often uncertain.

facts.text: Agni has red hair standing on end like a halo of flame and is seated on a ram (agamas); Cleveland describes him with flames rising behind and the goat as his mount.
facts.quote: the hair or jata of the head which should also be of red colour, standing on end and forming a sort of prabhamandala. He should be seated upon a ram.

facts.text: The Vishnudharmottara: bearded, four-armed, three-eyed, chariot drawn by four parrots, holding flames, trident and rosary, Svaha on his lap.
facts.quote: he is bearded, four-armed, four-tusked, three-eyed, riding a chariot with smoke standard drawn by four parrots

facts.text: The Kandiyur (Travancore) Agni has two goat heads, seven arms and three legs.
facts.quote: It has two heads which are of the goat, seven arms and three legs.

facts.text: Disputed: Rao's Chidambaram 'Agni' with a bull behind him may instead be Yajnapurusha, a minor form of Vishnu (Banerjea).
facts.quote: the Chidambaram figure may really represent Yajnapurusa, one of the minor manifestations of Visnu

rows.name: Yama
rows.features_other: Dark like a rain-cloud with side tusks; attendants Chitragupta (stylus and palm leaf, the record-keeper) and Kala with a noose; as Dharma, judge of the dead, he may hold a balance (no token).
rows.identify_by: A god with staff and noose seated on or beside a he-buffalo.

look_alikes.name: durga mahishasuramardini (see shiva_devi topic)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: With Durga the buffalo is a demon she is killing; with Yama it is his calm mount under a male god.

look_alikes.name: shani
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Shani holds a staff but has no buffalo and stands in a planet row.

look_alikes.name: yama/yamantaka in Tibetan and Nepalese art (see buddhist topic)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Tibetan Yama is buffalo-headed and dances on a bull; Indian Hindu Yama is human-headed.

rows.regions_styles: South quarter of Ashtadikpala sets; Kashmir and North-West miniature steles (Cleveland, 800s).
rows.cautions: An identification says who the figure is, not how old it is or whether it is genuine; the same forms are still made today.

facts.text: Yama is dark, two-armed, with side tusks, seated on a lion throne or a he-buffalo, holding sword and shield, or fruit and leaves, or staff and noose.
facts.quote: He may be seated either on a simhasana or on a he-buffalo.

facts.text: As Dharma, judge of the dead, Yama holds a balance with figures on each pan (Cleveland miniature stele, 800s).
facts.quote: which is suggested by the balance he holds in his hands with two figures on each extreme of the scale.

rows.name: Varuna
rows.features_other: Noose (pasha) is his weapon; seated on a makara, fish or crocodile, or in a chariot drawn by seven geese (Vishnudharmottara); fish banner; white umbrella; Ganga and Yamuna as attendants.
rows.identify_by: A god with a noose seated on a makara (or a goose), guardian of the west.

look_alikes.name: ganga
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Ganga also stands on a makara but is a goddess with a water pot.

look_alikes.name: brahma
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Brahma also has a goose but four heads.

rows.regions_styles: West quarter of Ashtadikpala sets; the Met's 6th-8th-century sandstone Varuna rides a goose.
rows.cautions: An identification says who the figure is, not how old it is or whether it is genuine; the same forms are still made today.

facts.text: Varuna is white, pacific, seated or standing on a fish, makara or crocodile; two arms (boon and noose) or four (boon, noose, snake, water pot).
facts.quote: as seated or standing upon a fish or makara (a kind of aquatic animal, more mythical than real) or a crocodile.

facts.text: The Vishnudharmottara seats him in a chariot drawn by seven geese; a Met sculpture (19.90) shows Varuna with a noose riding a goose, though Banerjea says sculptures usually show him on a makara, not a swan.
facts.quote: usually show the two-armed god either standing or seated, not on a swan, but on a Makara.

rows.name: Vayu
rows.features_other: Rides a deer or antelope (token wanted: mount 'deer/antelope'); holds a banner (dhvaja) that seems to stream in the wind; hair dishevelled; appears in haste; mouth open. Father of Bhima and Hanuman.
rows.identify_by: Guardian of the north-west with a fluttering banner and a deer as mount.

look_alikes.name: chandra (see navagraha)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Chandra (the Moon) is sometimes given an antelope too, but holds water-lilies and sits among the planets.

rows.regions_styles: North-west quarter of Ashtadikpala sets.
rows.cautions: An identification says who the figure is, not how old it is or whether it is genuine; the same forms are still made today.

facts.text: Vayu holds a banner and a staff and may sit on a lion throne or on a deer; the deer is more common in sculpture; he should appear to move in haste.
facts.quote: he may be seated either on a simhasana or on a deer ; the latter is more often met with in sculptures as the vehicle of Vayu.

rows.name: Nirrti
rows.features_other: Rides on a man's shoulders (naravahana; token wanted) or an ass; fierce, with tusks and hair on end; blue.
rows.identify_by: The south-west guardian, a fierce god with sword and shield riding on a man.

look_alikes.name: kubera
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Kubera can also sit on a man but is pot-bellied and holds a purse or mace.

look_alikes.name: shitala
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Shitala rides an ass but is a goddess with broom and pot.

rows.regions_styles: South-west quarter of Ashtadikpala sets.
rows.cautions: An identification says who the figure is, not how old it is or whether it is genuine; the same forms are still made today.

facts.text: Nirrti is blue, seated on a throne, a lion or the shoulders of a man (an ass in the Vishnudharmottara), fierce, with sword and shield.
facts.quote: seated either on a bhadrapitha, a lion or riding on the shoulders of a man. The Vishnudharmottara states that he must be seated on an ass

rows.name: Ishana
rows.features_other: Shiva as guardian of the north-east; tiger skin; snake sacred thread; four-armed form plays a vina.
rows.identify_by: A Shiva-like figure with trident and bull placed in the north-east of a set of guardians.

look_alikes.name: shiva (see shiva_devi topic)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Ishana is Shiva; only his place in a set of eight guardians makes him Ishana.

rows.regions_styles: North-east quarter of Ashtadikpala sets.
rows.cautions: An identification says who the figure is, not how old it is or whether it is genuine; the same forms are still made today.

facts.text: Ishana has three eyes, white color, tiger skin, jata crown with crescent, rides a white bull; two arms hold trident and skull cup.
facts.quote: From the description given of him, we know he is the same as Mahadeva or Siva.

rows.name: Ashtadikpala (Guardians of the Eight Directions)
rows.features_other: Eight figures: Indra (east, elephant), Agni (south-east, ram), Yama (south, buffalo), Nirrti (south-west, man or ass), Varuna (west, makara), Vayu (north-west, deer), Kubera (north, man, ram or elephant), Ishana (north-east, bull).
rows.identify_by: A set of eight seated or standing gods each on a different mount, on a ceiling or at the corners of a temple.

look_alikes.name: navagraha
look_alikes.how_to_tell: The nine planets stand in a row, with the bust-only Rahu; guardians each have a mount.

rows.regions_styles: Ceilings of front mandapas, corners of upper storeys of the vimana; North Indian wall corners (Khajuraho type).
rows.cautions: An identification says who the figure is, not how old it is or whether it is genuine; the same forms are still made today. A single guardian cut from a set is an architectural fragment.

facts.text: The eight guardians: Indra east, Agni south-east, Yama south, Nirrti south-west, Varuna west, Vayu north-west, Kubera north, Ishana north-east.
facts.quote: 1. Indra, the lord of the east, 2. Agni, the Lord of the south-east, 3. Yama, of the south, 4. Nirruti, of the south-west, 5. Varuna, of the west

facts.text: They are placed on the ceiling of the front mandapa, the corners of an upper storey of the vimana, or in a prakara.
facts.quote: the ceiling of the front mandapa, the eight corners of one of the upper-storeys of the vimana

rows.name: Kama (Manmatha)
rows.features_other: Bow of sugarcane and five flower arrows; standard-bearer holding a makara (or fish) banner; consorts Rati and Priti; friend Vasanta (Spring). His parrot mount, common in later pictures, was not found in a read source (gap).
rows.identify_by: A youthful god with a sugarcane bow and flower arrows, often with Rati beside him.

look_alikes.name: lalita / tripurasundari (see shiva_devi topic)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Lalita also holds a sugarcane bow and flower arrows but is a goddess with noose and goad.

look_alikes.name: rati
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Rati is his consort: female, holding fruit and lotus.

look_alikes.name: rama (see vishnu_krishna topic)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Rama's bow is a war bow, not sugarcane, and he has no flower arrows.

rows.regions_styles: Hoysala (Halebidu), Karnataka (Nuggehalli), later Pandya Tenkasi (15th century, four-armed, tall conical crown).
rows.dating_clues: Rao notes period features at Tenkasi: the manner of moustaches and long conical crown are of that period and place.
rows.cautions: An identification says who the figure is, not how old it is or whether it is genuine; the same forms are still made today.

facts.text: Manmatha carries a sugarcane bow in the left hand and five flower arrows in the right; his flag-bearer holds the makara banner; Priti and Rati stand beside him.
facts.quote: made to carry a bow of sugar-cane in the left hand and to hold in the right hand five flowery arrows.

facts.text: At Halebidu Manmatha stands with sugarcane bow and flower arrow, Rati on his left with fruit and lotus, standard-bearer on his right.
facts.quote: is seen standing with a bow of sugar-cane in his left hand and an arrow of flowers in the right hand.

rows.name: Rati
rows.features_other: Stands at Kama's left.
rows.identify_by: The woman beside a god with a sugarcane bow.

look_alikes.name: mithuna
look_alikes.how_to_tell: A mithuna couple has no sugarcane bow or banner-bearer.

rows.regions_styles: Hoysala and later South Indian reliefs.
rows.cautions: An identification says who the figure is, not how old it is or whether it is genuine; the same forms are still made today.

facts.text: At Halebidu Rati holds a fruit in her right hand and a lotus in her left.
facts.quote: To the left of Manmatha is the figure of his wife Rati holding a fruit in her right hand and a lotus in the left hand.

rows.name: Revanta
rows.features_other: Booted like Surya; holds a whip and reins; an attendant holds an umbrella over him; hunting companions, dogs and sometimes robbers in the scene.
rows.identify_by: A booted rider on a horse with an umbrella-bearer, in East Indian (Bengal, Bihar, Orissa) stone or bronze.

look_alikes.name: khandoba
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Khandoba rides with his consort Mhalsa, carries Shaiva weapons (sword, drum, trident) and comes from Maharashtra or Karnataka; Revanta wears boots and holds a whip, East India.

look_alikes.name: kalki (see vishnu_krishna topic)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Kalki, Vishnu's horse avatar, holds a sword and conch or discus.

rows.regions_styles: Eastern India (Bengal, Bihar, Orissa), Pala period; also known in Gujarat; almost unknown in South India.
rows.cautions: An identification says who the figure is, not how old it is or whether it is genuine; the same forms are still made today.

facts.text: Revanta rides a horse, engaged with companions in hunting (Brihatsamhita); the Ghatnagar image shows him booted with whip, reins and an umbrella-bearer.
facts.quote: The booted god rides on horseback holding a whip in his right hand and the reins in his left, with an attendant holding an umbrella over his head

facts.text: Rao is silent on Revanta because his images are almost unknown in South India; his worship was much in vogue in Eastern India.
facts.quote: Rao is silent about the images of Revanta, probably because they are almost unknown in Southern India.

rows.name: Ayyappa / Sasta (Aiyanar)
rows.features_other: A crooked stick (Tamil 'sendu', the vajradanda) in the right hand; left leg hanging and right leg raised with the elbow resting on its knee; modern Kerala images sit with a band (yogapatta) around the raised knees (single source); cock banner; wives Purana and Pushkala (Tamil) or Madana and Varnani (Suprabhedagama).
rows.identify_by: A youthful god seated with one knee raised, holding a crooked stick, sometimes on an elephant. In Kerala he is Ayyappan of Sabarimala; in Tamil villages Aiyanar.

look_alikes.name: indra
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Indra on his elephant holds a vajra; Sasta holds a crooked stick.

look_alikes.name: yoga narasimha (see vishnu_krishna topic)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Narasimha also sits with a yogapatta band round his knees but has a lion's head.

look_alikes.name: skanda/murugan (see shiva_devi topic)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Skanda holds a spear (vel) and rides a peacock.

rows.regions_styles: Kerala (Malayalam country: a Sasta shrine in the south-west corner of every temple; mountain temples of Sabarimala, Achankovil, Kulattupuzha, Aryankavu) and Tamil Nadu (Aiyanar village shrines); Chola bronzes such as Gajarudha Sasta (Valuvur).
rows.dating_clues: Rao: the deity is unknown north of the Godavari and absent from early Sanskrit works. Modern Swamimalai castings of Ayyappan are sold widely.
rows.cautions: An identification says who the figure is, not how old it is or whether it is genuine; the same forms are still made today. New lost-wax bronzes of Ayyappan are cast and sold today, including through online sellers (seller_listings_2026).

facts.text: Sasta (Arya, Hariharaputra) is a Dravidian deity, favourite of the Malayalam country; in the Tamil country he is mostly called Ayyanar.
facts.quote: This deity is peculiar to the extreme south of India, especially to Malabar and Travancore where he has the largest number of worshippers.

facts.text: The deity of Sabarimala is Aiyappan (Sasta), the most important Sasta temple, visited by pilgrims during the annual Mandala-puja.
facts.quote: Sabarimala Aiyappan (Sasta)

facts.text: He is the son of Shiva by Mohini, the female form of Vishnu (Suprabhedagama).
facts.quote: The Suprabhedagama very distinctly mentions that Sasta was born of Mohini

facts.text: Karanagama form: seated with left leg hanging, right leg raised vertically with the left elbow on its knee, a crooked stick in the right hand; vehicle and banner the elephant; alternatively bull vehicle and cock banner.
facts.quote: with his left leg hanging down the seat and the right one folded and rested upon the seat vertically.

facts.text: Most images of Ayyappan show him seated in yogapattasana, with a band around the knees.
facts.quote: Most iconography of Ayyappan depict him in a yogapattasana, a seated position

rows.name: Manasa (snake goddess)
other_names: Padmavati (name shared with the Jain yakshi)
rows.features_other: Seven snakes spread their hoods as a canopy over her head and she holds an eighth; a child (Astika) on her lap in one text; an emaciated bearded sage (Jaratkaru) on her right and a crowned male (Vasuki or Astika) on her left; a pitcher under the lotus seat; Snuhi (sij) plant used in her worship; also worshipped as a pot with snakes.
rows.identify_by: A goddess seated with one leg pendant under a canopy of seven cobra hoods, holding a snake, in Bengal or Bihar work.

look_alikes.name: padmavati (see jain topic)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: The Jain yakshi Padmavati also has a snake hood but attends Parshvanatha, often with a small Jina in the headdress.

look_alikes.name: nagini
look_alikes.how_to_tell: A nagini usually has a snake's lower body or one to three hoods and no child or emaciated sage.

look_alikes.name: hariti / janguli (see buddhist topic)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Hariti holds a child but has no snake canopy; the Buddhist snake goddess Janguli appears in Buddhist settings.

rows.regions_styles: Bengal and Bihar stone images of the 900s-1100s; 11th-century repousse copper (Met); 19th-century Kalighat paintings; 20th-century Madhubani paintings.
rows.dating_clues: Bhattasali: the many stone images of the 10th-12th century across Bengal show her cult was established by then.
rows.cautions: An identification says who the figure is, not how old it is or whether it is genuine; the same forms are still made today.

facts.text: Most Bengal images show her seated on a lotus with the right leg pendant, seven snakes spreading their hoods over her head and an eighth in her left hand, a fruit in the right hand in boon-giving.
facts.quote: Seven snakes spread their hoods like a canopy over her head and the goddess holds the eighth snake in her left hand.

facts.text: An emaciated bearded man (Jaratkaru) sits at her right and a crowned male at her left; often a pitcher under the seat.
facts.quote: To her right is represented an emaciated bearded man, while a crowned male figure sits on her left.

facts.text: A dhyana quoted by Raghunandana gives her a young child on her lap and two snakes in her hands; Bhattasali notes the likeness to Hariti.
facts.quote: She has a young child (on her lap).

facts.text: Museums identify Bengal and Bihar works of the 10th-11th centuries as Manasa, the snake goddess.
facts.quote: Manasa, the Snake Goddess

rows.name: Shitala
rows.features_other: Broom and winnowing fan (tokens wanted: 'broom', 'winnowing fan'); a pitcher or ewer; nim branches and leaves are used against the disease in her cult; Crooke lists seven smallpox sisters in North India.
rows.identify_by: A goddess riding a donkey with a broom, winnowing fan and water pot.

look_alikes.name: jyeshtha (see shiva_devi topic)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Jyeshtha also rides an ass and holds a broom but is pot-bellied with a crow banner and sits with two attendants (a bull-headed son and a daughter).

look_alikes.name: nirrti
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Nirrti is a male guardian with sword and shield who may ride an ass.

look_alikes.name: parnashabari (see buddhist topic)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: The Buddhist disease goddess Parnashabari wears leaves and tramples disease figures; Dacca steles show Shitala fleeing from her.

rows.regions_styles: North India and Bengal; popular painted and printed images; small brass shrine figures.
rows.cautions: An identification says who the figure is, not how old it is or whether it is genuine; the same forms are still made today.

facts.text: The ass is the animal on which Sitala rides; feeding a donkey is one remedy in an epidemic.
facts.quote: Another device is to feed a donkey, which is the animal on which Sitala rides.

facts.text: She carries a broom and winnowing fan, and in one hand a pitcher and ewer (Crooke, for Matangi-Sitala); a Dacca stele shows Sitala with broom and winnowing basket leaving on her donkey.
facts.quote: Sitala, the Brahmanical goddess of epidemics, with a broom stick in the right hand and the winnowing basket (kula) in the left, is departing

rows.name: Khandoba
rows.features_other: Rides a (white) horse, often with his wife Mhalsa seated in front of or behind him; dogs around the horse; the demon Malla (Mani-Malla) he killed; turmeric (bhandar) worship. Brass plaques and small horse-and-rider castings are typical of Maharashtra.
rows.identify_by: A warrior on horseback with a sword (often a drum), with his consort on the same horse and dogs below. Typically Maharashtra brass.

look_alikes.name: revanta
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Revanta wears boots and holds a whip; Khandoba has a consort on the horse and Shaiva weapons.

look_alikes.name: bhairava (see shiva_devi topic)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Bhairava stands naked with a dog; Khandoba rides a horse.

look_alikes.name: rajasthani hero and folk riders (Pabuji, Ramdev)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Rider deities of Rajasthan and Gujarat appear on Rajasthani phad cloths and plaques; Khandoba belongs to the Deccan and usually has Mhalsa with him.

rows.regions_styles: Jejuri near Pune is his chief temple; brass figures of Maharashtra dated 17th-18th century in museums (Met).
rows.dating_clues: The Met dates its brass Khandoba groups to the 17th-18th centuries by style; the same forms are still cast for worship.
rows.cautions: An identification says who the figure is, not how old it is or whether it is genuine; the same forms are still made today.

facts.text: Khandoba rides a horse: the Mallari-mahatmya gives him a white horse, and at Jejuri a hollow in the rock is shown as the print of Khandoba's horse.
facts.quote: His vehicle is to be a white horse
