facts.text: Mallari (Shiva as Khandoba) holds a drum (damaru) and sword and is surrounded by seven dogs (Mallari-mahatmya).
facts.quote: In the hands are to be seen a damaru and a khadga. His vehicle is to be a white horse and he must be surrounded by seven dogs.

facts.text: At Jejuri, Shiva appeared as the warrior Khandoba to slay the demon Mani-Malla; the dark shrine holds three pairs of images of Khandoba (Martand) and Mhalsa, in gold, silver and stone.
facts.quote: In this dark chamber behind a long stand three pairs of images of Martand or Khanderay and Mhalsa.

facts.text: Museum brass groups show Khandoba on a horse, with Mhalsa on horseback, and with a mahout on an elephant (Maharashtra, 17th-18th centuries).
facts.quote: Khandoba and Mhalsi on Horseback

rows.name: Yaksha (nature spirit)
rows.features_other: Massive, frontal, pot-bellied male, heavy jewelry, turban (sirastraka); flask or money bag; dwarf yakshas support bracket figures and thrones; yakshas act as guardians and gate-keepers.
rows.identify_by: A stout, frontal, richly jewelled male nature spirit with no specific god's attributes; often colossal (Parkham) or a guardian or bearer.

look_alikes.name: kubera
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Kubera, their lord, carries a purse or mongoose and sits on treasure pots.

look_alikes.name: dvarapala_shaiva
look_alikes.how_to_tell: A temple door guardian carries a club or trident and stands at a doorway, often fanged.

look_alikes.name: jain yaksha (see jain topic)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: A Jain yaksha sits beside a Jina as his attendant.

rows.regions_styles: Maurya and Shunga stone statues (Parkham, Patna), Bharhut and Sanchi railings, Kushan Mathura red sandstone, terracottas.
rows.dating_clues: Early yakshas of the Maurya-Shunga period are the oldest Indian stone figures in the round; style is what museums date them by.
rows.cautions: An identification says who the figure is, not how old it is or whether it is genuine; the same forms are still made today. Old names given to these statues are often wrong: the Mathura 'Manasa Devi' statue is, by its inscription, the Yakshi Layava. Early yaksha and yakshi figures have been faked (Cleveland holds a base catalogued as a 20th-century fake).

facts.text: Yakshas appear chiefly as attendants, guardians and gate-keepers; they can take any shape and are grouped with nagas and gandharvas.
facts.quote: it is chiefly as attendants, guardians and gate-keepers that the Yaksas appear in Buddhist art

facts.text: The Parkham image, a colossal yaksha inscribed with the name Kunika, is the oldest known Indian stone sculpture in the round.
facts.quote: The Parkham image is of great importance as the oldest known Indian stone sculpture in the round

facts.text: Cleveland reads a large pot-bellied terracotta as perhaps Kubera or a yaksha worshipped for wealth.
facts.quote: suggest that the image may represent Kubera, or a yaksha worshiped for wealth and prosperity.

rows.name: Yakshi (female nature spirit)
rows.features_other: Voluptuous woman in heavy jewelry with a broad jewelled girdle (mekhala), often grasping a tree branch (ashoka) and touching her breast or standing on a dwarf; on railing pillars of stupas. Token wanted: 'holds a tree branch'.
rows.identify_by: A nearly nude, heavily jewelled woman with a tree or on a dwarf, from an early railing pillar or bracket.

look_alikes.name: shalabhanjika
look_alikes.how_to_tell: The same woman-and-tree pose used as a bracket figure at the top of a pillar or gateway.

look_alikes.name: ganga
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Ganga has a makara under her feet and a water pot.

look_alikes.name: mithuna
look_alikes.how_to_tell: A mithuna is a couple.

look_alikes.name: manasa
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Manasa has a snake canopy; note that the Mathura 'Manasa Devi' is a yakshi.

rows.regions_styles: Bharhut, Sanchi, Mathura (Kushan red sandstone), Chandraketugarh terracotta and wood (Bengal).
rows.dating_clues: As for yaksha; Coomaraswamy traces the type from pre-Maurya terracottas.
rows.cautions: An identification says who the figure is, not how old it is or whether it is genuine; the same forms are still made today. Some early female figures are catalogued only 'probably a yakshi' (Cleveland, Met): the identification is often uncertain.

facts.text: No motif is more characteristic of Indian art than the woman and tree; the women of early railing pillars are yakshis, as inscriptions at Bharhut prove.
facts.quote: There is no motif more fundamentally characteristic of Indian art from first to last than is that of the Woman and Tree.

facts.text: Cleveland's railing pillar yakshi grasps an ashoka branch with one hand and touches her breast with the other.
facts.quote: grasping the branch of an ashoka tree with one hand and touching her breast full of nourishing milk with the other.

facts.text: The 'Manasa Devi' statue at Mathura is, by its inscription, the Yakshi Layava.
facts.quote: the so-called statue of Manasa Devi at Mathura (really the image of Yaksi Layava, as the inscription on the pedestal informs us)

rows.name: Shalabhanjika (woman-and-tree bracket figure)
rows.features_other: A woman bending from the trunk of a tree and holding a branch, carved as the bracket between a pillar and the beam; in Hoysala temples (Belur, Halebidu) she may dance, play music, hold a mirror or a parrot, with a dwarf below and drummers. The mirror and parrot are from general knowledge, not from a read source.
rows.identify_by: A slanting figure of a woman under a tree canopy that fits an angle between post and beam.

look_alikes.name: yakshi
look_alikes.how_to_tell: A yakshi on a railing pillar stands upright; the shalabhanjika is a bracket figure, slanting outward.

look_alikes.name: apsaras
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Celestial women on wall surfaces have no tree.

rows.regions_styles: Sanchi and Mathura gateway brackets (150-200 CE, Cleveland); Hoysala bracket figures of Karnataka; carved wooden brackets of later temples and houses.
rows.cautions: An identification says who the figure is, not how old it is or whether it is genuine; the same forms are still made today. Detached temple brackets are architectural fragments.

facts.text: Gateway architraves were supported by brackets carved with women grasping the branch of a tree.
facts.quote: brackets carved with figures of voluptuous women grasping the branch of a tree.

facts.text: Hoysala bracket figures keep the woman-and-tree motif, supported by a dwarf yaksha, often dancing and with drummers.
facts.quote: Hoysala bracket figures, however, which preserve the motif of woman and tree, supported by a dwarf Yaksa, are often in dancing positions

rows.name: Apsaras / Surasundari (celestial woman)
rows.features_other: Beautiful, ornamented women on temple walls and lintels, dancing, flying, adjusting ornaments or playing instruments; no fixed attributes. Male counterparts: gandharvas (musicians), vidyadharas (flying garland-bearers), kinnaras (bird-legged).
rows.identify_by: A beautiful ornamented woman in movement on a temple wall, with no god's attributes and no tree.

look_alikes.name: yakshi
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Yakshis stand frontally with a tree; Coomaraswamy warns that railing-pillar women are not dancing girls.

look_alikes.name: shalabhanjika
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Bracket figures are tied to a tree and an architectural angle.

look_alikes.name: sarasvati
look_alikes.how_to_tell: A woman with a vina and book is Sarasvati.

rows.regions_styles: Bharhut (named apsarases, dancing); medieval North Indian and Rajasthani wall figures (Met 'Dancing Apsaras', 13th-14th c.); Karnataka (gandharvas, Met).
rows.cautions: An identification says who the figure is, not how old it is or whether it is genuine; the same forms are still made today. Wall figures are fragments of temples.

facts.text: Apsarases have no special iconographic trait; they are shown as very beautiful women from the earliest period, dancing at Bharhut.
facts.quote: The Apsarasas did not appear to have had any peculiar iconographic trait of their own, inasmuch as they are usually shown in the forms of exceedingly beautiful damsels

facts.text: Railing-pillar women with instruments may be gandharvis or apsarases, but none dance; calling them dancing girls is an error.
facts.quote: none are represented as actually dancing, and to call them dancing girls is certainly an error.

rows.name: Naga (serpent deity)
rows.features_other: A hood of one, three, five or seven cobra heads behind the head; sometimes a human upper body ending in snake coils (token wanted: 'snake lower body'); as attendants nagas hold fly whisks or join hands in salutation; the flask or water bottle marks the water-spirit.
rows.identify_by: A male figure with a fan of cobra hoods behind his head and no other god's emblems.

look_alikes.name: balarama (see vishnu_krishna topic)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Balarama also has a snake hood but holds a plough and pestle (the Met catalogues one figure as 'Balarama or Nagaraja').

look_alikes.name: parshvanatha (see jain topic)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: The Jina Parshva sits or stands naked in meditation under seven hoods.

look_alikes.name: buddha with muchalinda (see buddhist topic)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: The Buddha sits in meditation on the snake's coils, with cranial bump and robe.

look_alikes.name: ketu
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Ketu has a snake tail but stands in a planet row.

rows.regions_styles: Bharhut and Sanchi; Kushan Mathura nagas (Cleveland); Andhra nagas (Goli, Nagarjunakonda); Gupta Nagarajas; Himachal Nag Devta temples.
rows.cautions: An identification says who the figure is, not how old it is or whether it is genuine; the same forms are still made today.

facts.text: Indian art shows nagas in three ways: as a many-headed serpent, as a human with a serpent hood, or as a human upper body joined to snake coils.
facts.quote: first, the form of the serpent, usually many-headed ; second, the human form universally characterized by means of the polycephalous serpent-hood ; third, a combination of the two

facts.text: Nagaraja has a five-headed cobra hood; the Silparatna makes nagas half human below the navel, with hoods of one, three, five or seven heads, carrying sword and shield.
facts.quote: Their heads must be covered with hoods having one, three, five or seven heads

facts.text: Cleveland identifies a Kushan naga by the serpent coils and the bottle of water in his hand.
facts.quote: The coils of a serpent's body and the bottle of water in his hand confirm the identity of this figure as a water serpent divinity

rows.name: Nagini (serpent goddess)
rows.features_other: Fewer hoods than her male partner (often one or three); may have a snake's lower body; often paired with a naga, tails intertwined.
rows.identify_by: A woman with a cobra hood, often beside a naga.

look_alikes.name: manasa
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Manasa has a canopy of seven snakes, holds a snake, and may have a child and an emaciated sage beside her.

look_alikes.name: padmavati (see jain topic)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Padmavati attends Parshvanatha.

look_alikes.name: sarasvati
look_alikes.how_to_tell: A nagini with a vina is still a nagini if a hood is present.

rows.regions_styles: Mamallapuram 'Descent of the Ganga' rock (naga with seven hoods, nagini with fewer); Hoysala Halebidu; Khiching (Orissa); Madras Museum.
rows.cautions: An identification says who the figure is, not how old it is or whether it is genuine; the same forms are still made today.

facts.text: At Mamallapuram the naga's hood has seven cobra heads while the nagini has fewer.
facts.quote: Both carry a hood, which in the case of the male consists of no less than seven cobra-heads, whereas the female has to be content with a

facts.text: Rao and Banerjea illustrate naga-and-nagini pairs and naginis (Halebidu, Madras Museum, Khiching, one with a vina).
facts.quote: Naga and Nagini ; Stone; Halebidu.

rows.name: Nagakal (serpent stone)
rows.features_other: A small stone slab carved with one cobra standing on its tail, a many-headed cobra, a naga couple with intertwined tails, or a half-human naga; set up under a pipal or nim tree.
rows.identify_by: A flat slab with a cobra or two intertwined snakes, without a temple setting.

look_alikes.name: naga
look_alikes.how_to_tell: A naga image is a figure; a nagakal is a votive slab, often several placed together under trees.

rows.regions_styles: South India, especially Karnataka (Mysore) and Tamil Nadu; also the Deccan (Badami, Aihole).
rows.dating_clues: Votive slabs are made continuously; most are recent.
rows.cautions: An identification says who the figure is, not how old it is or whether it is genuine; the same forms are still made today.

facts.text: Naga images are set up by scores under pipal trees; childless people vow to install them.
facts.quote: It is a common sight all over India to meet with the Naga images set up under big pipal trees by scores and worshipped occasionally.

facts.text: The commonest nagakal shows a single cobra standing on its tail with hood spread; many are polycephalous.
facts.quote: The simplest and perhaps commonest type of these snake-slabs exhibit a single cobra standing, as it were, on the tip of his tail

rows.name: Kirtimukha (face of glory)
rows.features_other: A horned mythic beast's mask from whose mouth stylized foliage pours; set above temple entryways and, in miniature, on a god's crown.
rows.identify_by: A fierce mask without a body, spewing foliage, at the top of a frame or arch.

look_alikes.name: rahu
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Rahu has a human face and appears in the planet row, often with hands.

look_alikes.name: bhuta
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Bhuta masks are separate metal masks worn by dancers, not carved crowns of arches.

look_alikes.name: mohra
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Mohras are face plaques of named gods with crowns and jewelry, not fanged foliage masks.

rows.regions_styles: All of India; Pallava temples (in full relief by the 800s); North Indian pediments (Cleveland, 1000s); Nepal and Tibet (as Kala) on Himalayan work.
rows.dating_clues: Coomaraswamy notes the kirttimukha head 'now in full relief' as a feature of later Pallava work; a regional style clue only.
rows.cautions: An identification says who the figure is, not how old it is or whether it is genuine; the same forms are still made today. The story behind the mask (a monster made by Shiva that devoured its own body) was not found in a read source here.

facts.text: Horned mythic beasts spewing stylized foliage were built into temples above entryways; the name means 'face of glory'.
facts.quote: Known as the 'face (mukha) of glory (kirti),' the protective mask emanates divine energy from the heart of the temple.

facts.text: A miniature kirttimukha can sit at the top of a god's jata crown (Khiching Ganesha).
facts.quote: The well-arranged jata with a miniature kirttimukha in the centre on the top of the elephant-head

facts.text: In later Pallava (Aparajita) style the kirttimukha head is carved in full relief.
facts.quote: the kirttimukha head now in full relief

rows.name: Mithuna (loving couple)
rows.features_other: A man and woman embracing, from affectionate to explicitly erotic; on temple exteriors, terracotta roundels, ivory plaques and box panels.
rows.identify_by: A couple embracing with no divine attributes, extra arms or mounts.

look_alikes.name: uma-maheshvara (see shiva_devi topic)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Shiva with Parvati has four arms, a trident or snake, and the bull.

look_alikes.name: kama
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Kama with Rati holds a sugarcane bow.

look_alikes.name: radha-krishna (see vishnu_krishna topic)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Krishna is dark and plays a flute.

rows.regions_styles: Kushan Mathura terracotta; Andhra (Nagarjunakonda pillars); Gupta terracotta roundels (Ahichchhatra); Khajuraho and Rajasthan (900s-1000s); Orissa (1200s-1300s, Konarak region); South Indian ivory panels (1600s-1700s).
rows.cautions: An identification says who the figure is, not how old it is or whether it is genuine; the same forms are still made today. Wall and roundel figures are temple fragments; ivory raises the ivory rules in the general cautions.

facts.text: Amorous couples were among the most frequent images on the outside of sacred buildings and were thought auspicious.
facts.quote: Amorous couples were among the most prevalent imagery on the exterior of sacred sites in early India. Their life-affirming imagery was considered auspicious.

facts.text: Mithunas appear from Kushan terracottas to Orissan stone and South Indian ivory in open-access collections.
facts.quote: Loving Couple (Mithuna)

rows.name: Dvarapala of a Shiva temple (door guardian)
other_names: Chanda and Prachanda (names in some traditions)
rows.features_other: Guardians stand in pairs beside a shrine door; the read sources give the drum, a skull-topped staff and the third eye (Cleveland) and four arms in developed Pallava work. Heavy clubs, fangs, horns, snakes and a raised warning finger (tarjani) are commonly described but were not confirmed in a read source here.
rows.identify_by: A pair of guardians at a doorway leaning on clubs, carrying Shiva's emblems; the Shaiva emblems decide the temple.

look_alikes.name: dvarapala_vaishnava
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Vishnu's guardians Jaya and Vijaya carry the discus, conch and mace.

look_alikes.name: bhairava (see shiva_devi topic)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Bhairava is the god himself, naked with a dog; a guardian stands at a door in a pair.

look_alikes.name: yaksha
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Yakshas also guard gates in early art but carry no Shaiva emblems.

rows.regions_styles: Pallava, Chola and later Tamil stone; Hoysala Karnataka (Cleveland, 1200s); ivory openwork panels from Mysore or Tamil Nadu (Met, late 1700s).
rows.dating_clues: Coomaraswamy lists four-armed dvarapalas as a feature of developed (later Pallava) style.
rows.cautions: An identification says who the figure is, not how old it is or whether it is genuine; the same forms are still made today. Single guardians are often cut from temple doorways.

facts.text: Guardians at Shiva temples sometimes appear as a form of the god himself, holding a drum and a staff topped with Brahma's head, with a third eye.
facts.quote: Guardians at Shiva temples sometimes appear as a form of the deity himself.

facts.text: Four-armed dvarapalas are a characteristic of the developed Pallava style.
facts.quote: the representation of dvarapalas with four arms

rows.name: Jaya and Vijaya (door guardians of Vishnu)
rows.features_other: Paired guardians at the door of a Vishnu shrine, or flanking Vishnu with Lakshmi and Bhudevi; reborn in myth as Hiranyaksha and Hiranyakashipu.
rows.identify_by: A four-armed guardian holding Vishnu's discus and conch with a mace.

look_alikes.name: dvarapala_shaiva
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Shaiva guardians carry trident, drum or snakes.

look_alikes.name: vishnu (see vishnu_krishna topic)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Vishnu stands at the centre, usually with consorts; the guardians stand at the sides or doors, often leaning on a mace.

rows.regions_styles: South Indian Vishnu temples; steles of Vishnu with consorts.
rows.cautions: An identification says who the figure is, not how old it is or whether it is genuine; the same forms are still made today.

facts.text: Jaya and Vijaya, the door-keepers of Vishnu, hold discus, conch and mace in three hands, the fourth in fear-not.
facts.quote: stand Jaya and Vijaya, the two door-keepers of Vishnu with chakra, sankha and gada in three of their hands, while the fourth one is held in the abhaya pose.

rows.name: Deepalakshmi (lamp-bearing woman)
rows.features_other: A standing woman holding a shallow oil lamp bowl (for oil and wick) in both hands in front of her; often in pairs; bronze or brass, sometimes very large; temple and household lamps. Token wanted: 'lamp'.
rows.identify_by: A standing woman holding out a lamp bowl with both hands; the lamp is the object, the woman its stand.

look_alikes.name: devotee
look_alikes.how_to_tell: A devotee or donor joins hands in salutation; the lamp bearer holds a bowl with a wick lip.

look_alikes.name: lakshmi (see vishnu_krishna topic)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Lakshmi as goddess holds lotuses and may be flanked by elephants; Deepalakshmi holds a lamp.

rows.regions_styles: South India (Tamil Nadu, Kerala); Vijayanagara period examples in museums; Chingleput district bronze of the 1700s-1800s (Cleveland).
rows.dating_clues: Swamimalai and other workshops cast new Deepalakshmi pairs in the traditional form today.
rows.cautions: An identification says who the figure is, not how old it is or whether it is genuine; the same forms are still made today. New lost-wax Deepalakshmis are made and sold today (seller_listings_2026); the form alone says nothing about age.

facts.text: Deepalakshmi is a temple lamp in the form of Lakshmi holding a lamp bowl as an offering of light.
facts.quote: Deepalakshmi is temple lamp that is represented as Lakshmi, the goddess of beauty and wealth.

facts.text: The Tamil paavai vilakku shows a woman holding the vessel for the lamp's fuel and wick; it is linked with the Karttikai Dipam festival.
facts.quote: embodies a woman holding a vessel for the lamp's fuel in which the wick is put.

rows.name: Devotee or donor figure (bhakta)
rows.features_other: Two-armed human figure with hands joined in salutation (anjali) or carrying an offering (tray of garlands); kings among the saints wear crowns; Brahmin saints a small tuft; the sixty-three Shaiva saints and twelve Alvars have their own images in South Indian temples.
rows.identify_by: A two-armed human figure with joined hands, without a god's emblems or extra arms.

look_alikes.name: sambandar
look_alikes.how_to_tell: A child saint with cymbals or dancing.

look_alikes.name: manikkavachakar
look_alikes.how_to_tell: A saint holding a palm-leaf book.

look_alikes.name: deepalakshmi
look_alikes.how_to_tell: A woman holding a lamp bowl.

rows.regions_styles: South Indian temple bronzes and stone (Shaiva and Vaishnava saints); Kushan Mathura devotee figures (Cleveland).
rows.cautions: An identification says who the figure is, not how old it is or whether it is genuine; the same forms are still made today. Saint images are temple property in South India; see the general cautions on stolen temple bronzes.

facts.text: Bhaktas may carry items associated with them or hold their hands in anjali, the attitude of worship; they may sing, dance or do puja.
facts.quote: they may have their hands held in the anjali pose, or the attitude of worship. They may be sculptured as singing, dancing or doing puja.

facts.text: Many Shiva temples have about seventy-three images of bhaktas: the sixty-three saints plus later ones such as Manikkavachakar.
facts.quote: that is why we see in many Siva temples not sixty-three, but about seventy-three images of bhaktas.

rows.name: Dhokra (tribal lost-wax brass)
rows.features_other: A craft, not a single figure: brass cast by the lost-wax method, popularised by nomadic communities of eastern and central India (Bastar in Chhattisgarh is the best known). Surfaces built from thin wax threads give a corded look; idols of local and Hindu deities (in Bastar: Bheemdev, Persa Pen, Jangubai) and animals (lion, fish, elephant, swan, tortoise, bull). Token wanted: kind 'craft tradition'.
rows.identify_by: A rough-surfaced brass figure covered in fine cord-like ridges, with simplified features, cast in one piece.

look_alikes.name: bhuta
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Tulu bhuta brasses come from coastal Karnataka and are smoother, often masks or human-and-animal images used in bhuta shrines.

look_alikes.name: khandoba
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Maharashtra brass Khandoba riders are cast smooth with a consort on the horse.

rows.regions_styles: Bastar (Chhattisgarh) and eastern India (West Bengal, Odisha); a living craft.
rows.dating_clues: Museum records of Bastar pieces are mostly dated to the 20th century (V&A, National Crafts Museum, as seen in search summaries); the Incredible India page says the craft's exact origins are unknown. Wear, dirt and patina can be added; age claims for Dhokra need evidence beyond the look.
rows.cautions: Most Dhokra figures in the Western market are recent and made to be sold; old and new are made by the same method. An identification says who the figure is, not how old it is or whether it is genuine; the same forms are still made today.

facts.text: Bastar Dhokra is made by molding, sun drying, melting wax, dewaxing and casting, with specialised tools for drawing wax threads; it includes idols of local and Hindu deities and animal figures.
facts.quote: specialised tools for extracting wax threads from wax blocks

facts.text: A local 1894 lost-wax method in the Central Provinces: clay model, wax coat (beeswax, resin, oil), clay coat, a clay crucible joined to the mold, then inverted so the metal runs in; idols and toys were cast this way.
facts.quote: instruments and idols, toys &c., are mostly cast.

facts.text: The exact origins of the Bastar craft are unknown.
facts.quote: While the exact origins of the craft remain unknown.

facts.text: Museum records date Bastar Dhokra figures to the 20th century (V&A Mata Devi citing Reeves 1962; National Crafts Museum, mid-20th century).

rows.name: Bhuta figures and masks (Tulu Nadu)
rows.features_other: Two kinds of object: (1) brass images kept in bhuta shrines, human or animal (boar, tiger, fowl), brought out for festivals; (2) a metal mask worn by the dancer possessed by the bhuta, with an arch of coconut leaves. Panjurli has the form of a boar. Sword and bell belong to the officiant.
rows.identify_by: A metal mask or rough brass figure from coastal Karnataka (South Canara/Tulu Nadu), with bulging eyes, often moustached; a boar mask points to Panjurli.

look_alikes.name: varaha (see vishnu_krishna topic)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Vishnu's boar avatar has four arms with discus and conch and lifts the earth goddess; Panjurli is a boar mask or boar image without Vishnu's emblems.

look_alikes.name: mohra
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Himachal mohras are face plaques of Shiva or Devi with crowns, from the western Himalaya.

look_alikes.name: kirtimukha
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Kirtimukha is a carved architectural mask, not a wearable one.

rows.regions_styles: South Canara (Mangalore, Udupi) and neighboring coastal Karnataka; Met holds an early 20th-century copper-alloy mask of the spirit deity Jumadi.
rows.dating_clues: Masks and images are renewed and recast for shrines; Western museum examples are mostly 19th-20th century.
rows.cautions: An identification says who the figure is, not how old it is or whether it is genuine; the same forms are still made today. Masks are sacred shrine property; old bhuta masks on the market often lack any record of how they left the shrine.

facts.text: Inside a bhuta shrine are images roughly made in brass, in human shape or like animals (pigs, tigers, fowls), brought out on festival occasions.
facts.quote: Inside the Bhutasthanam there is usually a number of images, roughly made in brass, in human shape, or resembling animals, such as pigs, tigers, fowls, &c.

facts.text: At an 1872 Mangalore festival brass images of five bhutas were set on the altar; Panjurli has the form of a hog.
facts.quote: brass images of the five Bhutas to be invoked that night ... The last mentioned has the form of a hog

facts.text: The possessed dancer wears a metal mask; in 1872 a second mask had a pig's snout.
facts.quote: put on a metal mask, and his servant held in his hand a similar mask with a pig's snout to it.

rows.name: Mohra (Himalayan deity mask)
rows.features_other: Cast or repousse metal (brass, copper alloy, silver, gold) faces or busts of a village god or goddess (Shiva, Devi and local devtas), fixed on the deity's palanquin (rath) for festivals and stored in the temple treasury; a CSMVS Shiva mohra (seen only in a search summary) shows a linga below the face and a third eye.
rows.identify_by: A metal face or bust of a deity, flat at the back with fixing holes, from Himachal Pradesh (Kulu, Mandi, Chamba).

look_alikes.name: nepalese processional masks (see buddhist topic)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: The Met's 14th-16th-century repousse 'processional masks' are Nepalese (Kathmandu Valley); Newar style differs from Himachal work and the record decides.

look_alikes.name: bhuta
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Bhuta masks are worn by dancers in coastal Karnataka.

look_alikes.name: mukhalinga (see shiva_devi topic)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: A mukhalinga is a linga with one or more faces carved or cast on the shaft, for a shrine.

rows.regions_styles: Western Himalaya (Kulu, Mandi, Chamba); LACMA dates one to about 1400; others are catalogued as 20th century.
rows.dating_clues: Dates range from about 1400 (LACMA) to the 20th century (CSMVS, per search summary); mohras are still cast by craftsmen in Mandi and Chamba districts.
rows.cautions: An identification says who the figure is, not how old it is or whether it is genuine; the same forms are still made today. New mohras are made today for temples; Nepalese masks are sometimes sold as Indian.

facts.text: Village gods are carried in a palanquin (rath) at fairs, decked with silver or gold masks kept in the temple treasure-house.
facts.quote: the gold and silver masks that are put over the idol on ceremonious occasions.

facts.text: Processional busts, popularly called masks (mohra), are carried on palanquins.
facts.quote: Processional busts, popularly known as masks (mohra), are carried on palanquins

facts.text: The craft is kept alive today by craftsmen mostly in Mandi and Chamba districts.
facts.quote: The 10th century craft has been kept alive by craftsmen mostly settled in Mandi and Chamba districts.

rows.name: Third eye (sign)
rows.features_other: Vertical on the forehead for Shiva and his forms; horizontal for Indra; texts also give three eyes to Agni, Ishana, Sasta, Ganesha and (in one text) Sarasvati, and to the guardian of a Shiva temple.
rows.identify_by: A third eye says the figure is divine and most often Shaiva; its direction (vertical or horizontal) separates Shiva from Indra.

look_alikes.name: sign_tilaka
look_alikes.how_to_tell: A painted forehead mark (tilaka) is a sect mark worn by devotees and also shown on gods; an eye has a pupil and lids.

rows.regions_styles: All India.
rows.cautions: A sign narrows the field; it does not identify a figure alone.

facts.text: In heads of Shiva the third eye is usually vertical; Indra's is horizontal.
facts.quote: in the heads of Siva the position of the third eye is usually vertical, Indra's third eye being shown horizontally

rows.name: Srivatsa mark (sign)
rows.features_other: In Hindu sculpture a small four-petalled flower in a rhombus or a triangle on the right side of Vishnu's chest; Buddhas and Jinas also bear it (on Jinas usually in the centre of the chest).
rows.identify_by: A small diamond, flower or triangle on the chest points to Vishnu and his avatars, or to a Jina.

look_alikes.name: jain srivatsa (see jain topic)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: A naked figure in meditation with the mark in the middle of the chest is a Jina.

look_alikes.name: kaustubha jewel
look_alikes.how_to_tell: The kaustubha is a jewel hung at Vishnu's neck, not a mark on the skin.

rows.regions_styles: All India.
rows.cautions: Small and often worn away; absence proves nothing.

facts.text: The srivatsa is shown as a four-petalled flower in a rhombus or an equilateral triangle, on the right side of Vishnu's chest (Banerjea repeats Rao's words, so this counts as one source; he adds that he recognized the mark on medieval northern and eastern Vishnus).
facts.quote: In sculpture this mole is represented by a flower of four petals arranged in the form of a rhombus, or by a simple equilateral triangle, and is invariably placed on the right side of the chest.

facts.text: The breasts of Vishnu, the Buddha and the Jinas are marked with the srivatsa.
facts.quote: The breasts of Visnu, Buddha and the Jinas are also characterised by the srivatsa mark.

rows.name: Crowns and hair (sign): kirita, karanda, jata
rows.features_other: Kirita-makuta: tall conical jewelled crown, for Vishnu (and emperors); Surya's is much the same. Karanda-makuta: short bowl- or basket-shaped crown for most other gods and all goddesses, a sign of subordinate rank. Jata-makuta: matted locks piled into a tall crown, for Brahma and Shiva (Shiva's with crescent and skull). Kesabandha hairdo for Sarasvati, kuntala for Lakshmi.
rows.identify_by: The crown type narrows the identity: tall cylinder of jewels = Vishnu or Surya; piled matted locks = Shiva or Brahma (or an ascetic); small basket crown = a goddess or lesser god.

look_alikes.name: sign_halo
look_alikes.how_to_tell: A halo is a disc or ring behind the head, not on it.

rows.regions_styles: All India; crown shapes are regional (tall conical later Pandya crowns, Rao on Tenkasi).
rows.dating_clues: Crown shapes help place region and school.
rows.cautions: Rules are ideals; sculptors varied them (Rao's Madras bronze Brahma wears a kirita, not jata).

facts.text: The kirita-makuta is for Narayana (Vishnu); the karanda-makuta, bowl-shaped and short, for other gods and all goddesses and shows subordinate status; the jata-makuta for Brahma and Rudra.
facts.quote: The kirita-makuta should be worn exclusively by Narayana among the gods.

facts.text: There is very little difference between the crown worn by Vishnu and that worn by Surya in extant images.
facts.quote: The extant images show that in most cases there is very little difference between the crown worn by Visnu and that worn by Surya.

rows.name: Sacred thread (sign)
rows.features_other: A cord over the left shoulder and under the right arm, on most later Hindu gods; Shiva and Ganesha may wear a snake as the thread; a deer skin worn the same way on Brahma and ascetics.
rows.identify_by: Says the figure is a deity or twice-born man; a snake as thread points to Shiva or Ganesha.

look_alikes.name: sign_crowns
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Unrelated; listed so the reader checks both.

rows.regions_styles: All India.
rows.dating_clues: Banerjea: the sacred thread appears on images of gods from the Gupta period on and is not usually found in earlier images; a jewelled thread sometimes accompanies the cotton one in medieval work. A dating tendency, not a test.
rows.cautions: Modern copies of any period include or omit the thread at will.

facts.text: The sacred thread is found on images of the gods from the Gupta period onward; earlier images do not usually show it.
facts.quote: is found on the images of the gods from the Gupta period onwards; in the earlier images it is not usually to be found.

facts.text: In later images the thread runs across the chest from the left shoulder.
facts.quote: In almost all the later representations of Hindu gods and goddesses we may see the yajnopavita running across the chest from left to right.

rows.name: Halo (sign): siraschakra and prabhavali
other_names: tiruvasi (Tamil, the arch of a bronze)
rows.features_other: Siraschakra: a disc or lotus behind the head, attached by a rod hidden in flowers. Prabhavali: a ring or oval around the whole figure, often edged with tongues of flame; may carry the god's emblems (conch and discus for Vishnu) or Vishnu's ten avatars.
rows.identify_by: Emblems carved on a prabhavali help identify the god inside it; a flaming ring round a dancing figure is Nataraja's.

look_alikes.name: kirtimukha
look_alikes.how_to_tell: A kirtimukha is a carved face that may top an arch; the halo is the ring itself.

rows.regions_styles: All India; South Indian bronzes have detachable arches (tiruvasi).
rows.cautions: Arches and halos of South Indian bronzes are often lost or replaced; a replacement arch is not evidence about the figure.

facts.text: The siraschakra is the halo round the head; the prabhavali a ring round the whole person, with tongues of flame.
facts.quote: the former is, however, a ring of light that surrounds the whole person of a god, while the latter is a circular halo that is shown close to the head.

facts.text: The prabhavali often carries the god's own emblems: conch and discus for Vishnu, axe and noose for Shiva or Ganesha, sometimes the ten avatars.
facts.quote: sankha and chakra are found in association with the prabhavali of Vishnu

rows.name: Forehead marks (sign): Shaiva and Vaishnava tilaka
rows.features_other: Shaiva: three horizontal lines of white ash (tripundra, vibhuti). Vaishnava: an upright mark (urdhvapundra), usually two white vertical lines joined at the root of the nose (Vishnu's footprint), with a red or yellow line between (Sri Vaishnavas red; Madhvas a black line ending in a turmeric dot). Seen on painted faces of gods and devotees and on wooden and painted images. Token wanted: 'horizontal forehead lines' and 'vertical forehead mark'.
rows.identify_by: Three horizontal lines point to a Shaiva setting; a U or Y-shaped vertical mark to a Vaishnava one.

look_alikes.name: sign_third_eye
look_alikes.how_to_tell: A third eye is an eye, not painted lines.

rows.regions_styles: All India; in South India the mark is called nama (namam).
rows.cautions: Smarta Brahmins, who worship all the main gods, also wear the three horizontal lines, so the mark says sect leaning, not exclusive allegiance.

facts.text: The Shaiva mark is three horizontal strokes of white ash (tripundra); the Vaishnava an upright mark (urdhvapundra) representing Vishnu's footprint.
facts.quote: That of the Saivas consists of three horizontal strokes (tri-pundra) made with the white ashes of burnt substances (vibhuti)

facts.text: Vaishnava sub-sects vary the mark: two perpendicular white lines joined at the root of the nose (Sri Vaishnavas with a red line between; Madhvas with a black line ending in a turmeric dot).
facts.quote: two perpendicular lines made with Gopichandana, and joined at the root of the nose like that of the Sri Vaishnavas

facts.text: Smarta Brahmins of the Lower Carnatic are distinguished by three horizontal stripes of cow-dung ash though they honour Brahma, Vishnu and Shiva alike.
facts.quote: They are readily distinguished by three horizontal stripes on the forehead, made with the ashes of cowdung

rows.name: Buddha calling the earth to witness (earth-touching Buddha)
rows.features_other: Right arm hangs over the right knee, fingers pointing down to touch the ground or the lotus; left hand lies palm-up in the lap (in Tibetan and Nepalese images it often holds an alms bowl). A vajra may lie on the lotus in front (the 'diamond throne'). Pala steles often add the Bodhi tree with heart-shaped leaves above.
rows.identify_by: A plain-robed Buddha seated with legs locked whose right hand reaches down over the knee to touch the earth. This is the moment of enlightenment at Bodh Gaya.

look_alikes.name: akshobhya
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Same gesture. Akshobhya is told apart only by a vajra set upright before him or on the pedestal, blue color in paintings, or his place in a set of five Buddhas; Bhattacharyya says a lone sculpture often cannot be told from the historical Buddha.

look_alikes.name: buddha-crowned
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Crowned and jeweled Buddhas may make the same gesture but wear a crown, earrings and necklaces over the robe.

look_alikes.name: medicine-buddha
look_alikes.how_to_tell: The Medicine Buddha's right hand also rests on the knee, but palm outward holding a sprig or fruit (myrobalan), and the left holds a bowl.

look_alikes.name: buddha-life-scenes-stele
look_alikes.how_to_tell: If small scenes surround the central earth-touching Buddha, the item is a life-scenes stele rather than a single image.

rows.regions_styles: Pala-Sena Bihar and Bengal (black chlorite steles and bronzes, 8th-12th c.); Burma from Pagan onward (bronze, lacquered wood); Tibet and Nepal (gilt copper, often with alms bowl); Thailand (Ayutthaya, Chiang Saen, Bangkok); Sri Lanka uses it less than the meditation pose.
rows.dating_clues: Style places an image in a school (Pala, Pagan, Mandalay, Tibetan), not in a year; the gesture has been made for many centuries and still is.
rows.cautions: An identification says who the figure is meant to be, never how old the item is or whether it is old at all: the same forms are still made today for worship and to be sold (Nepalese and Tibetan workshops never stopped; Coomaraswamy 1927 notes good Nepalese metal work 'even up to quite recent times'). India's Antiquities and Art Treasures Act 1972 restricts export of antiquities over 100 years old (see general_cautions).

facts.text: The Sadhanamala describes the Vajrasana Buddha as showing the earth-touching gesture with the right hand while the left rests on the lap, dressed in red robes, seated on a vajra on a double lotus.
facts.quote: Savyakarena Bhūsparśamudrām-utsaṅgasthitavāmahastaṃ kāṣāyavastrāvaguṇṭhanam

facts.text: Getty: the earth-touching gesture shows the Buddha calling the earth to witness his resistance to Mara; the right arm stretches down, fingers extended, tips touching the earth.
facts.quote: The right arm is stretched downwards, all the fingers are extended, the tips touching the earth, the palm turned underneath

facts.text: A vajra lying in front of the Buddha on the lotus throne can indicate the 'diamond throne' (Vajrasana).
facts.quote: The 'diamond' throne is sometimes indicated by a vajra lying in front of Buddha on the lotus throne.

facts.text: Bhattacharyya: the seven past Buddhas usually all show the earth-touching gesture, the gesture of Akshobhya, so a sculpture of Akshobhya cannot be identified unless colored or otherwise marked.
facts.quote: we are unable to identify a sculpture of the latter unless it is coloured or if no other identification mark is present

facts.text: In Tibet the historical Buddha's symbol is the begging bowl (patra) and his color golden.
facts.quote: Symbol: patra (begging-bowl). Colour: golden.

facts.text: Cleveland catalogues a Pagan-style (Burma, 1100s) Buddha in earth-touching gesture carved from solid wood, covered in black lacquer and gilded, and notes lacquer is perishable so such works are rare.
facts.quote: As is typical of Burmese works, this sculpture was carved from a solid piece of wood. Its surface was covered in black lacquer and then gilded

rows.name: Meditating Buddha
rows.features_other: Both hands lie in the lap, right on top of left, palms up; legs locked so the figure forms a triangle. Sri Lankan images often have a flame finial on the cranial bump.
rows.identify_by: A Buddha seated with legs locked and both hands resting palm-up one on the other in the lap, with nothing in them.

look_alikes.name: amitabha
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Amitabha makes the same gesture; Getty notes the meditation gesture is also Amitabha's. A lone figure cannot be told apart except by red color in paintings or a set context; Amitabha in a bodhisattva's crown is always this form.

look_alikes.name: amitayus
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Amitayus also meditates but is crowned and jeweled and holds a vase of nectar in his lap.

look_alikes.name: medicine-buddha
look_alikes.how_to_tell: The Medicine Buddha's left hand in the lap holds a bowl, and the right hangs over the knee with a fruit.

look_alikes.name: buddha-muchalinda
look_alikes.how_to_tell: If a many-headed serpent hood rises behind the meditating Buddha, it is the Muchalinda scene.

look_alikes.name: jain-tirthankara (jain topic)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Seated Jain tirthankaras also meditate with hands in the lap, but are nude or plainly unclothed with no robe line, have a srivatsa mark on the chest and an emblem on the pedestal; no cranial bump.

rows.regions_styles: Sri Lanka (Anuradhapura dolomite images; Kandyan bronzes and ivories); Gandhara; Gupta; Chola-period Nagapattinam bronzes.
rows.dating_clues: The gesture appears in the earliest Buddha images and is still made; regional style, not the gesture, suggests a school.
rows.cautions: An identification says who the figure is meant to be, never how old the item is or whether it is old at all: the same forms are still made today for worship and to be sold (Nepalese and Tibetan workshops never stopped; Coomaraswamy 1927 notes good Nepalese metal work 'even up to quite recent times'). Sri Lankan ivory figures fall under ivory trade rules.

facts.text: Getty: in the meditation gesture both hands lie on the lap, the right on top of the left, palms upward, and with the legs locked the figure forms a triangle; footnote: also the gesture of Amitabha.
facts.quote: In this pose both hands lie on the lap, the right on top of the left, with the palms turned upwards, and the figure, with the legs closely locked, formed a perfect triangle

facts.text: The Sadhanamala verse on the five Jinas gives meditation (dhyana) as the gesture of Amitabha.
facts.quote: Bodhyagrī-Varado-Dhyānam mudrā Abhaya-Bhūsparśau

facts.text: Coomaraswamy illustrates an Anuradhapura (Sri Lanka) dolomite Buddha seated in jhana with hands in dhyana mudra; the AIC catalogues an 18th-century Kandyan bronze in the same gesture.
facts.quote: Buddha seated in jhana, the hands in dhyana mudra. Anuradhapura, Ceylon. Dolomite

rows.name: Teaching Buddha (turning the wheel of the law)
rows.features_other: Both hands held before the chest, thumb and forefinger of each forming circles that touch (dharmacakra). The first sermon may instead be shown by a wheel flanked by two deer on the pedestal. In mainland Southeast Asia (Dvaravati) the teaching gesture (vitarka) is often made with one or both raised hands.
rows.identify_by: A plain-robed Buddha with both hands raised before the chest, fingers forming linked circles; a wheel between two deer on the base marks the first sermon in the Deer Park at Sarnath.

look_alikes.name: vairocana
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Vairocana makes the same gesture; in Nepal and Tibet he is usually crowned and jeweled, and white in paintings.

look_alikes.name: maitreya
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Maitreya as a Buddha also teaches, but is often seated with both legs pendant (European fashion) or carries his water pot and stupa motif.

look_alikes.name: prajnaparamita
look_alikes.how_to_tell: A jeweled goddess with the teaching gesture and a book on a lotus is Prajnaparamita.

rows.regions_styles: Gupta Sarnath (5th c.); Pala Bihar; Dvaravati Thailand and early Burma (vitarka); Tibet and Nepal.
rows.dating_clues: Getty: early images marked the sermon by a wheel on the statue; later the hand gesture alone was used. This is a tendency, not a dating rule.
rows.cautions: An identification says who the figure is meant to be, never how old the item is or whether it is old at all: the same forms are still made today for worship and to be sold (Nepalese and Tibetan workshops never stopped; Coomaraswamy 1927 notes good Nepalese metal work 'even up to quite recent times').

facts.text: Getty: to indicate the sermon in the Deer Park at Benares a wheel appeared on the statue; in later images the hand gesture called dharmacakra mudra was used; a wheel flanked by gazelles also stood for the sermon.
facts.quote: When the sculptor wished to indicate the sermon in the deer park at Benares, a wheel was apparent somewhere on the statue, but in later images the fact was indicated by a pose of the hands

facts.text: The Sadhanamala verse gives the teaching gesture (bodhyagri, i.e. dharmacakra) to Vairocana.
facts.quote: Bodhyagrī-Varado-Dhyānam mudrā Abhaya-Bhūsparśau

facts.text: Cleveland: a Mon-Dvaravati (Thailand, 600s) bronze Buddha in the teaching gesture wears a plain robe that shows awareness of Sarnath images.
facts.quote: this Buddha wears a plain robe that indicates the artist's awareness of images made at the workshops of Sarnath

rows.name: Buddha with the fear-not gesture
rows.features_other: Right hand raised to the shoulder, palm outward, fingers up; the left often holds the gathered end of the robe (standing) or lies on the lap (seated). Kushan Mathura seated images sit before a halo with lions on the throne.
rows.identify_by: A Buddha whose right hand is raised, palm out, fingers upward: the gesture of the earliest Indian Buddha images and of many standing Buddhas.

look_alikes.name: amoghasiddhi
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Amoghasiddhi makes the same gesture; he is green in paintings, seated, and in Tibet and Nepal often crowned.

look_alikes.name: buddha-boon-giving
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Boon-giving has the hand lowered with the palm out, not raised.

look_alikes.name: green-tara
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Tara is female, jeweled and holds a lotus; some Nepalese Taras raise the hand in the same gesture.

rows.regions_styles: Kushan Mathura (red mottled sandstone, 2nd c.); Gandhara (schist); Gupta Mathura and Sarnath standing Buddhas; Kashmir brass; Sri Lanka standing images; Burma and Thailand.
rows.dating_clues: Getty: in the early Indian images the right hand is generally raised palm outward. The gesture continues in all later schools.
rows.cautions: An identification says who the figure is meant to be, never how old the item is or whether it is old at all: the same forms are still made today for worship and to be sold (Nepalese and Tibetan workshops never stopped; Coomaraswamy 1927 notes good Nepalese metal work 'even up to quite recent times').

facts.text: Getty: in early Indian images of the Buddha the right hand is generally raised, fingers upward, palm outward, the left on the lap palm up; footnote names this abhaya mudra, used in the episode of the mad elephant.
facts.quote: In the early Indian images of the Buddha, the right hand is generally raised, the fingers extending upward, the palm turned outward

facts.text: The Sadhanamala verse gives the fear-not (abhaya) gesture to Amoghasiddhi.
facts.quote: Bodhyagrī-Varado-Dhyānam mudrā Abhaya-Bhūsparśau

facts.text: Cleveland: a Kashmir brass standing Buddha (c. 900) signals 'no fear' with the right hand and bears a Tibetan inscription naming its owner, a royal monk; wear from ritual bathing is noted.
facts.quote: With his right hand he signals that we should have no fear.

rows.name: Buddha with the boon-giving gesture
rows.features_other: Right arm lowered, palm turned outward, fingers pointing down. A standing Buddha with this gesture on a stepped or ladder base may show the descent from heaven.
rows.identify_by: A Buddha whose lowered right hand shows the open palm to the viewer, fingers down.

look_alikes.name: ratnasambhava
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Ratnasambhava makes the same gesture; yellow in paintings, often crowned in Nepal and Tibet; the jewel is his emblem.

look_alikes.name: buddha-descent
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Cleveland notes that a standing Buddha gesturing down with the palm out usually signals the descent from the Heaven of the Thirty-three; look for a ladder or attendant gods.

look_alikes.name: buddha-earth-touching
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Earth-touching has the palm turned inward toward the knee, fingertips touching the ground, and the Buddha is seated.

look_alikes.name: avalokiteshvara-padmapani
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Padmapani and Tara often give boons too, but are jeweled and hold a lotus.

rows.regions_styles: South Indian Buddhist bronzes from Nagapattinam (Chola period, c. 11th c.); Gupta and post-Gupta; Burma; Nepal.
rows.dating_clues: Not datable by gesture.
rows.cautions: An identification says who the figure is meant to be, never how old the item is or whether it is old at all: the same forms are still made today for worship and to be sold (Nepalese and Tibetan workshops never stopped; Coomaraswamy 1927 notes good Nepalese metal work 'even up to quite recent times').

facts.text: The Sadhanamala verse gives boon-giving (varada) to Ratnasambhava.
facts.quote: Bodhyagrī-Varado-Dhyānam mudrā Abhaya-Bhūsparśau

facts.text: The Art Institute of Chicago catalogues an 11th-century Chola-period Nagapattinam standing Buddha 'with Left Hand in Gift Giving Gesture (varadamudra)'.
facts.quote: Standing Buddha with Left Hand in Gift Giving Gesture (varadamudra)

rows.name: Standing Buddha
rows.features_other: The left hand usually gathers the hem of the robe. Robe treatment is the main regional sign: heavy toga-like folds (Gandhara); clinging robe with string-like folds (Kushan and Gupta Mathura); smooth robe that clings with no folds shown (Gupta Sarnath, 5th c.); frilled double hem (Nagapattinam and Pagan); flaring 'fish-tail' hem and inlaid glass borders (Mandalay).
rows.identify_by: A Buddha standing, robed as a monk, usually with the right hand raised or lowered and the left gathering the robe; identify the scene by gesture and base, the school by the robe.

look_alikes.name: buddha-descent
look_alikes.how_to_tell: A standing Buddha with lowered right palm on a ladder or flanked by Indra and Brahma is the descent from heaven.

look_alikes.name: gandhara-bodhisattva
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Gandharan bodhisattvas stand too but are bare-chested princes with jewelry, turban or long hair and sandals, not monk's robes.

look_alikes.name: jain-tirthankara (jain topic)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Standing Jain tirthankaras stand stiff with arms hanging straight at the sides (kayotsarga), nude or plainly clothed, never gesturing.

rows.regions_styles: Gandhara (schist, 2nd-3rd c.); Kushan and Gupta Mathura (red sandstone); Gupta Sarnath (buff sandstone, 5th c.); Kashmir brass; Pagan Burma (bronze, silver-inlaid eyes); Sri Lanka; Mandalay (lacquered and gilt wood with glass inlay, 19th c.).
rows.dating_clues: Cleveland dates the clinging, fold-less robe to Sarnath workshops of the 400s and says the form spread to Southeast Asia; AIC links Pagan frilled double hems to Nagapattinam bronzes. These are school markers; copies of every school exist.
rows.cautions: An identification says who the figure is meant to be, never how old the item is or whether it is old at all: the same forms are still made today for worship and to be sold (Nepalese and Tibetan workshops never stopped; Coomaraswamy 1927 notes good Nepalese metal work 'even up to quite recent times'). Gandhara standing Buddhas are among the most faked items (see styles: gandhara-modern-fakes).

facts.text: Cleveland: a plain robe clinging to the body without interrupting its contours was a new development in Sarnath workshops in the 400s CE; the form spread by portable images to Southeast Asia.
facts.quote: Depicting the Buddha in a plain robe that clings to the body, without interrupting the beauty of its contours, was a new development in the sculptural workshops of Sarnath during the 400s CE.

facts.text: Getty: Gandhara Buddhas have Grecian features, long wavy hair in a knot, and the right arm and shoulder are never bare, the robe draped in Grecian fashion.
facts.quote: The right arm and shoulder are never bare, but are covered by the monastic garment draped in the Grecian fashion over the left shoulder.

facts.text: AIC: a Pagan-period (Burma, c. 12th c.) standing bronze Buddha with silver-inlaid eyes shows a frilled double hem like Nagapattinam processional bronzes.
facts.quote: the frilled double-hem of the Buddha's gossamer sanghati (monastic robe), which is a common feature of Buddhist processional bronzes from the coastal entrepôt of Nagapattinam

rows.name: Crowned and jeweled Buddha
rows.features_other: A Buddha in monk's robe who also wears a crown, earrings, necklaces and armlets. Burmese crowned Buddhas range from Pagan-period wood to 19th-century gilded and lacquered wood with colored glass, some on an elephant throne (AIC). Gestures vary; the AIC also catalogues Khmer crowned Buddhas teaching.
rows.identify_by: A Buddha with the robe and gestures of a Buddha but wearing a crown and jewels; bodhisattvas are jeweled too but wear princely skirts and scarves, not a monk's robe.

look_alikes.name: avalokiteshvara-padmapani
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Bodhisattvas wear a dhoti and scarves with a bare chest and hold attributes (lotus, sword, flask); a crowned Buddha wears the monk's robe and holds nothing, or makes Buddha gestures.

look_alikes.name: amitayus
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Amitayus is crowned and meditates holding a vase of nectar.

look_alikes.name: vairocana
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Crowned Buddha teaching on a lion throne in Kashmir, Nepal or Tibet may be Vairocana or another cosmic Buddha.

rows.regions_styles: Kashmir (8th c. brass, 'cosmic Buddha'); Pala Bihar; Pagan and later Burma (Jambupati type; Arakan; Mandalay 19th c. lacquered wood with glass); Ayutthaya and Bangkok Thailand; Khmer crowned Buddhas on the naga.
rows.dating_clues: Getty: in Siam and Burma the cranial bump is often covered by an ornate tapering head-dress like a stupa. Crowned Buddhas exist across many centuries; the form alone does not date an item.
rows.cautions: An identification says who the figure is meant to be, never how old the item is or whether it is old at all: the same forms are still made today for worship and to be sold (Nepalese and Tibetan workshops never stopped; Coomaraswamy 1927 notes good Nepalese metal work 'even up to quite recent times'). The legend behind the Burmese name Jambupati is not in the sources read here.

facts.text: Cleveland: an 8th-century Kashmir brass seated on a lion throne may be one of the earliest cosmic Buddhas, because he wears a crown and jewels, unlike earthly Buddhas unadorned like monks.
facts.quote: he wears a crown and jewels, unlike the earthly Buddhas who are unadorned like monks

facts.text: Getty: Buddhas in Siam and Burma often have the cranial bump covered by an ornate tapering head-dress somewhat resembling a stupa.
facts.quote: The Buddhas, however, in Siam, as well as in Burma, often have the ushnisha covered by an ornate head-dress which is tapering in shape and somewhat resembles a stupa

facts.text: The AIC holds Burmese crowned Buddhas from the Pagan period (late 12th-early 13th c., wood) to the late 19th century (gilded and lacquered wood with colored glass, on an elephant throne) and a c. 17th-century bronze titled 'Jeweled and Crowned Buddha (Jambupati)'.
facts.quote: Jeweled and Crowned Buddha (Jambupati)

facts.text: Shway Yoe: the great brass seated image of the Maha Myat Muni (Arakan) pagoda in Mandalay was brought over the hills from Arakan in 1784, cast in three sections.
facts.quote: The huge brass image, twelve feet in height, was brought over the hills from Akyab in the year 1784

rows.name: Reclining Buddha (the Buddha's passing, parinirvana)
rows.features_other: Lies on the right side, head resting on the right hand or a pillow, legs together; mourning monks, Vajrapani or twin sal trees may be shown.
rows.identify_by: A robed Buddha lying on his right side with his head on his right hand or a pillow: the death and final release of the Buddha at Kushinagara.

look_alikes.name: vishnu-anantashayana (vishnu_krishna topic)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Vishnu reclines too, but on a coiled serpent with hoods over him, with four arms and a crown, and Lakshmi often at his feet.

rows.regions_styles: Gandhara relief panels; Pala manuscript paintings and steles (as the top scene); Burma, Thailand and Sri Lanka (large reclining images); Tibetan paintings.
rows.dating_clues: Not datable from the pose.
rows.cautions: An identification says who the figure is meant to be, never how old the item is or whether it is old at all: the same forms are still made today for worship and to be sold (Nepalese and Tibetan workshops never stopped; Coomaraswamy 1927 notes good Nepalese metal work 'even up to quite recent times'). Sources read here do not say whether open or closed eyes separate a 'resting' from a 'passing' Buddha in Burmese and Thai images.

facts.text: Getty: the Buddha entering Nirvana is shown lying on the right side with the right hand under the head, often with the disciples Sariputra and Maudgalyayana.
facts.quote: He is represented lying on the right side with his right hand under his head.

facts.text: The Sinhalese image canon Sariputra treats images of the Buddha in the three postures of sitting, standing and reclining.
facts.quote: we shall now describe the dimensions of images of Buddha in the three postures of sitting, standing and reclining

facts.text: The Smithsonian holds a Pala-Sena palm-leaf painting of the Parinirvana from a Prajnaparamita manuscript (Bengal or Bihar, early 12th c.).
facts.quote: Parinirvana of Buddha, from a Prajnaparamita manuscript

rows.name: Buddha descending from the Heaven of the Thirty-three
rows.features_other: A standing Buddha on or beside a ladder or triple stair, right hand lowered palm outward; the ladder alone, with footprints, can stand for the scene in early art.
rows.identify_by: A standing Buddha with a ladder or stair: his return to earth at Sankasya after teaching his mother in heaven.

look_alikes.name: buddha-boon-giving
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Without a ladder or stair, a standing Buddha with lowered palm cannot be shown to be the descent; read it as boon-giving.

look_alikes.name: buddha-life-scenes-stele
look_alikes.how_to_tell: The descent is one of the standard eight scenes; on a stele it appears among others around a central Buddha.

rows.regions_styles: Gandhara reliefs; Pala eight-scene steles; Burma (Pyu and Pagan plaques); Thailand.
rows.dating_clues: None from the scene.
rows.cautions: An identification says who the figure is meant to be, never how old the item is or whether it is old at all: the same forms are still made today for worship and to be sold (Nepalese and Tibetan workshops never stopped; Coomaraswamy 1927 notes good Nepalese metal work 'even up to quite recent times').

facts.text: Getty: a ladder with footprints on the top and bottom rungs denoted the Buddha's descent from heaven in early aniconic art.
facts.quote: A ladder with footprints on the top and bottom rungs denoted his descent from the Tushita heaven

facts.text: Foucher counts the 'triple ladder' as the characteristic decoration that makes this scene instantly recognizable, unlike the Great Miracle of Sravasti.
facts.quote: it has neither the exceptional role of the monkey or the elephant, nor the characteristic decoration of the triple ladder

facts.text: Cleveland: when a standing Buddha gestures down with his right hand, palm facing out, he usually signals his descent from the Heaven of the Thirty-three Gods, where he taught his mother.
facts.quote: When the standing Buddha gestures down with his right hand, with the palm facing out, he usually signals his miraculous descent from the Heaven of the Thirty-three Gods

rows.name: Buddha sheltered by the serpent king Muchalinda
rows.features_other: The Buddha sits on the coils of a serpent whose five or seven hoods spread over his head; sometimes only the hood is shown behind him.
rows.identify_by: A meditating Buddha seated on serpent coils with a fan of snake hoods above his head.

look_alikes.name: parshvanatha (jain topic)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: The Jain Parshvanatha also has a snake hood, but is nude (or plainly clothed), stands stiff or sits without a robe, and has no cranial bump; Muchalinda Buddha wears a monk's robe.

look_alikes.name: balarama / naga deities (other_hindu topic)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Hindu serpent deities and Balarama with a hood hold weapons or a plough; the Buddha holds nothing.

rows.regions_styles: Khmer (Cambodia; Cleveland and AIC examples of the 11th-13th c., often crowned); Thailand; Getty also records it in Tibet as the 'Liberator of the Nagas'.
rows.dating_clues: Not datable from the form.
rows.cautions: An identification says who the figure is meant to be, never how old the item is or whether it is old at all: the same forms are still made today for worship and to be sold (Nepalese and Tibetan workshops never stopped; Coomaraswamy 1927 notes good Nepalese metal work 'even up to quite recent times'). Khmer naga Buddhas are often sold as 'Indian'; Cambodian sources and US repatriations to Cambodia are outside this file.

facts.text: Getty: Gautama may be shown seated on the coils of a serpent with its hood of five or seven heads spread over him, or on a lotus throne with only the hood protecting his head; the Naga king Mucalinda sheltered him for seven days.
facts.quote: seated on the coils of a serpent with its hood of five or seven heads spread over him, or seated on a lotus throne with only the serpent's hood protecting his head

rows.name: Fasting or ascetic Buddha
rows.features_other: Ribs, veins and sunken belly shown; may have moustache and beard (Gandhara and East Asian).
rows.identify_by: A seated Buddha with a starved, skeletal body before his enlightenment, when he tried extreme fasting.

look_alikes.name: chamunda / bhringi (shiva_devi topic)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Hindu emaciated figures (Chamunda, Bhringi) wear skull garlands or dance and hold weapons; the fasting Buddha sits in meditation.

rows.regions_styles: Gandhara schist; Kashmir ivory (8th c.); Chinese and Japanese images.
rows.dating_clues: None.
rows.cautions: An identification says who the figure is meant to be, never how old the item is or whether it is old at all: the same forms are still made today for worship and to be sold (Nepalese and Tibetan workshops never stopped; Coomaraswamy 1927 notes good Nepalese metal work 'even up to quite recent times'). Gandhara fasting Buddhas are a prized subject and Gandhara is heavily faked (see styles: gandhara-modern-fakes). Kashmir ivories fall under ivory rules.

facts.text: Getty: the Buddha as an ascetic is shown very emaciated and often with moustache and beard; Gandhara images may have a beard when the Buddha is in ascetic form.
facts.quote: He is represented very emaciated and often with moustache and beard

facts.text: Cleveland: an 8th-century Kashmir ivory shows in three scenes the Buddha's fasting until his limbs withered, then accepting Sujata's food offering.
facts.quote: A brilliantly carved ivory depicts, in three successive scenes, the Buddha's early experimentation with fasting until his limbs withered.

rows.name: Stele or plaque with scenes from the Buddha's life (eight great events)
rows.features_other: A central earth-touching Buddha surrounded by small scenes: birth, first sermon, death (at the top), and the four 'secondary' miracles (taming the elephant, the monkey's gift of honey, the Great Miracle of Sravasti, the descent by the triple ladder). Small soft-stone versions served pilgrims.
rows.identify_by: One main Buddha framed by several small scenes, often with a reclining Buddha at the top.

look_alikes.name: buddha-earth-touching
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Without the surrounding scenes it is a single enlightenment image.

rows.regions_styles: Pala Bihar (Bodh Gaya) black stone and kaolin plaques, 10th-12th c.; Burma (Pagan, small kaolin plaques, sets of eight); carried to Nepal and Tibet.
rows.dating_clues: Cleveland records a 12th-century Newari prayer on one Indian plaque, showing it went to Nepal; an inscription can date an addition, not necessarily the carving.
rows.cautions: An identification says who the figure is meant to be, never how old the item is or whether it is old at all: the same forms are still made today for worship and to be sold (Nepalese and Tibetan workshops never stopped; Coomaraswamy 1927 notes good Nepalese metal work 'even up to quite recent times').

facts.text: Foucher: eight towns of Madhyadesa divided the legend of the Buddha, each with a holy place preserving the vestiges of one of the eight principal miracles; four (birth, illumination, first preaching, death) were recognized first.
facts.quote: In their immediate neighbourhood were eight specially holy places, supposed to preserve the vestiges of the eight principal miracles of the Master.

facts.text: Cleveland: a Pala kaolin plaque shows the Buddha at enlightenment surrounded by scenes of his life, including his death at the top; a prayer in 12th-century Newari script shows it was taken to Nepal.
facts.quote: A prayer written in a 12th-century Newari script indicates that this Indian sculpture was taken to Nepal.

rows.name: Footprints, empty throne, wheel and tree (the Buddha shown by symbols)
rows.features_other: Paired footprints (often with wheels on the soles), a vacant seat, a wheel flanked by deer, a tree with an altar, a riderless horse or a ladder stand for the Buddha.
rows.identify_by: No figure at all: a pair of footprints, a wheel, an empty seat or a tree receives the worship.

look_alikes.name: vishnupada (vishnu_krishna topic)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Hindu Vishnu footprints carry Vaishnava marks (conch, discus); Buddhist ones carry wheels and auspicious symbols. Read the marks, and any inscription.

rows.regions_styles: Early Indian stupas (Bharhut, Sanchi, Amaravati); Sri Lanka, Burma and Thailand footprint slabs.
rows.dating_clues: Getty and Foucher describe the symbols as the early Indian way of showing the Buddha; footprint slabs continued to be made long after images appeared, so symbols alone do not date an item.
rows.cautions: An identification says who the figure is meant to be, never how old the item is or whether it is old at all: the same forms are still made today for worship and to be sold (Nepalese and Tibetan workshops never stopped; Coomaraswamy 1927 notes good Nepalese metal work 'even up to quite recent times').

facts.text: Getty, following Foucher: up to the first century the Indian sculptors made no image of the Buddha; his birth was shown by footprints, his departure by a riderless horse, his first meditation by a vacant seat. (Getty is quoting Foucher, so this is one line of evidence.)
facts.quote: they succeeded in 'representing the life of Buddha without Buddha'

rows.name: Amitabha (Buddha of Infinite Light)
rows.features_other: In paintings red. In Nepal and Tibet often crowned and jeweled; in sets of five on crowns, steles, stupas and manuscript covers. Appears as the tiny seated Buddha in the crown of Avalokiteshvara.
rows.identify_by: One of the five cosmic (Jina, 'Dhyani') Buddhas, who look alike and differ by gesture and color: Amitabha makes the meditation gesture and is red.

look_alikes.name: buddha-meditation
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Same gesture; only color, set context or the Sukhavati paradise setting separates them.

look_alikes.name: amitayus
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Amitayus is crowned and holds a vase of nectar; Getty says Tibetans never confuse the two, though Chinese and Japanese images do.

rows.regions_styles: Pala Bihar and Bengal (from the 9th c.); Nepal (stupa niches, crowns, gilt copper); Tibet; Western Himalayas (Tabo, Ladakh).
rows.dating_clues: Not datable from the form.
rows.cautions: An identification says who the figure is meant to be, never how old the item is or whether it is old at all: the same forms are still made today for worship and to be sold (Nepalese and Tibetan workshops never stopped; Coomaraswamy 1927 notes good Nepalese metal work 'even up to quite recent times'). A single cosmic Buddha in sculpture often cannot be told from the historical Buddha making the same gesture (Bhattacharyya 1924).

facts.text: The Sadhanamala verse names the five Jinas with their colors (white, yellow, red, green, blue) and gestures (teaching, boon-giving, meditation, fear-not, earth-touching) for Vairocana, Ratnasambhava, Amitabha, Amoghasiddhi and Akshobhya respectively.
facts.quote: Varṇāḥ amīṣāṃ sitaḥ pīto rakto haritamecakau

facts.text: Amitabha's small seated image in the crown is the distinctive mark of Avalokiteshvara/Padmapani.
facts.quote: small image of his Dhyani-Buddha, Amitabha, in his crown

rows.name: Akshobhya (the Imperturbable)
rows.features_other: In paintings blue. In Nepal and Tibet often crowned and jeweled; in sets of five on crowns, steles, stupas and manuscript covers. A vajra may stand upright on the pedestal before him.
rows.identify_by: One of the five cosmic (Jina, 'Dhyani') Buddhas, who look alike and differ by gesture and color: Akshobhya makes the earth-touching gesture and is blue.

look_alikes.name: buddha-earth-touching
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Same gesture; Akshobhya is marked by a vajra placed upright in front of him or on the pedestal, blue color in paintings, or a vahana of two elephants.

rows.regions_styles: Pala Bihar and Bengal (from the 9th c.); Nepal (stupa niches, crowns, gilt copper); Tibet; Western Himalayas (Tabo, Ladakh).
rows.dating_clues: Not datable from the form.
rows.cautions: An identification says who the figure is meant to be, never how old the item is or whether it is old at all: the same forms are still made today for worship and to be sold (Nepalese and Tibetan workshops never stopped; Coomaraswamy 1927 notes good Nepalese metal work 'even up to quite recent times'). A single cosmic Buddha in sculpture often cannot be told from the historical Buddha making the same gesture (Bhattacharyya 1924).

facts.quote: Varṇāḥ amīṣāṃ sitaḥ pīto rakto haritamecakau

facts.text: Cleveland: on a Kurkihar (Bihar) Pala bronze of the late 800s, the double-headed vajra placed on top of the pedestal in front of the figure marks a tantric image, and the gestures identify him as one of the five cosmic Buddhas.
facts.quote: The double-headed thunderbolt, or vajra, placed on top of the pedestal in front of the figure indicates that this is a tantric image.

rows.name: Vairocana (the Illuminator)
rows.features_other: In paintings white. In Nepal and Tibet often crowned and jeweled; in sets of five on crowns, steles, stupas and manuscript covers.
rows.identify_by: One of the five cosmic (Jina, 'Dhyani') Buddhas, who look alike and differ by gesture and color: Vairocana makes the teaching gesture and is white.

look_alikes.name: buddha-teaching
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Same gesture; Vairocana is often crowned in Nepalese and Tibetan images and white in paintings; a lone figure may not be separable.

look_alikes.name: buddha-crowned
look_alikes.how_to_tell: A crowned teaching Buddha on a lion throne in Tibetan or Himalayan art is often read as Vairocana.

rows.regions_styles: Pala Bihar and Bengal (from the 9th c.); Nepal (stupa niches, crowns, gilt copper); Tibet; Western Himalayas (Tabo, Ladakh).
rows.dating_clues: Not datable from the form.
rows.cautions: An identification says who the figure is meant to be, never how old the item is or whether it is old at all: the same forms are still made today for worship and to be sold (Nepalese and Tibetan workshops never stopped; Coomaraswamy 1927 notes good Nepalese metal work 'even up to quite recent times'). A single cosmic Buddha in sculpture often cannot be told from the historical Buddha making the same gesture (Bhattacharyya 1924).

facts.text: Cleveland catalogues a Central Tibetan image (c. 1150-1200) titled 'Tantric Buddha Vairochana as Vajrasattva', showing the overlap between crowned cosmic Buddhas.
facts.quote: Tantric Buddha Vairochana as Vajrasattva

rows.name: Ratnasambhava (Jewel-born)
rows.features_other: In paintings yellow. In Nepal and Tibet often crowned and jeweled; in sets of five on crowns, steles, stupas and manuscript covers.
rows.identify_by: One of the five cosmic (Jina, 'Dhyani') Buddhas, who look alike and differ by gesture and color: Ratnasambhava makes the boon-giving gesture and is yellow.

look_alikes.name: buddha-boon-giving
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Same gesture; color (yellow), a crown in Himalayan images or a set context identify Ratnasambhava.

rows.regions_styles: Pala Bihar and Bengal (from the 9th c.); Nepal (stupa niches, crowns, gilt copper); Tibet; Western Himalayas (Tabo, Ladakh).
rows.dating_clues: Not datable from the form.
rows.cautions: An identification says who the figure is meant to be, never how old the item is or whether it is old at all: the same forms are still made today for worship and to be sold (Nepalese and Tibetan workshops never stopped; Coomaraswamy 1927 notes good Nepalese metal work 'even up to quite recent times'). rows.name: Amoghasiddhi (Infallible Success)
rows.features_other: In paintings green. In Nepal and Tibet often crowned and jeweled; in sets of five on crowns, steles, stupas and manuscript covers.
rows.identify_by: One of the five cosmic (Jina, 'Dhyani') Buddhas, who look alike and differ by gesture and color: Amoghasiddhi makes the fear-not gesture and is green.

look_alikes.name: buddha-fear-not
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Same gesture; green color, the double vajra (visvavajra, his symbol per Getty) or a set context identify Amoghasiddhi.

look_alikes.name: green-tara
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Green Tara, his emanation, may wear his small image in her crown.

rows.regions_styles: Pala Bihar and Bengal (from the 9th c.); Nepal (stupa niches, crowns, gilt copper); Tibet; Western Himalayas (Tabo, Ladakh).
rows.dating_clues: Not datable from the form.
