facts.text: Bhattacharyya: Amoghasiddhi is distinguished from the other Jinas by the green color of his body and the abhaya gesture of his right hand; seven Sadhanamala deities bear his image on the crown, all female.
facts.quote: Amoghasiddhi is distinguished from the other Dhyani Buddhas by the green colour of his body, and the Abhaya Mudra he displays in his right hand

rows.name: Vajrasattva (Diamond Being)
rows.features_other: Crowned and jeweled; holds the vajra upright against the chest in the right hand and the bell on the left hip; may embrace his consort (yab-yum).
rows.identify_by: A crowned, jeweled seated figure holding a vajra at the heart and a bell at the hip.

look_alikes.name: vajradhara
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Vajradhara holds the same vajra and bell, but with the wrists crossed over the chest.

look_alikes.name: vajrapani
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Vajrapani holds a vajra but no bell, and in Tibet is usually wrathful and striding.

rows.regions_styles: Nepal (very common in Newar Buddhism, gilt copper), Tibet; Pala manuscript covers.
rows.dating_clues: Not datable from form.
rows.cautions: An identification says who the figure is meant to be, never how old the item is or whether it is old at all: the same forms are still made today for worship and to be sold (Nepalese and Tibetan workshops never stopped; Coomaraswamy 1927 notes good Nepalese metal work 'even up to quite recent times').

facts.text: Bhattacharyya: Vajrasattva, the sixth Dhyani Buddha, is generally represented with the priestly symbols vajra and bell (ghanta).
facts.quote: is usually represented with the priestly symbols, the Vajra and the Ghanta

facts.text: Getty: he is always seated, crowned and dressed as a bodhisattva, holding the vajra against the breast with the right hand and the bell on the hip with the left; unlike the other Dhyani Buddhas he is always crowned.
facts.quote: He generally holds the vajra against his breast with the right hand ... With the left, he holds the ghanta on his hip

rows.name: Vajradhara (Holder of the Vajra)
rows.features_other: Arms crossed on the breast holding vajra and bell (vajra-humkara gesture); crowned and jeweled; may embrace a consort with crossed arms behind her back. (token wanted: crossed-arms vajra-humkara gesture)
rows.identify_by: A crowned seated figure whose wrists cross over the chest, holding a vajra in one hand and a bell in the other.

look_alikes.name: vajrasattva
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Vajrasattva holds the vajra at the heart and the bell at the hip, arms not crossed.

rows.regions_styles: Tibet, Nepal.
rows.dating_clues: Not datable.
rows.cautions: An identification says who the figure is meant to be, never how old the item is or whether it is old at all: the same forms are still made today for worship and to be sold (Nepalese and Tibetan workshops never stopped; Coomaraswamy 1927 notes good Nepalese metal work 'even up to quite recent times').

facts.text: Getty: Vajradhara is always seated with legs locked, wears the bodhisattva crown, and has his arms crossed on the breast in the vajra-humkara gesture holding vajra and ghanta.
facts.quote: His arms are crossed on his breast in the vajra-hum-kara mudra holding the vajra and ghanta.

rows.name: Amitayus (Buddha of Infinite Life)
rows.features_other: Crowned and jeweled like a bodhisattva; both hands in meditation in the lap holding a vase (kalasha) of the nectar of long life.
rows.identify_by: A crowned, jeweled seated Buddha holding a long-necked vase in his lap with both hands.

look_alikes.name: amitabha
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Amitabha is a plain-robed monk with empty hands in the lap.

look_alikes.name: medicine-buddha
look_alikes.how_to_tell: The Medicine Buddha is plain-robed and holds a bowl, with a fruit in the right hand on the knee.

look_alikes.name: maitreya
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Maitreya's water pot is held at the side or on a lotus at the shoulder, not in the lap with both hands.

rows.regions_styles: Tibet, Mongolia and China (AIC: Mongolian and Chinese 18th-c. gilt bronzes); Nepal (Cleveland thangka).
rows.dating_clues: Not datable from the form.
rows.cautions: An identification says who the figure is meant to be, never how old the item is or whether it is old at all: the same forms are still made today for worship and to be sold (Nepalese and Tibetan workshops never stopped; Coomaraswamy 1927 notes good Nepalese metal work 'even up to quite recent times'). Chinese and Mongolian Amitayus figures are often sold as Tibetan or Nepalese.

facts.text: Getty: Amitayus, Amitabha as bestower of long life, has the meditation gesture and the ambrosia vase as symbol; the image holds the vase in its lap; Tibetans never confuse the two forms.
facts.quote: Amitayus (Dispenser of Long Life) is the name given to Amitabha in his character of bestower of longevity, and the Tibetans, unlike the Chinese and Japanese, never confuse the two forms.

facts.text: The AIC catalogues an 18th-century Mongolian gilt bronze as 'Buddha Amitayus Holding a Vase of Longevity (Kalasa)'.
facts.quote: Buddha Amitāyus Holding a Vase of Longevity (Kalasa)

rows.name: Medicine Buddha
rows.features_other: Plain-robed Buddha, blue in paintings; left hand in the lap holds a bowl; right hand on the knee palm outward holds a myrobalan fruit or sprig (lemon-like, five-sided).
rows.identify_by: A robed Buddha holding a bowl in the lap and a small fruit or plant sprig in the right hand extended over the knee.

look_alikes.name: buddha-earth-touching
look_alikes.how_to_tell: The earth-touching Buddha's right hand turns palm-in and touches the ground; the Medicine Buddha's palm faces out and holds a fruit.

look_alikes.name: amitayus
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Amitayus is crowned and holds a vase.

rows.regions_styles: Tibet (sets of eight Medicine Buddhas; Smithsonian thangka), China, Japan.
rows.dating_clues: Not datable.
rows.cautions: An identification says who the figure is meant to be, never how old the item is or whether it is old at all: the same forms are still made today for worship and to be sold (Nepalese and Tibetan workshops never stopped; Coomaraswamy 1927 notes good Nepalese metal work 'even up to quite recent times').

facts.text: Getty: the Medicine Buddha is blue, seated with legs crossed in monastic robe; his left hand in meditation holds a branch or fruit of the myrobalan; an addendum says he may hold a bowl in the left hand with the fruit in the right hand in boon-giving gesture.
facts.quote: Mania may hold in his left hand in dhyana mudra a bowl resembling a begging-bowl, in which case the medicinal fruit is usually held in the right hand in varamudra.

rows.name: Avalokiteshvara Padmapani (Lotus-bearer)
rows.features_other: Slender princely youth with jewels; left hand holds the stem of a lotus that blooms at the shoulder; right hand gives boons or reassures; a small seated Amitabha Buddha in the crown or piled hair.
rows.identify_by: A jeweled bodhisattva holding a lotus stem whose crown or topknot carries a tiny seated meditating Buddha (Amitabha).

look_alikes.name: maitreya
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Maitreya carries a water pot (flask) and has a small stupa, not a seated Buddha, in his headdress; Grünwedel warns of the danger of confusing the two.

look_alikes.name: green-tara
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Tara is female (breasts), and her lotus is a closed blue lotus.

look_alikes.name: lakshmi (other_hindu topic)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Lakshmi holds lotuses too, but is female and often flanked by elephants pouring water.

look_alikes.name: khasarpana-lokeshvara
look_alikes.how_to_tell: If four small attendants (Tara, Sudhanakumara, Bhrikuti, Hayagriva) surround him, he is Khasarpana.

rows.regions_styles: Gandhara (with a Buddha in the turban); Kashmir brasses with silver and copper inlay; Pala black stone steles (Nalanda) and bronzes; Nepal (high-copper gilt bronzes, stone steles); Tibet; Sri Lanka (8th c. bronzes).
rows.dating_clues: Cleveland: 11th-century Nepalese bronzes are solid cast with exceptionally high copper content, giving a warm color. Sources read here give no wider dating rule.
rows.cautions: An identification says who the figure is meant to be, never how old the item is or whether it is old at all: the same forms are still made today for worship and to be sold (Nepalese and Tibetan workshops never stopped; Coomaraswamy 1927 notes good Nepalese metal work 'even up to quite recent times'). Nepalese images are often wrongly called Tibetan (Coomaraswamy 1927).

facts.text: Getty: Padmapani is shown as a slight, graceful youth dressed like an Indian prince, his hair in a mitre-shaped knot behind the five-leaved crown in which is a small image of Amitabha, his distinctive mark.
facts.quote: His hair is drawn up in a mitre-shaped ushnisha behind the five-leaved crown, in which is a small image of Amitabha (his distinctive mark)

facts.text: Cleveland: the tiny seated meditating Buddha Amitabha in the crown identifies the figure as Avalokiteshvara.
facts.quote: In the center of his crown is the tiny seated image of the meditating Buddha Amitabha that identifies this figure as Avalokitesvara specifically.

facts.text: The Sadhanamala Khasarpana dhyana describes the god with Amitabha in the crown, boon-giving right hand and a lotus with stalk in the left.
facts.quote: Amitābhakṛtaśekharam ... dakṣiṇe varadakaraṃ vāmakareṇa sanālakamaladharam

facts.text: Cleveland: 11th-century Nepalese bronzes are solid cast with an exceptionally high copper content, which gives warmth to the surface.
facts.quote: Nepalese bronzes of the 11th century are solid cast and have an exceptionally high copper content in the alloy

rows.name: Khasarpana Lokeshvara (with four attendants)
rows.features_other: Two-armed Avalokiteshvara seated at ease, boon-giving with a lotus, ALWAYS with four small figures: green Tara, the boy Sudhanakumara (book under arm, hands joined), four-armed Bhrikuti, and the wrathful Hayagriva; a pot-bellied hungry ghost (preta) below catches nectar from his hand.
rows.identify_by: Padmapani seated at ease with four small attendants around him and a starving ghost at his feet.

look_alikes.name: avalokiteshvara-padmapani
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Lokanatha may have only two attendants (Tara and Hayagriva); Khasarpana must have all four.

rows.regions_styles: Pala Bihar and Bengal (black stone steles; small kaolin plaques, 11th-12th c.).
rows.dating_clues: Not datable from iconography.
rows.cautions: An identification says who the figure is meant to be, never how old the item is or whether it is old at all: the same forms are still made today for worship and to be sold (Nepalese and Tibetan workshops never stopped; Coomaraswamy 1927 notes good Nepalese metal work 'even up to quite recent times').

facts.text: Bhattacharyya (from the Sadhanamala): Khasarpana is invariably accompanied by Tara, Sudhanakumara, Bhrikuti and Hayagriva; Lokanatha may have only Tara and Hayagriva.
facts.quote: The peculiar feature of this god is that he is invariably accompanied by the four divinities, Tara, Sudhanakumara, Bhrkuti and Hayagriva.

facts.text: Cleveland: a Pala kaolin plaque (reign of Ramapala, late 1000s) shows Khasarpana in royal ease with Amitabha in the crown, a hungry ghost with distended belly, a small figure with a manuscript, green Tara and four-armed Bhrikuti.
facts.quote: A hungry ghost with a distended belly praises him in the lower left corner of this plaque

rows.name: Shadakshari Lokeshvara (Lord of the Six Syllables)
other_names: Lord of Om mani padme hum
rows.features_other: Four arms: the front pair joined at the chest (sometimes clasping a jewel), the back right holds a rosary, the back left a lotus. Mantra: Om mani padme hum.
rows.identify_by: A seated four-armed bodhisattva whose front hands are pressed together at the heart, the other two holding a rosary and a lotus.

look_alikes.name: avalokiteshvara-eleven-headed
look_alikes.how_to_tell: The eleven-headed form has a stack of heads; Shadakshari has one head.

rows.regions_styles: Pala (Sarnath group), Tibet (Getty: the form held to be incarnate in the Dalai Lama), Nepal.
rows.dating_clues: Not datable.
rows.cautions: An identification says who the figure is meant to be, never how old the item is or whether it is old at all: the same forms are still made today for worship and to be sold (Nepalese and Tibetan workshops never stopped; Coomaraswamy 1927 notes good Nepalese metal work 'even up to quite recent times').

facts.text: The Sadhanamala describes Shadakshari Lokeshvara as white, four-armed, carrying the lotus in the left and the rosary in the right, the other two hands joined against the breast.
facts.quote: vāmataḥ padmadharaṃ dakṣiṇato'kṣasūtradharam aparābhyāṃ hastābhyāṃ hṛdi sampuṭāñjalisthitaṃ

facts.text: Cleveland: a Tibetan kaolin plaque of Shadakshari (c. 1200s) has the six-syllable mantra in Sanskrit and Tibetan scripts beside his head, lotus upper left, rosary upper right, front hands pressed together.
facts.quote: Shadakshari-Lokeshvara, a four-armed manifestation of Avalokiteshvara, is known as the “Lord of the Six Syllables.”

rows.name: Simhanada Lokeshvara (Lion's Roar)
rows.features_other: Seated on a lion in royal ease, wearing NO ornaments and a tiger or antelope skin; at his right a trident with a white snake wound round it, at his left a lotus bearing a flaming sword (sometimes a bowl of flowers).
rows.identify_by: An unadorned bodhisattva at royal ease on a lion, flanked by a snake-entwined trident and a lotus carrying a sword.

look_alikes.name: manjushri
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Manjushri on a lion is jeweled and has the book or blue lotus; Simhanada wears no ornaments and has the snake-wound trident (Getty, Bhattacharyya).

look_alikes.name: shiva (shiva_devi topic)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: The trident and snake recall Shiva, but Simhanada rides a lion, has a sword on a lotus and often Amitabha in the hair; Shiva rides Nandi the bull.

rows.regions_styles: Pala Bihar (Magadha), Mahoba, Nepal (Patan viharas keep pairs of Simhanada images), Tibet.
rows.dating_clues: Not datable.
rows.cautions: An identification says who the figure is meant to be, never how old the item is or whether it is old at all: the same forms are still made today for worship and to be sold (Nepalese and Tibetan workshops never stopped; Coomaraswamy 1927 notes good Nepalese metal work 'even up to quite recent times').

facts.text: The Sadhanamala describes Simhanada as white, three-eyed, with chignon crown, without ornaments, clad in tiger skin, seated on a lion in royal ease, with a white trident entwined by a white serpent to the right and a lotus bearing a flaming sword at the left.
facts.quote: dakṣiṇe sitaphaṇiveṣṭitaṃ triśūlaṃ ... vāmahastād utthaṃ padmopari jvalatkhaḍgam

facts.text: Bhattacharyya: that Simhanada wears no ornaments is important because it distinguishes him from some varieties of Manjushri.
facts.quote: The fact that Simhanada wears no ornaments is very important because this distinguishes him from some of the varieties of Manjusri.

rows.name: Eleven-headed (and thousand-armed) Avalokiteshvara
rows.features_other: Heads stacked in tiers (three tiers of three, a tenth head, and Amitabha on top); the main hands joined at the chest (namahkara); Getty, after Eitel, says this form always carries a book and a thunderbolt; a six-armed Himalayan bronze holds prayer beads and wears an antelope skin; the thousand arms of the painted form spread like a halo with an eye in each palm.
rows.identify_by: A bodhisattva with a pyramid of heads (eleven in all, the topmost a Buddha) and many arms, the front hands joined in prayer.

look_alikes.name: shadakshari-lokeshvara
look_alikes.how_to_tell: One head and four arms.

look_alikes.name: brahma / vishvarupa Vishnu (other topics)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Hindu many-headed gods have heads side by side (Brahma: four) or animal heads (Vishvarupa); the eleven-headed form stacks human heads under a Buddha head.

rows.regions_styles: Western Himalayas and Kashmir (c. 1000, gilt bronze with silver and copper inlay); Tibet (thangkas, bronzes); Nepal; Tang and later China (Guanyin) and Japan.
rows.dating_clues: Not datable.
rows.cautions: An identification says who the figure is meant to be, never how old the item is or whether it is old at all: the same forms are still made today for worship and to be sold (Nepalese and Tibetan workshops never stopped; Coomaraswamy 1927 notes good Nepalese metal work 'even up to quite recent times'). Chinese eleven-headed Guanyin figures are often sold as Tibetan.

facts.text: Getty: in his manifestation with eleven heads Avalokiteshvara is the 'all-sided one'; the heads are in three tiers of three with the tenth on top and his own (Amitabha's) image above.
facts.quote: Avalokitesvara, in three tiers of three, with the tenth head on top and his own image above them all.

facts.text: Cleveland: on a thousand-armed thangka each hand has an eye in the palm; on a c. 1000 gilt bronze the eleven heads follow texts naming placid, fierce, howling and laughing faces surmounted by Amitabha.
facts.quote: Each hand has an eye in the palm to see the suffering of all beings

rows.name: Maitreya (the future Buddha)
rows.features_other: Water flask (oval or pointed in Gandhara, round in India) in the left hand or on a lotus at the shoulder; a small stupa (caitya) in the headdress; a scarf tied at the left hip; may hold the nagakesara flower; as a Buddha he often sits with both legs pendant (European fashion) and teaches.
rows.identify_by: A bodhisattva holding a water flask, with a tiny stupa in his hair or crown; or a Buddha seated on a throne with both feet down.

look_alikes.name: avalokiteshvara-padmapani
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Padmapani has a seated Buddha (Amitabha), not a stupa, in the crown and holds a lotus rather than a flask; Grünwedel warns they are easily confused.

look_alikes.name: gandhara-bodhisattva
look_alikes.how_to_tell: A Gandharan bodhisattva with long hair in a loop and a flask is Maitreya; with a turban and no flask he is usually Siddhartha.

look_alikes.name: brahma (other_hindu topic)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Brahma also holds a water pot but has four heads and a goose mount.

look_alikes.name: budai (Chinese 'laughing Buddha')
look_alikes.how_to_tell: The fat laughing Chinese monk with a sack (Budai) is a Chinese figure, not an Indian Maitreya; sources read here do not discuss it.

rows.regions_styles: Gandhara (schist, flask, long hair); Pala Bengal (silver with turquoise inlay); Nepal (gilt copper; wood); Western Tibet; Sri Lanka, Burma and Thailand (the one bodhisattva of Theravada); Pyu Burma; China, Korea, Japan.
rows.dating_clues: Getty: vase oval or pointed in Gandhara, round in Indian sculpture. A tendency only.
rows.cautions: An identification says who the figure is meant to be, never how old the item is or whether it is old at all: the same forms are still made today for worship and to be sold (Nepalese and Tibetan workshops never stopped; Coomaraswamy 1927 notes good Nepalese metal work 'even up to quite recent times'). A Gandharan Maitreya was among the antiquities the Manhattan DA returned to Pakistan in 2022 (The Art Newspaper).

facts.text: The Sadhanamala gives Maitreya, when a minor god, the chowrie in the right hand and the nagakesara flower in the left; as principal god he is yellow, three-faced, four-armed, teaching.
facts.quote: Maitreya-Bodhisattvaṃ gauraṃ dvibhujaṃ jaṭāmukuṭinaṃ savyakareṇa cāmararatnadhāriṇam avasavyena nāgakesarapuṣpa...dhāriṇam

facts.text: Bhattacharyya: Maitreya is distinguished from Padmapani mainly by the small stupa (caitya) he bears on his crown.
facts.quote: He is distinguished from Padmapani mainly by the figure of a small caitya, which the former bears on his crown.

facts.text: Grünwedel: the most important attribute of the modern (Tibetan) Maitreya is the water flask (Skt. mangalakalasa), with the rosary; a Nepal-style bronze shows a stupa on the crown.
facts.quote: The modern attributes are the water flask or bottle (Tib. bum-pa; Skt. mangalakalasa)—the most important requisite, and the rosary.

facts.text: Getty: in Indian sculpture the standing Maitreya holds a round vase, in Gandhara sculptures oval or pointed; he is the only bodhisattva in Southern Buddhism, with statues in Ceylon, Burma and Siam.
facts.quote: in the left is a vase which is round, while in the sculptures of the Gandhara school the vase is oval or pointed in shape.

facts.text: Cleveland: a Nepalese figure with pendant legs is identified as Maitreya, the next figure to achieve enlightenment.
facts.quote: The pendant legs of this image indicate that he is the next historical figure to achieve enlightenment

rows.name: Manjushri (Bodhisattva of Wisdom)
rows.features_other: Usually brandishes a (flaming) sword in the raised right hand and holds a palm-leaf book against the breast or on a blue lotus at the left shoulder; or both rest on lotuses. Other forms hold only the blue lotus (utpala). Often rides a lion. May have a small Akshobhya in the crown. Wrathful form: buffalo-headed Yamantaka/Vajrabhairava.
rows.identify_by: A jeweled bodhisattva with a sword raised in the right hand and a book (often on a lotus) at the left.

look_alikes.name: simhanada-lokeshvara
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Simhanada on a lion wears no jewels and has a snake-wound trident; Manjushri is jeweled and has the book or blue lotus.

look_alikes.name: prajnaparamita
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Prajnaparamita also has the book on a lotus but is female and usually teaches with four arms.

look_alikes.name: vajrapani
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Vajrapani holds a vajra, not a sword.

rows.regions_styles: Pala Bengal and Bihar (Arapacana in stone and bronze, the most common form), Nepal (gilt copper, 15th c.), Tibet, China, Japan.
rows.dating_clues: Bhattacharyya: no Manjushri in Gandhara or Mathura sculpture; images appear at Sarnath, Magadha, Bengal and Nepal. So a 'Gandharan' Manjushri is doubtful.
rows.cautions: An identification says who the figure is meant to be, never how old the item is or whether it is old at all: the same forms are still made today for worship and to be sold (Nepalese and Tibetan workshops never stopped; Coomaraswamy 1927 notes good Nepalese metal work 'even up to quite recent times').

facts.text: Bhattacharyya (Sadhanamala, Arapacana): identification marks are the book against the breast and the brandished sword in the right hand; no form of Manjushri is so widely represented in stone and bronze.
facts.quote: vāme hṛdi gṛhītapustakam ... dakṣiṇe udyatakhaḍgakaram

facts.text: Getty: Manjushri has two types, one with sword and book (the more usual, commoner in bronzes), the other with the blue lotus (oftener in paintings and sculpture).
facts.quote: one with the sword and book, which is his more usual form, and the other with the utpala or blue lotus.

facts.text: Bhattacharyya: Manjushri's image is not found in the Gandhara and Mathura sculptures.
facts.quote: His image is not to be found in the Gandhara and Mathura sculptures

rows.name: Vajrapani (Holder of the Thunderbolt)
rows.features_other: Gentle forms (Kashmir, Nepal, Pala): a prince holding or resting a hand on a vajra, with snakes as ornaments (a knotted snake at the hips in a Nepalese bronze). In Gandhara reliefs he is the thunderbolt-bearing attendant of the Buddha. A wrathful Tibetan form is very common; the sources read here do not describe it in detail.
rows.identify_by: A figure whose main attribute is the vajra (double-ended thunderbolt), without the bell that Vajrasattva also holds.

look_alikes.name: vajrasattva
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Vajrasattva holds vajra AND bell, seated peacefully.

look_alikes.name: mahakala
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Mahakala holds a chopper over a skull cup; Vajrapani's main attribute is the vajra.

look_alikes.name: indra (other_hindu topic)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Indra holds a vajra too but rides the elephant Airavata and has a tall crown and, in Hindu images, many eyes on the body.

rows.regions_styles: Gandhara reliefs (attendant of the Buddha); Kashmir (8th c. bronzes with silver); Nepal (7th-8th c. copper); Pala; Sri Lanka (9th c. bronze); Tibet.
rows.dating_clues: Not datable from form.
rows.cautions: An identification says who the figure is meant to be, never how old the item is or whether it is old at all: the same forms are still made today for worship and to be sold (Nepalese and Tibetan workshops never stopped; Coomaraswamy 1927 notes good Nepalese metal work 'even up to quite recent times').

facts.text: Getty: Vajrapani is both the ferocious emanation of Vajradhara and the Dhyani-Bodhisattva of Akshobhya; in early legends accompanying Gautama he is a minor deity; Grünwedel identifies him with Sakra or Indra.
facts.quote: VAJRAPANI is both the ferocious emanation of Vajradhara and the spiritual reflex, the Dhyani-Bodhisattva, of Akshobhya

facts.text: Cleveland: Vajrapani means 'he who holds the thunderbolt'; his thunderbolt and club derive from images of Zeus and Hercules brought to the region; a Kashmir bronze sits on a rocky mountain with lions, wearing snakes as ornaments.
facts.quote: The attributes of the thunderbolt and the club were derived from images of Zeus and Hercules

facts.text: Grünwedel: in the Nirvana scenes of Gandhara the figure is identified by the legends as Sakka, Satamanyu or Vajrapani, 'the bearer of the thunderbolt'.
facts.quote: the personage in question appears to be clearly identified by the legends as Sakka, Satamanya, or Vajrapani—the bearer of the thunderbolt.

rows.name: Gandharan bodhisattva (princely figure: Siddhartha, Maitreya or Avalokiteshvara)
rows.features_other: Bare-chested prince with muscular Greco-Roman torso, Indian garments, heavy jewelry including a diagonal string of amulets, elaborate turban or looped long hair. Identity rests on small signs: a flask (Maitreya), a seated Buddha or Buddha pedestal in the diadem (Avalokiteshvara). Specialists often read a turbaned figure with no attribute as Siddhartha, the Buddha before renunciation; the sources read here do not state that rule.
rows.identify_by: A Gandharan prince-figure in jewels and turban; read the flask, the little Buddha in the turban, or their absence.

look_alikes.name: maitreya
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Holds a flask; long hair in a loop rather than a turban.

look_alikes.name: avalokiteshvara-padmapani
look_alikes.how_to_tell: A seated Buddha or lotus pedestal at the center of the diadem marks Avalokiteshvara (Cleveland 1985.31).

look_alikes.name: panchika
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Panchika is a heavier, bearded yaksha with a spear and purse, often with Hariti.

rows.regions_styles: Gandhara (Peshawar valley, Swat, Taxila; Pakistan and Afghanistan), gray-blue schist, 2nd-4th c.; stucco heads at Hadda and Taxila (3rd-5th c.).
rows.dating_clues: School style only. Modern Pakistani workshops copy these closely in schist (see gandhara-modern-fakes).
rows.cautions: An identification says who the figure is meant to be, never how old the item is or whether it is old at all: the same forms are still made today for worship and to be sold (Nepalese and Tibetan workshops never stopped; Coomaraswamy 1927 notes good Nepalese metal work 'even up to quite recent times'). Gandharan bodhisattvas are among the items most often faked and most often repatriated to Pakistan; see styles: gandhara-modern-fakes.

facts.text: Cleveland: bodhisattvas are shown as royal figures because the Buddha was a prince; the Gandharan example wears elaborate jewelry including a string of amulets diagonally across the chest; the garments are Indian, the muscular torso Greco-Roman.
facts.quote: He wears elaborate jewelry, including a string of amulets diagonally across his chest. The garments are Indian, but the muscular torso is derived from Greco-Roman sources.

facts.text: Cleveland: the water bottle in the left hand indicates Maitreya; the remains of a lotus pedestal for a Buddha at the center of a diadem identify a stucco head as Avalokiteshvara.
facts.quote: The water bottle in his left hand indicates that this figure depicts the bodhisattva Maitreya.

rows.name: Green Tara
rows.features_other: Seated with the right leg pendant, the foot on a small lotus; right hand in boon-giving; left hand in the teaching (vitarka) gesture holds the stem of a closed blue lotus (utpala) at the shoulder; may wear a small Amoghasiddhi in the crown; may be flanked by Marichi and Ekajata.
rows.identify_by: A jeweled goddess seated with the right leg stepping down onto a small lotus, right hand giving boons, left holding a closed blue lotus.

look_alikes.name: white-tara
look_alikes.how_to_tell: White Tara sits with both legs locked, usually has eyes on palms, soles and forehead, and an open lotus.

look_alikes.name: avalokiteshvara-padmapani
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Padmapani is male (flat chest) with Amitabha in the crown.

look_alikes.name: parvati / lakshmi (other topics)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Hindu goddesses often sit at ease too; look for Tara's blue lotus held in vitarka, a Buddha in the crown, and a Buddhist context. Without them a seated goddess can be uncertain.

rows.regions_styles: Pala Bengal and Bihar; Nepal (from the 10th c., copper alloy, gilt copper; wood); Tibet (gilt bronze with inlay); Yongle-mark Ming China (gilt bronze).
rows.dating_clues: Not datable; Chinese Yongle-mark Taras are a separate class, and marks are claims to check.
rows.cautions: An identification says who the figure is meant to be, never how old the item is or whether it is old at all: the same forms are still made today for worship and to be sold (Nepalese and Tibetan workshops never stopped; Coomaraswamy 1927 notes good Nepalese metal work 'even up to quite recent times'). Getty notes artists sometimes give Green Tara the open lotus of White Tara, so lotus shape alone is not conclusive.

facts.text: Getty: Green Tara sits on a lotus throne with the right leg pendent, the foot on a small lotus; right hand in charity mudra; left in argument mudra holding the blue lotus in profile.
facts.quote: She is represented seated on a lotus-throne, the right leg pendent, with the foot supported by a small lotus

facts.text: The Sadhanamala describes Khadiravani Tara as green, with Amoghasiddhi on her crown, showing the boon-giving gesture and the utpala in her right and left hands.
facts.quote: Haritām Amoghasiddhimukuṭīṃ varadotpaladhāridakṣiṇavāmakarām

facts.text: Getty: the utpala is shown with all petals closed or the central petals closed; artists sometimes erroneously give Green Tara the full-blown lotus of White Tara.
facts.quote: The artists, however, do not always follow tradition and sometimes erroneously give the green Tara the full-blown lotus of the white Tara

rows.name: White Tara
rows.features_other: Seated with legs locked, soles up; right hand boon-giving, left holding the stem of a full-blown lotus; third eye on the forehead and, in the 'seven-eyed' form, eyes on the palms and soles. A six-armed, three-faced white Tara also exists in the Sadhanamala. (token wanted: eyes on palms and soles)
rows.identify_by: A seated goddess with both legs crossed, right hand giving boons, an open lotus at the left shoulder, and extra eyes on forehead, palms and soles.

look_alikes.name: green-tara
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Green Tara has the right leg pendant and a closed blue lotus, and no eyes on palms or soles.

rows.regions_styles: Tibet, Mongolia (most popular there), Nepal; rare in China.
rows.dating_clues: Not datable.
rows.cautions: An identification says who the figure is meant to be, never how old the item is or whether it is old at all: the same forms are still made today for worship and to be sold (Nepalese and Tibetan workshops never stopped; Coomaraswamy 1927 notes good Nepalese metal work 'even up to quite recent times').

facts.text: Getty: White Tara is seated with legs locked, soles upward; right hand in charity, left holding the stem of the full-blown lotus in argument mudra; she generally has the third eye, and with eyes on palms and soles is called 'Tara of the Seven Eyes', most popular in Mongolia.
facts.quote: if there are eyes on the palms of her hands and the soles of her feet, she is called 'Tara of the Seven Eyes'

facts.text: The Sadhanamala also describes a white Tara with three faces and six arms (boon-giving, rosary and arrow at right; utpala, lotus and bow at left) wearing Amoghasiddhi on the crown.
facts.quote: Sitatārāṃ trimukhāṃ ṣaḍbhujāṃ

rows.name: Prajnaparamita (Perfection of Wisdom)
rows.features_other: A jeweled goddess, the personified scripture. Two arms: teaching, with a book on a blue lotus at the left shoulder. Four arms: front pair teaching, back pair holding book and rosary (or lotus with book and fear-not). Small Akshobhya in the headdress.
rows.identify_by: A seated goddess in teaching gesture with a palm-leaf book on a lotus or in a raised hand.

look_alikes.name: manjushri
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Manjushri is male and holds a sword.

look_alikes.name: saraswati (other_hindu topic)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Saraswati holds a book too, but usually plays a vina and rides a swan.

look_alikes.name: green-tara
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Bhattacharyya notes a teaching Tara can resemble Prajnaparamita; Tara's attendants Marichi and Ekajata decide it.

rows.regions_styles: Pala Bihar and Bengal (stone; manuscript paintings of the Ashtasahasrika Prajnaparamita); Java (very popular); Nepal. Getty: almost unknown in Tibet.
rows.dating_clues: Not datable.
rows.cautions: An identification says who the figure is meant to be, never how old the item is or whether it is old at all: the same forms are still made today for worship and to be sold (Nepalese and Tibetan workshops never stopped; Coomaraswamy 1927 notes good Nepalese metal work 'even up to quite recent times').

facts.text: Getty: Prajnaparamita may have two or four arms; with two the book is on a blue lotus at the left shoulder and the hands teach; with four the upper hands carry book and rosary, the lower are in dharmacakra; popular in Nepal and Java, almost unknown in Tibet.
facts.quote: If she has four arms the upper hands carry the book and rosary ... while the lower hands in both cases are in dharmacakra mudra.

facts.text: Bhattacharyya: Prajnaparamita is the embodiment of the Mahayana scripture of the same name, said to have been restored from the nether regions by Nagarjuna.
facts.quote: Prajnaparamita is the embodiment of the Mahayana Scripture of the same name

rows.name: Marichi (Goddess of the Dawn)
rows.features_other: Three faces, one of them a sow's head (at the left in India, at the right in Tibet, per Getty); original hands hold needle and thread (token wanted: needle and thread); other symbols an ashoka branch and vajra; a chariot drawn by seven pigs driven by Rahu (a head without body) or a legless goddess (token wanted: seven pigs as mount).
rows.identify_by: A many-armed goddess with a sow's face among her three heads, riding a chariot pulled by seven pigs.

look_alikes.name: varahi (shiva_devi topic)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Hindu Varahi is boar-faced with a single head and rides a buffalo; Marichi has three faces and seven pigs.

look_alikes.name: surya (other_hindu topic)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Surya's chariot has seven horses, not seven pigs.

look_alikes.name: vajravarahi (no row)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Vajravarahi has one face with a small sow's head by the ear, dances on a corpse and is the consort of Chakrasamvara (Bhattacharyya).

rows.regions_styles: Pala Bihar and Bengal (stone steles); Tibet; Japan (Marishiten, per Getty).
rows.dating_clues: Not datable.
rows.cautions: An identification says who the figure is meant to be, never how old the item is or whether it is old at all: the same forms are still made today for worship and to be sold (Nepalese and Tibetan workshops never stopped; Coomaraswamy 1927 notes good Nepalese metal work 'even up to quite recent times').

facts.text: Bhattacharyya: like the Hindu sun god Marichi has a chariot, but drawn by seven pigs instead of seven horses; the charioteer is a legless goddess or Rahu.
facts.quote: the chariot of Marici is drawn by seven pigs while the chariot of the sun is drawn by seven horses.

facts.text: Getty: she has three heads, the right one a sow's head in Tibet (in India always at the left), and usually six arms, the original pair holding thread and needle.
facts.quote: She has three heads, of which the one at the right is a sow's head (while in India it is always placed at the left)

facts.text: Disputed identity: Getty lists Vajravarahi as another name of Marichi; Bhattacharyya says the belief that they are the same has 'very little basis' (different arms, mounts, mantras).
facts.quote: There is a belief that Marici is the same as Vajravarahi, but there is very little basis for the theory.

facts.text: Disputed arm count: Bhattacharyya says Marichi can never have four arms and must have two, eight, ten or twelve according to the Sadhanas; Getty says she usually has six.
facts.quote: Marici can never have four arms: she must have either two, eight, ten or twelve arms according to the Sadhanas.

rows.name: Vasudhara (Goddess of Abundance)
rows.features_other: Two-armed form: boon-giving hand and ears of grain. Six-armed Nepalese form: a sheaf of grain, an overflowing vase, jewels, a book on a lotus, and one hand raised (sometimes cupped to the ear). Consort of Jambhala. Seated (leg position not recorded in the sources read; token wanted: seated, unspecified).
rows.identify_by: A seated goddess holding a sheaf of grain and a vase of plenty; in Nepal usually with six arms.

look_alikes.name: lakshmi / annapurna (other topics)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Hindu Lakshmi holds lotuses and is bathed by elephants; Annapurna holds a ladle and bowl; Vasudhara's grain sheaf and book with Buddhist setting mark her.

look_alikes.name: green-tara
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Tara holds a blue lotus and no grain.

rows.regions_styles: Nepal (among the most popular Newar deities; gilt copper with stones, 11th c. onward); Pala; Tibet.
rows.dating_clues: A dated Newari inscription (Nepal era 202 = 1082 CE) on a Smithsonian Vasudhara shows inscriptions can date such images; undated ones cannot be dated by type.
rows.cautions: An identification says who the figure is meant to be, never how old the item is or whether it is old at all: the same forms are still made today for worship and to be sold (Nepalese and Tibetan workshops never stopped; Coomaraswamy 1927 notes good Nepalese metal work 'even up to quite recent times').

facts.text: Bhattacharyya: Vasudhara is the consort of Jambhala; her form (like her attendant yakshinis) is yellow, carrying ears of corn and showing the boon-giving gesture.
facts.quote: Vasudhara who is yellow in complexion, carries the ears of corn and shows the Varada Mudra in her two hands.

facts.text: Cleveland: in Nepal this counterpart of the god of wealth is among the most popular divinities; in her six arms she holds jewels, an overflowing pot, a sheaf of wheat, and a Buddhist text on a lotus.
facts.quote: In each of her six arms she holds objects pertaining to life and abundance: jewels, an overflowing pot, and a sheaf of wheat.

facts.text: Smithsonian S2012.2, a Nepalese gilt copper Vasudhara, carries an inscription dated Nepal era 202 (February-March 1082).
facts.quote: on Thursday, the third lunar day of the bright fortnight of the month of Phalguna of Nepal era 202 (Feb–March 1082)

rows.name: Hariti (protector of children)
rows.features_other: A matronly goddess, usually seated, holding a child in her lap with other children climbing on her; may hold a pomegranate or a cornucopia; often paired with her consort Panchika (token wanted: child held in the lap; seated, unspecified).
rows.identify_by: A seated woman with a child on her lap and more children around her, sometimes with a pomegranate.

look_alikes.name: panchika
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Her consort: a male yaksha with spear and purse.

look_alikes.name: jain-ambika (jain topic)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Ambika also holds a child but sits on a lion under a mango tree with mangoes; Hariti has several children and no lion.

look_alikes.name: shashthi / skandamata (other topics)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Hindu mother-and-child goddesses carry Skanda or ride a lion or cat; read the setting.

rows.regions_styles: Gandhara (schist; flowing drapery, no head covering); Pala Bihar (black stone); Nepal (where Getty says she was believed to prevent smallpox); Java; Central Asia; China and Japan.
rows.dating_clues: Not datable.
rows.cautions: An identification says who the figure is meant to be, never how old the item is or whether it is old at all: the same forms are still made today for worship and to be sold (Nepalese and Tibetan workshops never stopped; Coomaraswamy 1927 notes good Nepalese metal work 'even up to quite recent times'). Gandharan Hariti groups are faked like other Gandharan sculpture.

facts.text: Getty: Hariti, protectress of children, was originally a yakshini who devoured children until the Buddha hid her last child under his begging bowl; Gandhara showed her in flowing garments holding a child with others climbing about her, sometimes with a pomegranate.
facts.quote: the Gandhara school represented Hariti in flowing garments, holding a child and with several children climbing about her

facts.text: Foucher: the 'fairy with the children and the genius with the purse' are a tutelary pair in Gandhara as in Roman Gaul; Hariti, from an ogress, became a matron.
facts.quote: this conjugal association of the fairy with the children and the genius with the purse

facts.text: Getty, after Yi-tsing: her statues stood in the porches or refectories of monasteries opposite the god of wealth, Kuvera.
facts.quote: her statues were always found either in the porches or refectories of the Buddhist monasteries, opposite the god of Wealth, Kuvera.

rows.name: Panchika (yaksha general, consort of Hariti)
rows.features_other: A yaksha in princely dress leaning on a lance and holding a purse of gold (token wanted: purse / money bag); usually seated beside Hariti.
rows.identify_by: A male figure with a spear and a money purse seated beside a goddess with children.

look_alikes.name: jambhala
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Jambhala holds a mongoose spewing jewels and a citron; no spear.

look_alikes.name: kubera (other_hindu topic)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Foucher: scholars long called him Kubera, but texts name him Panchika; Kubera alone has no spear and often a mongoose or money bag.

rows.regions_styles: Gandhara (schist and stucco, 2nd-4th c.); a Takht-i-Bahi stupa relief shows the pair (Getty, citing Stein).
rows.dating_clues: Not datable.
rows.cautions: An identification says who the figure is meant to be, never how old the item is or whether it is old at all: the same forms are still made today for worship and to be sold (Nepalese and Tibetan workshops never stopped; Coomaraswamy 1927 notes good Nepalese metal work 'even up to quite recent times'). Gandharan Hariti and Panchika groups are faked like other Gandharan sculpture.

facts.text: Foucher: in the male figure of the pair scholars long recognized Kuvera, but the texts name him Panchika, general of the yakshas, which is why he nearly always leans on a lance; the purse of gold in his right hand shows him as a dispenser of riches.
facts.quote: the texts merely designate him as their « general », by his name Pañcika, and it is in virtue of this title that he is nearly always leaning upon a lance.

facts.text: Getty (citing Stein): a Takht-i-Bahi stupa relief shows Kuvera seated beside Hariti, who holds a cornucopia.
facts.quote: representing Kuvera seated beside Hariti, who holds a cornucopia filled with flowers and fruit.

rows.name: Jambhala (Buddhist god of wealth)
rows.features_other: Corpulent (protruding belly), jeweled; holds a citron (jambhara fruit) in the right hand and in the left a mongoose spewing jewels (the mongoose is in origin a purse made of mongoose skin, Getty). Seated in the lalita posture. The AIC holds a Tibetan ivory Jambhala seated on a dragon. (token wanted: mongoose)
rows.identify_by: A fat, seated god holding a mongoose that vomits jewels; usually also a lemon-shaped fruit.

look_alikes.name: kubera (other_hindu topic)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Hindu Kubera is also pot-bellied with a money bag; a mongoose spewing jewels and a Buddhist setting (Buddha in the crown) point to Jambhala.

look_alikes.name: ganesha (other_hindu topic)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Ganesha is pot-bellied but elephant-headed.

look_alikes.name: panchika
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Panchika leans on a spear beside Hariti.

rows.regions_styles: Pala Bengal (Vikrampur) and Bihar; Sri Lanka (8th c. bronze, Coomaraswamy); Java; Nepal (from the 11th c.); Tibet (AIC ivory Jambhala on a dragon).
rows.dating_clues: Getty: Nepalese statues go back to the 11th century, Indian ones in Magadha are earlier. Not a dating rule for an item.
rows.cautions: An identification says who the figure is meant to be, never how old the item is or whether it is old at all: the same forms are still made today for worship and to be sold (Nepalese and Tibetan workshops never stopped; Coomaraswamy 1927 notes good Nepalese metal work 'even up to quite recent times').

facts.text: The Sadhanamala gives single Jambhala golden color, two arms, the citron in the right hand and a jewel-raining mongoose in the left.
facts.quote: Śrī-Jambhalaṃ pītavarṇaṃ dvibhujaṃ dakṣiṇahaste vījapūrakadharaṃ vāmahastena ratnapravarṣamāṇa-nakulīdharam

facts.text: Bhattacharyya: the mongoose is the receptacle of all gems; when Jambhala presses it, it vomits riches; noticing the mongoose makes him easy to recognize.
facts.quote: By noticing this mongoose in actual representations it is easy to recognize the possessor to be Jambhala.

facts.text: Getty: the mongoose (nakula) is in origin a bag made of mongoose skin, replacing the long narrow sack of earlier images; a Gandhara Kuvera holds such a bag.
facts.quote: The nakula, however, is merely a bag made of the skin of a mongoose, replacing the long narrow sack of the earlier images.

facts.text: Coomaraswamy: an 8th-century Sinhalese bronze Jambhala (Kubera), now in Boston, holds a citron in the right hand and a mongoose in the left.
facts.quote: Jambhala (Kubera), seated, r. hand with a citron (jambhara), l. hand holding a mongoose

rows.name: Mahakala (Great Black One, protector)
rows.features_other: Wrathful dark protector, fanged, with five skulls on the head and a garland of heads, snake ornaments and protruding belly, wearing tiger skin (Sadhanamala) or an elephant skin (Getty); holds a chopper (token wanted: chopper / kartri) and a skull cup; the six-armed form treads on one or two elephants.
rows.identify_by: A short, wrathful dark figure in flames holding a chopper and a skull cup, sometimes treading on elephants.

look_alikes.name: bhairava / shiva as mahakala (shiva_devi topic)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Hindu Bhairava and Shiva as Mahakala (Cleveland 1955.296, a Rajput painting) carry Shaiva emblems; the chopper-and-skull-cup pair, the five-skull crown and the elephants underfoot point to the Buddhist protector. Specialist reading advised.

look_alikes.name: vajrapani
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Wrathful Vajrapani raises a vajra.

look_alikes.name: yamantaka (no row)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Yamantaka/Vajrabhairava is buffalo-headed with many arms.

rows.regions_styles: Tibet and Mongolia (gilt copper, painted stone, thangkas); Nepal; Qing China; Japan (as Daikokuten, a quite different jolly god of wealth).
rows.dating_clues: Not datable.
rows.cautions: An identification says who the figure is meant to be, never how old the item is or whether it is old at all: the same forms are still made today for worship and to be sold (Nepalese and Tibetan workshops never stopped; Coomaraswamy 1927 notes good Nepalese metal work 'even up to quite recent times').

facts.text: The Sadhanamala describes two-armed Mahakala as dark, three-eyed, blazing, holding the chopper and skull cup in right and left hands, garlanded with heads, with snake ornaments and protruding belly.
facts.quote: Śrī-Mahākālabhaṭṭārakaṃ dvibhujam ekamukhaṃ kṛṣṇavarṇaṃ trinayanaṃ mahājjvalaṃ kartrikapāladhāriṇam

facts.text: Getty: the six-armed white Mahakala holds a wish-jewel over a skull cup at the breast, with chopper, small drum, trident and elephant goad in the other hands, and stands on two elephants; distinctive mark: treads on one or two elephants.
facts.quote: Distinctive mark: treads on one or two elephants.

rows.name: Padmasambhava (Guru Rinpoche)
rows.features_other: A deified 8th-century Indian teacher, not a god: seated with legs locked, the vajra in the right hand, a bowl or skull cup in the left lap, and the khatvanga (magic staff) pressed against him. (token wanted: deified teacher as kind; his distinctive hat is not described in the sources read)
rows.identify_by: A seated teacher holding a vajra and a skull cup or bowl with a staff pressed against his left side.

look_alikes.name: tibetan teachers (Tsongkhapa, Milarepa and others)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Portraits of other teachers lack the khatvanga-vajra-skull cup set; inscriptions on the base often name the person.

rows.regions_styles: Tibet, Bhutan, Sikkim, Nepal (Nyingma tradition); gilt copper and clay images, thangkas.
rows.dating_clues: Not datable.
rows.cautions: An identification says who the figure is meant to be, never how old the item is or whether it is old at all: the same forms are still made today for worship and to be sold (Nepalese and Tibetan workshops never stopped; Coomaraswamy 1927 notes good Nepalese metal work 'even up to quite recent times').

facts.text: Getty: Padmasambhava, invited to Tibet in the 8th century, is shown seated with legs locked, the right hand holding the vajra and the left in his lap with the patra, and his special symbol the khatvanga pressed against him.
facts.quote: He is represented seated on a lotus asana with the legs locked, the right hand holding the vajra, and the left, lying in his lap, the patra.

facts.text: AIC: the main form of Guru Rinpoche Padmasambhava, the 'Lotus Born', is seated with vajra and skull cup; he was an Indian Buddhist adept of the 8th century.
facts.quote: is seated in the center with vajra and skull cup

rows.name: Deities in union (yab-yum): Chakrasamvara, Hevajra, Vajrasattva with consort
rows.features_other: A male deity embracing a female partner who faces him; the male's main hands may cross behind her back holding vajra and bell; wrathful couples step on prostrate figures (Getty on Kalacakra: up to 24 arms). Peaceful couples (Vajrasattva, Manjuvara) sit.
rows.identify_by: Two figures in close embrace, the female facing the male; count heads and arms and look at the trampled figures to name the pair.

look_alikes.name: uma-maheshvara / lakshmi-narayana (shiva_devi, vishnu_krishna topics)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Hindu divine couples sit side by side, the goddess on the god's knee facing the viewer, not facing him in embrace.

look_alikes.name: vajrasattva
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Vajrasattva may be shown alone or in union; peaceful, seated, holding vajra and bell.

rows.regions_styles: Nepal (Newar gilt copper with jewel inlay, 16th-17th c. and later), Tibet, Mongolia, Qing China; Pala tantric texts.
rows.dating_clues: Not datable.

facts.text: Getty: Vajrasattva may press his shakti against his breast in the yab-yum attitude, his right hand holding the vajra, the left the bell on his hip; the yum holds the skull cup and vajra.
facts.quote: whom he presses against his breast in the yab-yum attitude, with the right hand holding the vajra, while the left holds the ghanta on his hip.

facts.text: The Smithsonian holds a Nepalese gilt copper with jewel inlay titled 'Sri Cakrasamvara and Vajravarahi' (16th-17th c.); Cleveland a Tibetan 'Manjuvara with consort (yab-yum)'.
facts.quote: Sri Cakrasamvara and Vajravarahi

rows.name: Rishabhanatha (Adinatha)
rows.features_other: Locks of hair falling on the shoulders (token wanted: hair locks on shoulders). 'hair in a bun' is the nearest token and is not exact.
rows.identify_by: A bull on the pedestal; locks of hair falling on the shoulders (the only Jina shown so); Cakreśvarī on Garuḍa with discs at the pedestal end.

look_alikes.name: bahubali
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Bāhubalī (his son) also stands in kāyotsarga, but has vines twining round arms and legs.

look_alikes.name: mahavira
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Without the bull or the hair locks a Jina is not identifiable; check the back inscription, which usually names the Jina.

rows.regions_styles: Seated or standing; in Western India (Gujarat, Rajasthan) mostly as small brass or bronze images, single or on five-Jina and twenty-four-Jina altarpieces; also marble temple images.
rows.dating_clues: The hair locks are a firm identifying sign from about the 1st century CE; they say nothing about date.
rows.cautions: An emblem identifies which Jina is meant, nothing more: it cannot date the item or show whether it is old. Jain brass images are still cast and consecrated in Gujarat and Rajasthan in the same forms, and the inscription on the back can be younger or older than the casting (see rows inscription-form and inscription-reading). Emblems are small and often worn; on multi-Jina altarpieces only the central Jina usually has one.

facts.text: Emblem is the bull in both traditions.
facts.quote: (5) the bull, - vrisha, balada

facts.text: Rishabha is the only Jina shown with long locks of hair on the shoulders; the locks appear from about the 1st century CE at Mathura and Chausa.
facts.quote: the only one depicted with long locks of hair (Cleveland 1969.228)

facts.text: Traditions disagree on why: Svetambara story (Triṣaṣṭi) says Indra asked him to keep a lock; Digambara Purāṇas and the Paumacariya say he plucked all his hair like the other Jinas.
facts.quote: this hair-creeper brought by the wind to your golden shoulders shines like an emerald. So let it remain.

facts.text: Yaksha Gomukha and yakshi Cakreśvarī in both traditions; Gomukha is bull-faced.
facts.quote: Rishabha has for Yaksha Gomukha, with the head of an ox (Burgess 1903 IA)

rows.name: Ajitanatha

look_alikes.name: mahavira

facts.text: Svetambara yakṣī Ajitabalā; Digambara yakṣī Rohiṇī.
facts.quote: With the Svetambaras the Yakshini is Ajitabala (Burgess 1903 IA)

rows.name: Sambhavanatha
