rows.name: Naminatha
rows.identify_by: A blue lotus (water-lily) on the pedestal.

look_alikes.name: padmaprabha
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Blue lily (Nami) versus red lotus (Padmaprabha): only color or the inscription separates them.

rows.regions_styles: Seated or standing; in Western India (Gujarat, Rajasthan) mostly as small brass or bronze images, single or on five-Jina and twenty-four-Jina altarpieces; also marble temple images.
rows.dating_clues: Style and inscription only. Emblems and yakṣa-yakṣī pairs appear on Jina images from the Gupta period on; Kushan images from Mathura have none, so an image without an emblem is not necessarily early.
rows.cautions: An emblem identifies which Jina is meant, nothing more: it cannot date the item or show whether it is old. Jain brass images are still cast and consecrated in Gujarat and Rajasthan in the same forms, and the inscription on the back can be younger or older than the casting (see rows inscription-form and inscription-reading). Emblems are small and often worn; on multi-Jina altarpieces only the central Jina usually has one.

facts.text: Emblem blue water-lily.
facts.quote: (5) the blue water-lily - nilotpala, with the Digambaras, sometimes the Asoka tree

facts.text: Digambara yakṣī Cāmuṇḍī, four-armed with rosary, rod and sword, crocodile cognizance (Mysore).
facts.quote: Chamundi, his Yakshini, has four hands having rosary, rod and sword, and the crocodile as cognizance

rows.name: Neminatha (Arishtanemi)
rows.identify_by: A conch on the pedestal; Ambikā with a child at the pedestal end; in early images Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma flank him.

look_alikes.name: munisuvrata
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Conch versus tortoise.

look_alikes.name: ambika
look_alikes.how_to_tell: A goddess with a child and lion is Nemi's yakṣī; a large Ambikā with a small Jina above is an Ambikā image, not a Nemi image.

rows.regions_styles: Seated or standing; in Western India (Gujarat, Rajasthan) mostly as small brass or bronze images, single or on five-Jina and twenty-four-Jina altarpieces; also marble temple images.
rows.dating_clues: Style and inscription only. Emblems and yakṣa-yakṣī pairs appear on Jina images from the Gupta period on; Kushan images from Mathura have none, so an image without an emblem is not necessarily early.
rows.cautions: An emblem identifies which Jina is meant, nothing more: it cannot date the item or show whether it is old. Jain brass images are still cast and consecrated in Gujarat and Rajasthan in the same forms, and the inscription on the back can be younger or older than the casting (see rows inscription-form and inscription-reading). Emblems are small and often worn; on multi-Jina altarpieces only the central Jina usually has one.

facts.text: Emblem conch; complexion black.
facts.quote: (4) black - syama; (5) a conch, - sankha

facts.text: Yakṣī Ambikā (Digambara Kūṣmāṇḍinī) with children and a lion; yakṣa Gomedha (Sarvāhṇa).
facts.quote: the Yakshini is Kushmandini, - four-armed, with two children in her lap, and a lion as cognizance.

facts.text: In Kushan and Gupta Mathura sculpture Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma, his cousins, flank Nemi.
facts.quote: Balarama and Krsna joined Neminatha as his cousins in the Kusana period

rows.name: Parshvanatha
rows.identify_by: A seven-hooded snake canopy over the head (also three, nine, eleven or a thousand in texts); snake coils behind the body; snake emblem on the pedestal.

look_alikes.name: suparshvanatha
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Supārśva has five (or one or nine) hoods and a svastika emblem.

look_alikes.name: padmavati
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Padmāvatī and Dharaṇendra also have hoods but have four arms holding objects and are not in meditation.

look_alikes.name: jina-seated
look_alikes.how_to_tell: A seated figure under a seven-hooded snake wearing a monastic robe, with no śrīvatsa, is a Buddha sheltered by Mucalinda, not Pārśva.

rows.regions_styles: Among the most numerous Jina images everywhere; Karnataka chlorite and Central Indian sandstone examples in Chicago and Cleveland; very common as Western Indian brass.
rows.dating_clues: Style and inscription only. Emblems and yakṣa-yakṣī pairs appear on Jina images from the Gupta period on; Kushan images from Mathura have none, so an image without an emblem is not necessarily early.
rows.cautions: An emblem identifies which Jina is meant, nothing more: it cannot date the item or show whether it is old. Jain brass images are still cast and consecrated in Gujarat and Rajasthan in the same forms, and the inscription on the back can be younger or older than the casting (see rows inscription-form and inscription-reading). Emblems are small and often worn; on multi-Jina altarpieces only the central Jina usually has one. Hood count is a strong sign but not absolute: images with other counts exist.

facts.text: Pārśva is shown with seven snake hoods; his iconography was the first of all the Jinas to be fixed (c. 1st century BCE).
facts.quote: The seven-headed snake canopy was associated with Parsvanatha in c. first century B. C.

facts.text: Texts and images also give three, seven, eleven or nine hoods, and a thousand in one Tīrthakalpa list.
facts.quote: snakes canopy him with three or seven or eleven hoods.

facts.text: The snake king Dharaṇendra spread his hoods over Pārśva in the storm sent by Meghamālin (Kamaṭha); the pair Dharaṇendra-Padmāvatī became his attendants.
facts.quote: Dharanendra spread his many hoods over the head of the Arhata and the Yakshini Padmavati held a white umbrella

facts.text: Pārśva and Supārśva are the only Jinas with snake hoods; all Jinas otherwise look alike.
facts.quote: identically alike ... with the exception of the snake-crests over Suparsva and Parsvanatha

facts.text: Rūpamaṇḍana: Malli and Pārśva are blue.
facts.quote: Malli and Parsva blue

rows.name: Mahavira (Vardhamana)
rows.identify_by: A single lion at the center of the pedestal (not the pair of lions that support every lion throne).

look_alikes.name: jina-seated
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Two lions at the pedestal corners are the throne (siṃhāsana) of any Jina; Mahāvīra's emblem is one lion in the center.

look_alikes.name: ambika
look_alikes.how_to_tell: A lion under a goddess with a child is Ambikā's mount; under a goddess with book and lute, Siddhāyikā's.

rows.regions_styles: Seated or standing; in Western India (Gujarat, Rajasthan) mostly as small brass or bronze images, single or on five-Jina and twenty-four-Jina altarpieces; also marble temple images.
rows.dating_clues: Style and inscription only. Emblems and yakṣa-yakṣī pairs appear on Jina images from the Gupta period on; Kushan images from Mathura have none, so an image without an emblem is not necessarily early.
rows.cautions: An emblem identifies which Jina is meant, nothing more: it cannot date the item or show whether it is old. Jain brass images are still cast and consecrated in Gujarat and Rajasthan in the same forms, and the inscription on the back can be younger or older than the casting (see rows inscription-form and inscription-reading). Emblems are small and often worn; on multi-Jina altarpieces only the central Jina usually has one.

facts.text: Emblem lion in both traditions.
facts.quote: (5) a lion - kesari-simha

facts.text: Lion-throne lions are a standard feature of Jina images from the Gupta period on.
facts.quote: simhasana (lion-throne), prabhamandala (nimbus)

facts.text: Yakṣa Mātaṅga on an elephant; yakṣī Siddhāyikā on a lion with book and lute.
facts.quote: The unfailing attributes by which Siddhaika may be identified in art are her lion mount in combination with objects such as the book, the lute

rows.name: Seated Jina (any Tirthankara) and how to tell it from a Buddha
rows.features_other: Right palm laid over the left in the lap; eyes fixed on the tip of the nose; no ornaments on Digambara images; wheel marks on palms and soles on some images.
rows.identify_by: A plain human figure seated cross-legged, both hands in the lap (right over left), with a diamond-shaped śrīvatsa on the chest; never more arms or heads, never a gesture other than meditation; an emblem and a yakṣa-yakṣī pair on the pedestal.

look_alikes.name: buddha (buddhist topic)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: A Buddha wears a monastic robe and often makes other gestures (earth-touching, teaching, fear-not); a Jina is nude or wears only a lower garment, always meditates, and carries a śrīvatsa on the chest. The cranial bump does NOT separate them: both have it.

look_alikes.name: dakshinamurti (shiva topic)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Śiva as teacher has four arms, a raised leg and attributes; the Jina has two arms in the lap.

look_alikes.name: panchatirthi
look_alikes.how_to_tell: A single seated Jina with four smaller Jinas around it on one plate is a five-Jina altarpiece.

rows.regions_styles: North Indian images sit in full padmāsana; South Indian Jinas often simply cross the legs. Western Indian brass (Gujarat, Rajasthan) dominates what collectors meet.
rows.dating_clues: Kushan Mathura heads may lack the cranial bump and curls; from about the 7th-8th century the full set of attendants appears; style can suggest a period but workshops still cast traditional forms.
rows.cautions: Identification as a Jina is a reading of signs; it cannot date the item or show it is old. South Indian and some eastern Indian Jinas lack the śrīvatsa, so its absence does not prove a Buddha. Seated Buddhas from Nepal and Tibet are sometimes sold as Jain and vice versa.

facts.text: Jinas are shown in only two postures: seated cross-legged in meditation or standing in kāyotsarga; never reclining.
facts.quote: They are shown only in two postures, seated cross-legged, in dhyana-mudra or standing erect in kayotsarga

facts.text: The seated Jina has the right hand laid over the left in the lap, palm up.
facts.quote: the right hand laid over the left in the lap with the palm upwards

facts.text: The śrīvatsa on the chest distinguishes a seated Jina from a Buddha; it is absent on many South Indian Jinas.
facts.quote: from the Srivatsa mark executed on the chest of a Tirthankara, one can easily distinguish it from that of the Buddha. In the Tirthankara images from South India, this particular symbol is, however, conspicuous by its absence.

facts.text: Jinas, like Buddhas, are shown with a cranial protuberance (uṣṇīṣa); the Vivekavilāsa prescribes it.
facts.quote: During this time Jinas, like Buddhas, were depicted with the protuberance atop the head (Cleveland 1969.228)

facts.text: Buddha images wear a robe, sometimes plain and clinging so the body shows through.
facts.quote: Depicting the Buddha in a plain robe that clings to the body (Cleveland 1943.278)

facts.text: North Indian seated Jinas are usually in padmāsana, South Indian ones with legs simply crossed.
facts.quote: Usually the North Indian images are shown in padmasana, the South Indian images with legs crossed.

facts.text: Bṛhatsaṃhitā (6th c.): the Arhat's god is shown nude, young, calm, arms reaching the knees, śrīvatsa on the chest.
facts.quote: should be shown nude, young and beautiful in appearance, with a tranquil expression and arms reaching down to the knees; his breast should have the (auspicious) Srivatsa mark

rows.name: Standing Jina in kayotsarga (any Tirthankara)
rows.features_other: Arms hang straight to the knees, fingers together turned slightly in, not touching the thighs; heels slightly apart; frontal and symmetrical.
rows.identify_by: A rigidly frontal standing figure, arms hanging straight down without touching the body, usually nude, with a śrīvatsa; no gesture and nothing held.

look_alikes.name: bahubali
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Bāhubalī stands the same way but has vines twining up his arms and legs and anthills with snakes at his feet.

look_alikes.name: buddha (buddhist topic)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: A standing Buddha wears a robe and usually raises the right hand (fear-not).

rows.regions_styles: Common in Digambara images (Karnataka, Central India, Deogarh, Khajuraho); 21 of the 24 are said to have reached liberation in this posture.
rows.dating_clues: Kushan standing Jinas are nude and attended by two disciples; no yakṣa-yakṣī before the Gupta period.
rows.cautions: Posture identifies a Jina (or Bāhubalī), not which one, and says nothing about age.

facts.text: In kāyotsarga the arms hang straight down to the knees, fingers turned slightly inward, not touching the thighs; heels slightly apart.
facts.quote: erect with arms hanging straight down to the knees, the fingers together and turned slightly inwards but not touching the thighs.

facts.text: Twenty-one Jinas attained liberation in kāyotsarga; Ṛṣabha, Nemi and Mahāvīra seated.
facts.quote: Twenty-one of the Tirthakaras are said to have attained Moksha in the Kayotsarga (Guj. Kaiisagga) posture

facts.text: Standing nude Jinas mark Digambara images.
facts.quote: his nudity links him to the digambara (sky-clad) sect of Jainism (Mia 98.246)

rows.name: Srivatsa mark (on a Jina's chest)
rows.features_other: A raised diamond or four-petalled mark at the center of the chest; on Western Indian brass often inlaid in silver.
rows.identify_by: A small diamond or flower-like mark in the middle of the chest of a seated or standing Jina.

look_alikes.name: shitalanatha
look_alikes.how_to_tell: A śrīvatsa on the PEDESTAL is Śītala's Svetambara emblem; on the chest it is on every Jina.

rows.regions_styles: Standard on North and Western Indian Jinas; often absent in South India and sometimes in Bihar, Orissa and Bengal.
rows.dating_clues: None.
rows.cautions: Absence of a śrīvatsa does not make a figure a Buddha (South Indian Jinas usually lack it).

facts.text: Every Jina, seated or standing, shows the śrīvatsa, a diamond-shaped chest mark.
facts.quote: Whether standing or seated, the jina image always shows a Srivatsa mark on the chest

facts.text: Silver-inlaid śrīvatsa marks are found on Western Indian brass altarpieces.
facts.quote: have inlaid silver auspicious marks on their chests srivatsa (Mia 2000.30)

facts.text: Jina images from Bihar, Orissa and Bengal sometimes omit the śrīvatsa; South Indian ones usually do.
facts.quote: do not show certain traditional features, such as Yaksa-Yaksi pairs ... and sometimes srivatsa also.

rows.name: Snake hoods over a Jain figure: how to count and read them
rows.features_other: Seven hoods: Pārśva. Five (also 1 or 9): Supārśva. Hoods over a four-armed figure: Dharaṇendra (5 or 7) or Padmāvatī (1, 3, 5 or 7).
rows.identify_by: Count the hoods, then look at the arms: two arms in meditation = a Jina (7 Pārśva, 5 Supārśva); four arms holding things = Dharaṇendra or Padmāvatī.

look_alikes.name: parshvanatha
look_alikes.how_to_tell: seven hoods, snake emblem

look_alikes.name: suparshvanatha
look_alikes.how_to_tell: five hoods, svastika

look_alikes.name: padmavati
look_alikes.how_to_tell: four arms, goad, noose, lotus, fruit; small Pārśva above

look_alikes.name: dharanendra
look_alikes.how_to_tell: four arms with snakes; tortoise or elephant-faced in texts

rows.regions_styles: Everywhere; Mathura from the 1st century BCE.
rows.dating_clues: Pārśva's seven hoods are the earliest fixed Jina sign (c. 1st century BCE).
rows.cautions: Counts vary in texts and images; worn or broken hoods are easy to miscount.

facts.text: Pārśva has seven hoods and Supārśva five.
facts.quote: Suparsva's image differs from other Tirthakaras in having five snake-hoods over his head

facts.text: Variant counts: Pārśva 3, 7, 9 or 11 (and 1,000 in one list); Supārśva 1, 5 or 9.
facts.quote: the canon of the numbers of hoods cited above is not always regular.

facts.text: Kalpasūtra paintings show Dharaṇendra with seven hoods and Padmāvatī with three beside a standing Pārśva; Padmāvatī images show varying hood counts.
facts.quote: flanked on the left by Dharanendra with seven hoods and on the right by Padmavati with three hoods.

facts.text: In the Mysore drawings both of Pārśva's attendants have five hoods.
facts.quote: Both attendants have five snake-hoods (sesha-phana) over their heads.

rows.name: Digambara or Svetambara image? (nude vs clothed, inlaid eyes)
rows.features_other: Svetambara images: a lower garment (often an incised hem at waist and knees), crowns and ornaments added in worship, eyes shown or inlaid (silver, sometimes other materials). Digambara images: fully nude, no ornaments, eyes half-closed.
rows.identify_by: Visible genitals and no garment line = Digambara; a waist-cloth line and open or inlaid eyes = Svetambara.

look_alikes.name: jina-seated
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Kushan Mathura Jinas are nude but predate the sectarian split in art; nudity there is not a sect marker.

rows.regions_styles: Svetambara brass dominates Gujarat and western Rajasthan; Digambara images predominate in Karnataka, Central India, Delhi region and eastern Rajasthan.
rows.dating_clues: Sectarian differences in images are not visible in Kushan art.
rows.cautions: Sect is a reading of the image, not of its age or whether it is genuine.

facts.text: Digambara Jina statues are always nude; Svetambaras show theirs clothed and adorn them with crowns and ornaments.
facts.quote: Their statues of the Tirthakaras are always represented as nude (nirvastra); whereas the Svetambaras represent theirs as clothed and decorate them with crowns and ornaments.

facts.text: Svetambara images often show the eyeballs; earlier images show half-closed eyes without eyeballs.
facts.quote: In Svetambara images the eye-ball is often represented.

facts.text: A Western Indian brass altarpiece dated 1579 has inlaid silver eyes on its central Jina.
facts.quote: The central ... figure, has inlaid silver eyes (Mia 2000.30)

facts.text: Nudity in Kushan Mathura images does not mark a sect.
facts.quote: the sectarian distinction relating to nudity or drapery did not, atleast in sculptures, originate as early as the Kushan period.

rows.name: The setting of a Jina image: triple umbrella, lion throne and attendants
rows.features_other: Triple umbrella over the head; halo; lion throne; two fly-whisk (cāmara) bearers; garland-bearing flying figures; a drummer above; elephants; the yakṣa at the Jina's right and the yakṣī at his left at the pedestal ends; wheel of the law with deer at the center; sometimes the nine planets (navagraha) in a row at the base.
rows.identify_by: A triple umbrella over the head and a yakṣa-yakṣī pair at the pedestal ends mark a Jina image even when the main figure is worn.

look_alikes.name: bahubali
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Bāhubalī has a single umbrella, not three.

look_alikes.name: buddha (buddhist topic)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Buddhist steles have bodhisattva attendants, not a yakṣa-yakṣī pair with a Jina emblem between.

rows.regions_styles: The full frame is fixed by c. 9th-10th century; Western Indian brass reduces it to a pierced arch with umbrella, cāmara-bearers and tiny attendants.
rows.dating_clues: Yakṣa-yakṣī pairs and emblems appear from the Gupta period; earlier (Kushan) images have neither.
rows.cautions: Frames were often cast separately; a Jina may have been fitted to a frame or pedestal from another image.

facts.text: All Tirthankara figures have a triple umbrella over the head.
facts.quote: All the figures of Tirthakaras have a triple umbrella or tiara over their heads

facts.text: The yakṣa is placed at the Jina's proper right, the yakṣī at his left; the nine planets may sit in a row at the base.
facts.quote: at the proper right of the Jina is a male figure representing the Yaksha ... at the left end of the throne is the corresponding female

facts.text: The eight prātihāryas are the aśoka tree, rain of flowers, divine sound, cāmaras, lion throne, halo, drum and umbrella.
facts.quote: simhasana (lion-throne), prabhamandala (nimbus), camaradhara attendant, hovering maladhara (sura-puspavrsti), chatra (parasol), caitya-tree and divyadhvani (divine music).

facts.text: Fully developed Jina images (c. 9th-10th century on) contain emblem, yakṣa-yakṣī, prātihāryas, wheel with worshippers, small Jinas and at times the navagrahas.
facts.quote: The fully developed Jina images invariably contain distinguishing emblems, Yaksa-Yaksi pairs, astapratiharyas, dharmacakra with worshippers, diminutive Jina figures and at times navagrahas

facts.text: Independent yakṣīs and yakṣas are recognized by a small Jina at their head or at the top of the image.
facts.quote: the keynote to recognise is the presence of a small Jina figure either at their head or at the top of the statue.

rows.name: Five-Jina altarpiece (panchatirthi)
rows.features_other: One larger central Jina (the mūlanāyaka) with four smaller Jinas: usually two standing in kāyotsarga at the sides and two seated above; yakṣa and yakṣī at the pedestal ends; inscription on the back.
rows.identify_by: A single brass plate or frame carrying five Jinas, one large in the middle. The central Jina's emblem and the back inscription name it.

look_alikes.name: chaturvimshatipatta
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Count the Jinas: five versus twenty-four.

look_alikes.name: tritirthi (no row)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Three Jinas (tritīrthī) or two (dvitīrthī) also occur, mostly at Digambara sites.

rows.regions_styles: Very common Western Indian (Gujarat, Rajasthan) brass of the 14th-17th centuries; dozens are recorded in Buddhisāgarasūri's corpus of metal-image inscriptions.
rows.dating_clues: Inscriptions on the back give a Vikrama Saṃvat date; style must agree with it (see inscription-reading).
rows.cautions: Still cast today; age cannot be read from the type.

facts.text: The Pañcatīrtha is a plate of metal or stone with five images on it.
facts.quote: The Panchatirtha is a plate of metal or stone with five images upon it

facts.text: Quintuple images are frequently seen as bronzes, with one central main image and smaller secondary figures.
facts.quote: In the cases of triple or quintuple images, frequently seen as bronzes but also found as stone sculptures, there is usually one mulanayaka

facts.text: The inscriptions themselves call the item a pañcatīrthī, e.g. an Ajitanātha pañcatīrthī consecrated in Saṃvat 1494.
facts.quote: saṃvat 1494 varṣe vaiśākha vadi 11 ... śrī-ajitanātha-pañcatīrthī kā[ritā] pra[tiṣṭhitā] (Buddhisāgara no. 93, normalized from OCR)

rows.name: Twenty-four-Jina altarpiece (chaturvimshatipatta, chovisi)
rows.features_other: One large central Jina with emblem and attendants, two larger flanking Jinas, and 21 (or 23) small Jinas sketched in rows around a pointed arch; often silver and copper inlay; long donor inscription on the back.
rows.identify_by: Count small seated Jinas around a central one: 23 + 1 = 24.

look_alikes.name: panchatirthi
look_alikes.how_to_tell: five Jinas only

look_alikes.name: buddha (buddhist topic)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Buddhist 'thousand Buddha' plaques show robed Buddhas with varied gestures.

rows.regions_styles: Western India from the 9th century (Akota) to the 19th; museum examples dated 1089, 1498 and 1579.
rows.dating_clues: Back inscriptions name donor and date; the Art Institute of Chicago dates one to 1089 and another to 1498, Mia one to 1579.
rows.cautions: Still made; recently cast items may carry copied inscriptions.

facts.text: Burgess: the Chauvīsvaṭa is a slab, usually marble, carved with the 24 Tirthankaras.
facts.quote: the Chauvisvata is a slab, usually of marble, carved with representations of the twenty-four Tirthakaras.

facts.text: When all 24 are shown in one frame, the central image is larger with emblem and attendants; two flanking ones may be larger than the other 21 'sketched in rudimentary outline'.
facts.quote: the central image is shown larger and with the recognition mark and the attendant figures.

facts.text: Inscriptions call these items caturviṃśati-paṭṭa, e.g. a Śreyāṃsa twenty-four-Jina plaque consecrated by Ratnaśekharasūri of the Tapā gaccha.
facts.quote: svaśreyase śrī-śreyāṃsa caturviṃśati-paṭṭaḥ kāritaḥ tapā śrī-ratnaśekharasūri ... pratiṣṭhitaḥ (Nahar no. 4, normalized)

facts.text: Such portable plaques were usually commissioned by lay people and presented to temples.
facts.quote: Portable plaques of this type were usually commissioned by the Jain laity and presented to their temples.

rows.name: Four-faced Jain image (chaumukha, sarvatobhadra)
rows.features_other: Four Jinas back to back on one square pedestal, facing the four directions; seated or standing; same Jina four times or four different Jinas.
rows.identify_by: Four identical-looking Jinas back to back, one facing each side.

look_alikes.name: chaturmukha linga (shiva topic)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: A four-faced liṅga shows four heads of Śiva around a shaft, not four whole seated or standing figures.

rows.regions_styles: From the Kushan period at Mathura (four different standing Jinas) to modern brass; often only Ṛṣabha (hair locks) and Pārśva (hoods) are identifiable.
rows.dating_clues: Kushan examples show four different standing Jinas; images of the same Jina four times start c. 7th-8th century.
rows.cautions: Type cannot date the item.

facts.text: In a caumukha four figures are placed back to back on one pedestal facing four directions.
facts.quote: In the caumukha image the four figures are placed back to back on one pedestal facing the four directions.

facts.text: Most four-different-Jina caumukhas show the emblems of only Ṛṣabha and Pārśva.
facts.quote: in most of the cases show the cognizances of only two, generally those of Rsabhanatha and Parsvanatha, of the four Jinas.

facts.text: DISPUTED origin: Jain and Fischer (following U. P. Shah) see the caumukha as a development of the samavasaraṇa preaching hall; Tiwari rejects this because Kushan examples show four different standing Jinas.
facts.quote: A further development of samavasarana is caumukha, four faced image. (Jain & Fischer) / this view is not acceptable (Tiwari)

rows.name: Siddhachakra plate (navapada yantra)
rows.features_other: A round or square metal plate with a lotus of four or eight petals: the Arhat in the center, then Siddha, Ācārya, Upādhyāya and Sādhu, and (Svetambara) right faith, knowledge, conduct and austerity; Digambara versions put the Jina image, Jina temple, wheel of the law and scripture in the petals. Horizontal versions stand on eight small feet with a spout for bath water; upright versions stand on a pyramidal base with lions.
rows.identify_by: A lotus diagram with tiny seated figures or syllables in a center and petals, on a plate with a spout or a stand.

look_alikes.name: buddhist mandala (buddhist topic)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: A Siddhacakra has nine places (five beings plus four virtues) and tiny Jinas or Jain monks with brooms and mouth-cloths.

look_alikes.name: hindu yantra (other_hindu topic)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Hindu yantras show interlocking triangles and seed syllables, not five revered beings.

rows.regions_styles: Very common in Svetambara household and temple shrines in Gujarat and Rajasthan; South Indian types have flames round the rim.
rows.dating_clues: None known from type; stone-panel Siddhacakras are recent.
rows.cautions: Mass-produced in brass today; type cannot date it.

facts.text: The Siddhacakra is a square brass plate with a spout for water, a central eight-petalled flower with the Arhat in the middle and the Siddha, Ācārya, Sādhu and Upādhyāya on four petals, tapas, darśana, cāritra and jñāna on the others.
facts.quote: The Siddhachakra is a square brass plate, found in the shrines. It has a sort of spout in front, to allow water to run off

facts.text: It is one of the most popular Jain yantras; Digambaras often call it navadevatā; it embodies the five-fold salutation (pañca-namaskāra).
facts.quote: The siddhacakra, the circle of the siddha or liberated one, is one of the most popular yantra of the Jaina.

facts.text: DISPUTED placement: Burgess puts the Ācārya on the right, the Sādhu on the left and the Upādhyāya in front by the spout; Jain and Fischer's painted type has Ācārya right, Upādhyāya left, Sādhu at the bottom.
facts.quote: the right hand by the Acharya; the left by the Sadhu or Muni; and the front, next to the spout, by the Upadhyaya

facts.text: Horizontal metal yantras have eight small feet and a gargoyle or outlet for ritual water; upright bronzes stand on a tapering base with lions.
facts.quote: metal yantra to be placed horizontally on the ground, with eight small feet, like a low stool. A gargoyle or other outlet is attached

rows.name: Bahubali (Gommateshvara)
rows.features_other: Vines or creepers twining round arms, legs and chest; anthills with snakes at his feet; lizards and scorpions on the body; sometimes two sisters (Brāhmī, Sundarī) or two vidyādharīs pulling away the vines; a single umbrella. Not a Tirthankara (token wanted: kind 'saint / kevalin').
rows.identify_by: A standing nude ascetic in kāyotsarga with vines climbing his limbs.

look_alikes.name: jina-standing
look_alikes.how_to_tell: A Jina has no vines or anthills and has a triple umbrella.

look_alikes.name: rishabhanatha
look_alikes.how_to_tell: His father Ṛṣabha may stand in the same pose but has hair locks on the shoulders and a bull emblem.

rows.regions_styles: Much more popular among Digambaras (Karnataka: Shravanabelagola colossus, Karkala, Venur; Ellora; Deogarh, Khajuraho); rare Svetambara images wear a dhoti.
rows.dating_clues: Earliest North Indian images c. 9th century (Prabhāsa Pāṭaṇa).
rows.cautions: Modern brass and stone Bāhubalīs are made in quantity in Karnataka and Rajasthan.

facts.text: Bāhubalī, Ṛṣabha's son, stood in kāyotsarga for a year; images show creepers round the body and snakes from anthills at the feet.
facts.quote: The Bahubali representations show snakes issuing out of the ant-hills which developed near his feet and creepers entwined round his body

facts.text: Digambaras call him Gommaṭeśvara and worship him equally with the Tirthankaras.
facts.quote: the Digambaras call him Gomatesvara-Svami, and worship him equally with the Tirthakaras

facts.text: Bāhubalī worship was much less popular among Svetambaras; their rare images show him wearing a dhoti.
facts.quote: U. P. Shah records only two Svetambara images of Bahubali, which in Keeping with the white-clad tradition, show him with dhoti.

facts.text: The Khajuraho Bāhubalī has a single umbrella instead of the triple one.
facts.quote: A single umbrella, instead of the triple one, is depicted overhead

rows.name: Ambika (Kushmandini)
rows.features_other: A child on her lap and often a second child standing at her side or holding her finger; a bunch of mangoes in a hand; a mango tree above; a small Jina (Nemi) at the top.
rows.identify_by: A goddess with a child on her lap, a bunch of mangoes and a lion, under a mango tree with a small Jina above.

look_alikes.name: durga / parvati (shiva_devi topic)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Both may ride a lion; Ambikā holds a child and mangoes and has a small Jina above her head.

look_alikes.name: hariti (buddhist topic)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Hārītī holds children too but has no lion and no Jina above.

look_alikes.name: siddhayika
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Siddhāyikā also rides a lion but holds a book and lute, no child.

rows.regions_styles: Worshipped by both sects everywhere; among the commonest Jain goddess images in brass and stone.
rows.dating_clues: One Kushan Mathura image (year 9) already shows her on the back of a Jina.
rows.cautions: Identification only; cannot date.

facts.text: Ambikā's chief marks are the mango tree or bunch of mangoes, the lion mount and a child on her lap or beside her.
facts.quote: The mango tree or a bunch of mangoes, the lion mount, and the child on her lap or standing by her or both are her chief marks of identification.

facts.text: Digambara Kūṣmāṇḍinī: four-armed, two children in her lap, lion cognizance.
facts.quote: Kushmandini, - four-armed, with two children in her lap, and a lion as cognizance.

facts.text: Pratiṣṭhāsāroddhāra 176: green, under a mango tree, rides a lion that was her husband, mangoes in the left hand for her son Priyaṅkara on her lap, the other son Śubhaṅkara holding her finger.
facts.quote: who rests under a mango tree and rides a lion that was her husband in her previous existence

facts.text: The Rūpamaṇḍana counts Ambikā with Cakreśvarī, Padmāvatī and Siddhāyikā as the four most venerable yakṣīs.
facts.quote: Cakresvari, Ambika, Padmavati and Siddhaika.

rows.name: Padmavati
rows.features_other: Cobra hoods (1, 3, 5 or 7) over the head; mount a cock or a cock-headed snake (kukkuṭa-sarpa) in Svetambara texts; a small Pārśva (hooded Jina) above. Mount token wanted: cock / cock-snake.
rows.identify_by: A four-armed goddess with snake hoods over her crown, holding goad, noose, lotus and fruit, with a small hooded Jina above.

look_alikes.name: parshvanatha
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Pārśva is two-armed and in meditation.

look_alikes.name: dharanendra
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Her male partner; often beside her with five or seven hoods.

look_alikes.name: nagini figures (other_hindu topic)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Look for the small hooded Jina above her head.

rows.regions_styles: Very popular in Karnataka (Humcha) and Western India; brass images common in household shrines.
rows.dating_clues: None from type.
rows.cautions: Identification only.

facts.text: Triṣaṣṭi: Padmāvatī rides a kurkuṭa snake, gold-colored, with lotus and noose in the right hands, fruit and goad in the left.
facts.quote: The Goddess Padmavati mounted on a kurkuta snake, gold-coloured, carrying a lotus and a noose in her right hands, a fruit and a goad in her left hands

facts.text: Rūpamaṇḍana: red, rides a cock, holds lotus, noose, goad and citron.
facts.quote: Padmavati has red complexion and she rides on a cock.

facts.text: Her images carry a varying number of hoods and two to four arms.
facts.quote: crowned with a varying number of cobra-hoods and two to four arms

rows.name: Dharanendra (Parshva Yaksha)
rows.features_other: Snake king; cobra-hood crown (five or seven); in Svetambara texts elephant-faced, dark, riding a tortoise, holding snakes, citron and mongoose. Head token wanted: elephant face (yakṣa).
rows.identify_by: A four-armed male with snake hoods and snakes in the upper hands, at Pārśva's right or on his own.

look_alikes.name: padmavati
look_alikes.how_to_tell: female partner, goad and noose

look_alikes.name: balarama (vishnu_krishna topic)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Balarāma has a snake canopy but holds a plough and pestle.

rows.regions_styles: Pedestals of Pārśva images everywhere; separate Deccan bronzes.
rows.dating_clues: None from type.
rows.cautions: Identification only.

facts.text: Pārśva's yakṣa is named Pārśva in the texts; Dharaṇendra is often treated as the yakṣa. Texts make him dark, elephant-faced, cobra-crowned, riding a tortoise, with snakes, citron and mongoose.
facts.quote: the actual name of Parsvanatha's yaksa given in the literature is Parsva, not Dharanendra, who is described as riding a tortoise

facts.text: Mysore drawings: Dharaṇendra four-handed with a snake in each upper hand, tortoise as symbol, five hoods.
facts.quote: four-handed, with a snake in each upper hand and a tortoise as symbol

rows.name: Jain Sarasvati (Shrutadevi)
rows.features_other: Holds a lute (vīṇā) (token wanted: lute / vīṇā); a miniature Jina over her head distinguishes her from Hindu Sarasvatī; Svetambara images mostly on a swan, Digambara on a peacock.
rows.identify_by: A goddess with book, lute, rosary and lotus, and a tiny Jina above her head.

look_alikes.name: sarasvati (other_hindu topic)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Hindu Sarasvatī has no small Jina above her head.

look_alikes.name: siddhayika
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Siddhāyikā holds book and lute too but rides a lion.

rows.regions_styles: Both sects; the 11th-12th-century marble Sarasvatīs of Rajasthan and Gujarat are famous; brass images common.
rows.dating_clues: None from type.
rows.cautions: Without the small Jina an image cannot be called Jain with confidence.

facts.text: In most Svetambara images Sarasvatī rides a swan, in Digambara ones a peacock; standard attributes lotus, lute, book, rosary.
facts.quote: In most of the Svetambara images she is mounted on a swan, in those of the Digambara on a peacock.

facts.text: A miniature Jina over her head distinguishes Jain from Hindu Sarasvatī.
facts.quote: In some images a miniature jina figure appears over her head, and this distinguishes them from Hindu images of Sarasvati.

facts.text: Sarasvatī is regarded as a messenger-goddess of all the Tirthankaras and is often figured in temples and houses.
facts.quote: she is regarded as a Sasanadevi or messenger of all the Tirthakaras, and is frequently figured in temples and private houses.

rows.name: Chakreshvari (Apraticakra)
rows.features_other: The discus (cakra) and the Garuḍa mount (a flying human-bodied eagle) are her constant signs; Svetambara images four or eight arms, Digambara up to twenty.
rows.identify_by: A many-armed goddess holding discs, on Garuḍa, with a small Jina (Ṛṣabha) above.

look_alikes.name: vaishnavi (vishnu / devi topics)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Vaiṣṇavī also has discus and Garuḍa; look for the small Jina above and a bull-emblem Jina nearby.

rows.regions_styles: Both sects; Gyaraspur, Deogarh, Western Indian brass.
rows.dating_clues: None from type.
rows.cautions: Identification only.

facts.text: Cakreśvarī rides Garuḍa and holds discs; Svetambara images have four or eight arms, Digambara two to twenty.
facts.quote: the cakra as one attribute and the eagle mount (as a two- or four-armed flying human being) are her unfailing identification marks.

facts.text: Cakreśvarī resembles Vaiṣṇavī, consort of Viṣṇu.
facts.quote: Cakresvari, the Yaksini of the Jina looks like the Vaisnavi, the wife of Brahmanic Visnu.

rows.name: Siddhayika (Mahavira's yakshi)
rows.features_other: Lute (vīṇā) and book; green or blue complexion in texts; Digambara Mysore drawings show only two hands and a haṃsa cognizance.
rows.identify_by: A goddess on a lion holding a book and a lute.

look_alikes.name: ambika
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Ambikā has a child and mangoes.

look_alikes.name: jain-sarasvati
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Sarasvatī rides a swan or peacock.

rows.regions_styles: Pedestals of Mahāvīra images; Vimala Vasahī, Mt Abu.
rows.dating_clues: None.
rows.cautions: Identification only.

facts.text: Siddhāyikā's unfailing signs are the lion mount with book, lute, fear-not gesture and citron.
facts.quote: Siddhāyikām harita-varṇām simha-vāhanam catur-bhujam, pustak-ābhaya (Nirvāṇakalikā via Tiwari)

facts.text: Digambara Siddhāyinī has only two hands (Mysore drawings).
facts.quote: Siddhayini alone has only two hands.

rows.name: Jain eight auspicious symbols (ashtamangala)
rows.features_other: Svetambara set: svastika, śrīvatsa, nandyāvarta, vardhamānaka (powder box or dish), bhadrāsana (seat), kalaśa (full pot), pair of fish, mirror. Digambara set: umbrella, banner, pot, fly whisk, mirror, seat, fan, vessel. Cast as brass plaques (often in groups of four) for worship; carved on lintels, painted on book covers; drawn in rice.
rows.identify_by: A row or plaque of small symbols: svastika, a nine-armed svastika (nandyāvarta), a pair of fish, a full pot, a mirror.

look_alikes.name: buddhist ashtamangala (buddhist topic)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: The Buddhist set includes the endless knot, conch, umbrella, banner and wheel; the Jain Svetambara set has the nandyāvarta, śrīvatsa, powder box and seat.

rows.regions_styles: Everywhere; brass aṣṭamaṅgala plaques are a common Western Indian household object.
rows.dating_clues: Mathura āyāgapaṭas show an earlier, different set.
rows.cautions: Symbols alone do not identify a Jina; a svastika, śrīvatsa, nandyāvarta, fish or pot under a Jina is an emblem.

facts.text: Svetambara set: svastika, śrīvatsa, nandyāvarta, vardhamānaka, seat, pitcher, fish, mirror.
facts.quote: to wit, a Svastika, Srivatsa, Nandyavarta, Vardhamanaka, state-seat, pitcher, fish and a mirror. (Bhattacharya)

facts.text: Digambara set (Ādipurāṇa, Jambudīvapaṇṇatti): umbrella, banner, pot, chauri, mirror, seat, fan, vessel.
facts.quote: Umbrella, banner, pot, chauri (fly whisk), mirror, seat, fan, and vessel proceed before the Lord

facts.text: The later standard symbols are cast on bronze plaques arranged in groups of four for worship.
facts.quote: The later standardized symbols are found cast on bronze plaques arranged in groups of four for worship in Jaina shrines.

rows.name: Inscription on the back of a Jain brass image: its usual form
rows.features_other: Not a figure: the incised Sanskrit (often Sanskritized Gujarati/Marwari) text on the back or pedestal of the image (token wanted: kind 'inscription').
rows.identify_by: Read in this order: (1) 'saṃvat 1527 varṣe vaiśākha sudi 3' = Vikrama Saṃvat year, month, fortnight (sudi bright / vadi dark), day, often weekday; (2) caste and lineage of the donor (e.g. śrīmāla-jñātīya, ukeśa/osavāla-jñātīya, prāgvāṭa) and gotra; (3) donor 'sā.' (sāha) with wife (bhāryā, bhā.) and sons; (4) purpose: 'śreyase / śreyorthaṃ' (for the merit of ...); (5) the Jina: 'śrī-śāntinātha-bimbaṃ' (image of Śāntinātha), or 'pañcatīrthī', 'caturviṃśati-paṭṭaḥ'; (6) 'kāritaṃ' (caused to be made) 'pratiṣṭhitaṃ' (consecrated; abbreviated 'pra.' or 'prati.') by a named monk 'śrī-...-sūribhiḥ' of a named gaccha (Tapā, Kharatara, Añcala, Pūrṇimā, Nāgendra, Upakeśa ...); (7) sometimes the town.

look_alikes.name: buddhist donative inscription (buddhist topic)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Jain inscriptions name a Jina ('-nātha-bimbaṃ') and a gaccha and sūri; Buddhist ones name a Buddha or bodhisattva and usually the deyadharma formula (not verified here).

rows.regions_styles: Western India, 12th-19th centuries, overwhelmingly 15th-16th; collected in Nahar's Jaina Lekha Saṅgraha and Buddhisāgarasūri's Jaina Dhātu Pratimā Lekha Saṅgraha.
rows.dating_clues: The Saṃvat date is the date of consecration (pratiṣṭhā), not necessarily of casting. Vikrama Saṃvat runs about 57 years ahead of CE (Saṃvat 1165 = c. 1108 CE in Mia's record). Some inscriptions use the Vīra (Mahāvīra) era instead, and misreading the era has produced impossible dates.
rows.cautions: An inscription shows what an image claims, not what it is: see inscription-reading. OCR'd and published readings contain errors; donor and caste names are spelled many ways.

facts.text: Nahar lists what inscriptions usually record: year, month, lunar day, weekday; lineage, gotra and family names; gaccha, branch and gaṇa; names of ācāryas and pupils; places; sometimes craftsmen, kings and ministers.
facts.quote: लेखों पर प्रायः निम्नलिखित बातें लिखी रहती हैं: वर्ष, मास, तिथि, वार आदि ... वंश, गोत्र ... गच्छ, शाखा, गण ... आचार्यों के नाम (inscriptions usually contain: year, month, lunar day, weekday; lineage, gotra; gaccha, branch; ācāryas' names)

facts.text: Typical example (Nahar no. 9): Saṃvat 1527, Vaiśākha bright 3; a Śrīmāla-caste donor with wife and sons, for the merit of his daughter, had an image of Śāntinātha made; consecrated by Lakṣmīsāgarasūri, successor of Ratnaśekharasūri of the Tapā gaccha; resident of Dhandhuka.
facts.quote: saṃvat 1527 varṣe vaiśākha su[di] 3 śrīmāla jñātīya ... putrī ramāī śreyorthaṃ śrī śāntinātha bimbaṃ kāritaṃ pratiṣṭhitaṃ śrī tapā gacche (normalized from OCR)

facts.text: The same formula 'X-bimbaṃ kāritaṃ pratiṣṭhitaṃ ... gacche ... sūribhiḥ' runs through Buddhisāgarasūri's corpus of metal-image inscriptions.
facts.quote: svaśreyorthaṃ śrī-sumatinātha-bimbaṃ kāritaṃ pratiṣṭhitaṃ tapāgacche (Buddhisāgara, normalized)

facts.text: A museum translation of a dated Jain inscription: made in Saṃvat 1165, dark half of Jyeṣṭha, 5th day, a Wednesday, by Jaluka son of Avasara of the Prāgvāṭa lineage (Mia 98.211; translation Phyllis Granoff).
facts.quote: This image was caused to be made in samvat 1165 in the dark half of the month Jyestha, 5th day, a Wednesday

facts.text: Nahar concentrated on metal images because stone inscriptions wear illegible sooner.
facts.quote: पत्थर पर का लेख कुछ काल में अस्पष्ट हो जाता है। अतएव ... धातु परके लेखों को अधिक पढ़ने का प्रयास किया है (stone inscriptions become unclear in time, so I tried to read more of the metal ones)

facts.text: Caste names appear in many spellings: Nahar found the Osvāl caste written eight ways (Ukeśa, Upakeśa, Osavāla ...).
facts.quote: ओसवाल ज्ञातिके नाम लेखोंमें आठ प्रकार से लिखे हुए मिलते हैं (the Osvāl caste name is found written in eight ways)

rows.name: What a Jain image inscription can and cannot tell (copied and misread dates)
rows.features_other: Not a figure (token wanted: kind 'inscription').
rows.identify_by: Use the inscription to name the Jina, donor, caste, gaccha and consecrating monk; then check that the style, casting and wear agree with the date before believing it.
rows.regions_styles: Western Indian brass, 11th-19th centuries; older pieces are much rarer.
rows.dating_clues: The date records consecration; the named monk can be checked against the gaccha's known succession (Nahar's index gives ācāryas with dates). A date that is impossible for the style may be a misread era (Vīra vs Vikrama) or a copied text.
rows.cautions: Later bronzes do carry older inscriptions: a 2023 SOAS study found five of six examined Jain bronzes younger than their inscriptions, and two bronzes (Norwich and Chandigarh) with identical inscriptions down to illegible parts. How often this happens across the market is NOT known (no survey found). An inscription is evidence to weigh, never proof of age or genuineness; specialists examine the image from all sides and its metal.

facts.text: Five of six Jain bronzes studied were younger than their inscriptions suggest; a Norwich bronze (SADACC 275.2) bears an inscription identical, down to illegible parts, to one on a Chandigarh museum bronze (2007.27.3); the authors advise examining images from all sides and analysing the material.
An Ajmer twenty-four-Jina image inscribed 'Vīra Saṃvat 1263' would date to c. 600 CE, which is stylistically impossible; the editors suggest Vikrama Saṃvat was meant.
facts.quote: This date corresponds to A. D. 600 which is stylistically impossible.

facts.text: Inscriptions usually name the Jina outright ('śrī-pārśvanātha-bimbaṃ', 'śrī-vāsupūjya-bimbaṃ'), which identifies the image better than a worn emblem.
facts.quote: śrī pārśvanātha bimbaṃ kāritaṃ pratiṣṭhitaṃ ... śrī vāsupūjya bimbaṃ kāritaṃ (Nahar nos. 8, 3, normalized)

facts.text: Nahar's corpus provides indexes of castes, gotras, gacchas and ācāryas with dates, the tools for checking a donor or monk.
facts.quote: Containing Index of Places, glossary of names of Shravaka Castes and Gotras of Gachhas and Acharyas with dates.

paintings.title: Indian paintings: schools, and the writing and seals on them

facts.text: Artists' names on Akbar-period illustrations were added afterward by clerks of the court or imperial library, not by the painters, and some were corrected by smearing gold paint over a wrong name.
facts.quote: none of them is in the writing of the artist himself. They were subsequently added by the clerks or munshis, employed either at the court of Akbar or in the office of the imperial library.

facts.text: Most Akbar-period pictures are the work of two artists, one making the sketch (tarh) and one doing the painting ('amal); a third sometimes painted the faces.
facts.quote: In the majority of Akbari pictures two artists only have combined, the one making the tarrah or sketch, and the other doing the 'amal, work, or painting.

facts.text: The Hamza-nama, the first major project of Akbar's workshop, was painted on cotton (mounted on paper), in 14 volumes of 100 illustrations, of which a little over 10 percent survive.
facts.quote: Originally in 14 volumes of 100 illustrations each, just a little more than 10 percent of the pages survive.

facts.text: European prints in Akbar's collection supplied distant cityscapes and rolling hills in late Akbar-period paintings such as the Akbar-nama of c. 1602-03.
facts.quote: European prints had made their way into Akbar's collection, and they provided the visual source for distant cityscapes, rolling hills, and less densely colored paintings.

facts.text: The halo was not used in Akbar-period painting; portraits of Akbar or his predecessors with a halo were made after Jahangir introduced it, or the halo was added later.
facts.quote: it is found in no likenesses of his predecessors painted previous to his own reign

facts.text: Akbar-period manuscript pages carry manuscript folio and picture numbers, e.g. 'Folio 229, painting 97' on a Chester Beatty Akbar-nama page; its borders were added in the 1700s and the calligraphy on the back was mounted upside down.
facts.quote: Folio 229, painting 97 from the so-called Chester Beatty Akbarnama

schools.cautions: Artists' names written on Akbar-period pages are later clerks' attributions and were sometimes corrected; they are evidence, not signatures. Pages from dispersed manuscripts were often remounted with borders and calligraphy of other dates. Style can place a page in the reign; it cannot prove that a page is not a later copy.
schools.name: Mughal painting, reign of Akbar
schools.region: North India: Agra, Fatehpur Sikri, Lahore (the imperial workshop moved with the court)
schools.patrons: Emperor Akbar; great nobles such as Abd al-Rahim Khan-i Khanan (patron of the Freer Ramayana)
how_to_recognize: Mostly book illustration: crowded, energetic narrative scenes for Persian texts (Hamza-nama, Tuti-nama, Akbar-nama, Razm-nama, Ramayana), with Persian text panels on the same or facing page
The early Hamza-nama pages are very large and painted on cotton, not paper
No halo around the emperor's head in paintings made during his reign; a halo on Akbar was added under or after Jahangir
Late in the reign, distant cityscapes and rolling hills borrowed from European prints
Many hands on one picture: one designed, another painted, sometimes a third did the faces
schools.writing_found: Persian (nasta'liq) notes in the margin or below the picture naming the artists, often two names, one for the design (tarh) and one for the painting ('amal); these were written by court or library clerks, not by the painters. Manuscript folio numbers and picture numbers (e.g. 'painting 126'). Persian text of the story. Later library notes and seals (see the mughal_seals topic).

look_alikes.how_to_tell: Jahangir-period work favors single portraits, natural-history studies and album pages, and gives the reigning emperor a halo
18th- and 19th-century copies repeat Akbar-period compositions with stiffer, less experienced drawing and deviations from the original
Deccani pages of the same date have different figure types, colors and poetic, fantastic subjects; museum attribution rests on comparison, not on one sign

schools.later_copies: Brown records later facsimiles of genuine Akbar-period pictures (e.g. British Museum album Or. 18807) with deviations and a less experienced hand. Bazaar artists kept tracings of famous pictures to reproduce them on demand.

facts.text: Jahangir adopted the halo for the reigning emperor; in Mughal painting it was reserved for the ruling sovereign, and Rajput painters later borrowed it as an imperial motif.
facts.quote: In Mughal painting it was reserved strictly for the ruling sovereign of the empire

facts.text: Album leaves often have calligraphy on one side and a painting on the other, the two unrelated.
facts.quote: on one side of a Mughal miniature a few lines of poetry ... and the reverse occupied by a painting, but in no case has either work any relation to the other.

facts.text: A portrait of Raja Suraj Singh Rathor in the Prince Khurram Album (assembled 1612) is inscribed in the lower inner border in the prince's own hand.
facts.quote: inscribed in hand of Shah Jahan in lower inner border: shabihi Raja Suraj-Singh Rathor

facts.text: A single album page can combine work of three dates: a Jahangir-period painting (c. 1620), calligraphy dated AH 1020 (1611-12) and borders of the mid-18th century.
facts.quote: ca. 1620; borders mid-18th century; calligraphy AH 1020 (1611-12)

facts.text: A later hand sometimes misidentified sitters: Brown notes a durbar picture wrongly inscribed 'Jahangir Padshah'.
facts.quote: The original picture is erroneously inscribed 'Jahangir Padshah' in the writing of a later hand.

schools.cautions: A halo dates the custom, not the sheet: later painters gave haloes to emperors in copies. An inscription naming the emperor can be wrong (Brown records a picture 'erroneously inscribed Jahangir Padshah in the writing of a later hand').
schools.name: Mughal painting, reign of Jahangir
schools.region: North India: Agra, Lahore, Allahabad (Jahangir's court as prince, c. 1600-04), and wherever the court traveled
schools.patrons: Emperor Jahangir (as Prince Salim from c. 1600); princes such as Khurram (later Shah Jahan)
how_to_recognize: Single portraits and small scenes for albums (muraqqa') rather than crowded book pages
The reigning emperor shown with a gold halo (nimbus); no one else in the royal house gets one
Close, naturalistic studies of animals, birds and flowers
Wide album borders decorated in gold, with calligraphy on the reverse
Jahangir-period dress (pointed-skirted jama, short sash, small turbans) is a dating clue that also appears in Rajput and Pahari pictures of the time
schools.writing_found: Persian names of sitters, sometimes in an emperor's own hand (e.g. shabih-i Raja Suraj Singh Rathor, 'likeness of Raja Suraj Singh Rathor', written by Shah Jahan as prince). Occasionally a tiny artist's name hidden on a detail of the picture, which may be the painter's own. Unrelated Persian calligraphy on the back of album leaves. Library notes and seals (see mughal_seals).

look_alikes.how_to_tell: Shah Jahan-period portraits are more formal and polished, with heavier gold and lavish flowered borders
Later portraits of Jahangir repeat a fixed type (same pose, same costume, same background); a museum may date such a 'Jahangir' to c. 1800

schools.later_copies: Portraits of Jahangir were copied for two centuries from tracings; museums hold Jahangir portraits dated early 18th century (a tracing) and c. 1800.

facts.text: Brown characterizes Shah Jahan-period painting by lavish display and over-elaboration of color and detail.
facts.quote: the lavish display which is the main characteristic of the painting under Shah Jahan, that sense of over-ripeness which is the sure sign of decline.

facts.text: A Shah Jahan album page is inscribed 'amal-i Bichitr, 'the work of Bichitr', below a portrait of Aurangzeb that was added to the page after 1658.
facts.quote: inscribed below portrait : 'amal-i Bichitr

facts.text: Some tiny Shah Jahan-period portraits were first set as 'portrait jewels' and later mounted on album pages with 18th-century borders.
facts.quote: Originally, it was in a gemstone setting as a 'portrait jewel' to be worn by family and supporters at court.

facts.text: Shah Jahan built and occupied the Delhi palace-fort in 1648; before that Akbar preferred Agra and Jahangir Lahore, so 'Delhi qalam' names the court manner, not the place a picture was painted.
facts.quote: It does not follow, however, that all the pictures in the Delhi qalam were painted at the Mughal capital

schools.cautions: Imperial pages were altered: a portrait of Aurangzeb was painted into a Shah Jahan sunburst page after 1658. Borders were often added in the 1700s. An 'amal-i inscription is an attribution that may be later or apocryphal (see deccani_bijapur).
schools.name: Mughal painting, reign of Shah Jahan
schools.region: Agra, Lahore, and Delhi (Shahjahanabad, palace occupied 1648)
schools.patrons: Emperor Shah Jahan; Prince Dara Shikoh
how_to_recognize: Formal, highly finished court portraits and darbar scenes; emperor in profile with a halo
Lavish gold and jewel-like detail; standing courtiers in profile against plain grounds
Album borders filled with gold flowers, birds or small figures (e.g. the Late Shah Jahan Album)
Tiny portraits made as 'portrait jewels' to be worn, later remounted on album pages
schools.writing_found: Persian attributions in nasta'liq such as 'amal-i Bichitr ('the work of Bichitr') below the portrait; Persian titles of the emperor (e.g. 'Padshah Jahan' under a sunburst); calligraphy on the reverse; library notes and seals (mughal_seals).

look_alikes.how_to_tell: Jahangir-period work is less formal, with more natural-history subjects and lighter borders
Shah Jahan hunting or darbar subjects were repainted in the late 18th century (one is dated c. 1790 by the Freer Gallery)

schools.later_copies: Late-18th-century versions of Shah Jahan subjects (e.g. 'Shah Jahan and his son Dara Shikoh hunting', ca. 1790, Freer Gallery F1907.196).

facts.text: Brown dates the end of the Mughal school's living phase to the middle of the 17th century; Coomaraswamy puts its practical end at Aurangzeb's death in 1706. The two disagree by half a century.
facts.quote: it begins with Akbar (a.d. 1556 to 1606), and is practically finished with the death of Aurangzeb in 1706.

facts.text: A Muhammad Shah-period court scene (c. 1735) carries a Persian note on the back saying 'Chitarman the painter carried out the task' at the emperor's command, and a seal of a servant of Muhammad Shah.
facts.quote: Chitarman-i musawwar amal nimud

facts.text: Muhammad Shah (r. 1719-48) commissioned Hindu subjects, and mid-1700s Mughal painting favored scenes of court women's domestic life.
facts.quote: scenes of domestic life among women of the court were a favorite subject for the imperial artists.

facts.text: As the court declined, painters moved to Lucknow, Hyderabad, Patna, Mysore and Tanjore, producing local styles (qalams); some Muslim families stayed in Delhi as bazaar painters.
facts.quote: So came into use the word qalam, which may be freely translated by the word 'style'

schools.cautions: Brown and Coomaraswamy (writing 1916-24) judged post-1650 Mughal painting harshly; that is their taste, not a statement about any particular item.
schools.name: Later Mughal painting (Aurangzeb to Bahadur Shah II)
schools.region: Delhi; painters dispersed to Lucknow, Murshidabad, Hyderabad, Patna and the Rajput and Pahari courts
schools.patrons: Aurangzeb (little patronage), Muhammad Shah (r. 1719-48) and later emperors; nobles; increasingly the bazaar and, after c. 1800, the British
how_to_recognize: Under Muhammad Shah: court women on terraces, night and festival scenes, Hindu subjects, tiered compositions
Repeated stock types for portraits: same pose, hands, costume and background
Paler, smoother finish; copies after earlier imperial portraits are common
schools.writing_found: Persian notes on the back, e.g. an artist's statement of commission with a servant's seal naming Muhammad Shah; Persian or later Urdu and English labels naming the sitter.

look_alikes.how_to_tell: Provincial (Lucknow, Murshidabad) work of the same decades is attributed by style and provenance; inscriptions rarely settle it
Copies of earlier emperors made in this period are late Mughal works, not works of the earlier reign

schools.later_copies: See mughal_later_copies and delhi_ivory_miniatures.

facts.text: After the mid-17th century portrait painting became a trade of reproducing copies by paper stencils and pouncing; painters' families kept large stocks of tracing-paper stencils.
facts.quote: From the type-portrait careful tracings were made, and by means of 'pouncing' each copy, any number of duplicates could be prepared.

facts.text: Bazaar artists copied pictures of earlier periods and styles, which has caused confusion in classification.
facts.quote: as they not infrequently consist of copies of pictures belonging to an earlier period and style, some confusion in classifying these has naturally arisen.

facts.text: Museums hold later Mughal-emperor portraits: 'Emperor Jahangir holding an orb', tracing and color, early 18th century (Freer F1907.592); 'Portrait of Emperor Jahangir', c. 1800 (Art Institute 1981.249).
facts.quote: Tracing and color on paper

facts.text: In stock portraits the figure always appeared with the same pose, look, hands, costume and background.
facts.quote: a stereotyped composition with the same pose, the same look, the same arrangement of the hands, the same costume, the same background

schools.cautions: A copy can itself be two or three hundred years old; 'copy' is not 'fake'. A label naming Akbar or Shah Jahan is not a date. Never treat an emperor's name as evidence of age.
schools.name: Later copies and stock portraits of Mughal emperors (18th-20th century)
schools.region: Delhi, Agra, Lucknow, Lahore, Jaipur; today Jaipur, Udaipur and Delhi workshops
schools.patrons: Bazaar buyers, Indian gentry, British visitors, later tourists
how_to_recognize: The same pose, look, hands, costume and background recur across many sheets of the same sitter
Pricked or dotted outlines (pouncing) or tracing paper, the tools for reproducing a type
Portraits of earlier emperors (Akbar, Jahangir, Shah Jahan) painted much later; museums date some to c. 1790-1800
Weaker drawing and deviations from the known original
schools.writing_found: Later Persian, Urdu or English labels naming the emperor; such labels date from the copy, and may misname the sitter.

look_alikes.how_to_tell: An original court portrait is unique in its drawing; a stock type repeats, and is usually weaker
The 19th- and 20th-century Delhi trade put the same stock emperor portraits on ivory or bone disks

schools.later_copies: This row is itself the later-copies row for Mughal portraiture.

facts.text: Calligraphy on one side and a painting on the other of an album leaf are normally unrelated works.
facts.quote: in no case has either work any relation to the other.

facts.text: Museum records give separate dates for picture, border and calligraphy, e.g. painting c. 1620, borders mid-18th century, calligraphy AH 1020 (1611-12).
facts.quote: ca. 1620; borders mid-18th century; calligraphy AH 1020 (1611-12)

facts.text: Pages were remounted with later borders, sometimes carelessly: an Akbar-nama page has borders added c. 1700s and its reverse calligraphy mounted upside down; a Golconda drawing of c. 1680-1700 has a border added in the 1800s.
facts.quote: borders added c. 1700s and mounted upside down

facts.text: Some Deccani album pages have gold-sprinkled borders.
facts.quote: mounted with gold-sprinkled borders

schools.cautions: Painting, border and calligraphy may be three different dates. Date each part separately; a dated calligraphy panel does not date the painting on the other side.
schools.name: Album leaves (muraqqa' pages): borders, calligraphy and remounting
schools.region: Mughal, Deccani and provincial courts; Persian and Indian albums
schools.patrons: Emperors, princes and nobles who assembled albums; later dealers who remounted pages
how_to_recognize: A painting set in ruled margins inside a wider border of a different paper, often blue, buff or gold-sprinkled, decorated in gold
A calligraphy panel (Persian verses in nasta'liq) on the reverse, unrelated to the picture
Borders sometimes contain small figures or flowers that suit the sitter (scholars and soldiers around a general)
schools.writing_found: Persian calligraphy on the reverse (sometimes signed and dated by the calligrapher, e.g. AH 1020); captions or attributions in the margins; library seals and notes (see mughal_seals).

look_alikes.how_to_tell: Fakers paint on old manuscript or album pages; but genuine album leaves also carry unrelated old text, so the text alone decides nothing

schools.later_copies: Borders were added or replaced in the 18th and 19th centuries; museum records state 'borders added c. 1700s' or 'border added 1800s'.

facts.text: From Shah Jahan's reign onward painters drifted from the center and set up bazaar schools in Lucknow, Hyderabad, Poona, Benares, Mathura, Mysore and Tanjore; the change of setting produced distinct provincial styles.
facts.quote: There is a distinctive character in the work of the Lucknow artists

facts.text: About 1730 the decline of Mughal patronage drove the ancestors of the Patna painters from Delhi to Murshidabad; from there some later moved to Patna.
facts.quote: About 1730 the general decline of patronage which attended the break-up of the Mughal empire forced these artists to migrate again, and they left Delhi and settled at Murshidabad.

facts.text: A Murshidabad ragamala page of c. 1755 names its mode in gold at the top.
facts.quote: identified at top in gold: ragini todi

facts.text: Brown (1918) describes early-19th-century Lucknow painting as mainly portraiture, much affected by European influence.
facts.quote: much impregnated with bad European influence. Portraiture was the main theme

schools.cautions: Attribution between Lucknow, Murshidabad and Delhi is often uncertain even for museums ('Murshidabad or Lucknow').
schools.name: Provincial Mughal painting: Lucknow (Awadh) and Murshidabad (Bengal), 18th century
schools.region: Lucknow and Faizabad (Awadh); Murshidabad (Bengal)
schools.patrons: Nawabs of Awadh; Nawabs of Bengal at Murshidabad; nobles; later British officials
how_to_recognize: Mughal manner on a provincial scale: court ladies on terraces, night and festival scenes, river views, ragamala sets
Murshidabad ragamala pages may name the ragini in gold at the top
Lucknow work of the late 18th and early 19th centuries shows strong European influence and portraiture
schools.writing_found: Persian or Devanagari ragini names (e.g. 'ragini todi' in gold); Persian calligraphy on reverse; later British labels.

look_alikes.how_to_tell: Delhi and provincial work of the same decades overlap; museums often write 'Murshidabad or Lucknow'
Patna and Company work after c. 1760-1800 drops the court subjects for scenes of trades and castes, on European paper

schools.later_copies: Not separately documented in sources read (see gaps).

facts.text: Bijapur kept its independence until conquered by Aurangzeb in 1686.
facts.quote: kept its independence until conquered by Aurangzeb in 1686

facts.text: The Adil Shahs of Bijapur adopted the halo in their portraiture.
facts.quote: the Adil Shahs of Bijapur, adopted the symbol in their portraiture

facts.text: Pages of Ibrahim Adil Shah II's Kitab-i Nauras (1618) carry Deccani Urdu lyrics in nasta'liq script.
facts.quote: Deccani Urdu (Karnati) lyrics in nasta'liq script

facts.text: A Bijapur 'marbled picture' (c. 1650) uses more applications of marbled colorant than any other known example, and bears an apocryphal attribution inscription.
facts.quote: apocryphal inscription lower left: 'amal-i mir Kalan 904

schools.cautions: Attribution inscriptions on Deccani pages can be apocryphal: Cleveland catalogues one as 'apocryphal inscription lower left: amal-i mir Kalan'. Bijapur fell to Aurangzeb in 1686, which ends the court style.
schools.name: Deccani painting: Bijapur (Adil Shahi court)
schools.region: Bijapur, Karnataka (Deccan)
schools.patrons: Sultan Ibrahim Adil Shah II (r. 1580-1627), Muhammad Adil Shah (r. 1627-56)
how_to_recognize: Poetic, dreamlike pictures and portraits; musical and literary themes
Marbled paper used for whole pictures (rare virtuoso technique)
Rulers sometimes shown with a halo, a Mughal device the Adil Shahs adopted
European figures observed in detail (ruffs, cuffs)
schools.writing_found: Persian and Deccani Urdu (Dakhni) verse in nasta'liq, e.g. Ibrahim Adil Shah II's Kitab-i Nauras songs; Persian verso labels naming the scene; later and sometimes apocryphal attributions such as 'amal-i Mir Kalan.

look_alikes.how_to_tell: Golconda and Bijapur are separated by museums on stylistic grounds; sources read give no single sign
Mughal pages of the same date are more documentary; Deccani pages more lyrical and fantastic

schools.later_copies: No source read describes later copies specific to Bijapur.

facts.text: Deccan artists developed composite creatures made up of many figures, for albums shown at elite gatherings.
facts.quote: created inventive images of composite creatures made up of figures that invite extended close looking.

facts.text: A Golconda portrait of Sultan Abdullah Qutb Shah (c. 1635) uses subdued colors with gold accents and is mounted with gold-sprinkled borders.
facts.quote: executed with subdued colors that complement the gold accents

facts.text: A Golconda composite elephant (c. 1590) has Persian verses in nasta'liq in the top and bottom borders.
facts.quote: Calligraphy of Persian verses in top and bottom borders, in nasta'liq script

schools.cautions: The end date (1687, Mughal conquest) comes from general history, not from the sources read (single-sourced as a date; see gaps).
schools.name: Deccani painting: Golconda (Qutb Shahi court)
schools.region: Golconda and Hyderabad, Telangana (Deccan)
schools.patrons: Qutb Shahi sultans, e.g. Abdullah Qutb Shah (1614-74)
how_to_recognize: Composite creatures (an elephant made of many animals and figures) for album entertainment
Portraits in subdued colors with gold accents, sometimes on gold-sprinkled borders
Persian verses in nasta'liq panels above and below the picture
schools.writing_found: Persian verses in nasta'liq in top and bottom borders; later borders.

look_alikes.how_to_tell: Distinguished by specialists on style; sources read give no one sign
Composite animals were also traced and recolored in 18th-century Mughal workshops (Freer F1907.642, a tracing)

schools.later_copies: Composite-animal pictures were traced and copied in the 18th century (Freer F1907.642, 'tracing and color on paper').

facts.text: Hyderabad painting is close to the Delhi manner but more minute and smaller in handling.
facts.quote: a form of painting very much akin to the Delhi qalam, but rather more minute in its technique and smaller in handling generally.

facts.text: Museums date Hyderabad and Aurangabad ragamala and terrace scenes to the 18th century (e.g. Cleveland 2013.291, c. 1720-30; Freer F1924.8, c. 1725; Cleveland 2003.344, Aurangabad, mid-1700s).

schools.cautions: Brown saw it as a link between Mughal painting and the southern (Mysore, Tanjore) developments; that is his hypothesis.
schools.name: Deccani painting: Hyderabad and Aurangabad (18th-19th century)
schools.region: Hyderabad and Aurangabad (Deccan)
schools.patrons: Nizams of Hyderabad (Asaf Jahi) and their nobles
how_to_recognize: Close to Delhi-style Mughal painting but more minute in technique and smaller
Ladies on terraces, ragamala sets
schools.writing_found: Ragini names; Persian labels.

look_alikes.how_to_tell: Brown: Hyderabad work is 'more minute' than Delhi work of the time

schools.later_copies: Not documented in sources read.

facts.text: A Mewar elephant-fight painting (c. 1670-75) carries a long Devanagari caption naming Maharana Raj Singh, his companions and the elephants, and a price 'Price 115 rupees' written in red.
facts.quote: Price 115 rupees [in red]

facts.text: A painting from Bundi (c. 1740) bears an Udaipur royal inventory number on its back, along with a 20th-century collector's seal.
facts.quote: Verso: Udaipur inventory 21/57

facts.text: Wall paintings survive in the island palaces of Udaipur, and Udaipur is presumed one of the great Rajasthani centers.
facts.quote: Wall-paintings are still preserved at Udaipur (the island palaces)

facts.text: An inscription in nagari in the upper margin identifies a Mewar noble (Rao Ram Chand of Bedla, 1740s), in the manner of Amar Singh II period painting.
facts.quote: An inscription in the upper margin in nagari identifies the subject as Rao Sri Ram Chand

schools.cautions: An inventory number or price on the back records a royal collection, not the painter's school; collections absorbed works from other courts.
schools.name: Rajput painting: Mewar (Udaipur)
schools.region: Mewar, southern Rajasthan; capital Udaipur; thikanas such as Bedla, Devgarh, Sawar
schools.patrons: Maharanas of Mewar (e.g. Raj Singh I, r. 1652-80; Amar Singh II, r. 1698-1710; Bhim Singh, r. 1778-1828) and nobles
how_to_recognize: Bold flat color and strong outline in 17th-century manuscript sets (Bhagavata Purana, Gita Govinda, Sat Sai)
18th- and 19th-century court scenes, processions, elephant fights and portraits of the Maharana
Long Rajasthani captions in Devanagari across the top margin identifying people, places and animals
schools.writing_found: Rajasthani in Devanagari: names of the Maharana and courtiers, place, event, even elephants' names; royal inventory numbers and prices on the back (e.g. 'Price 115 rupees' in red); Udaipur palace inventory numbers (e.g. 'Udaipur inventory 21/57').

look_alikes.how_to_tell: Udaipur also collected other schools' paintings: a Udaipur inventory number shows ownership, not that Mewar painters made it
Udaipur is a center of modern miniature production; modern copies of Mewar court scenes exist (see that row)

schools.later_copies: Modern miniatures in Mewar style are made for the market; see tourist_miniatures_paper.

facts.text: A Bundi ragamala page of c. 1610 shows a noble in Mughal dress including a Jahangir-period turban, and is labeled with the ragini name and a number.
facts.quote: ramakali. 11

facts.text: Museums attribute many 18th-century pages to 'Bundi or Kota', 'Bundi-Kota' or 'Bundi or Raghogarh'.
facts.quote: Bundi or possibly Kota

schools.cautions: The 'Bundi/Kota/Uniara/Raghogarh' boundary is uncertain in museum attributions.
schools.name: Rajput painting: Bundi
schools.region: Bundi, Hadoti region, southeastern Rajasthan (related to Kota and Uniara)
schools.patrons: Hada Rajput rulers of Bundi
how_to_recognize: Ragamala and Rasikapriya sets from c. 1610 onward; early pages show nobles in Jahangir-period Mughal dress
Dark night skies, lush foliage, dawn suns behind trees in Krishna scenes
Shares a vocabulary with Kota; museums often write 'Bundi or Kota'
schools.writing_found: Short Devanagari labels naming the ragini with a set number (e.g. 'ramakali. 11', 'gujari ragani. 14'); explanatory Rajasthani captions; later collectors' seals and inventory numbers.

look_alikes.how_to_tell: Kota broke away from Bundi in 1624 and specialised in royal hunts; many 18th-century pages are 'Bundi or Kota'

schools.later_copies: Not specifically documented in sources read.

facts.text: Beginning around 1660 Kota artists made images of rulers hunting, with calligraphic contour lines and highly textured landscapes.
facts.quote: Beginning around 1660, artists in Kota began creating extraordinary images of rulers hunting game

facts.text: A Kota hunt of 1787 names the ruler, gives the date as Samvat 1844 and names the painter Hans Raj Joshi.
facts.quote: samvat 1844 vasakih sudi 14 ... Joshi Hans Raj

facts.text: A Kota darbar painting is dated Samvat 1889 (1832) in two Devanagari inscriptions, one naming the painter.
facts.quote: chabi darabara sari rama siga ji ri cha samata 1889 posa badi 5

facts.text: Kota became an independent kingdom in 1624 and its artists were known for dynamic, idealized portrayals of rulers.
facts.quote: Kota artists were known for dynamic and idealized portrayals of their rulers

schools.cautions: Convert Samvat dates by subtracting 57 (or 56 for the part of the year after the new year); see heirloomapp.io/marks/indian-dates.
schools.name: Rajput painting: Kota
schools.region: Kota, Hadoti region, southeastern Rajasthan
schools.patrons: Raos and Maharaos of Kota (e.g. Jagat Singh, Umed Singh, Ram Singh II, r. 1827/28-66)
how_to_recognize: Royal hunts in dense jungle: from c. 1660, animals drawn with calligraphic contour lines in textured landscapes
Idealized, dynamic portrayals of the ruler; later (19th c.) blocks of lavender, salmon, orange and teal
Ram Singh II-period processions, hunts and darbars with many figures
schools.writing_found: Devanagari inscriptions with the ruler's titles, the event, a Vikram Samvat date (e.g. 'samvat 1844 ... sudi 14' = 1787) and sometimes the painter's name (e.g. Hans Raj Joshi); numbers on the back.

look_alikes.how_to_tell: Hunt subjects and the ruler's names in the caption point to Kota; style overlaps

schools.later_copies: Not specifically documented in sources read.

facts.text: Fresh palette and dramatically elongated eyes, especially on the women, are hallmarks of the most celebrated Kishangarh works.
facts.quote: The fresh palette and dramatically elongated eyes, especially on the women, are hallmarks of the most celebrated works from this Rajput court.

facts.text: A Kishangarh manuscript written in Samvat 1802 (1744-45) carries Rajasthani captions with scene numbers above each picture.
facts.quote: bhava 35

facts.text: A Kishangarh painting of c. 1750-60 has a Persian-script attribution 'amal-i Sitram.
facts.quote: upper left: amal-i Sitram

schools.cautions: Facial type alone is a weak sign: the Kishangarh face is easy to copy.
schools.name: Rajput painting: Kishangarh
schools.region: Kishangarh (and Rupnagar), central Rajasthan
schools.patrons: Rathore rulers of Kishangarh, especially Savant Singh (r. 1748-57, poet as Nagari Das) and Sardar Singh
how_to_recognize: Dramatically elongated eyes, especially on women; fresh palette
Lake and garden settings with white marble terraces
Savant Singh and his consort Bani Thani as Krishna and Radha
schools.writing_found: Devanagari captions in Rajasthani with scene numbers (e.g. 'bhava 35'); Devanagari numbers; occasionally a Persian-script attribution ('amal-i Sitaram); Jain colophons in manuscripts painted at Kishangarh with Samvat dates.

look_alikes.how_to_tell: The 'Bani Thani' face is among the most copied images in modern miniature workshops (no source read documents this; see gaps)

schools.later_copies: Modern copies of the Bani Thani image are widely sold; not documented in sources read.

facts.text: Coomaraswamy singles out the enormous turbans of the rajas of Jodhpur in Rajasthani portraits.
facts.quote: particularly the enormous erections of the rajas of Jodhpur

facts.text: A Jodhpur painting dated 1817 has a Devanagari note on the back recording that it was 'opened' in V.S. 1864 Bhadrapad sudi 14.
facts.quote: Ghera Khulayo 1864 Bhadrapad Sud 14

facts.text: A Marwar ragamala page of c. 1630 shows a youth in the pearl and ruby earrings fashionable under Jahangir.
facts.quote: he wears the pearl and ruby earrings that came into style during the reign of the Mughal emperor Jahangir

schools.cautions: A Samvat note on the back may record a later event (opening, inventory) rather than the painting date.
schools.name: Rajput painting: Marwar (Jodhpur, Nagaur)
schools.region: Marwar, western Rajasthan: Jodhpur, Nagaur, Pali
schools.patrons: Rathore rulers of Jodhpur (e.g. Man Singh, r. 1803-43) and thakurs
how_to_recognize: Early 17th-century ragamala sets with Jahangir-period jewelry and dress
18th-19th-century equestrian portraits and court scenes
Very large turbans on Jodhpur rulers in portraits
schools.writing_found: Devanagari notes on the back with Samvat dates, sometimes recording when a painting was opened or inventoried ('ghera khulayo', 'opened', V.S. 1864); ragini names on the front.

look_alikes.how_to_tell: Neighboring Rathore court; attributions rest on style and inscriptions

schools.later_copies: Not specifically documented in sources read.

facts.text: Bikaner paintings carry Devanagari notes on the back naming the painter (Ruknuddin, Nur Muhammad), the text, the folio and a Samvat date.
facts.quote: rukdin ro sam. 1743 pota raskapriya am.52

facts.text: A Bikaner artist portrayed Raja Jagat Singh of Kota (c. 1670-75) with a nimbus and flowers in each hand, imperial motifs from portraits of Shah Jahan.
