facts.quote: represented by a Bikaner artist with a radiant nimbus and holding flowers in each hand

facts.text: Coomaraswamy names Bikaner among the great centers of Rajasthani painting, with early-17th-century murals in the old palace and Chinese clouds on lacquered shields.
facts.quote: particularly at Bikaner, where true Chinese clouds are painted on the lacquered shields

schools.cautions: Bikaner artists also painted rulers of other states (a Bikaner artist's portrait of Raja Jagat Singh of Kota), so the sitter does not decide the school.
schools.name: Rajput painting: Bikaner
schools.region: Bikaner, northwestern Rajasthan
schools.patrons: Rathore rulers of Bikaner (e.g. Anup Singh, r. 1669-98)
how_to_recognize: Refined, Mughal-influenced style practiced by Muslim artist families (usta) at a Hindu court
Rasikapriya and Bhagavata Purana sets; portraits with Mughal imperial motifs
Old palace wall paintings and Chinese-style clouds on lacquer
schools.writing_found: Devanagari notes on the back with the artist's name, the text, folio number and a Samvat date (e.g. 'rukdin ro sam. 1743 ... am. 52' = by Ruknuddin, 1686, folio 52).

look_alikes.how_to_tell: Bikaner work often looks Mughal; Hindu subjects and Devanagari verso notes with Samvat dates point to Bikaner

schools.later_copies: Not specifically documented in sources read.

facts.text: The most familiar Rajasthani painting is 18th-century Jaipur, including large working drawings mostly pricked for pouncing.
facts.quote: working drawings (mostly pricked for reproduction by pouncing) designed for two large paintings on cloth

facts.text: Jaipur portraits are differentiated from Mughal ones by a more monumental, idealized treatment with less relief; copies of Mughal works occur among them.
facts.quote: clearly differentiated from Mughal works by a more monumental and idealistic treatment, and less relief.

facts.text: A large Jaipur ragamala set of c. 1750-70 is in the Art Institute of Chicago (1962.147 series), public domain.

schools.cautions: Pricked outlines show a design meant for reproduction; they do not by themselves date a sheet.
schools.name: Rajput painting: Amber and Jaipur
schools.region: Amber, then Jaipur (founded 1727), eastern Rajasthan
schools.patrons: Kachhwaha rulers (e.g. Sawai Jai Singh, Sawai Pratap Singh), long-serving Mughal generals such as Raja Ram Singh of Amber
how_to_recognize: 18th-century ragamala sets: polished, delicate and 'jewelled', with formal gardens and fountains
Large cartoons pricked for pouncing, made for big paintings on cloth
Portraits more monumental and idealized than Mughal ones, with less modeling; white accordion-pleated court skirts
19th-century popular work in cruder forms, Vaishnava and musical subjects
schools.writing_found: Ragini names; Devanagari captions; numbers. Pouncing holes along outlines on working drawings.

look_alikes.how_to_tell: Jaipur painters also copied Mughal works; Coomaraswamy says copies of Mughal works are sometimes found among Jaipur portraits
Jaipur is today a main center of new miniatures made in old styles

schools.later_copies: Jaipur workshops produce modern miniatures in Mughal and Rajput styles; see tourist_miniatures_paper. Coomaraswamy (1916) notes Jaipur, with Mathura, as a center for paper stencils (sanjhi).

facts.text: Early Pahari ('Jammu') pictures have hot coloring, silver as well as gold, and sometimes beetle-wing fragments for jewelry.
facts.quote: A remarkable feature is the occasional use of fragments of beetles' wings to represent jewellery

facts.text: Most of these pictures have red borders on which a legend may be written in white.
facts.quote: Most of the pictures have red borders, on which a legend may be written in white

facts.text: The characteristic inscriptions are short labels in the local dialect in Takri script.
facts.quote: the most characteristic inscriptions are short labels in the local dialect, written in the very illegible Dogra Takri character.

facts.text: Pages of the Shangri Ramayana (c. 1700-25) are numbered on the front and carry a book-and-chapter reference on the back.

schools.cautions: Terminology changed: Coomaraswamy (1916) called this group 'Jammu'; museums now say Basohli or name other hill states. Beetle wing has flaked away on many pages.
schools.name: Pahari painting: Basohli (and related early Pahari styles)
schools.region: Basohli and neighboring hill states (Jammu, Nurpur, Mankot, Bilaspur), Jammu and Kashmir / Himachal Pradesh
schools.patrons: Balauria rajas of Basohli (e.g. Kirpal Pal) and neighboring hill rajas
how_to_recognize: Hot, saturated color; red borders on which a label may be written in white; parts of the picture crossing the border
Very large eyes, pupil centered even in profile; sloping forehead
High horizon with a narrow strip of stormy sky; crimson lightning in night scenes
Fragments of green beetle wing-case used for emeralds in jewelry; silver as well as gold
schools.writing_found: Short labels in Takri script in local Pahari dialect; Sanskrit verses in Devanagari, often on the back; chapter and folio numbers (e.g. Shangri Ramayana 'bal. 70' and '13').

look_alikes.how_to_tell: Guler and Kangra work after c. 1740 is cooler, more naturalistic and finer in line, without beetle wing

schools.later_copies: Not specifically documented in sources read.

facts.text: Members of a Guler artist family had worked in the Mughal imperial workshop at Lahore and brought naturalism and refinement to Guler.
facts.quote: Some members of a family of artists of Guler had worked in the Mughal imperial workshop in Lahore

facts.text: A portrait of Raja Dilip Singh of Guler (c. 1707) is labeled on the back in Takri.
facts.quote: verso, in Takri: Shri Dalip Singh

facts.text: A Guler page of c. 1750-60 bears the purple Mandi inventory stamp with a handwritten number.
facts.quote: A purple stamped cartouche (the Mandi inventory stamp) with handwritten number 268.

facts.text: Coomaraswamy reports that painters still practiced at Guler in his day, and that hill portraits are inscribed with the names of the Rajas of Guler, Suket, Mandi and others.
facts.quote: One finds inscribed on these portraits the names of the Rajas of Guler, Sukhet, Mandi, Patyala, &c.

schools.cautions: A royal stamp of another state (Mandi) on a Guler painting shows later ownership.
schools.name: Pahari painting: Guler
schools.region: Guler, Kangra Valley, Himachal Pradesh
schools.patrons: Rajas of Guler, especially Dalip Singh (r. 1695-1741) and Govardhan Chand; the family of Pandit Seu, Manaku and Nainsukh
how_to_recognize: Naturalism and delicate refinement learned from the Mughal workshop (trees, faces, belted tunics, floral carpets)
Fine line, cool palette, portraits of hill rajas
schools.writing_found: Takri labels with the raja's name on the back (e.g. 'Shri Dalip Singh'); Devanagari verses; royal inventory stamps (Mandi inventory cartouche with number on a Guler page); collectors' stamps (e.g. Chughtai, Lahore).

look_alikes.how_to_tell: Guler painters' families moved to Kangra under Sansar Chand; museums often write 'Guler or Kangra'
Chamba portraits use straight hookah pipes, striped trousers and big bolsters (Cleveland)

schools.later_copies: Not specifically documented in sources read.

facts.text: Kangra sets of the Eight Nayikas are often inscribed with verses of Keshavdas's Rasikapriya, always in Nagari characters.
facts.quote: such inscriptions are always in Nagari characters, a pleasing contrast to the almost illegible Takri of Jammu.

facts.text: A painting of Raja Sansar Chand attacking Kangra Fort is inscribed in Takri and Persian with the date Samvat 1839 (1782).
facts.quote: Inscriptions in Takri and Persian.

facts.text: Nearly all very late Kangra or Garhwal examples draw the fingers sharply pointed and with little feeling.
facts.quote: the fingers are sharply pointed and drawn with little feeling

facts.text: In Kangra Sikh paintings the faces of young men are unshaven, which never appears in Pahari work for Hindu patrons.
facts.quote: the faces of young men are unshaven, a peculiarity that never appears in Pahari art executed for Hindu patrons

facts.text: Pages from the collection of the Lahore painter-collector Abdur Rahman Chughtai carry his seal or stamps, e.g. a Kangra Bhagavata Purana page (1775-80) and a Guler portrait.
facts.quote: Verso: personal seal of Abdur Rahman Chughtai.

schools.cautions: The verse inscribed on a Kangra picture identifies the subject, not the date.
schools.name: Pahari painting: Kangra
schools.region: Kangra (Nadaun, Sujanpur Tira, Alampur), Himachal Pradesh; related Garhwal work
schools.patrons: Raja Sansar Chand (r. 1775-1823) and successors (Aniruddh Chand, r. 1823-33)
how_to_recognize: Lyrical Krishna and Radha subjects, heroines (nayikas), Bhagavata Purana and Nala-Damayanti sets
Soft, sweet sentiment; slender women; misty hill landscapes
Very late Kangra and Garhwal hands have sharply pointed fingers drawn with little feeling
Sikh-period portraits show young men unshaven
schools.writing_found: Hindi verses in Devanagari (Nagari) from the Rasikapriya of Keshavdas and other poets, on the front or back; Sanskrit text on the back; Takri and Persian on some court pictures with Samvat dates (e.g. Samvat 1839 = 1782); collectors' seals.

look_alikes.how_to_tell: Guler work before c. 1775 is the source of the Kangra style; attributions often read 'Guler or Kangra'
Modern Kangra-style paintings are made in Himachal; no source read gives test signs

schools.later_copies: Not specifically documented in sources read beyond the general tourist trade.

facts.text: Early Chamba portraiture features a straight hookah pipe, striped trousers, large bolsters and a particular sitting posture.
facts.quote: a straight Hookah pipe, striped trousers, large bolsters, and the sitting posture of the raja.

facts.text: A Chamba Dashavatara page of c. 1765 is captioned in Takri on the top border.
facts.quote: [[top border, in Takri]] sri raja ram lachhamana avatara

facts.text: Coomaraswamy says he cannot speak with authority about Chamba painting.
facts.quote: I regret, however, that I cannot speak with authority about the painting of Chamba

schools.cautions: Coomaraswamy (1916) could not characterize Chamba painting; modern attributions rest on later scholarship summarized in museum records.
schools.name: Pahari painting: Chamba
schools.region: Chamba, Himachal Pradesh
schools.patrons: Rajas of Chamba, e.g. Chhatar Singh (r. 1664-90), Raj Singh (r. 1764-94)
how_to_recognize: Early portraits: straight hookah pipe, striped trousers, large bolsters, a particular seated posture
Later (Raj Singh period) Guler-influenced series such as the Dashavatara
schools.writing_found: Takri captions on the top border naming the subject (e.g. 'sri raja ram lachhamana avatara'); Takri or Devanagari labels naming the raja ('raja catara singha camba vala').

look_alikes.how_to_tell: Later Chamba work was painted by Guler-trained artists; museums write 'Guler or Chamba'

schools.later_copies: Not documented in sources read.

facts.text: A Mandi painting of c. 1645-55 shows Hindu deities enthroned like Mughal rulers, with delicate contours, small heads and profile faces.
facts.quote: the delicate contours, small-headed figures, and the profile (rather than frontal) representations of deities

facts.text: A portrait of Raja Hari Sen of Mandi (c. 1650) wears Jahangir-era fashion and carries only a number, '111'.
Paintings that passed through the Mandi royal collection bear a purple stamped cartouche with a handwritten number.
facts.quote: A purple stamped cartouche (the Mandi inventory stamp) with handwritten number 268.

schools.cautions: The Mandi inventory stamp is an ownership mark, not a school mark.
schools.name: Pahari painting: Mandi
schools.region: Mandi, Himachal Pradesh
schools.patrons: Sen rajas of Mandi, e.g. Hari Sen (c. 1650), Sidh Sen, Shamsher Sen (r. 1727-81)
how_to_recognize: 17th-century works mixing Hindu devotional subjects with Mughal style: small-headed figures, delicate contours, deities in profile like rulers
18th-century portraits of Shaiva rulers (ash marks, whistle in turban)
schools.writing_found: Takri or Devanagari labels (e.g. 'sri damyan', 'Honorable Minister'); numbers; the purple Mandi royal inventory stamp (a cartouche with a handwritten number), found also on paintings from other states.

look_alikes.how_to_tell: A Mandi stamp shows the painting was in the Mandi royal collection; the painting itself may be Guler or another school

schools.later_copies: Not documented in sources read.

facts.text: Patna painters migrated from Murshidabad; the Patna style was technically good though 'hard in feeling'.
facts.quote: the Patna style although hard in feeling was quite good in technique

facts.text: Shiva Lal's workshop sold sets of 'Native Characters' at one or two rupees a picture, and mica sets in boxes of twelve for two rupees ten annas.
facts.quote: The sets of mica pictures were sold in boxes of twelve for two rupees ten annas a box.

facts.text: Early Patna painters gave up Mughal stippling for soft English-style washes; from 1850 Shiva Lal's workshop returned to a coarser stippling that resembles a print.
facts.quote: shadow is shown with soft washes of colour, as in an English water-colour.

facts.text: Ishwari Prasad, the last painter of the Patna school, made a Sweet-seller in 1943.
facts.quote: Ishwari Prasad (b. 1870). Sweet-seller, 1943.

schools.cautions: Archer's artist names (Sewak Ram, Hulas Lal, Shiva Lal, Ishwari Prasad) rest largely on family tradition recorded in the 1940s.
schools.name: Company School: Patna
schools.region: Patna and Bankipore, Bihar; artists also hawked work to Dinapore, Benares, Allahabad, Calcutta
schools.patrons: British officials and residents; Indian gentry and merchants; the bazaar
how_to_recognize: Single figures and small groups of trades, castes and festivals ('Native Characters') with little or no background
Brilliant, clearly separated colors, little shading; early work uses soft English-style washes, later (from c. 1850) coarse stippling
Sold in sets (firka); mica sets of twelve; portrait miniatures on ivory and paper
schools.writing_found: English captions on mounts or flyleaves (trade names, 'native man'); occasional artist names known from family tradition; prices recorded by the last painter's family.

look_alikes.how_to_tell: Patna painters came from Murshidabad c. 1760-1800; early sheets are close
Mica pictures are on translucent mineral sheets, not paper

schools.later_copies: The school's last painter, Ishwari Prasad, was still painting in the 1940s (a 'Sweet-seller' dated 1943), so 20th-century Patna-style sheets exist.

facts.text: At Murshidabad painters also painted sheets of mica for Muharram processions.
facts.quote: painting sheets of mica for use in Muharram processions

facts.text: A Murshidabad Muharram scene of 1795-1810 is painted in watercolor on watermarked paper.
facts.quote: Watercolor on watermarked paper

facts.text: Murshidabad and Patna local styles had a passing reputation in the first half of the 19th century.
facts.quote: Such migrations produced the purely local styles of Murshidabad and Patna

schools.cautions: A watermark date only sets the earliest possible date for the painting.
schools.name: Company School: Murshidabad
schools.region: Murshidabad, Bengal
schools.patrons: Nawabs of Bengal; British officials of the East India Company
how_to_recognize: Late Mughal provincial style shading into British taste: Muharram processions, Nawabs' festivals, trades
Some on European watermarked paper (c. 1795-1810)
Painted mica sheets for Muharram processions
schools.writing_found: English or Persian identifications; watermarks in the paper (dates in watermarks give a date after which the sheet was painted).

look_alikes.how_to_tell: Patna was founded by painters who left Murshidabad; early Patna and late Murshidabad overlap
Earlier Murshidabad work (before c. 1770) is court ragamala and terrace painting for Indian patrons

schools.later_copies: Not documented in sources read.

facts.text: W. G. Archer found no evidence of an important general school of Company painting at Calcutta, but it was a notable center for natural-history painting from 1770-90 (the Impeys, Mrs Wheler, Nathaniel Middleton); the artists were up-country Kayasths from Patna or Murshidabad, or Muslim descendants of Mughal artists.
facts.quote: The artists who executed plant and animal studies were either up-country Kayasths from Patna or Murshidabad, or Muhammadan descendants of former Mughal artists.

facts.text: A Company School parrot of c. 1820, made by an Indian artist for a British civil servant in Calcutta, is inscribed in Persian at lower right.
facts.quote: recto, lower right in persian

facts.text: Company bird studies of c. 1780-1820 are painted on watermarked paper.
facts.quote: Watercolor on watermarked paper

schools.cautions: Many such drawings are now dispersed from albums; the inscription is usually the owner's, not the artist's.
schools.name: Company School: Calcutta (natural history and scenes for the British)
schools.region: Calcutta (Kolkata), Bengal
schools.patrons: British residents and officials, e.g. collectors of natural-history albums
how_to_recognize: Birds, animals and plants painted with precision on plain unpainted grounds
Watercolor on European (often watermarked) paper
Artists from Patna and Murshidabad, or descendants of Mughal painters
schools.writing_found: Persian or English names of the bird or plant, sometimes Latin names added by the owner; watermarks.

look_alikes.how_to_tell: Patna sets are of people and trades; Calcutta specialized in natural history for British patrons

schools.later_copies: Not documented in sources read.

facts.text: A Lucknow set picture of the early 1830s, made for a British buyer, adds a cursory landscape and awkward shadows to suit British preferences for depth and realism.
facts.quote: the artist creates a cursory landscape setting and awkward shadows under the figures to accord with the preferences of British collectors

facts.text: Fraser Album pages (Delhi region, c. 1815-20) are in Cleveland and the Art Institute of Chicago, public domain.
Delhi painters, descendants of the Mughal school, developed a style of miniature portraiture of the Mughal dynasty; older examples, generally on ivory, date to about 1860s.
facts.quote: Some of the older Delhi miniatures, executed about fifty years ago, generally on ivory, express a certain amount of feeling and quality

schools.cautions: Brown (1918) judged 'modern Delhi painting' of low merit; that is taste, not dating evidence.
schools.name: Company School: Lucknow and Delhi
schools.region: Lucknow (Awadh); Delhi and the surrounding region (Haryana); also Agra and Punjab (Lahore, Amritsar) later
schools.patrons: British officials (e.g. the Fraser brothers, c. 1815-20), travelers
how_to_recognize: Sets of servants, trades and 'types' made for British buyers, with cursory landscapes and awkward cast shadows added for European taste
Delhi: highly finished portraits of local people and rulers (Fraser Album); views of Mughal monuments (Taj Mahal, Akbar's tomb) on paper or ivory
Punjab Company sets of the later 19th century (Lahore, Amritsar)
schools.writing_found: English captions naming trade or sitter; Persian names; later dealers' labels.

look_alikes.how_to_tell: Ivory or bone plaques of the same monuments and emperors were made for travelers from the 19th century onward
Delhi bazaar painters also made stock emperor portraits

schools.later_copies: Views of Mughal monuments were produced for visitors into the 20th century (e.g. Art Institute 'Akbar's Tomb, Sikandra', 19th/20th century).

facts.text: In the early 20th century descendants of Mughal painters in Delhi bazaars reproduced any member of the dynasty to order on disks of ivory or bone, as characterless copies.
facts.quote: reproducing on disks of ivory or bone any member of the dynasty according to order, but these are mere characterless copies

facts.text: Coomaraswamy says nothing of Mughal art survives but the modern Delhi miniatures on ivory, made by tradesmen for tourists.
facts.quote: Nothing survives of it but the modern Delhi miniatures on ivory, the work of tradesmen catering for tourists.

facts.text: British miniaturists such as John Smart, who came to India in the late 18th century, introduced painting on ivory there.
facts.quote: actually came to India to paint the portraits of Europeans, and thus introduced painting on ivory into India.

facts.text: India banned trade in imported ivory by inserting section 49C in the Wild Life (Protection) Act in 1991; ivory dealers' challenges failed in the Delhi High Court (1997) and the Supreme Court (2003).

schools.cautions: Painting on ivory in India followed British portrait miniaturists of the late 18th century, so an emperor portrait on ivory is not 16th- or 17th-century imperial work, whatever emperor it names. Ivory: trade in ivory is restricted in India (Wild Life (Protection) Act as amended 1991) and in many importing countries; whether a plaque is ivory or bone needs a specialist; no legal advice is given here.
schools.name: Delhi ivory and bone miniatures (portraits of emperors, monuments)
schools.region: Delhi and Agra; later Jaipur and other tourist centers
schools.patrons: British residents and travelers, tourists
how_to_recognize: Small oval or round disks or rectangular plaques painted with Mughal emperors and empresses or monuments (Taj Mahal, Delhi Fort, tombs)
Stock portraits: the same emperor types repeated
Often framed in sets, sometimes in brooches or boxes
schools.writing_found: Persian, Urdu or English names of the emperor or monument painted on the plaque or written on the back; dealers' labels.

look_alikes.how_to_tell: The 20th-century trade continued the same subjects on bone and other materials; material and condition matter more than subject
Genuine 17th-century Mughal portraits are on paper; Mughal painting on ivory belongs to the late 18th century onward

schools.later_copies: Still made in Delhi bazaars in 1916-24 'on disks of ivory or bone', according to Coomaraswamy and Brown.

facts.text: At Murshidabad painters painted mica sheets for Muharram processions; Patna workshops later sold mica sets in boxes of twelve.
facts.quote: The sets of mica pictures were sold in boxes of twelve for two rupees ten annas a box.

facts.text: The British Library holds a set of 24 gouache-on-mica paintings of occupations, transport, hunting and festivals 'by a Trichinopoly artist', c. 1850, inscribed on old mounts.
facts.quote: By a Trichinopoly artist ... Gouache on mica ... Inscribed on old mounts with notes.

facts.text: Patna mica paintings are marked by brilliant color, e.g. a figure silhouetted against a bright red ochre background.
facts.quote: The same brilliance of colour distinguishes the paintings on mica

schools.cautions: Mount papers and captions can be later than the mica; a watermark on the mount dates the mount.
schools.name: Mica paintings (Murshidabad, Patna, Benares, Trichinopoly)
schools.region: Murshidabad, Patna, Benares (north and east India); Trichinopoly (Tiruchirappalli, south India)
schools.patrons: Indian households (Muharram use, novelties) and British buyers of souvenir sets
how_to_recognize: Small translucent mineral sheets (often about 4 x 6 inches), painted in opaque color, usually mounted on paper
Sets of trades, castes, festivals, transport, deities; south Indian sets show couples by caste
Brilliant colors against plain or red-ochre grounds; paint flakes easily
schools.writing_found: English captions on the paper mounts ('Inscribed on old mounts with notes'); box labels; mount papers may carry watermarks.

look_alikes.how_to_tell: Same subjects on paper; hold to the light: mica is translucent and layered
Reverse-glass paintings are on rigid glass with gold foil; mica is thin and flexible

schools.later_copies: Not documented in sources read.

facts.text: The southern style of Company School painting is distinguished by bold outlines, saturated color and heavy gold; a Tanjore set picture keeps a 19th-century British inscription on its tissue fly-sheet.
facts.quote: distinguished by its bold outlines, saturated color, and heavy application of gold

facts.text: Trichinopoly artists painted sets of south Indian castes, occupations and festivals c. 1850.

schools.cautions: British inscriptions reflect the owner's view, sometimes mocking; they are not the painter's caption.
schools.name: Company School: Tanjore and Trichinopoly sets on paper
schools.region: Thanjavur (Tanjore) and Tiruchirappalli (Trichinopoly), Tamil Nadu
schools.patrons: Officers and officials of the East India Company and later British residents
how_to_recognize: Sets of castes, professions, deities and temple festivals for British buyers
Bold outlines, saturated color and heavy gold (the 'southern style' of Company painting)
Often bound in albums with tissue fly-sheets
schools.writing_found: English inscriptions by British owners on fly-sheets or mounts describing the caste or trade; sometimes Tamil or Telugu names.

look_alikes.how_to_tell: Tanjore gesso paintings are on wooden panels with raised gilded relief and glass stones; Company sets are flat watercolor on paper
Trichinopoly also painted the same subjects on mica

schools.later_copies: South Indian watercolors on paper continued to c. 1910 (Art Institute holds Thanjavur watercolors dated c. 1910, not public domain).

facts.text: Kalighat painters were Bengali Hindus of the patua community; prominent later painters Nirbaran Chandra Ghosh and Kali Charan Ghosh died in 1930.
facts.quote: Kalighat painters, on the other hand, were Bengali Hindus of the patua community.

facts.text: Kalighat pictures sold to pilgrims for between a pice and an anna, which demanded a rapid, simplified style.
facts.quote: The actual charges, as we know from later evidence, ranged from a pice to one anna

facts.text: Kalighat paintings were done on mill-made paper, without decoration, and usually feature only one or two characters.
facts.quote: The paintings were completed on mill-made paper, stripped of decoration and traditionally feature only one or two characters.

facts.text: Silver paint was used to define contours, more sparingly in the later period; museum records describe the medium as gum tempera with tin (or silver paint).
facts.quote: Silver paint which was formerly used to define contours is resorted to more sparingly.

facts.text: Kalighat images were sold as pilgrim souvenirs to locals and to the British; some carry English captions added by owners.
facts.quote: This image would have been sold as a pilgrim souvenir to both locals and the colonial British

facts.text: By 1920 almost all the original painters' descendants had stopped painting, and by 1930 the school had ended.
facts.quote: In 1920 almost all the descendants of the original artists had ceased to paint and by 1930 the school had ended.

schools.cautions: Kalighat works were cheap and often survive in albums assembled by British visitors; the album date, not the style, may be the best date evidence.
schools.name: Kalighat painting (Calcutta bazaar painting)
schools.region: Around the Kali temple at Kalighat, Calcutta (Kolkata), Bengal
schools.patrons: Pilgrims to the Kalighat temple, Calcutta residents, British visitors
how_to_recognize: Watercolor on cheap machine-made (mill) paper, usually one or two large figures on a plain ground
Bold, sweeping brush outlines; shading only to stress outlines
Silver (tin) paint for jewelry and contours, used more sparingly after c. 1870
Gods and goddesses (Kali, Durga, Krishna, Rama) and satires of Calcutta 'babus', courtesans and scandals
schools.writing_found: Usually no inscription by the painter; English or Bengali captions sometimes added by buyers (e.g. 'Ganesha rides on the mouse'; 'Bashoodeva'); album page numbers.

look_alikes.how_to_tell: Woodcuts, line drawings and lithographs of the same subjects were cheaper substitutes from c. 1870-1930; 20th- and 21st-century patua artists still paint in the style and usually sign and date
Company painting was made for British patrons by other artists (Patna/Murshidabad), with fine detail and small scale

schools.later_copies: See kalighat_later.

facts.text: From 1890 to 1930 Kalighat production was cheapened with line drawings and woodcuts.
facts.quote: in a desperate attempt to cheapen production, line-drawings as well as woodcuts were also produced.

facts.text: Calcutta woodcuts copying Kalighat subjects were printed on paper that missionaries intended for Bibles, as cheap alternatives to paintings.
facts.quote: Woodcuts such as this were made on paper that Christian missionaries intended for the production of Bibles.

facts.text: A Kalighat-style watercolor of a 'babu' taking a selfie is signed and dated 'Bhaskar Chitrakar 2020'.
facts.quote: The artist's signature and date, "Bhaskar Chitrakar 2020"

facts.text: A mid-1900s Kalighat painting in Cleveland is signed in Bengali script.
facts.quote: The artist signed his name in Bengali script in the lower right.

schools.cautions: A Kalighat-style painting can be new; sources read do not give a test for telling old from new beyond signature, paper and paint.
schools.name: Kalighat-style woodcuts, lithographs and later patua paintings
schools.region: Calcutta (Kolkata) and Bengal villages (patua/chitrakar families)
schools.patrons: Calcutta buyers; later collectors and tourists
how_to_recognize: Woodcuts printed in black on thin paper, sometimes hand-colored, repeating Kalighat designs
Line drawings without color (1890-1930)
Modern patua paintings in Kalighat style, often on better paper, signed and dated, sometimes with modern subjects (a 2020 'babu' taking a selfie)
schools.writing_found: Modern works are usually signed (Bengali or English script) and dated by the artist, e.g. 'Bhaskar Chitrakar 2020'; earlier woodcuts may carry printed captions.

look_alikes.how_to_tell: 19th-century Kalighat paintings are unsigned, on cheap mill paper, with tin/silver paint; a signature and date usually indicate 20th-century or later work

schools.later_copies: Kalighat style is practiced today; museum examples include a painting signed and dated 2020 (Smithsonian NMNH, CC0).

facts.text: Tanjore painting on wood is watercolor heavily gilt and encrusted with precious stones or paste gems.
facts.quote: a water-colour painting on wood, but heavily gilt and encrusted with precious stones or paste gems.

facts.text: After the death of Sivaji, the last Tanjore raja (r. 1833-55), most painters turned to other crafts; a few families made 'bazaar' religious pictures with much gilding and paste gems.
facts.quote: execute "bazaar" pictures of religious subjects much appreciated by the local Hindus

facts.text: Tanjore paintings are panel paintings on solid wood planks, locally called palagai padam; jackfruit wood was used traditionally. Brown (1918) likewise describes the form as painting on wood.
facts.quote: Tanjore paintings are mainly panel paintings done on solid wood planks, and hence referred to as palagai padam in local parlance.

facts.text: Present-day makers paste cardboard on the board, stretch cotton cloth over it with gum, coat it with chalk powder and tamarind-seed paste, build relief, apply gold foil and set stones.
facts.quote: after the cardboard is pasted to wooden board, Cotton fabric is then stretched and pasted on the board

facts.text: The Art Institute of Chicago holds a 19th-century Thanjavur Shiva Nataraja in 'opaque watercolor with gilded paper on canvas on wood' (2018.593, not public domain).
facts.quote: Opaque watercolor with gilded paper on canvas on wood

schools.cautions: Brown (1918) already called the 19th-20th-century output 'bazaar pictures'; age cannot be told from style. Plywood and cardboard backing indicate modern work; solid wood alone does not prove age.
schools.name: Tanjore (Thanjavur) paintings: gilded gesso on wood
schools.region: Thanjavur (Tanjore) and Tiruchirappalli, Tamil Nadu; Pudukkottai
schools.patrons: Maratha rajas of Tanjore (Serfoji/Sarabhoji II, Shivaji II, d. 1855), temples, Hindu households; today a large commercial market
how_to_recognize: Central deity (Krishna, Rama's coronation, Balaji, Lakshmi) facing out, with attendants, under an arch
Painted on a wooden panel covered with cloth and a chalk-and-gum ground; raised relief built up in the gold areas
Gold leaf or foil on the relief; glass or paste 'gems' set in jewelry and arches
Saturated reds, greens and blues; round faces
schools.writing_found: Rarely any inscription; sometimes names of deities; modern works may have a maker's label or certificate on the back.

look_alikes.how_to_tell: Mysore paintings use a thinner gesso on paper with little relief and no inset glass; Tanjore panels have thick relief and glass stones
Reverse-glass paintings are painted behind glass, flat, with foil; no wooden relief

schools.later_copies: Tanjore panels are produced in quantity today. Present-day workshop practice uses plywood with cardboard and cotton cloth, a chalk-and-tamarind-seed or chalk-and-glue paste, and gold foil; older panels were on solid planks (jackfruit wood).

facts.text: The Art Institute of Chicago catalogues Thanjavur reverse-glass paintings of the 19th and early 20th centuries ('opaque watercolor and gold foil on reverse glass').
facts.quote: Opaque watercolor and gold foil on reverse glass

schools.cautions: Only one source (Art Institute records, none public domain) was read for this row.
schools.name: South Indian reverse-glass paintings (Thanjavur)
schools.region: Thanjavur and south India
schools.patrons: Hindu households, temples, merchants
how_to_recognize: Painted on the back of a glass sheet, seen through the glass; flat surface
Gold or silver foil behind the glass in jewelry and borders
Deities (Durga, Krishna, Rama and Sita's marriage, Ganesha) and courtly figures
schools.writing_found: Not documented in sources read.

look_alikes.how_to_tell: Gesso paintings have raised relief on wood; reverse-glass paintings are flat under glass

schools.later_copies: Not documented in sources read.

facts.text: The Mysore school reached its height under Krishnaraja Wodeyar in the first half of the 19th century and dispersed after his death in 1868.
facts.quote: On the death of Krishnaraja, in 1868, these artists were dispersed and the school became extinct.

facts.text: Mysore gesso paste (zinc oxide and gum) gives only a slightly raised effect under gold foil.
facts.quote: This paste is used to give a slightly raised effect of carving to those parts of the painting that require embellishments

facts.text: Earlier Mysore painters built the base from 10-20 layers of paper; today artists use mount board, synthetic colors and Fevicol.
facts.quote: Now days, artists have changed the technique of using the base. They use mount board

facts.text: The Art Institute of Chicago holds a Mysore 'Coronation of Rama' of the late 19th or early 20th century in opaque watercolor with gold leaf on paper and wood (2018.594, not public domain).
facts.quote: Opaque watercolor with gold leaf on paper and wood

schools.cautions: Brown (1918, 1924) wrote that the court school became extinct after 1868; the present-day craft is a later revival or continuation, so Mysore-style works are often 20th-21st century.
schools.name: Mysore painting
schools.region: Mysore (Mysuru), Karnataka
schools.patrons: Wodeyar rulers, especially Mummadi Krishnaraja Wodeyar (r. 1799-1868); temples and households
how_to_recognize: Hindu deities and court scenes with delicate detail
Thin gesso (raised only slightly) under gold leaf; less relief than Tanjore, no inset glass
Older works on paper built up in layers; today on mount board
schools.writing_found: Not documented in sources read; Kannada labels possible (see gaps).

look_alikes.how_to_tell: Tanjore has thick relief on wood with glass stones; Mysore has thin gesso on paper

schools.later_copies: Mysore paintings are made today; present practice uses mount board with an ivory or cartridge sheet, zinc-oxide-and-gum gesso, gold foil, synthetic colors and Fevicol in place of gum.

facts.text: Painted-cloth pichhvais form the backdrop to the worship of Krishna as Shri Nathji in the Pushti Marg; long exposure leaves them faded and worn.
facts.quote: As a result of long-term exposure, these textiles are usually faded and worn.

facts.text: Brown lists Nathdwara as one of the three Rajput qalams recognized by Indian connoisseurs, with Jaipur and Kangra.
facts.quote: Rajput. (1) Jaipur. (2) Kangra. (3) Nathdwara.

facts.text: A Nathdwara painting of c. 1890 uses a new synthetic pink pigment imported from Europe.
facts.quote: the pink created by a new synthetic pigment imported from Europe.

facts.text: Commercial Nathdwara painting today replaces earth colors and brushwork with canvas, acrylic colors and spray guns; studios range from devoted painters to producers for the tourist trade.
facts.quote: earth colours and traditional brush works are replaced by canvas, and acrylic colours and spray guns are used

facts.text: A pichhvai of c. 1820-30 attributed to the Hyderabad region is painted, mordant-dyed and wax-resisted cotton with gold and mica.
facts.quote: Cotton, painted, mordant-dyed, wax resisted, with gold and mica gilding

schools.cautions: New pichhvais are made in Nathdwara, Udaipur and elsewhere in quantity; size and subject do not indicate age. Synthetic pigments (e.g. a European synthetic pink c. 1890 in a Nathdwara painting) show that a late-19th-century date is possible but do not date a work by themselves.
schools.name: Nathdwara pichhvais and Nathdwara paintings
schools.region: Nathdwara (near Udaipur), Rajasthan; Kota and Kankroli shrines; some pichhvais made in south India for the cult
schools.patrons: Pushti Marg (Vallabha sampradaya) temples and devotees; pilgrims; today decorators and collectors
how_to_recognize: Large painted cotton hangings hung behind the image of Shri Nathji (Krishna lifting Mount Govardhan): the dark frontal icon with one arm raised
Gopis, cows, lotus ponds, festival themes; borders of cows or Krishna episodes
Old cloth hangings are usually faded and worn from long use
Smaller paintings on paper of Shri Nathji in festival dress, and portraits of the head priests (Tilkayats), sold to pilgrims
schools.writing_found: Devanagari names of festivals or priests on paper paintings; rarely inscriptions on pichhvais. Not well documented in sources read.

look_alikes.how_to_tell: Printed Shri Nathji images (and photographs) were widely sold; Nathdwara painting itself absorbed print and photo styles
Kota painted Pushti Marg shrine images too (e.g. worship at Kankroli, c. 1880)

schools.later_copies: Many pichhvais on the market are modern: present-day commercial work uses canvas, machine-made cloth, acrylic paint and spray guns, and some studios produce for the tourist trade.

facts.text: In January 1934 W. G. Archer, British Collector in Madhubani District, saw the wall paintings after the Bihar earthquake brought down compound walls.
facts.quote: In January 1934, W.G. Archer, the local British Collector in Madhubani District, "discovered" the ancient wall painting tradition

facts.text: During the 1966-68 drought the All India Handicrafts Board encouraged Mithila women to transfer their wall paintings to paper to be sold; the first paintings on paper were exhibited in Delhi in 1967.
facts.quote: In the wake of a drought in 1966, the All India Handicrafts Board encouraged women of the Mithila region make paintings on paper

facts.text: Mithila paintings stay two-dimensional, with no horizon line, filled spaces, deities full face and humans in profile, and a painted frame.
facts.quote: deities are usually full face, humans in profile; paintings begin with a painted frame mimicking the wooden beams that framed the wall paintings

facts.text: Since the 1970s women of many castes, and a few men, have taken up painting on paper.
facts.quote: Over the past 50 years hundreds of other women, from a wide array of castes, communities, and villages – and even a few men – have also taken up painting on paper.

schools.cautions: Paintings on paper begin in the late 1960s. A Mithila painting on paper offered as 19th-century or earlier contradicts the sources. The wall tradition is older, but walls rarely survive.
schools.name: Mithila (Madhubani) painting on paper
schools.region: Mithila region, Madhubani and Darbhanga districts, Bihar (villages such as Jitwarpur and Ranti)
schools.patrons: Originally household ritual wall and floor painting by women for weddings and festivals; on paper from the late 1960s for sale (All India Handicrafts Board), then collectors and tourists
how_to_recognize: Flat, two-dimensional images with no horizon or perspective; every empty space filled with flowers, foliage or patterns
Deities usually full face, humans in profile; a painted frame mimicking the beams that framed wall paintings
Ink and bright colors (or line-only work in black and red) on handmade or wove paper
Subjects: deities, kohbar (marriage-chamber) designs, Ramayana, village life, and newer social subjects
schools.writing_found: Devanagari captions naming deities (e.g. 'jaya shankar-ji'); artists' names and dates are common on later works (not systematically documented in sources read).

look_alikes.how_to_tell: Kalighat has one or two large figures on blank ground; Mithila fills every space

schools.later_copies: Produced in quantity since 1967; designs are widely reproduced as prints and on textiles.

facts.text: Ravi Varma lived 1848-1906 (Smithsonian Libraries name heading).
facts.quote: Ravi Varma,1848-1906

facts.text: Ravi Varma's works were declared art treasures under the 1972 Act and cannot be exported from India; the nine artists are Abanindranath Tagore, Amrita Sher-Gil, Gaganendranath Tagore, Jamini Roy, Nandalal Bose, Nicholas Roerich, Rabindranath Tagore, Raja Ravi Varma and Sailoz Mookherjea.
facts.quote: can never be exported out of the country.

facts.text: The ASI declared the nine artists' works 'art treasures' in 1976 and 1979 (Ravi Varma in 1979, according to one source).
facts.quote: not being antiquities, to be art treasures, having regard to their artistic and aesthetic value.

facts.text: Ravi Varma sent ten paintings of Indian life to the Chicago exhibition (1893) and won two medals.
facts.quote: Mr. Ravi Varma contributed to the Chicago International Exhibition ten paintings representing native life and character

facts.text: Coomaraswamy called Ravi Varma's work 'pseudo-Indian art'.
facts.quote: I need not refer to the pseudo-Indian art of Ravi Varma.

schools.cautions: India declared the works of nine artists, including Raja Ravi Varma, 'art treasures' under the Antiquities and Art Treasures Act, 1972 (notifications of 1976 and 1979); such works may not be exported from India. Facts only; not legal advice. Coomaraswamy (1916) dismissed Ravi Varma's art as 'pseudo-Indian'; his popularity contradicts that judgment, which is a matter of taste.
schools.name: Raja Ravi Varma: oil paintings
schools.region: Kilimanoor and Travancore (Kerala); Bombay and courts across India (Baroda, Mysore)
schools.patrons: Maharajas of Travancore and Baroda, princely and wealthy sitters
how_to_recognize: European academic oil technique on canvas: modeled figures, perspective, theatrical lighting
Hindu mythological heroines (Shakuntala, Damayanti, Lakshmi, Saraswati) and portraits
The same compositions are far more often met as prints (see ravi_varma_press)
schools.writing_found: Signature on oils (form not documented in sources read); printed 'Ravi Varma' signature appears in many prints.

look_alikes.how_to_tell: A print shows a regular printed texture under magnification and no raised brushwork; a varnished or overpainted print can mislead (no source read gives a test; see gaps)

schools.later_copies: Later painted copies of Ravi Varma compositions exist (not documented in sources read).

facts.text: Ravi Varma set up a lithographic press in Bombay at his own expense to print his works in color for the masses.
facts.quote: establishment by the artist at his own expense of a Lithographic Press in Bombay for the purpose of printing his works in colours and placing them within the reach of the masses.

facts.text: The press was established in 1894 at Girgaum, Bombay; its first chromolithograph was 'The Birth of Shakuntala' (1894).
The Varma brothers sold the majority interest to the German technician Fritz Schleicher in 1901; he shortened the name to 'F.A.L. Press, Bombay'. Other accounts give 1903 for the sale.
facts.quote: F.A.L. Press—Bombay

facts.text: Imprints read 'Ravi Varma Press Karli Bombay' (c. 1900), 'Ravi Varma Press Karla Lonavala' (1910, 1928) and 'Ravi Varma Press Malavli Lonavala' (c. 1930).
facts.quote: Ravi Varma Press Karla Lonavala

facts.text: The press operated under Schleicher (d. 1935) and successors until a fire destroyed it in 1972; it was briefly revived and shut in 1975, and its remaining prints and stones were auctioned in 2000.
By 1916 German oleographs after Indian drawings hung in Hindu shops and houses.
facts.quote: German oleographs after genuine earlier drawings

schools.cautions: A printed 'Ravi Varma' signature does not mean he supervised that print. Dates of the move to Malavli (1899 or 1901) and of the sale to Fritz Schleicher (1901 or 1903) differ between sources. Whether old prints count as 'antiquities' under Indian law was not found in sources read.
schools.name: Ravi Varma Press chromolithographs (from 1894)
other_names: Ravi Varma Fine Art Lithographic Press
schools.region: Girgaon (Girgaum), Bombay, from 1894; Ghatkopar (1898); Malavli near Karla and Lonavla from c. 1899-1901
schools.patrons: Mass market across India: households, shops, advertisers (calendars)
how_to_recognize: Color lithographs of Ravi Varma's mythological paintings and others (Shakuntala, Lakshmi, Saraswati, Krishna, Rama), often with a printed signature
Printed imprint line in the lower margin naming the press and place
Later issues used as advertising calendars (e.g. Vinolia soap, 1927 and 1930)
schools.writing_found: Printed imprints such as 'Ravi Varma Press, Karli, Bombay' (c. 1900), 'Ravi Varma Press, Karla-Lonavala' (1910, 1928), 'Ravi Varma Press, Malavli-Lonavala' (c. 1930); titles in English, Devanagari or other scripts; printed 'Ravi Varma' signature.

look_alikes.how_to_tell: Other presses imitated and pirated Ravi Varma Press images; the imprint names the press
An original oil has brushwork and canvas; a print has printed texture on paper

schools.later_copies: After the 1901 sale, prints bearing Varma's signature proliferated with declining quality; the press kept printing until a fire in 1972 (briefly revived, shut 1975). Rival presses imitated and pirated its images. Its remaining stock and stones were auctioned in 2000, so late impressions exist.

facts.text: In 1888 T. N. Mukharji wrote that Kalighat painting was declining because of cheaper colored lithographs of gods made by ex-students of the Calcutta School of Art.
facts.quote: The industry is on the decline owing to cheaper coloured lithograph representations of Gods and Goddesses turned out by the ex-students of the Calcutta School of Art

facts.text: By 1890-1930 oleographs and printed pictures were so common that hand painting seemed out of date.
facts.quote: The oleograph and the printed picture were now so general that hand-painting seemed out of date.

facts.text: Demand for 'framing pictures' led to many presses in India, with Sivakasi a major center, where artists such as M. Ramalingam and C. Kondiah Raju sometimes imitated or drew on Ravi Varma Press images.
Advertising calendars carried god images: Vinolia soap calendars of 1927 (Saraswati) and 1930 (Lakshmi) used Ravi Varma Press prints.

schools.cautions: Printed images are reproductions; their age is read from press imprints, calendar dates and printing method, not from the subject. Framing and old glass can be later than the print.
schools.name: Bazaar, calendar and framing prints of gods (c. 1880-present)
schools.region: Calcutta, Bombay, Poona, later Sivakasi (Tamil Nadu), Delhi, Mathura; some printed in Germany
schools.patrons: Households, shrines, shops; advertisers issuing calendars
how_to_recognize: Mass-printed color images of deities, saints and national figures, often framed under glass in homes
Chromolithographs (layered flat colors, grainy texture) and later offset prints (regular dot screen)
Calendar pads or advertisers' names along the bottom; printed imprint of the press
schools.writing_found: Printed captions in English and Indian scripts; press imprints; advertisers' names and calendar years; artists' printed signatures (e.g. later Sivakasi artists).

look_alikes.how_to_tell: Read the imprint: many presses copied Ravi Varma Press images
Kalighat works are hand-painted watercolors; color lithographs replaced them from the 1880s

schools.later_copies: Continuously reprinted; old images are reissued. A calendar year printed on the sheet dates that issue.

facts.text: Fakers sometimes take old manuscripts or albums, clear the surface of the writing and paint over it; ordinary paper is stained with tea to look old.
facts.quote: artists get hold of old manuscripts or albums, clear the surface of any written material and then paint over it.

facts.text: Fakes proliferate especially at tourist centers, makeshift galleries and five-star hotel shopping arcades, painted in easy-to-use poster colors.
facts.quote: fakes are proliferating, especially at tourist centres, makeshift galleries and shopping arcades of five-star hotels.

facts.text: Genuine Mughal album leaves often have unrelated calligraphy on the reverse, so unrelated text on the back is not by itself a sign of a fake.
facts.quote: in no case has either work any relation to the other.

facts.text: In old Rajput painting the color forms a thin skin that flakes when the paper is rubbed or bent, revealing the underdrawing.
facts.quote: the colouring forms a thin skin on the surface of the paper, and readily flakes away when the paper is rubbed or bent, revealing the under-drawing beneath.

schools.cautions: Sources read give no reliable visual test. Old paper does not make an old painting, and painting over a cleared manuscript or album page destroys the original text. Only a specialist with the item in hand, ideally with pigment analysis and provenance, can judge age.
schools.name: 20th- and 21st-century miniatures sold as old (on paper)
schools.region: Jaipur, Udaipur, Delhi, Kishangarh, Bikaner and other tourist centers; also sold online
schools.patrons: Tourists, hotel arcades, online buyers
how_to_recognize: Mughal or Rajput subjects in a familiar 'classic' composition (emperors, Bani Thani, hunts, ragamala) in bright poster or gouache colors
Paper stained with tea to look old, or real old paper (manuscript and account-book pages, album pages) with the original writing cleared and painted over
Writing on the back or showing through that has nothing to do with the picture (also true of genuine album leaves, so it decides nothing)
schools.writing_found: Old Devanagari or Persian text on the reused page; added fake inscriptions or seals; sellers' descriptions such as 'painted on antique paper'.

look_alikes.how_to_tell: Genuine album leaves also carry unrelated calligraphy; a specialist judges the painting itself, paper, pigments and provenance
18th-19th-century copies are old works in their own right; modern tourist work is recent

schools.later_copies: This row is itself about later work.

facts.text: Delhi bazaar painters in the early 20th century painted the Mughal dynasty to order on disks of ivory or bone.
facts.quote: reproducing on disks of ivory or bone any member of the dynasty according to order

facts.text: India's 1991 amendment to the Wild Life (Protection) Act inserted a total prohibition on trade in imported ivory.

schools.cautions: Material identification (ivory, bone, celluloid or other plastic) needs a specialist; the sources read give no test. Ivory items are subject to trade law in India and in many importing countries; facts only, no legal advice.
schools.name: Modern miniatures on ivory, bone, camel bone and plastic
schools.region: Delhi, Jaipur, Udaipur and other tourist centers
schools.patrons: Tourists
how_to_recognize: Small oval or rectangular plaques with Mughal emperors and empresses, Taj Mahal, hunting or lovers scenes
Often in sets, frames, boxes or jewelry
schools.writing_found: Names of emperors in English or Urdu; sometimes artist names; dealers' labels.

look_alikes.how_to_tell: 19th-century Delhi ivory miniatures and 20th-century tourist plaques share subjects; age and material need a specialist

schools.later_copies: This row is itself about later work.

facts.text: Rajput painters prepared numbered series of pictures, without text or with the text written behind, above or below.
facts.quote: they prepared a series of portfolio pictures consecutively numbered, and either without any text, or with the appropriate text inscribed behind, or sometimes above or below.

facts.text: Samvat dates on paintings convert by subtracting 57: V.S. 1743 is given as A.D. 1686, V.S. 1844 as 1787 and V.S. 1889 as 1832 in museum transcriptions; Coomaraswamy gives Samvat 1832 as A.D. 1775.
facts.quote: Samvat, 1832 (a.d. 1775), the fifth day of the bright fortnight of Phalgun

facts.text: A Guler portrait in Cleveland carries Devanagari numerals 53, Arabic numerals 2.74, 'No.138', two purple Chughtai Museum Trust (Lahore) stamps and a black Urdu 'Chughtai' stamp.
facts.quote: Two purple ink stamps: Chughtai Museum Trust ... Lahore-16 Pakistan

facts.text: Pahari court paintings may carry Persian as well as Takri inscriptions with a Samvat date.
facts.quote: Inscriptions in Takri and Persian.

schools.cautions: A Samvat note may record a later event (an inventory or 'opening') rather than the painting date. An inventory stamp shows where a painting was kept, not where it was made. See heirloomapp.io/marks/indian-dates for Samvat conversion.
schools.name: Writing on the backs of Rajput and Pahari paintings: Samvat dates, numbers, inventory stamps, collectors' seals
schools.region: Rajasthan and the Punjab Hills; later collectors in Lahore and elsewhere
schools.patrons: Royal libraries (toshakhana) of Udaipur, Mandi, Kota and other states; 20th-century collectors such as Abdur Rahman Chughtai (Lahore)
how_to_recognize: Devanagari or Takri notes on the back: subject, ruler's name, artist's name, folio number, Vikram Samvat date with month and lunar half (sudi/badi)
Royal inventory numbers and prices (e.g. 'Udaipur inventory 21/57'; 'Price 115 rupees'); purple stamped cartouches (Mandi)
Collectors' stamps (e.g. purple 'Chughtai Museum Trust ... Lahore' stamps, Chughtai's Urdu seal)
schools.writing_found: Vikram Samvat (V.S.) year: subtract 57 (or 56 late in the Indian year) for the Common Era year, e.g. V.S. 1743 = 1686, V.S. 1844 = 1787, V.S. 1889 = 1832; Devanagari and Arabic numerals; English notations added by dealers.
schools.later_copies: Inscriptions and stamps can be added or copied; not documented in detail in sources read.

facts.text: Abu'l Fazl lists Akbar's seals: a round steel seal with his name and his ancestors' names back to Timur in riqa' script, a nasta'liq seal with his name only, a mihrab-shaped judicial seal with a verse, the small round 'uzuk', a square seal reading Allahu Akbar jalla jalaluhu, and a separate harem seal.
facts.quote: Maulana Maqsud, the seal-engraver, cut in a circular form upon a surface of steel, in the riqa' character, the name of his Majesty and those of his illustrious ancestors up to Timurlang

facts.text: The uzuk is the small round seal; Jahangir records entrusting his own uzuk seal to trusted nobles, and his translators gloss uzuk as a Turkic word for a signet ring.
facts.quote: The round small seal goes by the (Chaghatai) name of Uzuk

facts.text: A manuscript of Jerome Xavier's life of Christ, copied for Akbar's court in AH 1013, bears Akbar's seal with that date.
facts.quote: bearing the seal of Akbar (also giving the date 1013 AH)

facts.text: British Museum manuscripts from the imperial library carry inspection notes and seals of the reigns of Akbar, Jahangir and Shah Jahan on the first page.
facts.quote: the first page contains several 'Arz-didahs and seals of the reigns of Akbar, Jahangir and Shahjahan.

seals.cautions: Akbar's own seals are much rarer on books than the notes and seals of later reigns. The A'in describes seals for documents (farmans, letters, harem orders); which of them was pressed on books is not stated there.
native: راستی موجب رضای خداست / کس ندیدم که گم شد از ره راست
seals.translit: Allāhu Akbar, jalla jalāluhu (square seal); Rāstī mūjib-i riżā-yi khudāst, kas nadīdam ki gum shud az rah-i rāst (verse on the mihrab-shaped judicial seal); uzuk (the small round seal)
seals.meaning: 'God is Most Great, glorious is His glory' (square seal); 'Uprightness is the means of pleasing God; I never saw anyone lost on the straight road' (judicial seal). The large round seal carried Akbar's name and those of his ancestors back to Timur.
seals.date_note: Engraved by Maulana Maqsud of Herat at the start of the reign; later recut by Tamkin and improved by Mulla 'Ali Ahmad of Delhi (A'in-i Akbari). A manuscript at the Asiatic Society of Bengal carries Akbar's seal with the date AH 1013 (1604-05).
seals.where_on_object: Fly-leaf or first page of manuscripts from the imperial library, among the inspection notes; Akbar's seals were made chiefly for orders and letters.
seals.what_it_tells: A genuine impression shows the book was in Akbar's library or chancery; it says nothing about when the text was copied or the paintings made.

facts.text: A British Museum copy of Barani's Tarikh-i Firuzshahi bears on fol. 16 the seal of Hamida Banu dated AH 957, and its first page carries inspection notes and seals of successive librarians of Shah Jahan and Dara Shikoh.
facts.quote: bears on fol. 16 the seal of Hamidah Banu, the wife of Humayun and mother of Akbar, dated A.H. 957

seals.cautions: Known to us from one catalogue entry; Seyller's 1997 study is said to trace other manuscripts with her seal, but it was not read for this file.
seals.translit: Ḥamīda Bānū bint-i 'Alī Akbar 957
seals.meaning: Hamida Banu, daughter of 'Ali Akbar, [AH] 957
seals.owner: Hamida Banu Begum, wife of Humayun and mother of Akbar
seals.date_note: Seal dated AH 957 (1550-51).
seals.where_on_object: Inside the text block (fol. 16 in the British Museum Tarikh-i Firuzshahi).
seals.what_it_tells: One of the few seals of Humayun's household known on a book; shows the volume belonged to the imperial women's books before the later librarians' notes.

facts.text: Jahangir's note in the Khamsa of Nizami (BL Or.6810) records that the book entered his library on 5 Azar of year 1 (Nov 1605), calls it a select (khassa) book with 22 paintings, 16 by Bihzad, 5 by Mirak and 1 by 'Abd al-Razzaq, and values it at 5,000 rupees.
facts.quote: On the fifth of Azar year 1 (Nov 1605) [this book] entered the library of this supplicant at the Divine Court.

facts.text: A note in the same form and with the same date is on the fly-leaf of the Akbarnama in the Victoria and Albert Museum; Percy Brown judged it authentic.
facts.quote: on the fifth Azar of the first year (1605) this book was entered in the library of this suppliant at the gate of God. Written by Nur ud-Din Jahangir, son of Akbar Padshah.

facts.text: Habitual notes by the emperors on their best manuscripts begin with Jahangir and continue under Shah Jahan, after whom the practice seems to stop; over 20 manuscripts carry notes by both.
facts.quote: the habitual notes by the Mughal emperors, found on their most valuable manuscripts, really only began with Jahangir and were continued by Shah Jahan, after whom the practice seems to have been discontinued.

seals.cautions: The Persian wording was not available in the sources read (only translations). Jahangir's attributions inside such notes are opinions, not records (he gave 16 of 22 paintings in BL Or.6810 to Bihzad).
seals.meaning: 'God is Great. On the fifth of Azar, year 1 [this book] entered the library of this supplicant at the Divine Court. Written by Nur al-Din Jahangir son of Akbar Padshah.'
seals.owner: Jahangir (r. 1605-1627), in his own hand
seals.date_note: The two notes found by both sources are dated 5 Azar of regnal year 1 (November 1605), a few weeks after his accession.
seals.where_on_object: Fly-leaf or opening page, often beside the illuminated rosette (shamsa).
seals.what_it_tells: The emperor's own entry of a prized book into his library; it may add a count of paintings, the painters' names and a value.

facts.text: Shah Jahan's notes in two British Library manuscripts (Or.6810 and Grenville XLI) record entry into his library on the day of his accession, 25 Bahman / 8 Jumada II 1037 (14 Feb 1628).
facts.quote: entered the library of this supplicant at the Divine Court on the twenty-fifth of the month of Bahman Ilāhī, corresponding to the eighth of the month of Jumādā II year 1037 Hijri

facts.text: The Khuda Bakhsh (Bankipore) Timurnama carries an autograph of Shah Jahan together with inspection notes and official seals of Mughal nobles.
facts.quote: Besides the autograph of Shah Jahan there are several 'Ard-didahs and official seals of the nobles of the Mughal Courts of India.

seals.cautions: Persian wording not available in the sources read (translations only). Single dated formula seen on two British Library books; other dates occur.
seals.meaning: 'God is Great. This [book] entered the library of this supplicant at the Divine Court on 25 Bahman Ilahi, corresponding to 8 Jumada II 1037 Hijri, which is the day of the blessed accession. Written by Shihab al-Din Muhammad Shah Jahan Padshah, son of Jahangir Padshah, son of Akbar Padshah Ghazi.'
seals.owner: Shah Jahan (r. 1628-1658), in his own hand
seals.date_note: Several notes carry his accession day, 8 Jumada II 1037 / 14 February 1628, as the day the book entered his library.
seals.where_on_object: Fly-leaf or opening page, often under Jahangir's note.
seals.what_it_tells: The book was in the imperial library at Shah Jahan's accession; a note dated on the accession day marks books inherited from Jahangir's library.

facts.text: Imperial-library manuscripts carry seals of the reigns of Akbar, Jahangir and Shah Jahan.
facts.quote: seals of the reigns of Akbar, Jahangir and Shahjahan

facts.text: Mughal manuscripts taken to Persia by Nadir Shah in 1739 and later found in European libraries bear the seals of Jahangir and Shah Jahan.
facts.quote: Some, bearing the seals of Jahangir and Shah Jahan, as well as evidences of a temporary sojourn in Persia, and later in Constantinople

facts.text: The Salar Jung Museum's Persian manuscripts include a seal of Prince Salim (Jahangir), which the cataloguer lists among the rare seals.
facts.quote: Amongst rare seals are those of Prince Salim ( Jahangir), Ibrahim Qutb Shah of Golconda and 'Ali Adil Shah II of Bijapur.

facts.text: Jahangir wrote that as prince he entrusted his own uzuk seal to the Amir al-Umara and later to his son Parwiz.
facts.quote: I had entrusted, in consequence of my extreme confidence in him, my own uzuk seal to the Amiru-l-umara

seals.cautions: The legend of Jahangir's seal was not transcribed in any source read for this file (gap). A rare item: the Salar Jung cataloguer singled out Prince Salim's seal as one of the rare seals in that collection.
seals.owner: Jahangir (as Prince Salim and as emperor)
seals.date_note: Prince Salim's seal predates his accession in 1605.
seals.where_on_object: Fly-leaf or first page among inspection notes.
seals.what_it_tells: The book was in Jahangir's library (or Salim's princely library).

facts.text: The opening of BL Or.6810 shows Shah Jahan's seal dated 1037 (1628) with the notes of Jahangir and Shah Jahan.
facts.quote: Folio 3r containing a shamsah, the classification, Shah Jahan’s seal dated 1037 (1628) and inscriptions by Jahangir and Shah Jahan

facts.text: An India Office manuscript has several seals of Shah Jahan, to whose library it belonged, dated AH 1045 and 1046.
facts.quote: several seals of the emperor Shahjahan, to whose library this MS. belonged, with the dates A.H. 1045 and 1046

facts.text: A British Museum history bears inspection notes and official seals of the reigns of Shah Jahan and 'Alamgir, the earliest dated AH 1037.
facts.quote: It bears several 'Arz-didahs and official seals of the reigns of Shahjahan and 'Alamgir, the earliest of which is dated A.H. 1037.

seals.cautions: The legend was not transcribed in the sources read (gap). Catalogues sometimes call officials' seals of the reign 'seals of Shah Jahan'; the wording of the legend is what decides.
seals.owner: Shah Jahan and his library
seals.date_note: Dated impressions read 1037 (1628, his accession year), 1045 and 1046 (1635-37).
seals.where_on_object: Fly-leaf, often next to the rosette and the emperors' notes.
seals.what_it_tells: Entry into Shah Jahan's library; the year on the seal gives the earliest possible date for the impression, not the date of the manuscript.

facts.text: An India Office manuscript carries a seal of 'Alamgir dated AH 1079 (1668-69) on the fly-leaf.
facts.quote: A seal of 'Alamgir's, from A. H. 1079 (A. D. 1668, 1669), on the fly-leaf.

facts.text: British Museum manuscripts carry inspection notes of Aurangzeb's reign dated by regnal year, e.g. years 13 and 37, and years 2 and 46.
facts.quote: three 'Arz-Didah, the first two of which are dated the 13th and the 37th year of the reign (of Aurangzib).

seals.cautions: Legend not transcribed in the sources read (gap). Under Aurangzeb the emperors' personal notes stop; the marks are officials' seals and inspection notes.
seals.owner: Aurangzeb 'Alamgir (r. 1658-1707) and his library
seals.where_on_object: Fly-leaf or first page, with inspection notes dated by regnal year.
seals.what_it_tells: The book was in the imperial library under Aurangzeb; his librarians kept inspecting and transferring books through his reign.

facts.text: A seal of Farrukhsiyar (d. AH 1131/1719) and various seals of Muhammad Shah occur on India Office manuscripts.
facts.quote: Various seals of Muhammadshah on fol. 9a.

facts.text: A painting made for Muhammad Shah (c. 1735) carries on its verso a note that the painter Chitarman did the work on the emperor's verbal command, and the seal of 'the devoted servant [of] Muhammad Shah, Padshah-i Ghazi'.
facts.quote: The seal refers to "the devoted servant [of the house of] Muhammad Shah, Padshah-i Ghazi."

facts.text: A Khuda Bakhsh manuscript has a note that it was bought at Hyderabad for the library of Bahadur Shah, and another carries two seals of Mirza Khurram Bakht, grandson of Shah 'Alam.
facts.quote: A note on fol. 1 says that this copy was purchased at Hyderabad for the Library of Bahadur Shah

seals.cautions: Late Mughal seals appear on books bought long after they were made (one was bought at Hyderabad for Bahadur Shah's library), so they date the ownership, not the item.
seals.owner: Later Mughal emperors and princes (Farrukhsiyar, Muhammad Shah, Shah 'Alam II's family, Bahadur Shah II)
seals.where_on_object: Fly-leaf, first page, or verso of a painting.
seals.what_it_tells: The book or painting was in the Delhi court's possession in the 18th or 19th century.

facts.text: Cleveland's portrait of Suraj Singh Rathor from the Prince Khurram Album is labeled in Shah Jahan's hand 'shabih-i Raja Suraj-Singh Rathor'.
facts.quote: inscribed in hand of Shah Jahan in lower inner border: shabihi Raja Suraj-Singh Rathor

facts.text: A partly erased ascription to Basawan on a Cleveland portrait of a Jain monk may be in Jahangir's distinctively large hand.
facts.quote: It may have been written by the Mughal emperor Jahangir, since it appears to be in his distinctively large hand.

facts.text: A note on folio 3r of a British Library Divan of Hafiz (Grenville XLI), possibly by Jahangir, says the work was completed at Allahabad where he held court as Prince Salim.
facts.quote: Folio 3r contains a note, possibly by Jahangir, saying that the work was completed at Allahabad where he held court as Prince Salim.

facts.text: Jahangir and Shah Jahan wrote in their own hands on manuscripts and album pages (library entries, attributions, sitters' names), as recorded independently by Cleveland, the British Library and Percy Brown.
facts.quote: Emperor Shah Jahan himself wrote the label inscription under the painting.

seals.cautions: Hands are identified by curators on style ('his distinctively large hand'); a label 'Jahangir Padshah' or a painter's name can be added later by others (see attribution_reliability).
seals.translit: shabīh-i Rāja Sūraj Singh Rāthor
seals.meaning: 'Likeness of Raja Suraj Singh Rathor' (a sitter's label in Shah Jahan's hand)
seals.owner: Jahangir and Shah Jahan, writing on album pages and fly-leaves
seals.where_on_object: Lower border of album portraits; above or below a painting; fly-leaf.
seals.what_it_tells: An emperor's label names the sitter or the painter; such labels are what albums were catalogued from.

facts.text: Rieu repeatedly identifies imperial-library books by the 'Arz-didahs and seals on their first page.
facts.quote: This MS. appears to have belonged to the imperial library of India : the first page contains several 'Arz-didahs and seals

facts.text: The Khuda Bakhsh catalogue describes the same notes ('Ard-didahs') of the time of Shah Jahan and Aurangzeb at the beginning and end of manuscripts, mostly faded.
facts.quote: There are several 'Ard-didahs and seals of the time of Shah Jahan and Aurangzib both at the beginning and end of the copy, but almost all of them are faded.

facts.text: A partly obliterated 'Arzdidah gives the dates 16 and 31, read as Jahangir's 16th regnal year and AH 1031.
facts.quote: the dates 16 and 31 are still faintly legible. The first is apparently meant for the sixteenth year of the reign of Jahangir

facts.text: Inspection notes kept being written in the 18th century: one dated Lucknow in the first year of 'Shahjahan II' (AH 1173) and one of AH 1206 beside the seal of the Awadh minister Tikait Rai.
facts.quote: an 'Arzdidah dated Lucknow, the first year of Shuhjahan II. (A.H. 1173).

facts.text: Librarians' inspection notes on British Library Delhi Persian manuscripts are dated in regnal years and Hijri months (e.g. 30 Rajab, year 32 of Shah Jahan).

seals.cautions: Notes are often faded, partly obliterated or erased. A fly-leaf covered with notes can be moved from another book (see pasted_flyleaf). A note belongs to the book it was written for, not necessarily to the text now bound with it.
seals.translit: 'arż-dīda (pl. 'arż-dīdahā)
seals.meaning: 'Seen at the review': a short note by a library official recording that the book was presented and checked, with the date (regnal year and often the Hijri or Ilahi month), sometimes the folio count and value, and the official's seal.
seals.owner: Officials of the Mughal imperial library; later also used in successor courts (Lucknow)
seals.date_note: From Akbar's reign (before 1605). Earliest dated in the sources read: notes of Akbar's and Jahangir's reigns (one dated regnal year 16 = AH 1031/1621-22). Latest seen: AH 1169, AH 1173 (dated at Lucknow, 'first year of Shah Jahan II') and AH 1206 (1791-92) with an Awadh minister's seal.
seals.where_on_object: First page or fly-leaf at the front, sometimes the last page; often many notes crowded together.
seals.what_it_tells: The item was in the Mughal imperial library (or a court that copied its practice) on the dates given; a run of notes shows the book was re-inspected over decades.

facts.text: Jahangir's note in Or.6810 is dated 5 Azar of year 1; Shah Jahan's is dated 25 Bahman Ilahi and 8 Jumada II 1037 together.
facts.quote: the twenty-fifth of the month of Bahman Ilāhī, corresponding to the eighth of the month of Jumādā II year 1037 Hijri

facts.text: A gift note in BL Add.5600 is dated 8 Amurdad Ilahi, regnal year 20 of Jahangir (August 1625).
facts.quote: On the 8th of the month Amurdād ilāhī year 20 of the blessed accession [of Jahāngīr] (August 1625)

facts.text: Aurangzeb-era inspection notes carry regnal years such as 2, 13, 37 and 46.
facts.quote: dated respectively the second and forty-sixth year

facts.text: Tipu Sultan's later seals use his mawludi era with the digits written right to left (5121 for 1215).
facts.quote: A further innovation was to record the numbers from right to left instead of the usual way round

facts.text: James Grant's Persian seal is dated 1193 of the Bengali era.
facts.quote: sannah Bangalah 1193

seals.cautions: Dates on notes must be converted with care; scholars disagree on at least one well-known note (see the dispute in noble_gift_and_ownership_notes).
seals.translit: sana-yi julūs (regnal year); māh-i ... ilāhī (Ilahi solar month: Farvardin ... Amurdad, Azar, Bahman ...)
seals.meaning: How the notes are dated: by the emperor's regnal year (julus), by the Ilahi solar months introduced under Akbar, by the Hijri year, or by several at once; Tipu Sultan used his own mawludi era; British seals may use the Bengali era.
seals.owner: all Mughal library notes
seals.where_on_object: Inside the notes and on seals.
seals.what_it_tells: A regnal year without the ruler's name is ambiguous: year 8 can mean Jahangir's or Shah Jahan's reign.

facts.text: Akbar's library was arranged by the value of the books and the standing of their subjects.
facts.quote: Each part of the Library is subdivided, according to the value of the books and the estimation in which the sciences are held of which the books treat.

facts.text: Nearly all the finest imperial copies carry gradings and valuations; Jahangir valued the Or.6810 Khamsa at 5,000 rupees.
facts.quote: nearly all the finest copies carry gradings and valuations.

facts.text: A Rampur Raza Library manuscript copied by Mir 'Ali of Herat is said to have been valued by Shah Jahan at one thousand rupees.
facts.quote: regarded as an important manuscript by Shah Jahan, who valued it at one thousand rupees.

seals.cautions: A historical value is not a modern market value. Modern dealers' prices in pencil or ink are a different thing (see dealer_price_marks).
seals.translit: qīmat (value), with the sum in rupees or mohurs
seals.meaning: A note of the book's value set by the library (or a price paid by an owner).
seals.owner: Mughal emperors and librarians; later private owners
seals.date_note: Earliest dated example in the sources: Jahangir's note of 1605.
seals.where_on_object: In the emperor's or librarian's note on the fly-leaf.
seals.what_it_tells: How highly the court rated the book; values were revised at later inspections.

facts.text: BL Or.6810 was classed as 'Select' (khassa) and 'Class one grade one' (avval avval).
facts.quote: This manuscript was classified as ‘Select’ (khāṣṣah), and ‘Class one grade one’ (avval avval)

facts.text: Akbar's library was subdivided by the value of the books.

seals.cautions: Only a handful of books reached the top grade; Seyller is reported to list just five others of equal status to Or.6810.
seals.translit: khāṣṣa (select); avval avval (class one, grade one)
seals.meaning: Library grading of a book's quality and rank.
seals.owner: Mughal imperial library
seals.where_on_object: Fly-leaf, with the emperor's note.
seals.what_it_tells: The book was among the most valued in the imperial library.

facts.text: BL Delhi Persian 918, 44 and 1263 record transfers between library keepers Mun'im Bayg, Murad Bayg and 'Azim Bayg, one certified by the inspector Muhammad Rashid.

seals.cautions: Known here from one study (Shapouran 2024) read through a summary; the reading of one librarian's name is uncertain in that study.
seals.translit: taḥvīl (transfer into the custody of ...)
seals.meaning: A note that the book passed from one librarian's custody to the next.
seals.owner: Officials of the Mughal imperial library under Aurangzeb and his successors
seals.date_note: Dated examples on BL Delhi Persian manuscripts: to Mun'im Bayg in regnal year 19 (1676); from Mun'im Bayg to Murad Bayg in year 50 (1706) and in year 3 of Bahadur Shah (1709); from Murad Bayg onward in 1708 or 1713.
seals.where_on_object: Fly-leaf among the inspection notes.
seals.what_it_tells: A chain of custody inside the library; useful for dating when a book was in Delhi.

facts.text: Muhammad Tahir 'Inayat Khan (Ashna) held the post of Daroghah-i Kutub Khanah, keeper of the imperial library, from Shah Jahan's 31st year and retired in Aurangzeb's first year.
facts.quote: filled in succession the offices of Daroghah i Huzur and of Daroghah i Kutub Khanah, or keeper of the imperial library. He retired from the service in the first year of Aurangzib

facts.text: His round seal on BL Delhi Persian manuscripts shows they had entered the library by Shah Jahan's 31st year.
Khuda Bakhsh manuscripts bear seals of 'Inayat Khan Shah Jahani dated AH 1044 and 1048, with those of 'Abd al-Rashid Daylami and other nobles of Shah Jahan's court.
facts.quote: This copy also bears the seals, dated a.h. 1044 and 1048, of 'Inayat Khan Shah Jahani, 'Abd-ur-Rashid-i-Daylami, and of several other noblemen of Shah Jahan's court

seals.cautions: His seal predates his office: a seal of 1044 does not mean the book entered the library in 1044.
seals.translit: 'Ināyat Khān Shāhjahānī ('Āshnā')
seals.meaning: Seal of Muhammad Tahir 'Inayat Khan, pen-name Ashna, keeper of Shah Jahan's library
seals.owner: Muhammad Tahir 'Inayat Khan 'Ashna' (d. AH 1081/1670-71)
seals.date_note: His seals on books are dated AH 1044 and 1048 (1634-39); he became keeper of the imperial library (Daroghah-i Kutubkhana) in Shah Jahan's 31st year (AH 1068) and retired in Aurangzeb's first year.
seals.where_on_object: Fly-leaf, round seal beside inspection notes.
seals.what_it_tells: The book was in Shah Jahan's library by the time of his inspection (one note is dated year 32, May 1658).

facts.text: The earliest of the notes and seals on a British Museum history bears the name of Amanat Khan Shahjahani with the date 1042.
facts.quote: the earliest of which bears the name of Amanat Khan Shahjahani, with the date 1042.

facts.text: A first page is covered with notes and seals of successive librarians of Shah Jahan and of Dara Shikoh.
facts.quote: The first page is covered with 'Arz-Didahs and seals of successive librarians of Shahjahan and Dara Shikuh.

facts.text: The poet Mir Yahya Kashi was appointed librarian by Shah Jahan.
facts.quote: Shahjahan appointed him to the office of librarian and entrusted to him the task of writing a poetical record of his reign.

seals.cautions: Catalogues call these men 'nobles' or 'librarians' loosely; the seal legend decides the office. Names in faded seals are often unreadable.
seals.owner: Officials of Shah Jahan's and Dara Shikoh's libraries: Amanat Khan Shahjahani, 'Abd al-Rashid Daylami, Mir Yahya Kashi (librarian), and others
seals.date_note: Amanat Khan Shahjahani's mark is dated 1042 (1632-33).
seals.where_on_object: First page or fly-leaf.
seals.what_it_tells: Library custody under Shah Jahan; Rieu also records separate librarians of Prince Dara Shikoh.

facts.text: Jahangir names Maktub Khan as superintendent of the library and picture gallery and later raises him to a rank of 1,500.
