facts.quote: Maktub Khan, the superintendent of the library and picture gallery, and one of my old servants

facts.text: Percy Brown repeats that Maktub Khan was in sole charge of both library and picture gallery.
facts.quote: the superintendence of Maktub Khan, who we learn was in sole charge of both the library and picture gallery

seals.cautions: No seal of Maktub Khan was described in the sources read.
seals.translit: Maktūb Khān, dārogha of the kutubkhāna and taṣvīrkhāna
seals.meaning: Superintendent of Jahangir's library and picture gallery
seals.owner: Maktub Khan
seals.where_on_object: (no seal described in the sources read)
seals.what_it_tells: Names the official in charge when Jahangir-period notes were written.

facts.text: Round seal of Qabil Khan, Aurangzeb's librarian, reading 'khana-zad-i 'Alamgir Padshah', on BL Delhi Persian 918, 44 and 1263.
On fol. 5a of a British Museum manuscript are several inspection notes of Aurangzeb's reign with the seals of Sa'd al-Din Khan and others.
facts.quote: several 'Arzdidahs of the reign of Aurangzib, with the seals of Sa'd ud-Din Khan and others.

seals.cautions: Names and readings come from one recent study read through a summary; several seals there are damaged.
seals.translit: khāna-zād-i 'Ālamgīr Pādshāh (Qābil Khān); Sayyid 'Alī al-Ḥusaynī murīd-i 'Ālamgīr pādshāh
seals.meaning: 'House-born servant of 'Alamgir Padshah' (seal of the librarian Qabil Khan); 'Sayyid 'Ali al-Husayni, disciple of 'Alamgir padshah'
seals.owner: Qabil Khan (Aurangzeb's librarian), Sayyid 'Ali al-Husayni, and later keepers Mun'im Bayg and Murad Bayg
seals.date_note: Qabil Khan's seal occurs with notes of regnal year 29 (1685-86); Sayyid 'Ali's seal is dated 106[9] (1658-59).
seals.where_on_object: Fly-leaf.
seals.what_it_tells: Inspection under Aurangzeb; British Museum books also carry Aurangzeb-period notes with the seal of Sa'd al-Din Khan and others.

facts.text: Seal on the verso of a painting for Muhammad Shah: 'the devoted servant [of] Muhammad Shah, Padshah-i Ghazi'.
Aurangzeb's librarian Qabil Khan styled himself khana-zad-i 'Alamgir Padshah; another official, murid-i 'Alamgir padshah.
A court librarian's seal reads 'banda-yi dargah ... kitabdar', dated AH 934 (1527-28); Rieu does not name the court.
facts.quote: At the end is impressed the seal of a court librarian, بندهٔ درگاه زرقوم کتابدار, with the date A.H. 934.

facts.text: A Hyderabad seal reads 'Ghulam Muhyuddin Fidwi-e-Nizamul Mulk, 1130'.
facts.quote: Seals: Ghulàm Muhyuddin Fidwi-e-Nizamul Mulk, 1130.

facts.text: The painter Bichitr signs 'amal-i banda-yi dargah Bichitr' (work of the servant of the court, Bichitr).
facts.quote: ascription in lower right corner: amal - i bandieh dargah Bichitr

seals.cautions: 'Devoted servant of Muhammad Shah' is not Muhammad Shah's seal. The date in such a seal is the year it was cut.
seals.translit: fidvī (devoted servant), khāna-zād (house-born servant), murīd (disciple), banda-yi dargāh (servant of the court)
seals.meaning: Humility formulas that tie a seal-owner to a ruler; they mark officials' and nobles' seals, and also appear in painters' signatures.
seals.owner: Mughal officials, nobles and painters; Deccan officials
seals.date_note: Examples in the sources run from a seal dated AH 934 (1527-28, court not named) through the 18th century.
seals.where_on_object: In seal legends on fly-leaves and versos; in signatures on paintings.
seals.what_it_tells: The seal is an official's or noble's, not the emperor's own; the ruler named gives the reign.

facts.text: A Khuda Bakhsh manuscript that was in Shah Jahan's library bears the seal of Jahan Ara Begam, which the cataloguer calls very rare.
facts.quote: The most interesting of all the seals is that of Jahan Ara Begam, which is very rare and not found in any other MS. in this Library.

seals.cautions: The cataloguer calls it very rare (one example in the Khuda Bakhsh collection); legend not transcribed in the source read.
seals.owner: Jahan Ara Begam (1614-1681), eldest daughter of Shah Jahan
seals.where_on_object: Among the seals and notes on the opening leaves.
seals.what_it_tells: The book passed through the princess's own collection.

facts.text: BL Add.5600 (a Shahnama refurbished c. 1616) has a gold note that Jahangir gave it to Mu'taqid Khan in August 1625, a note by the same man (now Ilahvirdi Khan) passing it to his brother, an owner's note with seal by the brother's son, and a note that it was bought for 700 rupees at Lahore.
facts.quote: purchased for 700 rupees at Lahore at the desire of Nawab Khān Jahān Bahādur.

facts.text: DISPUTED: Seyller and Losty read the gift note dated 1 Azar, regnal year 8, as Jahangir's year 8 (November 1613); Sims-Williams argues it is Shah Jahan's year 8 (November 1635), since the book was still in 'Abd al-Rahim's studio in 1616.
facts.quote: have interpreted this date as referring to the eighth year of Jahāngīr’s reign (November 1613) which is problematic.

facts.text: A Khuda Bakhsh manuscript carries a mutilated seal of a noble of 'Alamgir's time followed by a note recording the price of the manuscript as fifteen rupees.
facts.quote: This is followed by a note which records the price of the MS. as fifteen rupees.

facts.text: Ethé dates many undated India Office manuscripts by the seals and notes of former owners.
facts.quote: Seals and notes of former owners on fol. 1a

seals.cautions: Dates in such notes can be read more than one way (regnal year 8 of which emperor?); see the dispute recorded in the facts.
seals.translit: min mutamallakāt-i ... (from the possessions of ...); ba-... 'ināyat kardand / farmūdand (was given to ...); kharīd namūda shud (was bought)
seals.meaning: Owners' and gift notes: who owned the book, who gave it to whom, sometimes what was paid.
seals.owner: Mughal nobles and later owners
seals.date_note: Examples in the sources run from 1625 into the 18th century.
seals.where_on_object: Fly-leaf or first page, usually followed by the writer's seal.
seals.what_it_tells: A chain of private owners outside the imperial library, e.g. a Jahangir gift in 1625, then brothers and sons, then a purchase at Lahore.

facts.text: Cleveland's Tutinama (c. 1560) has ascriptions such as ''amal Basawan' and ''amal Daswant'; other Cleveland pages read ''amal-i Mushfiq sana 1015', ''amal-i Bichitr' and ''amal-i Muhammad Hashim'.
facts.quote: 'amal basāwan | the work of Basavanta

facts.text: Brown: Akbar-period illustrations were issued unsigned by mostly Hindu painters, and the names were written later by Muslim, often Persian, clerks.
facts.quote: the names which they now bear were written later by Muhammadan and very often by Persian clerks. Unfortunately the reliability of all these inscriptions is open to question

facts.text: Abu'l Fazl names Daswanth and Basawan as Akbar's leading painters, the names that recur in these ascriptions.
facts.quote: 4. Basawan. In back grounding, drawing of features, distribution of colours, portrait painting, and several other branches, he is most excellent

seals.cautions: Percy Brown: in Akbar's books the names were added later by clerks and their reliability is 'open to question'; mistakes were painted over in gold and rewritten. A great name (Bihzad) is sometimes added by a later hand.
seals.translit: 'amal-i [name] / 'amal [name]
seals.meaning: 'Work of [name]': the commonest Mughal ascription of a painting to a painter.
seals.owner: Written by library clerks, by emperors, and sometimes by the painters themselves
seals.date_note: Examples in the sources run from the Cleveland Tutinama (c. 1560) to the 1760s.
seals.where_on_object: Lower margin under the picture in Akbar-period manuscripts; small, inside the painting (on a pillar, rock, book or the ground) in later work; below album portraits.
seals.what_it_tells: Who the court believed painted the picture. In Akbar-period manuscripts it is usually a clerk's label, not a signature.

facts.text: A Chingiznama page at Cleveland (c. 1596-1600) is inscribed: outline drawing by Lal, color work by Dharam Das, important portraits by Padarath.
facts.quote: Outline drawing by Lal, [color] work by Dharam Das, important portraits by Padarath

facts.text: Brown: usually two artists combined, one making the tarh (sketch), the other the 'amal (painting); sometimes a third did the chihra-numa (portraiture) and rarely a fourth the surat (figure drawing).
facts.quote: the one making the tarrah or sketch, and the other doing the 'amal, work, or painting. On occasion, however, there may also have been a third who did the chihra-numa or portraiture

seals.cautions: Brown found the same names on pictures of very different quality and suspected some labelled sets are contemporary copies; credits record the workshop's view, not a signature.
seals.translit: ṭarḥ-i [A], 'amal-i [B], chihra-numā(-yi) [C]
seals.meaning: 'Design (outline) by A, painting by B, faces (important portraits) by C': the split credits of Akbar's workshop.
seals.owner: Akbar's library clerks
seals.where_on_object: Lower margin under the picture, in small nasta'liq.
seals.what_it_tells: Several painters worked on one picture; the first name drew the design, the second colored it, a third did the faces.

facts.text: Cleveland's posthumous portrait of Muhammad Shah is signed 'raqam-i kamtarin Muhammad Reza-i Hindi', with the date 1178 (1764).
facts.quote: raqam-i kamtarin Muhammad Reza-i Hindi

facts.text: A 1755 painting at Cleveland is signed twice, 'amal-i Fayzullah on a pillar capital and 'bi-qalam-i Fayzullah Musavvir walad-i Faqirullah Musavvir' with the year.
facts.quote: bi - qalam i Fayzullah Musavvir walad - i Faqirullah Musavvir dar sanna 1755

facts.text: A Jahangir-period painting in BL Or.7573 is signed in Arabic 'sawwarahu al-'abd Muhammad Rida'.
facts.quote: ṣawwarahu al-‘abd Muḥammad Riḍā (‘painted by the slave [of God] Muḥammad Riżā’)

seals.cautions: 'kar-i' is named here but no source read for this file gives an example (gap). Any signature can be copied onto a later picture.
seals.translit: raqam-i kamtarīn [name] (written/drawn by the humblest ...); bi-qalam-i [name] (by the pen of ...); ṣawwarahu al-'abd [name] (painted by the servant [of God] ...); kār-i [name] (work of ...)
seals.meaning: Other ways painters and clerks sign or ascribe paintings.
seals.owner: Painters
seals.date_note: Examples in the sources: c. 1611 (Muhammad Riza), 1755 (Fayzullah), 1764 (Muhammad Riza Hindi).
seals.where_on_object: Bottom center of the picture, inside the painting, or in the margin.
seals.what_it_tells: Signatures with a date and parentage (e.g. 'Fayzullah the painter son of Faqirullah the painter, 1755') are stronger evidence than a bare name.

facts.text: Brown: where a name is microscopically inscribed on some detail of the picture, it may have been written by the artist himself.
facts.quote: Occasionally, where the name is microscopically inscribed on some detail of the picture, it may have been written by the artist himself

facts.text: Cleveland examples: ''amal-i Fayzullah' on the capital of a central pillar (1755); ''amal 'Aqil Khan' signed in the lower right of the miniature (c. 1765).
facts.quote: on capital of central pillar: 'amal - i Fayzullah

seals.cautions: Microscopic names need magnification; do not confuse with later margin labels.
seals.meaning: Tiny names painted into a detail of the picture
seals.owner: Painters
seals.date_note: Cleveland examples are dated 1755 and c. 1765.
seals.where_on_object: On a pillar capital, a book, a rock, a sword hilt, the lower right corner of the picture.
seals.what_it_tells: A microscopic name inside the picture may be the painter's own writing, unlike margin labels.

facts.text: Jahangir writes that Abu'l Hasan has become Nadir al-Zaman and Ustad Mansur has the title Nadir al-'Asr.
facts.quote: Truly he has become Nādira-i-zamān (“the wonder of the age”). Also, Ustād Manṣūr has become such a master in painting that he has the title of Nādiru-l-ʿAṣr

facts.text: Brown lists an India Office (Johnson album) painting of an old pilgrim 'painted by Nadir uz-Zaman' and notes Jahangir's habit of inventing such titles.
facts.quote: Jahangir had a playful way of devising these and conferring them on those who pleased him with their handiwork.

seals.cautions: Titles were famous and are easy to add to a later copy.
seals.translit: Nādir al-Zamān (Abu'l Hasan); Nādir al-'Aṣr (Ustad Mansur)
seals.meaning: 'Wonder of the Age' titles given by Jahangir to his favorite painters; they appear in ascriptions.
seals.owner: Abu'l Hasan and Ustad Mansur
seals.where_on_object: In the ascription or signature.
seals.what_it_tells: An ascription to 'Nadir al-Zaman' means Abu'l Hasan; to 'Nadir al-'Asr', Mansur.

facts.text: Brown saw frequent corrections of artists' names in the British Museum Darabnama: clerks smeared a wrong name with gold paint and wrote another across it.
facts.quote: deleting his first incorrect inscription with a smear of gold paint, and then writing across it another name.

facts.text: The names of Mirak and Bihzad were written under a painting in BL Or.6810 at an unknown date; Jahangir in 1605 claimed 16 of its pictures for Bihzad.
facts.quote: The names of both Mirak, the older master, and of Bihzad have been written underneath it at an unknown date

facts.text: A Cleveland portrait of a Jain monk carries a later spurious attribution to Bihzad above a palm tree.
facts.quote: Later spurious attribution to the famed Persian painter Bihzad (1450–1535) inscribed above palm tree.

facts.text: Brown illustrates a painting on which Bihzad's name was 'clumsily inscribed by a recent hand', and another 'erroneously inscribed Jahangir Padshah in the writing of a later hand'.
facts.quote: The original picture is erroneously inscribed ‘ Jahangir Padshadi ’ in the writing of a later hand.

facts.text: Jahangir claimed he could name the painter of any work, and even who painted the eyes and eyebrows of a face.
facts.quote: without the names being told me, I say on the spur of the moment that it is the work of such and such a man.

seals.cautions: Treat every name as a reading to test against style, not as proof. Never take a name as evidence that an item is old or genuine.
seals.meaning: How far to trust names written on Mughal paintings
seals.where_on_object: Margins, fly-leaves, inside the painting.
seals.what_it_tells: Ascriptions tell what someone believed at some date; contemporary clerks erred, emperors claimed attributions, and later hands added famous names.

facts.text: A Mughal Shahnama page at Cleveland has '25 / Haidar Kashmiri' in the left margin.
facts.quote: Persian inscription in left margin, in nasta‘liq script: 25 / Haidar Kashmiri

facts.text: The 89 paintings of BL Add.5600 are numbered consecutively 1-91, with one number and a gap where a page is missing.
facts.quote: These are numbered consecutively 1-91, only lacking no. 37

facts.text: A Bikaner Bhagavata Purana page at the National Museum of Asian Art carries a folio number, chapter notes and various other inventory numbers.
facts.quote: Various other inventory numbers.

seals.cautions: Numbers are easy to add and often added by later owners and dealers; several systems may coexist on one page.
seals.meaning: Numbers written on illustrated pages: the picture's place in the manuscript, folio numbers, later inventory numbers
seals.owner: Mughal and later libraries; Rajput courts; collectors
seals.where_on_object: Margin beside the painter's name, top or bottom margin, verso.
seals.what_it_tells: A picture number shows the page came from a series or a manuscript; it helps match detached pages to their book.

facts.text: A Bundi painting at Cleveland has on its verso an Udaipur inventory number '21/57', plus the Urdu and English signature, seal and number of the 20th-century painter-collector Chughtai.
facts.quote: Verso: Udaipur inventory 21/57 Chughtai signature in both Urdu and English Chughtai seal and number 117

facts.text: A Malwa ragamala page at Cleveland has the seal of Datia state on its reverse.
facts.quote: On reverse is seal of Datia state

facts.text: A Bikaner page at the National Museum of Asian Art has a purple stamp and Khet Singh's signature stamped in purple ink.
facts.quote: Purple stamp and Khet Singh signature stamped out with purple ink.

seals.cautions: These marks are part of the painting_schools topic too; ink stamps (purple) are modern administrative marks, not original to the painting.
seals.meaning: Stamps, seals and inventory numbers of Rajput and Central Indian court collections found on paintings
seals.owner: Mewar (Udaipur), Bikaner, Datia and other court collections
seals.where_on_object: Verso of the painting.
seals.what_it_tells: The painting was in a named court collection; Udaipur numbers are written as two numbers with a slash.

facts.text: A ragamala page at the National Museum of Asian Art has, in a later hand in blue ink, '8000' crossed out and 'Rs. 5000'.
facts.quote: (top) in a later hand in blue ink, 8000 crossed out; Rs. 5000

facts.text: A purchase note on BL Add.5600 records 700 rupees paid at Lahore in the 17th century, an example of a historical price note.

seals.cautions: Do not confuse with Mughal library valuations (valuation_note). A crossed-out higher price shows haggling, nothing about age.
seals.meaning: Prices written on paintings by later owners and dealers
seals.owner: Dealers and owners
seals.date_note: Written 'in a later hand'; no date given by the source.
seals.where_on_object: Verso or margins, in pencil, blue or black ink.
seals.what_it_tells: A rupee price in a later hand is a trade mark, not a historical valuation.

facts.text: Tipu Sultan's personal seal is dated 1186 (1772/73), before his accession at the end of 1782; a wax seal possibly dated 1219 is 'quite a few years earlier than the document it is connected to'.
facts.quote: The seal predates Tipu's accession to the throne at the end of 1782 after the death of his father Hyder ʻAli.

facts.text: British officers' Persian seals were usually dated to the year their Mughal titles were granted.
facts.quote: the date of his seal which presumably corresponded with the date of his being awarded his titles.

facts.text: Ethé dates undated manuscripts by their seals ('No date. A seal from AH 1172 ...').
facts.quote: No date. A seal from a. h. 1172 (a. d. 1758, 1759)

facts.text: 'Inayat Khan's seals are dated AH 1044 and 1048, but he became keeper of the library only in AH 1068.

seals.cautions: Owners kept using a seal for years: 'Inayat Khan's seals of 1044 and 1048 predate his librarianship of 1068; Tipu's personal seal of 1186 predates his accession.
seals.meaning: The year engraved in a seal is the year the seal was cut (often when its owner received a title or office), not the year it was pressed on the book.
seals.where_on_object: Inside the seal, usually under or beside the name.
seals.what_it_tells: A dated seal gives only the earliest possible date of the impression, and therefore a latest possible date for the copying of an undated manuscript.

facts.text: Rieu: a first page covered with seals and inspection notes of Shah Jahan's reign had been cut from a copy of Jami's Yusuf and Zalikha and cunningly pasted onto a later history, giving it a deceptive appearance of antiquity.
facts.quote: The first page of this MS. imparts to it a deceptive appearance of antiquity ; for it is covered with seals and 'arz-didahs, several of which are of the reign of Shahjahan.

facts.text: Khuda Bakhsh: the last figure of a colophon date had been changed to '9', which the cataloguer detected through the seal of Sultan Muhammad Qutb Shah on the title page.
facts.quote: The last figure of the date has been changed to “ 9.” This would have passed unobserved but for the seal (on the title-page) of Sultan Muhammad Qutb Shah

seals.cautions: Check that the fly-leaf belongs to the text: Rieu found a leaf with Shah Jahan-period notes from a copy of Jami's Yusuf and Zulaykha pasted onto a history written c. 1705, with a spurious preface to disguise missing pages. A Golconda manuscript's colophon date had its last figure changed, caught only through a royal seal.
seals.meaning: Fly-leaves with imperial notes moved from another book; dates in colophons altered
seals.date_note: Recorded in 19th- and early-20th-century catalogues; the practice is older.
seals.where_on_object: First leaf (pasted down), colophon.
seals.what_it_tells: A crowded imperial fly-leaf proves only that that leaf was in the imperial library.

facts.text: Sprenger (1854): Lucknow's royal library was checked only by counting volumes, so good books were taken out and bad ones put in their place; a librarian sold 1,100 rupees' worth of books in a week.
facts.quote: merely to count the volumes, and to make the librarian responsible for the numbers not diminishing. The consequence is that many good books have been abstracted and bad ones put in their place.

facts.text: Ivanow (1924): a copy listed with Shah Jahan's seal is now a worm-eaten, worthless modern copy.
facts.quote: a copy dated 902 AH., bearing the seal of Shahjahan. But at present there is a defective and worm-eaten quite worthless, modern copy

seals.cautions: Both the Lucknow royal library in the 1840s and the Asiatic Society of Bengal lost valuable copies this way.
seals.meaning: Valuable books taken out of court libraries and cheap copies put in their place
seals.date_note: Recorded by Sprenger (1854) and Ivanow (1924).
seals.what_it_tells: A library number or listing does not prove the book now under it is the one listed.

facts.text: In BL Add.5600, 55 original illustrations were covered with paper and painted over in India c. 1616, and 35 more added in blank spaces.
facts.quote: The remaining 55 original illustrations were covered with paper which was then painted over.

facts.text: A Gulistan copied in Bukhara in 1567/68 was 'improved' in Jahangir's reign with seven more paintings; a 1557-58 Layla Majnun had its five paintings added some fifty years later.
facts.quote: The manuscript was 'improved' again in Jahangir's reign when seven more paintings were added, probably between 1605 and 1609.

facts.text: Cleveland's Panj Ganj pages have Herat text of c. 1500-20 with paintings and borders added in the Deccan in 1603-7; Cleveland's Kevorkian Album shamsa portrait was altered after 1658 to show Aurangzeb.
facts.quote: The portrait of Aurangzeb was probably added when he took over the imperial library after seizing the throne from his father, Shah Jahan, in 1658

facts.text: The Kashmiri-style illumination and blue leather binding of BL Or.2361 (copied 1662-65) date from a later period, probably the 19th-century changes of ownership.
facts.quote: the manuscript’s Kashmiri-style illumination and gold-tooled blue leather binding date from a later period

seals.cautions: Look for paper pasted over earlier pictures, paintings in a later style than the script, and portraits with altered faces.
seals.meaning: Paintings added to older manuscripts, painted over earlier pictures, or altered to show a later ruler
seals.owner: Mughal workshops and later restorers
seals.where_on_object: The painted pages themselves; bindings and illumination.
seals.what_it_tells: A book's text, paintings, illumination and binding can be of different dates and places; seals date only the ownership.

facts.text: Cleveland's Baburnama page (c. 1589) has outer margins added about the mid-1900s.
facts.quote: c. 1589; outer margins added c. mid-1900s

facts.text: Akbar's Khamsa (BL Or.12208) had 42 illustrated folios, 5 now in the Walters Art Museum; a Divan of Hafiz is split between the British Library and the Chester Beatty Library.
facts.quote: 5 of which are now in the Walters Art Museum, Baltimore

facts.text: Brown notes that mounting pictures from a book or album separately under glass was already standard museum practice in 1924.
facts.quote: To carry out this plan, however, in the case of an illustrated book or a muraqqa raises many debatable issues, as it necessitates taking the pictures out of the volume and mounting them separately.

seals.cautions: Remargining can hide or remove margin ascriptions and numbers. Parts of one manuscript can sit in different museums.
seals.meaning: Single pages cut from manuscripts and albums, often given new margins
seals.where_on_object: Margins and borders.
seals.what_it_tells: A detached page has usually lost the fly-leaf where the library seals and notes were; margins may be modern.

facts.text: Brown: Nadir Shah's sack of Delhi in 1739 made the first inroad; the Rohilla wars and the Marathas took more; the final dispersal came in 1857.
facts.quote: When the Persian monarch, Nadir Shah, sacked Delhi in the year 1739, the first real inroad was made on the imperial library of Mughal manuscripts and miniatures

facts.text: The British Library's Delhi Persian manuscripts, with imperial library notes, reached London after 1857; one may have been taken from a noble's descendants then.
Several British Library notes and seals are erased or damaged; the Salar Jung and Khuda Bakhsh catalogues record many seals as defaced or faded.
facts.quote: Seals: Defaced.

seals.cautions: Mughal seals were sometimes scraped off after looting; their absence proves nothing.
seals.meaning: How the Mughal imperial library was scattered, and how that shows on books
seals.where_on_object: Later seals and notes stacked after the Mughal ones.
seals.what_it_tells: Persian and Ottoman seals after Mughal ones point to Nadir Shah's 1739 booty; Lucknow, Hyderabad and British seals to 18th- and 19th-century sales; the British Library 'Delhi Persian' collection was taken from the palace in 1857.

facts.text: Many manuscripts from the Lucknow royal library bear the vermilion stamps of Sulaiman Jah and Amjad 'Ali, with verse legends.
facts.quote: once belonged to the Royal library of Lucknow, and bears the vermillion stamps of two kings of Oude, Sulaiman Jah and Amjad 'Ali, containing the following inscriptions in verse.

facts.text: A manuscript once at the court of Awadh contains the characteristic red seals of Nasir al-Din Haidar and Amjad 'Ali Shah.
facts.quote: it contains the characteristic red seals of Nāṣir al-Dīn Ḥaydar (r. 1827-37) and Amjad ʻAlī Shāh (r. 1842-47).

facts.text: Two independent catalogues record red (vermilion) seals of these two Awadh kings on books from the Lucknow royal library.

seals.cautions: Rieu names the owner 'Sulaiman Jah'; the British Library identifies the same red seals as Nasir al-Din Haidar's (our identification links the two). Lucknow books often carry earlier Mughal notes too.
seals.native: خوش است مهر کتبخانهٔ سلیمان جاه / بهر کتاب مزین چو نقش بسم الله
seals.translit: Khush ast muhr-i kutubkhāna-yi Sulaymān Jāh / ba-har kitāb muzayyan chu naqsh-i bismillāh
seals.meaning: 'Fine is the seal of the library of Sulayman Jah, adorning every book like the words In the name of God' (translation ours).
seals.owner: Nasir al-Din Haidar, King of Awadh (r. 1827-1837), titled Sulayman Jah
seals.where_on_object: Vermilion (red) impression on the first page or fly-leaf.
seals.what_it_tells: The book was in the royal library at Lucknow.

facts.text: Rieu prints the verse legend of Amjad 'Ali's vermilion stamp.
British Library and Khuda Bakhsh manuscripts carry Amjad 'Ali Shah's red seals at the beginning and end.
facts.quote: Several seals of Amjad ‘Ali Shah and Wajid ‘Ali Shah, the late kings of Oudh, are fixed at the beginning and the end of the copy.

seals.cautions: Usually found with Nasir al-Din Haidar's or Wajid 'Ali Shah's seals. Sprenger heard in 1854 that the Lucknow libraries had been given up to pillage, so many such books left Lucknow without any record.
seals.native: ناسخ هر مهر شد چون شد مزین بر کتاب / خاتم امجد علی شاه زمان عالیجناب
seals.translit: Nāsikh-i har muhr shud chun shud muzayyan bar kitāb / khātam-i Amjad 'Alī Shāh-i zamān-i 'ālī-janāb
seals.meaning: 'When it adorned the book it cancelled every other seal: the seal of Amjad 'Ali, king of the age, of exalted rank' (translation ours).
seals.owner: Amjad 'Ali Shah, King of Awadh (r. 1842-1847)
seals.where_on_object: Red impression, at the beginning and end of the book.
seals.what_it_tells: The book was in the Lucknow royal library in the 1840s.

facts.text: Khuda Bakhsh manuscripts carry several seals of Wajid 'Ali Shah and Amjad 'Ali Shah, 'the later kings of Oude'.
facts.quote: Several seals of the later kings of Oude, viz. Wajid ‘Ali Shah and Amjad ‘Ali Shah, are affixed at the end of the manuscript.

seals.cautions: Legend not transcribed in the source read (gap).
seals.owner: Wajid 'Ali Shah, last King of Awadh (r. 1847-1856)
seals.where_on_object: Beginning and end of the book, with Amjad 'Ali Shah's seals.
seals.what_it_tells: The book was in the Lucknow royal library until its dispersal.

facts.text: The Lucknow royal library held Hafiz Rahmat Khan's whole library, was enriched by Ghazi al-Din Haidar, and was kept in three parts: the Moti Mahal, the Farah Bakhsh palace, and the Topkhana (arsenal).
facts.quote: It contained the whole of the literary treasures of Hafitz Rahmat Khan, and was subsequently much enriched more particularly by Ghaziy aldyn Haydar.

facts.text: Muhammad Salih was librarian of the Moti Mahal under Ghazi al-Din Haidar.
facts.quote: made for Ghazi ud Din by Muhammad Salih, librarian of the Moty Mahall

facts.text: Many British Museum manuscripts are described as 'from the royal library of Lucknow'.
facts.quote: From the royal library of Lucknow.

seals.cautions: A Lucknow seal on a Mughal book shows a later owner, not the maker.
seals.meaning: The royal library of the Nawabs and Kings of Awadh at Lucknow
seals.owner: Kings of Awadh; librarian Muhammad Salih of the Moti Mahal (d. c. 1840)
seals.date_note: Sprenger catalogued it in 1848-50; by 1854 he heard it had been 'given up to pillage'.
seals.what_it_tells: Lucknow absorbed the library of the Rohilla chief Hafiz Rahmat Khan and many Mughal books; Hamilton and other British collections bought from it.

facts.text: The seal of Maharajah Tikait Rai, dated 1203, is on the first page of a British Museum manuscript, with an 'Arz-didah of AH 1206.
facts.quote: The seal of Maharajah Tiket Rai, with the date 1203, is found on its first page, as well as an 'Arz-didah, dated A.H. 1206.

facts.text: William Yule's manuscripts derive partly from the library of the Awadh diwan Maharaja Tikait Rai.
facts.quote: the Dīwān of Awadh Maharaja Tikait Rai Bahadur (1760–1808)

seals.cautions: Legend not transcribed in the sources read.
seals.owner: Maharaja Tikait Rai, diwan of Awadh (1760-1808)
seals.date_note: Seal dated 1203 (1788-89), with an inspection note of AH 1206 on the same page.
seals.where_on_object: First page.
seals.what_it_tells: The book was in the library of Awadh's Hindu finance minister; several later passed to the British collector William Yule.

facts.text: The library's first seal carried the Persian inscription 'Hast in muhr bar kutub khana-i wali-i Rampur farzana', meaning 'this is the seal of the library by the wise ruler of Rampur'.
facts.quote: The first signet of the library was conceptualised in a Persian inscription: Hast in Muhr Bar Kutub Khana: Waali-i-Rampur Farzana.

facts.text: The library got its own seal in 1851-52, under Nawab Muhammad Sa'id Khan.
facts.quote: during his reign, the library got its own seal, in 1851-1852.

seals.cautions: Known only from journalists' accounts that seem to rest on the library's own text; the seals of individual Nawabs were not found (gap).
seals.native: هست این مهر بر کتب‌خانهٔ والی رامپور فرزانه
seals.translit: Hast īn muhr bar kutubkhāna-yi wālī-yi Rāmpūr farzāna
seals.meaning: 'This is the seal on the library of the wise ruler of Rampur'
seals.owner: Rampur State library (now Rampur Raza Library), Nawabs of Rampur
seals.date_note: One account dates the first library seal to 1851-52, under Nawab Muhammad Sa'id Khan (r. 1840-1855); the library traces its founding to Nawab Faizullah Khan, 1774.
seals.where_on_object: Fly-leaf or first page.
seals.what_it_tells: The book or album belonged to the Rampur state library.

facts.text: Stewart (1809): all volumes rebound at Seringapatam have the names of God, Muhammad, Fatima, Hasan and Husain in a central medallion, the four caliphs in the corners, 'Sirkari Khodadad' at the top and 'Allah Kafy' at the bottom.
facts.quote: At the top is “ Sirkari Khodadad,” (the government given by God); and at the bottom, “ Allah Kafy,” (God is sufficient).

facts.text: Sims-Williams lists the stamped inscriptions in detail (front top Sarkar-i Khudadadi; pendants Allah kafi; Qur'an verses on back and spine) and notes a contemporary binding still with the Prize Agents' label of 1799.
facts.quote: Front top: Sarkār-i Khudādādī ‘God-given government’

seals.cautions: Not all Tipu bindings carry the stamps, and many were altered in restoration. Some volumes still carry the 1799 Prize Agents' labels.
seals.translit: Sarkār-i Khudādādī (top); Allāh, Muḥammad, 'Alī, Fāṭima, Ḥasan, Ḥusayn (central medallion); Allāh kāfī (pendants); the four caliphs' names (corners)
seals.meaning: 'The God-given government' (Tipu's name for his state); 'God is sufficient'
seals.owner: Tipu Sultan's library at Seringapatam (Srirangapatna), Mysore (r. 1782-1799)
seals.where_on_object: Stamped on the outside of leather bindings made at Seringapatam.
seals.what_it_tells: The book was rebound for Tipu's library; captured in 1799, the library went to the East India Company (London deposits 1806-08 and 1837) and Fort William College, Calcutta.

facts.text: Tipu's personal rectangular seal reads Tipu Sultan 1186 (1772/73).
facts.quote: The rectangular seal is inscribed Tīpū Sulṭān 1186 (1772/73), measuring 16 x 11.5 mm

facts.text: A few of Tipu's books were impressed with his private signet 'Tipu Sultan'; only a small number of Asiatic Society manuscripts bear it; India Office manuscripts also carry 'a seal of Tipu Sultan'.
facts.quote: A few were impressed with the private signet “‘Typu Sultan.”

seals.cautions: Only a small share of Tipu's books carry his seal (28 found among several hundred at the British Library).
seals.translit: Tīpū Sulṭān 1186
seals.meaning: 'Tipu Sultan, [AH] 1186'
seals.owner: Tipu Sultan
seals.date_note: Rectangular seal, 16 x 11.5 mm, dated 1186 (1772/73), before his accession.
seals.where_on_object: Top or margin of the opening page.
seals.what_it_tells: Tipu personally valued the book (mostly poetry, history, letter-writing).

facts.text: Official seals of 1215 and 1223 mawludi; the 1796 regulations prescribe the special seal with the tughra in the shape of a tiger's mouth and six tiger stripes.
facts.quote: It reads: Tipū Sulṭān 3221 [ie. 1223] Maw lū d-i Muḥammad (1795/96).

seals.cautions: Digits run right to left; read 5121 as 1215 mawludi, not a Hijri year.
seals.translit: Tīpū Sulṭān 5121 [= 1215]; Tīpū Sulṭān 3221 [= 1223] Maw-lū-d-i Muḥammad
seals.meaning: Official seals in Tipu's mawludi era: 1215 (1787/88) and 1223 (1795/96); the second has the name as a tughra shaped like a tiger's mouth with tiger stripes, and the letters of mawlud-i Muhammad in the corners.
seals.owner: Tipu Sultan's government
seals.where_on_object: Head or right side of documents and official manuals.
seals.what_it_tells: An official Seringapatam document or manual, not a library book.

facts.text: A Tipu library manuscript once belonged to the Qutb Shahs and has seals of Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah and of Muhammad Qutb Shah, the latter dated 1021 (1612/13).
facts.quote: includes the seals of Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah (r. 1580-1612) and his successor Muhammad Qutb Shah (r. 1612-26) – his seal dated 1021 (1612/13).

facts.text: Khuda Bakhsh manuscripts bear seals of Sultan Muhammad Qutb Shah and of 'Abd Allah Qutb Shah, sixth king of the dynasty.
facts.quote: The MS. bears the seal of ‘Abd Ullah Qutb Shah, the sixth king of the Qutb Shahi dynasty of Golconda

facts.text: The Salar Jung collection includes a rare seal of Ibrahim Qutb Shah.
A Golconda portrait at the National Museum of Asian Art has 'Abdullah Qutub Shah' written in the top verso margin.
facts.quote: Top verso margin: Abdullah Qutub Shah

seals.cautions: Legends not transcribed in the sources read (gap). A Qutb Shahi seal helped expose an altered colophon date (see pasted_flyleaf_and_altered_dates).
seals.owner: Qutb Shahi kings of Golconda: Ibrahim, Muhammad Quli (r. 1580-1612), Muhammad (r. 1612-26), 'Abd Allah
seals.date_note: Muhammad Qutb Shah's seal is dated 1021 (1612/13).
seals.where_on_object: Title page or fly-leaf.
seals.what_it_tells: The book was in the Golconda royal library; many such books later reached Mughal, Hyderabad, Mysore and British owners.

facts.text: The Salar Jung collection includes a rare seal of 'Ali 'Adil Shah II of Bijapur.
Some books in Tipu Sultan's library had formerly belonged to the kings of Bijapur and Golconda.
facts.quote: Some of them had formerly belonged to the Mohammedan Kings of Bijapore and Golcondah

seals.cautions: Only a mention was found; legends not transcribed (gap).
seals.owner: 'Adil Shahi kings of Bijapur, e.g. 'Ali 'Adil Shah II
seals.where_on_object: Fly-leaf or title page.
seals.what_it_tells: The book was in the Bijapur royal library before the Mughal conquest.

facts.text: Salar Jung Museum manuscripts carry seals of Munir al-Mulk dated 1206 and of Hyder Yar Khan, 'ancestor of the collector'.
facts.quote: Seals : 4 of Hyder Yar Khan, ancestor of the collector,

facts.text: Rieu and the British Library record manuscripts from the Hyderabad libraries of Samsam al-Mulk Shahnavaz Khan and Munir al-Mulk.
facts.quote: library of Samsam ul-Mulk in Haidarabad

seals.cautions: The Nizams' own seals and the Asafiya (state) library stamp were not found in the sources read (gap).
seals.owner: Hyderabad nobles under the Nizams: the Salar Jung family (Munir al-Mulk, seal dated 1206; Hyder Yar Khan, seal dated 1184), Samsam al-Mulk Shahnavaz Khan, officials styled 'servant of Nizam al-Mulk'
seals.where_on_object: Fly-leaf and first page.
seals.what_it_tells: The book was in a Hyderabad noble library; Salar Jung family seals mark books now in or once in the Salar Jung Museum.

facts.text: Sims-Williams lists dated Persian seals of Swinton, Browne, Johnson, Grant, Rotton, Yule, Price and Skinner in British Library manuscripts.
facts.quote: Bookplate of Richard Johnson (1753-1807) based on his seal dated 1780: Mumtāz al-Dawlah Mufakhkhar al-Mulk Richārd Jānsan Bahādur Ḥusām Jang, 1194.

facts.text: Company officials used Persian seals because they acted, in theory, as servants of the Mughal emperor.
facts.quote: This was a long-established practice in India where officials of the East India Company were theoretically acting as ‘servants’ of the Mughal emperor

facts.text: European owners' Persian seals are recorded independently in other catalogues: Halhed's Persian seal (Rieu), a seal of Major Polier dated AH 1181 (Khuda Bakhsh), and Claude Martin's seal on several folios (Ivanow).
facts.quote: It belonged some time to Claude Martin, whose seal appears on several folios.

seals.cautions: These seals are in Persian and look 'Mughal'; read the name before assuming an Indian owner. They date the owner, not the book.
seals.meaning: Persian-script seals of British (and other European) officers, often with Mughal titles and a date
seals.owner: East India Company officers and European adventurers, e.g. Archibald Swinton (1174), James Browne (1191), Richard Johnson (1194), James Grant (Bengali era 1193), Richard Rotton (regnal year 32 of Shah 'Alam II), William Yule (1213), William Price (1226), James Skinner (1830), Antoine Polier (1181), Claude Martin, Nathaniel Brassey Halhed
seals.date_note: Dated examples in the sources run from 1174 (1760/61) to 1830; British officials in the Persian Gulf still used Persian-script seals into the 20th century.
seals.where_on_object: Fly-leaf, first or last page; sometimes as a printed bookplate.
seals.what_it_tells: A European owner in India in the 18th-19th century; the titles and date usually mark the year the Mughal emperor granted the titles.

facts.text: Johnson's titles were granted by Shah 'Alam II on 4 Rabi' I 1194 (10 March 1780); his collection was bought by the Company in February 1807.
facts.quote: Richard Johnson’s bookplate inscribed in English and Persian with his name and Mughal titles

seals.cautions: A Johnson bookplate or seal does not prove the British Library ever owned the item; Or.6810 was sold separately and bought back from a dealer in 1908.
seals.translit: Mumtāz al-Dawla Mufakhkhar al-Mulk Richārd Jānsan Bahādur Ḥusām Jang, 1194
seals.meaning: 'Richard Johnson, chosen of the dynasty, exalted of the kingdom, valiant, sharp blade in war, [AH] 1194 (1780)'
seals.owner: Richard Johnson (1753-1807), East India Company official at Lucknow and Hyderabad
seals.date_note: The two British Library posts give different manuscript counts: 'an estimated 1000' (2014) and 716 (2017).
seals.where_on_object: Seal and printed bookplate in English and Persian.
seals.what_it_tells: The item belonged to Johnson, whose 64 albums and manuscripts went to the East India Company library in 1807 (now British Library); a few left the collection earlier and were sold.

facts.text: A British Museum Divan bears the seal of the College of Fort William.
facts.quote: This volume bears the seal of the college of Fort William.

facts.text: The college seal was still in use in 1924 by the Board of Examiners, who stamped it on their acquisitions.
facts.quote: The seal of the College, however, is still in use with the Board of Examiners (now at Dehli), the direct successors of the College, who stamp it on their acquisitions.

seals.cautions: Ivanow notes the Board of Examiners still stamped the college seal on its acquisitions in 1924, so the seal alone does not date the acquisition to the college years.
seals.owner: College of Fort William, Calcutta, and its successor the Board of Examiners
seals.date_note: Still stamped by the Board of Examiners in 1924 (Ivanow).
seals.where_on_object: Fly-leaf or first page.
seals.what_it_tells: The book passed through the college library (which held much of Tipu's library) before the Asiatic Society of Bengal, the India Office or the British Museum.

facts.text: A Khuda Bakhsh manuscript has the seal of the library of Nawwab Sayyid Vilayat 'Ali Khan of Patna beside a note; the name of Sayyid Khwurshid Nawwab, who gave it, appears in several places.

rows.name: Bidri ware
rows.date_note: Tradition places the origin at Bidar under the Bahmani and Barid Shahi rulers (15th-16th century); museum examples are cataloged from about 1650 (Cleveland). Still made at Bidar and Hyderabad.
rows.identify_by: A cast vessel of gray zinc alloy, blackened all over, with silver (sometimes gold or brass) wire or sheet hammered into cut channels so the bright metal sits flush with or slightly above the matt black ground.
how_to_recognize: Matt, dead-black surface; the alloy under scratches is pale gray, not yellow
Inlay is silver wire or sheet set into engraved channels; floral, poppy, diaper or star patterns
Cast and lathe-turned forms (hookah bases, pandan, surahi, basins); a lead plug may close the casting hole in the base
Heavy for its size but does not dent or rust; breaks only under a hard blow
rows.marks_and_labels: Old pieces are rarely marked; sources describe no maker's stamps. Exhibition-era and later pieces may carry dealer labels; 20th-century Hyderabad work may carry cooperative or emporium labels (not described in the sources).
rows.later_production: Declining by the 1880s (Mukharji) and nearly extinct at Murshidabad; promoted for the European market from the 1880s (vases, tumblers, cups and saucers, salt-cellars). The Nizam's government revived it in the first half of the 20th century with a department at the Central School of Arts and Crafts, Hyderabad; by 1961 it was made in cooperative workshops for emporia and export, in new forms. Registered as a Geographical Indication (Karnataka).
rows.how_to_tell_old: Sources give no reliable test of age. The Salar Jung catalogue says museum dating "is only approximate and is based on design". Pointers the sources do give: 20th-century Hyderabad work introduced new Western forms (cigarette cases, ash trays, cuff links) and figures copied from the Ajanta murals; Lucknow fish motifs belong to the Oudh court style; some old pieces are heavier because of more lead in the alloy, but weight is not a test on its own.

look_alikes.name: Moradabad 'bidri' (black-lac brass)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Moradabad makers imitated bidri with tinned brass or copper whose ground was cut away and filled with black lac; it is brass or copper underneath (yellow or red where scratched), the black is a lac filling, not a chemically blackened alloy, and it is far lighter in tone where worn.

look_alikes.name: Koftgari (gold or silver on blued steel)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Koftgari is on iron or steel, which is magnetic and may rust; bidri is a non-magnetic zinc alloy that sources say does not rust.

look_alikes.name: Blackened or patinated brass and modern copies
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Brass shows yellow where the surface is worn or scratched; bidri alloy is gray-white under the black.

look_alikes.name: Black pottery imitating bidri
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Birdwood notes bidri "is also imitated in pottery"; ceramic is lighter, rings differently and shows a fired body at chips.

rows.features_other: Alloy: mostly zinc with a little copper (ratios recorded from 16:1 to 4:1), sometimes lead or tin. Blackened with a paste of sal ammoniac and saltpetre or the saltpetre-bearing earth of Bidar fort.
rows.cautions: Sources note the alloy is brittle and can break if dropped. No legal cautions given.

facts.text: The ware takes its name from Bidar, north-west of Hyderabad in the Nizam's dominions.
facts.quote: This peculiar art-ware derived its name from the town of Bidar, its original home

facts.text: The body is cast from an alloy of zinc and copper whose proportions varied by place; Lucknow added steel powder and Murshidabad tin.
facts.quote: This is an alloy of copper and zinc, the proportion in which each metal is used varying in different places.

facts.text: Salar Jung Museum gives zinc to copper as 16 to 1, with lead in heavier items.
facts.quote: The mixture of zinc and copper is in the ratio of 16 to I.

facts.text: Early writers disagreed on the alloy: Heyne (1817) found tin and copper, Wilkins zinc; Birdwood (1880) gave copper, lead and tin; later writers give zinc.
facts.quote: He examined the alloy used, and found it to consist of 24 parts of tin to i of copper.

facts.text: Blackening is done with a paste of sal ammoniac and saltpetre (with blue vitriol at Murshidabad and Lucknow); the black does not affect the inlay.
facts.quote: performed at Bidar by the application of a paste made of salammoniac and saltpetre, ground up with brackish water.

facts.text: A saltpetre-bearing clay from Bidar fort is used to blacken the alloy.
facts.quote: A particular clay containing salt-petre found in Bidar Fort, diluted in water, is generally used for blackening the alloy.

facts.text: Bidri does not rust and breaks only under a severe blow; Watt adds that it is heavy and clumsy.
facts.quote: Bidri does not rust, and only breaks by a severe blow, but it is very heavy and clumsy.

facts.text: The casting hole in the base is closed with lead before final polishing.
facts.quote: the hole in the bottom of the vessel left in the place of the opening through which the molten alloy was poured into the mould, is closed with lead

facts.text: Four seats of manufacture in the 1880s: Bidar, Lucknow, Purnea and Murshidabad; Watt adds a little at Kashmir.
facts.quote: At present, the four chief seats of Bidri manufacture are Bidar itself, Lucknow in Oudh, Purniah, and Murshidabad in Bengal.

facts.text: Usual forms: hookah bases, surahi water bottles, spittoons, pandan betel boxes, abkhora cups; for Europeans, vases, tumblers, cups and saucers, plates, trays and salt-cellars.
facts.quote: For European use, flower vase, tumbler, cup and saucer, plates of various sizes, trays, salt-cellar, and other articles are made.

facts.text: In the 20th century new forms appeared: cigar boxes, cigarette cases, ash trays, cuff links, dress studs, and designs taken from the Ajanta murals.
facts.quote: With the increase of interest in the Ajanta murals, many of their decorative motifs found their way in the designing of new fashioned Bidri Ware

facts.text: Dating of museum bidri is approximate and based on design.
facts.quote: The dating of the pieces is only approximate and is based on design

facts.text: Bidriware is a registered Geographical Indication (application 20, filed 24 January 2005 by the Karnataka State Handicrafts Development Corporation, certificate 30 January 2006).
facts.quote: Bidriware

rows.name: Bidar and Hyderabad bidri
rows.date_note: Courtly Deccan bidri of the 17th-18th centuries (Cleveland, AIC examples); revived in Hyderabad in the 20th century and made today in Bidar and Hyderabad.
rows.identify_by: Deccan bidri with naturalistic flowers (poppy plants, roses) or diapers of small silver crosses and stars, wire and sheet inlay together, often on large hookah bases, basins and pandans.
how_to_recognize: Poppy-plant and flowering-plant patterns drawn fairly naturally
Diagonal diapers of tiny silver stars or crosses in wire
Combination of wire (tarkashi) and sheet (tehnishan) inlay is common
Courtly forms: bell- or globe-shaped hookah bases, wide-rimmed basins (sailabchi), lidded pandans
rows.marks_and_labels: No maker's marks described in the sources. 1903 exhibition pieces were sold by named dealers (Haji Hasan, an Arab trader of Hyderabad).
rows.later_production: In the 1880s the Bidar trade was in the hands of Lingayat Hindus and declining; Hyderabad became the revival center in the 20th century (Nizam's government, then Andhra Pradesh cooperative workshops), making cigarette cases, ash trays, vases and cuff links for emporia and export.
rows.how_to_tell_old: Sources give no reliable test of age. The Salar Jung catalogue says museum dating "is only approximate and is based on design". Pointers the sources do give: 20th-century Hyderabad work introduced new Western forms (cigarette cases, ash trays, cuff links) and figures copied from the Ajanta murals; Lucknow fish motifs belong to the Oudh court style; some old pieces are heavier because of more lead in the alloy, but weight is not a test on its own.

look_alikes.how_to_tell: Koftgari is on iron or steel, which is magnetic and may rust; bidri is a non-magnetic zinc alloy that sources say does not rust.

look_alikes.name: Blackened or patinated brass and modern copies
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Brass shows yellow where the surface is worn or scratched; bidri alloy is gray-white under the black.

look_alikes.name: Black pottery imitating bidri
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Birdwood notes bidri "is also imitated in pottery"; ceramic is lighter, rings differently and shows a fired body at chips.

facts.text: The poppy plant is one of the oldest Hyderabad bidri patterns; the other common one is a diaper of minute silver crosses or stars in wire.
facts.quote: One of the oldest and at the same time most beautiful patterns employed in true bidri portrays the poppy plant

facts.text: Bidar floral decoration is drawn more naturalistically than the conventional patterns of upper India and Purnea.
facts.quote: The patterns are generally of a floral description, more or less natural at Bidar and conventional in Upper India.

facts.text: At Bidar the trade was in the hands of Lingayat Hindus; copper was sometimes inlaid as well as silver and gold.
facts.quote: At Bidar the trade is in the hands of Hindus of the Lingayet sect.

facts.text: The Nizam's government opened a bidri department at the Central School of Arts and Crafts and a center at Hyderabad in the first half of the 20th century.
facts.quote: They opened a department for it in the Central School of Arts and Crafts

facts.text: By 1961 many bidri items, particularly old ones, were being shipped abroad.
facts.quote: a large number of Bidri Wares, particularly old ones, are being shipped out of the country.

rows.name: Lucknow bidri
rows.date_note: Flourished under the Nawabs and Kings of Oudh (later 18th to mid-19th century); small output continued (13-31 workmen in 1881-82).
rows.identify_by: Bidri with large patches of silver in raised (zarbuland) work, often including fish among the flowers, the fish being the Oudh court emblem.
how_to_recognize: Fish motifs among flowers
Large silver patches standing slightly above the black ground (zarbuland), sometimes chased
Later Lucknow work turned to minute realistic patterns like Purnea
rows.marks_and_labels: None described. Makers named at the 1903 exhibition: Chandu Beg, Kadar Beg.
rows.later_production: Declining by the 1880s; Watt (1903) shows Lucknow work moving from raised zarbuland to minute realistic designs. Sources give no later production figures.
rows.how_to_tell_old: Sources give no reliable test; the fish emblem points to Lucknow work but was used over a long period.

look_alikes.name: Tanjore encrusted ware
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Mukharji says zarbuland imitates Tanjore work, but Tanjore applied silver sits on red copper or yellow brass, not on black zinc alloy.

facts.text: Lucknow bidri often includes a fish among the flowers, from the Oudh kings' 'Dignity of Fish' (mahi maratib).
facts.quote: In Lucknow, the figure of a fish is frequently introduced among the floral decoration

facts.text: Lucknow made a raised form called zarbuland, in which the inlay stands slightly above the surface; gilt silver was sometimes used.
facts.quote: A modified form of Bidri-work, called Zarbuland is made at Lucknow, in which the patterns are slightly raised

facts.text: In 1881 there were 13 bidri workers in Lucknow (Rs 4,000 output); in 1882, 31 (Rs 4,500).
facts.quote: In 1881 there were 13 men engaged in Bidri manufacture in the town of Lucknow

facts.text: The Oudh Gazetteer did not even mention bidri among Lucknow manufactures.
facts.quote: in the Oudh Gazetteer ... no mention is made of Bidri-ware among the manufactures of Lucknow

rows.name: Purnea and Murshidabad bidri
rows.date_note: Murshidabad work dates from the early 19th century (Mir Ilahi Bakhsh); both centers were declining in the 1880s-1900s. End date is an estimate: sources describe no later production.
rows.identify_by: Bengal bidri with large, deeply set patches of silver or gold cut as flowers or animals, richly polished, sometimes with Chinese-looking ornament.
how_to_recognize: Large patches of sheet silver or gold, not wire (Watt, 1903)
Strictly conventional patterns; sometimes Chinese in character
Rich surface polish
Two grades at Purnea: gharki (deep, well finished) and karna-bidri (plainer)
rows.marks_and_labels: None described. Murshidabad maker named in 1903: Trailokya Nath Dass.
rows.later_production: Murshidabad: eight workmen in the 1880s, 'slowly perishing'. Purnea: four brazier families cast the blanks at Bellori. No 20th-century figures in the sources.
rows.how_to_tell_old: Sources give no test of age. Watt warns that Birdwood's 1880 plates of Purnea bidri do not represent the work being made in 1903.
