rows.cautions: Region token: Purnea is now in Bihar (token wanted); Murshidabad is in West Bengal.

facts.text: Purnea made two grades: gharki, deeply set and well finished, and karna-bidri, plainer.
facts.quote: Two kinds of ware are made in Purniah: the best called Gharki, in which the patterns are deeply set and well finished

facts.text: Purnea patterns are strictly conventional and sometimes Chinese in character, which Birdwood thought came by way of Sikkim or Bhutan.
facts.quote: Sometimes the decoration of the Purniah bidri is Chinese in character

facts.text: In Purnea and Murshidabad wire alone was not used by 1903; silver or gold was cut in fairly large patches as flowers or animals.
facts.quote: In Purnea and Murshidabad, wire alone is never used (at the present day)

facts.text: Murshidabad bidri was introduced at the start of the 19th century by Mir Ilahi Bakhsh and was declining in the 1880s.
facts.quote: its manufacture at Murshidabad dates from the commencement of the present century, when it was introduced by one Mir Ilahi Bakhsh.

facts.text: Purnea's alloy is zinc with only a little copper.
facts.quote: Bidri is also made at Purniah, in the Bhagalpur division of Bengal, where only zinc is mixed with copper in the alloy

rows.name: Tarkashi (wire inlay)
rows.date_note: Used throughout bidri history.
rows.identify_by: Bidri decoration made of silver (or gold) wire hammered into engraved lines, giving fine lines, stars and diapers.
how_to_recognize: Thin, even lines of silver in channels
Often combined with sheet inlay (tehnishan)
Diapers of small stars or crosses
rows.later_production: Still used in Bidar and Hyderabad.
rows.how_to_tell_old: The technique does not date a piece.

look_alikes.name: Koftgari wire on steel
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Same idea of hammered wire, but on iron or steel; Watt notes ordinary koftgari wire can be felt on the surface.

rows.features_other: The term tar-kashi is also used for brass-wire inlay in wood (JIA 1916); that is a different craft.

facts.text: Roy Choudhury lists tarkashi as inlay of wire, one of five bidri techniques; the Salar Jung Museum repeats this.
facts.quote: tarkashi (inlay of wire), taihnishan (inlay of sheet), zarnishan (low relief), zarbuland (high relief) and aftabi

facts.text: Mukharji distinguishes thin leaf inlay for ordinary work from gold or silver wire in better work.
facts.quote: Very thin leaf is used for the ordinary kinds, while in the more durable workmanship, gold or silver wire is employed.

facts.text: A combination of wire and sheet inlay is very common.
facts.quote: A combination of tarkashi and taihnishan is very common.

rows.name: Tehnishan (flush sheet inlay)
rows.identify_by: Pattern deeply cut and the silver or gold sheet set into it and polished flush, so the inlay is level with or below the black ground. The same term names the deep, best grade of koftgari on steel.
how_to_recognize: Inlay flush with the surface, smooth to the touch
Shapes (leaves, petals) of sheet metal, not lines of wire
rows.later_production: Still used.
rows.how_to_tell_old: The technique does not date a piece.

facts.text: Watt names two main bidri forms by depth: teh nashan, deeply cut, with the inlay finished within or below the surface, and zar nashan or zar buland, raised.
facts.quote: These are known as Teh Nashan, or deeply cut work and Zar Nashan, (or Zar buland), raised work.

facts.text: Roy Choudhury defines taihnishan as inlay of sheet.
facts.quote: taihnishan (inlay of sheet)

facts.text: The same name (tah-i-nishan, teh nashan) is used for true, deep damascening of gold wire into grooves cut in steel.
facts.quote: This is the true damascening in which the design is cut out in grooves on steel

rows.name: Zarnishan (low-relief inlay)
rows.identify_by: Bidri inlay left in low relief above the black ground.
how_to_recognize: Silver stands slightly proud of the surface
Edges of the inlay can be felt
rows.later_production: Still used.
rows.how_to_tell_old: Not a dating feature.

facts.text: Roy Choudhury defines zarnishan as low relief, distinct from zarbuland, high relief.
facts.quote: zarnishan (low relief), zarbuland (high relief)

facts.text: Watt treats zar nashan and zar buland as one raised form.
facts.quote: Zar Nashan, (or Zar buland), raised work.

rows.name: Zarbuland (high-relief inlay)
rows.date_note: Associated with Lucknow from the 18th-19th century.
rows.identify_by: Bidri in which shaped silver pieces are raised well above the surface, filled with lead behind and held by hammering the ground metal over their edges, then chased.
how_to_recognize: Silver forms in clear relief, chased on top
Typical of Lucknow; fish, flowers and leaves
Sometimes gilt silver
rows.later_production: Still used occasionally.
rows.how_to_tell_old: Not a dating feature.

look_alikes.name: Tanjore encrusted copper and brass
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Similar method of holding relief metal, but on copper or brass, with Hindu deities.

facts.text: In zarbuland the pattern is raised and chased rather than set level with the surface.
facts.quote: the patterns are slightly raised and not set even with the surface as in the ordinary Bidri-ware.

facts.text: Watt describes the method: silver leaf shaped, its hollow filled with soft lead, pressed into the engraved outline and secured by hammering the ground metal round it.
facts.quote: the cavity thus formed filled with a piece of soft lead

facts.text: Zarbuland greatly resembles Tanjore encrusted ware.
facts.quote: Zar Nashan or Zar buland work greatly resembles Tanjore encrusted ware.

rows.name: Aftabi (cut-out overlay)
rows.identify_by: Bidri in which a silver sheet laid over the surface is cut out in a pattern so the black alloy shows through the openings.
how_to_recognize: Large areas of silver with the design showing black through cut-outs
The reverse of ordinary bidri, where silver lines sit on black
rows.later_production: Still used.
rows.how_to_tell_old: Not a dating feature.

facts.text: Roy Choudhury defines aftabi as cut-out designs in an overlaid metal sheet, usually treated separately from other techniques.
facts.quote: aftabi (cut out designs in overlaid metal sheet)

rows.name: Moradabad brass
rows.date_note: A town of 'comparatively modern origin' (Dampier 1894); the bold black-lac 'bidri' style was current about 1850, the minute marori and charakwan styles by 1900. Production continues, now largely industrial.
rows.identify_by: Brass (often tinned) or copper engraved through the surface, with the cut-away ground filled with black or colored lac, so a white-metal or yellow pattern stands on a colored ground or the reverse.
how_to_recognize: Lac filling in engraved recesses: hard, slightly glossy, can chip or melt with heat
Tinned (silver-looking) surface cut through to yellow brass in many pieces
Black-lac ground with white floral pattern (old 'bidri' style); minute all-over pattern (marori); colored pattern on bare brass (charakwan)
Later pieces: colored flowers, deities or scenes called 'enamel' though they are lac
rows.marks_and_labels: Old work unmarked; makers named at the 1903 exhibition (Sheik Hafiz Azizuddin, Mahomed Yarkhan). Export pieces may be stamped INDIA or MADE IN INDIA. Sources found give no dated rule for 'INDIA' or 'MADE IN INDIA' stamps on brass; treat them only as signs of an export piece, not of a date.
rows.later_production: Sales to Europeans took off after 1876, when a stall for travelers was opened at an Allahabad hotel (Mukharji 1888). Already working to European orders by 1894 (candlesticks, ash trays in 'gaudy red and blue'); export to England and the West 'daily growing larger' (Dampier 1894). By the 1940s-60s Moradabad had some 250 small factories and about 25,000 workers, about a fifth of output ornamental brassware, with spinning lathes, power presses and electroplating tanks (Khanna 1963). Moradabad Metal Craft is a registered Geographical Indication (certificate 2014).
rows.how_to_tell_old: Sources give a style sequence, not a test: the bold black-lac style is the oldest described; minute marori and European-pattern charakwan came later; colored flowers and Hindu mythological scenes in lac are the newest (about 1900 on) and were thought 'foreign to the Mohamedan originals'. Spun and pressed shapes and electroplating belong to the industrial 20th-century trade. Sources found give no dated rule for 'INDIA' or 'MADE IN INDIA' stamps on brass; treat them only as signs of an export piece, not of a date.

look_alikes.name: Bidri ware
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Bidri is a cast, chemically blackened zinc alloy with silver inlay; Moradabad 'bidri' is brass or copper with black lac in the recesses.

look_alikes.name: Benares brass
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Benares work is chased or punched bare brass, often with Hindu deities, usually without lac.

look_alikes.name: Kashmir tinned copper
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Kashmir work is copper (red where cut), tinned, with black lac or no filling, in Persian rosette or shawl patterns; Moradabad is mostly brass.

look_alikes.name: Jaipur colored brass
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Jaipur copied Moradabad marori and charakwan work with more colors, and also made engraved mythological trays.

look_alikes.name: Painted brass (Tilhar, Bareilly)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Designs painted with commercial enamel paint on the surface, not filled into engraved recesses.

rows.features_other: Tinning: token wanted. Lac is a shellac compound, not lacquer in the Asian sense.

facts.text: Moradabad is chiefly famous for its lacquered (lac-filled) work; the better class uses mainly black lac.
facts.quote: Moradabad is a town of comparatively modern origin and is chiefly famous for its lacquered work

facts.text: Moradabad ornament was designed to imitate bidri: tinned copper with the ground cut away and filled with black lac, leaving a white-metal pattern; locally this was called bidri.
facts.quote: This form was known locally as bidri.

facts.text: Moradabad had two styles: sada, tinned then engraved to show yellow brass, and siyah-kalam, with the ground cut away and filled with black lac; red and green lac went with inferior work.
facts.quote: In the Siyah-kalam work the ground of the vessel is graved out, bringing out in relief the floriated patterns.

facts.text: The trade grew from 1876, when the North-Western Provinces Agricultural Department had an Allahabad hotel-keeper open a stall for Europeans travelling home.
facts.quote: their sale went up by leaps and bounds.

facts.text: The oldest and best Moradabad work has bold, simple outlines; later work turned to minute enrichment.
facts.quote: the oldest and best of Moradabad work is marked by bold and simple outlines, not overloaded with detail

facts.text: Moradabad Metal Craft is a registered Geographical Indication (filed 9 February 2009, certificate 31 March 2014).
facts.quote: Moradabad Metal Craft (Word Mark)

facts.text: Birdwood describes Moradabad tin soldered on brass and incised through to the brass, sometimes with the ground filled with black lac as in Kashmir.
facts.quote: At Moradabad, in the North West Provinces, tin is soldered on brass, and incised through to the brass in floriated patterns

facts.text: The bold early style gave way to minute marori work and then charakwan, with the pattern in lac and the ground in bare brass; the charakwan pattern came from an English calico print.
facts.quote: The chief pattern employed in charakwan work is admittedly European

facts.text: Colored flowers and mythological subjects in lac were a recent development by 1903, and the colored parts were wrongly called enamel.
facts.quote: the colour portions are spoken of (though incorrectly) as enamel.

facts.text: Cheap red-and-blue candlesticks and ash trays made for European buyers had no artistic merit, and European orders debased the craft.
facts.quote: the gaudy red and blue vulgarisms that are generally offered for sale, the candlesticks, ash tray, &c., are of no artistic merit

facts.text: Export from Benares and Moradabad to England and the West was growing in 1894.
facts.quote: the export trade from such places as Benares and Moradabad to England and the west generally, is daily growing larger.

facts.text: Where tinning forms part of Moradabad decoration, Hindu workmen were employed.
facts.quote: Where tinning forms part of the decoration of a brass vessel, as in the well-known Moradabad ware, Hindu workmen are employed

facts.text: Mid-20th-century Moradabad: about 20% ornamental brassware, 70% domestic utensils, 10% cutlery and electroplated nickel-silver; 55 spinning lathes and 80 plating tanks recorded.
facts.quote: It is estimated that 20 % of the total production at Moradabad is of ornamental brass-ware articles

rows.name: Lac-colored (so-called enamelled) brass and copper
rows.date_note: Recorded as an old craft in 1903; still made.
rows.identify_by: Engraved or chased brass or copper whose recesses are filled with black or colored lac melted in with a hot iron and then rubbed back, imitating enamel at much lower cost.
how_to_recognize: Color sits in engraved hollows and is soft compared with vitreous enamel: it scratches, chips and softens with heat
Colours glossy when new and dull with age
Often on a tinned, gilt or silvered ground
rows.later_production: Made in large quantities for export and tourists through the 20th century (Moradabad, Jaipur).
rows.how_to_tell_old: Kipling notes the glossy new colors dull within months, so dullness is not a sign of age. No test given.

look_alikes.name: Vitreous enamel (meenakari)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: True enamel is glass fused in a kiln: hard, glassy, cannot be scratched with a pin and cracks rather than dents.

look_alikes.name: Painted metal
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Paint lies on the surface rather than in engraved recesses (Tilhar and Bareilly trays used Aspinall's enamel paint).

facts.text: Watt classes tinned, painted and lac-colored wares together as goods imitating enamel; the main centers were Moradabad, Jaipur, Peshawar and Kashmir.
facts.quote: all the goods that may be spoken of as imitating enamelled wares.

facts.text: The lac is applied with a hot bolt, the excess removed with sand, brick-dust or a file, and the surface polished.
facts.quote: the excavations thus made are then loaded with black or variously coloured lac (lakh) applied by a hot bolt

facts.text: Kashmir also filled graven patterns with red, green and black lac; the gloss fades within months.
facts.quote: When the brass is new and the colours are glossy, the effect is disagreeably smart, but in a few months this vulgar glimmer is lost

facts.text: Painted brass trays from Tilhar and Bareilly used Aspinall's enamel paints.
facts.quote: These are made at Tilhar, near Shahjahanpur.

rows.name: Benares (Varanasi) brass
rows.date_note: Old center of Hindu brass (images and ritual vessels); the export trade in chased trays grew from about the 1870s. Still made.
rows.identify_by: Bare polished brass chased or punched all over, often with Hindu deities in panels, raised (ubhar) work or copper set against brass; sold widely in Europe as 'Benares brass'.
how_to_recognize: Chased and punched surface (dots made with a punch, lines with chisels), no lac
Hindu deities and mythological scenes, lotus and floral borders
Ubhar (raised) work hammered up from the back on a lac block
Copper and brass together (ganga-jamni)
Shallow all-over patterns on thin trays
rows.marks_and_labels: Generally unmarked. Some exported pieces stamped INDIA or MADE IN INDIA; Sources found give no dated rule for 'INDIA' or 'MADE IN INDIA' stamps on brass; treat them only as signs of an export piece, not of a date.
rows.later_production: By 1880 'a large quantity' of exported Benares brass had reached England; by 1894 a large trade in European types (paper knives, jardinières, salvers) for winter tourists; in 1903 Watt found nearly all of it poor and in 'degraded European shapes'. In the early 1960s Varanasi had some 500 foundries and 9-10,000 workers (Khanna 1963). Pilgrims also took home Banarsi lotas. Benaras Metal Repousse Craft is a registered Geographical Indication (certificate 2016).
rows.how_to_tell_old: Sources give no test. They contrast 'fine old patterns' with cheap shallow chasing and European shapes, but say even good pieces were cheap; age cannot be read from the type.

look_alikes.name: Moradabad brass
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Moradabad work has lac-filled grounds and Islamic floral patterns; Benares is bare chased brass, often with Hindu figures.

look_alikes.name: Jaipur brass
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Jaipur work also shows engraved Hindu figures and repoussé arabesques; sources give no reliable way to tell them apart without a label.

look_alikes.name: Tanjore and Madras brass
look_alikes.how_to_tell: South Indian work is more often embossed (repoussé) and encrusted with copper or silver.

look_alikes.name: Kashmir and Peshawar copper
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Copper (red), often tinned, with Persian patterns.

facts.text: Benares is a chief center of Hindu ornamental brass: idols, ritual implements, bells, open-work shields, embossed panels and brass trays relieved with copper.
facts.quote: brass idols, brass and copper sacrificial implements phul bells, open-work brass shields, embossed panels, and brass trays relieved with copper.

facts.text: Exported Benares brass reached England in quantity by 1880; Birdwood thought it rickety and over-ornamented with shallow chasing.
facts.quote: A large quantity of the exported domestic brass work of Benares has in recent years found its way into this country.

facts.text: Benares brass was sold all over Europe by 1888.
facts.quote: The ware is now largely sold not only in India but all over Europe.

facts.text: Benares engravers worked freehand, with no tracing or pattern, repeating the traditional figures of the gods.
facts.quote: The workers in brass have no tracing or pattern.

facts.text: Benaras Metal Repousse Craft is a registered Geographical Indication (filed 24 January 2013, certificate 31 May 2016).
facts.quote: BENARAS METAL REPOUSE CRAFT

facts.text: Benares punched brass was cheap and the best-known Indian metalwork in Europe.
facts.quote: It is, however, cheap and is the best known style of Indian metal work met with in Europe

facts.text: By 1894 Benares made goods of European type, paper knives, jardinières and salvers, for tourists.
facts.quote: of late years has sprung up a large manufacture of goods of European type— paper knives

facts.text: Raised work (ubhar ka kam) is beaten up on a wax or lac block and finished with chisels; it was called the prettiest Benares process.
facts.quote: is the prettiest of all the ornamental processes for which Benares is famous.

facts.text: The engraver (naqqashwala) traces figures with a tracer and makes dots with a punch (moti).
facts.quote: the tray is passed on to the graver, who is technically known as the naqqashwala

facts.text: Indian chasers use hammer, chisel and punch, not a burin.
facts.quote: there is no burin or graver in any Indian workshop. The hammer, chisel and punch are alone employed

facts.text: In 1903 Watt excluded Benares brass from the Delhi exhibition because the items were bad imitations and in European shapes.
facts.quote: Many were in degraded European shapes and purposes.

rows.name: Ganga-jamni (two-metal) work
rows.date_note: Named after the meeting of the Ganges (white) and Jumna (dark) rivers.
rows.identify_by: Any work that sets two contrasting metals together: copper with brass or bell metal on Benares salvers, or gold with silver on koftgari steel.
how_to_recognize: Two metal colors side by side (red copper and yellow brass; or gold and silver)
rows.later_production: Common in later Benares trays.
rows.how_to_tell_old: Not a dating feature.

facts.text: At Benares, gangajamni is ornamental ware combining copper and brass or copper and bell metal.
facts.quote: Gangajamni is the name given to a kind of ornamental ware, in which a very beautiful effect is produced by the combined use of copper and -brass or copper and bell- metal.

facts.text: In koftgari, Ganga-Jamni means gold and silver used together; some gold is alloyed with copper for a pink tint.
facts.quote: At times when both gold and silver are used [Ganga-Jamna], certain parts of the gold are mixed with copper

rows.name: Jaipur brass
rows.date_note: Art-ware output grew with the Jaipur School of Art (founded 1866) and the Jeypore Exhibition of 1883; much increased by 1903. Still made.
rows.identify_by: Polished brass trays, vases and boxes with repoussé arabesques or engraved Hindu mythological scenes, pierced betel boxes, and colored-lac imitations of Moradabad work.
how_to_recognize: Repoussé arabesques in rich but not crowded relief
Engraved mythological figures; later in many colors on a metal ground
Pierced floral and geometric patterns on pan and soap boxes
Large trays mounted as tables
rows.marks_and_labels: School of Art and firms (Panna Muhammad Alla Buksh & Co.; Nur Buksh Khuda Buksh) exhibited under their names; sources describe no stamps.
rows.later_production: Watt (1903) says the trade from Jaipur had 'immensely increased' and 'Jaipur tables' had become a distinct item of trade within ten or fifteen years.
rows.how_to_tell_old: No test given in the sources.

look_alikes.name: Moradabad brass
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Jaipur imitated Moradabad marori and charakwan with more colors; without a label the two are hard to separate.

facts.text: Jaipur salvers and Hindu-shaped vases engraved with mythological figures and pierced boxes were made at the School of Art and in the bazaar; repoussé arabesque trays were newly introduced under Hendley.
facts.quote: Salvers, vases of Hindu shapes engraved with mythological figures, soap boxes, pan boxes, &c., pierced with floral and geometrical patterns

facts.text: Jaipur tables (brass trays on stands) had become a distinct trade item by 1903.
facts.quote: the famous Jaipur tables, that within the past ten or fifteen years have assumed the condition of a distinct item of trade.

facts.text: Jaipur had recently taken to imitating Moradabad marori and charakwan work with many colors.
facts.quote: Jaipur has taken to imitating Moradabad in the production of marori and charakwan work

facts.text: Zinc surahis and hookahs enriched with brass bands were made at Chirawa and Jhunjhunu.
facts.quote: Surahis or water bottles and hookas are made in zinc and enriched with brass bands

rows.name: Kashmir engraved and tinned copper
rows.date_note: 19th-century Srinagar work described from the 1870s-1900s; still made.
rows.identify_by: Copper wares of Persian form (aftaba ewers with tasht basins, samovars, round trays) chased all over in minute shawl, rosette or arabesque patterns, usually tinned so the cut lines show red, often with the ground filled with black lac.
how_to_recognize: Red copper lines showing through a white tinned surface
Minute patterns from shawl designs, rosettes on a black ground, or arabesques
Persian forms: aftaba and tasht, samovar, Bokhara jar, kangri-shaped salt-cellars
European forms (teapots, claret jugs) covered with shawl patterns for export; trays mounted as walnut tables
rows.marks_and_labels: Sources name makers (Lassoo, Subhana, Habib Joo of Srinagar) but describe no stamps. Pieces sent to England to be electroplated may carry British plate marks only (not described in detail).
rows.later_production: Much was made for Europeans: tea sets, claret jugs and salvers chased in copper and sent to England to be electroplated or gilded (1886); smiths made a finer grade specially for plating and copper trays framed in carved walnut as tables (1895). Watt (1903) found cheapened Kashmir copper and brass 'almost unsaleable'. Amritsar's Kashmiri colony and Peshawar made similar ware.
rows.how_to_tell_old: No test in the sources. Watt says older Kashmir copper was often not tinned but gilt, with sparer, better-spaced arabesques; electroplated or gilt Kashmir copper may pass for silver or gold.

look_alikes.name: Peshawar and Amritsar copper
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Same family of Persian-style chased tinned copper; sources say Peshawar work is hard to tell from imports and Amritsar copied Kashmir patterns.

look_alikes.name: Persian (Iranian) and Central Asian copper
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Sources say Persian pieces served as models in Srinagar; without inscriptions or labels they are hard to separate.

look_alikes.name: Moradabad brass
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Mostly brass, lac-filled; Kashmir is mostly copper, tinned.

look_alikes.name: Silver or silver-gilt plate
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Electroplated or gilt Kashmir copper looks like silver; copper shows at worn edges and there are no silver marks.

rows.features_other: Tinning (kalai) makes copper safe for food; token wanted: tinning, electroplating.
rows.cautions: Old tinned copper used for food should be re-tinned (sources explain tinning is for safety); no further cautions given.

facts.text: Kashmir and Amritsar furnished most of the brass and copper sold to Europeans in the 1880s; Kashmir art is Persian in origin.
facts.quote: Cashmere and Amritsar at the present moment furnish the greater part of such brass and copper ware as is sold to Europeans.

facts.text: In Kashmir tin is soldered on copper that has been deeply graven, and the sunken ground is filled with a black composition like niello.
facts.quote: In Cashmere tin is soldered on copper which has been previously deeply graven over with a diffused floral design

facts.text: Copper vessels used by Muslims for cooking and eating must be tinned for safety, which made tinned ornament essentially Muslim in origin.
facts.quote: The Muhammadans use copper cooking and eating vessels, and hence these have to be tinned before they can be employed with safety.

facts.text: Kashmiri smiths made European tea sets, claret jugs and salvers in chased copper that were sent to England to be electroplated or gilded.
facts.quote: in elaborately chased copper which are sent home to be electro-plated.

facts.text: Copper trays framed as tables in carved walnut were in large demand by 1895.
facts.quote: A large demand has arisen for the beautiful copper trays framed as tables in carved walnut-wood

facts.text: Competition after taxes were lifted lowered prices of Srinagar copper work from seven to three rupees a seer.
facts.quote: Copper-work which sold at seven rupees per seer in the days of taxation now sells at three rupees

facts.text: Kashmir copper was sold by weight (by the seer) in the 1880s.
facts.quote: Chased and tinned copper and lacquered brass are sold-by the Cashmeeree seer

facts.text: Three Kashmir patterns: rosettes on a black ground, arabesques, and modern patterns; formerly copper was gilt rather than tinned, with better-spaced ornament.
facts.quote: Formerly Kashmir used to turn out copper, not tinned but with Arabesque designs showing on the gold (sometimes even gilt) surface.

facts.text: By 1903 cheapened Kashmir copper and brass had become almost unsaleable.
facts.quote: the brass and copper wares of Kashmir from being once in great demand have become almost unsaleable.

facts.text: Watt saw 'imitation old Thibetan' brasses made by Lassoo of Srinagar.
facts.quote: collection of old Thibetan (and imitation old Thibetan) brasses

rows.name: Kashmiri samovar
rows.date_note: Recorded as a popular Kashmiri institution in 1895 and in exhibitions from 1886; still made.
rows.identify_by: A copper tea urn with an internal charcoal tube, a tap and a lid, chased and often tinned, used for Kashmiri tea (kahwa and salt tea).
how_to_recognize: Central chimney for charcoal inside the body
Tap near the base, handles, domed lid
Chased tinned copper with Kashmiri patterns
rows.later_production: Made in Kashmir, Amritsar and Peshawar for local use and for sale.
rows.how_to_tell_old: No test given.

look_alikes.name: Russian and Persian samovars
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Sources say the Kashmiri samovar follows the Russian type; Russian samovars are usually of brass or plated with factory stamps.

look_alikes.name: Kashmiri ewer (aftaba)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: An ewer has a spout and no charcoal chimney.

rows.features_other: Form token wanted: samovar (closest token used: ewer).

facts.text: Kashmiri sweet and salt tea are both made in the Russian samovar, a popular institution in Kashmir.
facts.quote: Both are made in the Russian samovar, which is a popular institution in Kashmir.

facts.text: Large samovars were made at Amritsar and Peshawar; at Amritsar the Kashmiri colony introduced the copper samovar with a heating arrangement.
facts.quote: the large samovar itself is made at Amritsar and Peshawar.

facts.text: A Kashmir samavar in arabesque tinned copper was shown by the Kashmir State at Delhi in 1903.
facts.quote: a samavdr (No. 4905), Rs. 37, by Kashmir State

rows.name: Meenakari (Indian enamel)
rows.date_note: Hendley took the enamelled crutch staff of Raja Man Singh of Jaipur (court of Akbar, late 16th century) as the oldest surviving Indian enamel. Still made.
rows.identify_by: Vitreous enamel fused into recesses chased, engraved, repoussé or die-stamped in gold, silver or copper (champlevé), the colors fired one after another from hardest to softest.
how_to_recognize: Glassy, hard colors in recesses with thin metal lines between
Translucent colors over hatched gold catch the light (best Jaipur work)
Opaque colors on stamped silver (Multan) or painted on copper (Kashmir)
Often on the backs of jewelled ornaments
rows.marks_and_labels: Sources describe no marks; firms (Sughan Chand Sobhag Chand of Jaipur) and named enamellers are recorded.
rows.later_production: By 1903 Watt saw a shift from large pieces to small trade jewelry (sleeve links, lockets, brooches) and from field-color designs to crowded ones; skilled Jaipur enamellers had moved to Delhi.
rows.how_to_tell_old: Watt: older Jaipur work used a field color, often creamy white; work of the 'past few decades' (before 1903) dropped it for crowded designs with no field. This is a style pointer, not a test.

look_alikes.name: Lac-colored brass
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Lac is soft and scratches with a pin; vitreous enamel is glass, hard and glossy, and chips rather than dents.

look_alikes.name: Painted metal
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Paint lies on a flat surface; enamel fills chased or stamped recesses and has a glassy depth.

look_alikes.name: Chinese cloisonné
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Chinese cloisonné uses soldered wire cells over the whole surface; Indian enamel is mostly champlevé, the colors laid in hollows cut or stamped in the metal.

rows.cautions: Sources record red lead in the glass recipe; no handling cautions are given in the sources.

facts.text: Indian enamel is champlevé, not cloisonné: the colors lie in hollows in the metal.
facts.quote: The Indian enamel is not however like the Chinese and Japanese “ cloisonné,” but “champlevé,’

facts.text: Colors are applied in order of their resistance to fire, hardest first.
facts.quote: The enameller or minakar now applies the colours in the order of their hardness

facts.text: Jaipur enamellers bought their colors in vitreous lumps from Lahore, made by Muslim bracelet-makers (manihars).
facts.quote: The colours are obtained in opaque vitreous masses from Lahore

facts.text: Enamelling is done on gold at Jaipur, Alwar, Delhi and Benares; on silver at Multan, Bahawalpur, Kashmir, Kangra, Lucknow and others; on copper in Kashmir and the Punjab.
facts.quote: At Jeypore enamelling is done on gold, silver, and copper

facts.text: A pure red is the test of an enameller's skill.
facts.quote: The power of producing a good pure red is the measure of the ability of the enameller.

facts.text: The glass base recorded is 100 parts quartz, 50 borax and 200 red lead.
facts.quote: a glass composed of loo parts of quartz, 50 borax and 200 red lead.

rows.name: Jaipur enamel
rows.date_note: From the late 16th century (Man Singh's staff); 18th-century items in Cleveland; still made.
rows.identify_by: Translucent enamel on high-carat gold, famous for a fiery red with greens and blues, the gold engraved so finely that little metal shows; older work often on a white field.
how_to_recognize: High-carat gold (Watt: 22 carat)
Translucent ruby red, emerald green, blues over hatched gold
White or creamy field in older work
Enamelled backs to kundan-set jewels
rows.marks_and_labels: None described.
rows.later_production: By 1903 skilled men had moved to Delhi and production had turned to small jewelry for trade; Egerton (1880) notes Jaipur State took all output of its own enamellers.
rows.how_to_tell_old: Only the style pointer given under meenakari (field color versus crowded design). Museum catalogues differ on technique names (Cleveland calls some Jaipur pieces 'cloisonné').

look_alikes.name: Lac-colored brass
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Lac is soft and scratches with a pin; vitreous enamel is glass, hard and glossy, and chips rather than dents.

look_alikes.name: Painted metal
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Paint lies on a flat surface; enamel fills chased or stamped recesses and has a glassy depth.

look_alikes.name: Chinese cloisonné
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Chinese cloisonné uses soldered wire cells over the whole surface; Indian enamel is mostly champlevé, the colors laid in hollows cut or stamped in the metal.

look_alikes.name: Delhi and Benares enamel on gold
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Watt and the 1886 Punjab list say Delhi work was 'little inferior' to Jaipur; without provenance sources give no way to separate them.

facts.text: The best enamel on gold is produced at Jaipur, famous for its fiery red.
facts.quote: it is universally acknowledged that the best work on gold is produced at Jeypore

facts.text: Jaipur enamel is done on the purest gold, so finely engraved that the surface becomes a sheet of translucent enamel.
facts.quote: It is invariably done on the purest gold (22 carat)

facts.text: The Jaipur ground is generally a dazzling white.
facts.quote: the ground in that of Jaipur is generally of a dazzling white.

facts.text: Recent Jaipur work had dropped the field color and turned to small jewelry for the trade.
facts.quote: Within the past few decades this has been discontinued

facts.text: Cleveland catalogues several Jaipur gold items as cloisonné enamel, while 19th-century sources call Jaipur work champlevé.
facts.quote: cloisonne enamel on gold

rows.name: Benares (Varanasi) enamel
rows.date_note: Recorded 1880-1903; still made.
rows.identify_by: Enamel on gold used mainly as a colored ground for set stones or in large patches imitating jewels, with brilliant reds.
how_to_recognize: Enamel as ground color behind diamonds or other stones
Rich warm translucent colors (pachisi markers shown 1903)
rows.later_production: Declining and made to order by 1888 (Mukharji); revived as 'gulabi meenakari' (pink enamel), registered as a Geographical Indication in 2015. Sources found do not give 20th-century figures.
rows.how_to_tell_old: No test given.

facts.quote: In Benares the art of enamelling seems confined to the production of large patches of colour in imitation of jewels

facts.text: Benares had long been famous for enamel on gold, but by 1888 the craft was declining and done only to order.
facts.quote: Benares has long been famous for its enamel in gold. The industry is on the decline, and is now only done to order.

facts.text: Banaras Gulabi Meenakari Craft (pink enamel) is a registered Geographical Indication (filed 24 January 2013, certificate 23 March 2015).
facts.quote: Banaras Gulabi Meenakari Craft

facts.text: Benares is one of the centers enamelling on gold, with brilliant reds like Jaipur and Delhi.
facts.quote: The brilliant reds attained by the Jaipur, Delhi and Benares workers on gold

rows.name: Lucknow and Rampur enamel
rows.date_note: Mughal-period transparent enamel on silver hookah fittings is attributed to Lucknow or Rampur; recorded 1880-1903.
rows.identify_by: Silver minutely engraved and enamelled mainly in translucent green and blue with small touches of yellow and brown, often with animals and birds among flowers.
how_to_recognize: Green and blue on silver, so dense it looks like verdigris from a distance
Animals, birds and figures scattered over flowers
Hookah bowls, boxes, bangles
rows.later_production: Watt (1903) judged current Lucknow work inferior but expensive; old pieces of higher merit 'occasionally' found.
rows.how_to_tell_old: Watt says some fine old pieces once called Lucknow may be misattributed; no test given.

look_alikes.name: Kashmir silver enamel
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Kashmir silver enamel is in two shades of blue, rich and translucent, in shawl patterns.

facts.text: Lucknow and Rampur enamel shows an etched silver pattern with green and blue and small patches of yellow and brown.
facts.quote: an etched pattern on silver in which green and blue with a small patch of yellow and brown enamel is given.

facts.text: Lucknow and Benares are among the centers of enamel listed by Birdwood and Hendley; Hendley lists Lucknow among silver enamelling centers.
facts.quote: The art is practised everywhere in India, at Lucknow and Benares

facts.text: Watt questions whether Birdwood's fine plate 38 hookah, attributed to Lucknow or Rampur, is correctly identified.
facts.quote: so far superior to anything of the present day as to leave some doubt of the identification here made being correct.

rows.name: Multan and Bahawalpur blue enamel
rows.date_note: Recorded 1872-1903; still made in Pakistan.
rows.identify_by: Small silver ornaments struck in a die and filled with opaque enamel in shades of blue (Multan), or larger chased silver and gold vessels in rich deep or slightly translucent blue (Bahawalpur).
how_to_recognize: Die-stamped raised silver lines separating opaque blues
Little red or yellow, and those of poor quality
Bahawalpur: larger vessels, rich deep blue, sometimes raised white slip
rows.later_production: No later figures in the sources.
rows.how_to_tell_old: No test given.

rows.features_other: Region note: Multan and Bahawalpur are in Pakistan (Punjab).

facts.text: Multan enamel is on silver struck in a die, leaving small silver rims between opaque colors, mostly blues.
facts.quote: The articles are in silver, struck off from a die so as to leave small rims of silver to demark the patches of colour.

facts.text: A slightly translucent blue enamel is peculiar to Bahawalpur, where large items are made.
facts.quote: A slightly translucent blue enamel is peculiar to Bahawalpur.

rows.name: Kashmir enamelled copper, brass and silver
rows.date_note: 'Of late years a great development' (1886); recorded to 1903 and later.
rows.identify_by: Gilt copper or brass (sometimes silver) with shawl, arabesque or rosette patterns punched up and filled with opaque, readily fusible enamel, mostly blues with red and yellow.
how_to_recognize: Opaque blues, never translucent on copper and brass
Gilding combined with enamel
Shawl-pattern (boteh) ornament; rosettes; 'mosaic' large patches
Persian and Central Asian forms (aftaba and tasht, Bokhara jars, gourd-shaped tumba)
rows.marks_and_labels: Makers named in 1886-1903 (Habib Joo, Subhana, Lassoo of Srinagar); no marks described.
rows.later_production: A large trade in the 1880s-1900s for Europeans; Watt and Kipling call it bright and cheap.
rows.how_to_tell_old: Watt notes the copper and brass enamels dull with age; not a test of date.

look_alikes.name: Lac-colored brass
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Lac is soft and scratches with a pin; vitreous enamel is glass, hard and glossy, and chips rather than dents.

look_alikes.name: Persian enamel
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Watt says a painted Kashmir plate might be mistaken for Persian but for its Hindu subject.

facts.text: Kashmir's most costly copper ware is enamelled and gilt, with somewhat crude colors.
facts.quote: The most costly, and on the whole the most effective, is the enamelled and gilt copper ware

facts.text: Kashmir copper and brass enamels are never translucent; the pattern is punched and the hollows charged with fusible glass paint.
facts.quote: The copper and brass enamels are never translucent

facts.text: Lawrence thought Kashmir enamel on brass the best and said copper does not lend itself to enamel.
facts.quote: Of the enamel work, the enamels on brass are, I think, the best

facts.text: Kashmir enamel is cut in shawl patterns filled with turquoise blue, sometimes with dark green.
facts.quote: the ground, of the usual shawl pattern ornamentation cut in gold, is filled in with turquoise blue.

rows.name: Pratapgarh thewa (gold on glass)
rows.date_note: Recorded from the 1880s; still made at Pratapgarh by a few families.
rows.identify_by: A plaque of green (or red, or at Ratlam blue) glass with a pierced and chased gold-leaf picture fused to its face, backed with bright silver foil, sold as plaques set in jewelry and boxes.
how_to_recognize: Flat glass plaque, deep green with a mirror-like silver backing
Fine gold figures, hunting scenes, landscapes or flowers on the surface
Set in a silver or gold frame as a brooch, pendant, belt plaque or box lid
rows.marks_and_labels: None described in the sources; makers named in 1886: Jagan Nath and Nabh Chand.
rows.later_production: Still made at Pratapgarh by a few families; registered as a Geographical Indication (Thewa Art Work, certificate 2014). Sources found give no production figures.
rows.how_to_tell_old: No test given.

look_alikes.name: Enamel
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Thewa is glass with applied gold, not enamel fused into metal; Hendley and Watt call it quasi-enamel.

look_alikes.name: Ratlam work
look_alikes.how_to_tell: The same technique on blue glass.

facts.text: Pratapgarh 'green enamels' are not true enamels.
facts.quote: The so-called green enamels made at Pertabgarh, ... are not true enamels.

facts.text: The medallions are green glass with figures, landscapes and flowers in gold, backed by silver foil.
facts.quote: The medallions are composed of green glass, upon which quaint patterns of figures, landscapes, and flowers are traced in gold.

facts.text: The method was a secret of two or three families; Hendley gives two unconfirmed explanations (acid-etched glass filled with gold powder, or cut gold leaf).
facts.quote: The mode of preparation is kept most carefully secret by the two or three families who practice the art.

facts.text: Watt describes gold leaf punched and chased on lac, framed in silver wire and fused onto semi-molten glass.
facts.quote: The glass is then semi-fused, and while still hot the rim of silver and film of gold are slipped over the edge

facts.text: Thewa Art Work is a registered Geographical Indication (filed 17 October 2011, certificate 31 March 2014).
facts.quote: Thewa Art Work

facts.text: Ratlam made similar work on blue glass.
facts.quote: In Ratlam a similar form of imitation enamelling is practised, a shade of blue being produced.

rows.name: Koftgari (gold and silver on steel)
rows.date_note: Mughal and Deccani arms from the 17th century carry it (museum examples); a large trade in domestic and tourist items from the mid-19th century; still made (Udaipur Koftgari GI, filed 2021).
rows.identify_by: Gold or silver wire or leaf hammered onto steel that has been cross-hatched or grooved, then heated, burnished and often blued, so the gold pattern stands on a dark ground.
how_to_recognize: Steel or iron ground (magnetic), often blued or blackened
Fine gold or silver scrolls and flowers; on good work the wire lies in cut grooves and is filed smooth (teh-nishan)
Ordinary work: cross-hatched ground under the gold; the wire can be felt standing on the surface
Cheapest (dewali): gold leaf on scratched lines, very thin
rows.marks_and_labels: Sialkot makers sometimes worked inscriptions, Qur'anic verses, spells, poetry or their own names into the wire (1886). Exhibition pieces were sold under makers' names.
rows.later_production: After the Sikh wars Sialkot and Gujrat koftgars turned to domestic and decorative articles (trays, caskets, inkstands, paper-cutters, cigar cases) and kept making decorative swords, shields and helmets as curiosities; Jaipur, Alwar, Sirohi and Lahore also produced 'large quantities' by 1903. Tourist demand pushed cheap shallow and gold-leaf work.
rows.how_to_tell_old: Sources give grades of work, not dates: deep teh-nishan is the costly best grade; shallow koftgari and gold-leaf dewali were the cheap tourist grades. A cheap grade does not prove a late date, and a good grade does not prove an early one.

look_alikes.name: Bidri ware
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Bidri is a blackened, non-magnetic zinc alloy; koftgari is gold or silver on iron or steel, which a magnet picks up and which can rust.

look_alikes.name: Dewali (gold-leaf imitation koftgari)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Gold leaf rubbed onto scratched steel: very thin, no wire felt, wears off easily.

look_alikes.name: Persian, Caucasian and Ottoman gold-overlaid steel
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Same technique across the Islamic world; Smithsonian notes record Qajar and Dagestani koftgari. Without inscriptions or form clues, origin is uncertain.

look_alikes.name: Japanese or Spanish (Toledo) damascene
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Factory souvenir damascene on steel or iron is very even, often with machine-cut grounds; sources consulted do not discuss it (gap).

rows.features_other: Terms are used inconsistently: Watt calls deep wire inlay 'teh nashan or deep koftgari'; Egerton and the 1913 Madras book reserve 'koft' for overlay on a hatched surface and call inlay into undercut grooves true damascening.

facts.text: Koftgari began with the ornament of swords and other weapons.
facts.quote: The art of damascening appears to have taken its origin with the ornamentation of swords and other weapons.

facts.text: The steel is hatched with deep cross lines, the gold wire hammered onto it along the pattern, heated and burnished; the gold stands above the surface.
facts.quote: the blade is first ‘ hatched ” or cut across with sharp and deep lines where it is intended to place the pattern

facts.text: Three grades in 1903: teh nashan (deep), ordinary (shallow, wire felt on the surface) and dewali (gold leaf, the cheapest imitation).
facts.quote: the cheapest form of all is a sort of imitation koftgari. This is called Dewali

facts.text: A cheap koft made with gold leaf on etched lines was common; it does not last.
facts.quote: There is a cheap kuft work done by simply laying gold leaf on the steel plate

facts.text: True damascening is costly, so for the needy and the tourist workmen use filed outlines and gold leaf; shields were made this way very cheaply.
facts.quote: to meet the demand of the needy, and of the tourist, who likes a good deal for his money

facts.text: Koft overlay on roughened iron is often mistaken for damascening, which inlays thicker metal into undercut grooves.
facts.quote: because it is so often mistaken for damascening

facts.text: The Udaipur Koftgari Metal Craft GI was filed in 2021 and certified in 2023.
facts.quote: Udaipur Koftgari Metal Craft

rows.name: Sialkot and Gujrat koftgari
rows.date_note: Localized at Kotli Loharan (Sialkot district) and Gujrat by the 1880s; still made in Pakistan.
rows.identify_by: Punjab steel or iron wares (shields, helmets, armor sets, trays, caskets, inkstands, surahis) covered in gold and silver arabesque wire on a blued ground, often for Europeans.
how_to_recognize: Shields (dhal), helmets and chahar-aina armor sets as well as trays and caskets
Dense foliated gold and silver scrolls; inscriptions in Arabic or Persian sometimes worked in wire
European forms (inkstands, paper-cutters, cigar cases)
rows.marks_and_labels: Inscriptions and makers' prayers in the wire are recorded (1886); otherwise no stamps described.
rows.later_production: Heavy 19th-century trade for Europeans: Kotli and Gujrat made 'chiefly ornamental small wares for decorative purposes'; bargaining forced 'a cheap and superficial sort of work' (1886).
rows.how_to_tell_old: No test given; sources warn that much later work is thin and lightly gilt.

look_alikes.name: Bidri ware
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Bidri is a blackened, non-magnetic zinc alloy; koftgari is gold or silver on iron or steel, which a magnet picks up and which can rust.

facts.text: On the decline of Sikh power the koftgars of Sialkot and Gujrat turned to domestic articles but still made damascened sword hilts, scabbards, shields and helmets.
facts.quote: On the decline of the Sikh power, the koftgari workers of Sialkot and Gujerat diverted their skill to the ornamentation of articles for domestic use.

facts.text: Shields, helmets and other arms were still made and sold as curiosities in 1886.
facts.quote: Shields, helmets, and other arms, are still made and sold as curiosities

facts.text: The art was localized at Kotli (Sialkot) and Gujrat, making chiefly small decorative wares; bargaining forced cheap, superficial work.
facts.quote: compels the men to a cheap and superficial sort of work in which the gold is inferior and lightly applied

facts.text: Sialkot makers worked Qur'anic verses, spells, poetry and even a maker's prayer into the wire.
facts.quote: in one a prayer by the maker, Sharifud-din, for good fortune at this Exhibition.

facts.text: Gujrat blacksmiths made the daggers, knives and nut-cutters that the koftgars decorated.
facts.quote: The blacksmiths of Gujrat (Panjab) make daggers, knives, betel-nut cutters, scissors, and other articles of cutlery for the Koftgars

facts.text: Baden-Powell records koftgari shields, inkstands and caskets from Sialkot and Gujrat at the Punjab exhibitions.
facts.quote: Koftgari was exhibited from Gujrat and Sealkot

rows.name: Rajasthan koftgari (Jaipur, Alwar, Udaipur, Sirohi)
rows.date_note: Court arms of the 18th-19th centuries; School of Art and tourist work from the 1880s; Udaipur koftgari GI (2021).
rows.identify_by: Gold and silver damascening on Rajput sword hilts, shields and armor, later on trays and goblets; Sirohi work sets gold against a frosted silver ground.
how_to_recognize: Rajput hilts (talwar with disc pommel) covered in gold koftgari
Sirohi: gold on frosted silver background
School of Art trays and goblets in deep teh-nishan
rows.marks_and_labels: None described.
rows.later_production: By 1903 Jaipur, Alwar and Sirohi turned out 'large quantities'; at Alwar in 1888 only one State-employed man did koft work on knives, scissors and nut-cutters.
rows.how_to_tell_old: No test given.

look_alikes.how_to_tell: Bidri is a blackened, non-magnetic zinc alloy; koftgari is gold or silver on iron or steel, which a magnet picks up and which can rust.

look_alikes.how_to_tell: Gold leaf rubbed onto scratched steel: very thin, no wire felt, wears off easily.
