look_alikes.how_to_tell: Factory souvenir damascene on steel or iron is very even, often with machine-cut grounds; sources consulted do not discuss it (gap).

facts.text: Damascening of sword handles reached high proficiency at Jaipur, Alwar, Datia, Jodhpur and Sirohi.
facts.quote: In Jaipur, Alwar, Datia, Jodhpur and in Serhoi, the art of damascening sword handles attained high proficiency.

facts.text: Sirohi work sets gold against a frosted silver ground.
facts.quote: a background of frosted silver is given round the gold

facts.text: The Jaipur industry was said to have been introduced from Gujrat in the Punjab.
facts.quote: The industry was introduced from Gujrat in the Punjab.

facts.text: At Alwar in 1888 one man, employed by the State, did koft work on knives, scissors and betel-nut cutters.
facts.quote: But there is only one man who is engaged in this kind of work, and he is employed by the State.

rows.name: Tanjore (Thanjavur) art plate
rows.date_note: Older Tanjore work of brass with applied copper (flush); silver figures on copper are a 19th-century 'modern' adaptation (1886); the plate form is made today (GI filed 2006, certified 2007).
rows.identify_by: A brass or copper plate or vessel with separately made figures of Hindu deities and floral panels in silver, copper or brass set into undercut outlines and held by hammering the ground metal over their edges, usually in relief.
how_to_recognize: Three metals: yellow brass, red copper and white silver together
Central deity (Krishna, Vishnu, Lakshmi, Ganesha) with radiating panels or a border of dancing figures
Applied pieces held at the edges, not soldered
Modern pieces: silver figures embossed from dies in high relief, often a single large boss
rows.marks_and_labels: Makers of the Pathar (Kammalar) community are named in 1903 (Karupanna Pathar & Co., Amnuga Pathar, Guvmsawmy Pathar); sources describe no stamps. Modern plates may carry GI or emporium labels.
rows.later_production: European buyers were 'the chief patrons' by 1886; silver encrustation may have come from European suggestion, and die-stamped silver patches replaced hand-chased pieces by 1903. The Madras School of Arts also made Tanjore-type trays. Registered GI (Thanjavur Art Plate, filed 2006, certificate 2007); the modern plate, framed for display, is a common gift item.
rows.how_to_tell_old: Sources describe a style change rather than a test: old Tanjore and Tirupati work was smooth, with copper or silver laid flush and many small hand-chased pieces; modern work has figures in high relief made from dies. Age cannot be read from the type alone.

look_alikes.name: Lucknow zarbuland bidri
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Raised silver on a black zinc ground rather than on copper or brass.

look_alikes.name: Trichinopoly work
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Brass encrusted with zinc rather than silver (Watt 1903).

look_alikes.name: Benares brass with copper
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Copper and brass set together (ganga-jamni) but chased in the metal, not applied as separate relief pieces.

look_alikes.name: Swami silver (Madras silver)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Solid silver with repoussé deities; Tanjore plates are base metal with applied silver (covered elsewhere in the Heirloom silver reference).

facts.text: Tanjore metal work has three varieties: copper and silver, brass and copper, and graven brass.
facts.quote: The copper and silver, the brass and copper, and graven brass, are the three chief varieties of the Tanjore metal work.

facts.text: Silver figures on copper are a modern adaptation of the older art of covering brass with copper figures, made for European customers.
facts.quote: The encrusting of copper-ware with silver figures is a modern, but very pleasing, adaptation of the older art of covering brass with copper figures

facts.text: The applied items are fixed by hammering the ground metal over their edges in an undercut outline.
facts.quote: the metal is merely fastened at its edges, by an undercut outline which is afterward hammered over the edges of the applied metal

facts.text: Old Tanjore and Tirupati work was smooth; relief ornament is the bane of modern Tanjore work.
facts.quote: The finished article also, in both cases, was smooth, not with the ornament in relief, which is the bane of modern Tanjore work

facts.text: By 1903 large patches of die-blocked silver leaf replaced the many small hand-chased items of earlier work.
facts.quote: the substitution of large patches of fine silver leaf, blocked out on a die, in place of the multitude of small pieces (hand chased)

facts.text: A common Tanjore salver shows Krishna on a cow playing to the gopis, framed by figures of Krishna in arches; rims may show the Ras Mandala dance.
facts.quote: The most common salver from Tanjore shewed in the centre Krishna, seated on a cow, playing to the Gopis

facts.text: Thanjavur Art Plate is a registered Geographical Indication (application 63, filed 26 July 2006, certificate 24 September 2007).
facts.quote: Thanjavur Art Plate

rows.name: Kuthuvilakku (South Indian standing oil lamp)
rows.date_note: Ancient form; surviving domestic and temple examples mostly 18th-20th century; still made (Nachiarkoil Kuthuvilakku GI).
rows.identify_by: A cast brass or bell-metal oil lamp on a round foot with a tall knopped stem and a shallow oil bowl with several wick spouts, often topped by a finial such as a hamsa (swan), parrot or peacock.
how_to_recognize: Heavy cast brass or bronze, in screw-together sections
Round foot, knopped stem (deepa-briksha), dish with 4 to many wick lips
Finial bird (hamsa, peacock) or emblem
Ghee or oil lamps have pointed lips; camphor burners plain round pans
rows.marks_and_labels: Sources describe no marks. Dowry and temple lamps may be engraved with donors' names in Tamil or Malayalam (not described in the sources; gap).
rows.later_production: Made continuously for homes, temples and dowries; Nachiarkoil (near Kumbakonam) lamps registered as a Geographical Indication (filed 2010, certificate 2013). Modern shop lamps are widely made.
rows.how_to_tell_old: Sources give no reliable test of age for South Indian brass lamps. The Madras Museum warned that crude modelling and heavy corrosion are 'so uncertain as guides' because buried metal corrodes fast and workmen 'still produce plenty of work quite as primitive in technique'; Gangoly notes extant temple and museum lamps 'are not very old' although the forms are ancient.

look_alikes.name: Deepalakshmi figure lamp
look_alikes.how_to_tell: A cast female figure holding the oil dish, not a stem lamp.

look_alikes.name: Nepal and Tibet standing lamps
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Watt and the Madras book note similar forms in Nepal and Tibet; Nepalese lamps are often made by lost-wax with more elaborate figures.

facts.text: Standing lamps of good weight are frequent dowry gifts; wicks range from four to two hundred or more.
facts.quote: The larger ones, particularly standing !amp of good weight, are frequent articles included in marriage dowrys.

facts.text: The hamsa lamp has the wick receptacle on a knobbed upright rod surmounted by a swan; the stem is called the deepa-briksha.
facts.quote: the whole is surmounted by an effigy of a swan or hamsa which dominates the design.

facts.text: Pointed burning pans are for wick lamps in ghee or oil; plain round concave pans are for camphor.
facts.quote: Those which are pointed at one end are intended for a wick placed in ghee or oil

facts.text: Lamps are the most popular temple gift and are recorded in many temple inscriptions.
facts.quote: the offering of lamps has become the most popular.

facts.text: Nachiarkoil Lamps, popularly Nachiarkoil Kuthuvilakku, are a registered GI (filed 8 February 2010, certificate 4 March 2013).
facts.quote: "Nachiarkoil Lamps" - popularly known as "Nachiarkoil Kuthuvilakku"

rows.name: Hanging chain lamp
rows.date_note: Long-lived temple form; still made.
rows.identify_by: A brass oil lamp suspended from a cast chain, often with a bird or deity finial above the oil dish.
how_to_recognize: Cast chain of figured links
Oil dish with wick lips below a bird (hamsa, parrot) or figure
Hook at top
rows.marks_and_labels: None described.
rows.later_production: Made throughout; Jaipur firms won prizes for hanging lamps in 1903.
rows.how_to_tell_old: Sources give no reliable test of age for South Indian brass lamps. The Madras Museum warned that crude modelling and heavy corrosion are 'so uncertain as guides' because buried metal corrodes fast and workmen 'still produce plenty of work quite as primitive in technique'; Gangoly notes extant temple and museum lamps 'are not very old' although the forms are ancient.

look_alikes.name: Nepal hanging lamps
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Nepal sent 'perhaps the best series ever shown' of hanging, standard and hand lamps to Delhi in 1903.

facts.text: Hanging lamps and their chains are among the most beautiful Indian brass, Watt says.
facts.quote: few articles of Indian production are more beautiful, especially the chains by which these are suspended.

facts.text: Shop lamps in the Punjab hung from elaborate chains; Jagadhri had a name for brass ware.
facts.quote: In the shops they hang from elaborate but clumsy chains.

facts.text: Sinhalese hanging lamps vary the hamsa type with an ordinary bird.
facts.quote: A variation of the hamsa type is met with in a class of Sinhalese hanging lamps

rows.name: Deepalakshmi (figure lamp), as a look-alike
rows.date_note: Form traced to early Tamil literature; extant items 'not very old' (1916); made in quantity today.
rows.identify_by: A cast standing female figure holding an oil dish in both hands in front of her, used in pairs before a deity or as a memorial lamp. Recorded here as a look-alike for the stem lamp and for bronze images.
how_to_recognize: Female figure, wide hips, small waist, hands holding a lamp pan
Often on a pedestal; sometimes a bird on one arm
Usually in pairs
rows.marks_and_labels: None described.
rows.later_production: Made for temples and homes; modern versions are very common.
rows.how_to_tell_old: Sources give no reliable test of age for South Indian brass lamps. The Madras Museum warned that crude modelling and heavy corrosion are 'so uncertain as guides' because buried metal corrodes fast and workmen 'still produce plenty of work quite as primitive in technique'; Gangoly notes extant temple and museum lamps 'are not very old' although the forms are ancient.

look_alikes.name: Bronze temple image
look_alikes.how_to_tell: An image (murti) has its own iconography and no oil pan; the Deepalakshmi's hands hold the lamp dish.

rows.cautions: A figure lamp is not evidence of an antique bronze; India's Antiquities and Art Treasures Act 1972 controls export of items over 100 years old.

facts.text: The female statue holding the wick is technically called Deepa Lakshmi; male versions are rare.
facts.quote: The statue holding the wick is generally a female figure and is technically known as Deepa Lakshmi.

facts.text: Figure lamps are used in pairs either side of a god, or singly kept lit as memorials, and are also called Kamakshi or Amman lamps.
facts.quote: These lamps are commonly used in pairs, placed on either side of a god.

facts.text: Early Tamil poems refer to lamps held by statues, some said to be made by the Yavanas.
facts.quote: Pouring oil (ghee) fully into lamps held by the statue that was skilfully made by the Yavanas

rows.name: Betel box (pandan)
rows.date_note: Made in every metal craft discussed here (bidri, Lucknow copper, Delhi enamel, Malabar brass); still used.
rows.identify_by: A lidded box, often with a tray of small inner compartments, for betel leaves, sliced areca nut, lime and spices.
how_to_recognize: Lidded box with small inner boxes or compartments
Shapes: round, square, oval, fish or leaf shaped
Malabar type: steep roof-shaped lid, fitted construction
rows.marks_and_labels: None described.
rows.later_production: Made in all centers for local use and for sale; Delhi made small heart-shaped mirror boxes in 'large quantities' for the bazaars.
rows.how_to_tell_old: No test given; the type was made continuously.

look_alikes.name: Spice box
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Smaller; sources treat betel and spice boxes together.

look_alikes.name: Hookah base
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Bidri pandans and hookah bases share decoration; a hookah base has an open neck and no lid.

facts.text: The pandan holds betel leaves, sliced areca nut, lime and spices and was indispensable in well-to-do households.
facts.quote: The Pandan, or betel-case, is an article indispensable to well-to-do natives

facts.text: Betel and spice boxes in metal exist in an immense variety in South India; a roof-lidded box is made only in Malabar.
facts.quote: Figure 156 is a form only commonly made in Malabar.

facts.text: Lucknow made beaten brass and copper pandans and trays.
facts.quote: The ornamental work done at Lucknow consists chiefly of beaten brass and copper pandans and trays

facts.text: Delhi made small oblong or heart-shaped boxes with a pierced, engraved lid and a mirror under a second lid.
facts.quote: A second lid discloses a looking-glass rather rudely set in red cement.

rows.name: Sarota (betel-nut cutter)
rows.date_note: Surviving decorative examples mostly 18th-20th century; still made.
rows.identify_by: A pair of hinged nippers with a steel blade and brass handles, used to slice areca nut, often cast with figures (lovers, horses, birds) or damascened.
how_to_recognize: Hinged nipper form with a short iron or steel blade
Brass handles cast as birds, horses, dancers or lovers
Punjab (Karnal) type set with bits of mirror and colored glass
Some damascened in gold wire (Rajasthan, Punjab)
rows.marks_and_labels: None described.
rows.later_production: Karnal cutters were 'prepared for export, and sold in almost all large towns in Upper India' (1888); made in quantity since.
rows.how_to_tell_old: No test given in the sources.

look_alikes.name: Southeast Asian and Sri Lankan nut cutters
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Very similar forms in Sri Lanka, Thailand and Indonesia (Smithsonian holds examples); attribution needs comparison.

rows.features_other: Form token wanted: nut-cutter / tool (closest used: toy).

facts.text: The sarota is a pair of nippers with brass handles and iron blades for slicing betel nut.
facts.quote: Betel nut cutters, ‘Sarota.’ These are of brass with iron blades, they are like a pair of sugar nippers

facts.text: Karnal made fanciful cutters whose brass handles were set with mirrors and colored glass, sold throughout Upper India.
facts.quote: the handles being of brass with quaint projections in which small mirrors and pieces of coloured glass are fixed.

facts.text: South Indian areca-nut cutters are often elaborately finished, amusing and ingenious.
facts.quote: They are often elaborately finished and amusing and ingenious in design.

facts.text: Damascened nut-cutters were shown in 1903, and Alwar's State koftgar decorated betel-nut cutters.
facts.quote: Knives, scissors, and betel-nut cutters are decorated in Koft work at Alwar.

rows.name: Dhokra (pointer)
rows.date_note: Pointer only; a fuller entry is needed (gap).
rows.identify_by: Lost-wax cast brass figures and vessels made by itinerant metalsmith communities of eastern and central India, with surfaces built from fine wax threads.
how_to_recognize: Thread-like surface relief from wax strands
Figures of animals, riders, deities; measures and lamps
rows.marks_and_labels: None described.
rows.later_production: Made in quantity for sale; registered GIs: Bastar Dhokra (certificate 2008), Adilabad Dokra (filed 2015), Bengal Dokra (certificate 2018).
rows.how_to_tell_old: Not covered here (gap).

look_alikes.name: Benares and Jaipur cast brass figures
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Smooth cast and chased surfaces rather than wax-thread relief.

rows.features_other: Region token wanted: Chhattisgarh, Telangana.

facts.text: The Bengal brass monograph lists Dhokra-kamar among the sub-castes of Kamars.
facts.quote: (7) Dhokra-kamar

facts.text: Bastar Dhokra, Adilabad Dokra and Bengal Dokra are registered Geographical Indications.
facts.quote: Bengal Dokra

rows.name: Talwar (Indian sabre)
rows.date_note: Mughal and Rajput period onward; decorative examples made into the 20th century.
rows.identify_by: A curved single-edged sabre with a hilt of a short grip, straight or slightly curved quillons and a disc pommel, often with a knuckle guard, the hilt frequently koftgari in gold or silver.
how_to_recognize: Disc pommel with a small finial
Short grip suited to a closed hand
Curved blade, sometimes watered (crucible) steel
Hilt koftgari in gold or silver; inscriptions in Persian or Arabic on some blades
rows.marks_and_labels: Blades may carry inscriptions, armoury marks or smiths' names; Smithsonian notes say some inscriptions were added later.
rows.later_production: Decorative talwars with koftgari hilts were made as curiosities from the 1880s (Sialkot, Lahore, Jaipur, Sirohi).
rows.how_to_tell_old: Sources give no single test. They record that decorative arms (shields, helmets, swords, armor sets) were still being made in Sialkot, Gujrat, Lahore and Jaipur as curiosities from the 1880s, often in cheap shallow or gold-leaf koftgari; Smithsonian catalog notes flag later scabbards and later-added inscriptions on 19th-century swords. A specialist's examination of blade, hilt and fittings is needed.

look_alikes.name: Persian shamshir
look_alikes.how_to_tell: More strongly curved blade and a pistol-grip hilt without a disc pommel.

look_alikes.name: Decorative tourist copy
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Thin blade, cheap gold-leaf or shallow koftgari, new scabbard; sources give no single test.

rows.cautions: Export of items over 100 years old from India is controlled under the Antiquities and Art Treasures Act 1972; local laws on carrying or selling bladed weapons may apply. No other cautions given in the sources.

facts.text: The talwar (sabre) is in almost universal use across India.
facts.quote: such as the Talwar (No. 395), or sabre, are in almost universal use

facts.text: Talwar hilts were damascened in gold at Alwar, Jaipur, Datia, Jodhpur and Sirohi; Sirohi hilts in ganga-jamni koftgari were cheap exhibition items in 1903.
facts.quote: The hilt, of the ordinary shape, is exquisitely damascened in gold

facts.text: A Smithsonian 19th-century tulwar has a Rajput (Udaipur) style hilt overlaid with gold koftgari; another's scabbard is 'likely later' and inscriptions 'possibly added later'.
facts.quote: Scabbard likely later.

rows.name: Katar (push dagger)
rows.date_note: Widely used from the 16th century; made decoratively later.
rows.identify_by: A dagger with an H-shaped hilt: two side bars joined by one or more cross grips, the blade continuing straight forward from the fist.
how_to_recognize: H-shaped hilt gripped crosswise
Broad triangular blade, often thickened at the point
Variants: forked blade, scissor katar opening into three blades, blade chiselled with hunting scenes
Hilt often gold-damascened
rows.marks_and_labels: Not described beyond decoration.
rows.later_production: Decorative katars were made at Sialkot, Jaipur and elsewhere for sale.
rows.how_to_tell_old: Sources give no single test. They record that decorative arms (shields, helmets, swords, armor sets) were still being made in Sialkot, Gujrat, Lahore and Jaipur as curiosities from the 1880s, often in cheap shallow or gold-leaf koftgari; Smithsonian catalog notes flag later scabbards and later-added inscriptions on 19th-century swords. A specialist's examination of blade, hilt and fittings is needed.

look_alikes.name: Pata (gauntlet sword)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: A long sword blade fixed to an armoured gauntlet; the katar is a short dagger.

rows.cautions: Export of items over 100 years old from India is controlled under the Antiquities and Art Treasures Act 1972; local laws on carrying or selling bladed weapons may apply. No other cautions given in the sources.

facts.text: The katar is a distinctively Indian weapon; Egerton calls it, with the straight sword, probably the national arms of India, used over a very wide range.
facts.quote: The “Katar,” dagger, together with the straight sword are probably the national arms of India.

facts.text: Hendley lists katars with carved and long blades among Indian arms shown in 1911.
facts.quote: An usual type of KATAR with carved blade.

rows.name: Khanjar (curved dagger)
rows.date_note: Mughal period onward.
rows.identify_by: A dagger with a double-curved, double-edged blade and a pistol-shaped or animal-head hilt, often of jade, ivory or horn, worn tucked in the belt.
how_to_recognize: Doubly curved two-edged blade
Hilt of jade, rock crystal, ivory, horn or steel, sometimes carved as a horse or ram head
Gold koftgari or set stones on the hilt
rows.marks_and_labels: Not described.
rows.later_production: Copies and composite pieces are common (sources give no figures).
rows.how_to_tell_old: Sources give no single test. They record that decorative arms (shields, helmets, swords, armor sets) were still being made in Sialkot, Gujrat, Lahore and Jaipur as curiosities from the 1880s, often in cheap shallow or gold-leaf koftgari; Smithsonian catalog notes flag later scabbards and later-added inscriptions on 19th-century swords. A specialist's examination of blade, hilt and fittings is needed.

look_alikes.name: Ottoman and Persian khanjar
look_alikes.how_to_tell: The same name and form across the Islamic world; Smithsonian notes record an Ottoman 'khanjar of Kurdish shape'.

rows.cautions: Export of items over 100 years old from India is controlled under the Antiquities and Art Treasures Act 1972; local laws on carrying or selling bladed weapons may apply. No other cautions given in the sources. Ivory hilts fall under ivory trade rules (see the shared ivory note).

facts.text: The khanjar has a doubly curved two-edged blade.
facts.quote: Dagger; ‘Khanjar;’ doubly-curved two-edged blade

facts.text: Curved daggers called khanjar were worn tucked into the belt by Mughal men.
facts.quote: Daggers with curved blades, known as khanjar, were worn tucked into the belt

rows.name: Dhal (round shield)
rows.date_note: Hide and steel shields of the 17th-19th centuries; decorative steel shields made from the 1880s to be sold.
rows.identify_by: A round convex shield with four (sometimes more) bosses, of hide (buffalo, rhinoceros), lacquered or painted, or of steel with koftgari.
how_to_recognize: Circular and convex, usually four bosses for the inner grips
Hide shields lacquered in colors with gilt bosses (Rajasthan)
Steel shields chased and gold-damascened (Lahore, Sialkot, Jaipur)
rows.marks_and_labels: Not described.
rows.later_production: Shields in cheap koftgari were made 'at very cheap rates' for tourists at Jaipur (1883) and sold as curiosities at Sialkot (1886); steel shields with koftgari were standard exhibition pieces in 1903.
rows.how_to_tell_old: Sources give no single test. They record that decorative arms (shields, helmets, swords, armor sets) were still being made in Sialkot, Gujrat, Lahore and Jaipur as curiosities from the 1880s, often in cheap shallow or gold-leaf koftgari; Smithsonian catalog notes flag later scabbards and later-added inscriptions on 19th-century swords. A specialist's examination of blade, hilt and fittings is needed.

look_alikes.name: Persian steel shields
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Hendley 1913 lists Persian steel shields damascened in gold beside Indian ones.

look_alikes.name: Papier-mâché shields
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Egerton records lacquered papier-mâché shields; light in weight.

rows.cautions: Export of items over 100 years old from India is controlled under the Antiquities and Art Treasures Act 1972; local laws on carrying or selling bladed weapons may apply. No other cautions given in the sources. Rhinoceros-hide shields may fall under wildlife trade rules (sources do not discuss this).

facts.text: Shields (dhal) are circular and convex with bosses, of buffalo or rhinoceros hide, sometimes papier-mâché or silk.
facts.quote: Men of high rank, chiefly Brahmins, who have an objection to wearing any kind of leather, use a shield, “ Dhal bafta,”

facts.text: Cheap koft shields were made for tourists at Jaipur.
facts.quote: Shields are thus prepared at very cheap rates.

facts.text: Sialkot shields were still made and sold as curiosities.
facts.quote: Shields, helmets, and other arms, are still made and sold as curiosities

rows.name: Later decorative arms and armor
rows.date_note: From the mid-19th century for exhibitions, Europeans and tourists; continuing.
rows.identify_by: Swords, daggers, shields, helmets and armor sets made after fighting use ended, chiefly to display koftgari and to sell to collectors and tourists.
how_to_recognize: Complete matching sets (shield, helmet, chahar-aina armor, gauntlets) in bright koftgari
Thin or shallow gold (ordinary or dewali grade)
Blades of indifferent quality; hilts and scabbards newer than blades on composite pieces
rows.marks_and_labels: Exhibition and dealer labels; makers' names in wire on some Sialkot work.
rows.later_production: Recorded from 1883 (Jaipur), 1886 (Sialkot), 1903 (Delhi exhibition sets priced from Rs 14 to Rs 1,871) and noted as 'tourist trade' in Smithsonian catalog notes.
rows.how_to_tell_old: Sources give no single test. They record that decorative arms (shields, helmets, swords, armor sets) were still being made in Sialkot, Gujrat, Lahore and Jaipur as curiosities from the 1880s, often in cheap shallow or gold-leaf koftgari; Smithsonian catalog notes flag later scabbards and later-added inscriptions on 19th-century swords. A specialist's examination of blade, hilt and fittings is needed.

look_alikes.name: Period arms
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Earlier fighting arms with wear consistent with use; sources give no single test.

look_alikes.name: Imitation arms
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Egerton notes Kashmiri copies of Daghestan pistols 'not to be distinguishable from the originals' and clever imitations of European arms.

rows.cautions: Export of items over 100 years old from India is controlled under the Antiquities and Art Treasures Act 1972; local laws on carrying or selling bladed weapons may apply. No other cautions given in the sources.

facts.text: With modern firearms, metalworkers turned from arms to boxes and vessels for patrons who were 'now usually tourists in search of curios'.
facts.quote: to give pleasure to his patrons, who are now usually tourists in search of curios.

facts.text: Sialkot and Gujrat still made damascened sword hilts, scabbards, shields and helmets in 1903, and as curiosities in 1886.
facts.quote: To this day, however, they still prepare damascened sword and dagger handles, scabbards, shields, helmets, etc.

facts.text: Egerton notes skilled Indian imitations of European arms and Kashmiri imitations of Daghestan pistols.
facts.quote: they are imitated in Kashmir so as not to be distinguishable from the originals.

facts.text: A Smithsonian catalog note records a 19th-century 'tourist trade' mace in silver koftgari.
facts.quote: 19th C. tourist trade Persian devils head mace, silver koftgari overlaid.

rows.name: Agra marble inlay (pietra dura)
rows.date_note: As architecture the inlay is Mughal (Itimad-ud-Daula's tomb, Agra Fort palaces, Taj Mahal, completed 1648). As portable small items (plates, boxes, chess boards, tabletops, paperweights) the sources describe a revival of about 1850 and a tourist and export trade from then on; no source describes surviving portable items made before the revival.
rows.identify_by: Hardstones (carnelian, jasper, agate, lapis, malachite, mother-of-pearl and others) cut to petal-by-petal shapes and set flush into grooves cut in white Makrana marble, almost always in Mughal flower-scroll patterns copied from the Taj and Agra Fort.
how_to_recognize: White marble ground (Makrana, Rajasthan); black marble grounds also used
each petal or leaf is a separate shaped piece of stone set into a groove cut to fit it, not painted or laid on top
floral scrolls, flower sprays and vine borders in the Taj style; parrots and butterflies occur as Hindu-taste motifs
joins: in good work no cement line shows; in poor work the white lime-and-gum cement shows around the stones
forms: plates (often with shaped rims), round or octagonal tabletops, chess boards, box lids, paperweights, panels
rows.marks_and_labels: Sources name the Agra firms (Nathu Ram & Sons, the largest workshop c.1903-06; Behari Lal & Sons; Parusram) as exhibitors, but none describes a stamped, signed or labelled mark on the work. Unknown: whether or when firm labels were applied.
rows.later_production: Revived about 1850 and made since for tourists and export: Birdwood (1880) says nearly all specimens in England were produced under Dr J. Murray's patronage after the revival; by 1906 the work was 'confined mostly to small articles' (paper-weights, chess boards, box covers) made by 80-100 inlayers in Agra. Production continues today for the tourist market (no modern source gathered on volume).
rows.how_to_tell_old: The sources give no test that dates a portable piece. They grade quality, not age: in first-class work 'no joining will be apparent', while cheap work shows cement; mother-of-pearl roses in pink cement were made for visitors; cheap tourist pieces were made by 1906. Treat any portable Agra inlay as post-1850 unless documented. No source gathered describes how to tell modern resin, glass or painted imitations from stone; that is a gap.

look_alikes.name: Florentine (Italian) pietra dura
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Birdwood (1880) and Watt (1903) contrast the two: Italian commesso often uses pictorial subjects (fruit, birds, landscapes) and black or colored stone grounds, while Agra work keeps to stylised Mughal flower scrolls on white marble. Sources give no material test; provenance and style are the guide.

look_alikes.name: Delhi, Bhera and Amritsar inlay
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Wilberforce (1906) says Punjab inlay copies Agra designs; Bhera work uses green serpentine ('false jade') and mottled 'Purbeck marble' grounds rather than white marble.

look_alikes.name: Mysore inlaid marble
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Watt saw one Mysore slab of bluish marble inlaid with gourd-flower designs; rare.

look_alikes.name: Resin, glass or painted imitations
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Not described in the sources gathered (gap).

rows.features_other: Stones named by Crosthwaite with sources: Makrana white marble, black marble (Rajputana), yellow marble (Jaisalmer), jasper (Cambay), bloodstone (Jabalpur), agate and onyx (Ken river), carnelian (Cambay, Banda), carbuncle (Jaipur), jade (Kumaon), lapis (Badakhshan, Ceylon), coral, malachite, turquoise. Token wanted: hardstone/semiprecious stone (using gemstones).
rows.cautions: Old items may count as antiquities in India if over 100 years (Antiquities and Art Treasures Act 1972; covered in other phase-3 topics). Heavy tabletops crack at old cement repairs; sources say nothing on conservation.

facts.text: Crosthwaite calls the craft manabbat-kari, 'sometimes called Indian pietra dura', and traces three stages: bold stone mosaic (Sikandra gateway), arabesque inlay (Itimad-ud-Daula), then naturalistic flowers (Taj screen, Agra Fort).
facts.quote: Manabbat-kari, which is sometimes called Indian pietra dura, is itself a development with or without foreign impulse from a rough mosaic work, which characterized the earlier style of the Moghal epoch.

facts.text: The process: marble rough-hewn and polished with Jumna sand; stones cut with a wire bow, ground to the shape of steel patterns (a pattern for every petal), set in grooves with lime-and-gum cement, then polished.
facts.quote: In making the groove the exact size and no more lies the difference between good and bad workmanship. If the groove is too big, the cement ... will be apparent (Crosthwaite). Birdwood: in good work not a trace [of cement] should appear between the encrusted stones and the marble.

facts.text: Portable work in 1906: mostly small articles; 80-100 inlayers in Agra; an elaborate tray took two workmen two months and cost about Rs 200.
facts.quote: At present the inlay work is confined mostly to the production of small articles, such as paper-weights, chess-boards, covers of boxes, &c.

facts.text: Agra inlay on small household items was revived about 1850 after nearly dying out; nearly all specimens then in England were made under Dr J. Murray's encouragement.
facts.quote: revived about thirty years ago through the exertions of Dr. J. Murray ... Nearly all the specimens of this work in England, at Windsor and elsewhere, were produced under his fostering care.

facts.text: Mukharji (1888) records the Taj mosaic 'now employed' on plates, cups and boxes, with prices: table Rs 300-600, box Rs 30-100, plate Rs 10-50, chess board Rs 100-200; mother-of-pearl 'recently introduced ... not with good effect'.
facts.quote: The mosaic work of the Tajmahal is now employed in the decoration of plates, cups, boxes, and other small objects.

facts.text: At the 1902-03 Delhi exhibition the best Agra items to be sold were by Nathu Ram & Sons (round table Rs 437, chess board Rs 1,625, plates) and Behari Lal & Sons; Watt rated Bharatpur inlay 'in some respects superior' to Agra.
facts.quote: The inlaid marble work of Bharatpur is in some respects superior to that of Agra.

facts.text: Tourists encouraged cheap work by 1906, though Crosthwaite thought high-class firms were unaffected.
facts.quote: the globe-trotters who throng into Agra and Benares during the cold weather, tempt the stone-carver and inlayer to prostitute their art by producing cheap and nasty imitations (Crosthwaite). Havell: a few families at Agra ... chiefly employed in making curiosities for tourists.

facts.text: DISPUTED origin: Birdwood (1880) called Agra inlay 'Florentine in origin' and credited Austin de Bordeaux; Mukharji (1888) reports Birdwood's later JIA paper arguing it is Eastern; Watt (1903) cites earlier marble-on-sandstone inlay (Tughlaq, Humayun) for an indigenous origin; Crosthwaite (1906) says European influence existed but 'its extent will never be known'.
facts.quote: While Florentine in origin and style, the designs have a thoroughly local character of their own (Birdwood 1880).

rows.name: Mother-of-pearl inlay on marble (Agra, Bhera)
rows.date_note: Mukharji (1888) calls mother-of-pearl in Agra inlay a recent introduction; Fatehpur Sikri has an early-17th-century architectural example.
rows.identify_by: Pieces of mother-of-pearl set into marble, typically as roses in a pinkish cement, made for visitors at Agra; also with jade and Purbeck marble at Bhera.
how_to_recognize: iridescent shell pieces, often roses or flower heads
pink or colored cement around the shell (Crosthwaite)
shell chips easily, so edges are often damaged
rows.marks_and_labels: None recorded.
rows.later_production: Made for visitors from the 1880s (Mukharji 1888; Crosthwaite 1906). Continues in the modern souvenir trade (no source gathered).
rows.how_to_tell_old: No dating test in the sources. Crosthwaite says first-class workmanship was rarely spent on it.

look_alikes.name: Hardstone parchin kari
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Hardstone has no iridescence; mother-of-pearl shows a rainbow sheen and layered structure at chips.

facts.text: Mother-of-pearl roses set in rose-colored cement were 'much manufactured to be sold to visitors' at Agra; the shell chips, so first-class work rarely used it.
facts.quote: Mother of pearl roses, inlaid with a rose-coloured cement, are much manufactured for sale to visitors (Crosthwaite). Mukharji: Mother-o'-pearl has recently been introduced in the work, but not with good effect.

facts.text: Watt names Bhera and Agra as the places where mother-of-pearl is inlaid on stone; Bhera made a Purbeck-marble chess table inlaid with mother-of-pearl and green jade (Rs 2,500).
facts.quote: a corresponding industry exists both in Bhera and Agra in inlaying mother-of-pearl on stone

rows.name: Taj Mahal and monument models
rows.date_note: Recorded as sold to visitors by 1888 (Mukharji); exhibited 1903 (Watt). Earlier production not documented in the sources gathered.
rows.identify_by: Small-scale models of the Taj Mahal and other Agra and Fatehpur Sikri monuments carved in white marble, alabaster or soapstone (sometimes in ivory) for visitors.
how_to_recognize: domed tomb on a plinth with four minarets; detachable parts common
marble (cold, heavy, crystalline), alabaster (softer, more translucent), or soapstone (soapy, warm gray, scratches with a fingernail)
ivory models are smaller and made in Delhi
rows.marks_and_labels: None recorded; makers named at exhibitions (Nathu Ram & Sons; Permanand Brothers of Agra).
rows.later_production: A visitor trade by 1888 (marble model about Rs 500) and through the 20th century; still made (no modern source gathered).
rows.how_to_tell_old: No dating test in the sources.

look_alikes.name: Ivory Taj models
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Stubbs (1900) says ivory Taj models sold in Agra were officially said to be imported from Delhi.

rows.features_other: Alabaster: token wanted.
rows.cautions: Ivory models fall under the ivory rules (see ivory rows).

facts.text: Marble and soapstone models of the Taj were made and sold to visitors; a fine marble model cost Rs 500.
facts.quote: models of which, both in marble and soap-stone, are made and sold to visitors (Mukharji). Watt: the Taj, made by Nathoo Ram and Sons, Rs. 625, is doubtless the best example [of alabaster and soapstone].

facts.text: Ivory models of the Taj were sold in Agra but said to be made in Delhi.
facts.quote: such models of the Taj as are sold in Agra are imported from Delhi (Stubbs). Dutt: an ivory Taj from Delhi, has a peculiar value of its own.

facts.text: Soapstone models of the Fatehpur Sikri ruins were made at Fatehpur Sikri.
facts.quote: At Fattehpur Sikri models in soapstone are made of the celebrated Mahommedan ruins of that city (Birdwood). Watt: The model of Salim Chisti's tomb at Fatehpur Sikri by Permanand Brothers of Agra.

rows.name: Agra soapstone carving
rows.date_note: Described as a modern development of the jali tradition in the Journal of Indian Art (vol. I, 1884-86, quoted by Mukharji 1888).
rows.identify_by: Boxes, trays, dishes, inkstands and models carved and pierced in a tough warm-gray Rajputana steatite, sold cheaply in Agra workshops.
how_to_recognize: soft, soapy feel; warm gray, sometimes greenish or cream
sharp floral or arabesque relief; pierced (jali) lids and sides on boxes
light enough to buy as a souvenir; scratches easily
rows.marks_and_labels: None recorded.
rows.later_production: Cheap work for visitors from the 1880s; Crosthwaite (1906) says carved soapstone boxes could be bought 'very cheaply in any of the karkhanas at Agra'. Still made (no modern source gathered).
rows.how_to_tell_old: No dating test in the sources.

look_alikes.name: Alabaster
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Alabaster is translucent at thin edges and whiter; soapstone is opaque and greasy to the touch. Sources name both materials for Agra fretwork boxes but give no test.

look_alikes.name: Orissa and Gaya soapstone
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Orissa pieces are figure groups and idols, often blackened (Havell 1906); Agra work is mostly floral boxes and trays.

rows.features_other: Alabaster also used for the same boxes (token wanted: alabaster).

facts.text: The best soapstone carving comes from Agra; carved soapstone boxes were cheap in Agra workshops; marble, alabaster and soapstone fretwork boxes were sold to sight-seers.
facts.quote: The best soap-stone carving, however, undoubtedly comes from Agra ... Beautifully carved boxes of soap-stone can be purchased very cheaply in any of the karkhanas at Agra (Crosthwaite). Watt: a small hexagonal box from Agra, price Rs. 37 ... by Nathu Ram and Sons.

facts.text: The Journal of Indian Art described Agra soapstone carving as a modern offshoot of the jali craft, in a tough warm-gray Rajputana steatite, made into boxes and trays for drawing-room use.
facts.quote: The specimens of carving in soap-stone belong to a modern development of the same hereditary art. The material, which also comes from Rajputana, is a stratite of particularly tough texture and a warm grey tint.

facts.text: Soapstone was also carved into dishes and inkstands at Fatehpur Sikri, and at Gohari (NW Provinces).
facts.quote: it is also carved into ornamental dishes, inkstands, and other objects. Soapstone ornaments are also made at Gohari

rows.name: Pierced marble and alabaster screens and panels (small jali)
rows.date_note: Architectural jali is Mughal (Fatehpur Sikri, 1566 on); small panels to be sold recorded from 1888.
rows.identify_by: Small slabs or screens of white marble or alabaster pierced through in geometric lattice, copying the Taj and Fatehpur Sikri screens, sold as souvenirs and decorative panels.
how_to_recognize: through-cut geometric or floral lattice
white marble (Makrana) or alabaster; red sandstone for architectural pieces
small slabs sized for display, not building
rows.marks_and_labels: None recorded.
rows.later_production: Small slabs or screens in marble and alabaster 'in imitation of the marble screens of the Tajmahal' were made at Agra for about Rs 30-40 in 1888. Varanasi soft-stone jali work was registered as an Indian GI in 2017-18 (application 556), showing the craft continues.
rows.how_to_tell_old: No dating test in the sources. Crosthwaite notes pierced stone becomes brittle after two centuries outdoors (architectural, not small panels).

look_alikes.name: Plaster jali
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Wilberforce (1906) says Delhi plaster relief is so well polished it 'may easily be mistaken for real stone work'; plaster is lighter and chalky at breaks.

rows.features_other: Alabaster: token wanted.

facts.text: At Agra fine marble and alabaster work was made in imitation of the Taj screens; a small slab cost about Rs 30-40.
facts.quote: In the same place is also made exquisitely fine work in marble and in alabaster in imitation of the marble screens of the Tajmahal; price about R30 to R40 for a small slab or screen (Mukharji). Crosthwaite: a small trade is carried on in fret-work boxes, made of marble, alabaster, and soapstone, which are sold to sight-seers.

facts.text: Varanasi Soft Stone Jali Work is a registered Indian geographical indication (application 556, 2017-18).

rows.name: Orissa and Gaya soapstone and black-stone carving
rows.date_note: Present-day (c.1880-1906) work described; the families descend from temple carvers. Gaya carvers are said to descend from masons brought from Jaipur about 1766.
rows.identify_by: Small idols, figure groups (Krishna and the gopis), animals and puja vessels carved in soft soapstone at Puri or in harder black chlorite/potstone at Gaya and near Balasore, often blackened.
how_to_recognize: small Hindu figure groups and animals
soft gray soapstone, frequently stained black to pass for harder stone (Havell)
Gaya work in a harder dark potstone or black chlorite
cups and dishes in black chlorite from the Nilgiri estate near Balasore
rows.marks_and_labels: None recorded.
rows.later_production: By 1906 the Puri temple carvers lived by making small soapstone carvings for the bazaar; Gaya families made idols and animals. Still made (Konark stone carving registered as an Indian GI in 2008-09, application 87).
rows.how_to_tell_old: No dating test in the sources. Havell says blackening was a contemporary practice, so a black surface does not show age.

look_alikes.name: Harder stone (black chlorite, basalt) sculpture
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Havell: soapstone carvings 'are generally coloured black to make them resemble the more expensive work in handstone'; soapstone scratches easily.

rows.features_other: Black chlorite and potstone are not soapstone strictly; token wanted: other soft stone / chlorite. Gaya is in present Bihar (token Bengal used for the old Bengal Presidency).
rows.cautions: Old temple images and fragments may be antiquities (India's 1972 Act; see other topics).

facts.text: Puri carvers worked soapstone from near Cuttack because it was easiest and sold cheaply, and usually blackened it to resemble costlier stone.
facts.quote: The soapstone-carvings are generally coloured black to make them resemble the more expensive work in handstone, a process which depreciates the real artistic merit which many of them possess.

facts.text: Animals were carved in black chlorite at Gaya; black chlorite from the Nilgiri estate near Balasore was made into cups and dishes.
facts.quote: Animals are carved in black chlorite at Gaya in the Patna division of Bengal (Birdwood). Havell: The ordinary work of those two families is carving small idols, puja vessels, and animals.

facts.text: Konark stone carving is a registered Indian geographical indication (application 87, 2008-09).

rows.name: Jaipur marble figures and idols
rows.date_note: Described as current work in 1880-1906.
rows.identify_by: White (also black and red) marble images of Hindu deities and animals, often painted in bright colors and gold, made at Jaipur and copied at Delhi.
how_to_recognize: conventional frontal deities and animals
white marble, sometimes black or red
painted red, green, yellow, blue and gilded details (Birdwood)
sets of deities in graded sizes were sold (Watt)
rows.marks_and_labels: None recorded.
rows.later_production: A large commercial trade by 1903 (complete sets of idols in assorted sizes on sale); Delhi carvers copied Jaipur work. Still made in Jaipur (no modern source gathered).
rows.how_to_tell_old: No dating test in the sources; paint is renewed on worshipped images, so fresh paint says nothing.

look_alikes.name: Cast resin or marble-dust figures
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Not covered by the sources (gap).

rows.cautions: Images from temples may be antiquities (India's 1972 Act).

facts.text: In Rajputana idols were largely carved in white marble and brightly colored with paint and gold.
facts.quote: In Rajputana also idols are largely carved in white marble, and brilliantly colored in red, green, yellow, and blue paint and gold (Birdwood). Watt: several complete sets of Hindu idols, in assorted sizes ... all more or less in conventional forms.

facts.text: Delhi marble models of animals and deities were 'entirely in imitation of Jaipur work'.
facts.quote: Marble models of animals, figures of deities and heroes are sometimes made. The work is entirely in imitation of Jaipur work, and is wholly conventional

rows.name: Bhera 'false jade' and stone inlay
rows.date_note: Recorded 1872-1906; the lapidaries were blacksmiths who turned from weapons to caskets and tables after the Arms (Disarmament) Act.
rows.identify_by: Knife and sword hilts, caskets, tea sets and small tables of green serpentine ('false jade', softer than true jade) and mottled limestone, sometimes inlaid with mother-of-pearl or mounted with Sialkot gold damascening, from Bhera (Shahpur District).
how_to_recognize: pale to dark green translucent stone, softer than nephrite
mottled 'Purbeck marble' (suleimani) grounds
inlay of contrasting stones and mother-of-pearl in Agra-derived designs
pairs with gold-damascened steel mounts
rows.marks_and_labels: None recorded; makers named (Muhammad Din, Fazal Din, Muhammad Amin).
rows.later_production: A small industry of about 25 men in six shops (1905), selling through Delhi and Lahore; declining except at durbars.
rows.how_to_tell_old: No dating test in the sources.

look_alikes.name: True jade (nephrite or jadeite)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Watt and Kipling: the Bhera stone is softer than the jade imported from Burma and China; sources give no field test.

look_alikes.name: Mughal jewelled jade
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Watt separates court jewelled jade (true or false jade set with gems) from Bhera trade wares.

rows.features_other: Token wanted: serpentine/jade.

facts.text: The green Bhera stone was identified as false jade, a pure serpentine (bowenite), called sang-i-yeshm, softer than true jade and brought down the Indus from Afghanistan.
facts.quote: has been classed as false jade or rather a very pure form of serpentine called Bowenite; it is known in the vernacular as sang-i-yeshm. It is softer and more easily worked than the jade (Watt).

facts.text: Bhera lapidaries were blacksmiths who forged blades and inlaid stones; after the Disarmament Act they turned to caskets and tables; designs copied from Agra work.
facts.quote: The passing of the Disarmament Act has now caused them to turn their skill and energies into the more peaceful occupation of carving caskets and tables.

rows.name: Cambay and Banda agate ware
rows.date_note: Ancient trade (Broach and Cambay agates since Pliny's time per Birdwood); the small items for Europeans described are 19th-early 20th century.
rows.identify_by: Cups, small boxes, knife and sword handles, paper-knives, brooches and beads cut and polished from agate, carnelian and moss agate at Cambay, Banda and Jabalpur, much of it for European buyers.
how_to_recognize: polished translucent banded or mossy stone
carnelian red to flesh tones
small boxes 3-4 in., knife handles, studs and buttons
rows.marks_and_labels: None recorded.
rows.later_production: A large export and souvenir trade by the 1880s-1900s; Ball (quoted by Watt and Mukharji) believed many European seaside 'pebbles' were cut in India.
rows.how_to_tell_old: No dating test. Watt records that most Cambay stones were heated (baked) to bring out or change color, so strong color is not a sign of age or of natural color.

look_alikes.name: Dyed or heated agate
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Watt (from J. M. Campbell): stones were sun-baked or fired in cowdung to turn browns white or chestnut and yellows red; only a few types were left unbaked.

rows.features_other: Token wanted: agate/hardstone.

facts.text: Cambay stones were collected near Ratanpur and most were baked to change their color.
facts.quote: All others are baked to bring out their colours. After exposure to the sun or by being baked in a fire of cowdung, light browns become white and dark browns deepen into chestnut.

facts.text: Agates from the Ken river (Banda) were made into brooches, studs, knife-handles and paper-weights 'chiefly for European use'.
facts.quote: agates are found in the bed of the river Ken in the District of Banda, which are made into brooches, studs, knife-handles, paper-weights, &c., chiefly for European use (Mukharji). Crosthwaite: In Banda city there are four Muhammadan firms, which cut and polish semi-precious stones.

rows.name: Murshidabad ivory carving
rows.date_note: Tradition (Dutt 1901) places the start under the Nawabs, when a Hindu copied a Muhammadan carver brought from Delhi; the trade served East India Company Europeans at Kasimbazar and Berhampore from the later 18th century and declined by 1901 (about 25 carvers).
rows.identify_by: Ivory figures and groups made by the Bhaskar caste of Murshidabad and Berhampore: Durga panels under a classical canopy, peacock-prow boats (mayurpankhi), caparisoned elephants, bullock carts, palanquins, processions and chessmen, often carved from a single block without joins.
how_to_recognize: flat panel of Durga with attendant deities under columns and canopy
peacock boats, elephants with howdahs, processions, figures of trades and castes
carvers avoided joins (Dutt), so larger pieces are costly and small pieces are single-block
ivory preferred from Assam or Burma, soft and white; Watt calls the goods flimsy and brittle compared with Travancore
no figure of Krishna: Dutt says the Vaishnava carvers would not carve or sell him
rows.marks_and_labels: None recorded; makers named at exhibitions (Tulsi Khatumber, Manick and Ram Kishore Bhaskar; Nilmani, Girish Chandra, Murari Mohan, Nimai Chandra Bhaskar). Calcutta retailers (S. J. Tellery & Co., H. C. Ganguli & Co.) bought from the carvers.
rows.later_production: For the European market from the later 18th century; by 1901 Dutt says carvers had 'sacrificed quality to quantity' and depended on European tourists and residents; Watt (1903) says the flat Durga panel was copied at Delhi and Patiala and sold all over India.
rows.how_to_tell_old: No reliable dating test in the sources. Watt found 'no antique examples' at any ivory center and Dutt's list of stock models changed little; European-form pieces (candelabra, wall brackets, chessmen after Layard's Nineveh) are datable only by form and provenance.

look_alikes.name: Delhi and Patiala copies of Murshidabad Durgas
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Watt says the flat Durga style was first made at Murshidabad and copied at Delhi and Patiala; sources give no visual test.

look_alikes.name: Bone or resin figures
look_alikes.how_to_tell: See bone row; Burns: ivory lacks the pores of bone.

rows.cautions: Ivory: India banned trade in imported ivory and articles made from it from 2 April 1992 (Wild Life (Protection) Amendment Act 1991, ss. 49B-49C), after protecting the Indian elephant in 1977; the Supreme Court upheld the ban in 2003. UK: since 6 June 2022 the Ivory Act 2018 bans dealing in elephant (and now hippo, killer whale, narwhal, sperm whale) ivory without a registered exemption, e.g. items made before 3 March 1947 with under 10% ivory, portrait miniatures made before 1918 up to 320 sq cm, or a certificate for pre-1918 items of outstandingly high value; owning, gifting and bequeathing are not banned. US: Asian elephants are Endangered and African Threatened under the ESA; interstate sale is generally barred except for ESA antiques (100+ years old, not repaired with ivory after 27 Dec 1973) and de minimis items, and several states add their own bans. Facts only, not legal advice; check current rules.

facts.text: Ivory carving at Murshidabad was in the hands of the Bhaskar (image-maker) caste of Vaishnavas, a branch of the carpenter caste; about 25 carvers remained in 1901.
facts.quote: The ivory-carvers of Murshidabad are all Hindus and belong to the Baisnav sect. The caste is called Bhaskar, or image maker, and is a branch of the carpenter caste (Dutt).

facts.text: Stock articles and prices c.1901 included Durga groups Rs 50-300, Jagannath car processions, palanquins, chessmen, elephants, bullock carts, peacock barges, figures of trades, combs, bangles, card cases, photo frames and caskets.
facts.quote: The following is a list of the ivory articles usually made in Murshidabad with their prices

facts.text: Murshidabad carvers preferred soft Assam or Burma ivory; Watt contrasts Travancore's stable green ivory with Murshidabad's 'flimsy brittle goods'.
facts.quote: Murshidabad carvers generally prefer Assam or Burma ivory to others, as it is both light and soft (Dutt). Watt: the purity, opacity and stability of the Travancore ivories when compared with the flimsy brittle goods of Murshidabad.

facts.text: Bengal carvers made table ornaments 'for the European market mainly'; the industry rose with the Europeans of Kasimbazar and Berhampore and then depended on tourists.
facts.quote: the Bengal ivory workers have produced for some years past a large assortment of table ornaments ... for the European market mainly (Watt). Dutt: looks to European tourists or residents for encouragement.

facts.text: Watt calls the flat Durga panel 'a modern abomination' first made at Murshidabad and copied at Delhi and Patiala.
facts.quote: This flat and flimsy style of ivory work was first made in Murshidabad but it is now copied in Delhi and Patiala and finds a market all over India.

rows.name: Delhi ivory carving
rows.date_note: Watt (1903): hardly an ivory industry in Delhi 'some 40 years ago' (c.1860s); a leading center by 1900, mainly for tourists. Older Mughal ivory existed but no continuity is documented.
rows.identify_by: Pierced and carved ivory for European buyers made in the Dariba workshop of Lala Faqir Chand Raghu Nath Dass and others: elephants with chains and trappings cut from one block, bullock carts, peacock boats, Hindu pantheons, paper-knives with elephant handles, card cases and lace-like pierced caskets.
how_to_recognize: deep, regular pierced tracery (perforation), often a pierced shell over an inner carved block
figures stiff, 'left side invariably concave and its right convex' because carved close to the curve of the tusk (Ellis)
elephants loaded with howdahs and chains of tiny loose links
boxes may combine carving with painted ivory miniatures
rows.marks_and_labels: None recorded; sources name the firm of Lala Faqir Chand Raghu Nath Dass but no mark.
rows.later_production: Mostly for tourists by 1900 (Ellis: Americans and Russians bought the best). Stock models priced from Rs 1-2 (camels, horses) to Rs 2,000-2,500 (elephants, pantheons) in 1900.
rows.how_to_tell_old: No dating test in the sources. Ellis notes stock models were reproduced 'time after time'.

look_alikes.name: Bone fretwork
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Stubbs: bone fretwork in the same style was sold in every bazaar; see bone row.

look_alikes.name: Chinese and Japanese ivory
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Sources compare Delhi figures unfavorably with Chinese work (Baden-Powell) but give no test.

rows.cautions: Ivory: India banned trade in imported ivory and articles made from it from 2 April 1992 (Wild Life (Protection) Amendment Act 1991, ss. 49B-49C), after protecting the Indian elephant in 1977; the Supreme Court upheld the ban in 2003. UK: since 6 June 2022 the Ivory Act 2018 bans dealing in elephant (and now hippo, killer whale, narwhal, sperm whale) ivory without a registered exemption, e.g. items made before 3 March 1947 with under 10% ivory, portrait miniatures made before 1918 up to 320 sq cm, or a certificate for pre-1918 items of outstandingly high value; owning, gifting and bequeathing are not banned. US: Asian elephants are Endangered and African Threatened under the ESA; interstate sale is generally barred except for ESA antiques (100+ years old, not repaired with ivory after 27 Dec 1973) and de minimis items, and several states add their own bans. Facts only, not legal advice; check current rules.

facts.text: Delhi ivory carving grew from almost nothing c.1860 to a leading center by 1903 because of sight-seers; goods met European demand.
facts.quote: in Delhi, some 40 years ago, there hardly existed an ivory-carving industry while to-day Delhi is one of the chief centres of the craft in India. This remarkable development is doubtless entirely the result of the great influx of sight-seers (Watt). Ellis: Year by year the tourist element increases in volume.

facts.text: Delhi stock designs c.1900: elephants Rs 2-2,000, bullock carts Rs 4-1,500, peacock ships, Hindu pantheons Rs 4-2,500, chessmen, camels, horses, palanquins, paper-knives, card cases, boxes, picture frames.
facts.quote: Below is appended a list of the stock designs, with minimum and maximum prices

facts.text: Ellis and Watt describe the stiff, lopsided animals caused by carving close to the tusk's outer surface to save material.
facts.quote: an animal ... apparently taken out of a child's Noah's Ark, without joints, and with its left side invariably concave and its right convex.

facts.text: Baden-Powell (1872) found the only respectable Punjab ivory work at Delhi and Amritsar: boxes, crochet needles with tiny figures, minute toys.
facts.quote: The places where ivory carving is done are numerous, but the only respectable work comes from Delhi and Amritsar.

rows.name: Delhi miniature painting on ivory
other_names: Taj and Jama Masjid ivory views
rows.date_note: A 19th-century Delhi trade for Europeans (portraits of Mughal emperors and empresses, views of the Taj, Jama Masjid, Delhi and Agra buildings); in the 1880s artists copied photographs. Start date approximate; sources gathered do not fix it.
rows.identify_by: Thin plates of ivory painted in watercolor with portraits of Mughal rulers and beauties or views of Mughal buildings, sold loose, framed, set in jewelry, or let into carved ebony and sandalwood boxes.
how_to_recognize: very fine single-hair brushwork (ek bal qalam)
portraits full face (do-chashm) or profile (ek-chashm)
subjects: Mughal emperors and empresses, the Taj, Jama Masjid, Delhi Fort
oval plaques set in Nagina ebony or sandalwood boxes bound with silver or plated brass
later work copies photographs
rows.marks_and_labels: Some painters signed, but the sources gathered do not describe signatures; artists claimed Persian descent and also worked in Calcutta and Bombay.
rows.later_production: By 1888 the Delhi painters sold large amounts in Calcutta and Bombay; prices Rs 10-100. Painting on ivory also at Benares, Trichinopoly and Jaipur. Continued as a souvenir trade in the 20th century (no source gathered on modern bone or plastic plaques).
rows.how_to_tell_old: No dating test in the sources. Photographic-looking portraits point to after the introduction of photography (Kipling, quoted by Mukharji).

look_alikes.name: Bone or plastic plaques
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Not covered by the sources (gap); see bone row for structure.

look_alikes.name: European portrait miniatures on ivory
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Subjects and style differ; Birdwood calls Delhi work 'in the style of European miniatures'. UK Ivory Act exempts pre-1918 portrait miniatures up to 320 sq cm (registration needed).

rows.cautions: Ivory: India banned trade in imported ivory and articles made from it from 2 April 1992 (Wild Life (Protection) Amendment Act 1991, ss. 49B-49C), after protecting the Indian elephant in 1977; the Supreme Court upheld the ban in 2003. UK: since 6 June 2022 the Ivory Act 2018 bans dealing in elephant (and now hippo, killer whale, narwhal, sperm whale) ivory without a registered exemption, e.g. items made before 3 March 1947 with under 10% ivory, portrait miniatures made before 1918 up to 320 sq cm, or a certificate for pre-1918 items of outstandingly high value; owning, gifting and bequeathing are not banned. US: Asian elephants are Endangered and African Threatened under the ESA; interstate sale is generally barred except for ESA antiques (100+ years old, not repaired with ivory after 27 Dec 1973) and de minimis items, and several states add their own bans. Facts only, not legal advice; check current rules.

facts.text: Delhi was the chief center of miniature painting on ivory; subjects were Mughal court portraits and Mughal buildings; work set into carved ebony caskets and jewelry.
facts.quote: Portraits of emperors, empresses, and other beauties of the Muhammadan Court, and pictures of the chief buildings in Northern India, like the Taj at Agra, and the Juma Masjid at Delhi, are favourite subjects (Mukharji). Baden-Powell: Delhi Boxes ... noticed in the Fine Art section on account of the ivory paintings on them.

facts.text: Ivory for painting was sawn into thin plates, pressed four to nine months to season, planed and chalk-polished.
facts.quote: The plates are then generally placed in a press with the object of preserving the flattened shape, and kept in that position for four to nine months

facts.text: Delhi sandalwood and ebony boxes were 'set with oval Delhi miniatures and bound with silver or plated brass', Rs 2-8 to 25 each (1888).
facts.quote: Delhi has its specialty in carved sandalwood and ebony boxes set with oval Delhi miniatures and bound with silver or plated brass (Mukharji). Watt: [Nagina ebony] has been taken advantage of by the miniature painters of Delhi to set off their choicest productions.

rows.name: Amritsar and Punjab ivory (combs, card cases, bangles)
rows.date_note: The Golden Temple's Darshani door ivory inlay probably dates from Ranjit Singh's restoration of 1802 (Watt); combs, card cases and bangles recorded 1872-1903.
rows.identify_by: Ivory combs with geometric pierced work, paper-cutters, card cases, surmadanis (antimony boxes) shaped as fruit or vegetables, toys and turned bangles from Amritsar, Patiala and Ludhiana.
how_to_recognize: combs with geometric open-work panels
ivory stained red and green (Darshani door; bangles)
Patiala: shallow surface floral tracery, poor joinery
fruit-shaped surmadanis (mango, brinjal, chili, maize)
rows.marks_and_labels: None recorded.
rows.later_production: Amritsar comb-making 'probably originated with the Sikhs' (Kipling, quoted by Ellis); by 1900 Ellis found Amritsar and Patiala in decline and Amritsar work comparable only with cheaper Delhi goods. Billiard balls at Ludhiana were a modern trade.
rows.how_to_tell_old: No dating test in the sources. Ellis says an old set of bangles fetched about two-thirds the price of a new uncolored one, so color fashion changed c.1900.

look_alikes.name: Bone and horn combs
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Burns: high-caste Poona women thought bone combs impure; cheap foreign bone and horn combs undercut ivory c.1900; see bone and horn rows.

rows.cautions: Ivory: India banned trade in imported ivory and articles made from it from 2 April 1992 (Wild Life (Protection) Amendment Act 1991, ss. 49B-49C), after protecting the Indian elephant in 1977; the Supreme Court upheld the ban in 2003. UK: since 6 June 2022 the Ivory Act 2018 bans dealing in elephant (and now hippo, killer whale, narwhal, sperm whale) ivory without a registered exemption, e.g. items made before 3 March 1947 with under 10% ivory, portrait miniatures made before 1918 up to 320 sq cm, or a certificate for pre-1918 items of outstandingly high value; owning, gifting and bequeathing are not banned. US: Asian elephants are Endangered and African Threatened under the ESA; interstate sale is generally barred except for ESA antiques (100+ years old, not repaired with ivory after 27 Dec 1973) and de minimis items, and several states add their own bans. Facts only, not legal advice; check current rules.

facts.text: Amritsar made great quantities of ivory combs, paper-cutters and card cases with geometric open-work; the comb trade is linked to Sikh custom.
facts.quote: At Amritsar great quantities of combs are made, an industry which probably originated with the Sikhs (Kipling, quoted by Ellis). Watt: With the Sikhs ... the use of a comb, to be worn in the hair, became almost a matter of faith.

facts.text: Patiala work is shallow floral surface tracery with good designs but bad joinery; a Patiala howdah is among the oldest authentic Punjab ivories.
facts.quote: In PATIALA a fairly old industry exists in shallow surface floral tracery ... the workmanship and joinery are very bad.

facts.text: Ivory bangles (churas) were turned in large numbers and colored; by 1900 fashion favored uncolored ones.
facts.quote: fashion now lays down that they are to be worn in the natural colour (Ellis). Baden-Powell: One of the commonest form of work in ivory, is the manufacture of colored ivory bracelets.

rows.name: Travancore ivory carving
rows.date_note: Watt (1903) describes current work from the School of Art, Trivandrum, and older South Indian ivories of the 17th-18th centuries; continuity between them is not documented.
rows.identify_by: Massive, solid, finely finished ivory carving in deep relief and in the round: deities (Vishnu on the serpent), caskets with Ramayana panels, hand mirrors, brush backs, model temple doorways and shrines, often on buffalo-horn stands.
how_to_recognize: solid, heavy ivory rather than thin panels
figures carved fully in the round, finished behind as well as in front (Watt)
floral scrolls springing from lion-griffins or yali heads
green (fresh) ivory that is white, opaque and stable
stands in buffalo horn
rows.marks_and_labels: None recorded; the School of Art, Trivandrum is named as maker of prize pieces.
rows.later_production: Made for the Maharaja's presentation and exhibitions and for sale from the late 19th century; the School of Art won a gold medal at Delhi 1903.
rows.how_to_tell_old: No dating test. Watt warns that old South Indian ivories are hard to separate from Ceylon work.

look_alikes.name: Ceylon (Kandyan) ivory
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Watt: 'it is more difficult to separate the Ceylon from the Travancore and Mysore ivories than these from the purely Dravidian work'.

look_alikes.name: Mysore ivory
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Watt: Travancore keeps ancient conventional designs; Mysore favors modern jungle scenes.

facts.text: Watt ranked Travancore and Mysore ivories foremost in India; Travancore pays more attention to statuary than any other center.
facts.quote: The ivory carvings of Travancore and Mysore must be given the very foremost position among the ivories of India.

facts.text: Travancore ivory is pure, opaque and stable because carvers use fresh ('green') ivory.
facts.quote: The purity, opacity and stability of the Travancore ivories ... are doubtless largely due to the superiority of the green ivory invariably employed

facts.text: Travancore was one of the chief ivory-carving centers of India in the later 19th century.
facts.quote: Ivory is carved all over India, but chiefly at ... Travancore, Vizagapatam, and Vizianagram, in Madras (Birdwood). Watt: four localities in India ... famous for their ivory manufactures; these are DELHI ... MURSHIDABAD ... MYSORE and TRAVANCORE.

rows.name: Mysore ivory carving
rows.date_note: A settee back-rest in the Mysore palace was believed to be early 17th-century (Watt); current work c.1903 included realistic jungle and hunting scenes.
rows.identify_by: Ivory caskets and panels from Mysore with realistic jungle, hunting and elephant-catching scenes and Chalukyan-style scrolls shared with Mysore sandalwood carving.
how_to_recognize: realistic jungle scenes with foreground, distance and clouds
Chalukyan floral scrolls like Mysore sandalwood
old pieces gilded, stained and lac-engraved in pale green and magenta (Watt)
rows.marks_and_labels: None recorded.
rows.later_production: Palace commissions and exhibition pieces c.1900; the same Gudigar carvers also carved ivory (Thurston/D'Cruz).
rows.how_to_tell_old: Watt describes an old original and a later copy of the same back-rest: the copy used iron rods that discolored the ivory, was not gilded or stained, and was framed in wood. That is a single example, not a general test.

look_alikes.name: Mysore sandalwood carving
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Same designs; material differs (see sandalwood row).

facts.text: The sandalwood carvers (Gudigars) of Mysore were also specialist ivory carvers.
facts.quote: The sandal-wood carvers are also expert in carving ivory (Thurston/D'Cruz). Watt: Mysore (fig. i) modern jungle scenery, in which a high proficiency has been attained both in sandal-wood and ivory.

facts.text: A palace back-rest believed early 17th century was later copied; the copy's iron rods discolored the ivory.
facts.quote: It is made of more massive ivory but is spoiled by having iron rods driven through it ... The ivory of the new copy has been discoloured by the iron

rows.name: Mysore ivory inlay on rosewood and ebony
rows.date_note: Watt says the art 'has for long been followed in Mysore'; Mukharji cites the ivory-inlaid doors of Tipu Sultan's tomb (late 18th century). The 1900s palace commission expanded it.
rows.identify_by: Ivory set into rosewood, ebony or sheesham in Carnatic and Mughal patterns, the ivory engraved with fine designs filled with black lac.
how_to_recognize: ivory pieces engraved and the lines filled with black lac
darker durable wood ground (rosewood, ebony)
surfaces not overloaded with ivory (Watt, contrasting Hoshiarpur)
rows.marks_and_labels: None recorded; firms named: Ahamed Ali and Mahomed Mukhdum, Ganesiam & Co., Yusuf Ali & Sons.
rows.later_production: Doors and furniture for the new Mysore palace c.1900; tables, teapoys and small articles for sale (teapoy Rs 50 in 1888). 'Mysore Rosewood Inlay' was registered as an Indian GI in 2004-05 (application 24); modern work often uses substitutes for ivory (no source gathered).
rows.how_to_tell_old: No dating test in the sources.

look_alikes.name: Hoshiarpur inlay
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Watt: Mysore designs are more artistic, workmanship better and wood more durable; Hoshiarpur spots ivory or bone all over sheesham.

look_alikes.name: Vizagapatam lac-engraved ivory
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Watt says Mysore ivory is 'richly loaded with black lac after the fashion practised in Vizagapatam'; Vizagapatam work is veneer on boxes, Mysore is inlay into solid wood.

facts.text: Mysore inlay puts ivory on sheesham, rosewood or ebony and blackens engraved designs in the ivory with lac.
facts.quote: A peculiarity of Mysore work and the one that gives it its great charm, is the fact that the surface of the ivory is ornamented with black designs.

facts.text: In Mysore town, ebony cabinet work and furniture were inlaid with ivory in Carnatic and Mughal patterns; a teapoy cost Rs 50; Tipu Sultan's tomb has ivory-inlaid doors.
facts.quote: Cabinet work and furniture of ebony wood are inlaid with ivory in the town of Mysore. The work is done in the old conventional Carnatic and Mughul patterns.

facts.text: Mysore inlaid ivory into dark woods (ebony, rosewood, sheesham) for cabinets, tables, teapoys and palace doors, c.1888-1903.
facts.quote: Mysore, where ivory on shishaw, rosewood or ebony, is the form of the art adopted (Watt). Mukharji: Cabinet work and furniture of ebony wood are inlaid with ivory in the town of Mysore.

facts.text: 'Mysore Rosewood Inlay' is a registered Indian GI (application 24, 2004-05).

rows.name: Vizagapatam ivory-veneered boxes and furniture
rows.date_note: Museum examples: writing box ca. 1740 (Cooper Hewitt), casket ca. 1760-65 (Met). Watt (1903) says European-style floral designs had been used for 50-60 years and older items used pale green, blue and pink lac rather than black.
rows.identify_by: Boxes (writing slopes, work boxes, tea caddies, jewel caskets, chess boards, picture frames) and furniture of sandalwood or other wood veneered with ivory, tortoiseshell or buffalo and bison horn; the ivory engraved and filled with lac (sgraffito), or overlaid with pierced and carved ivory fretwork.
how_to_recognize: thin ivory veneer sheets pinned with ivory or silver pins over a wood carcass
engraved lines filled with black lac on white ivory (later work) or green, blue and pink lac (older work, per Watt)
European flowers (eyebright, convolvulus, rose) and scrolls; also Hindu mythological figures
tortoiseshell or horn veneer under a pierced ivory trellis
rows.marks_and_labels: None recorded; Watt names makers of 1903 (Ganugula Ramalingam, Lala Venkata Das, Golti Lakshmaya, Ganugula China Veerama). No source describes stamps or labels.
rows.later_production: Watt: three or four workshops employing about 60 people (1903); work for European buyers 'for many years past'. Bidie (quoted by Mukharji) says expensive but 'much in demand as drawing-room ornaments'.
rows.how_to_tell_old: Watt gives one clue: older pieces (palace chairs, Government House, Calcutta) are colored with pale green or blue and pink lac, more recent ones with black alone. He also says the European floral repertoire dates from the previous 50-60 years. No other test.

look_alikes.name: Mysore ivory inlay
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Mysore ivory is inlaid into solid wood; Vizagapatam ivory is a veneer or applique on boxes.

look_alikes.name: Bone veneer
look_alikes.how_to_tell: See bone row.

Tortoiseshell: marine turtle shell is covered by CITES; in the UK worked items made before 3 March 1947 need no commercial-use certificate, but whole or polished shells are not worked specimens (govuk_worked).

facts.text: Vizagapatam veneered sandalwood and other woods with tortoiseshell or bison and buffalo horn, overlaid with ivory fretwork and carved ivory.
facts.quote: chess-tables and men, dressing cases, work-boxes, tea-caddies, jewel-cases, glove-boxes, picture-frames, etc., have for many years past been extensively manufactured in sandal and other woods, veneered with tortoise-shell or bison and buffalo-horn (Watt). Mukharji: chiefly of sandal-wood, which are decorated with ivory fret-work, tortoise-shell, horn.

facts.text: Ivory surfaces were engraved and filled with colored lac, then scraped and polished.
facts.quote: By a process of what might be called sgraffito, lakh variously coloured is fused over the surface of the engraved ivory (Watt). Bidie (in Mukharji): adorned with etchings in black of mythological figures ... or with floral forms.

facts.text: Older Vizagapatam items used pale green or blue and pink lac; recent ones black alone.
facts.quote: The older samples ... are mostly ornamented by pale green or blue and pink lakh, not by black alone, as in the more recent goods.

facts.text: A state palanquin of Vizagapatam ebony and ivory with European flowers etched in black was given to the Prince of Wales (1875-76).
facts.quote: Although the details of the decoration are European, consisting of scrolls of convolvuluses and fuchsias, etched in black on the ivory

rows.name: Hoshiarpur ivory and bone inlay
rows.date_note: Long made for local use (chaukis, pen cases, walking sticks); extended to European tables, cabinets and boxes through C. Coldstream's efforts from about the 1870s-80s (Kipling via Mukharji; Watt).
rows.identify_by: Dark sheesham wood spotted all over with small pieces of ivory (or bone) and sometimes brass in minute floral, geometric and herring-bone patterns, made at Hoshiarpur and Jullundur and sold through Simla, Lahore and Amritsar dealers.
how_to_recognize: small even specks and sprigs of white inlay over most of the surface
sheesham ground, sometimes with blackwood (Diospyros, called abnus) strips
ivory from bangle and comb waste; bone and camel bone also used
herring-bone borders in ivory and black wood
rows.marks_and_labels: None recorded; makers named at Delhi 1903 (Jeyram Das and Karam Chand; Atma Ram and Ganga Ram).
rows.later_production: By 1903 'the shops of the Indian art-dealers have been flooded with tables, cabinets, etc., elaborately spotted all over with ivory or bone' (Watt). Prices 1888: table Rs 45, box Rs 25.
rows.how_to_tell_old: No dating test. Ellis: camel bone is hard to tell from ivory in inlay except by an expert, but bone 'quickly loses its gloss and brilliancy'.

look_alikes.name: Mysore ivory inlay
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Mysore uses larger engraved, lac-filled ivory pieces in more open designs on rosewood or ebony.

look_alikes.name: Bone-inlaid copies
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Watt: in low-class work 'bone takes the place of ivory in inlaying'.
