US: Asian elephants are Endangered and African Threatened under the ESA; interstate sale is generally barred except for ESA antiques (100+ years old, not repaired with ivory after 27 Dec 1973) and de minimis items, and several states add their own bans. Facts only, not legal advice; check current rules. Bone is not covered by ivory laws, but a seller must know which it is.

facts.text: Hoshiarpur inlaid ivory (or bone) and brass on sheesham; the trade in European furniture was inspired by Mr Coldstream; by 1903 art-dealers' shops were flooded with it.
facts.quote: recently the shops of the Indian art-dealers have been flooded with tables, cabinets, etc., elaborately spotted all over with ivory or bone (Watt). Kipling (in Mukharji): The extension of this trade to articles of European use is mainly due to the efforts of Mr. Coldstream.

facts.text: DISPUTED: Ellis (1900) says Hoshiarpur inlayers used some camel bone that only an specialist can detect; Kipling (quoted by Mukharji) says bone use is 'frequently alleged' but waste ivory was enough.
facts.quote: To some extent camel-bone is also used by the in-layers of Hoshiarpur, and except to the expert it is in inlaid work difficult to detect the difference (Ellis).

facts.text: Baden-Powell (1872) records boxes of dark sheesham inlaid with a flower pattern in ivory from the Punjab.
facts.quote: Boxes of dark shisham wood, inlaid with a flower pattern in ivory.

rows.name: Monghyr ebony boxes inlaid with ivory
rows.date_note: Recorded 1880-1903 as a long-standing trade; dates of origin unknown.
rows.identify_by: Black ebony work-boxes and small furniture from Monghyr (Bihar) inlaid with ivory or horn, formerly small stiff flower sprays, by 1903 rows of ivory discs on a punched and incised ebony ground.
how_to_recognize: black ebony carcass
ivory roundels in sets of three at intervals, ground incised and punched (later style, Watt)
earlier: minute stiff sprays of ivory flowers
geometric carved designs (Birdwood)
rows.marks_and_labels: None recorded.
rows.later_production: Small and shrinking by 1888 (six or eight carpenters); by 1903 cabinets, card tables and tea tables for quasi-European furnishing, cheap compared with other ebony work.
rows.how_to_tell_old: Watt describes a change of style about 1900 (flower sprays to roundels); no other test.

look_alikes.name: Nagina ebony
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Nagina carves floral relief with a punched ground; Monghyr inlays ivory.

facts.text: Monghyr was famed across Bengal for black ebony work-boxes inlaid with ivory, known to the trade as 'Monghyr boxes'.
facts.quote: For many years this town has been famed all over Bengal for turning out black ebony work-boxes, inlaid with ivory (Watt). Mukharji: Only in Monghyr ivory and horn are sometimes inlaid on furniture or small articles made of ebony wood.

facts.text: Ebony was carved at Monghyr in a conventional style like Bijnor (Nagina), latterly inlaid with ivory.
facts.quote: Ebony is excellently carved at Bijnur ... and in a similar conventional style at Monghyr in Bengal.

rows.name: Sadeli micro-mosaic ('Bombay boxes')
rows.date_note: Watt: came from Shiraz via Sindh 'perhaps 300 years or so ago'; doors at Amber (1630) are cited; a Met writing box in the technique is dated late 16th-early 17th century. Mass 'Bombay box' trade is 19th century.
rows.identify_by: Rods of tin wire, ebony, sandalwood, brazilwood, ivory (white and green-stained) and stag horn glued in bundles so that slices show tiny geometric 'blooms', laid as veneer ribbons on glove boxes, work boxes, desks and card cases.
how_to_recognize: veneer of minute repeating stars, hexagons and chevrons in cross-section
materials alternate white ivory or bone, black ebony, red-brown wood, silvery tin
ribbons framing panels of carved sandalwood or ebony
made at Surat, Bombay, Ahmedabad, Baroda, Kutch
rows.marks_and_labels: None recorded. Named pattern types (Birdwood, quoted by Mukharji): chakar-gul, katki-gul, tinkonia-gul and others.
rows.later_production: 'Ubiquitous' by 1880 (Birdwood): glove boxes, blotters, book stands, work boxes, desks and card cases; taught to Parsis after Hindus.
rows.how_to_tell_old: No dating test in the sources.

look_alikes.name: Kota horn marquetry
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Kota (Etawa) builds horn veneers inlaid with ivory and mother-of-pearl decorated with black lac (Watt).

look_alikes.name: European Tunbridge ware
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Not discussed in the sources (gap).

facts.text: Bombay boxes are a micro-mosaic of tin wire, sandalwood, ebony, sappan wood, ivory (white and green) and stag horn rods, introduced from Shiraz via Sindh.
facts.quote: In Bombay the inlay is made up of tin wire, sandal-wood, ebony, sappan [brazil] wood, ivory, white, and stained green, and stag horn (Birdwood). Watt: It would appear that the art came to India from Persia (Shiraz) through Sind, perhaps 300 years or so ago.

facts.text: Watt says sadeli was first taken up by Hindus, then taught to Parsis; 'Bombay boxes' came to include carved sandalwood boxes made in Gujarat.
facts.quote: The so-called Bombay boxes were apparently Sadeli boxes though the expression was early made to embrace carved wood or ivory boxes (Watt). Birdwood: the generic term Bombay boxes includes the sandalwood carving of Ahmedabad, Surat, and Bombay.

rows.name: Ceylon (Kandyan) ivory
rows.date_note: Museum examples date from the 16th century (caskets); Kandyan work continued to 1815 and after; Coomaraswamy (1908) describes surviving craftsmen.
rows.identify_by: Ivory combs (often double-sided, carved and fretted with figures and plants), statuettes of Kandyan characters and deities, caskets, door-jamb plaques, book covers and turned boxes and fan handles decorated with lac-filled incised circles.
how_to_recognize: double-sided combs with figure or plant panels
turned ivory boxes, fan handles and gaming pieces with incised dots and circles filled with colored lac
statuettes partly colored: dress details picked out in red and hair blackened
caskets with gilt silver mounts (Kandy)
rows.marks_and_labels: None recorded.
rows.later_production: Coomaraswamy (1908) says Kandyan craftsmen still made ivory figurines of drummers and chiefs; most craftsmen had turned to tourist brass trays. No figures gathered on 20th-century tourist ivory.
rows.how_to_tell_old: No dating test. Watt and Coomaraswamy both note how hard it is to separate Ceylon ivory from Travancore and Mysore work.

look_alikes.name: Travancore and Mysore ivory
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Watt: harder to separate Ceylon from Travancore and Mysore than these from Dravidian work.

look_alikes.name: Bone combs
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Coomaraswamy illustrates some combs that are bone, not ivory.

facts.text: Ceylon ivory is valued above African for density and tint, but supply was small because few Ceylon elephants have large tusks.
facts.quote: Ceylon ivory is valued in the East above African on account of its density of texture and delicacy of tint; but the quantity obtainable must always have been small.

facts.text: DISPUTED value: Watt (1903) says Ceylon ivory had for years been becoming shorter and less valuable than Indian.
facts.quote: For some unaccountable reason Ceylon ivory has been for years past becoming shorter and less valuable than the Indian.

facts.text: Sinhalese ivory combs are numerous and varied, carved and fretted, some made of bone; turned ivory is decorated with lac-filled dots and circles.
facts.quote: The number and variety of Sinhalese ivory combs is surprising ... No. 2, perhaps the most beautiful, is of bone

facts.text: Kandyan carvers made carved double-sided ivory combs and ivory caskets; dated museum examples run from the 16th to the 18th century.
facts.quote: The number and variety of Sinhalese ivory combs is surprising (Coomaraswamy). Met catalogue: Double-Sided Comb, Sri Lanka, 18th century, ivory (1984.182); Casket, Sri Lanka, second half 16th century (2024.482).

facts.text: Watt saw a 'Cingalese' cabinet lent by South Kensington that closely resembled modern Patiala ivory.
facts.quote: there is a cabinet described as 19th Century Cingalese work. This is exceedingly like much of the Patiala ivory of to-day.

rows.name: Burmese ivory carving (Moulmein)
rows.date_note: Recorded c.1901-03; Moulmein named as the main center with Pyinmana; Rangoon carving had moved to Moulmein.
rows.identify_by: Whole or half tusks carved with 20-30 Buddha figures and scenes under a pierced foliate trellis, sword (da) and knife handles, picture frames, chessmen and stands for silver bowls.
how_to_recognize: whole tusk carved with tiers of figures inside a lace-like trellis
bold undulating foliage and rosettes as on Burmese boat carving
figures in the conventional Burmese manner even on European forms (Pratt)
often on silver or wood stands
rows.marks_and_labels: None recorded; makers named: Maung Po Hla (Moulmein); Beato & Co. (Rangoon dealers).
rows.later_production: Made for European buyers and Buddhist patrons c.1900; Beato & Co. offered carved tusks at Rs 1,000 each in 1903.
rows.how_to_tell_old: No dating test in the sources.

look_alikes.name: Chinese pierced ivory
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Not discussed (gap).

rows.cautions: Ivory: India banned trade in imported ivory and articles made from it from 2 April 1992 (Wild Life (Protection) Amendment Act 1991, ss. 49B-49C), after protecting the Indian elephant in 1977; the Supreme Court upheld the ban in 2003. UK: since 6 June 2022 the Ivory Act 2018 bans dealing in elephant (and now hippo, killer whale, narwhal, sperm whale) ivory without a registered exemption, e.g. items made before 3 March 1947 with under 10% ivory, portrait miniatures made before 1918 up to 320 sq cm, or a certificate for pre-1918 items of outstandingly high value; owning, gifting and bequeathing are not banned. US: Asian elephants are Endangered and African Threatened under the ESA; interstate sale is generally barred except for ESA antiques (100+ years old, not repaired with ivory after 27 Dec 1973) and de minimis items, and several states add their own bans. Facts only, not legal advice; check current rules.

facts.text: Burmese ivory centers were Moulmein, Pyinmana and Rangoon; products: da and knife handles, frames, paper-cutters, bowl stands, chessmen, chairs, Buddha images, and whole carved tusks.
facts.quote: Whole tusks are carved with as many as 20 to 30 statues shown within a trellis-like covering of pierced ivory (Watt). Pratt: The chief articles made are handles for das, knives and forks, and paper knives.

facts.text: Even European-pattern articles kept the Burmese style.
facts.quote: Even where articles are made after European patterns, they are still executed in the conventional Burmese style.

rows.name: Bone and camel bone (ivory substitutes)
rows.date_note: Recorded as widespread c.1888-1903; modern production not covered by the sources.
rows.identify_by: Bone, often camel bone, cut, pierced and inlaid in the same forms as ivory: fretwork boxes, pen-box fittings, surmadanis, combs, and inlay on Hoshiarpur and Nagina woodwork.
how_to_recognize: Burns: elephant ivory is free of the pores and vessels found in bone and shows crossing curved lines on a transverse section; bone shows small dark pits or streaks (gap: modern ID guide not retrieved)
bone pieces are small and flat (no large solid blocks)
Ellis: camel bone quickly loses gloss and brilliancy; polishing restores it only for a time
rows.marks_and_labels: None.
rows.later_production: By 1900 the ordinary bazaar buyer was 'quite content' with bone (Stubbs); bone replaced ivory in cheap inlay (Watt). Peshawar camel-bone surmadanis were singled out as artistic.
rows.how_to_tell_old: No age test. Material test only (see how_to_recognize).

look_alikes.name: Ivory
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Burns: ivory 'free from vessels, or pores such as occur in bone' and takes a finer smoothness; the crossing curved lines on a cross-section are peculiar to elephant ivory.

look_alikes.name: Plastic and resin
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Not covered by the historical sources (gap).

rows.cautions: Bone is not covered by ivory trade bans, but buyers and sellers should establish which material an item is before sale; ivory sold as bone, or bone as ivory, both cause problems.

facts.text: Bone was extensively used as a substitute for ivory in inferior inlaying; Peshawar made artistic camel-bone surmadanis.
facts.quote: BONE is extensively used as a substitute for ivory in inferior inlaying, but in Peshawar surma-danis (antimony boxes) are artistically made from camel bone (Watt). Ellis: camel-bone ... is, however, more perishable and liable to decay, and quickly loses its gloss and brilliancy.

facts.text: In Cawnpore and Lucknow bazaars small fretwork articles were usually bone; ivory was used only to order, chiefly for European residents.
facts.quote: The ordinary purchaser is quite content with his articles if they are made of bone, and in Cawnpore ... the only customers for ivory work are the European residents.

facts.text: Ivory differs from bone in lacking pores and vessels and in the crossing curved lines of the tusk section.
facts.quote: free from vessels, or pores such as occur in bone; and although containing a large proportion of lime, it has none of the harsh, meagre character of bone

rows.name: 'Fish tooth' (walrus, mammoth or hippo ivory) hilts
rows.date_note: Watt (1903) believed the trade had existed for centuries, judging from old weapons in princely armouries.
rows.identify_by: Sword and dagger hilts of a dirty oily-yellow ivory with a patchy crystalline texture, called 'fish tooth' in every Indian language and more prized than elephant ivory for hafts.
how_to_recognize: dirty, oily yellow color
texture 'as if crystallized into patches' (Watt)
used mainly for sword and dagger hilts
sometimes inlaid with ivory pegs (Ceylon)
rows.marks_and_labels: None.
rows.later_production: Not described.
rows.how_to_tell_old: No test.

look_alikes.name: Elephant ivory
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Watt: elephant ivory is whiter and evenly textured; 'fish tooth' is oily yellow with crystalline patches.

rows.cautions: Walrus ivory is outside the UK Ivory Act species list but may need other permits (govuk_ivory); in the US walrus is protected by the Marine Mammal Protection Act with exemptions for pre-1972 items (usfws_ivory factsheet). Hippo ivory is now covered by the UK Ivory Act.

facts.text: 'Fish tooth' was a cured ivory substitute more valued than ivory for sword and dagger hafts; Watt identified it as mainly Siberian mammoth ivory, perhaps with hippo and walrus.
facts.quote: So far as the writer has been able to discover, the fish tooth of Indian trade is mainly, if not entirely, the so-called fossil ivory of Siberia

facts.text: In Ceylon a fibrous hilt material called 'unicorn horn' is probably the same as Watt's 'fish tooth'.
facts.quote: A peculiar fibrous material sometimes used, and called unicorn horn ... is probably identical with the so-called fish-tooth

rows.name: Buffalo and bison horn carving
rows.date_note: Ratnagiri bison-horn work was said c.1897 to be four or five generations old.
rows.identify_by: Combs, cups, boxes, buttons, stick and knife handles and figures of buffalo or bison horn (cow horn avoided for religious reasons), softened by heat and molded, engraved, stained jet black, or inlaid with ivory and metal.
how_to_recognize: translucent amber to black horn, thin sections glow when held to light
molded trays and boxes, engraved line ornament (Ratnagiri)
jointed horn insects and animals stained like jet (Madura)
Mysore horn inlaid with ivory and copper
Kota: horn veneer pieces inlaid with ivory and mother-of-pearl
rows.marks_and_labels: None recorded; Ratnagiri makers named (Vithal Gangaram Wadaya; Gopat Shiveram Wadaya; Bhikkoo Vishram Wadaya).
rows.later_production: A trade in combs, buttons and handles c.1900; foreign horn combs undercut ivory combs (Burns). Sambhal Horn Craft (Uttar Pradesh) was registered as an Indian GI in 2023-24 (application 674).
rows.how_to_tell_old: No dating test in the sources.

look_alikes.name: Tortoiseshell
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Not discussed (gap); horn lacks the mottled blond-and-brown pattern of hawksbill shell.

look_alikes.name: Rhinoceros horn
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Watt: rhino-horn cups were prized by Hindus but scarce. Rhino horn is strictly controlled (govuk_worked: contact APHA before selling any rhino specimen).

rows.cautions: Rhinoceros horn cups or carvings are strictly regulated; UK guidance says to contact APHA's CITES team before selling any rhino specimen (govuk_worked).

facts.text: Buffalo and bison horn were used because of religious objections to cow horn; buffalo horn is the most used, mostly as veneer, but also for combs, cups, handles and toys.
facts.quote: The chief forms of horn used in the Indian Art Industries are buffalo and bison, since there are religious objections to the use of cow-horn (Watt). Birdwood: Bison horn is carved into figures and otherwise wrought at Ratnagiri, Sawuntwadi, and elsewhere.

facts.text: Ratnagiri horn was softened with coconut oil before a fire, molded, turned and engraved; the commonest item was a Nandi bull carrying a tray under a cobra.
facts.quote: A portion of horn is kept moist with cocoanut-oil and heated before a fire until it becomes almost as soft as wax (Aitken, quoted by Watt).

facts.text: Kandyan horn combs were cut from buffalo horn transversely; turned horn boxes carried lac-filled circles like ivory.
facts.quote: The combs are made of buffalo horn cut transversely, the tops of the horns being used for tool- and knife-handles and the like.

facts.text: Sambhal Horn Craft is a registered Indian GI (application 674, 2023-24).

rows.name: Mysore and Kanara sandalwood carving (Gudigar work)
rows.date_note: Described as stagnant 'for the last century' in 1903 (Thurston/D'Cruz); Birdwood (1880) cites an 1871 exhibition cabinet. Earlier dating not documented.
rows.identify_by: Boxes, caskets, cabinets, card cases, frames and figures of sandalwood carved by the Gudigar caste of Sorab and Sagar (Shimoga) and North Kanara in deep relief and undercutting, the whole surface covered with interlaced foliage around medallions of Hindu deities, with animals and birds.
how_to_recognize: entire surface carved; no plain ground
pinnate foliage in fan-like sprays with rolled tips; deities in canopied panels (Watt)
recurring elephant-headed creature with foliated tail and goose carrying a flower spray
fragrant pale brown wood; best is dark heartwood
joinery and fittings poor: glued blocks, plain bazaar drawer knobs (Watt; Thurston)
rows.marks_and_labels: None recorded; makers named at Delhi 1903 (Shapur Subbrayappa, Sagar Dudda Puttappa, Banarsi Subhana of Sorab, Jade Gopalappa of Sorab).
rows.later_production: By 1903 card cases, pencil cases, watch stands, frames, album covers, inkstands and paper-cutters were made for Europeans; caskets Rs 250-600; best work on commission for presentation and exhibitions. About 35 carvers in Mysore in 1903.
rows.how_to_tell_old: No dating test in the sources. Glued joints that 'give way' are a known fault of new work, not a sign of age (Watt).

look_alikes.name: Gujarat and Bombay sandalwood
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Birdwood and Watt: Surat and Bombay work is low relief, mostly foliage; Mysore and Kanara work is high relief with mythological subjects.

look_alikes.name: Canton (Chinese) sandalwood
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Rice (quoted by Thurston) thought Sorab carving superior to Bombay or Canton; no visual test given.

rows.cautions: Sandalwood is a protected commercial timber in India; sources gathered say nothing about rules for old carved items (gap).

facts.text: Sandalwood carving was confined to Gudigar families of Sorab and Sagar (Shimoga) and relatives in North Kanara; about 35 artisans in 1903.
facts.quote: The art of sandal-wood carving is confined to a few families, belonging to the Gudigar caste, in the Sorab and Sagar taluks of the Shimoga district (Thurston/D'Cruz). Watt: not more than eight families with 35 artizans in all.

facts.text: Articles for Europeans included card cases, watch stands, frames, album covers, inkstands, paper-cutters and walking sticks; for the native market combs, toys, images and shrines.
facts.quote: The articles turned out for Europeans are card-cases, pencil-cases, watch-stands, mirror and photograph frames, album covers, ink-stands, paper-cutters

facts.text: Joinery and fittings were poor in fine sandalwood work.
facts.quote: the joinery is unsatisfactory and the fittings worthless (Watt). Thurston/D'Cruz: The only flaw ... is their inferior and clumsy joining work.

facts.text: Canara and Mysore sandalwood is high relief with mythological subjects; Surat and Bombay work low relief and mostly foliage.
facts.quote: The Surat and Bombay work is in low relief, and the designs consist almost entirely of foliated ornament; the Canara and Mysore work is in high relief, the subjects being chiefly mythological (Birdwood).

rows.name: Surat, Ahmedabad and Bombay sandalwood carving
rows.date_note: Recorded 1880-1903; earlier dating not documented.
rows.identify_by: Sandalwood glove boxes, work boxes, shawl boxes, frames, cabinets and book covers carved in low but deep-cut relief with large-leaved foliage, temples and figures in a Jain-influenced style, often framed with sadeli bands.
how_to_recognize: foliage large and bold with upturned tips and serrate edges (Watt)
Ahmedabad: Krishna and gopis in a wood above a river band with fish, tortoises and water-fowl (Birdwood)
houses and figures 'jumbled together' without perspective (Watt)
often combined with sadeli micro-mosaic borders
rows.marks_and_labels: None recorded; makers named (Jamsetji Nasarwanji Petigara, Surat; Parbhudas Rughnath Petigara, Ahmedabad; Harkison Parshotam).
rows.later_production: A trade in glove boxes and similar articles for Europeans by 1880 under the 'Bombay box' name; Mukharji cites some 800 Parsi sandalwood carvers and inlayers.
rows.how_to_tell_old: No dating test in the sources.

look_alikes.name: Mysore sandalwood
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Mysore is high relief with deities in canopied panels.

facts.text: Bombay, Surat and Ahmedabad sandalwood shows a Jain tendency, bold freely cut foliage with upturned leaf tips, and temples and figures without perspective.
facts.quote: In the Bombay, Surat and Ahmedabad work ... there may be traced a strongly Jaina tendency.

facts.text: Gujarat and Bombay sandalwood carving is low relief dominated by foliage, unlike the high-relief mythological Mysore and Kanara work.
facts.quote: The Surat and Bombay work is in low relief, and the designs consist almost entirely of foliated ornament (Birdwood). Watt: The foliage is large, bold, deeply and freely cut, with the individual leaves having upturned tips.

facts.text: Birdwood says 'Bombay boxes' includes the sandalwood carving of Ahmedabad, Surat and Bombay as well as inlaid wood.
facts.quote: the generic term Bombay boxes includes the sandalwood carving of Ahmedabad, Surat, and Bombay, as well as inlaid wood

rows.name: South Indian rosewood (blackwood) carving
rows.date_note: Madras School of Arts wood-carving class from 1877 (Thurston); Bombay and Ahmedabad blackwood carving recorded by Birdwood 1880. Furniture is covered by the furniture topic.
rows.identify_by: Deep-cut carving in dark Indian rosewood ('blackwood', Dalbergia latifolia) and teak with Dravidian temple ornament (yalis, pillars, deities), often framing copper repousse panels, made at the Madras School of Arts and in Madura and Travancore.
how_to_recognize: dark purple-brown to black heavy wood that takes deep undercutting
Dravidian architectural motifs: yali brackets, temple pillar orders, deities in niches
copper repousse panels set in blackwood frames (Madras School of Arts)
European furniture forms with Dravidian ornament
rows.marks_and_labels: None recorded; foremen named (Meenakshi Asari of Ramnad; R. Kalimuthu Asari).
rows.later_production: From 1877 the Madras School of Arts carved European furniture with Dravidian ornament; demand among Europeans exceeded supply (Thurston).
rows.how_to_tell_old: No dating test in the sources.

look_alikes.name: Ebony
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Ebony is jet black and very hard; blackwood shows purple-brown grain.

look_alikes.name: Burmese teak carving
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Burmese work is pale teak with figure-crowded deep relief (Tilly; Maffey).

rows.features_other: Rosewood and blackwood are the same tree in these sources (Dalbergia latifolia). Some Dalbergia species are CITES-listed; sources gathered do not address old items (gap).

facts.text: The Madras School of Arts carved chiefly teak and blackwood ('rosewood', Dalbergia latifolia), especially the latter, for European furniture with Dravidian details, often framing copper repousse panels.
facts.quote: the great bulk of the work done in the school has been in teakwood, and blackwood or rosewood (Dalbergia latifolia), more particularly the latter. Copper repousse panels in blackwood frames are an exceedingly effective combination

facts.text: Watt lists Madras red-wood 'sometimes called black-wood' among the main ornamental woods and notes deep undercutting possible in teak, red-wood and walnut; Birdwood records blackwood carving at Bombay, Ahmedabad and Dholera.
facts.quote: the deep under-cutting and sculpture that is possible with teak, red-wood and walnut (Watt). Birdwood: The blackwood carving of Bombay, Ahmedabad, and Dholera, has already been mentioned.

rows.name: Saharanpur wood carving
rows.date_note: Shisham doors and frames are older; the dudhi vine-pattern trade and machine fretwork in tun date from the later 19th century ('in the last generation', Maffey 1903).
rows.identify_by: Three strands: carved shisham doors and frames (Hindu mistris); white dudhi wood plates, frames and caskets in vine-leaf pattern (largely gone by 1903); and machine-fretted tun (Indian cedar, 'cigar-box wood') brackets, trays, octagonal folding tables and screens exported to Europe and America by the thousand, sometimes with brass inlay.
how_to_recognize: fretted jali panels with perfect machine symmetry, touched up by chisel (Maffey)
soft reddish tun wood with a dull red polish, or dark shisham
shallow punched leaf pattern on the unfretted strips
octagonal folding tables and wall brackets
brass wire or sheet inlay on tun (Saharanpur 'tun carving and brass inlay')
rows.marks_and_labels: None recorded.
rows.later_production: By 1903 the machine-fretted tun trade dominated, exported 'by the thousand' and sold at railway stations; dudhi carving was 'practically extinct'. Saharanpur Wood Craft was registered as an Indian GI in 2013-14 (application 184), so the trade continues.
rows.how_to_tell_old: No dating test. Maffey: machine fretsaw cutting (five or six panels at once) was in use by 1903, so machine-cut fretwork alone does not prove modern date.

look_alikes.name: Kashmir walnut carving
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Kashmir carving is deep undercut naturalistic leaves in walnut, not fretwork in tun.

look_alikes.name: Simla and Hoshiarpur fretwork
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Watt: Simla and Punjab low-class work also uses the fretsaw and cheaper woods.

facts.text: Saharanpur's best-known products by 1903 were cheap fretted tun articles for tourists; the industry was modern and sprang up 'in the last generation'.
facts.quote: the cheap articles of fretted tun-wood, such as are sold on railway-station platforms ... the industry is quite modern, having sprung up in the last generation (Maffey). Watt: cut by the machine fret-saw and exported to Europe and America by the thousand.

facts.text: Fretwork panels were sawn by machine several at a time, then touched up with a chisel to hide the machine finish.
facts.quote: one passage of the machine fret-saw is actually doing five or six panels of jali work at once.

facts.text: Saharanpur dudhi (white wood) carving in vine pattern was formerly extensive, sold in large quantities to European tourists in the 1880s, and nearly extinct by 1903 because dudhi discolors.
facts.quote: They have of late attracted European attention and are sold in large quantities to European tourists. A soft white wood called Dudhi ... is used (Mukharji). Maffey: have now lost favour owing to their tendency to rapid discoloration.

facts.text: Saharanpur Wood Craft is a registered Indian GI (application 184, 2013-14).

rows.name: Nagina ebony carving
rows.date_note: Local ebony work on gunstocks and charpai legs is older; European demand began about 1873 when the Collector of Bijnor ordered picture frames (Maffey 1903, 'about thirty years ago').
rows.identify_by: Small black 'ebony' (actually Diospyros tomentosa heartwood from Central India) pen boxes, caskets, trays, frames, book covers and walking sticks carved in crisp shallow floral relief on a ground punched with tiny circles; sometimes inlaid with ivory, silver or mother-of-pearl.
how_to_recognize: dense black wood, carving never deep, no undercutting (Maffey)
Muhammadan floral and geometric diaper; dog-tooth borders
background punched in minute circles (Watt)
frames used for Delhi ivory miniatures
rows.marks_and_labels: None recorded; makers named (Abdulla, Moula Buksh, Murad Buksh).
rows.later_production: Steady European demand from the 1870s; prices 1888: table Rs 90, box Rs 16, paper-knife 12 annas; by 1903 cheaper machine-fretted goods were sold at railway stations alongside hand work.
rows.how_to_tell_old: No dating test in the sources.

look_alikes.name: Monghyr ebony
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Monghyr inlays ivory into ebony; Nagina carves relief.

look_alikes.name: Ebonized wood
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Not covered by the sources (gap).

rows.cautions: Ivory-inlaid items fall under ivory rules (see ivory rows).

facts.text: Nagina 'ebony' (abnus) is Diospyros tomentosa heartwood imported from Central India; carving is shallow because the wood is hard.
facts.quote: their so-called ebony (abnus): the latter (Diospyros tomentosa) is a black and heavy heart-wood imported from Central India (Maffey). Kipling (in Mukharji): the old heart-wood of the Kinum (Diospyros tomentosa), incorrectly called abnus or ebony.

facts.text: Nagina carving is crisp surface floral work with a background punched in minute circles; it occurs nowhere else.
facts.quote: The effect of the carving is enhanced by the clever way the background is punched in minute circles (Watt). Birdwood: Ebony is excellently carved at Bijnur.

facts.text: European demand began when the Collector of Bijnor ordered carved picture frames about thirty years before 1903.
facts.quote: Not until about thirty years ago did the industry attract European attention.

rows.name: Kashmir walnut carving
rows.date_note: Older Kashmir woodwork was pine/deodar lattice (pinjra) and khatamband ceilings. Realistic deep-undercut walnut carving began 'some 8 or 10 years' before 1903 at European suggestion (Watt); in 1888 walnut chairs were only occasionally made to order (Mukharji).
rows.identify_by: Walnut boxes, small tables, screens, trays and frames carved in deep undercut naturalistic relief with chinar (plane) leaves, lotus and water lilies, grapes and dragons, made in Srinagar for European buyers.
how_to_recognize: deep undercutting, foliage standing free of the ground
naturalistic chinar leaves, lotus and water lilies, vine
dark brown walnut, often dull from undercutting (Watt)
folding or pedestal tables, boxes, screens
rows.marks_and_labels: None recorded; Srinagar carvers and dealers named in 1903 (Jubbar Khan, Habib Joo, Lussoo, Subhana, Khizra).
rows.later_production: Bought 'with avidity' at Delhi 1903 (small tables Rs 20-100); a continuing tourist and export trade through the 20th century; Kashmir Walnut Wood Carving was registered as an Indian GI in 2011-12 (application 182).
rows.how_to_tell_old: Sources support only an earliest date: no deep-cut naturalistic walnut carving before about the 1890s (Watt; Mukharji). They give no test to separate early from later 20th-century work.

look_alikes.name: Mango wood stained to look like walnut
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Mukharji: at Agra inferior frames were mango wood 'often painted to make it look like walnut wood'.

look_alikes.name: Saharanpur fretwork
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Fretted tun or shisham, not undercut walnut.

look_alikes.name: Simla walnut furniture
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Baden-Powell (1872) and Kipling record Simla carpenters carving walnut and kakkar (Pistacia) to supplied European patterns.

facts.text: Kashmir's realistic walnut carving was recent in 1903 and originated from a European suggestion 8-10 years earlier; Watt disliked its undercutting.
facts.quote: The wood-work of Kashmir to-day seems to have originated by a European suggestion, given some 8 or 10 years ago.

facts.text: In 1888 carved walnut chairs were only occasionally made in Kashmir to order for Europeans and the industry was a possibility rather than a trade.
facts.quote: In Kashmir carved walnut chairs are occasionally made to order for Europeans, which are finished in the plains or in England.

facts.text: Deep-carved walnut for European buyers was a new Kashmir trade at the end of the 19th century: rare in 1888, eagerly bought by 1903.
facts.quote: In Kashmir carved walnut chairs are occasionally made to order for Europeans (Mukharji 1888). Watt: the avidity with which every bit of this modern Kashmir work was purchased.

facts.text: Kashmir Walnut Wood Carving is a registered Indian GI (application 182, 2011-12).

rows.name: Burmese teak carving
rows.date_note: Architectural tradition is old; portable items for Europeans recorded c.1900-03. Burmese prisoners also carved teak in Indian central jails (Maffey 1903).
rows.identify_by: Pale teak carved in very deep, crowded relief and openwork with figures (nats, Buddhist and courtly scenes), flame-like foliage, peacocks and dragons: screens, panels, gong stands, figures, overmantels, tables.
how_to_recognize: teak, often left pale and unpolished (Maffey) or gilded and lacquered
figures carved in high relief, sometimes cut from the same block (Tilly)
exuberant layered undercutting ('the marvellous', Watt)
forms: gong stands, rudder chairs, screens, panels, half-life-size figures
rows.marks_and_labels: None recorded; carvers named (Maung Po Thit, Maung Po Nyun, Saya Khin of Amarapura); dealers Beato & Co., Rangoon.
rows.later_production: Watt (1903) complains of 'putrid adaptations' made for the European market; prices c.1903: panel 15 in. Rs 25, figure 3.5 ft Rs 65, screens Rs 600-2,000.
rows.how_to_tell_old: No dating test in the sources.

look_alikes.name: Indian jail-made Burmese-style carving
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Maffey: Burmese prisoners in Indian central jails worked in teak in their own style; identifiable by pale unpolished teak but otherwise the same.

look_alikes.name: Chinese carved camphor or teak
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Not covered (gap).

facts.text: Burmese wood-carving is mainly teak and was applied chiefly to building exteriors, so it is bold and solid.
facts.quote: The main characteristics of Burmese wood-carving have been decided by the fact that it has been chiefly applied to the adornment of the exteriors of buildings and that teak is almost invariably used (Tilly). Watt: The marvellous is a distinct feature of both the wood and the ivory-carving of Burma.

facts.text: Watt organized the Delhi 1903 Burmese series to show original work 'rather than in the frequently putrid adaptations of it that are prepared for the European market'.
facts.quote: rather than in the frequently putrid adaptations of it that are prepared for the European market

facts.text: Burmese prisoners carved teak in the central jails of the United Provinces; their work is recognized by pale unpolished teak and Burmese style.
facts.quote: Teak or sagon (Tectona grandis) is used in the central jails by Burmese prisoners, and their work is as readily identified by the pale unpolished nature of the wood

rows.name: Ceylon low-country calamander and ebony boxes
rows.date_note: Dutch-influenced forms (bible-boxes) in calamander and ebony and ivory-inlaid work-boxes formerly made at Matara (Coomaraswamy 1908). Dates not fixed by the sources.
rows.identify_by: Boxes in European (Dutch) forms made in the Ceylon low country of calamander (striped Diospyros) or ebony, with scalloping and fluting, or work-boxes with compartments inlaid with ivory scrolls (Matara).
how_to_recognize: calamander: fawn ground with dark brown to black waves and blotches (Tennent)
ebony: even intense black (Tennent)
Dutch box forms; ivory plates with scroll and floral ornament in fittings
rows.marks_and_labels: None recorded.
rows.later_production: Calamander was 'nearly eradicated' by 1860 through overcutting (Tennent), so later pieces are rarer or use substitutes; no source on 20th-century tourist ebony carving (elephants), which is a gap.
rows.how_to_tell_old: No dating test in the sources.

look_alikes.name: Indian rosewood
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Tennent: calamander 'resembles rose-wood, but surpasses it both in beauty and durability'.

look_alikes.name: Vizagapatam boxes
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Vizagapatam veneers ivory over sandalwood; Ceylon low-country boxes are solid calamander or ebony with inset ivory.

rows.cautions: Ivory: India banned trade in imported ivory and articles made from it from 2 April 1992 (Wild Life (Protection) Amendment Act 1991, ss. 49B-49C), after protecting the Indian elephant in 1977; the Supreme Court upheld the ban in 2003. UK: since 6 June 2022 the Ivory Act 2018 bans dealing in elephant (and now hippo, killer whale, narwhal, sperm whale) ivory without a registered exemption, e.g. items made before 3 March 1947 with under 10% ivory, portrait miniatures made before 1918 up to 320 sq cm, or a certificate for pre-1918 items of outstandingly high value; owning, gifting and bequeathing are not banned. US: Asian elephants are Endangered and African Threatened under the ESA; interstate sale is generally barred except for ESA antiques (100+ years old, not repaired with ivory after 27 Dec 1973) and de minimis items, and several states add their own bans. Facts only, not legal advice; check current rules.

facts.text: Low-country Ceylon made Dutch-form 'bible-boxes' in calamander or ebony and ivory-inlaid work-boxes at Matara.
facts.quote: A type of box commonly met with in the low-country is the bible-box, an evident copy of a Dutch form, usually made in calamander or ebony

facts.text: Ceylon ebony (Diospyros ebenum) is exceptionally even and black; calamander, the most esteemed cabinet wood, was nearly eradicated by 1860.
facts.quote: Notwithstanding its value, however, the tree is nearly eradicated, and runs considerable risk of becoming extinct in the island (Tennent). Coomaraswamy: calamander now almost extinct as a result of the increased demand.

rows.name: Jadau (gem-set gold jewelry)
rows.date_note: Museum examples catalogued 18th century (Cleveland 1966.516, Met 15.95.54); the craft is older but its start date was not established from the sources read. Still made.
rows.identify_by: Gold jewelry in which stones are set by the kundan method (pure gold pressed round each stone), often with an enamelled back; 'jadau' or 'jarao' means 'set with stones'.
how_to_recognize: Stones held by a burnished rim of soft yellow gold rather than claws or prongs.
Stones (often flat-cut diamonds, rubies, emeralds, or glass) usually sit on foil, so the back of each stone is not visible.
The reverse is often enamelled (see meenakari) unless the stones are set 'clear'.
Made by a chain of specialists: goldsmith, chaser, enameller (minakar), stone setter (kundansaz or murassiakar).
rows.marks_and_labels: Traditional jadau is not normally marked; it is exempt from India's mandatory hallmarking (see heirloomapp.io/marks/indian-hallmarks/). A jeweler's name may appear on a modern box or certificate, not on the piece.
rows.later_production: Made continuously; 1903 Delhi Exhibition shows Jaipur firms (Sughan Chand Sobhag Chand) producing large stocks of modern gem-set and enamelled jewelry. A geographical-indication application for 'Kundan Meena Jewellery' (Jaipur) was filed 13 Dec 2022 and is under examination.
rows.how_to_tell_old: Sources give no reliable test of age for jadau. Watt (1903) dates a change in Jaipur enamel backs (loss of a plain field color in recent decades), which bears on the enamel only.

look_alikes.name: Imitation kundan (glass and foil in base metal)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Base-metal or plated frame, light weight; see the imitation_kundan row. Note that glass and foil also occur in genuine gold pieces.

look_alikes.name: Silver-gilt gem-set jewelry
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Cleveland catalogues several 19th-century Delhi pendants and armlets as gilt silver with gems and enamel; a gold color alone does not show gold.

rows.features_other: Pearls are common (token wanted: pearl).

facts.text: Baden-Powell (1872) describes the division of labor: the goldsmith makes the form, the enameller (minakar) enamels the back, and the murassiakar or kundansaz sets the stones on lac with foil made by the bindligar; Hendley (1909) repeats this account.
facts.quote: If jewels are to be set, the enamelling at the back is done by a 'minakar,' and then the stone is set into the places prepared by the goldsmith, &c. by the 'murassiakar' or 'kundansaz,'

facts.text: Mukharji (1888) gives the same sequence: after the goldsmith, the article is enamelled on the back and then goes to the setter of jewels; he names Delhi as the headquarters of stone setting.
facts.quote: After the goldsmith has finished his work the article goes to the enameller to be enamelled on the back, and then it comes to the setter of jewels.

facts.text: Gem-set jewelry and gold were also made in silver-gilt: Cleveland catalogues 19th-century Delhi pendants (1916.280) and armlets (1916.274, 1916.286) as gilt silver with stones and enamel.
facts.quote: Gilt silver with diamonds, emeralds, rubies, pearls, and enamel

facts.text: Maclagan's Punjab returns list jewel-sellers under local names including murassa saz, kundan and jarya.
facts.quote: There are also 90 jewel-sellers (... murassa saz ; kundan ... ; jarya), all in towns.

facts.text: Kundan, polki and jadau jewelry are exempt from India's mandatory gold hallmarking: S.O. 2481(E) of 23 June 2021 added 'special categories of jewelry, namely Kundan, Polki and Jadaau' to the exemptions; the World Gold Council lists the same exemption.
facts.quote: special categories of jewellery, namely Kundan, Polki and Jadaau;

facts.text: A GI application 'Kundan Meena Jewellery' by a Jaipur jewelers' artisans' association was filed 13 Dec 2022 and shows status 'Examination'.
facts.quote: Kundan Meena Jewellery Status Examination ... Jaipur, Rajasthan ... Date of Filing 13-12-2022

rows.name: Kundan setting
rows.date_note: Described in detail 1872-1905; museum items catalogued 18th century. Still practised.
rows.identify_by: Each stone is fixed by pressing strips of very pure gold foil (kundan) around its edge until they consolidate into a burnished rim; the stone sits on lac and a foil.
how_to_recognize: A smooth, slightly irregular rim of bright, soft gold around every stone; no claws.
Stones usually foiled from behind; Baden-Powell notes the back of a stone may be colored, but not the foil.
Lac fills the setting cup behind the foil.
rows.marks_and_labels: None traditionally. Exempt from mandatory hallmarking (see heirloomapp.io/marks/indian-hallmarks/).
rows.later_production: Continuous; also widely imitated in base metal with glass (see imitation_kundan).
rows.how_to_tell_old: No reliable test of age is given in the sources read.

look_alikes.name: Bezel or rub-over setting (European)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: A rim raised from the cup itself and pushed over the stone; Baden-Powell calls this the European way and contrasts it with the added kundan rim.

look_alikes.name: Imitation kundan
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Glass in a plated or base-metal frame, glued rather than set in gold foil; see imitation_kundan.

rows.features_other: Kundan is also the name of the purest grade of gold used for the foil (Charles 1905).
rows.cautions: Old reports say a setter could replace gold pared away with lac, so weight is not a guide to gold content.

facts.text: Kundan is the name of the purest, very highly refined gold, beaten out like gold leaf and used for setting stones; it gave its name to the technique.
facts.quote: The purest form of gold is kundan; it is very highly refined and of a beautiful, rich colour, and is commonly beaten out like gold leaf.

facts.text: The setter puts lac in the hollow, presses in a foil (dank) from the bindligar, places the stone, and then presses thin gold foil all round its edge until a rim forms and is burnished.
facts.quote: The esteemed method however is to put a 'kundan' on: that is, to press with a probe or silai thin gold foil all round the edge of the gem till a rim is formed

facts.text: Stones are sometimes set 'clear' but more usually with a foil behind; the back of the stone may be colored to deepen it.
facts.quote: They sometimes set jewels 'clear,' but more usually with a foil behind, and sometimes they color the back of the stone to deepen it, but they never color the foil itself.

facts.text: Claw settings were made only by workmen who had learned European jewelry making.
facts.quote: The art of fixing gems by little claws is only done by those who have learned the way of making European jewellery.

facts.text: Hoey (1880, quoted by Charles 1905) reports that the setter may keep part of the kundan gold issued to him and sometimes puts lac in place of metal he has pared away.
facts.quote: he also sometimes puts in lac in place of metal which he has pared away from the fitting

facts.text: Unless stones are set clear, the finer items are enamelled on the back.
facts.quote: Unless the stones are clear set, all the finer specimens are beautifully enamelled on the back.

facts.text: Kundan, polki and jadau jewelry are exempt from India's mandatory gold hallmarking: S.O. 2481(E) of 23 June 2021 added 'special categories of jewelry, namely Kundan, Polki and Jadaau' to the exemptions; the World Gold Council lists the same exemption.
facts.quote: special categories of jewellery, namely Kundan, Polki and Jadaau;

rows.name: Polki (flat, uncut or lightly cut diamonds)
rows.date_note: 19th-century sources describe flat 'lasque' and table diamonds in Indian jewelry; the trade word 'polki' was not found in the period sources read.
rows.identify_by: Diamonds left flat or only slightly polished, with a large flat top and little depth, set in kundan with a foil behind.
how_to_recognize: Thin, flat diamonds with irregular outlines (triangular or free-form), sometimes mere scales.
Foil backing gives the depth and reflection the thin stone lacks.
Set in kundan; the back is usually closed and enamelled.
rows.marks_and_labels: None on the piece; exempt from hallmarking. Laboratory reports may accompany modern pieces.
rows.later_production: Very large modern production. A Jaipur laboratory reported glass-filled CVD synthetic diamonds cut as polkis in 2019.
rows.how_to_tell_old: No age test in the sources read. Gemological testing is needed to tell natural, filled and synthetic polkis apart.

look_alikes.name: Glass or rock crystal in kundan
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Herklots (1832) already mentions crystals and foils in gold ornaments; only testing tells stone from glass when foiled.

look_alikes.name: Glass-filled or synthetic (CVD) polki
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Square, tabular outlines are a warning sign; natural polkis are usually triangular or irregular. Laboratory testing (color flashes in fissures, spectroscopy) is needed.

look_alikes.name: Rose-cut diamonds
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Faceted dome on a flat base; GIA describes polki as a simple, ancient relative of the rose cut.

rows.cautions: Polki-cut stones may be glass-filled or synthetic (Choudhary 2019); only laboratory testing settles it.

facts.text: Indian jewelers used very thin flat diamonds: Hendley calls them 'mere scales or lasques', Birdwood defines a lasque as a flat shallow parallelogram, and notes the Indian fondness for table and point diamonds.
facts.quote: A flat shallow parallelogram is called a lasque

facts.text: Birdwood observed that Indian jewelers valued effect over the commercial quality of gems, using 'mere splinters and scales of diamonds'.
facts.quote: the flawed 'tallow drop' emeralds, and foul spinel rubies, large as walnuts, and mere splinters and scales of diamonds, which he so lavishly uses

facts.text: GIA describes polki as flat uncut diamonds, or diamonds cut to look flat, set kundan-style with 24K gold foil, the foil acting as the stone's pavilion.
facts.quote: flat uncut diamonds, or diamonds cut to look flat, set in the Kundan style with 24K gold foil

facts.text: In 2019 the GJEPC Gem Testing Laboratory, Jaipur, reported three glass-filled polki-cut CVD synthetic diamonds submitted as natural; square tabular shapes typical of CVD growth were a clue, natural polkis being usually triangular or irregular.
facts.quote: This was the first time we had encountered glass-filled CVD synthetic diamond polkis

facts.text: Kundan, polki and jadau jewelry are exempt from India's mandatory gold hallmarking: S.O. 2481(E) of 23 June 2021 added 'special categories of jewelry, namely Kundan, Polki and Jadaau' to the exemptions; the World Gold Council lists the same exemption.
facts.quote: special categories of jewellery, namely Kundan, Polki and Jadaau;

rows.name: Meenakari (enamel) on jewelry
rows.date_note: Jaipur items catalogued 18th century (Cleveland 1966.515); Watt (1903) calls Jaipur the oldest school. Banaras pink (gulabi) meenakari GI certificate 23 Mar 2015.
rows.identify_by: Translucent or opaque colored glass fused into engraved hollows on gold (Jaipur, Delhi, Benares) or silver (Multan, Lucknow, Kashmir); on jadau it usually covers the back.
how_to_recognize: Jaipur: done on high-carat gold; the plate is engraved so only fine gold lines separate the colors; hatched floors give play of light under translucent red, green and blue.
Reverse of a stone-set piece enamelled with flowers, birds or animals.
Benares: enamel used as large patches of color in imitation of jewels or as a ground for set stones.
Multan: die-struck silver in two or three shades of opaque blue.
rows.marks_and_labels: Not marked traditionally. Some Nathdwara devotional pendants carry 'Sri Nath ji' and footprints on the back (Hendley).
rows.later_production: Watt (1903) records a large modern trade in sleeve links, lockets, bracelets and brooches, and the decoration of jewelry backs, controlled by Jaipur dealers who employed the best enamellers.
rows.how_to_tell_old: Watt (1903) says older Jaipur enamel used a field color, most often creamy white, which recent work had dropped for crowded designs with no field color. Single source; not a test on its own.

look_alikes.name: Painted or cold enamel (resin)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: No source read describes resin imitations; not covered.

look_alikes.name: Thewa
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Gold foil fused onto a single sheet of green or red glass, not enamel in engraved cells; see thewa.

rows.features_other: Kashmir 'enamel' on silver is often painted with a fusible paint and fired at moderate heat (Watt).

facts.text: Watt (1903) says Jaipur enamel is done on the purest gold (22 carat) and engraved so that only faint gold lines remain between colors.
facts.quote: invariably done on the purest gold (22 carat), and the plate is so engraved that all but the faintest lines of the metal disappear

facts.text: In Jaipur the chaser engraves the pattern, hollows the plate and hatches the floor of each pit to increase the play of the translucent enamel and help it adhere; Watt (1903) quotes this account from Hendley.
facts.quote: hollows out the plate, and hatches the floor of the pits to increase the play of colours of the translucent enamel

facts.text: Watt (1903) says recent Jaipur work had given up the old field color (often creamy white) for intricate designs, and that enamel had shifted to decorating the backs of jewelry and small items such as lockets and brooches.
facts.quote: Formerly every attention was given to effect, and a background or field colour was regularly employed, most frequently a rich creamy white.

facts.text: Benares enamel is mostly large patches of color in imitation of jewels or as a ground for set stones.
facts.quote: the art of enamelling seems confined to the production of large patches of colour in imitation of jewels, or as a setting to jewels

facts.text: Jaipur enamellers bought their colors as opaque glass from Lahore makers and applied them in order of hardness, hardest first (Hendley, quoted by Watt 1903).
facts.quote: The colours are obtained in opaque vitreous masses from Lahore, where they are prepared by Muhammadan manikars or bracelet makers.

facts.text: Kipling (quoted by Mukharji 1888) says Delhi enamel is often spoiled by being done on gold too thin to stand the heat.
facts.quote: The enamel work is often spoiled by being done on gold too thin to withstand without distortion the heat of the enamel fire.

facts.text: Banaras Gulabi Meenakari Craft is a registered GI (filed 24 Jan 2013, certificate 23 Mar 2015).
facts.quote: Banaras Gulabi Meenakari Craft Status Registered ... Certificate Date 23-03-2015

facts.text: Gem-set Indian jewelry is commonly enamelled on the back: described by Baden-Powell (1872), Mukharji (1888) and Watt (1903), and seen on Cleveland's 18th-century Jaipur pendant 1966.515.
facts.quote: The enameling on the back depicts a peacock with a pair of peahens amid flowers.

rows.name: Thewa (gold foil fused on glass)
rows.date_note: Items catalogued 19th century (Met 53.167, 60.159); exhibited Delhi 1902-03 (Partabgarh State prize). GI registered 2014. Still made.
rows.identify_by: A thin sheet of gold, pierced and chased with figures (hunting scenes, gods, animals), fused onto a plaque of deep green (sometimes red or blue) glass, framed in silver or gold with foil behind.
how_to_recognize: Flat plaques of dark green glass with flat gold figures cut out and pressed onto the surface.
Silver or gold wire frame round the glass; silver foil underneath for brilliance.
Usually brooches, pendants, bracelet links, boxes and belt plaques.
rows.marks_and_labels: Not traditionally marked. Modern makers (the Rajasthan Thawa Kala Sansthan, Pratapgarh holds the GI) may sign or label boxes; not checked.
rows.later_production: Made for European use by 1900 (belts, brooches, plates shown 1903); Delhi jewelers mounted Partabgarh plaques with miniatures (Kipling, 1888). Ratlam made a blue imitation (Watt).
rows.how_to_tell_old: No test of age in the sources read.

look_alikes.name: Ratlam blue imitation
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Watt (1903) says Ratlam made a similar work in a shade of blue.

look_alikes.name: Enamel (meenakari)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Thewa has one continuous glass ground under applied gold, not separate enamel colors in engraved cells.

facts.text: Watt (1903) describes the process: a frame of silver wire is made to the size of a green or red glass item; gold leaf is laid on lac, the pattern punched and chased, and fused onto the semi-molten glass; silver foil goes underneath.
facts.quote: Before mounting the article, a piece of silver tin-foil is placed underneath the glass to give it brilliancy.

facts.text: Hendley describes Partabgarh plaques as green glass with sporting pictures in gold on a deep green ground; Kipling (1888) calls it a semi-translucent green incrusted with gold-chased figures and animals.
facts.quote: They are of green glass with quaint sporting pictures in gold, which are seen on the rich deep green ground.

facts.text: Partabgarh State won a third prize at Delhi 1903 'for the quasi-gold enamel characteristic of that State'.
facts.quote: Third Prize with bronze medal to Partabgarh State for the quasi-gold enamel characteristic of that State

facts.text: Thewa Art Work is a registered GI, applicant Rajasthan Thawa Kala Sansthan, Pratapgarh (filed 17 Oct 2011, certificate 31 Mar 2014).
facts.quote: Thewa Art Work Status Registered Applicant Name Rajasthan Thawa Kala Sansthan ... Certificate Date 31-03-2014

facts.text: The Met catalogues 19th-century Rajasthan thewa items as 'Pierced gold foil over glass (thewa work)'.
facts.quote: Pierced gold foil over glass (thewa work)

facts.text: Three sources agree on the essentials: gold figures cut out and applied to a deep green glass ground, from Partabgarh in southern Rajputana.
facts.quote: the quasi-enamel of Partabgarh in Rajputana, in which quaint figures are cut out in gold and applied to a deep emerald-green glass ground.

rows.name: Navaratna (nine-gem) jewelry
rows.date_note: Met and Cleveland examples catalogued 18th-19th century; described as a talisman from Sanskrit sources. Still made.
rows.identify_by: Nine different stones set together, often in a fixed order, standing for the nine planets; worn as an armlet, ring, pendant or bracelet.
how_to_recognize: Nine stones of different colors in a row or ring, often round a central ruby.
Armlet form (nauratan bazuband) tied with silk cords; also rings.
rows.marks_and_labels: Not marked traditionally.
rows.later_production: Made continuously; a stock item of modern Indian jewelers.
rows.how_to_tell_old: No test in the sources read.

look_alikes.name: Any multi-stone piece
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Sources disagree on which nine stones; substitutes (garnet for ruby, glass) are common, so the count of nine colors is the guide, not the exact stones.

rows.features_other: Disputed: the list of nine gems differs between sources.

facts.text: The navaratna is an amulet of nine gems; Hindus wore it against evil planetary influences, each gem linked to a planet.
facts.quote: The nava-ratna or nao-ratan, an amulet or talisman composed of 'nine gems'

facts.text: Sources list different nine stones: Birdwood gives coral, topaz, sapphire, ruby, flat diamond, cut diamond, emerald, hyacinth and carbuncle; Hendley gives diamond, ruby, cat's-eye, pearl, zircon (gomeda), coral, emerald, topaz, sapphire; Hoey (via Charles) has lapis lazuli in place of cat's-eye.
facts.quote: Coral, Topaz, Sapphire, Ruby, flat Diamond, cut Diamond, Emerald, Hyacinth, and Carbuncle

facts.text: In the Punjab sapphires were uncommon and worn only in the nau ratn armlet.
facts.quote: sapphires are quite uncommon, and only worn in the 'nau ratn,' or armlet with nine gems.

facts.text: Mukharji (1888) describes the navaratna or navagraha as a ring set with the nine most precious stones.
facts.quote: A ring on which the nine most precious stones have been set.

facts.text: The Met's 19th-century navaratna bracelets include turquoise, garnets and agate among their stones.
facts.quote: Gold, enamel; inset with emeralds, turquoise, garnets, sapphires, diamonds, agate, coral

rows.name: Temple jewelry (Nagercoil and south Indian)
rows.date_note: Nagercoil (Vadasery) craft registered as a GI with certificate 13 Jul 2007 (logo registration 2016). Older south Indian gold-and-ruby items in museums are catalogued 17th-19th century.
rows.identify_by: South Indian jewelry with motifs from temple sculpture (Lakshmi, peacocks, yalis, lotuses), red and green 'kemp' stones set in lac; the Nagercoil craft makes it in silver overlaid with thin gold sheet, for dancers and brides.
how_to_recognize: Red and green stones in closed settings with lac behind.
Deity figures, peacocks, parrots, mango (paisley) motifs; sets of necklace, nethi chutti (forehead piece), hair and braid ornaments, belt.
Nagercoil work: a silver body overlaid with thin gold sheet; filigree and repoussé.
rows.marks_and_labels: Not traditionally marked. Modern solid-gold 'temple jewellery' sold by large jewelers should carry BIS hallmarks if sold new in India after 2021 (see heirloomapp.io/marks/indian-hallmarks/).
rows.later_production: Very large modern production for dance, brides and export; both gold-overlaid silver (Nagercoil) and solid gold (retail chains), and imitations.
rows.how_to_tell_old: No test of age in the sources read.

look_alikes.name: Gold-and-ruby south Indian jewelry (older)
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Solid gold with rubies and emeralds, e.g. Met 2018.197, 15.95.39, 19.111.4; Cleveland 1944.65. Material and weight differ from silver-based dance sets.

look_alikes.name: Gold-plated imitation temple sets
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Base metal (often copper or brass) under plating; see one_gram_gold.

rows.cautions: Gold-overlaid silver is not solid gold; describe metal only after testing.

facts.text: GJEPC's Solitaire (2026) describes Nagercoil work: silver shaped into forms, thin sheets of gold overlaid, set with red and green kemp stones in lac (arakku), with filigree and repoussé.
facts.quote: Silver is carefully shaped into desired forms, while thin sheets of gold are overlaid on the base metal and embellished with traditional red and green kemp stones (kuchu kal) set in arakku (lac).

facts.text: The craft is centered on Vadasery in Nagercoil (Kanyakumari district); the ornaments were worn by Bharatanatyam and Kuchipudi dancers and later became south Indian bridal jewelry.
facts.quote: The craft took root in Vadasery, a locality in Nagercoil

facts.text: 'Temple Jewellery of Nagercoil' is a registered GI (application 65, filed 26 Jul 2006, certificate 13 Jul 2007); a separate logo registration (application 515) has certificate 31 Mar 2016. GJEPC dates the GI to 2007-08.
facts.quote: Temple Jewellery of Nagercoil Status Registered ... Certificate Date 13-07-2007

facts.text: Hendley (1909) says ornaments given to adorn a consecrated temple image favor the five or nine pure gems, and that imitation jewelry is absolutely forbidden for this use.
facts.quote: Favourite ornaments are such as contain the five or nine pure gems (Ratan or Ratna). Imitation jewellery is absolutely forbidden.

facts.text: Kipling (via Mukharji 1888) says Madras 'swami' silver with Dravidian figures was imitated at Delhi by die-stamping and chasing; Birdwood calls it the Dravidian 'swami' jewelry of the Madras Presidency.
facts.quote: In the best Madras examples the figures are entirely hand-worked, but they are often made at Delhi by die-stamping, afterwards chased.

rows.name: Cuttack silver filigree
rows.date_note: Described as famous by 1880 (Birdwood) and exported widely by 1905; earlier start not established in sources read. GI certificate 1 Mar 2024. Still made.
rows.identify_by: Openwork silver (sometimes gold) made entirely of fine twisted and flattened wires bent into coils and scrolls inside a frame of thicker wire, soldered together, with a white, matte finish.
how_to_recognize: Lace-like open panels of coiled flat-twisted wire inside thicker outline wires.
Very light for its size; a 'snowy' white finish.
For European use: lily, leaf and butterfly brooches, bangles, necklaces, earrings (1888 price list).
rows.marks_and_labels: Traditional pieces are not normally marked. Pieces made for export may be stamped 'SILVER' or carry a retailer's or emporium label (see the origin-stamps rows for Central Cottage Industries Emporium and HHEC labels). BIS silver hallmarks are voluntary for old work (see heirloomapp.io/marks/indian-hallmarks/).
rows.later_production: Made for European buyers by 1888 (lily, leaf and butterfly patterns) and exported in 1905 to Calcutta, Delhi, Bombay, Cutch, Bangalore, Akyab and Mauritius; a mechanized workshop (Orissa Art Union, M. S. Das) by 1905. Copied elsewhere (Jhansi imitations, 1905).
rows.how_to_tell_old: No test of age in the sources read.

look_alikes.name: Dacca filigree
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Same process; Mookerji (1905) judges modern Dacca finish inferior to Cuttack. Origin usually cannot be told from the piece alone.

look_alikes.name: Karimnagar filigree
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Same family of technique (Telangana); see karimnagar_filigree. Sources read give no visual test between them.

look_alikes.name: Maltese, Genoese or Scandinavian filigree
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Birdwood notes the work is identical in character to European filigree; Charles (1905) found Maltese filigree in Indian shops. Look for European marks.

look_alikes.name: Trichinopoly filigree
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Watt (1903) calls it sturdier and better for wear than Cuttack or Dacca work.

facts.text: Cuttack's filigree is made by drawing wire through graduated holes, arranging thick outline wires and finer twisted, flattened wires on a mica sheet, and soldering them.
facts.quote: Over a tin-plate a piece of mica is placed. The thick wires are then arranged over the mica plate according to the outlines of the design.

facts.text: Purity: Mukharji (1888) says Cuttack filigree is made of pure silver (refined with lead); Mookerji (1905) records silver alloyed with copper at 16 to one-half.
facts.quote: In Cuttack the work is all filigrain, and is made of pure silver.

facts.text: Birdwood (1880): in Cuttack the work was generally done by boys, and it is distinct from the indigenous silver jewelry of the region.
facts.quote: In Cuttack the work is generally done by boys, whose sensitive fingers, and keener sight enable them to put the fine silver threads together

facts.text: By 1888 Cuttack made filigree for European use, with a price list of lily, diamond, leaf and butterfly patterns; Dacca, Lucknow, Delhi and Trichinopoly also made silver jewelry for Europeans.
facts.quote: ornaments for European use are chiefly made at Dacca, Cuttack, Lucknow, Delhi, and Trichinopoly. These are almost all made of silver, of European shape with Indian patterns.

facts.text: In the United Provinces (1905) most filigree in jewelers' shops was imported from Cuttack; local Jhansi copies were inferior and some were gold-plated with green stones.
facts.quote: the specimens of it which are sometimes seen in the jewellers' shops have generally been imported from Cuttack. Malta filigree silver is also occasionally found.

facts.text: 'Cuttack Silver Filigree (Chandi Tarakasi)' is a registered GI (filed 1 Jul 2021 by the Odisha State Co-operative Handicrafts Corporation; certificate 1 Mar 2024).
facts.quote: Cuttack Silver Filigree (Chandi Tarakasi) Status Registered ... Certificate Date 01-03-2024

rows.name: Karimnagar silver filigree
rows.date_note: Mukharji (1888) names Zelgandal (here read as Elgandal, the old seat of Karimnagar district; the identification is not stated by the source) for silver filigree in Hyderabad State. GI certificate 16 May 2007.
rows.identify_by: Silver filigree from Karimnagar (Telangana): fine twisted wire coiled inside thicker frames, soldered.
how_to_recognize: Openwork silver of coiled wire, as Cuttack work; boxes, trays, jewelry and ornaments.
rows.marks_and_labels: Not established from sources read; modern pieces may carry a co-operative society label.
rows.later_production: Registered GI held by the Karimnagar Silver Filigree Handicrafts co-operative society; current production for gifts and souvenirs (scale not found).
rows.how_to_tell_old: No test of age in the sources read.

look_alikes.name: Cuttack filigree
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Sources read give no visual test between the two.

facts.text: Mukharji (1888) names Zelgandal and Aurangabad as the only places in Hyderabad State noted for silver ware, made in filigree.
facts.quote: Zelgandal and Aurangabad are the only places in Haidrabad noted for their silver ware. The articles are made in filigrain work.

facts.text: 'Silver Filigree of Karimnagar' is a registered GI (application 53, filed 28 Apr 2006 by the Karimnagar Silver Filigree Handicrafts Mutually Aided Co-operative Welfare Society; certificate 16 May 2007; renewed to 2036).
facts.quote: Silver Filigree of Karimnagar Status Registered ... Certificate Date 16-05-2007

rows.name: Rajasthani, Sindhi and tribal silver jewelry
rows.date_note: Described as everyday village wear 1872-1909; the forms are old but individual items are usually 19th-20th century. Many are still made, and much is made for the export and tourist trade (not quantified in sources read).
rows.identify_by: Heavy, often solid silver neck rings (hasli), anklets, bracelets (kara) and armlets with knobbed or faceted ends, chased or engraved, worn by village and pastoral communities; poorer versions in bell metal, brass or zinc.
how_to_recognize: Weight: solid rings of several ounces; Herklots gives 3-4 oz for a silver kara and 4 oz to nearly a pound for a hasli.
Simple geometric chasing, knobbed or polygonal terminals.
Hollow forms may be filled with lac, resin or pellets that rattle (see hollow_filled_jewelry).
rows.marks_and_labels: Not marked traditionally. Export pieces may bear 'SILVER', 'INDIA' or emporium labels (see origin-stamp rows).
rows.later_production: Large later production for the home market and for tourists and export; amounts and dates not given in the sources read.
rows.how_to_tell_old: Sources read give no test of age. Old silver ornaments were valued by weight and often melted, so few survive unaltered.

look_alikes.name: Bell metal, brass or zinc ornaments
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Poorer wearers used bell metal (United Provinces) or zinc (Rajputana); color and a silver test distinguish them.

look_alikes.name: Electroplated base metal
look_alikes.how_to_tell: The Met catalogues some 19th-century anklets as 'silver or electroplated iron'; a magnet or test is needed.

rows.cautions: Zinc-alloy and low silver items exist side by side with good silver; describe metal only after testing.

facts.text: Those who could not afford silver wore foot and wrist ornaments of bell metal (United Provinces) or zinc (Rajputana).
facts.quote: those who cannot afford even silver have their foot and wrist ornaments made of bell metal. The same classes in Rajputana more commonly use zinc

facts.text: Birdwood (1880): in Sindh and Baluchistan solid silver torques, anklets and bracelets were very common; the beaten silver jewelry of the Gonds and other tribes was very primitive in character.
facts.quote: Solid silver torques, and anklets, and bracelets are very common, of a severe style of rectangular construction and ornamentation.

facts.text: Maclagan (1890): in the Punjab old unsoldered ornaments, such as old karas and haslis, sold at a higher rate per tola than lighter soldered or alloyed jewelry.
facts.quote: in Sialkot old karas and haslis fetch Re. 1 a tola, while old jewellery containing alloy will fetch only 12 annas a tola.

facts.text: Rohtak peasant jewelry shown in the Punjab Exhibition of 1881-82 was bought for the West End of London.
facts.quote: Remarkably good examples of peasant jewellery, which came from Rohtak, were purchased for the West End of London.

facts.text: The Met catalogues several 19th-century Indian anklets as 'Silver or electroplated iron'.
facts.quote: Silver or electroplated iron

facts.text: Heavy solid silver neck rings, anklets and bracelets were everyday village and tribal wear in north and west India in the 19th century.
facts.quote: Solid silver torques, and anklets, and bracelets are very common

rows.name: Kashmiri jewelry
rows.date_note: Described 1876-1909; Met bracelets catalogued 17th-19th century. Still made.
rows.identify_by: Gold (often reddish) and silver jewelry of the Kashmir valley, with filigree and enamel; the dejharu ear pendants of pure gold mark a married Kashmiri Pandit woman.
how_to_recognize: Dejharu: pendant ear ornaments of pure gold hung through the ear, given at marriage.
Gold work combining much filigree; Birdwood saw it mainly in 'ruddy gold'.
Silver jewelry by silversmiths who would copy any design given.
rows.marks_and_labels: Not marked traditionally.
rows.later_production: Much sold to visitors by the 1870s; Ince (1876, quoted by Hendley) warned that most 'precious' stones sold in Kashmir were imitations.
rows.how_to_tell_old: No test in the sources read.

look_alikes.name: Punjabi gold jewelry
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Birdwood says Kashmiri jewelry is identical in form with Punjabi.

rows.cautions: Stones sold with Kashmiri jewelry to visitors were often imitations (Ince 1876).

facts.text: Lawrence (1895): among a Kashmiri Pandit bride's gifts are the dij haru, ear ornaments of pure gold worn while her husband lives, and the chandanhar, a gold neck ornament given by her father-in-law.
facts.quote: The dij haru are ear-ornaments of pure gold, of the same mystic shape as the wegu ; these are worn by the wife while her husband lives.

facts.text: Birdwood (1880): Kashmiri jewelry is identical in form with Punjabi, but what he had seen was in gold, the best in 'ruddy gold' with much filigree.
facts.quote: the choicest specimens in 'ruddy gold,' combining a good deal of gold filigrain work.

facts.text: Ince's Kashmir Handbook (1876), quoted by Hendley, says Kashmiri jewelers set opals, carbuncles, bloodstones, agates and turquoises, but about three-fourths of those sold were clever imitations.
facts.quote: it is best to avoid, unless the purchaser is a good judge, as at least three-fourths of those sold are clever imitations.

facts.text: Lawrence: the Kashmiri silversmith works with hammer and chisel and will faithfully copy any design given to him.
facts.quote: The silversmith works with a hammer and chisel, and will faithfully copy any design which may be given to him.

facts.text: The Met catalogues a pair of Kashmir bracelets of gold and silver, 17th-19th century (15.95.43-44).
facts.quote: Bracelet, One of a Pair | 17th–19th century | Kashmir | Gold and silver

rows.name: Bengali gold jewelry
rows.date_note: Forms described in 1888 and 1905; 'Kolkatti Jewelry' registered as a GI (filed 2022). Still made.
rows.identify_by: Fine, light gold jewelry of Bengal: wire bracelets (chur), animal-headed bala bracelets, ratanchur hand ornaments, sinthi chains along the hair parting, and bead necklaces, with gold worn above the waist and silver below.
how_to_recognize: Light, intricate gold with fine wire and bead work.
Bala bracelets with tiger, crocodile or other animal heads at the ends; often jewelled or enamelled.
Ratanchur: a gold plate on the back of the hand chained to five finger rings.
Anklets in silver, not gold, by custom.
rows.marks_and_labels: Not marked traditionally. Pieces sold new after mid-2021 carry BIS hallmarks (see heirloomapp.io/marks/indian-hallmarks/).
rows.later_production: Calcutta drew the best craftsmen by 1905; 'Kolkatti Jewelry' GI filed 2022 by GJEPC and Bangiya Swarna Shilpi Samity. Production not quantified.
rows.how_to_tell_old: No test in the sources read.

look_alikes.name: Gold-washed silver
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Mookerji (1905) describes silver pieces with alternate scales gold-washed; a gold color is not proof of gold.

facts.text: Mukharji (1888) lists the ornaments then worn in Bengal, including the sinthi (chain along the hair parting ending in a jewelled pendant), nath, jhumka, hansuli, chur, ratanchur and bala.
facts.quote: Sinthi,—A long gold chain put on the middle of the head where the hair is parted until it reaches the brow, where it ends in a jewelled pendant.

facts.text: The bala is called the most important Bengali bracelet, made in gold, silver and baser metals, often jewelled or enamelled with animal heads at the ends.
facts.quote: This kind of bracelet is the most important of all the bracelets worn in Bengal.

facts.text: In Bengal gold was not worn below the waist, gold being the metallic representation of Lakshmi; Mukharji notes gold anklets were worn in Rajputana.
facts.quote: In Bengal gold ornaments are not worn below the waist, for gold is considered as the metallic representation of Lachhmi, the Goddess of Wealth.

facts.text: Mookerji (1905): Calcutta attracted the best artists from the interior; Murshidabad lists include Dara Har, choori and jhoomka in gold.
facts.quote: Calcutta has naturally attracted to itself the best artists from the interior

facts.text: 'Kolkatti Jewelry' is a GI application by the Gem and Jewelry Export Promotion Council and the Bangiya Swarna Shilpi Samity, filed 19 Apr 2022, shown as Registered.
facts.quote: Kolkatti Jewelry Status Registered Applicant Name 1. The Gem and Jewellery Export Promotion Council and 2. Bangiya Swarna Shilpi Samity

rows.name: Shell and ivory bangles (shankha, chura)
rows.date_note: Shell bracelets described as of great antiquity; fragments found in Hendley's Sambhar excavations. Customs described 1888-1909. Still worn (shell); ivory now restricted.
rows.identify_by: Marriage bangles cut from conch shell (Bengal) or turned from ivory or bone (Punjab, Rajasthan, Gujarat), often colored red, green or black and decorated with gold foil or tinsel.
how_to_recognize: Shankha: white conch-shell rings, sometimes dyed with lac and decorated with gold foil; given to a Bengali bride.
Chura: sets of colored ivory or bone rings; in Marwar graduated sets forming a cone up the forearm.
Color often hides the material (Kipling).
rows.marks_and_labels: None.
rows.later_production: Shell bangles largely out of fashion in Bengal by 1888 except in outlying districts, but still given at marriage; Dacca made refined shell bangles for the market. Modern plastic substitutes not covered by sources read.
rows.how_to_tell_old: No test in the sources read.

look_alikes.name: Bone, plastic or celluloid
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Kipling noted the material is so disguised by color that a cheaper substance would serve as well; testing by a specialist is needed. Not covered further by sources read.

rows.cautions: Ivory: India banned trade in imported ivory by the Wild Life (Protection) Amendment Act 1991 (section 49B), upheld by the Supreme Court in 2003. The UK Ivory Act 2018 prohibits dealing in ivory from 6 June 2022, with narrow exemptions (e.g. registered pre-1947 items with under 10% ivory). US rules not checked here. This is not legal advice.

facts.text: Conch-shell bracelets (sankha) were cut into rings, dyed with lac and decorated with gold foil; wearing them was a religious obligation for Bengali Hindu women and a set is presented to the bride by her father.
facts.quote: The wearing of shell-bracelets was considered a religious obligation by the Hindus of Bengal, and even now a set is always presented to the bride by her father

facts.text: Hendley found fragments of shell armlets in his excavations at Sambhar (Rajputana) and notes shell ornaments were by then more common in Eastern Bengal.
facts.quote: In the Sambhur excavations fragments of shell armlets were found, but ornaments in that material are more common now in Eastern Bengal.

facts.text: In the Punjab the bride's maternal uncle presents a set of ivory bangles colored red, green or black (Kipling, quoted by Mukharji 1888).
facts.quote: the Mama, or maternal uncle, of the bride is expected to present her with a set of ivory bangles coloured red, green, or black

facts.text: In western Rajputana, especially Marwar, broad ivory or bone armlets and bracelets in graduated sets were worn; one or two marked a married woman whose husband lived.
facts.quote: In the western parts of Rajputana, and especially in Mar war, from ancient times, it has been customary to wear broad ivory, or even bone, armlets and bracelets.
