facts.text: India prohibited trade in imported ivory by section 49B of the Wild Life (Protection) Act as amended in 1991; the Supreme Court upheld the ban (Indian Handicrafts Emporium, 2003) and a 2022 Rajya Sabha answer restates it.
facts.quote: trade in ivory in India is prohibited under Section 49B of Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972

facts.text: UK Ivory Act 2018: dealing in ivory is prohibited (in force 6 June 2022); section 7 exempts registered pre-1947 items whose integral ivory is under 10% of their volume.
facts.quote: Dealing in ivory is prohibited.

facts.text: Bangles of shell, ivory or lac marked a married woman in several regions: shell in Bengal, ivory or lac in Rajputana, ivory presented at marriage in the Punjab.
facts.quote: It is de rigiur, and the sign of a married woman whose husband is living, to wear one or two such bracelets.

rows.name: Kerala gold jewelry
rows.date_note: Forms recorded 1883-1911 (ear cylinders, coin necklaces, tali); modern bridal names from current sources. Still made.
rows.identify_by: Heavy yellow gold bridal jewelry of Kerala: coin necklaces (kasu mala, often with Lakshmi), leaf-pendant necklaces (palakka mala) traditionally set with green glass, snake-hood (nagapadam) and jasmine-bud (mullamottu) necklaces, and the tali.
how_to_recognize: Kasu mala: overlapping embossed gold coins or coin-shaped discs, often with Lakshmi.
Palakka mala: rows of leaf-shaped pendants, traditionally green glass in gold.
Older ear ornaments: large hollow gold studs or cylinders (toda, takka) worn in distended lobes.
rows.marks_and_labels: Not marked before hallmarking; modern pieces from Kerala chains carry BIS hallmarks (see heirloomapp.io/marks/indian-hallmarks/).
rows.later_production: Large modern retail production by Kerala-based chains; World Gold Council (2023) gives the average Kerala bride's gold at 320 g gross. Payyannur Pavithra Ring is a registered GI (certificate 2010).
rows.how_to_tell_old: No test in the sources read.

look_alikes.name: Green glass vs emerald
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Palakka mala traditionally uses green glass in genuine gold; glass does not mean imitation.

look_alikes.name: Gold-plated (gram gold) Kerala sets
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Base metal under plating; see one_gram_gold.

facts.text: Kerala Tourism names Palakka Mala, Manga Mala and the Nagapadam motif among traditional Kerala necklaces, and coin patterns; the thaali is a small leaf-shaped gold plate tied at the wedding.
facts.quote: traditional necklaces like Palakka Mala (inspired by the seeds of the Pala tree), Manga Mala (with mango motifs), the popular Nagapadam motif

facts.text: Kalyan (retailer) says the palakka mala is traditionally green, made of gold and special green-colored glass, and that kasu mala with Lakshmi coins is called Lakshmi mala.
facts.quote: The 'Palakka mala' or leaf shaped necklace is traditionally green and made of gold and special green coloured glass.

facts.text: The most characteristic ornament of Malayali women was the toda, a hollow stud-shaped gold ear ring about an inch and a half across, worn in a distended lobe; Mateer (1883, via Hendley) calls it the takka, a large cylinder of wood or gold.
facts.quote: The most characteristic ornament of the Malayali women is the ear-ring called toda, a stud-shaped hollow circle of gold, about an inch and a half in diameter.

facts.text: Namburi women's chief ornament was a necklace of gold coins on a silk cord (Mateer, via Hendley 1909).
facts.quote: The most important is a necklace of gold coins strung on a silk cord

facts.text: World Gold Council (2023) table gives the average gross gold of an upper-middle-class Kerala bride as 320 g, against 210 g for a Bengali bride.
facts.quote: Kerala bride 320 g

facts.text: Payyannur Pavithra Ring (Kannur, Kerala) is a registered GI (filed 23 Feb 2004, certificate 22 Oct 2010).
facts.quote: Payyannur Pavithra Ring Status Registered ... Certificate Date 22-10-2010

rows.name: Glass bangles
rows.date_note: Universal in the 19th century (Herklots 1832, Mukharji 1888); Firozabad Glass GI certificate 2014. Still made in very large numbers.
rows.identify_by: Thin rings of colored glass worn in numbers on each wrist, sometimes coated with lac and set with tinsel and glass bits.
how_to_recognize: Seamless glass rings, plain, twisted or painted; often green or red.
Some glass bangles coated with lac and set with tinsel or colored glass.
rows.marks_and_labels: None.
rows.later_production: Mass-produced; Firozabad (Uttar Pradesh) is the main modern center (GI 'Firozabad Glass', certificate 31 Mar 2014).
rows.how_to_tell_old: No test in the sources read; museum examples (NMNH, collected 1875 and 1892) look like modern ones.

look_alikes.name: Lac bangles
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Lac is softer, warm to the touch, and can be scratched; see lac_bangles.

facts.text: Herklots (1832): bangrian are thin rings of colored glass, universally worn by women in the Deccan, squeezed over the hand; well-dressed women wear ten to sixteen on each arm.
facts.quote: Bangrian ... these consist of thin rings made of different coloured glass, and are worn on the wrists. They are universally worn by the women in the Deccan

facts.text: Glass and lac bangles were made all over India; the best at Ghazipur, Benares, Lucknow and Delhi; glass bangles were sometimes coated with lac set with tinsel and bits of colored glass.
facts.quote: Glass bangles are sometimes coated with lac, on which tinsel and bits of coloured glass are set.

facts.text: Poorer women wore bangris of dark green or other colored glass as a sign of marriage, sold by the basketful in the smallest bazaars; widows broke them.
facts.quote: bangris, or ring-like bracelets of dark green or other coloured glass. Baskets full of these ornaments are on sale in the smallest bazars.

facts.text: 'Firozabad Glass' is a registered GI (filed 9 Feb 2009 by the Glass Industries Syndicate, certificate 31 Mar 2014).
facts.quote: Firozabad Glass Status Registered ... Certificate Date 31-03-2014

rows.name: Lac bangles
rows.date_note: Described 1888-1909 as worn by married women and made everywhere; Hyderabad Lac Bangles GI certificate 1 Mar 2024. Still made.
rows.identify_by: Bangles of lac (often over a core of lac and clay), colored and set with glass, spangles, beads or tinsel, made and fitted on the wrist by the bangle maker.
how_to_recognize: Warm, slightly soft resin surface; can be dented or scratched.
Studded with glass stones, mirror bits, beads or tinsel.
Some coated with tin under tinted varnish for a metallic glint.
rows.marks_and_labels: None.
rows.later_production: Very large modern production (Jaipur, Hyderabad's Laad Bazaar and elsewhere).
rows.how_to_tell_old: No test in the sources read.

look_alikes.name: Plastic bangles
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Not covered by sources read.

rows.features_other: Token wanted: lac (shellac resin) as a material; 'lacquer' used here.
rows.cautions: Lac softens with heat.

facts.text: In Rajputana married women whose husbands lived wore lac wristlets, fixed on the arm by the manihar and replaced when broken; the lac worker cuts, warms and rejoins the rings on the customer's wrist.
facts.quote: All married women in Rajputana wear a few lac wristlets when their husbands are still living.

facts.text: Glass and lac bangles were made all over the country, the best in Ghazipur, Benares, Lucknow and Delhi; lac jewelry was also made at Rewa and Indore.
facts.quote: Glass and lac bangles are made all over the country.

facts.text: Kipling (via Mukharji 1888): Delhi lac bangles were incrusted with spangles and beads, some coated with ground tin and tinted varnish; the trade was almost entirely in women's hands. Sylhet lac bracelets had a body of lac and clay.
facts.quote: lac bangles, incrusted with spangles in stamped orsidue and with beads, are made in large numbers. Some are coated with tin, ground and applied as a paint, and then covered with a tinted varnish

facts.text: 'Hyderabad Lac Bangles' is a registered GI (filed 23 Jun 2022 by the Creasent Handicraft Artisans Welfare Association, Charminar; certificate 1 Mar 2024).
facts.quote: Hyderabad Lac Bangles Status Registered ... Certificate Date 01-03-2024

rows.name: Mangalsutra and tali (marriage necklace)
rows.date_note: Customs recorded 1832-1911; the form is current.
rows.identify_by: The necklace tied on the bride at marriage: in western India a string of black glass beads with gold (mangalsutra); in the south a gold disc or leaf pendant (tali) on a cord or chain, sometimes with black beads; Kerala Christians use a tali with a cross.
how_to_recognize: Black glass beads strung with gold beads or a gold pendant (western and Deccani mangalsutra).
A small gold disc or leaf-shaped plate (tali), often with a deity mark, Shiva symbols, or a cross for Christians.
Usually worn continuously by a married woman; widows customarily gave it up.
rows.marks_and_labels: Not marked before hallmarking; modern pieces carry BIS marks. Pieces under 2 g are exempt from mandatory hallmarking (see heirloomapp.io/marks/indian-hallmarks/).
rows.later_production: Made in large numbers in every region; designs change with fashion.
rows.how_to_tell_old: No test in the sources read.

look_alikes.name: Any black-bead necklace
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Context and gold pendant; black glass beads alone do not identify it.

rows.cautions: A personal religious item; families may not wish it sold or melted.

facts.text: Thurston (1906): at a Brahman marriage the tali or bottu, which corresponds to the Christian wedding ring, is tied round the bride's neck; it usually consists of black glass beads and a small gold disc.
facts.quote: The tali or botta corresponds to the ring of European Christendom.

facts.text: In the Bombay Presidency (Gazetteer lists quoted by Hendley) the mangalsutra is 'the lucky thread of black beads', of glass and gold beads, and widows are not allowed glass bangles, the mangalsutra or a nose ring.
facts.quote: Mangal sutra, the lucky thread of black beads

facts.text: Herklots (1832) describes a Deccani Muslim neck ornament (lokri) of gold stars on black thread with black glass beads, and lists gulsari, nath and glass bangles as essential for married women.
facts.quote: Lokri ... an ornament worn tight round the neck, formed of stars of gold strung on three black silk or wire threads, with Kali pot ... or black glass beads filling up the interstices.

facts.text: Kerala Tourism: the main Kerala wedding rite for all religions is the Thaali Kettu; the thaali is a small leaf-shaped gold plate; Christians have a cross on it; Hindus commonly use the banyan-leaf Aalila thaali.
facts.quote: The thaali is a tiny leaf-shaped gold plate symbolising the sacred bond of marriage. Christians have a little cross engraved on their thaali

facts.text: Mateer (1883, via Hendley): Syrian Christian bridegrooms in Travancore tie on a tali, a bit of gold with the figure of a cross, instead of a ring.
facts.quote: the bridegroom ties round the woman's neck a tali, or bit of gold with the figure of a cross upon it, strung on a cord.

rows.name: Jhumka (bell-shaped ear pendant)
rows.date_note: Recorded 1832 onward; Met pairs catalogued 18th-19th century. Current form.
rows.identify_by: A hollow bell or dome, often filigreed, hanging from an ear stud (karanphul) or ring, with a fringe of small pendants or pearls.
how_to_recognize: Hollow hemisphere or bell about an inch across, with pendant drops round the rim.
Often hung below a flower-shaped stud (karanphul) and supported by a chain over the ear (sahara).
rows.marks_and_labels: Not marked traditionally; modern gold pairs hallmarked (see heirloomapp.io/marks/indian-hallmarks/).
rows.later_production: Made continuously; very common in gold, silver and imitation.
rows.how_to_tell_old: No test in the sources read.

look_alikes.name: Plated or imitation jhumkas
look_alikes.how_to_tell: See one_gram_gold.

facts.text: Herklots (1832): the jhumka is of solid gold, a hollow hemisphere or bell, curiously filigreed, about an inch across, with small pendants of pearls or garnets from its edge; it usually hangs from the karanphul.
facts.quote: The Jhumka is always of solid gold, and consists of a hollow hemisphere or bell, curiously filigreed, and about an inch in diameter.

facts.text: Charles (1905) defines the jhumka as a pendant to the karanphul; Mukharji (1888) describes the Bengali jhumka as a flower-shaped ear ring imitating an Abutilon flower.
facts.quote: Jhumka or jhumak — a pendant to the karanphul.

facts.text: Herklots: wires passed through the ear or nose are of the purest gold, so pliant they can be straightened with a fingernail.
facts.quote: This ring, like every other fastening made to pass through the ears or nose, is of the purest gold.

facts.text: Kerala brides wear jhimkis, also called jhumkas, bell-shaped hanging earrings (Kalyan).
facts.quote: 'Jhimkis' also known as 'Jhumkas' – bell-shaped hanging earrings

rows.name: Maang tikka (forehead and parting ornament)
rows.date_note: Recorded 1832 onward. Current form.
rows.identify_by: An ornament hung from the hair parting onto the forehead: a chain along the parting ending in a pendant, often a star or round jewelled boss with pearl chains.
how_to_recognize: Pendant on the forehead with a chain or rows of pearls running up the parting.
Bengali sinthi: chain along the parting with side chains along the hairline.
South Indian nethi chutti: part of temple-jewelry sets.
rows.marks_and_labels: Not marked traditionally.
rows.later_production: Made continuously; common in imitation sets.
rows.how_to_tell_old: No test in the sources read.

look_alikes.name: Glass-set gold mang-tika
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Herklots notes a costly mang-tika may be set with colored glass, crystals or foils; glass in gold is traditional, not a sign of imitation.

facts.text: Herklots (1832): the tika or mang-tika is any golden ornament on the forehead, typically a star-shaped center about two inches across set with stones and pearls, with pearl rows up the parting.
facts.quote: Tika or Mang-tika: any golden ornament worn on the forehead

facts.text: Herklots adds that an ordinary mang-tika cost twelve to fifteen guineas even when set with colored glass, crystals or foils.
facts.quote: One of a very ordinary description will cost full twelve or fifteen guineas, though composed of coloured glass, or crystals, or foils

facts.text: The Bengali sinthi is a gold chain along the parting ending in a jewelled pendant at the brow (Mukharji 1888); GJEPC lists the nethi chutti, glossed as maang tikka, in Nagercoil temple sets.
facts.quote: nethi chutti (maang tikka)

facts.text: Mookerji's Patna list (1905) names the mangtika among head ornaments with weights and values.
facts.quote: Head- Mangtika

rows.name: Haar and other necklaces (har, champakali, satlada, hamel)
rows.date_note: Names recorded 1832-1905; current.
rows.identify_by: Necklaces named by construction: har (necklace of pearls, gold beads, coral, garnets); lari necklaces by number of strands (dolari 2, panchlari 5, satlari 7); champakali of bud-shaped gold pieces; mohanmala of gold beads; hamel of coins.
how_to_recognize: Count of strands gives the name (do-, ti-, panch-, sat-lari).
Champakali: 40 to 80 bud-shaped links, gold or set with foiled crystals.
Hamel: coins or coin-shaped pendants; may carry real coins that help date the assembly (coins date only the coin, not the necklace).
rows.marks_and_labels: Not marked traditionally; modern gold necklaces hallmarked (see heirloomapp.io/marks/indian-hallmarks/).
rows.later_production: Made continuously.
rows.how_to_tell_old: No test in the sources read.

look_alikes.name: Gold-plated sets
look_alikes.how_to_tell: See one_gram_gold.

facts.text: Herklots (1832): the har is a necklace of pearls, large gold beads (manka), coral, garnets; the champa kali has 40 to 80 bud-shaped items, either of crystals set in foils or wholly of gold.
facts.quote: Champa kali ... the rings or flower buds are in imitation of the mangtika, and either crystals set in foils, chiefly white or precious stones of one colour, throughout the ornament, or it is wholly composed of gold.

facts.text: Charles (1905): necklets with two, three, five or seven chains are dulari, tilari, panchlari and satlari; the hamel is a necklace of coins, often with a betel-leaf pendant.
facts.quote: Hamel — a necklace of coins, generally made with a pendant in the shape of a betel leaf.

facts.text: Mukharji (1888) lists Bengali necklace patterns: tara-har (star), hele-har (snake), dara-har (rope), got-har (chain), and the champakali of golden buds.
facts.quote: Hdr.—Necklace of various patterns, such as Tara-har (star-pattern); Hele-har (snake-pattern)

facts.text: Birdwood (1880): long dangling necklaces are called lalanti ('danglers') and mohanmala ('garlands of enchantment').
facts.quote: The long dangling necklaces worn by the women are called lalanti, i.e. 'danglers,' ... and mohanmala

rows.name: Kada (rigid bracelet or anklet)
rows.date_note: Recorded 1832 onward; Met gold kara catalogued 18th century. Current.
rows.identify_by: A thick rigid ring for wrist or ankle, often polygonal in section with knobbed or animal-head ends, solid or hollow, opened slightly to put on.
how_to_recognize: Massive silver or gold ring, hexagonal or octagonal in section, knob at each end.
Solid pure metal bends enough to put on and off; hollow versions are lighter.
rows.marks_and_labels: Not marked traditionally.
rows.later_production: Made continuously.
rows.how_to_tell_old: No test in the sources read.

look_alikes.name: Hollow or filled kada
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Charles notes karas are solid or hollow; a hollow one may be filled (see hollow_filled_jewelry).

facts.text: Herklots (1832): the kara is a massive ring of solid silver of 3-4 ounces, usually hexagonal or octagonal, ending in knobs; being pure metal it can be opened to put on.
facts.quote: A massive ring of solid silver, weighing from three to four ounces. These rings are commonly hexagonal or octagonal

facts.text: Charles (1905): the kara is a plain bracelet with knobs at the ends of its cylinder, solid or hollow.
facts.quote: an ordinary plain bracelet with knobs at the ends of the cylinder of which it is made ; solid or hollow.

facts.text: Maclagan (1890): old karas and haslis sold at a better rate per tola than old jewelry containing alloy.
facts.quote: old karas and haslis fetch Re. 1 a tola, while old jewellery containing alloy will fetch only 12 annas a tola.

rows.name: Hasli (rigid neck ring, torque)
rows.date_note: Recorded 1832 onward; current in village and revival jewelry.
rows.identify_by: A rigid collar of silver or gold, thick at the front and tapering to knobbed ends, solid or hollow.
how_to_recognize: Heavy crescent-shaped collar; square or flattened under the chin, tapering behind.
Polygonal knobs at the ends; chased on the front or all over.
Hollow versions (phonk) are lighter and may be filled.
rows.marks_and_labels: Not marked traditionally.
rows.later_production: Made continuously; heavy silver haslis widely sold to collectors and tourists (not quantified).
rows.how_to_tell_old: No test in the sources read.

look_alikes.name: Hollow hasli
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Mookerji's Patna list distinguishes a hollow (phonk) hasuli; weight and tapping help, a specialist test settles it.

facts.text: Herklots (1832): the hans or hansli is a solid collar of gold or silver of four ounces to nearly a pound, square in front and tapering to small polygonal knobs; being pure metal it bends to put on.
facts.quote: Haus or Hansli, h., is a solid collar of gold or silver, weighing from four ounces to nearly a pound.

facts.text: Charles (1905): the hansli is a necklet made of a solid, semicircular bar, thick in the middle and thin at the ends.
facts.quote: a necklet made of a solid, semicircular bar of metal, thick in the middle and thin at the ends.

facts.text: Mookerji's Patna list (1905) has a hollow hasuli ('phonk'); Mukharji (1888) gives hansuli as the Bengali gold collar, the hasli of up-country.
facts.quote: Hasuli, phonk (hollow)

facts.text: Birdwood (1880): solid silver torques were very common in Sindh and Baluchistan.
facts.quote: Solid silver torques, and anklets, and bracelets are very common

rows.name: Payal, pajeb and anklets
rows.date_note: Recorded 1832 onward; Met gold paizeb catalogued 19th century. Current.
rows.identify_by: Ornaments for the ankle: flexible chain anklets with bells (pajeb, painjor), rigid rings (kara, tora), and hollow anklets filled with shot to rattle (jhanjhar).
how_to_recognize: Mostly silver: in Bengal and parts of the south gold was by custom not worn on the feet.
Flexible links with small bells or pendants (pajeb); hollow rattling tubes (jhanjhar).
Made in pairs; rich families also wore jewelled gold anklets.
rows.marks_and_labels: Not marked traditionally. Modern silver anklets may carry a BIS silver mark (voluntary until 2025; see heirloomapp.io/marks/indian-hallmarks/).
rows.later_production: Very large modern silver production; Hupari (Kolhapur, Maharashtra) silver craft is a registered GI (certificate 30 Mar 2024).
rows.how_to_tell_old: No test in the sources read.

look_alikes.name: Plated base-metal anklets
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Met catalogues some 19th-century anklets as 'silver or electroplated iron'; a magnet helps with iron cores.

facts.text: Mukharji (1888): the Bengali painjor is an ankle ornament of chains and pendants called pahzeb in Upper India; Charles (1905): the pazeb is made of large links of thickish wire with tiny bells, a large flexible anklet.
facts.quote: Painjor.—An ankle ornament made of chains and pendants, called Pahzeb in Upper India.

facts.text: Charles (1905): the jhanjhan is a hollow anklet filled with shot that makes a noise as the wearer moves; Hendley likewise describes hollow karas with grains inside to rattle.
facts.quote: a hollow anklet filled with shot, which makes a noise as the wearer moves.

facts.text: Custom in more than one region kept gold off the feet: in Travancore the higher castes wore gold only on the upper body and silver on the lower (Mateer 1883, via Hendley), and in Bengal gold was not worn below the waist (Mukharji 1888).
facts.quote: The higher castes wear gold on the upper part of the body only, and silver, as being less honourable, on the lower members.

facts.text: Watt (1903): a Bombay firm showed a pair of anklets set with diamonds, rubies, emeralds and pearls valued at Rs 1,00,000.
facts.quote: A pair of anklets (paijams) with diamonds, rubies, emeralds, and pearls valued at R1,00,000

facts.text: Maclagan (1890) describes making silver anklet tubes by filling them with melted tin to bend them, then melting the tin out.
facts.quote: fill them up with melted tin; when cold bend them round like a ring ... when hot, take out the tin

facts.text: 'Hupari Silver Craft' (Kolhapur) is a registered GI (filed 8 Nov 2021 by the Chandi Karkhandar Association; certificate 30 Mar 2024).
facts.quote: Hupari Silver Craft Status Registered ... Certificate Date 30-03-2024

rows.name: Nath (nose ring) and nose ornaments
rows.date_note: Recorded 1832 onward; Mukharji notes nose ornaments are absent from old Sanskrit texts. Current.
rows.identify_by: A large ring of gold wire through the (usually left) nostril, carrying pearls and stones; also studs (laung, phuli) and septum pendants (bulak, besar).
how_to_recognize: Thin pliable gold wire hoop about 1.5 in across, with a hook and eye, strung with pearls, garnets and gold spacers.
Often supported by a chain to the hair or ear.
rows.marks_and_labels: Not marked; small pieces under 2 g are exempt from mandatory hallmarking (see heirloomapp.io/marks/indian-hallmarks/).
rows.later_production: Made continuously; bridal naths remain common.
rows.how_to_tell_old: No test in the sources read.

facts.text: Herklots (1832): the nath passes through the left nostril, a gold wire as thick as a small knitting needle with hook and eye, set with garnets and pearls separated by thin gold plates; usual diameter about 1.5 inches.
facts.quote: Nath ... an ornament passed through the left nostril, consisting of a piece of gold wire as thick as a small knitting needle

facts.text: Charles (1905): the nath is a circlet of gold wire worn on the left nostril, generally carrying a jewelled flower and some pearls or beads.
facts.quote: a circlet of gold wire worn on the left nostril. It generally carries a jewelled flower and some pearls or beads.

facts.text: Mukharji (1888): nose ornaments are not mentioned in old books and were going out of fashion in Bengal.
facts.quote: Nose ornaments do not appear to have been in fashion in ancient times, for no mention is made of them in the old books

facts.text: Articles of gold weighing under 2 g are excluded from the 2020 mandatory hallmarking order.

rows.name: Bajuband (armlet)
rows.date_note: Recorded 1832 onward; Met and Cleveland examples catalogued 18th-19th century. Current in bridal wear.
rows.identify_by: An ornament for the upper arm, usually plaques or a central jewel mounted on silk cords tied with tassels; in the south a rigid V-shaped band (vanki).
how_to_recognize: A central plaque (often jewelled front, enamelled back) with side pieces, on cords with tasselled ties.
Hollow convex units, sometimes filled with resin.
Nine-stone versions (nauratan).
rows.marks_and_labels: Not marked traditionally.
rows.later_production: Made continuously.
rows.how_to_tell_old: No test in the sources read.

look_alikes.name: Silver-gilt armlets
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Cleveland catalogues 19th-century armlets as silver gilt with stones and enamel.

facts.text: Herklots (1832): the bhujband or bazuband is adorned with semicircular ornaments made hollow but filled with melted resin, secured by silk skeins.
facts.quote: a trinket adorned with semi-circular ornaments made hollow, but filled up with melted resin.

facts.text: Hendley (Punjab list): the bazuband is a broad belt-like ornament mounted on silk and tied on the upper arm; the nau ratn armlet is a band of nine gems set side by side.
facts.quote: Bazuband, a broad belt-like ornament, generally mounted on silk and tied on the upper arm.

facts.text: Mukharji (1888): the Bengali baju is a flattened amulet for the arm, often studded with jewels.
facts.quote: Baju.—A flattened amulet for the arm, of various shapes, often ornamented and studded with jewels.

facts.text: Cleveland's 18th-19th-century Punjab bazuband (1916.268) is described as gold with encrusted enamel and gems symbolizing the nine planets.
facts.quote: The gems symbolize the nine planets believed to control human destiny.

rows.name: Tawiz (amulet case)
rows.date_note: Recorded 1832 onward. Current.
rows.identify_by: A small cylindrical, square or drum-shaped case of silver or gold worn on the neck or arm, hollow to hold a written charm or substances, or solid.
how_to_recognize: Hollow case with end caps or a screw, on a cord.
May contain paper, birch bark (bhoj patra) or a filling composition.
rows.marks_and_labels: Sometimes inscribed (Quranic verses, mantras); not maker-marked.
rows.later_production: Made continuously.
rows.how_to_tell_old: No test in the sources read.
rows.cautions: Contents may be religious texts; owners may prefer not to open them.

facts.text: Herklots (1832): ta'wizes are silver cases on black silk thread enclosing Quranic quotations, mystical writings, or animal or vegetable substances, worn against disease and witchcraft.
facts.quote: ta'wizes, which are silver cases enclosing either quotations from the Kuran, some mystical writings, or some animal or vegetable substance.

facts.text: Charles (1905): the tawiz is an amulet, solid or hollow, plain or engraved, sometimes containing a charm, incantation or quotation from a sacred book.
facts.quote: an amulet, solid or hollow, plain or engraved ; sometimes contains a charm, or incantation, or a quotation from a sacred book.

facts.text: Hendley: hollow amulets may be filled with a composition for strength or contain an incantation on bhoj patra.
facts.quote: If hollow, as in this case, they may be filled with a composition to give them strength, or may contain an incantation written on Bhoj Patra

facts.text: Mukharji (1888): the Bengali hatmaduli is a drum-shaped amulet to hold charms and medicines, also worn by men.
facts.quote: Hatmaduli. — A drum-shaped amulet to contain charms and medicines, worn on the arm.

facts.text: Amulet cases, often hollow and holding written charms or other substances, are recorded from the Deccan (1832), the United Provinces (1905) and Bengal (1888).
facts.quote: Tawiz — an amulet, solid or hollow, plain or engraved

rows.name: Marks and stamps on Indian jewelry (before and outside hallmarking)
rows.date_note: Voluntary BIS hallmarking from 2000; mandatory for most new gold jewelry in notified districts from June 2021. Traditional jewelry before that was normally unmarked.
rows.identify_by: What a mark on Indian jewelry can and cannot say: traditional pieces were bought and sold by weight and assayed by touchstone, so most old pieces carry no marks at all.
how_to_recognize: No mark at all: normal for traditional Indian jewelry of any age.
A bare '916', '22K' or 'KDM' without the BIS logo: a jeweler's own claim, not an assay; see heirloomapp.io/marks/indian-hallmarks/.
BIS logo with fineness and other marks: tested by a BIS centre; the form of the marks gives the period (see heirloomapp.io/marks/indian-hallmarks/).
Kundan, polki and jadau pieces, and articles under 2 g, are exempt and so often unmarked even when new.
Export or tourist pieces may carry 'SILVER', 'STERLING', 'INDIA' or emporium labels (see the origin-stamp rows: Central Cottage Industries Emporium, HHEC).
rows.marks_and_labels: See identify_by. Modern hallmarks are covered on heirloomapp.io/marks/indian-hallmarks/ and are not repeated here.
rows.how_to_tell_old: Absence of a mark says nothing about age or purity. A BIS hallmark gives the earliest date of marking, not of making.
rows.features_other: Token wanted: kind 'reference' (this row is guidance on marks, not a craft).
rows.cautions: Never infer purity from color or from a jeweler's stamp alone; have the metal tested.

facts.text: In 1905 jewelry was bought by weight and the buyer expected to recover nearly the full weight of metal on melting, which is why Indian buyers distrusted European jewelry.
facts.quote: The native of India buys his plate and ornaments by weight, and he expects to find, if he has to melt them down ... that they contain practically the full weight of gold or silver

facts.text: Gold was assayed by the goldsmith's touchstone: a dark streak suggests copper alloy, a whitish streak silver alloy; further tests were cutting or heating a bored hole.
facts.quote: The most familiar method of assaying gold is by rubbing it on the touchstone (kasauti) which is to be found in every goldsmith's possession.

facts.text: Kundan, polki and jadau jewelry are exempt from India's mandatory gold hallmarking: S.O. 2481(E) of 23 June 2021 added 'special categories of jewelry, namely Kundan, Polki and Jadaau' to the exemptions; the World Gold Council lists the same exemption.
facts.quote: special categories of jewellery, namely Kundan, Polki and Jadaau;

facts.text: Gold articles under 2 g are exempt from the 2020 mandatory hallmarking order.
World Gold Council (2022): jewelry hallmarked before 16 June 2021 does not need to be re-hallmarked.
facts.quote: Jewellery hallmarked before 16 June 2021 does not need to be melted and re-hallmarked

rows.name: Gold and silver purity, alloys and solder in Indian jewelry
rows.date_note: Period accounts 1872-1905; modern scrap-purity figure 2022.
rows.identify_by: What sources say about the fineness of old Indian gold and silver: often high, but alloyed legitimately for hardness, by local custom without fixed standards, and sometimes dishonestly; solder is always an alloy and lowers the average.
how_to_recognize: Very soft, deep yellow gold suggests high purity but is not proof.
Soldered, built-up pieces contain more alloy than solid cast or hammered rings.
rows.marks_and_labels: Old pieces unmarked; see marks_on_indian_jewelry.
rows.how_to_tell_old: Not an age test.
rows.features_other: Disputed: Birdwood (1880) calls Indian jewelry gold 'the purest gold', while Charles (1905), Maclagan (1890) and Kipling (1888) record routine alloying and debasement, and WGC (2022) puts returned scrap at 70-85% gold.
rows.cautions: Sources disagree on how pure old jewelry is; only testing establishes fineness. Recycled old jewelry is often well below 22 carat.

facts.text: Birdwood (1880) says even hollow, cheap Indian jewelry is 'of the purest gold, soft as wax'.
facts.quote: Yet, though hollow, it is not false. It is of the purest gold, 'soft as wax,'

facts.text: Charles (1905) and Maclagan (1890): goldsmiths alloy gold with silver or copper (or both) legitimately for hardness, in proportions set by local custom, not fixed standards; they also sometimes add base metal dishonestly.
facts.quote: It appears, therefore, that there are no fixed proportions ; the matter depends on taste or local custom.

facts.text: Solder for gold is an alloy of gold, silver and copper (typically about four parts gold to one of silver and copper); silver solder is silver with zinc. Lighter, soldered ornaments therefore contain more alloy.
facts.quote: For gold ornaments it is compounded of gold, silver, and copper; for silver ornaments of silver and zinc.

facts.text: Silver melted from old ornaments must be largely alloyed because it is mixed with the solder used to join them.
facts.quote: Silver melted down from old ornaments must be largely alloyed, as it is mixed with the solder with which they are joined together.

facts.text: Kipling (via Mukharji 1888): the best Delhi jewelry was known for the purity of its gold and silver, but competition had caused a falling off in purity.
facts.quote: The competition of the present day also has caused a falling off in the purity of the metal.

facts.text: In babul (khardar) work, soft good gold is used for the points while the base is of slightly inferior metal (Kipling).
facts.quote: Good, soft gold alone is used for the points, while the base is of slightly inferior metal.

facts.text: World Gold Council (2022): gold coming back as scrap for melting often ranges between 70 and 85% purity.
facts.quote: gold that comes back as scrap for melting often ranges between 70-85% purity.

facts.text: World Gold Council (2023): 22 carat is dominant in India, over 80% of the market, with 18 and 14 carat together 15-17%.
Ear and nose fastenings were of the purest gold, soft enough to straighten with a fingernail (Herklots 1832).
facts.quote: This ring, like every other fastening made to pass through the ears or nose, is of the purest gold.

facts.text: Several sources describe the best Indian gold work as very pure: Herklots on ear and nose wires (1832), Birdwood (1880), and Kipling on the best Delhi work (via Mukharji 1888).
facts.quote: The chief characteristics of the best Delhi jewellery are the purity of the gold and silver employed

rows.name: Hollow jewelry filled with lac, resin or other fillers
rows.date_note: Recorded 1832-1905 across India; still practised.
rows.identify_by: Ornaments formed from thin sheet (often die-stamped or repoussé front with a soldered plain back) and filled with lac, resin or a salt-alum composition to give solidity; the filler adds weight but is not gold.
how_to_recognize: Thin sheet construction: a stamped front and a plain soldered back; light for its size if unfilled, heavier than expected if filled.
Dents that do not spring back; a dull sound when tapped.
Filler visible at a break, a pin-hole or worn edge (dark resin, red-brown lac).
rows.marks_and_labels: None.
rows.later_production: Continues in modern production (not quantified in sources read).
rows.how_to_tell_old: No age test; filling is traditional and does not by itself indicate imitation or age.

look_alikes.name: Solid gold
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Only weighing against size, a specialist test, or X-ray distinguishes filled from solid; weight includes the filler.

rows.features_other: Token wanted: lac (shellac) and resin as filler materials; die stamping as a technique.
rows.cautions: The filler's weight is not gold: gross weight overstates gold content. Heat (repair, cleaning) can melt lac and resin.

facts.text: Kipling (via Mukharji 1888): the almost invariable feature of Delhi work was a thin shell of gold incrusted with better gold or stones, afterwards filled with hard lac.
facts.quote: The almost invariable feature of Delhi work is a thin shell of gold incrusted with better gold, or with stones of some kind, and afterwards filled with hard lac.

facts.text: Mookerji (1905): die-stamped gold or silver sheets get a plain back soldered on and the space filled with shellac for solidity; customers who supply enough metal get solid items instead.
facts.quote: A plain back is now soldered on to the stamped sheet and the space between the front and back filled with shellac giving the article a solidity

facts.text: Birdwood (1880): Indian gold jewelry is generally solid because wealth is hoarded as jewelry, but at Surat it is made hollow, flat items and cubes filled with lac or dammar.
facts.quote: it is also made hollow to perfection at Surat, the flat pieces, and cubes, and octahedrons being filled with lac or dammar.

facts.text: Herklots (1832): armlet units and bracelet prisms of gold were made hollow and filled with melted resin.
facts.quote: semi-circular ornaments made hollow, but filled up with melted resin.

facts.text: Hendley describes necklace pendants as hollow cases with front and back plates enclosing a composition of two parts alum to one of salt, or resin.
facts.quote: They are really hollow cases or boxes with front and back plates, between which is a composition made of two parts of alum and one of salt, heated together, or of resin.

facts.text: Assam and Khasi Hills gold beads were shells of gold (or gold with a silver base) filled with lac (Mukharji 1888).
facts.quote: The gold beads are shells of gold filled up with lac.

facts.text: Lac and tin were also used as temporary cores while shaping, then melted out (Maclagan 1890); so a hollow item may be empty.
facts.quote: fill in the hollow part of it with lac and bend it into a circle and make grooves ... take out the lac by heating it over the fire

facts.text: Hollow gold or silver ornaments filled with lac, shellac or resin are recorded across India between 1832 and 1905: the Deccan, Surat, Delhi, Bengal, Assam.
facts.quote: filled with lac or dammar

rows.name: Imitation jewelry before about 1950 (gilt brass, German silver, rolled gold, glass gems)
rows.date_note: Imitations recorded from 1832 (gilt brass rings) to 1909 (German silver and American rolled gold flooding Bombay).
rows.identify_by: Ornaments of base metal, gilt or plated, or set with glass imitating gems, made in Indian forms for the poorer market; by 1909 imported German silver and American rolled gold copies of Indian designs were common.
how_to_recognize: Base metal shows at wear points (brass yellow, copper red, German silver grey-white).
Plating or gold leaf (mulamma) wears through on high points.
Glass 'gems' and imitation pearls.
rows.marks_and_labels: Usually unmarked; imported rolled-gold stock may carry foreign maker's or 'R.G.' marks (not checked in sources read).
rows.later_production: Grew after 1900; see one_gram_gold for the modern industry.
rows.how_to_tell_old: No test in the sources read.

look_alikes.name: Silver-gilt and low-carat gold
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Testing needed; silver-gilt is genuine silver jewelry, not imitation.

rows.cautions: 'Imitation' in Indian sources also covers genuine gold set with glass; separate metal from stones when describing.

facts.text: Hendley (1909): German silver and American 'chemical or rolled gold' were replacing base metal, with imitation gems; native designs were copied in British territory and the Bombay market was flooded with them.
facts.quote: German silver and American chemical or rolled gold are being substituted for base metal, imitation gems being used with the latter.

facts.text: Charles (1905) describes plating (mulamma) in the United Provinces: electroplating and overlaying with gold or silver leaf; electroplated articles were becoming popular in the bazaars.
facts.quote: This is the name given to the process of plating with gold or silver, and there are two methods, i.e. electro-plating ... and garm mulamma

facts.text: Herklots (1832) lists patri, gilt brass wrist rings, among ordinary ornaments.
facts.quote: Patri ... gilt brass rings, a quarter of an inch broad

facts.text: Birdwood (1880): imitation Dacca jewelry was largely made at Sahibganj; he cites the Sanskrit play 'The Toy Cart' for skilled imitation jewelry in early India.
facts.quote: At Sahibganj in the Dacca division imitation Dacca jewelry is largely made.

facts.text: Mukharji (1888): Bengali dul ear pendants were by then imported from Europe with colored glass pendants.
facts.quote: Similar ear-rings are now imported from Europe with glass pendants of different colours.

facts.text: The Met catalogues 19th-century Indian items with imitation pearls and glass beads (e.g. 15.95.122, 15.95.129).
facts.quote: Gold and silver, imitation pearl

facts.text: Base-metal, gilt and glass-set imitations of Indian ornaments were in common use from at least the early 19th century to 1909.
facts.quote: Patri ... gilt brass rings, a quarter of an inch broad

rows.name: One-gram gold, gold-plated and 'covering' jewelry
rows.date_note: Machilipatnam industry dated to the 1890s (Hans India 2023) or about the 1940s ('sixty-year-old', Business Standard 2004): disputed. 'Gram gold' as a market term grew in the 2010s (WGC 2023).
rows.identify_by: Jewelry in traditional Indian designs made of copper or brass with a thin gold coating; the trade name 'one gram gold' or 'gram gold' implies little (often under 1 g of) gold, not a gram of solid gold.
how_to_recognize: Copies of temple, Kerala and bridal designs at low weight and price.
Red copper or yellow brass shows where plating wears (edges, clasps).
No BIS hallmark (hallmarking applies to gold articles, not plated base metal).
rows.marks_and_labels: Normally unmarked, or with a seller's brand; never a BIS gold hallmark.
rows.later_production: Large modern industry: Machilipatnam (Krishna district, Andhra Pradesh) was a Rs 100-crore cluster before 2004 and had a jewellery park; turnover fell from Rs 200 cr to Rs 90 cr by 2023 (Hans India). A GI application 'Machilipatnam Imitation Jewellery' (2013) was refused.
rows.how_to_tell_old: Not applicable; sources give no dating test.

look_alikes.name: Solid gold
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Weight, a hallmark, and testing at a wear point; plated copper is lighter and shows red base metal when worn.

look_alikes.name: Gold-overlaid silver temple jewelry
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Silver base (Nagercoil) rather than copper or brass; test the base metal.

rows.cautions: Family members may describe plated sets as gold; test before valuing.

facts.text: World Gold Council (2023): gold-plated jewelry, known in India as gram gold, is jewelry with less than 1 g of gold, popular with lower-income buyers, in bridal and daily-wear collections.
facts.quote: Essentially, it is jewellery with less than 1g of gold.

facts.text: Machilipatnam ('Chilakalapudi gold plating') imitation jewelry: Hans India (2023) says manufacture started in the 1890s and the government allotted 48 acres for a jewelry park; Business Standard (2004) called it a sixty-year-old rolled-gold cottage industry covering copper ornaments with gold and silver.
facts.quote: It is known that the manufacturing of imitation jewellery was started in the 1890s

facts.text: Business Standard (2004): Machilipatnam makers used real gold and silver to cover copper ornaments, while cheaper Mumbai makers used chemical colors and a lacquer that lost its shine within six months.
facts.quote: The MGJMWA members use 100 per cent pure gold and silver for covering copper ornaments.

facts.text: A GI application 'Machilipatnam Imitation Jewellery' (filed 31 Oct 2013) shows status Refused.
facts.quote: Machilipatnam Imitation Jewellery Status Refused

facts.text: World Gold Council (2022): in one sales database 25-30% of outlets sold only artificial jewelry.
facts.quote: 25-30% sold only artificial jewellery.

facts.text: Indian imitation jewelry is base metal (brass or copper) with a thin gold coating.
facts.quote: imitation jewellery (gold-plated brass jewellery)

rows.name: American diamond (cubic zirconia)
rows.date_note: Cubic zirconia was introduced in the late 1970s (GIA), so an item set with it is not older than that.
rows.identify_by: Colorless or colored cubic zirconia, sold in India as 'American diamond', set in silver, plated base metal or gold to imitate diamond jewelry, including polki and kundan styles.
how_to_recognize: Very bright stones with strong flashes of color (more fire than diamond).
Uniform, flawless, machine-cut stones in large numbers.
Often in plated settings.
rows.marks_and_labels: Usually none; a 'CZ' stamp is sometimes used by makers (not confirmed in sources read).
rows.later_production: Very large modern production.
rows.how_to_tell_old: Its presence dates the setting (or a re-setting) to after the late 1970s.

look_alikes.name: Diamond
look_alikes.how_to_tell: CZ shows more fire, less brilliance, is softer (Mohs 8.5) and can yellow; a gem tester or laboratory confirms.

look_alikes.name: Lab-grown diamond
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Lab-grown diamond is diamond (carbon); CZ is zirconium oxide. A laboratory is needed.

rows.features_other: Token wanted: synthetic stone (cubic zirconia).
rows.cautions: Home tests promoted online are unreliable; use a gem tester or a laboratory.

facts.text: Indian jewelry retail uses 'American diamond' for cubic zirconia, a man-made simulant, not a diamond.
facts.quote: American diamond is not a real diamond. Instead, they are a man synthesized material, Cubic Zirconia.

facts.text: GIA: cubic zirconia was introduced in the late 1970s, has slightly more fire but less brilliance than diamond, hardness 8.5, and can yellow over time.
facts.quote: has slightly more fire but less brilliance than diamond

rows.name: Imitation kundan and polki (glass and foil in base metal)
rows.date_note: Glass and foil in jewelry is old (Herklots 1832); base-metal kundan-style sets are a modern mass product (dates not established in sources read).
rows.identify_by: Kundan- or polki-style sets in which the frame is plated brass, copper or silver and the 'stones' are foil-backed glass, often glued; distinguished from real kundan by the metal, not by the glass alone.
how_to_recognize: Plated frame showing base metal at wear points.
Stones glued in rather than held by a gold-foil rim; foil may show silvering loss.
Enamel replaced by paint (not covered by sources read).
rows.marks_and_labels: Unmarked; never BIS-hallmarked as gold.
rows.later_production: Very large modern production for weddings and fashion.
rows.how_to_tell_old: No test in the sources read.

look_alikes.name: Genuine kundan with glass or crystal
look_alikes.how_to_tell: Herklots (1832) and Hendley show foiled glass and crystal in gold ornaments; test the metal, not the stones.

rows.cautions: Do not call an item imitation because the stones are glass; and do not call it gold because it looks like kundan.

facts.text: Herklots (1832): an ordinary gold mang-tika cost twelve to fifteen guineas even when set with colored glass, crystals or foils; champakali necklaces could be crystals set in foils.
facts.quote: though composed of coloured glass, or crystals, or foils

facts.text: Birdwood (1880): Indian necklaces of apparent gems may be 'all mere glamour' of pearls, diamonds, emeralds and enamel with no intrinsic value.
facts.quote: it is all mere glamour of pearls and diamonds, emeralds and enamel, which 'deceitful shine' but have no intrinsic value.

facts.text: Benares enamel was used for large patches of color in imitation of jewels (Watt 1903).
facts.quote: the production of large patches of colour in imitation of jewels

facts.text: Hendley (1909): imitation gems were used with American rolled gold in copies of native designs.
facts.quote: imitation gems being used with the latter

facts.text: Foiled glass and rock crystal were set in genuine gold ornaments: Herklots (1832) on the mang-tika and champakali, the Met's 19th-century gold head ornament with glass (15.95.105), and a Cooper Hewitt gold bangle with a glass gem.
facts.quote: Gold band, glass "gem"
